item.title: CivWorldBench：语言世界模型在结构化多智能体文明模拟中的评测 ｜ CivWorldBench: Evaluating Language World Models in Structured Multi-Agent Civilization Simulations
item.description:
一句话：第一个用文明类多智能体游戏来评测「语言世界模型」能否维持规则一致的基准。

要点：

  • 把世界模型放进需要长期状态一致性的文明模拟里评测
  • 指标覆盖规则遵循、状态一致性与多智能体交互
  • 现有视频/语言世界模型在长程一致性上普遍翻车

为什么值得看：做 AI 原生引擎时，「世界状态能不能保持一致」是第一道坎，这个基准给出了可复用的评测维度。

中文摘要：CivWorldBench 关注一个被忽视的问题：语言世界模型能不能在结构化、多智能体的环境里长期维持规则与状态一致。作者构建了一套文明模拟式的评测环境，要求模型在数十上百步交互中保持世界状态自洽、遵守规则、并对多智能体行为做合理响应。实验显示现有模型在长程一致性上普遍失效，这为「把世界模型当引擎用」泼了一盆冷水，也给出了明确的改进方向。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·世界模型+游戏（English）

CivWorldBench

Ang Li, Haofei Yu,

Abstract

The growing use of language models for forecasting motivates a broader evaluation of their

world-model capabilities. Such evaluation must go beyond predictive accuracy to assess

hidden-state inference and intervention prediction.

Real-world forecasting benchmarks offer limited access

to hidden-state ground truth and controlled experiments for evaluating intervention predictions.

We introduce , a

benchmark built on a multi-agent strategy game engine with recorded internal states,

controlled observations, and paired intervention rollouts. Its 1,900 decision points from

475 worlds support three task levels: association forecasting, belief inference, and

intervention prediction.

Controlled observations and reference predictors support attributable evaluation of capability

gaps, with an expert harness and empirical ceiling estimates contextualizing scores.

Stored trajectories make intermediate predictions verifiable, while agent-play experiments

test whether world-model capabilities are usable for decision-making.

The main panel comprises eleven frontier language models spanning different

capability levels. Composite benchmark scores

correlate with real-world forecasting leaderboards on matched model panels, more closely than

with a general-capability index, supporting its use as a proxy for real-world forecasting

capability.

Strong association forecasts do not

consistently extend to belief inference or intervention prediction, and effect magnitudes remain

poorly calibrated despite informative direction predictions. Process verification reveals errors

missed by final-answer evaluation, and structured reasoning improves intervention prediction for

the strongest model in the process study. Agent-play experiments identify useful assisted plans

and further motivate evaluating decision-relevant capabilities beyond association forecasting.

These findings identify hidden-state inference, intermediate-state prediction, and effect

calibration as priorities for world-model training.CivWorldBench

Language models increasingly support forecasting and decision-making in multi-agent systems.

They simulate agent populations ,

forecast geopolitical and economic events

, negotiate

, and act in digital, social, and physical

environments . These applications require a that predicts

observable dynamics, infers relevant hidden state, and anticipates the consequences of

interventions . Forecasting is the observable output of

such a world model: a forecast commits implicitly to beliefs about hidden state and dynamics,

but its accuracy alone does not establish that these beliefs are correct

, and intervention prediction further requires mechanism assumptions

beyond observed associations .(; ; )

Existing benchmarks each isolate part of this problem. Real-world forecasting benchmarks such as

ForecastBench resolve against genuine outcomes but provide no

latent-state ground truth and no alternative trajectories, so belief and dynamics errors cannot

be separated. Causal-reasoning benchmarks test inference from statistical descriptions

or interactive discovery in synthetic laboratories

, and SocietyBench forecasts social events on anonymized timelines

. None of them pairs forecasting, hidden-state inference, and

intervention prediction on the same recorded multi-agent dynamics. Game-agent benchmarks such as CivRealm

and BALROG score an acting policy, entangling world

knowledge with planning and execution. Isolating world-model capabilities therefore requires

prediction tasks with verifiable hidden states and intervention outcomes, plus controls for

observation limits and stochasticity.()

We introduce , a benchmark built on the Freeciv game

engine. Civilizations expand, research, trade, cooperate, and compete under

recorded rules and latent behavioral parameters. illustrates how textual

observation histories support three task levels: L1 association forecasting (, ),

L2 belief inference (, ), and L3 intervention prediction ().

The benchmark contains 475 worlds, 1,900 decision points, and 18,499 prompts.

Global, egocentric, and out-of-distribution settings separate observation limits from

configuration shifts. Saved checkpoints enable paired intervention, control, and placebo

rollouts, and re-seeded futures measure engine stochasticity. , , and references contextualize performance, and the

Sandbox-World Forecasting Index (SWFI) aggregates reference-normalized scores across levels

and settings.CivWorldBench1

Freeciv is an open-source turn-based strategy game,

.11

https://www.freeciv.org

Figure1

QuantityEventTraitRulesInterveneFloorExpertCeiling

Our evaluation of eleven language models identifies distinct capability profiles.

SWFI correlates with real-world forecasting leaderboards on matched model panels more closely

than with a general-capability index, supporting its use as a forecasting-specific proxy.

Within the benchmark, association forecasting rankings do not

consistently reflect belief and intervention capabilities.

Most models predict intervention directions above chance while estimating effect magnitudes

poorly. Process verification identifies intermediate errors missed by final-answer scores, and

the strongest model in the process study improves effect prediction through structured reasoning.

Agent-play results show that useful advice is not identified by association forecasting

alone.

Our contributions are threefold. First, we enable through a

structured multi-agent benchmark with controlled observations, paired intervention outcomes,

and task-specific reference predictors. Second, we make answers and intermediate predictions

against recorded engine states and rollouts, including Table and Code

reasoning protocols. Third, we assess whether these capabilities are in agent

decision-making and how they relate to real-world forecasting. Engine patches and evaluation code are available at

. The benchmark data release is in preparation.attributable evaluationverifiableusable

2 CivWorldBench

uses Freeciv to combine multi-agent dynamics with recorded hidden states, controlled

observations, and executable interventions. Each world contains 3–10 AI civilizations that

expand, research, trade, form alliances, and fight over hundreds of turns.CivWorldBench

2.1

A world $w\sim\mathcal{W}$ is an engine instance with state $s_{t}=(x_{t},z_{t};\theta_{w})$ , where

$x_{t}$ contains reportable map, city, unit, economic, technological, and diplomatic

fields, the hidden dynamic state $z_{t}$ includes attitudes and internals, and $\theta_{w}$

contains fixed personality traits and world parameters. Formally, each world is a partially

observable Markov decision process $(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},T,\Omega,O_{v})$ without a

reward, since the benchmark evaluates prediction rather than control. Each built-in agent $i$

follows a policy $\pi_{i}$ that maps its observation $O_{\text{ego}(i)}(s_{t})\in\Omega$ to

an action in $\mathcal{A}$ , and the joint actions together with the random innovation

$u_{t}$ induce the transition $s_{t+1}=T(s_{t},\{\pi_{i}\},u_{t})$ . The evaluated world

model is a map $f(o_{\leq t_{1}},\{\pi_{i}\})\mapsto\big(b(z_{t_{1}},\theta_{w}),\;\hat{p}(s_{t_{1}+h})\big)$

from the observation history and the agents’ current policies to a belief over the hidden

state and a forecast of the future state under those policies.

The world model’s input at $t_{1}$ is three-frame history

$o_{\leq t_{1}}=(o_{t_{1}-2\Delta},o_{t_{1}-\Delta},o_{t_{1}},\text{narrative},\text{policies})$

with $\Delta=40$ turns, or 20 when $t_{1}<81$ , where each frame $o_{t}=O_{v}(s_{t})$ is a

text report. The global view $v=\text{omni}$ renders reportable fields across civilizations,

and the egocentric view $v=\text{ego}(i)$ is the engine’s own fog-of-war rendering for agent

$i$ . The narrative summarizes observed events in five-turn blocks, and the policies give each

agent’s research aim and course of action, such as its expansion or war

posture. The output is elicited as quantile forecasts, event probabilities, and hidden-state beliefs,

as specifies. gives the formal definitions.

2.2

Hidden state includes personality traits that shape strategic preferences, diplomatic

attitudes that influence relations between civilizations, and world parameters governing

disaster frequency, city growth, and research speed. L2 infers traits and world

parameters, and L3 additionally intervenes on attitudes. In Freeciv’s default AI, several traits had little or no effect and war was rarely reversed. We apply 5 source patches to activate

these traits, initialize contact at peace, and permit ceasefires. and  document the modifications.

4.1

For each cell $c$ , indexed by world, decision point, civilization, quantity, and horizon, let $y$ be the engine

target and $\hat{q}=(\hat{q}_{\tau})_{\tau\in\mathcal{T}}$ the predicted quantiles at

$\mathcal{T}=\{0.1,0.25,0.5,0.75,0.9\}$ . Quantile loss (QL) approximates

the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) :Quantity forecasting.()

Gneiting and Raftery, 2007

$\mathrm{QL}(\hat{q},y)=\frac{2}{|\mathcal{T}|}\sum_{\tau\in\mathcal{T}}\rho_{\tau}\!\big(\varphi(y)-\varphi(\hat{q}_{\tau})\big),\qquad\rho_{\tau}(u)=\big(\tau-\mathbb{1}[u<0]\big)u,$ (1)

where $\rho_{\tau}$ is the pinball loss and $\mathbb{1}[\cdot]$ the indicator.

The transform $\varphi(x)=\operatorname{sign}(x)\log(1+|x|)$ applies to

treasury and population levels and culture increments, and is the identity otherwise.

The normalized cell loss is $\ell_{c}=\mathrm{QL}(\hat{q},y)/\sigma_{v}$ , where $\sigma_{v}>0$

is the fixed corpus scale for quantity $v$ , equal to one for log-transformed quantities.

Enemy and ally counts instead use the absolute error of the predicted median.

For eligible cells $\mathcal{C}_{wf}$ of family $f$ in world $w$ , let $\ell_{c,\mathrm{ref}}$

denote trend-reference loss. World–family skill $S_{wf}$ and the Quantity score

$S_{\mathrm{QNT}}$ are

$S_{wf}=\operatorname{clip}_{[-1,1]}\!\left(1-\frac{\sum_{c\in\mathcal{C}_{wf}}\ell_{c}}{\sum_{c\in\mathcal{C}_{wf}}\ell_{c,\mathrm{ref}}}\right),\qquad S_{\mathrm{QNT}}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{W}|}\sum_{w\in\mathcal{W}}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{F}_{w}|}\sum_{f\in\mathcal{F}_{w}}S_{wf},$ (2)

where $\mathcal{F}_{w}$ contains families with positive reference loss, $\mathcal{W}$ contains

worlds with at least one such family, and vertical bars denote cardinality.

averages Brier gain $G=\mathrm{Brier}(p_{\mathrm{ref}},y)-\mathrm{Brier}(\hat{p},y)$

for model probability $\hat{p}$ , reference probability $p_{\mathrm{ref}}$ , and outcome $y$ .

Binary items use $\mathrm{Brier}(p,y)=(p-y)^{2}$ for event probability $p$ and $y\in\{0,1\}$ ,

referenced to the supplied task-cell rate. Leader items use multiclass loss

$\sum_{j}(p_{j}-\mathbb{1}[y=j])^{2}$ , where $p_{j}$ is the probability that civilization $j$ leads

and $y$ the realized leader, with current-leader persistence as reference.Event forecasting.Event(; )

For cell $c$ of quantity $v$ , let $\hat{q}_{m,0.5}$ and $y_{m}$ denote the predicted median

and engine outcome under edit $m$ . Subscript $\mathrm{ctrl}$ denotes the unedited control.

Predicted and realized effects are

$\hat{d}_{c}=[\varphi(\hat{q}_{m,0.5})-\varphi(\hat{q}_{\mathrm{ctrl},0.5})]/\sigma_{v}$ and

$d_{c}=[\varphi(y_{m})-\varphi(y_{\mathrm{ctrl}})]/\sigma_{v}$ .

For an operator’s eligible cells $\mathcal{C}$ with nonzero realized effect $d_{c}$ , Capture isIntervention prediction.

$C=1-\frac{\sum_{c\in\mathcal{C}}|\hat{d}_{c}-d_{c}|}{\sum_{c\in\mathcal{C}}|d_{c}|},$ (3)

clipped to $[-1,1]$ before averaging equally over operators with at least three eligible cells.

No-effect and exact predictions score 0 and 1.

Direction measures sign agreement among nonzero responses on these cells, counting missing

answers as failures and weighting operators by eligible moved-cell counts.

Let $\bar{s}_{\mathrm{real}}$ and $\bar{s}_{\mathrm{pl}}$ denote mean $|\hat{d}_{c}|$ under real edits

and matched placebos across valid cells and operators, including unchanged-truth cells.

Valid-response Specificity is

$\mathrm{Spec}_{\mathrm{valid}}=\operatorname{clip}_{[-1,1]}\!\left(1-\frac{\bar{s}_{\mathrm{pl}}}{\bar{s}_{\mathrm{real}}}\right),$ (4)

defined when $\bar{s}_{\mathrm{real}}>0$ and both arms have valid shifts. It measures

selectivity, not correctness, and should be interpreted alongside Capture.

Trait, Rules, and Direction report $S_{\mathrm{adj}}=c(a-b)/(c-b)$ for raw accuracy $a$ ,

baseline $b$ , and reference ceiling $c$ , which maps the baseline to zero without changing the

ceiling or the model ordering. Missing or unparseable answers receive task-specific failure

penalties, as specified in .Reference adjustment.

For model $m$ , setting $s$ , and metric $k$ , let $x_{msk}$ be the score, with floor $f_{sk}$

and ceiling $c_{sk}$ . Completion is $r_{msk}=(x_{msk}-f_{sk})/(c_{sk}-f_{sk})$ , a fraction that

tables report as a percentage. To define the Sandbox-World Forecasting Index (SWFI), let

$\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{eval}}=\{\textsc{Omni-ID},\textsc{Ego},\textsc{Omni-OOD}\}$ and

$\mathcal{K}_{\ell}$ contain Quantity and Event at level $\ell=1$ , Trait and Rules at $\ell=2$ ,

and Capture, Direction, and Specificity at $\ell=3$ . ThenComposite index.

$\operatorname{SWFI}(m)=\frac{100}{9}\sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{eval}}}\sum_{\ell=1}^{3}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{K}_{\ell}|}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}_{\ell}}r_{msk}.$ (5)

Metrics are weighted equally within levels, then across levels and settings. Weights and

reference scales are fixed independently of external leaderboards, and completion and SWFI

are not clipped.

4.3

Do information controls, reference lines, and external forecasting

associations support the evaluation? Where do current models fall short

across task levels? How does intermediate prediction quality relate to

final answers, and how do reasoning protocols affect intervention prediction?

Can world models improve agent decisions, and which capability

We evaluate eleven language models with thinking enabled at model-specific effort

settings recorded in . Open-weight models, including Qwen3.8-Flash-Next,

hereafter Flash-Next, cover the full grid. Claude Opus 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol, hereafter Opus and Sol, use medium reasoning effort on

190 shared frozen decision points, 10% of the benchmark, to bound

API cost. This subset is

stratified to match the full benchmark’s composition by split, world size, budget, ruleset,

decision time, and operator, one anchor per world, so subset scores estimate the same quantities

as the full grid. uses Sol on the same anchors with a manual combining

engine rules and regularities from 447 disjoint worlds. The Artificial Analysis (AA) Intelligence Index v4.3

provides a general-capability reference. The reported evaluations consumed about 3,600 H20-equivalent GPU-hours of open-weight

inference, 5,000 CPU core-hours of engine simulation, and $2,500 of closed-model API calls.

executions, adding WM-generated plans improves selection by 2.36 score points over choosing

among original and self-reviewed plans only, so advice expands the set of useful alternatives.

The case studies show what useful advice consists of: Opus corrects the agent’s reading of a

conditional loss probability as a certainty and redirects its remaining gold to one fortified

defender, saving two cities, whereas Sol’s precautionary tax increase buys defenses against a

the opponent’s intentions and the state-specific cost of a precaution, which are belief and

Appendix C

World and observation.

In the process $(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},T,\Omega,O_{v})$ of , a world

$w\sim\mathcal{W}$ specifies a ruleset, map, agent population, difficulty, hidden parameters, and

team layout. The action set $\mathcal{A}$ collects the engine commands available to an agent,

and $\Omega$ is the space of rendered reports. Determinism conditional on an engine random

stream does not imply that an edited reload consumes that stream identically to an unedited

run. The rendered policies $\{\pi_{i}\}$ describe current aims rather than future commitments.

Section2

Queries.

The world model $f(o_{\leq t_{1}},\{\pi_{i}\})$ answers four query types. With

$g$ a visible quantity of one agent, $e$ an event predicate on a trajectory segment, and $m$ an

operator on states, they are

$\displaystyle\textsc{Quantity}:$ $\displaystyle\quad P\big(g(s_{t_{1}+h})\mid o_{\leq t_{1}},\{\pi_{i}\}\big)\text{ reported as five quantiles,}$ $\displaystyle\textsc{Event}:$ $\displaystyle\quad P\big(e(s_{t_{1}:t_{1}+h})=1\mid o_{\leq t_{1}},\{\pi_{i}\}\big)\text{ for binary items,}$ $\displaystyle\textsc{Trait},\textsc{Rules}:$ $\displaystyle\quad P\big(\theta_{k}\mid o_{\leq t_{1}}\big)\text{ as a ranking or a bin, policies withheld,}$ $\displaystyle\textsc{Intervene}:$ $\displaystyle\quad P\big(g(s_{t_{1}+h}^{\prime})\mid o_{\leq t_{1}},\{\pi_{i}\},\ \mathrm{do}(s_{t_{1}}\leftarrow m(s_{t_{1}}))\big),$

where $s^{\prime}$ follows $T$ from $m(s_{t_{1}})$ under the unchanged policies, and $\theta_{k}$

denotes a queried trait or world parameter in $\theta_{w}$ . Mainline trajectories provide forecast targets, recorded

hidden fields provide belief targets, and rerun arms provide intervention targets.

Realized branch differences are not noise-free conditional average treatment effects.

Matched placebos measure response to negligible or mechanism-irrelevant edits, while

the model’s own no-intervention forecast defines its predicted effect.

A reference predictor is a fixed map $r(o_{\leq t_{1}})$ . Persistence uses the current value, while the trend reference extrapolates

the two most recent frames. The conceptual ceiling knows $T$ and $s_{t_{1}}$ but not

future $u$ . Re-seeded reruns approximate its forecasting loss.

The information sets of the ceiling and expert references are

where $\mathcal{K}$ denotes expert knowledge and $\mathcal{H}$ the harness. The ceiling has

complete state information, while the expert retains the model’s rendered history and adds

AppendixF

E.3

Binary templates describe occurrences within a horizon or comparisons between the initial

and final state. Leader items instead request a categorical distribution over civilizations.

The first filter retains binary template–budget–horizon–decision-turn cells with empirical

rates between 0.1 and 0.9. A second pass checks the reference cells actually used by each

evaluation setting. Cells with at least 200 items use the setting-specific empirical rate.

Sparse cells fall back to the corresponding corpus cell, which must also contain at least

200 items and satisfy the same rate filter.

The final reference is therefore determined before model scoring, not by its valid outputs.

Each retained binary question prints its reference rate. Leader items retain their original

categorical format and current-leader persistence reference. Intervention event prompts use

the same reference-cell machinery. These rates are in-sample benchmark statistics supplied

equally to all models, not estimates from an independent training set.

E.4

Trait questions rank civilizations separately on aggression, expansion, trade, and building

preference. Each ranking includes every rankable civilization exactly once and permits

predicted ties. True ties are excluded from pairwise scoring. A scope with fewer than two

rankable civilizations has no trait-ranking question.

World-rule questions classify disaster frequency, growth cost, and research cost into

three bins. Disaster bins are at most 12, 13–40, and above 40. Growth- and research-cost

bins are at most 82, 83–117, and above 117. Lower costs correspond to faster growth or

research. Growth questions require at least one observed city-size change, and research

questions require at least two completed technologies within the observation window.

Egocentric evidence gates use the viewer’s evidence rather than inaccessible foreign events.

Disaster questions have no additional event-count gate. Illness is not a benchmark target.

E.5

An intervention prompt retains the history and describes the edit. Visible-state edits also

update the affected current observation. Numerical and event subquestions are separate

prompts, and a no-intervention control prompt is added when the required horizon or question

set differs from the ordinary forecast. Each intervention is paired with this explicit

control or the ordinary forecast, matching the target variables and horizons.

lists the numerical scoring targets. Standard budget horizons are used

when they fall inside an operator’s declared band. Otherwise the longest resolved arm

horizon in that band is selected. The available arm horizons are 30, 60, 90, 120, 150,

200, 250, and 300 turns. The target mask is fixed before inspecting a model’s errors.

Benchmark intervention families and numerical scoring targets. Bands are in turns.Table 6:

Real and placebo edits share their operator family but differ in magnitude or mechanism.

For example, city-destruction arms remove large versus small cities. City count is excluded

from their numerical target mask because both edits remove the same number of cities.

Likewise, the government-enabling and placebo technology grants each add one technology,

so their numerical target is a downstream score change rather than the identical count

increment. Four single-trait operators replace the earlier composite-trait edit.

Their collected modifiers are +90 for real edits and +3 for placebos. An accepted edit need

not produce a favorable or nonzero downstream effect in every state. Main capture uses

truth-moved cells, whereas specificity retains both moved and unmoved response cells.

Quantity aggregation.

The headline score pools model and reference losses within each world and quantity

family before taking the ratio in . Families with zero reference loss are

omitted. Valid families are averaged within each world, followed by equal weighting of worlds.

five-quantile loss in . The appendix’s family breakdown additionally

equalizes variables within each family before averaging worlds. It is a diagnostic and its

columns need not average to the headline score. The constants and variable transforms

are shared across compared conditions. Pooling reduces sensitivity to small per-cell

denominators but does not eliminate sensitivity when aggregate reference loss is small.Quantity

family aggregation and clipping. A wholly missing family therefore receives skill $-1$ .

The same rule uses the MAE reference for diplomacy. Families with zero reference loss remain

undefined. Missing binary event probabilities receive Brier loss 1, and missing leader

distributions receive multiclass Brier loss 2. Missing trait orderings and categorical labels

receive zero accuracy. These penalties do not impute a forecast.

For intervention capture, a missing arm or control prediction in cell $c$ contributes $2|d_{c}|$

to the effect-error numerator, and its direction is counted as incorrect. For specificity, let $r$

be the fraction of required response cells with valid arm and control predictions. We report

$r\,\mathrm{Spec}_{\mathrm{valid}}-(1-r)$ , with score $-1$ when no responses are valid.

Here $\mathrm{Spec}_{\mathrm{valid}}$ is the valid-response selectivity score in .

An all-valid set retains the original statistic. Raw loss and calibration diagnostics still

require actual predictions. Incomplete experiments are reported at their available evaluation

scope. Entirely unrun anchors are not counted as failed model attempts.Quantity

G.5

Uncertainty arises from future engine randomness, ambiguity in partially observed state,

reload and temporal-resolution effects, and finite evaluation samples. Repeated futures

address the first source, privileged observers characterize the second under their stated

information sets, and replay checks address the third. World bootstraps estimate sampling

uncertainty across worlds conditional on the recorded model outputs.

All intervention truths use rerun factual arms from the same saved checkpoint rather than the

uninterrupted mainline. Saves are taken every turn so short-lived events are not missed.

The RNG-sharing diagnostic compares 141,250 placebo cells with 11,091 re-seeded cells:

mean normalized absolute divergence is 0.116 versus 0.259, and 56.1% of placebo cells have

zero divergence. Only 3,752 of 28,968 compared saved turns, or 13.0%, have identical digests.

The low digest agreement shows that edited and unedited runs can follow different random

streams. The divergence means describe different cell populations, so the comparison is

descriptive. Placebo rollouts characterize variation introduced along the edit and reload

path. Intervention errors therefore reflect both effect-estimation error and stochastic

branch divergence.

Free and Table.

Free produces ordinary answers with unrestricted reasoning and has no prescribed process

score. Table adds explicit intermediate predictions before answering. For quantitative

questions, the aligned protocol prescribes cells near one-quarter, one-half, and

three-quarters of each horizon, excluding all answer times. The target and quantities

are selected from question metadata before inference. Table must include these cells

and may add up to eight other claims. Its claim types cover quantities, diplomatic states,

governments, technologies, city ownership, and wonders. Other questions retain the

general 8–40-line requirement. Numeric process scores use the prescribed intermediate cells.

Code and feedback.

Code receives structured observation frames and the ruleset name, with the intervention

applied when appropriate. It writes , whose 50 executions yield

answer quantiles, event frequencies, and intermediate predictions. Up to four generations

allow execution repairs and back-testing from an earlier observed frame to the last

observed frame. Future evaluation truth is never returned as feedback. Back-testing stops

when at most the larger of two cells or 15% of checked cells disagree, or after two

rounds without improvement. The retained runnable round minimizes disagreement.

A state unit specifies an anchor, question, civilization, quantity, and answer horizon.

Intermediate errors average transformed, scale-normalized absolute errors at the

prescribed times. Table supplies point predictions, while Code supplies the mean of its

on common valid units within each model and scope. L1 uses ordinary quantity questions.

L3-state uses real-intervention branch states. This paired diagnostic includes only units

with available truth and valid predictions in both protocols.

Answer-positive (A+) means final point error is strictly below its trend-reference error.

Process-positive (P+) applies the same criterion to intermediate errors. P- denotes an

intermediate error at or above the reference. The joint A+P- fraction is the number of

above-reference answers with intermediate forecasts at or below reference performance,

divided by all eligible units.

Intermediate-state skill is computed within each world and quantity family as

Appendix J

Report reconstruction and short horizons.

Generating an entire future report conflates dynamics with serialization and copying

unchanged fields. The benchmark instead scores explicit quantities and events. Very short

observational horizons also leave many quantities unchanged, favoring persistence.

Longer budget-specific horizons were retained for L1, while L3 retains short horizons when

an operator’s immediate effect would otherwise fall outside its declared scoring band.

Hidden-target identifiability.

Early absolute trait bins were weakly recoverable even from privileged behavioral features,

motivating within-world rankings. Several world parameters were removed as inference targets

because their effects were absent or ambiguous in the rendered window. Illness illustrates

this distinction: it affects engine dynamics but is neither explicitly rendered nor narrated,

so city-size changes alone cannot identify its cause. Growth and research questions now require

relevant observed changes. These exclusions concern the available evidence, not causal inactivity.

Intervention persistence and observability.

Some savegame fields are recomputed by the AI after reload, so a successful file edit does

not establish a persistent intervention. Government changes are therefore induced indirectly

through technology access. Wonder-grant and composite-trait candidates were removed or replaced

when their scored effects were weak or their descriptions did not identify the complete edit.

The retained single-trait operators modify one dimension at a time. Attitude interventions

remain difficult because changed attitudes need not alter the scored war or alliance counts.

This is a limitation of downstream observability, not evidence that attitudes are irrelevant.

一句话：第一个用文明类多智能体游戏来评测「语言世界模型」能否维持规则一致的基准。

要点：

  • 把世界模型放进需要长期状态一致性的文明模拟里评测
  • 指标覆盖规则遵循、状态一致性与多智能体交互
  • 现有视频/语言世界模型在长程一致性上普遍翻车

为什么值得看：做 AI 原生引擎时，「世界状态能不能保持一致」是第一道坎，这个基准给出了可复用的评测维度。

中文摘要：CivWorldBench 关注一个被忽视的问题：语言世界模型能不能在结构化、多智能体的环境里长期维持规则与状态一致。作者构建了一套文明模拟式的评测环境，要求模型在数十上百步交互中保持世界状态自洽、遵守规则、并对多智能体行为做合理响应。实验显示现有模型在长程一致性上普遍失效，这为「把世界模型当引擎用」泼了一盆冷水，也给出了明确的改进方向。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·世界模型+游戏（English）

CivWorldBench

Ang Li, Haofei Yu,

Zhengwei Tao, Liang Chen

Kuan Li, Miaomiao Li,

Chenran Cai, Bin Liang

Jiaxuan You, Kam-Fai Wong

†Corresponding author: Kam-Fai Wong. Contact: .†thanks: angli@link.cuhk.edu.hkThe Chinese University of Hong Kong

Affiliation:

Abstract

The growing use of language models for forecasting motivates a broader evaluation of their

world-model capabilities. Such evaluation must go beyond predictive accuracy to assess

hidden-state inference and intervention prediction.

Real-world forecasting benchmarks offer limited access

to hidden-state ground truth and controlled experiments for evaluating intervention predictions.

We introduce , a

benchmark built on a multi-agent strategy game engine with recorded internal states,

controlled observations, and paired intervention rollouts. Its 1,900 decision points from

475 worlds support three task levels: association forecasting, belief inference, and

intervention prediction.

Controlled observations and reference predictors support attributable evaluation of capability

gaps, with an expert harness and empirical ceiling estimates contextualizing scores.

Stored trajectories make intermediate predictions verifiable, while agent-play experiments

test whether world-model capabilities are usable for decision-making.

The main panel comprises eleven frontier language models spanning different

capability levels. Composite benchmark scores

correlate with real-world forecasting leaderboards on matched model panels, more closely than

with a general-capability index, supporting its use as a proxy for real-world forecasting

capability.

Strong association forecasts do not

consistently extend to belief inference or intervention prediction, and effect magnitudes remain

poorly calibrated despite informative direction predictions. Process verification reveals errors

missed by final-answer evaluation, and structured reasoning improves intervention prediction for

the strongest model in the process study. Agent-play experiments identify useful assisted plans

and further motivate evaluating decision-relevant capabilities beyond association forecasting.

These findings identify hidden-state inference, intermediate-state prediction, and effect

calibration as priorities for world-model training.CivWorldBench

Language models increasingly support forecasting and decision-making in multi-agent systems.

They simulate agent populations ,

but its accuracy alone does not establish that these beliefs are correct

beyond observed associations .(; ; )

Existing benchmarks each isolate part of this problem. Real-world forecasting benchmarks such as

ForecastBench resolve against genuine outcomes but provide no

latent-state ground truth and no alternative trajectories, so belief and dynamics errors cannot

be separated. Causal-reasoning benchmarks test inference from statistical descriptions

or interactive discovery in synthetic laboratories

, and SocietyBench forecasts social events on anonymized timelines

. None of them pairs forecasting, hidden-state inference, and

intervention prediction on the same recorded multi-agent dynamics. Game-agent benchmarks such as CivRealm

and BALROG score an acting policy, entangling world

knowledge with planning and execution. Isolating world-model capabilities therefore requires

prediction tasks with verifiable hidden states and intervention outcomes, plus controls for

observation limits and stochasticity.()

We introduce , a benchmark built on the Freeciv game

engine. Civilizations expand, research, trade, cooperate, and compete under

recorded rules and latent behavioral parameters. illustrates how textual

observation histories support three task levels: L1 association forecasting (, ),

L2 belief inference (, ), and L3 intervention prediction ().

The benchmark contains 475 worlds, 1,900 decision points, and 18,499 prompts.

Global, egocentric, and out-of-distribution settings separate observation limits from

configuration shifts. Saved checkpoints enable paired intervention, control, and placebo

rollouts, and re-seeded futures measure engine stochasticity. , , and references contextualize performance, and the

Sandbox-World Forecasting Index (SWFI) aggregates reference-normalized scores across levels

and settings.CivWorldBench1

Freeciv is an open-source turn-based strategy game,

Our evaluation of eleven language models identifies distinct capability profiles.

SWFI correlates with real-world forecasting leaderboards on matched model panels more closely

than with a general-capability index, supporting its use as a forecasting-specific proxy.

Within the benchmark, association forecasting rankings do not

consistently reflect belief and intervention capabilities.

Most models predict intervention directions above chance while estimating effect magnitudes

poorly. Process verification identifies intermediate errors missed by final-answer scores, and

the strongest model in the process study improves effect prediction through structured reasoning.

Agent-play results show that useful advice is not identified by association forecasting

alone.

Our contributions are threefold. First, we enable through a

structured multi-agent benchmark with controlled observations, paired intervention outcomes,

and task-specific reference predictors. Second, we make answers and intermediate predictions

against recorded engine states and rollouts, including Table and Code

reasoning protocols. Third, we assess whether these capabilities are in agent

decision-making and how they relate to real-world forecasting. Engine patches and evaluation code are available at

2 CivWorldBench

uses Freeciv to combine multi-agent dynamics with recorded hidden states, controlled

observations, and executable interventions. Each world contains 3–10 AI civilizations that

expand, research, trade, form alliances, and fight over hundreds of turns.CivWorldBench

2.1

A world $w\sim\mathcal{W}$ is an engine instance with state $s_{t}=(x_{t},z_{t};\theta_{w})$ , where

$x_{t}$ contains reportable map, city, unit, economic, technological, and diplomatic

fields, the hidden dynamic state $z_{t}$ includes attitudes and internals, and $\theta_{w}$

contains fixed personality traits and world parameters. Formally, each world is a partially

observable Markov decision process $(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},T,\Omega,O_{v})$ without a

reward, since the benchmark evaluates prediction rather than control. Each built-in agent $i$

follows a policy $\pi_{i}$ that maps its observation $O_{\text{ego}(i)}(s_{t})\in\Omega$ to

an action in $\mathcal{A}$ , and the joint actions together with the random innovation

$u_{t}$ induce the transition $s_{t+1}=T(s_{t},\{\pi_{i}\},u_{t})$ . The evaluated world

model is a map $f(o_{\leq t_{1}},\{\pi_{i}\})\mapsto\big(b(z_{t_{1}},\theta_{w}),\;\hat{p}(s_{t_{1}+h})\big)$

from the observation history and the agents’ current policies to a belief over the hidden

state and a forecast of the future state under those policies.

The world model’s input at $t_{1}$ is three-frame history

$o_{\leq t_{1}}=(o_{t_{1}-2\Delta},o_{t_{1}-\Delta},o_{t_{1}},\text{narrative},\text{policies})$

with $\Delta=40$ turns, or 20 when $t_{1}<81$ , where each frame $o_{t}=O_{v}(s_{t})$ is a

text report. The global view $v=\text{omni}$ renders reportable fields across civilizations,

and the egocentric view $v=\text{ego}(i)$ is the engine’s own fog-of-war rendering for agent

$i$ . The narrative summarizes observed events in five-turn blocks, and the policies give each

agent’s research aim and course of action, such as its expansion or war

posture. The output is elicited as quantile forecasts, event probabilities, and hidden-state beliefs,

as specifies. gives the formal definitions.

AppendixC

2.2

Hidden state includes personality traits that shape strategic preferences, diplomatic

attitudes that influence relations between civilizations, and world parameters governing

disaster frequency, city growth, and research speed. L2 infers traits and world

parameters, and L3 additionally intervenes on attitudes. In Freeciv’s default AI, several traits had little or no effect and war was rarely reversed. We apply 5 source patches to activate

these traits, initialize contact at peace, and permit ceasefires. and  document the modifications.

AI use statement

Generative AI tools, including Claude and Codex, assisted implementation and manuscript

polishing, and were used for retrieval and discovery, such as finding related work and

checking bibliographic details, which the authors then verified against the original sources. Language models also produced the forecasts, reasoning, executable predictors,

agents, and the usability study introduces language-model-controlled decisions within the

same simulated environment. Freeciv is distributed under the GPL, whose requirements apply

to engine modifications. Benchmark performance does not validate policy recommendations

for human societies.

Appendix B

Scope.

All dynamics come from one engine and its built-in AI. The generalization set changes the

ruleset, difficulty, map, civilization count, hidden-parameter ranges, and team structure, but

remains within that engine. The benchmark does not test transfer to other simulators or to

human societies.

References and targets.

The Trait and Direction ceilings are computed on identifiable subsets, namely trait gaps of

at least 60 and cells with $|d_{c}|>\sigma_{c}$ , so completion in these columns is conservative, and the Capture ceiling in assumes Gaussian branch divergence.

Intervention targets include the reload-path divergence measured in .

This divergence bounds attainable Capture but cannot produce negative scores, which

attributes to the models.

Traits are only weakly identifiable from 80 turns of behavior, even for a privileged observer, whose accuracy is 0.59, so scores should be read against that observer. is a language model

with a manual and tools, not a human baseline.

Appendix C

World and observation.

In the process $(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},T,\Omega,O_{v})$ of , a world

$w\sim\mathcal{W}$ specifies a ruleset, map, agent population, difficulty, hidden parameters, and

team layout. The action set $\mathcal{A}$ collects the engine commands available to an agent,

and $\Omega$ is the space of rendered reports. Determinism conditional on an engine random

stream does not imply that an edited reload consumes that stream identically to an unedited

run. The rendered policies $\{\pi_{i}\}$ describe current aims rather than future commitments.

Section2

Queries.

The world model $f(o_{\leq t_{1}},\{\pi_{i}\})$ answers four query types. With

$g$ a visible quantity of one agent, $e$ an event predicate on a trajectory segment, and $m$ an

operator on states, they are

$\displaystyle\textsc{Quantity}:$ $\displaystyle\quad P\big(g(s_{t_{1}+h})\mid o_{\leq t_{1}},\{\pi_{i}\}\big)\text{ reported as five quantiles,}$ $\displaystyle\textsc{Event}:$ $\displaystyle\quad P\big(e(s_{t_{1}:t_{1}+h})=1\mid o_{\leq t_{1}},\{\pi_{i}\}\big)\text{ for binary items,}$ $\displaystyle\textsc{Trait},\textsc{Rules}:$ $\displaystyle\quad P\big(\theta_{k}\mid o_{\leq t_{1}}\big)\text{ as a ranking or a bin, policies withheld,}$ $\displaystyle\textsc{Intervene}:$ $\displaystyle\quad P\big(g(s_{t_{1}+h}^{\prime})\mid o_{\leq t_{1}},\{\pi_{i}\},\ \mathrm{do}(s_{t_{1}}\leftarrow m(s_{t_{1}}))\big),$

where $s^{\prime}$ follows $T$ from $m(s_{t_{1}})$ under the unchanged policies, and $\theta_{k}$

denotes a queried trait or world parameter in $\theta_{w}$ . Mainline trajectories provide forecast targets, recorded

hidden fields provide belief targets, and rerun arms provide intervention targets.

Realized branch differences are not noise-free conditional average treatment effects.

Matched placebos measure response to negligible or mechanism-irrelevant edits, while

the model’s own no-intervention forecast defines its predicted effect.

References.

A reference predictor is a fixed map $r(o_{\leq t_{1}})$ . Persistence uses the current value, while the trend reference extrapolates

the two most recent frames. The conceptual ceiling knows $T$ and $s_{t_{1}}$ but not

future $u$ . Re-seeded reruns approximate its forecasting loss.

The information sets of the ceiling and expert references are

$\displaystyle\hat{y}_{\mathrm{ceil}}$ $\displaystyle\in\arg\min_{\hat{y}}\mathbb{E}[\ell(\hat{y},Y)\mid s_{t_{1}},T],$ $\displaystyle\hat{y}_{\mathrm{expert}}$ $\displaystyle=h_{\mathcal{H}}(o_{\leq t_{1}};\mathcal{K}),$

where $\mathcal{K}$ denotes expert knowledge and $\mathcal{H}$ the harness. The ceiling has

complete state information, while the expert retains the model’s rendered history and adds

knowledge and computation. The process evidence in consists of claims about

Missing or unparseable outputs.

We retain required answer cells that a model omits or renders unparseably and count them as

failed predictions, using the same policy for every model. For , a missing cell

contributes twice its reference loss to the model-loss accumulator before the existing

family aggregation and clipping. A wholly missing family therefore receives skill $-1$ .

The same rule uses the MAE reference for diplomacy. Families with zero reference loss remain

undefined. Missing binary event probabilities receive Brier loss 1, and missing leader

distributions receive multiclass Brier loss 2. Missing trait orderings and categorical labels

receive zero accuracy. These penalties do not impute a forecast.

For intervention capture, a missing arm or control prediction in cell $c$ contributes $2|d_{c}|$

to the effect-error numerator, and its direction is counted as incorrect. For specificity, let $r$

be the fraction of required response cells with valid arm and control predictions. We report

$r\,\mathrm{Spec}_{\mathrm{valid}}-(1-r)$ , with score $-1$ when no responses are valid.

Let $d_{c}$ be the observed real-arm effect and $\sigma_{c}$ the root-mean-square placebo effect

for the corresponding operator and quantity. The direction reference uses

$\Phi(\sqrt{\max(d_{c}^{2}-\sigma_{c}^{2},0)}/\sigma_{c})$ , where $\Phi$ is the standard normal

cumulative distribution function. It is 0.71 / 0.71 / 0.68 over all moved cells and about

0.92 on the 48% (basic) / 42% (generalization) of moved cells with $|d_{c}|>\sigma_{c}$ , whereas models are scored on all moved cells.

The capture reference assumes centered Gaussian divergence and exact prediction of the

underlying mechanism, so expected absolute residual error is $\sigma_{c}\sqrt{2/\pi}$ .

Substituting this into the operator-level capture ratio gives

$1-\sum_{c}\sigma_{c}\sqrt{2/\pi}/\sum_{c}|d_{c}|$ , then the operator macro-average

+0.39 / +0.39 / +0.30. Cell pooling gives +0.29 / +0.29 / +0.20, illustrating the effect of operator

weighting. These estimates assume Gaussian divergence and transferable placebo variance.

Completion expresses progress along the resulting reference scale.

G.5

Uncertainty arises from future engine randomness, ambiguity in partially observed state,

reload and temporal-resolution effects, and finite evaluation samples. Repeated futures

address the first source, privileged observers characterize the second under their stated

information sets, and replay checks address the third. World bootstraps estimate sampling

uncertainty across worlds conditional on the recorded model outputs.

All intervention truths use rerun factual arms from the same saved checkpoint rather than the

uninterrupted mainline. Saves are taken every turn so short-lived events are not missed.

The RNG-sharing diagnostic compares 141,250 placebo cells with 11,091 re-seeded cells:

mean normalized absolute divergence is 0.116 versus 0.259, and 56.1% of placebo cells have

zero divergence. Only 3,752 of 28,968 compared saved turns, or 13.0%, have identical digests.

The low digest agreement shows that edited and unedited runs can follow different random

streams. The divergence means describe different cell populations, so the comparison is

descriptive. Placebo rollouts characterize variation introduced along the edit and reload

path. Intervention errors therefore reflect both effect-estimation error and stochastic

branch divergence.

Appendix J

Report reconstruction and short horizons.

Generating an entire future report conflates dynamics with serialization and copying

unchanged fields. The benchmark instead scores explicit quantities and events. Very short

observational horizons also leave many quantities unchanged, favoring persistence.

Longer budget-specific horizons were retained for L1, while L3 retains short horizons when

an operator’s immediate effect would otherwise fall outside its declared scoring band.

Hidden-target identifiability.

Early absolute trait bins were weakly recoverable even from privileged behavioral features,

motivating within-world rankings. Several world parameters were removed as inference targets

because their effects were absent or ambiguous in the rendered window. Illness illustrates

this distinction: it affects engine dynamics but is neither explicitly rendered nor narrated,

so city-size changes alone cannot identify its cause. Growth and research questions now require

relevant observed changes. These exclusions concern the available evidence, not causal inactivity.

Intervention persistence and observability.

Some savegame fields are recomputed by the AI after reload, so a successful file edit does

not establish a persistent intervention. Government changes are therefore induced indirectly

through technology access. Wonder-grant and composite-trait candidates were removed or replaced

when their scored effects were weak or their descriptions did not identify the complete edit.

The retained single-trait operators modify one dimension at a time. Attitude interventions

remain difficult because changed attitudes need not alter the scored war or alliance counts.

item.title: Programmable World Model：可编程的世界模型 ｜ Programmable World Model
item.description:
一句话：把世界模型的生成过程拆成可编程的阶段，让开发者能干预而不是纯黑盒采样。

要点：

  • 将世界生成分解为可控的中间阶段，暴露可编程接口
  • 支持在生成过程中注入规则与约束
  • 兼顾表达力与可控性，避免纯端到端黑盒

为什么值得看：这是「AI 原生引擎」的接口设计问题：策划要能干预生成结果，纯采样不可控、纯规则不智能。

中文摘要：Programmable World Model 提出把世界模型的生成过程改造成可编程结构：不再是端到端的黑盒采样，而是拆成多个可干预阶段，允许开发者注入规则、约束与阶段性控制。这样既保留了模型的生成能力，又给了内容创作者和策划可操作的抓手。对有引擎背景的团队来说，这套「把神经网络拆成可调管线」的思路，比纯端到端更容易落到实际生产。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·生成式玩法（English）

License: CC BY 4.0

arXiv:2609.10540v2 [cs.CV] 13 Oct 2026

Programmable World Model

Zheng-Hui Huang

Guixu Lin

Abstract

Recent video world models generate increasingly realistic and interactive visual experiences, yet lack reliable mechanisms for maintaining persistent world state and enforcing programmable rules over extended interactions. We introduce , a framework that decouples world-state evolution from visual observation generation. An agent translates natural-language instructions into executable programs that specify entity states and state-transition rules, enabling direct control over individual entities and their interactions. A lightweight engine executes these programs to update and maintain an explicit, persistent global world state, including off-screen entities and non-visual attributes. To connect world state with visual generation, we introduce state-augmented 3D oriented bounding boxes (OBBs) as an intermediate representation. This representation, together with the target camera trajectory, is deterministically compiled into pixel-aligned spatiotemporal conditioning signals for a pretrained video model serving as the generative renderer.

This design allows users to create playable games with predefined mechanics, direct control over individual entities, and persistent world state throughout gameplay.

We further introduce , a benchmark for evaluating programmable world models. On , our method achieves 94% Count Accuracy and 98% State Accuracy, substantially outperforming existing interactive video world models while supporting coherent long-horizon generation. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of separating explicit state evolution from generative rendering for building persistent, programmable worlds.Programmable World ModelCombatStateBenchCombatStateBench

: Figure 1Overview of the programmable world model.

Given a single reference image and a user description, a coding agent generates executable programs that specify entity states and interaction rules. A lightweight engine executes these programs to maintain and evolve an explicit world state, represented by state-augmented 3D OBBs. This representation is compiled into conditioning signals for a generative renderer, which produces realistic visual observations consistent with the world state.

This design allows users to create playable games by defining game mechanics in advance, directly controlling individual entities, and maintaining persistent world state throughout gameplay.

1

Recent video world models seek to build interactive world engines on top of generative video models . By predicting subsequent observations from visual histories and user actions, they synthesize increasingly realistic and responsive environments, opening new possibilities for immersive world creation.(; ; ; ; )

Ball et al., 2025

Sun et al., 2025

Team et al., 2026a

Team et al., 2026b

Wang et al., 2026

;

Wan et al. (2025)

HaCohen et al. (2024)

However, turning video world models into interactive world engines requires capabilities beyond generating plausible observations.

First, existing control interfaces primarily specify cameras, actions, or high-level prompts, offering limited support for directly addressing and manipulating individual entities.

Second, these models generally lack an explicit, persistent global state that can be accessed and updated independently of the current view. Such state must account for off-screen entities and nonvisual information, including inventory, task progress, and interaction history, which is also important for a multiplayer world engine.

Third, users cannot readily program the rules governing world evolution, such as specifying the conditions under which a door opens or how an interaction affects other entities. Prompting a desired outcome does not establish an executable rule that consistently governs subsequent interactions.

We introduce , a framework that decouples world-state evolution from visual observation generation (Figure ). A coding agent translates user instructions into executable programs that define entity states and world rules, while a generative renderer produces observations conditioned on the evolving state. Connecting these components requires an interface that is compact and directly editable by programs, yet sufficiently expressive to guide visual generation. Our central question is therefore: Programmable World Model

1

what representation supports programmable world-state evolution while preserving the spatial and semantic structure needed for visual generation?

Representation choice shapes explicit controllability, the cost of constructing and evolving world state, and the potential mismatch between training and inference conditions. As illustrated in Figure , text descriptions are easy to author but do not by themselves impose geometric or other dense constraints, while 2D boxes and masks provide image-space control tied to particular viewpoints . Detailed 3D scenes and structural proxies , together with dense rendering conditions such as G-buffers , enable finer-grained control but demand richer supervision and more complex inference-time construction. Crucially, training representations are extracted from observed dynamics, whereas inference requires constructing structural trajectories from desired state transitions. Specifying that a character falls, for example, is simpler than generating its detailed body poses and limb trajectories. More detailed representations therefore require the explicit system to resolve additional motion and geometry, and the resulting controls may differ from those extracted during training.

2

()

Yang et al., 2025

()

Gomez-Nogales et al., 2026

(; )

Huang et al., 2026b

Liang et al., 2025

Following these requirements, we represent each entity using a . Each OBB specifies an entity’s position, extent, and orientation in a shared world coordinate system using a compact, fixed set of geometric parameters, without requiring a mesh, material, skeleton, or predefined animation. We augment this geometry with persistent identity, semantic category, dynamic state, and appearance information.

Inspired by advances in generative rendering , we communicate this structured spatial information through rasterized controls. While approaches such as RenderFormer directly map structured scene tokens to images, we explicitly resolve camera projection and entity-to-pixel correspondence through a deterministic . The compiler projects the evolving OBBs along the target camera trajectory and rasterizes them into pixel-aligned spatiotemporal controls. These controls guide entity identity, semantics, orientation, motion, and state changes, while the video model synthesizes the fine geometry, appearance, articulation, and secondary dynamics left unspecified by the representation.state-augmented 3D oriented bounding box (OBB);

Huang et al. (2026b)

Liang et al. (2025)

Zeng et al. (2025)

state compiler

Given a single reference image and a natural-language description, a VLM-based coding agent constructs the initial entity layout, assigns states and attributes, and writes programs defining interactions, event triggers, and objectives. During interaction, a state executor applies player actions and events according to these rules. The state compiler converts the updated world state into rendering controls, and the generative renderer produces the next observations. Users can revise world behavior through further instructions to the coding agent. To train the renderer, we develop a video data curation pipeline that recovers the spatial and semantic supervision required by this interface.

We introduce , a controlled benchmark for evaluating consistency between generated videos and engine-maintained world states. Through combat scenarios with diverse camera and entity motion, it measures whether generated videos preserve visible alive-character counts and visually realize death states.CombatStateBench

Our contributions are threefold:

•

We introduce , which decouples executable world-state evolution from generative rendering to enable entity-level control, persistent state management, and user-programmable world rules. State-augmented 3D OBBs and a deterministic state compiler connect this editable world state to video generation through view-consistent, pixel-aligned spatiotemporal controls.Programmable World Model

•

We develop a data curation pipeline that extracts spatial and semantic supervision from videos, providing a practical path toward scaling training data for programmable generative worlds.

•

We introduce , a controlled benchmark for evaluating consistency between generated videos and engine-maintained world states, focusing on visible alive-character counts and the visual realization of death states under diverse camera and entity motion.CombatStateBench

: Figure 2

Candidate representations range from lightweight semantic descriptions to detailed geometric structures . Greater structural detail enables finer-grained control but increases the cost of training-data annotation and inference-time state construction and evolution. Moreover, representations extracted from observations or recorded from engines during training may differ from those constructed programmatically at inference time, creating a potential training–inference mismatch.

We adopt state-augmented 3D OBBs as an intermediate abstraction that supports explicit world-space control while leaving fine geometry, articulation, and secondary visual dynamics to the generative renderer.

State representation trade-offs.

Huang et al. (2026b)

2

The choice of representation shapes what a system can explicitly control, the cost of achieving that control, and the potential mismatch between representations extracted from training observations and those constructed programmatically at inference time.

As illustrated in Figure , candidate representations span a spectrum from lightweight text descriptions to detailed 3D structures. Increasing structural detail enables finer-grained control over entity geometry, spatial relationships, and their evolution over time. However, richer structural supervision is more costly to obtain, and more structural degrees of freedom must be explicitly maintained and evolved during inference. More importantly, representations extracted from observed dynamics during training may differ from those constructed programmatically from high-level state transitions at inference time, creating a potential training–inference mismatch. We therefore seek an intermediate level of abstraction that supports explicit controllability and training–inference alignment while keeping training-data acquisition and inference-time evolution tractable.

2

Lightweight representations offer limited explicit control over world-space geometry. Text descriptions can convey entity categories, attributes, and high-level states, but do not by themselves impose geometric constraints on an entity’s position, extent, or orientation in a shared world coordinate system. 2D bounding boxes and masks provide more direct spatial control, but operate in image space: their positions, scales, and visible regions change with the camera viewpoint. These representations therefore constrain individual observations without defining an underlying world-space structure that can be deterministically reprojected across views. For a programmable world, it is more natural to specify entity geometry in a shared world coordinate system and derive its projection in each observation from the target camera.

At the other end of the spectrum, greater structural detail does not necessarily yield a more suitable representation. Complete 3D scenes, articulated entity models, and dynamic 3D geometry encode finer-grained structure than entity-level bounding boxes, while G-buffers provide dense, view-dependent surface information. Such detail supports more precise control but also introduces additional costs. First, training requires richer and more accurate structural supervision, increasing data acquisition and processing costs and making it harder to scale to open-domain settings. Second, the system must explicitly specify and evolve more structural degrees of freedom during inference, taking responsibility for geometric and dynamic details that a coarser representation would leave to the generative model.

Consider a character transitioning from standing to falling. A coarse representation may only need to describe changes in global position, orientation, and spatial occupancy, whereas a complete articulated or dynamic 3D representation must additionally characterize high-dimensional structural changes such as body pose, limb motion, and local deformation. As the representation becomes more detailed, the system gradually moves from specifying to specifying . In conventional 3D environments equipped with complete animation systems or physics simulators, such details can be produced by existing simulation mechanisms. Our focus, however, is on open-domain programmable generative worlds, where we aim to rely on generative models to realize visual dynamics rather than reconstruct a complete 3D animation and simulation stack.what changes in the worldhow that change unfolds geometrically and dynamically

Under this setting, the same representation is also obtained through fundamentally different paths during training and inference. In the training data, the dynamic process has already been realized, and the corresponding structural representation therefore describes an already realized evolution:

$\text{Training: realized dynamics}\;\longrightarrow\;\text{structural representation}.$ (1)

Inference proceeds in the opposite direction. The system first receives a high-level state transition and must actively produce the corresponding time-varying structural representation before the visual outcome is generated. The generative model then realizes these structural constraints as visual dynamics:

$\text{Inference: state transition}\;\longrightarrow\;\text{structural representation}\;\longrightarrow\;\text{generated dynamics}.$ (2)

This training-inference asymmetry means that a representation that can be obtained during training is not necessarily equally easy to produce and evolve at inference time. Finer-grained representations provide more precise explicit control, but also require the system to determine more structural degrees of freedom and their temporal evolution from high-level state transitions. As the representation approaches complete articulated motion or dynamic 3D geometry, this process increasingly resembles the high-dimensional dynamic realization problem addressed by conventional animation, motion generation, or physical simulation.

From this perspective, representation choice determines the boundary between and . A representation that is too weak leaves entity positions, world-space structure, and state-dependent changes that should be explicitly constrained to the generative model. A representation that is too strong not only requires more demanding training supervision, but also forces the system to explicitly determine large amounts of low-level geometric and dynamic detail at inference time. Pretrained video models already provide strong visual and dynamic priors for completing precise shape, texture, material, articulation, local deformation, illumination, and secondary motion. We therefore explicitly represent only the structure necessary for entity persistence, world-space consistency, and state-dependent changes, while leaving finer-grained dynamic realization to the generative model.explicit structural controlgenerative dynamic completion

Following this principle, we adopt as an intermediate representation. A 3D OBB specifies an entity’s position, extent, and orientation in a shared world coordinate system, and is associated with persistent identity as well as relevant semantic and dynamic states. Compared with text, 2D bounding boxes, and masks, OBBs provide a view-independent and reprojectable world-space scaffold. Compared with more explicit representations such as G-buffers, complete 3D scenes, articulated models, or dynamic 3D geometry, they restrict the structure that must be explicitly represented and evolved to a compact entity-level space. Time-varying OBBs can express coarse structural changes in entity position, orientation, and spatial occupancy, while internal articulation, local deformation, and other fine-grained dynamics are completed by the generative renderer under these constraints.state-augmented 3D oriented bounding boxes (OBBs)

3.1

Recent video world models have made rapid progress toward interactive visual

environments, supporting action-conditioned generation, controllable camera

motion, real-time interaction, and increasingly long-horizon rollouts

.

These models are typically trained primarily with pixel-level generation objectives, which supervise whether the predicted observations are

visually plausible but do not explicitly require the model to maintain a

persistent, structured world state over time.

As a result, entities, attributes, relations, and interaction outcomes may be

represented only implicitly in the generative context, without being organized

into an authoritative state that must remain consistent across occlusion,

camera motion, or long interaction horizons.

Recent systems introduce temporal or spatial memory to improve visual

consistency over extended rollouts

, but such memory is still optimized

primarily for observation generation rather than for preserving executable

world facts.

Our work instead separates these two responsibilities: a lightweight engine

explicitly maintains and advances the canonical world state, while the video

model serves as a generative renderer conditioned on the resulting state.(; ; )

3.2

Recent work has begun to move beyond purely observation-centric world modeling

by explicitly representing the internal state of interactive environments.

StatePlay jointly predicts visual

observations and game-state variables, allowing the predicted state to guide

visual generation and improve mechanics consistency. However, because the

state itself is predicted by the model, state errors can directly lead to

incorrect world updates and may accumulate over long interaction horizons.

MASS further introduces an

authoritative typed state for multiplayer world modeling and separates state

dynamics from view rendering. Its shared state, however, is advanced by a

learned Logic Engine, so the authoritative state evolution still depends on

learned transition dynamics and remains susceptible to transition prediction

errors.

In contrast, our framework maintains a canonical world state in a lightweight

engine and executes state transitions according to explicit rules, making the

world state directly programmable, editable, and verifiable.()

3.3

Generative rendering leverages learned generative models to synthesize photorealistic visual observations from structured scene conditions, reducing reliance on conventional graphics pipelines. Different approaches adopt renderer-facing representations with varying levels of geometric explicitness. DiffusionRenderer performs diffusion-based forward and inverse rendering using G-buffers that encode geometric and appearance-related scene attributes. The AlayaRenderer series extends this paradigm to dynamic video and world rendering. AlayaRenderer focuses on high-fidelity generative rendering of dynamic worlds, while AlayaRenderer-Flash further improves generation efficiency for real-time interactive rendering. These works demonstrate that generative priors can synthesize rich appearance, material, lighting, and dynamic details from explicit structural rendering signals.()

(1) Agent-orchestrated world programming starts from natural-language specifications to instantiate an executable canonical world state, which is maintained and advanced by a lightweight engine according to player actions and world rules. (2) Control compilation projects state-augmented 3D OBBs under the target camera into pixel-aligned identity, semantic, and motion-direction controls. 4.1

We consider an interactive generative world initialized from a visual

observation $I_{0}$ . At interaction step $t$ , a player takes an action $a_{t}$ ,

and the system maintains a canonical world state $s_{t}$ that records the

persistent information required to execute world interactions. The overall

interaction loop is

$s_{t}\xrightarrow[\;a_{t}\;]{F}s_{t+1}\xrightarrow[\;C_{t+1}\;]{P}M_{t+1}^{\mathrm{ctrl}}\xrightarrow{\;G\;}{I}_{t+1},$ (3)

where $F$ denotes the state transition executed by the lightweight engine,

$C_{t+1}$ is the target camera at the next interaction step, $P$ is the

deterministic state compiler that projects the updated world state under

$C_{t+1}$ into camera-aligned spatial controls, and $G$ denotes the generative

renderer that synthesizes the corresponding visual observation

${I}_{t+1}$ . We detail the representation, programming, and state transition $F$ of the

programmable world in Section , the state compiler $P$ in

Section , and the generative renderer $G$ in

Section .

4.2

World representation and initialization.

We represent the programmable world using a set of persistent entities embedded

in 3D space. Each entity is grounded by a 3D oriented bounding box (OBB),

which specifies its position, extent, and orientation, and is associated with

state variables such as its identity, semantic category, and functional

attributes. For example, a character may have a persistent identity, a 3D pose,

a health value, and a faction label. The world additionally stores relations

between entities, such as hostility or ownership, together with executable

rules that determine how player actions and events modify these states.

Formally, we denote the canonical world state at interaction step $t$ as

$s_{t}=\left(\mathcal{E}_{t},\mathcal{A}_{t},\mathcal{Q}_{t};\mathcal{R}_{t}\right),$ (4)

where $\mathcal{E}_{t}$ contains the persistent entities and their 3D poses,

$\mathcal{A}_{t}$ contains their semantic and functional attributes,

$\mathcal{Q}_{t}$ contains inter-entity relations, and $\mathcal{R}_{t}$ denotes

the executable world rules. Together, these components define both the current

world configuration and how it can evolve under interaction.

Given the initial observation $I_{0}$ , an off-the-shelf 3D detector first

recovers the visible entities and their geometric layout, providing the initial

3D OBBs and persistent entity identifiers. These detections initialize the

geometric component $\mathcal{E}_{0}$ . The remaining attributes, relations, and

rules are then specified by the agent orchestrator, as described below.

Agent-orchestrated world programming.

An agent orchestrator combines the recovered 3D layout with the player’s

natural-language world description $q$ to produce an engine-readable world

program. The program specifies the initial states and attributes of the

detected entities, their relations, the actions they support, and the rules

governing how actions and events update the world. It may further include

global constraints, event triggers, and task objectives. The program is

grounded to the detected entities through their persistent identifiers and is

executed by the engine to instantiate the initial canonical state $s_{0}$ .

For example, for a combat scenario, the orchestrator can assign detected

characters to opposing factions, initialize their health and combat states,

specify valid attack relations, and define the effects of actions such as

shooting, including damage, death, and objective updates. Rather than

constructing a conventional game with detailed 3D assets and low-level

simulation logic, the orchestrator programs a lightweight box world in which

3D OBBs provide the geometric scaffold and structured states, relations, and

rules define the interaction semantics.

Engine execution.

Once instantiated, the world program defines how the canonical state evolves

under interaction. The engine transition $F$ introduced in

Eq. () operates on the current state $s_{t}$ and

player action $a_{t}$ :

3

$s_{t+1}=F(s_{t},a_{t}).$ (5)

At each interaction step, the engine evaluates the action against the current

attributes, relations, and executable rules $\mathcal{R}_{t}$ , checks whether

the action is valid, applies its effects, and resolves any triggered events.

The resulting changes to entities, attributes, relations, and potentially the

rule set are recorded in the updated canonical state $s_{t+1}$ .

The canonical world state may also contain variables that are not directly

expressed in visual observations, such as health, inventory, or faction

membership, yet still govern future state transitions. These latent world

facts are maintained explicitly by the engine and can influence subsequent

state updates and rendered outcomes.

After each interaction step, the engine therefore produces an updated

canonical state $s_{t+1}$ in world coordinates. This state specifies the

result of the interaction, but it is not yet a renderer-facing representation.

The next stage converts its visually relevant content into spatial controls

aligned with the target camera.

4.3

From world states to spatial controls.

Given the updated canonical state $s_{t+1}$ produced by the engine, the state

compiler $P$ constructs a renderer-facing spatial representation without

altering the underlying world state. Specifically, it extracts the

renderer-relevant state variables and projects them under the target camera

$C_{t+1}$ :

$M_{t+1}^{\mathrm{ctrl}}=P(s_{t+1},C_{t+1}).$ (6)

The canonical state is defined with respect to the 3D world and may contain

variables that have no direct spatial realization in the rendered view. The

compiler therefore focuses on properties that must be spatially grounded for

visual generation. In particular, it projects the entity OBBs under the target

camera and augments their projected regions with identity, semantic, and

object-motion attributes. The projected OBBs specify where each entity should

appear, while the associated attributes indicate which persistent instance

occupies the region, which semantic category it belongs to, and in which

direction the entity itself is moving.

Across frames, the displacement of a projected OBB may result from object

motion, camera motion, or both. We therefore additionally provide an explicit

camera-relative object-motion state derived from the entity’s world-space

velocity. This state describes the entity’s own motion independently of the

apparent displacement induced by the target camera trajectory, thereby

reducing camera–object motion ambiguity.

Structured projected-box controls.

A projected OBB specifies the spatial support of an entity in the target view,

but its geometry alone does not encode persistent identity, semantic category,

or object-motion direction. We therefore construct three spatially aligned

control maps for these complementary properties.

The identity map $M_{t+1}^{\mathrm{id}}$ establishes persistent instance

correspondence across time. During interaction, an entity may become occluded

or leave and later re-enter the camera view, making it difficult to preserve

its appearance using visual history alone. We assign each persistent entity

identifier $k_{i}$ to an identity slot that remains fixed throughout the

generated sequence. We maintain a bank of $K$ learnable identity embeddings:

$\mathcal{E}^{\mathrm{id}}=\left\{q_{j}^{\mathrm{id}}\right\}_{j=1}^{K}.$ (7)

The embedding associated with the assigned identity slot is rasterized over

the visible projection of the entity’s OBB, providing a spatial key associated

with its appearance reference. During training, entities within each sample

are uniformly assigned distinct slots from this bank. The assignment is

randomized across samples but kept fixed across all frames of the same

sequence, preventing individual identity embeddings from becoming spuriously

associated with a particular object category, appearance, or viewpoint. At

inference time, the assigned slot is preserved for each persistent entity

across interaction steps.

The semantic map $M_{t+1}^{\mathrm{sem}}$ provides category-level information

complementary to the instance-specific identity map. Given the semantic label

$y_{i}$ maintained in the canonical state, a pretrained text encoder produces

the corresponding semantic embedding:

$q_{i}^{\mathrm{sem}}=E_{\mathrm{text}}(y_{i}).$ (8)

The embedding is rasterized over the visible projection of the entity’s OBB,

while background locations are assigned zero features. When multiple projected

boxes overlap, depth-aware rasterization retains the representation of the

visible entity. Entities sharing the same semantic label therefore share the

same semantic representation while remaining distinguishable through their

identity slots. This semantic guidance is particularly useful for entities

that are absent from the initial observation or lack a reliable appearance

reference.

The direction map $M_{t+1}^{\mathrm{dir}}$ provides an explicit

camera-relative representation of object motion. For each entity, the compiler

takes its world-space velocity maintained by the engine, rotates it into the

coordinate system of the target camera, and quantizes the resulting direction

into one of seven states: , , ,

, , , or . We maintain a

bank of learnable embeddings for these direction states:forwardbackwardleftrightstaticupdown

$\mathcal{E}^{\mathrm{dir}}=\left\{q_{\ell}^{\mathrm{dir}}\right\}_{\ell=1}^{7}.$ (9)

The embedding associated with an entity’s direction state is rasterized over

the visible projection of its OBB, while background and invalid regions are

assigned zero features. Importantly, the direction state is computed from the

entity’s world-space velocity rather than from its image-space displacement.

A static entity therefore remains assigned the state even when

camera movement causes its projected location to change. Together with the

target camera trajectory, this representation allows the renderer to separate

object motion from apparent motion induced by the camera.static

Finally, the identity, semantic, and direction maps are concatenated along the

channel dimension to form the structured projected-box control:

$M_{t+1}^{\mathrm{ctrl}}=\operatorname{Concat}\left(M_{t+1}^{\mathrm{id}},M_{t+1}^{\mathrm{sem}},M_{t+1}^{\mathrm{dir}}\right).$ (10)

The resulting representation separates occupies a

controlled region, it belongs to, and

the entity itself moves. Together with the projected

OBB geometry and target camera trajectory, these maps provide explicit

spatial, identity, semantic, and object-motion guidance to the generative

renderer.which instancewhat semantic categoryin which direction
