3.2

As analyses in Figure , the variation in adjacent chunk’s clean-latent similarity across control regimes

motivates allocating computation according to the incoming controls. We thus propose an

action-aware scheduling and refresh policy to assign each chunk a control

state, to decide whether using residual reuse or full

computation at the selected interior denoising step.

2

Based on the chunk’s position in the rollout and the incoming controls, we

distinguish four control states, including $\operatorname{initial}$ , $\operatorname{transition}$ , $\operatorname{turning}$ , and $\operatorname{steady}$ .

The control state $C_{n}$ of the chunk $n$ is thus assigned as:Control-state assignment.

$C_{n}=\begin{cases}\operatorname{initial},&n=1,\\

\operatorname{transition},&n>1,\ T_{n}=1,\\

\operatorname{turning},&n>1,\ T_{n}=0,\ R_{n}=1,\\

\operatorname{steady},&n>1,\ T_{n}=0,\ R_{n}=0.\end{cases}$ (2)

Here, $T_{n}$ indicates whether a control transition occurs, and $R_{n}$ indicates

whether a turning control is active. The first chunk is assigned the initial

state without requiring a preceding control input.

For subsequent chunks,

transition takes priority over turning, so a chunk containing an action

change is classified as transition even when a turning control is also active.

Steady state means unchanged, non-turning controls, while the generated scene may continue to evolve without remaining static.

Given these state definitions, the next step is to determine the indicators from the incoming

control sequence.

For a given backbone, let $\mathbf{a}_{n,j}$ denote the $j$ -th

control input in the chunk $n$ , where $j\in\{1,\ldots,J\}$ and $J$ is the number of

control inputs per chunk. We denote this sequence action by $\mathbf{a}_{n,1:J}$ .

For $n>1$ , we additionally define

$\mathbf{a}_{n,0}=\mathbf{a}_{n-1,J}$ as the last control input of the

preceding chunk, allowing the same rule to detect changes both

across chunk boundaries and within a chunk. This auxiliary boundary action input is not included among the

current chunk’s $J$ control inputs.

We distinguish a comparison between consecutive control inputs from a test of

the current turning-control magnitude. Let

$\operatorname{switch}(\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b})\in\{0,1\}$ indicate whether the

command changes between two inputs, and let

$\operatorname{rot}(\mathbf{a})\geq 0$ denote the magnitude of the turning

control in an input.

For $n>1$ , the transition indicators $T_{n}$ and the turning indicators $R_{n}$ are computed as:

$\displaystyle T_{n}$ $\displaystyle=\max_{1\leq j\leq J}\operatorname{switch}\!\left(\mathbf{a}_{n,j},\mathbf{a}_{n,j-1}\right),$ (3) $\displaystyle R_{n}$ $\displaystyle=\mathbbm{1}\!\left[\max_{1\leq j\leq J}\operatorname{rot}\!\left(\mathbf{a}_{n,j}\right)>\tau_{\mathrm{turn}}\right],$

where $\mathbbm{1}[\cdot]$ denotes the indicator function, which returns

one when its argument is true and zero otherwise, and

$\tau_{\mathrm{turn}}$ is the backbone-specific turning threshold.

Checking $j=1$ detects a change at the chunk boundary, while checking

$j=\{2,\ldots,J\}$ captures changes within the chunk.

Given the control state $C_{n}$ , we determine whether to enable residual reuse

at one selected interior denoising step $s\in\{2,\ldots,S-1\}$ .

All remaining steps are fully computed, with the first initializing the

residual cache and the final preserving the model’s refinement.

Let $G_{n}\in\{0,1\}$ indicate whether full computation is required at the

selected step:Scheduling and refresh trigger.

$G_{n}=\begin{cases}1,&n=1,\\

T_{n},&n>1.\end{cases}$ (4)

Here, $G_{n}=1$ triggers a cache refresh in which the DiT transformer blocks are fully

computed, and the resulting residual updates the current chunk’s cache as the new residual cache.

When $G_{n}=0$ , the transformer-block output at the selected step is

approximated using the cached residual via Eq. ().

Initial chunks retain full computation to establish the rollout, and

transition chunks restore it at the selected step to accommodate changed

controls. Turning and steady chunks instead reuse the cached residual at

that step.

1

3.3

The action-aware scheduling and refresh policy controls residual reuse within each chunk. We further

introduce a frequency-mixed history prior guidance to

determine what cached information is safer to carry forward during reusing.

Here, we use information from the preceding chunk’s

clean latent.

As the analyses in Figure , even in the steady interaction regime,

low-frequency components encoding coarse scene layout remain more persistent

across chunks than high-frequency components encoding fine appearance details.

Transferring the preceding clean

latent without distinction can therefore impose details that no longer fit

the evolving scene.

To this end, we construct a history prior that

emphasizes coarse structure, and blend it into the current chunk’s first-step clean

estimate. This guidance is enabled only when $C_{n}=\operatorname{steady}$ since

during transitions and sustained turning, the inherited geometry may itself

be changing with the viewpoint.

2

Let $\boldsymbol{z}_{n-1}$ denote the preceding chunk’s clean latent, consisting of $L$ temporal latent frames. We use its

last frame, $\boldsymbol{z}_{n-1,L}$ , to construct the history prior

for the current chunk.

We decompose this latent into a low-frequency component

obtained by spatial average pooling and a high-frequency component defined

as the remaining difference:Frequency-mixed history prior construction.

$\displaystyle\boldsymbol{z}^{\mathrm{low}}_{n-1,L}$ $\displaystyle=\operatorname{AvgPool}_{3\times 3}(\boldsymbol{z}_{n-1,L}),$ (5) $\displaystyle\boldsymbol{z}^{\mathrm{high}}_{n-1,L}$ $\displaystyle=\boldsymbol{z}_{n-1,L}-\boldsymbol{z}^{\mathrm{low}}_{n-1,L}.$

Here, the $\mathrm{low}$ and $\mathrm{high}$ denote frequency

components. $\operatorname{AvgPool}_{3\times 3}$ denotes spatial average pooling

with a $3\times 3$ kernel, unit stride, and replicate padding, chosen for its

low computational cost. It operates independently on each latent frame and

channel, preserving spatial resolution without mixing information across the

temporal dimension.

The current chunk likewise contains $L$ temporal latent frames.

Position $k=1$ is closest in time to the

preceding chunk, and larger $k$ denotes a later position. Thus, $k$ indexes

positions within a latent chunk, while $s$ indexes denoising steps and $j$

indexes control inputs as shown in the previous sections. We construct a history prior latent frame $\boldsymbol{p}_{n,k}$

at each position, with the same shape as $\boldsymbol{z}_{n-1,L}$ :

$\boldsymbol{p}_{n,k}=w_{k}\bigl(\boldsymbol{z}^{\mathrm{low}}_{n-1,L}+\alpha_{k}\boldsymbol{z}^{\mathrm{high}}_{n-1,L}\bigr),\quad k=1,\ldots,L,$ (6)

where $\alpha_{k}$ weights the high-frequency component, with $\alpha_{1}=1$

and $\alpha_{k}=\alpha\in[0,1]$ for $k\geq 2$ . The temporal weights $w_{k}$ satisfy

$1=w_{1}\geq w_{2}\geq\cdots\geq w_{L}\geq 0$ . With $\alpha_{1}=w_{1}=1$ ,

the first prior frame preserves the preceding chunk’s last clean latent

frame in full. At later positions, $\alpha$ controls high-frequency

attenuation, while $w_{k}$ scales both frequency components according to

temporal distance. Stacking

$\{\boldsymbol{p}_{n,1},\ldots,\boldsymbol{p}_{n,L}\}$ along the temporal dimension yields the

history prior $\boldsymbol{p}_{n}$ for chunk $n$ . The model-specific values of

$\alpha$ and $w_{k}$ are reported in Section .

4.1

After constructing the history prior $\boldsymbol{p}_{n}$ from the preceding

chunk, we use it to guide the current chunk’s clean latent estimate.

Let $\widehat{\boldsymbol{z}}_{n}^{(s)}$ denote the clean latent estimate of chunk $n$

obtained at denoising step $s$ using the base sampler’s prediction

parameterization.

Both $\widehat{\boldsymbol{z}}_{n}^{(s)}$ and $\boldsymbol{p}_{n}$

span all $L$ temporal latent positions and have the same shape.

We then blend the

current estimate $\widehat{\boldsymbol{z}}_{n}^{(s)}$ with the history prior $\boldsymbol{p}_{n}$ :Guiding the clean latent estimate using the history prior.

$\widehat{\boldsymbol{z}}_{n}^{(s)}\leftarrow(1-\lambda)\widehat{\boldsymbol{z}}_{n}^{(s)}+\lambda\boldsymbol{p}_{n},$ (7)

where $\lambda\in[0,1]$ is the guidance strength and the arrow denotes an

in-place update of the clean estimate.

In this paper, we apply history prior guidance only at $s=1$ , when the earliest

control-conditioned clean latent estimate of the current chunk becomes

available. This leaves the remaining denoising steps to adapt the transferred

structure to the current controls and refine visual details.

The sampler uses the updated clean estimate to construct the next noisy

latent under its original timestep and noise schedule. Thus, the guidance introduces no additional DiT forward computation cost.

3.4

For each chunk, CtrlCache first determines its control state from the

incoming controls and then coordinates computation reuse and history transfer

accordingly. Initial and transition chunks retain full computation throughout

the denoising process, whereas turning and steady chunks reuse a cached

residual at one selected interior step. The first and final denoising steps

remain fully computed in all cases. In addition, steady chunks apply the

frequency-mixed history prior to the clean latent estimate at $s=1$ to promote

structural consistency across chunks. After generating the clean latent chunk

$\boldsymbol{z}_{n}$ , CtrlCache retains its last temporal frame $\boldsymbol{z}_{n,L}$ as the

history reference for the next chunk. The complete inference pseudocode is

provided in Appendix .

Table  reports the quantitative comparison on all three

backbones. Overall, CtrlCache attains the best WBench Overall score and the

closest agreement with the original model on every backbone, at a speedup

comparable to the caching baselines.

On Matrix-Game 2.0, CtrlCache is the only method that improves over Original

on all five WBench dimensions, raising Overall from 0.6543 to 0.6786 and

surpassing the relatively best EasyCache (0.6625) while delivering

On LingBot-World v1/ v2, CtrlCache achieves best Overall, PSNR, SSIM and LPIPS, while keeping a comparable

1.26 $\times$ and 1.21 $\times$ speedup, respectively.

The caching baselines remain marginally faster than CtrlCache on every

backbone, since their reuse criteria are free to skip computation at action

transitions.

CtrlCache instead spends that computation on transition chunks,

which is what yields the highest setting adherence and physics compliance on

all three backbones.

We keep residual reuse and the action-aware policy fixed and vary the

control states in which history prior guidance is applied.

By default, we only apply the frequency-mixed history prior guidance (Sec. ) on the steady state.

Restricting

guidance to steady chunks yields the highest Overall scores among the

evaluated variants, while extending it to turning or transition chunks

reduces performance. These results suggest that

the prior is most beneficial during steady interaction, whereas carrying

forward historical structure during turning or control transitions may

interfere with the required scene changes.Effect of the frequency-mixed history prior guidance.

D

5

We propose CtrlCache, a training-free framework that uses online controls

to guide both computation reuse and history transfer in interactive video

world models. Its action-aware scheduling and refresh policy controls

residual reuse and restores full computation at control transitions, while

frequency-mixed history prior guidance transfers persistent coarse structure

during steady interaction. Experiments on Matrix-Game 2.0 and

LingBot-World v1/ v2 show that CtrlCache improves WBench Overall over original models

and

achieves

comparable speedups. These findings highlight the value of

adapting acceleration to the control regime and the persistence of

historical information.

CtrlCache currently relies on backbone-specific action indicators

and a fixed reuse step that varies with each backbone’s denoising schedule.

We will explore more general control representations and adaptive

step selection in the future work.Limitation.

Appendix C

We sample 40 cases from the WBench navigation split and use generation seed

$42$ . For each backbone, all methods are evaluated on the same sampled cases

with the same seed. Original and accelerated runs also share the prompts,

controls, initial frames, and decoding settings, so fidelity is computed on

paired outputs.Evaluation split and paired runs.

We report five navigation-track dimensions that consist of Quality (the mean of six video

quality measures), Consistency (the mean of eight consistency measures),

Interaction (interaction adherence), Setting (the mean of scene and subject

adherence), and Physics (the mean of visual plausibility and causal fidelity).

WBench Overall is the unweighted arithmetic mean of these five dimension

scores. Each component is averaged over the cases for which that measure is

defined.WBench aggregation.

For each case, PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS are computed frame by frame between the

accelerated video and its paired Original video. We first average each metric

over frames within a video, then report the unweighted mean of the resulting

per-case values. Thus, each case contributes equally to the reported fidelity

metrics.Paired fidelity metrics.

For efficiency, we report mean DiT denoising latency and

speedup relative to Original. Timing uses CUDA synchronization and covers only DiT computation

during denoising, excluding KV-cache commit/update, model loading, condition preparation, VAE

decoding, and video encoding.Efficiency evaluation.

一句话：给交互式视频世界模型加控制感知的缓存复用，把推理成本压下来。

要点：

  • 识别相邻帧之间可复用的计算结果，避免重复推理
  • 缓存键与用户控制信号绑定，保证一致性不被破坏
  • 在交互式场景下显著降低每帧成本

为什么值得看：世界模型要当引擎用，首帧生成慢还能忍，每帧都要重新推理就没法玩。这类缓存优化是落地前提。

中文摘要：交互式视频世界模型的核心瓶颈是推理成本：用户每给一次输入就要重新生成，几乎无法实时。CtrlCache 的思路是做控制感知的缓存——找出相邻帧之间可以复用的中间结果，并把缓存与控制信号绑定，确保复用不会破坏画面一致性。作者在交互式场景下验证了这套方法能显著降低每帧开销，是「世界模型当引擎」路上必须解决的一类工程问题。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·世界模型+游戏（English）

CtrlCache: Accelerating Interactive Video World Models with Control-Aware Caching

Abstract

Interactive video world models need to generate each video chunk efficiently while responding faithfully to user controls.

Many systems use chunk-wise

autoregressive generation with few-step denoising, but each chunk still

requires several costly denoising iterations.

Training-free caching can reduce this cost, yet existing policies make reuse decisions primarily from model-internal denoising dynamics and do not

explicitly account for control transitions.

Actually, interactive

generation explicitly exposes a signal they do not use: the controls for a chunk arrive before it is denoised, so a schedule derived from them costs no forward pass.

To this end, we analyze adjacent chunks under different control regimes and

find that structural similarity drops around action changes, while low-frequency

structure remains more persistent than high-frequency detail.

Motivated by these observations, we propose , a training-free control-aware caching framework that adapts computation to the

current control sequence.

Specifically, the action-aware scheduling and refresh policy detects action

changes across and within chunks, and labels each chunk as initial, transition,

turning, or steady state.

At one selected interior

denoising step, initial and transition chunks retain full computation, while turning

and steady chunks reuse the transformer residual from the most recent fully computed step in the same chunk.

To exploit the persistence of low-frequency structure during steady

interaction, we further introduce a frequency-mixed history prior guidance

that incorporates complementary information from the preceding clean latent

without an additional DiT forward pass.

Evaluated on Matrix-Game 2.0 and LingBot-World v1/v2, CtrlCache achieves

1.21 $\times$ to 1.41 $\times$ DiT-backbone speedups without model retraining

while improving WBench Overall

scores over original inference across all three models.CtrlCache

Our CtrlCache adapts DiT computation to the incoming controls. The left panel shows how the control-aware policy selects

full computation, residual reuse, or refresh across representative control

states. The right panel summarizes WBench Overall and DiT-backbone speedup on

Matrix-Game 2.0 , LingBot-World v1 , and LingBot-World v2 . Here,

denotes a regular full DiT forward, denotes residual reuse at

the selected denoising step, and denotes a full forward at an

action transition.

Interactive video world models turn a stream of user controls into continuously evolving

visual environments, offering a foundation for interactive simulation and

virtual exploration. Recent methods  have made substantial progress toward

realistic, real-time, and long-horizon

interaction. However, efficient

inference remains essential since delays in generating each new segment directly

affect how promptly users can interact with the simulated world.(; ; ; ; ; )

Many recent interactive world models  generate video autoregressively in short chunks and adopt few-step diffusion to reduce sampling cost.

Yet each chunk still requires multiple expensive full forward through

the large diffusion transformer (DiT) backbone.

Training-free caching

can reduce this repeated computation by reusing intermediate computation,

ranging from

fixed reuse schedules  to adaptive ones driven by internal feature changes .

However, these methods were primarily developed for image or video

generation, and their reuse policies do not explicitly account for

action transitions during interactive generation.(; ; ; )

Yin et al., 2025

Huang et al., 2025

This motivates examining how the incoming control sequence can guide

computation allocation and the use of generated history.

We first analyze the similarity between the clean latent representations

of adjacent chunks under different control regimes, and

make two observations as shown in Figure .

First, latent similarity drops around action changes, suggesting

that

reuse policies should be applied more conservatively during these transitions.

Second, even during steady interaction, low-frequency components are

more persistent across chunks than high-frequency components,

suggesting that coarse scene layout carries over more reliably than

fine-grained appearance details.

2

These observations naturally raise two complementary design questions:

denoising cache should be reused or refreshed,

and content from the cached history is safer to carry forward if reusing them.

To this end, we introduce , a

training-free framework that couples control-aware computation allocation

with selective history cache transfer.

To decide , we introduce an .

It first assigns each chunk to one of four control states, $\operatorname{initial}$ , $\operatorname{transition}$ , $\operatorname{turning}$ , or $\operatorname{steady}$ , based on the incoming control sequence.

Then, at one interior denoising step, initial chunks execute the full DiT computation to initialize the cache, transition chunks do so to refresh it, and

turning and steady chunks instead permit reuse using the transformer residual cache from the

most recent fully denoising step in

the same chunk.

In this way, the denoising cache can be selectively reused according to the incoming controls.

This policy is applied both across chunk boundaries and within each chunk, since a single chunk spans

multiple action samples.

Transferring the preceding chunk’s clean latent frame without distinction, however, can

carry over fine details that no longer fit the evolving scene. Guided by

our frequency analysis, we further introduce a to address .

The guidance builds a history prior from that frame, which emphasizes low-frequency structure

of that frame,

attenuates its high-frequency detail, and

gradually reduces the history prior contribution at later positions in the new

chunk.

The prior is then blended into the clean latent estimate after the first denoising step

to stabilize the structural layout of subsequent chunks under acceleration,

without an additional computational cost.

We enable this guidance only for

steady chunks, since during control transitions and sustained turning,

the geometry inherited from the preceding chunk may become outdated as

the viewpoint changes.

Together, these designs adapt both computation reuse and history

transfer to the current interaction state without retraining the model.whenwhatCtrlCachewhenaction-aware scheduling and refresh policyfrequency-mixed history

prior guidancewhat

We evaluate CtrlCache on Matrix-Game 2.0  and

LingBot-World v1/v2

using the WBench navigation track .

Across all three backbones, CtrlCache achieves the highest WBench

Overall among all evaluated methods while delivering DiT-backbone

speedups ranging from $1.21\times$ to $1.41\times$ .

Among the accelerated methods, it also achieves the highest PSNR and

SSIM and the lowest LPIPS on every backbone, demonstrating the

strongest fidelity to the Original outputs. Overall, our main contributions are:()

We propose CtrlCache, a training-free control-aware caching framework

that uses action-aware scheduling and refresh to determine to

Extensive experiments on three interactive video world models demonstrate that CtrlCache accelerates the inference computation while improving WBench Overall scores, outperforming the evaluated caching baselines at comparable latency.

2

Interactive video world models

generate visual observations conditioned on controls throughout an ongoing

rollout. Early autoregressive systems model action-conditioned latent dynamics,

as in Genie  and iVideoGPT ;

diffusion world models extend this setting to action-conditioned games and

navigation .

Recent systems broaden control and scene coverage through multimodal or

open-world generation ,

while CausVid  and Self Forcing

establish causal few-step diffusion for streaming

generation. Long-horizon interaction and memory are further explored by The

Diffusion models generate images and videos through iterative denoising

, with each step requiring a backbone

forward pass; DiT  and related architectures therefore

offer substantial opportunities for intermediate-feature reuse. Training-free

caching methods use either predefined or adaptive schedules. Fixed schemes

include DeepCache , FORA ,

$\Delta$ -DiT , and PAB , which reuse

features at selected network modules or timestep intervals. Adaptive schemes

include TeaCache , EasyCache ,

FasterCache , ToCa , and AdaCache

, which adjust reuse according to feature

variation, token redundancy, or motion content. These methods reduce inference

cost without retraining. Recent work further studies structure-preserving

video caching and adaptive caching for video generation .

However, these works generally

ignore online action changes as

FlowCache extends caching to autoregressive video through independent chunk-wise

reuse decisions and bounded-history KV-cache compression, but does not interpret online action transitions.

X-Cache targets cross-chunk caching for autonomous-driving world models ,

a distinct application scenario from ours.

Light Interaction  addresses interactive video

generation, yet ties denoising reuse to sufficiently similar historical views,

making it less suited to open-ended interactions with few or no revisits. Our method instead derives its reuse and refresh decisions directly from the control sequence.

Action transitions trigger full computation and

cache refresh, while other control states permit residual reuse without trajectory revisitation.()

As illustrated in Figure , CtrlCache builds on

established residual reuse (Sec. ) and comprises two

complementary components. The

(Sec. ) uses the incoming controls to determine when to

reuse cached transformer residuals and when to restore full computation.

The (Sec. )

first constructs a history prior from the preceding chunk’s last clean latent

3.1

Let $n$ index the $n$ -th video chunk and $s\in\{1,\ldots,S\}$ as denoising steps within each chunk, where $S$ is the number of denoising steps per chunk.

To generate chunk $n$ , the interactive video world models  progressively denoise a noisy latent

conditioned on the incoming controls and previously generated history.

Each step performs a full forward pass through the

diffusion transformer (DiT), followed by a sampler update using the model

prediction. After the $S$ steps, the completed clean latent chunk provides

history for subsequent autoregressive generation.Chunk-wise autoregressive denoising.(; ; )

Rather than computing the whole DiT transformer blocks at every denoising step, following ,

we adopt the established approximation of applying a cached residual from the most recent full forward to

the current step’s input as the execution

mechanism underlying CtrlCache.

Let $\boldsymbol{f}^{\mathrm{in}}_{n,s}$ and

$\boldsymbol{f}^{\mathrm{out}}_{n,s}$ denote the feature tensors immediately before and after

the DiT transformer blocks for chunk $n$ at step $s$ . A full forward process produces

the residual $\boldsymbol{r}_{n,s}=\boldsymbol{f}^{\mathrm{out}}_{n,s}-\boldsymbol{f}^{\mathrm{in}}_{n,s}$ , which is cached for reuse within the current chunk.

At denoising step $s$ , if the scheduling policy permits reuse and a residual

from an earlier fully computed step is cached, the current transformer-block

output $\widetilde{\boldsymbol{f}}^{\mathrm{out}}_{n,s}$ can be approximated as:Residual reuse.()

3.2

As analyses in Figure , the variation in adjacent chunk’s clean-latent similarity across control regimes

motivates allocating computation according to the incoming controls. We thus propose an

action-aware scheduling and refresh policy to assign each chunk a control

state, to decide whether using residual reuse or full

computation at the selected interior denoising step.

2

Based on the chunk’s position in the rollout and the incoming controls, we

distinguish four control states, including $\operatorname{initial}$ , $\operatorname{transition}$ , $\operatorname{turning}$ , and $\operatorname{steady}$ .

The control state $C_{n}$ of the chunk $n$ is thus assigned as:Control-state assignment.

$C_{n}=\begin{cases}\operatorname{initial},&n=1,\\

\operatorname{transition},&n>1,\ T_{n}=1,\\

\operatorname{turning},&n>1,\ T_{n}=0,\ R_{n}=1,\\

\operatorname{steady},&n>1,\ T_{n}=0,\ R_{n}=0.\end{cases}$ (2)

Here, $T_{n}$ indicates whether a control transition occurs, and $R_{n}$ indicates

whether a turning control is active. The first chunk is assigned the initial

state without requiring a preceding control input.

For subsequent chunks,

transition takes priority over turning, so a chunk containing an action

change is classified as transition even when a turning control is also active.

Steady state means unchanged, non-turning controls, while the generated scene may continue to evolve without remaining static.

Given these state definitions, the next step is to determine the indicators from the incoming

control sequence.

For a given backbone, let $\mathbf{a}_{n,j}$ denote the $j$ -th

control input in the chunk $n$ , where $j\in\{1,\ldots,J\}$ and $J$ is the number of

control inputs per chunk. We denote this sequence action by $\mathbf{a}_{n,1:J}$ .

For $n>1$ , we additionally define

$\mathbf{a}_{n,0}=\mathbf{a}_{n-1,J}$ as the last control input of the

preceding chunk, allowing the same rule to detect changes both

across chunk boundaries and within a chunk. This auxiliary boundary action input is not included among the

current chunk’s $J$ control inputs.

We distinguish a comparison between consecutive control inputs from a test of

the current turning-control magnitude. Let

$\operatorname{switch}(\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b})\in\{0,1\}$ indicate whether the

command changes between two inputs, and let

$\operatorname{rot}(\mathbf{a})\geq 0$ denote the magnitude of the turning

control in an input.

For $n>1$ , the transition indicators $T_{n}$ and the turning indicators $R_{n}$ are computed as:

$\displaystyle T_{n}$ $\displaystyle=\max_{1\leq j\leq J}\operatorname{switch}\!\left(\mathbf{a}_{n,j},\mathbf{a}_{n,j-1}\right),$ (3) $\displaystyle R_{n}$ $\displaystyle=\mathbbm{1}\!\left[\max_{1\leq j\leq J}\operatorname{rot}\!\left(\mathbf{a}_{n,j}\right)>\tau_{\mathrm{turn}}\right],$

where $\mathbbm{1}[\cdot]$ denotes the indicator function, which returns

one when its argument is true and zero otherwise, and

$\tau_{\mathrm{turn}}$ is the backbone-specific turning threshold.

Checking $j=1$ detects a change at the chunk boundary, while checking

$j=\{2,\ldots,J\}$ captures changes within the chunk.

Given the control state $C_{n}$ , we determine whether to enable residual reuse

at one selected interior denoising step $s\in\{2,\ldots,S-1\}$ .

All remaining steps are fully computed, with the first initializing the

residual cache and the final preserving the model’s refinement.

Let $G_{n}\in\{0,1\}$ indicate whether full computation is required at the

selected step:Scheduling and refresh trigger.

$G_{n}=\begin{cases}1,&n=1,\\

T_{n},&n>1.\end{cases}$ (4)

Here, $G_{n}=1$ triggers a cache refresh in which the DiT transformer blocks are fully

computed, and the resulting residual updates the current chunk’s cache as the new residual cache.

When $G_{n}=0$ , the transformer-block output at the selected step is

approximated using the cached residual via Eq. ().

Initial chunks retain full computation to establish the rollout, and

transition chunks restore it at the selected step to accommodate changed

controls. Turning and steady chunks instead reuse the cached residual at

that step.

3.3

The action-aware scheduling and refresh policy controls residual reuse within each chunk. We further

introduce a frequency-mixed history prior guidance to

determine what cached information is safer to carry forward during reusing.

Here, we use information from the preceding chunk’s

clean latent.

As the analyses in Figure , even in the steady interaction regime,

low-frequency components encoding coarse scene layout remain more persistent

across chunks than high-frequency components encoding fine appearance details.

Transferring the preceding clean

latent without distinction can therefore impose details that no longer fit

the evolving scene.

To this end, we construct a history prior that

emphasizes coarse structure, and blend it into the current chunk’s first-step clean

estimate. This guidance is enabled only when $C_{n}=\operatorname{steady}$ since

during transitions and sustained turning, the inherited geometry may itself

be changing with the viewpoint.

2

Let $\boldsymbol{z}_{n-1}$ denote the preceding chunk’s clean latent, consisting of $L$ temporal latent frames. We use its

last frame, $\boldsymbol{z}_{n-1,L}$ , to construct the history prior

for the current chunk.

We decompose this latent into a low-frequency component

obtained by spatial average pooling and a high-frequency component defined

as the remaining difference:Frequency-mixed history prior construction.

$\displaystyle\boldsymbol{z}^{\mathrm{low}}_{n-1,L}$ $\displaystyle=\operatorname{AvgPool}_{3\times 3}(\boldsymbol{z}_{n-1,L}),$ (5) $\displaystyle\boldsymbol{z}^{\mathrm{high}}_{n-1,L}$ $\displaystyle=\boldsymbol{z}_{n-1,L}-\boldsymbol{z}^{\mathrm{low}}_{n-1,L}.$

Here, the $\mathrm{low}$ and $\mathrm{high}$ denote frequency

components. $\operatorname{AvgPool}_{3\times 3}$ denotes spatial average pooling

with a $3\times 3$ kernel, unit stride, and replicate padding, chosen for its

low computational cost. It operates independently on each latent frame and

channel, preserving spatial resolution without mixing information across the

temporal dimension.

The current chunk likewise contains $L$ temporal latent frames.

Position $k=1$ is closest in time to the

preceding chunk, and larger $k$ denotes a later position. Thus, $k$ indexes

positions within a latent chunk, while $s$ indexes denoising steps and $j$

indexes control inputs as shown in the previous sections. We construct a history prior latent frame $\boldsymbol{p}_{n,k}$

at each position, with the same shape as $\boldsymbol{z}_{n-1,L}$ :

$\boldsymbol{p}_{n,k}=w_{k}\bigl(\boldsymbol{z}^{\mathrm{low}}_{n-1,L}+\alpha_{k}\boldsymbol{z}^{\mathrm{high}}_{n-1,L}\bigr),\quad k=1,\ldots,L,$ (6)

where $\alpha_{k}$ weights the high-frequency component, with $\alpha_{1}=1$

and $\alpha_{k}=\alpha\in[0,1]$ for $k\geq 2$ . The temporal weights $w_{k}$ satisfy

$1=w_{1}\geq w_{2}\geq\cdots\geq w_{L}\geq 0$ . With $\alpha_{1}=w_{1}=1$ ,

the first prior frame preserves the preceding chunk’s last clean latent

frame in full. At later positions, $\alpha$ controls high-frequency

attenuation, while $w_{k}$ scales both frequency components according to

temporal distance. Stacking

$\{\boldsymbol{p}_{n,1},\ldots,\boldsymbol{p}_{n,L}\}$ along the temporal dimension yields the

history prior $\boldsymbol{p}_{n}$ for chunk $n$ . The model-specific values of

$\alpha$ and $w_{k}$ are reported in Section .

4.1

After constructing the history prior $\boldsymbol{p}_{n}$ from the preceding

chunk, we use it to guide the current chunk’s clean latent estimate.

Let $\widehat{\boldsymbol{z}}_{n}^{(s)}$ denote the clean latent estimate of chunk $n$

obtained at denoising step $s$ using the base sampler’s prediction

parameterization.

Both $\widehat{\boldsymbol{z}}_{n}^{(s)}$ and $\boldsymbol{p}_{n}$

span all $L$ temporal latent positions and have the same shape.

We then blend the

current estimate $\widehat{\boldsymbol{z}}_{n}^{(s)}$ with the history prior $\boldsymbol{p}_{n}$ :Guiding the clean latent estimate using the history prior.

$\widehat{\boldsymbol{z}}_{n}^{(s)}\leftarrow(1-\lambda)\widehat{\boldsymbol{z}}_{n}^{(s)}+\lambda\boldsymbol{p}_{n},$ (7)

where $\lambda\in[0,1]$ is the guidance strength and the arrow denotes an

in-place update of the clean estimate.

In this paper, we apply history prior guidance only at $s=1$ , when the earliest

control-conditioned clean latent estimate of the current chunk becomes

available. This leaves the remaining denoising steps to adapt the transferred

structure to the current controls and refine visual details.

The sampler uses the updated clean estimate to construct the next noisy

latent under its original timestep and noise schedule. Thus, the guidance introduces no additional DiT forward computation cost.

3.4

For each chunk, CtrlCache first determines its control state from the

incoming controls and then coordinates computation reuse and history transfer

accordingly. Initial and transition chunks retain full computation throughout

the denoising process, whereas turning and steady chunks reuse a cached

residual at one selected interior step. The first and final denoising steps

remain fully computed in all cases. In addition, steady chunks apply the

frequency-mixed history prior to the clean latent estimate at $s=1$ to promote

structural consistency across chunks. After generating the clean latent chunk

$\boldsymbol{z}_{n}$ , CtrlCache retains its last temporal frame $\boldsymbol{z}_{n,L}$ as the

history reference for the next chunk. The complete inference pseudocode is

provided in Appendix .

The caching baselines remain marginally faster than CtrlCache on every

CtrlCache instead spends that computation on transition chunks,

which is what yields the highest setting adherence and physics compliance on

all three backbones.

Building on naive residual reuse, we enable the action-aware policy in Sec.  to

restore full computation at control transitions, while steady and turning states do residual reuse.

It improves Overall on both backbones, as well as setting and physics

3.2

We keep residual reuse and the action-aware policy fixed and vary the

control states in which history prior guidance is applied.

By default, we only apply the frequency-mixed history prior guidance (Sec. ) on the steady state.

Restricting

guidance to steady chunks yields the highest Overall scores among the

evaluated variants, while extending it to turning or transition chunks

reduces performance. These results suggest that

the prior is most beneficial during steady interaction, whereas carrying

forward historical structure during turning or control transitions may

interfere with the required scene changes.Effect of the frequency-mixed history prior guidance.

D

5

We propose CtrlCache, a training-free framework that uses online controls

to guide both computation reuse and history transfer in interactive video

world models. Its action-aware scheduling and refresh policy controls

residual reuse and restores full computation at control transitions, while

frequency-mixed history prior guidance transfers persistent coarse structure

during steady interaction. Experiments on Matrix-Game 2.0 and

LingBot-World v1/ v2 show that CtrlCache improves WBench Overall over original models

and

achieves

comparable speedups. These findings highlight the value of

adapting acceleration to the control regime and the persistence of

historical information.

CtrlCache currently relies on backbone-specific action indicators

and a fixed reuse step that varies with each backbone’s denoising schedule.

We will explore more general control representations and adaptive

step selection in the future work.Limitation.

Appendix C

We sample 40 cases from the WBench navigation split and use generation seed

$42$ . For each backbone, all methods are evaluated on the same sampled cases

with the same seed. Original and accelerated runs also share the prompts,

controls, initial frames, and decoding settings, so fidelity is computed on

paired outputs.Evaluation split and paired runs.

We report five navigation-track dimensions that consist of Quality (the mean of six video

quality measures), Consistency (the mean of eight consistency measures),

Interaction (interaction adherence), Setting (the mean of scene and subject

adherence), and Physics (the mean of visual plausibility and causal fidelity).

WBench Overall is the unweighted arithmetic mean of these five dimension

scores. Each component is averaged over the cases for which that measure is

defined.WBench aggregation.

For each case, PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS are computed frame by frame between the

accelerated video and its paired Original video. We first average each metric

over frames within a video, then report the unweighted mean of the resulting

per-case values. Thus, each case contributes equally to the reported fidelity

metrics.Paired fidelity metrics.

For efficiency, we report mean DiT denoising latency and

speedup relative to Original. Timing uses CUDA synchronization and covers only DiT computation

during denoising, excluding KV-cache commit/update, model loading, condition preparation, VAE

decoding, and video encoding.Efficiency evaluation.

item.title: RIGen：从「跟随动作」到生成式玩法里的双向互动 ｜ RIGen: Beyond Action Following with Reciprocal Interaction in Generative Gameplay
item.description:
一句话：让生成式游戏不只是「玩家输入→模型输出」，而是模型也能主动推动玩法。

要点：

  • 指出当前生成式游戏只有单向动作跟随，缺乏真正的互动
  • 提出双向互动框架：环境/角色也会主动发起行为
  • 评估玩家体验层面的差异

为什么值得看：这是「AI 原生玩法」的核心设计问题：单向映射只是高级动画，双向互动才谈得上玩法。

中文摘要：现有生成式游戏大多把模型当成「动作翻译器」：玩家按键，模型输出画面或后果，本质仍是单向映射。RIGen 提出应该走向双向互动——不仅响应用户动作，环境与角色也能主动发起事件、施加压力，形成真正的博弈与叙事张力。论文给出了这套框架的实现与评估方法，是讨论「AI 原生玩法」时值得参考的一块拼图。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·生成式玩法（English）

License: CC BY 4.0

RIGen: Beyond Action Following with Reciprocal Interaction in Generative Gameplay

Abstract

Generative gameplay requires more than immediate responses to player actions.

Actions should have persistent consequences, while the generated world should

act according to its own state and rules, shaping the player’s situation and

subsequent choices. Video generation captures local dynamics, but limited

history, partially observed game state, and the need for contextual behavior

decisions make such interactions difficult to sustain through audiovisual

prediction alone. We introduce RIGen (Reciprocally Interactive Generation), a framework for

reciprocal interaction in generative gameplay. RIGen combines persistent state and configurable

rules, contextual interaction reasoning, and action-conditioned audiovisual

generation. Together, these components make interaction consequences and

actor behavior jointly determine generated content while maintaining

consistency between game state and visible outcomes. We construct a Xonotic

gameplay dataset to train an audiovisual generator for learning dynamics and

interactions. Further post-training enables RIGen-Arena, an interactive generative

first-person shooter (FPS) prototype.

Experiments demonstrate more reliable combat outcomes and reciprocal

interaction between the player and the generated world.

Project page: .

https://murphylmf.github.io/RIGen/

Players affect the generated world, whose rules, persistent state, and

characters in turn shape gameplay.

(a) Attacks have state-dependent consequences.

(b) Enemy actions, resource constraints, and respawn rules shape the

player’s survival and continued play.

(c) Opponents adapt their behavior to their health and current combat

conditions.Figure 1: Reciprocal interaction in RIGen.

1

Generative models offer a route to game experiences whose environments,

characters, and events can be created during

play .

Such experiences could be personalized to each player’s preferences and

choices. Realizing this potential requires reciprocal interaction: players

should be able to change the world through their actions, while the world

follows its own operating logic. Its characters act according to their

situation and goals, and its rules and events shape the player’s

circumstances and subsequent choices.(; )

Bruce et al., 2024

Yu et al., 2025

Recent video-based world models have made progress toward this goal.

DIAMOND  and GameNGen

demonstrate playable game simulation.

LingBot-World  and SCOPE

provide responsive camera and movement control, while

LingBot-World 2.0  and

Incantation  incorporate semantic guidance for

character behavior and interaction events.

Table  compares these systems across control,

gameplay, and output capabilities. It highlights the remaining gap in combining

reciprocal state changes with scene- and state-conditioned actor planning.()

Alonso et al., 2024

()

Valevski et al., 2025

()

Robbyant Team et al., 2026

()

Tong et al., 2026

()

Gao et al., 2026

()

Zhu et al., 2026b

The prevailing approach builds on video models that capture rich local dynamics

and generate continuous audiovisual feedback conditioned on player controls,

making them a natural foundation for interactive games. However, sustaining reciprocal interaction

through audiovisual prediction alone faces three challenges.

Responding to player actions

does not by itself determine how the world should act upon the player.

Actors must choose behavior based on current conditions and their own goals,

and the consequences must update player state and constrain subsequent

interactions.

Events beyond the model’s context window can

still have consequences for current interactions .

Gameplay variables such as health and

ammunition may not be recoverable from the visible scene, yet determine

whether an action can be executed and what outcome it should have.(1) Coordinating reciprocal interaction.(2) Limited history.()

Xiao et al., 2025

(3) Partially observed state.

In sustained combat, for example, accumulated damage must determine whether

the next hit is lethal, even when earlier attacks fall outside the video

context. The opponent’s remaining health and goals should shape whether

it attacks or retreats. Damage dealt by the opponent must likewise affect

the player’s health and ability to continue fighting.

To address these challenges, we introduce RIGen, a framework for reciprocal

interaction in generative gameplay (Figure ).

The layer maintains persistent gameplay variables and

configurable rules, including strategic goals and constraints.

The layer interprets the scene and player actions

to infer events and plan actor behavior under these conditions.

The layer realizes the resulting guidance

alongside player controls. Together, these layers let player actions change

the state that governs subsequent interactions. The world also acts

according to its own rules and goals, affecting the player’s state and

available actions.state and rulesinteraction reasoningaudiovisual generation

We instantiate RIGen in first-person shooter (FPS) environments.

Our experiments assess combat outcomes, while qualitative demonstrations

and RIGen-Arena illustrate state-dependent interactions and autonomous

enemy behavior that affects the player (Figure ).

We integrate

interaction prediction, executable state updates, and audiovisual generation

into a closed loop in which player actions change world state and world

behavior affects the player.

Model comparisons and controlled ablations demonstrate more reliable

realization of state-dependent interaction outcomes.

We construct a dataset covering

basic dynamics, controlled interactions, and sustained combat, pairing

audiovisual observations with player controls and interaction annotations,

with a reproducible data creation pipeline.

We build RIGen-Arena, integrating

few-step audiovisual generation with closed-loop interaction to support

Explicit state and generative rendering.

Prior systems combine structured state or game logic with generative

while planning-based video methods organize content before

Geometric rendering interfaces provide explicit spatial

state to generation through player actions and local interaction guidance,

without constructing explicit spatial trajectories.

3.1

RIGen couples three layers to align player actions, persistent state,

and generated audiovisual outcomes (Figure ).

The maintains persistent state, applies transition

rules, and specifies strategic constraints (Section ).

The reasons about action consequences and plans actor

behavior (Section ). The

models local dynamics under player controls and generation guidance

(Section ).State and Rule Engine

3.2

Interaction Agent

3.3

Audiovisual Generator

3.4

At each chunk boundary, the agent uses recent video, player controls, and

persistent state to predict interaction events and plan actor behavior.

The rule engine evaluates these events, and the updated state and planned

behavior jointly guide the next audiovisual chunk. After generation, the

agent checks which events occurred, and the rule engine uses this evidence

to determine the state for the next decision.

3.2

We represent gameplay as an event-driven state machine with numerical variables,

following standard state-based game AI .

The engine maintains player and enemy health and life/death state, player

ammunition, and opponent strategy modes, together with configurable rule

parameters such as the player’s per-shot damage and transition conditions.

Writing $s$ for the complete game state and $e$ for an interaction event

record, the engine maps $s$ to its successor $s^{\prime}$ through()

Millington & Funge, 2009

$s^{\prime}=\operatorname{Rules}(s,e).$ (1)

For example, firing requires a living player with available ammunition and

consumes a round regardless of whether the shot hits. A hit reduces the

target’s health by the configured damage, for either the player or an enemy.

Reaching zero health triggers death. If an opponent survives with low health,

a configured rule can switch its strategy from engagement to retreat.

The updated strategy guides the Interaction Agent’s next decision, such as

choosing a retreat direction suited to the current scene

(Section ).

3.3

3.3

Before generating chunk $o_{k}$ , we perform through

verification and state correction. The agent verifies $o_{k-1}$ using sampled

verification frames $\mathcal{I}_{k-1}$ , player controls $u_{k-1}$ , and local

guidance $p_{k-1}$ .

The rule engine then corrects the planned state $s_{k}^{\mathrm{plan}}$

using feedback $f_{k-1}$ :reconciliation

$\displaystyle f_{k-1}$ $\displaystyle=\operatorname{Verify}(\mathcal{I}_{k-1},u_{k-1},p_{k-1}),$ (2) $\displaystyle s_{k}$ $\displaystyle=\operatorname{Correct}(s_{k}^{\mathrm{plan}},f_{k-1}).$

Using this updated state, feedback, and current player controls $u_{k}$ ,

the agent proposes events $e_{k}$ and behavior $b_{k}$ :

$(e_{k},b_{k})=\operatorname{Agent}(o_{k-1},s_{k},u_{k},f_{k-1}).$ (3)

The rule engine computes a provisional successor $s_{k+1}^{\mathrm{plan}}$

and local interaction guidance $p_{k}$ without overwriting $s_{k}$ :

$\displaystyle s_{k+1}^{\mathrm{plan}}$ $\displaystyle=\operatorname{Rules}(s_{k},e_{k}),$ (4) $\displaystyle p_{k}$ $\displaystyle=\operatorname{Prompt}(s_{k+1}^{\mathrm{plan}},e_{k},b_{k}).$

The generator realizes this guidance as the next audiovisual chunk $o_{k}$

(Section ).

At the next boundary, verification of $o_{k}$ reconciles

$s_{k+1}^{\mathrm{plan}}$ with committed visual outcomes to obtain $s_{k+1}$ .

These observations take precedence over conflicting predictions, and the

corrected state conditions the next decision.

Implementation scope and verification details are given in

the appendix.

3.4

3.4

The global prompt $g$ describes the scene and character identity shared across

chunks. Local guidance $p_{k}$ specifies the current chunk’s actor behavior and

observable interaction outcomes, derived from the agent’s proposals and

rule-based state updates (Section ). Together, they form

text condition $c_{k}$ . Given audiovisual context $\mathcal{H}_{k}$ and player

controls $u_{k}$ , the generator produces the next chunk:

3.3

$c_{k}=(g,p_{k}),\qquad o_{k}\sim G_{\theta}(\mathcal{H}_{k},u_{k},c_{k}).$ (5)

The context $\mathcal{H}_{k}$ contains a first-frame anchor, a character reference,

and recent generated chunks with their controls and text conditions.

The generator denoises the target under these conditions, and the resulting

$o_{k}$ provides observations for the next interaction decision.

We instantiate $G_{\theta}$ with the LTX-2.3

audiovisual backbone, using coupled video and audio transformer streams

(Figure ). Continuous movement/camera controls

modulate video features through FiLM , while button inputs enter through causal

cross-attention. Audiovisual attention connects the two streams and is

causal across chunks and joint within each chunk. The anchor and reference

provide visual context without text or action updates.(; )

Perez et al., 2018

Chunk-wise prompt routing.

In both video and audio streams, each chunk attends only to the global prompt

and its corresponding local guidance through text cross-attention

(Figure ).

Historical chunks retain their original text conditions, while the target

receives the current guidance. The same routing is used in bidirectional and

causal training.

Training and continued generation.

Following the bidirectional-to-autoregressive adaptation used in

CausVid , we first train the model bidirectionally to follow player controls and

chunk-level guidance, then adapt it to autoregressive next-chunk prediction

conditioned on clean audiovisual history. Sliding-window training retains

a window of recent chunks alongside the first-frame anchor and character

reference, keeping $\mathcal{H}_{k}$ bounded during continued generation.

Training objectives and implementation details are provided in the appendix.()

5

RIGen-Arena is an interactive one-on-one FPS prototype in which the player fights an opponent,

with either side respawning after defeat to continue the match

(Figure ).

We initialize post-training for RIGen-Arena from the bidirectional model trained on

the Interaction subset. We first fine-tune it bidirectionally on the Arena

subset to adapt to sustained combat. We then train the adapted model to

generate chunks autoregressively using a sliding window of recent history

together with the first-frame anchor and character reference

(Section ).

3.4

We adopt the two-stage distillation recipe of

Causal-rCM . Teacher-forcing consistency distillation

first produces a few-step generator. Distribution matching then trains

this generator on its own autoregressive rollouts.()

Zheng et al., 2026a

We additionally train a video refiner to recover high-frequency details in

dynamic gameplay. Training pairs spatially degraded latents with the

original encodings of the same arena clips. We first train the refiner

bidirectionally with paired flow matching , then fine-tune it for causal,

chunk-wise refinement with a bounded history window.

At inference, it refines each generated chunk without access to future

chunks. We integrate the generator and refiner with the state and rule

engine and interaction agent to form RIGen-Arena.

Training objectives, sampling schedules, and implementation details are

provided in the appendix.()

Metrics.

Qwen3.8-27B  evaluates two interaction metrics offline.

(EB) measures adherence to prescribed enemy motion

within specified time windows. (FSA) measures

agreement between the final visible enemy state and its survival/death target.

FSA-S is the percentage of the 50 survival-target cases in which the enemy

is visibly alive at the end. FSA-D is the percentage of the 50 death-target

cases in which the enemy is visibly dead at the end. Overall FSA averages

these two rates. Incorrect or unjudgeable outcomes count as failures, so FSA

can fall below 50%. We also report Motion Smoothness (MS), Aesthetic Quality (AQ),

Subject Consistency (SC), Background Consistency (BC), and Dynamic Degree (DD),

following VBench . Scores are on a 0–100 scale.

Higher is better except for DD, which measures motion prevalence rather than quality.()

Results.

Table  shows that RIGen achieves 81% FSA,

compared with 29% for LingBot-World 2.0 and 4% for SCOPE, and higher EB

than both baselines. With the generator fixed, FSA falls to 39% with

motion-only guidance, 35% with semantic prompting, 64% with post-hoc

updates, and 76% without reconciliation. These results support predicting

interaction consequences before generation, executing state updates, and

reconciling them with visual feedback. Visual metrics remain nearly unchanged

across ablations. Lower AQ than LingBot-World 2.0 may reflect our smaller

training dataset. The appendix provides further details and analysis.

6.2

Combat responses.

Figure  compares visible combat responses

from the same initial image and attack requests. In this example, RIGen produces a hit reaction followed by a fall and a sustained downed state,

while the baseline opponents remain active under repeated fire despite

receiving text guidance specifying the correct combat outcomes.

State-dependent interactions.

Figure  varies initial enemy health, player

ammunition, and state-dependent opponent strategy from a shared starting

scene under the same player input requests.

The low-health opponent falls, depleted ammunition suppresses the third

shot, and an injured opponent switches from hold to retreat, moving left

and crouching at cover. These examples illustrate how explicit state and

strategy affect visible gameplay.

7

We presented RIGen, a framework for reciprocal interaction in generative

gameplay. Player actions change persistent world state, while world rules

and actor decisions affect the player. Quantitative comparisons demonstrate

more reliable combat outcomes, and qualitative results illustrate

state-dependent interactions and autonomous enemy behavior.

Limitations and future work.

RIGen is not yet real-time, supports only single-opponent FPS gameplay,

and relies on VLM perception and reasoning for interaction decisions and

state verification. Future work will optimize generation and agent inference,

extend to multiple opponents and broader action spaces and game genres,

and improve visual grounding and reasoning reliability.

Appendix A

A.1

We build on the LTX  audiovisual architecture, using

the LTX-2.3 22B dev backbone . Separate video and audio

autoencoders produce latent sequences processed by coupled transformer

streams. Each stream uses self-attention and text cross-attention, with

cross-modal attention connecting video and audio. At 20 video frames per

second, each generated chunk contains two video latent steps, corresponding

to 16 new frames, and 20 audio latent steps, corresponding to 0.8 seconds.

Generation is causal between chunks. Tokens within a chunk are denoised

jointly.()

HaCohen et al., 2026

()

Lightricks, 2026

The action interface provides four continuous movement/camera channels

and supports fire, jump, and reload inputs. For each generated video latent step, the eight aligned raw-frame vectors

are concatenated into a 32-dimensional continuous-action vector $J_{t}$ and broadcast

over spatial locations. After projection, per-layer networks produce feature

scale and shift through FiLM ()

Perez et al., 2018

$h^{\prime}_{\ell,t}=\bigl(1+\gamma_{\ell}(J_{t})\bigr)\odot h_{\ell,t}+\beta_{\ell}(J_{t}).$ (6)

Buttons remain at the raw-frame rate and enter through an additional

cross-attention residual. Each generated video latent attends to its eight

aligned action frames and earlier retained actions, with future actions masked. Temporal rotary embeddings

align these queries and keys. Continuous

scale/shift outputs and button-attention output projections are initialized

to zero. The action branches act on the video stream, while cross-modal

attention connects the resulting dynamics to audio.()

Su et al., 2024

Writing $z_{j}$ for the audiovisual latents of generated chunk $j$ , the causal

model uses a compact context

$[\text{first-frame anchor}\mid z_{k-4:k-1}\mid T_{k}\mid r].$ (7)

Here $r$ denotes the encoded character reference. At steady state, four

previous chunks are clean context and only the target

chunk $T_{k}$ is denoised. Tokens in each generated chunk attend to tokens in

that chunk and earlier chunks.

Reference-image tokens attend only to one another and are readable directly by

the target video chunk. Direct cross-modal attention excludes the reference.

The anchor and reference receive no action or text updates. As the window

advances, old history is removed and temporal positions are rebased locally.

The same layout supports zero to three history chunks during startup.

An optional cache reuses clean-context keys and values within a chunk’s

denoising steps. It is rebuilt when the window advances.

A.2

The generator’s prompt does not encode numerical health, hit counters, or internal

generation identifiers. High-frequency player controls remain in the action

tensors, while text specifies the actor behavior and consequences those

controls should realize.

Each chunk has its own text condition $c_{j}=(g,p_{j})$ . The global description

covers the environment, weapon, and character appearance. Local guidance

describes the current actor behavior, visibility, and observable interaction

outcomes. Each chunk’s combined text condition is encoded independently,

and the resulting context tokens are concatenated. The text attention mask routes both video

and audio queries to the corresponding prompt, with padding

excluded and anchor/reference queries receiving no text-attention update

in the causal model. In bidirectional adaptation,

the initial frame instead shares the first generated chunk’s prompt.

Historical chunks use their corresponding prompts, while the target

directly attends only to its current prompt. Historical context remains

available through audiovisual attention, which is causal across chunks

during autoregressive training and generation.

At inference, a deterministic text renderer converts the controller’s

structured predictions and rule-updated state into local guidance.

A.3

Generator training optimizes the audiovisual backbone and action branches

while freezing the text encoder and autoencoders.

The Interaction Agent uses InternVL3-8B  without

task-specific fine-tuning, while the rule engine and prompt compiler are

programmed. The loader aligns video, audio, player controls,

reference images, and chunk text conditions at shared temporal boundaries.()

Zhu et al., 2025

Training hyperparameters.

We train on 16 NVIDIA GB300 GPUs with a global batch size of 16 and

BF16 mixed precision. Table  lists the

generator learning rates. Consistency distillation and distribution matching

use AdamW with $\beta=(0,0.999)$ , weight decay $0.01$ , and 100 warmup steps.

The learned score model uses a learning rate of $10^{-5}$ .

Both refiner stages use 8-bit AdamW with a learning rate of $10^{-5}$ ,

$\beta=(0.9,0.999)$ , weight decay $0.01$ , and 100 warmup steps.

The domain LoRA has rank 384 and scaling parameter $\alpha=384$ .

Bidirectional adaptation uses chunk-specific text conditions and a linear-path

level $\sigma\in[0,1]$ , the noisy input and predicted clean estimate are
