$\displaystyle z_{k,\sigma}$ $\displaystyle=(1-\sigma)z_{k}+\sigma\epsilon_{k},$ (9) $\displaystyle\widehat{z}_{k}$ $\displaystyle=z_{k,\sigma}-\sigma v_{\theta}(z_{k,\sigma},\sigma\mid\mathcal{H}_{k},u_{k},c_{k}).$

Here $v_{\theta}$ predicts flow velocity, and $\mathcal{H}_{k}$ , $u_{k}$ , and $c_{k}$

follow Equation . Superscripts $v$ and $a$

denote video and audio. The target-chunk reconstruction objective is

5

$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{AR}}=\mathbb{E}\!\left[w(\sigma)\left(\operatorname{MSE}(\widehat{z}_{k}^{v},z_{k}^{v})+\lambda_{a}\operatorname{MSE}(\widehat{z}_{k}^{a},z_{k}^{a})\right)\right],$ (10)

where $w(\sigma)=\exp[-2(\sigma-0.5)^{2}]$ weights the noise level and

$\lambda_{a}=0.16$ weights the audio loss. Squared errors are averaged over

target tokens only.

This stage uses ground-truth history.

Bidirectional and autoregressive adaptation share the chunk-wise prompt

routing used at inference, but only autoregressive adaptation enforces

temporal causality through audiovisual attention.

Consistency distillation and startup coverage.

For few-step generation, the implementation follows the teacher-forcing

consistency initialization in Causal-rCM .

This recipe builds on Consistency Models ,

sCM , and rCM .

A frozen autoregressive teacher advances a noisy sample between nearby noise

levels. At the advanced point, the current student produces a clean estimate

without gradients, which serves as the consistency target for its prediction

at the starting point. Video and audio both contribute to this loss.

Checkpoint EMA is maintained separately.()

Zheng et al., 2026a

()

Song et al., 2023

()

Lu & Song, 2025

()

Zheng et al., 2026b

Startup and continued generation use the same sliding-window context layout. The

training recipe alternates an update with four history chunks and an update

with zero, one, two, or three history chunks.

The final Arena recipe further distills text classifier-free

guidance  into the student. The teacher combines conditional and text-unconditional

predictions while retaining player actions and visual context. The student

uses a single conditional forward pass per denoising step.()

Ho & Salimans, 2022

Self-forcing distribution matching.

After consistency distillation, we apply self-forcing distribution

matching  as the second stage of the

Causal-rCM  recipe. The objective follows

DMD  and DMD2 , with bidirectional-teacher

supervision of an autoregressive student as in CausVid .

One student starts from

the initial frame, generates four startup chunks, and continues for five

additional chunks using the same reference, chunk-wise prompt routing, and sliding

context. No ground-truth history is inserted into this rollout. Both the

startup chunks and the later chunks receive distribution-matching supervision.()

Huang et al., 2025

()

Zheng et al., 2026a

()

Yin et al., 2024b

()

Yin et al., 2024a

()

Yin et al., 2025

A frozen bidirectional score model and a learned score model for student

samples evaluate the same perturbed rollout with aligned controls and

semantic conditions. These score models receive no reference-image tokens,

so their text conditions describe character appearance explicitly.

The final Arena recipe applies text guidance to the

frozen score model, while the learned score model and student remain

conditional. Their normalized difference in denoised predictions

defines a stop-gradient target. The generator then replays the recorded final

denoising step of each chunk to optimize a masked video–audio regression

loss against that target. Rollout generation runs without gradients, avoiding storage of its full

computation graph.

Video refiner training.

We construct temporally aligned training pairs from the same arena clip.

Its original VAE encoding serves as the target. To construct the degraded

input, we spatially downsample the RGB frames, encode them, and apply a

frozen LTX-2.3 $2\times$ spatial upscaler v1.1

to restore the target spatial size.

We train a domain LoRA  on the refiner with truncated

flow matching  between

the original target and a noise-perturbed upsampled latent.

The refiner is first trained bidirectionally. Causal adaptation starts from

this checkpoint, conditions on the first frame, character reference, and

up to four clean history chunks, and applies loss only to the current

chunk. Training uses ground-truth history, while deployment uses previously

refined outputs. Both stages optimize only the domain LoRA, keeping the upsampler and

backbone frozen. The official LTX-2.3 distilled LoRA

v1.1  is disabled for this training loss and enabled

for few-step refinement at inference.()

Lightricks, 2026

()

Hu et al., 2022

()

Lipman et al., 2023

()

Lightricks, 2026

Inference settings.

The distilled Arena generator uses four denoising steps with noise levels

$(1,0.9375,0.8333,0.625,0)$ .

Refinement uses two denoising steps with noise levels

$(0.725,0.421875,0)$ , a classifier-free guidance scale of 1, and no

spatiotemporal guidance.

A.4

Prediction and state commitment.

At a chunk boundary, the controller retains the corrected state and uses

predicted events to compute provisional outcomes and local guidance.

Generation does not commit those predictions to the persistent ledger.

After decoding, verification produces the feedback used to obtain the next

retained state in Equation . The implementation

recomputes this state from the saved pre-generation state and observed

events, preventing predicted and verified damage from being counted twice.

The first chunk uses the initial frame and configured state without a

preceding verification step.

The retained gameplay state is stored independently of the generator’s

sliding visual context. When earlier frames leave that context, their

recorded interaction consequences remain available to subsequent rule

updates and enter generation through the current guidance.

2

Observation selection and shot prediction.

The online Arena implementation uses decoded RGB frames directly, without

an observation refiner. Within each chunk, it selects the first frame of

each uninterrupted firing interval and every fourth frame thereafter

(5 Hz at 20 FPS). Before generation, the latest available frame is the

preceding chunk’s last frame, or the initial image at startup. For each

selected firing time, a calibrated control-to-pixel mapping estimates the

image displacement from the intervening controls. We translate the latest

frame accordingly, take a $320\times 320$ crop centered on the screen, and

overlay a hollow green aiming ring. The Interaction Agent receives this

projected crop and a separate enemy appearance reference, and predicts

whether the enemy’s body overlaps the marked aiming region.

Visual verification.

After generation, we decode the corresponding actual firing frames,

the chunk’s final frame, and the frame three positions before it.

Together with the pre-generation frame, these form the sampled observations

$\mathcal{I}_{k-1}$ . A firing-frame audit receives the selected firing

frames in temporal order, with the same ring overlay, alongside the

pre-generation and two late frames. Unlike prediction, verification uses

full frames rather than center crops. The ring radius is 5% of the shorter

image dimension and leaves its interior unobstructed.

A separate state query places the final frame first and uses the

pre-generation and earlier late frame only as temporal context. It

classifies the enemy as alive, dead, or not visible in the final frame.

Both queries receive an appearance reference for identity only. Full

frames are padded to a $2{:}1$ canvas and the reference to a square,

without cropping their contents. Aim markers appear only in the VLM

inputs. The requested outcome is the condition being checked, not visual

evidence, and verification uses separate calls from prediction.

The rule engine specifies intended transitions, while committed visual

outcomes ground the state used for subsequent interaction. When an observed

outcome contradicts a prediction, the controller revises the affected state

and derives subsequent guidance from that revision. Numerical attributes

remain rule-maintained rather than directly estimated from images, and

occlusion alone is not treated as death.

Action constraints and opponent behavior.

Ammunition gates the executed fire commands and is consumed when a shot is

permitted, independently of whether it hits. Before an enemy can attack,

the Interaction Agent checks visual preconditions, including whether the

enemy is visible and facing the player. When these conditions hold, attacks

are sampled at a configured rate, and each attack hits with a preset

probability. Successful hits subtract a fixed

per-shot damage from player health. Reaching zero health disables player

controls and adds the corresponding terminal outcome to guidance.

For opponent behavior, the agent assesses movement feasibility from the

current scene. The behavior policy combines this assessment with retained

state and the configured strategy to select a movement description.

Attack rules and strategy-transition conditions can be edited in the rule layer.

Numerical state remains in the controller, while the generator receives

observable behavior and outcome descriptions. World-side events thus

combine visual assessment of the current scene with executable game rules

that update player state and constrain subsequent controls.

A.5

Reciprocal interaction concerns the causal effects of player actions on the

world and of world events on the player. It does not require every game

mechanic to be learned. Executable rules make damage, ammunition, and

termination conditions explicit and configurable, while scene-conditioned

behavior reasoning determines how actors act under those conditions.

Their combination connects world-side decisions to persistent consequences

for the player during continuous interaction.

Realizing these interactions also requires a generator that can express

their consequences. Explicit state specifies intended outcomes, and text

guidance communicates them, but the generator must learn to realize them

as visible behavior. We therefore develop interaction data, train the

conditioned generator, and connect event reasoning, executable updates,

and visual feedback in an online loop. The contribution is the reciprocal

generative gameplay enabled by this coordinated system, including its data

and training procedure. Reconciliation supplies feedback within this loop

by grounding subsequent decisions in committed observations.

Appendix B

All routes share the capture and alignment pipeline below. Counts refer to

accepted source recordings, excluding candidate jobs, prompt variants, and

overlapping training windows.

B.1

Execution and recording.

We specify the map, assets, initial conditions, actor policies, and player

controls before capture. The engine records gameplay demos together with

applied inputs, frame timing, state, and interaction events.

Requested controls and realized events are retained separately, with damage

labels taken from realized engine events. Offline replay renders the recorded

trajectory and game audio under a fixed client configuration. Presentation

settings, including HUD, crosshair, and effect suppression, are versioned

per route.

Renderer telemetry records camera position and orientation, transforms,

and projection parameters, synchronized with simulation ticks.

Time and action interface.

The capture pipelines use a 64 Hz simulation/control clock. Warm-up is

removed using the recorded capture boundary before aligning model time

zero. The model-facing stream uses 20 video frames per second, with four

continuous movement/camera channels and fire, jump, and reload inputs

under the shared action contract. Camera and movement values follow the recorded

applied controls. Button resampling preserves short active runs that might

otherwise disappear between sampled frames. In the long Interaction release,

the action profiles explicitly remove 64 warm-up ticks and align row zero

with the first video frame.

Native media differ across routes. Basic Dynamics stores 320 frames at 64 fps

and $1280\times 720$ resolution. Short and long Interaction sequences store 81 and 1,201

frames at 20 fps and $1280\times 720$ . Arena stores 1,201 frames at 20 fps

and $1664\times 960$ . Representative files in all four subsets contain

48 kHz stereo game audio. The model loader resizes video and resamples audio

according to the training configuration. The generator training configuration uses

$832\times 480$ video and 16 kHz stereo audio.

The 81-frame layout comprises an initial frame and five 16-frame chunks.

The 1,201-frame layout similarly supports 75 chunks.

Semantic labels and packaging.

We use Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite

() to separately annotate map style, weapon

appearance and operation, and player and enemy appearance.

Interaction releases add chunk-local motion,

visibility, damage, and death descriptions derived from telemetry.

Prompts distinguish no damage, nonlethal damage, a new death event, and an

already-dead actor. Off-screen intervals are described using visibility

records rather than invented visible motion. Player controls remain in

action tensors. Enemy movement and jumping belong to semantic conditions.

Where reference images are used, the manifest binds them to the appropriate

actor and time interval.()

Google DeepMind, 2026

gemini-3.1-flash-lite

B.2

Basic Dynamics contains 50,140 five-second clips across 28 maps and nine

weapons, including 39,539 without an enemy and 10,601 with a non-damaging

enemy distractor.

Movement, camera changes, firing, and local collision responses provide

the principal supervision. The supplement emphasizes pure idle,

idle-to-action, action-to-idle, interrupted action, smooth routes, and

wall impacts.

Route validation and camera filtering remove unsuitable trajectories.

B.3

Short interactions.

The short Interaction subset contains 42,000 recordings across five maps,

nine weapons, and 42 model–skin–color appearances.

Capture varies distance, opponent movement,

direction changes, stopping, jumping, visibility transitions, and firing.

Firing times are sampled deterministically from the scenario seed.

Weapon-specific schedules include isolated shots, repeated taps, and

bounded bursts. Opponent motion and jump programs are specified separately

from player controls.

Outcome labels follow the realized engine events, yielding 6,535 no-fire examples,

16,666 misses, 14,496 nonlethal-hit examples, and 4,303 kills.

The visibility allocation is 37,800 continuously visible examples,

2,100 exit-and-hold examples, and 2,100 exit-and-return examples.

The annotation identifies visibility transitions within each

0.8-second chunk. The underlying timestamped records also support

constructing annotations over windows of arbitrary duration within each

recording. This release describes view-frustum transitions, not

geometric occlusion behind arbitrary cover. Crosshair and casing effects are

disabled in its capture configuration.

Each recording has one

81-frame bidirectional view and one five-chunk autoregressive view.

Long interaction sequences.

Interaction-Long contains 1,791 accepted recordings with blood-hit effects

disabled during capture.

Each episode contains four actor slots, arranged either as distinct actors

or a controlled-return sequence, and zero, one, or two scheduled kills.

The accepted collection contains 900 controlled-return and 891

distinct-actor episodes.

The maps are Bromine, Courtfun, Geoplanetary, and Stormkeep. The weapons

are MachineGun, Rifle, and Shotgun. Scripted trajectories undergo collision

and ground-support checks. Camera schedules use frozen calibration traces,

with scan and aiming phases, rather than live feedback that tracks the

current enemy.

The reference bank contains 42 appearances with five clean views each.

Bindings expose the current actor reference, retain the outgoing reference

through its despawn transition, and mask intervals without an actor.

Each source episode provides fifteen 81-frame bidirectional windows.

The autoregressive view keeps each full sequence and its 75 chunk prompts.

B.4

Arena contains 1,800 one-minute

bot-versus-bot recordings in a compact arena, using MachineGun combat and

a fixed opponent appearance. Independent bot controls produce ongoing

movement and exchanges instead of prescribing a short outcome sequence.

The capture configuration bounds locomotion and camera motion and removes

crosshair and pickup clutter.

The release constructs the action stream from authoritative gameplay

records. Chunk descriptions summarize opponent motion, attacks, visibility,

nonlethal damage, kills, and player death from telemetry aligned with the

rendered camera. Fully off-screen chunks suppress visible-motion claims.

The manifest provides 75 prompts per episode and a fixed opponent

reference binding.

Arena trains RIGen-Arena.

B.5

Capture validation checks route geometry, camera behavior, and consistency

between scheduled interactions and recorded events. Manifest validation

checks media metadata, finite and aligned controls, complete prompt

schedules, and reference bindings.

Test set construction.

We reserve 100 Interaction recordings for quantitative evaluation. Their

maps and enemy appearances are excluded from all task-specific training

subsets, including Basic Dynamics, Interaction, Interaction-Long, and Arena,

and are not used in subsequent adaptation or distillation.

Appendix C

C.1

The 100 Xonotic scenarios comprise 50 survival targets and 50 death targets.

All RIGen variants in Table  use the same

Interaction-trained generator after sliding-window autoregressive training

on Interaction-Long, without Arena post-training or distillation.

SCOPE and LingBot-World 2.0 receive the prescribed

combat outcomes directly as text guidance.

Enemy motion is supplied by source annotations in place of online behavior

selection. The interaction agent handles hit, injury, and death reasoning

and correction of predicted state.

All variants use their own generated video history. Online interaction

variants compute guidance from that history, while RIGen (w/ Reference guidance)

uses frozen reference guidance.

Fixing enemy motion gives methods common behavior requirements and focuses

the comparison on motion adherence and combat-outcome realization, separating

behavior selection from its execution in generated video.

We combine controlled experiments, state-dependent branching examples, and

continuous closed-loop gameplay. Controlled experiments compare the

realization of specified interaction outcomes. Branch comparisons show how

state and strategy affect generated behavior, while RIGen-Arena demonstrates

the mutual effects of player actions and world events during continued play.

Together, these complementary evaluations examine outcome realization,

state dependence, and reciprocal interaction in the implemented system.

The external comparisons evaluate complete systems, including their data

and training recipes. Learning to realize interaction outcomes is part of

the proposed method. Specifying an outcome in text alone does not ensure

that a generator can express it. We therefore assess the resulting system

capability against external models and use fixed-generator ablations to

examine the online interaction mechanisms separately.

Evaluating generated trajectories.

Once a generated trajectory diverges from its source recording, source-engine

hit and visibility labels cannot automatically serve as ground truth for the

generated scene. Rule execution can be checked against configured transitions,

while judging whether a generated attack hits requires independent evidence

from the generated video itself. Autonomous behavior also admits multiple

valid choices under the same state, calling for task-based criteria that

accommodate alternative behaviors. Our benchmark uses prescribed motion and outcome

targets with video-based assessment. Event-level visual correctness and

autonomous decision quality require annotations or task criteria for the

generated trajectories, rather than direct reuse of source-engine labels.

C.2

Qwen3.8-27B  judges complete generated videos offline.()

Qwen Team, 2026

Enemy Behavior.

Enemy Behavior averages

satisfaction of directional motion checks within predefined time windows,

first within each video and then equally across the 100 scenarios. A check

receives credit only when the judge reports it as satisfied and cites visual

evidence within its time window. Lateral and depth motion are checked

separately, relative to the environment rather than camera-induced image

motion. For death-target cases, the prescribed lethal chunk and subsequent motion

requirements are excluded for all methods using the same fixed windows.

Final-state Agreement.

Final-state Agreement compares the enemy’s visible state in the final

0.8 seconds with its preassigned survival or death target. The target is

withheld from the judge. Unreadable outcomes and failures remain in the

denominator and receive no agreement credit.

Overall FSA uses all 100 cases. Survival-target and death-target success

rates each use the corresponding 50 cases, so overall FSA is their mean.

FSA tests whether the prescribed final combat outcome is actually realized.

Locally plausible motion and high visual quality do not establish that an

opponent survives or dies as required, making outcome agreement a distinct

interaction criterion. EB measures motion adherence, while qualitative

sequences illustrate intermediate combat responses.

Visual quality and dynamics.

The five visual metrics use the official dimension-specific VBench

pipelines on complete generated videos. Each reported score is the mean

per-video normalized score multiplied by 100. Dynamic Degree is the

percentage of videos meeting the official motion threshold.

The system also generates audio jointly with video.

C.3

The ablation rows in Table  compare inference-time variants using the

same video checkpoint, initial conditions, player inputs, and sampling settings.

1.

Predict interaction consequences before

generation, apply executable rules, and guide the current chunk.

Observe the generated chunk and reconcile predicted state with its

visible outcome before the next decision.Full RIGen.

2.

Retain player inputs, scene,

appearance, and source motion annotations. Remove hit, injury, and death

guidance and the online interaction VLM.Motion guidance only.

3.

The VLM maintains persistent textual

state and selects the next chunk’s combat outcome. Rules are supplied

as text, without an executable rule engine or an independent

verification-and-correction module. This variant compares agent-managed

state updates with executable rules and separate visual reconciliation.Semantic prompting.

4.

Generate first, observe events,

apply rules, and pass consequence guidance to the following chunk.

There is no pre-generation prediction of current-chunk consequences.Post-hoc event updates.

5.

Retain pre-generation prediction

and executable state updates, but do not correct the planned state from

post-generation verification. The next reasoning step still sees the

newly generated frames.Without reconciliation.

6.

Freeze reference event

guidance in advance and remove online VLM calls. Death instructions are

derived from source hit annotations combined with configured health and

damage rules. They specify a counterfactual task answer, not ground-truth

death in the source recording. The guidance is not revised from generated

observations, but autoregressive video context uses this variant’s own

outputs.RIGen (w/ Reference guidance).

C.4

Generation throughput at $832\times 480$ .

Parameters count the generation backbone.

Both RIGen settings include refinement.Table 2:

Runtime is measured on a single NVIDIA GB300 GPU.

In Table , Replay disables online VLM calls and

reuses the same guidance, while Online runs the interaction loop. Both

include refinement and remain below the target playback rate of 20 FPS.

一句话：让生成式游戏不只是「玩家输入→模型输出」，而是模型也能主动推动玩法。

要点：

  • 指出当前生成式游戏只有单向动作跟随，缺乏真正的互动
  • 提出双向互动框架：环境/角色也会主动发起行为
  • 评估玩家体验层面的差异

为什么值得看：这是「AI 原生玩法」的核心设计问题：单向映射只是高级动画，双向互动才谈得上玩法。

中文摘要：现有生成式游戏大多把模型当成「动作翻译器」：玩家按键，模型输出画面或后果，本质仍是单向映射。RIGen 提出应该走向双向互动——不仅响应用户动作，环境与角色也能主动发起事件、施加压力，形成真正的博弈与叙事张力。论文给出了这套框架的实现与评估方法，是讨论「AI 原生玩法」时值得参考的一块拼图。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·生成式玩法（English）

RIGen: Beyond Action Following with Reciprocal Interaction in Generative Gameplay

Abstract

Generative gameplay requires more than immediate responses to player actions.

Actions should have persistent consequences, while the generated world should

act according to its own state and rules, shaping the player’s situation and

subsequent choices. Video generation captures local dynamics, but limited

history, partially observed game state, and the need for contextual behavior

decisions make such interactions difficult to sustain through audiovisual

prediction alone. We introduce RIGen (Reciprocally Interactive Generation), a framework for

reciprocal interaction in generative gameplay. RIGen combines persistent state and configurable

rules, contextual interaction reasoning, and action-conditioned audiovisual

generation. Together, these components make interaction consequences and

actor behavior jointly determine generated content while maintaining

consistency between game state and visible outcomes. We construct a Xonotic

gameplay dataset to train an audiovisual generator for learning dynamics and

interactions. Further post-training enables RIGen-Arena, an interactive generative

first-person shooter (FPS) prototype.

Experiments demonstrate more reliable combat outcomes and reciprocal

interaction between the player and the generated world.

Project page: .

https://murphylmf.github.io/RIGen/

Players affect the generated world, whose rules, persistent state, and

characters in turn shape gameplay.

(a) Attacks have state-dependent consequences.

(b) Enemy actions, resource constraints, and respawn rules shape the

player’s survival and continued play.

(c) Opponents adapt their behavior to their health and current combat

conditions.Figure 1: Reciprocal interaction in RIGen.

1

Generative models offer a route to game experiences whose environments,

characters, and events can be created during

play .

Such experiences could be personalized to each player’s preferences and

choices. Realizing this potential requires reciprocal interaction: players

should be able to change the world through their actions, while the world

follows its own operating logic. Its characters act according to their

situation and goals, and its rules and events shape the player’s

circumstances and subsequent choices.(; )

Bruce et al., 2024

Yu et al., 2025

Recent video-based world models have made progress toward this goal.

DIAMOND  and GameNGen

demonstrate playable game simulation.

LingBot-World  and SCOPE

provide responsive camera and movement control, while

LingBot-World 2.0  and

Incantation  incorporate semantic guidance for

character behavior and interaction events.

Table  compares these systems across control,

gameplay, and output capabilities. It highlights the remaining gap in combining

reciprocal state changes with scene- and state-conditioned actor planning.()

Alonso et al., 2024

()

Valevski et al., 2025

()

Robbyant Team et al., 2026

()

Tong et al., 2026

()

Gao et al., 2026

()

Zhu et al., 2026b

The prevailing approach builds on video models that capture rich local dynamics

and generate continuous audiovisual feedback conditioned on player controls,

making them a natural foundation for interactive games. However, sustaining reciprocal interaction

through audiovisual prediction alone faces three challenges.

Responding to player actions

does not by itself determine how the world should act upon the player.

Actors must choose behavior based on current conditions and their own goals,

and the consequences must update player state and constrain subsequent

interactions.

Events beyond the model’s context window can

still have consequences for current interactions .

Gameplay variables such as health and

ammunition may not be recoverable from the visible scene, yet determine

whether an action can be executed and what outcome it should have.(1) Coordinating reciprocal interaction.(2) Limited history.()

Xiao et al., 2025

(3) Partially observed state.

In sustained combat, for example, accumulated damage must determine whether

the next hit is lethal, even when earlier attacks fall outside the video

context. The opponent’s remaining health and goals should shape whether

it attacks or retreats. Damage dealt by the opponent must likewise affect

the player’s health and ability to continue fighting.

To address these challenges, we introduce RIGen, a framework for reciprocal

interaction in generative gameplay (Figure ).

The layer maintains persistent gameplay variables and

configurable rules, including strategic goals and constraints.

The layer interprets the scene and player actions

to infer events and plan actor behavior under these conditions.

The layer realizes the resulting guidance

alongside player controls. Together, these layers let player actions change

the state that governs subsequent interactions. The world also acts

according to its own rules and goals, affecting the player’s state and

available actions.state and rulesinteraction reasoningaudiovisual generation

We instantiate RIGen in first-person shooter (FPS) environments.

Our experiments assess combat outcomes, while qualitative demonstrations

and RIGen-Arena illustrate state-dependent interactions and autonomous

enemy behavior that affects the player (Figure ).

1

Our contributions are threefold.

We integrate

interaction prediction, executable state updates, and audiovisual generation

into a closed loop in which player actions change world state and world

behavior affects the player.

Model comparisons and controlled ablations demonstrate more reliable

realization of state-dependent interaction outcomes.

We construct a dataset covering

basic dynamics, controlled interactions, and sustained combat, pairing

audiovisual observations with player controls and interaction annotations,

with a reproducible data creation pipeline.

We build RIGen-Arena, integrating

few-step audiovisual generation with closed-loop interaction to support

continued play under persistent game rules.(1) A system for reciprocal generative gameplay.(2) FPS gameplay dataset.(3) Interactive gameplay prototype.

2

Video generation and interactive worlds.

Video and audiovisual foundation models provide appearance and dynamics

priors .

Controllable visual simulation

has developed into generative game environments

and interactive content creation .

Recent work broadens scene coverage and streaming control ,

adds multiplayer or audiovisual interaction ,

and improves long-horizon consistency through memory .

We focus on persistent gameplay state and rule-governed interaction consequences.(; ; ; ; ; )

Explicit state and generative rendering.

Prior systems combine structured state or game logic with generative

rendering ,

while planning-based video methods organize content before

synthesis .

Geometric rendering interfaces provide explicit spatial

control .

Programmable World Model  compiles state-augmented 3D

bounding boxes into rendering controls, while Code World Model

compiles executable state into proxy videos. RIGen instead connects gameplay

state to generation through player actions and local interaction guidance,

without constructing explicit spatial trajectories.

The PixVerse Game Engine technical blog

describes a separation of game mechanics, agent orchestration, and generative

expression. We provide a concrete implementation for continuous player

control, connecting interaction prediction, executable state updates, and

video feedback, with corresponding generator training and controlled ablations.(; ; ; ; ; )

3.1

RIGen couples three layers to align player actions, persistent state,

and generated audiovisual outcomes (Figure ).

The maintains persistent state, applies transition

rules, and specifies strategic constraints (Section ).

The reasons about action consequences and plans actor

behavior (Section ). The

models local dynamics under player controls and generation guidance

(Section ).State and Rule Engine

3.2

Interaction Agent

3.3

Audiovisual Generator

3.4

At each chunk boundary, the agent uses recent video, player controls, and

persistent state to predict interaction events and plan actor behavior.

The rule engine evaluates these events, and the updated state and planned

behavior jointly guide the next audiovisual chunk. After generation, the

agent checks which events occurred, and the rule engine uses this evidence

to determine the state for the next decision.

3.2

We represent gameplay as an event-driven state machine with numerical variables,

following standard state-based game AI .

The engine maintains player and enemy health and life/death state, player

ammunition, and opponent strategy modes, together with configurable rule

parameters such as the player’s per-shot damage and transition conditions.

Writing $s$ for the complete game state and $e$ for an interaction event

record, the engine maps $s$ to its successor $s^{\prime}$ through()

Millington & Funge, 2009

$s^{\prime}=\operatorname{Rules}(s,e).$ (1)

For example, firing requires a living player with available ammunition and

consumes a round regardless of whether the shot hits. A hit reduces the

target’s health by the configured damage, for either the player or an enemy.

Reaching zero health triggers death. If an opponent survives with low health,

a configured rule can switch its strategy from engagement to retreat.

The updated strategy guides the Interaction Agent’s next decision, such as

choosing a retreat direction suited to the current scene

(Section ).

3.3

3.3

Before generating chunk $o_{k}$ , we perform through

verification and state correction. The agent verifies $o_{k-1}$ using sampled

verification frames $\mathcal{I}_{k-1}$ , player controls $u_{k-1}$ , and local

guidance $p_{k-1}$ .

The rule engine then corrects the planned state $s_{k}^{\mathrm{plan}}$

using feedback $f_{k-1}$ :reconciliation

$\displaystyle f_{k-1}$ $\displaystyle=\operatorname{Verify}(\mathcal{I}_{k-1},u_{k-1},p_{k-1}),$ (2) $\displaystyle s_{k}$ $\displaystyle=\operatorname{Correct}(s_{k}^{\mathrm{plan}},f_{k-1}).$

Using this updated state, feedback, and current player controls $u_{k}$ ,

the agent proposes events $e_{k}$ and behavior $b_{k}$ :

$(e_{k},b_{k})=\operatorname{Agent}(o_{k-1},s_{k},u_{k},f_{k-1}).$ (3)

The rule engine computes a provisional successor $s_{k+1}^{\mathrm{plan}}$

and local interaction guidance $p_{k}$ without overwriting $s_{k}$ :

$\displaystyle s_{k+1}^{\mathrm{plan}}$ $\displaystyle=\operatorname{Rules}(s_{k},e_{k}),$ (4) $\displaystyle p_{k}$ $\displaystyle=\operatorname{Prompt}(s_{k+1}^{\mathrm{plan}},e_{k},b_{k}).$

The generator realizes this guidance as the next audiovisual chunk $o_{k}$

(Section ).

At the next boundary, verification of $o_{k}$ reconciles

$s_{k+1}^{\mathrm{plan}}$ with committed visual outcomes to obtain $s_{k+1}$ .

These observations take precedence over conflicting predictions, and the

corrected state conditions the next decision.

Implementation scope and verification details are given in

the appendix.

3.4

3.4

The global prompt $g$ describes the scene and character identity shared across

chunks. Local guidance $p_{k}$ specifies the current chunk’s actor behavior and

observable interaction outcomes, derived from the agent’s proposals and

rule-based state updates (Section ). Together, they form

text condition $c_{k}$ . Given audiovisual context $\mathcal{H}_{k}$ and player

controls $u_{k}$ , the generator produces the next chunk:

3.3

$c_{k}=(g,p_{k}),\qquad o_{k}\sim G_{\theta}(\mathcal{H}_{k},u_{k},c_{k}).$ (5)

The context $\mathcal{H}_{k}$ contains a first-frame anchor, a character reference,

and recent generated chunks with their controls and text conditions.

The generator denoises the target under these conditions, and the resulting

$o_{k}$ provides observations for the next interaction decision.

We instantiate $G_{\theta}$ with the LTX-2.3

audiovisual backbone, using coupled video and audio transformer streams

(Figure ). Continuous movement/camera controls

modulate video features through FiLM , while button inputs enter through causal

cross-attention. Audiovisual attention connects the two streams and is

causal across chunks and joint within each chunk. The anchor and reference

provide visual context without text or action updates.(; )

()

Perez et al., 2018

Chunk-wise prompt routing.

In both video and audio streams, each chunk attends only to the global prompt

and its corresponding local guidance through text cross-attention

(Figure ).

Historical chunks retain their original text conditions, while the target

receives the current guidance. The same routing is used in bidirectional and

causal training.

Training and continued generation.

Following the bidirectional-to-autoregressive adaptation used in

CausVid , we first train the model bidirectionally to follow player controls and

chunk-level guidance, then adapt it to autoregressive next-chunk prediction

conditioned on clean audiovisual history. Sliding-window training retains

a window of recent chunks alongside the first-frame anchor and character

reference, keeping $\mathcal{H}_{k}$ bounded during continued generation.

Training objectives and implementation details are provided in the appendix.()

5

RIGen-Arena is an interactive one-on-one FPS prototype in which the player fights an opponent,

with either side respawning after defeat to continue the match

(Figure ).

We initialize post-training for RIGen-Arena from the bidirectional model trained on

the Interaction subset. We first fine-tune it bidirectionally on the Arena

subset to adapt to sustained combat. We then train the adapted model to

generate chunks autoregressively using a sliding window of recent history

together with the first-frame anchor and character reference

(Section ).

3.4

We adopt the two-stage distillation recipe of

Causal-rCM . Teacher-forcing consistency distillation

first produces a few-step generator. Distribution matching then trains

this generator on its own autoregressive rollouts.()

Zheng et al., 2026a

We additionally train a video refiner to recover high-frequency details in

dynamic gameplay. Training pairs spatially degraded latents with the

original encodings of the same arena clips. We first train the refiner

bidirectionally with paired flow matching , then fine-tune it for causal,

chunk-wise refinement with a bounded history window.

At inference, it refines each generated chunk without access to future

chunks. We integrate the generator and refiner with the state and rule

engine and interaction agent to form RIGen-Arena.

Training objectives, sampling schedules, and implementation details are

provided in the appendix.()

Metrics.

Qwen3.8-27B  evaluates two interaction metrics offline.

(EB) measures adherence to prescribed enemy motion

within specified time windows. (FSA) measures

agreement between the final visible enemy state and its survival/death target.

FSA-S is the percentage of the 50 survival-target cases in which the enemy

is visibly alive at the end. FSA-D is the percentage of the 50 death-target

cases in which the enemy is visibly dead at the end. Overall FSA averages

these two rates. Incorrect or unjudgeable outcomes count as failures, so FSA

can fall below 50%. We also report Motion Smoothness (MS), Aesthetic Quality (AQ),

Subject Consistency (SC), Background Consistency (BC), and Dynamic Degree (DD),

following VBench . Scores are on a 0–100 scale.

Higher is better except for DD, which measures motion prevalence rather than quality.()

Results.

Table  shows that RIGen achieves 81% FSA,

compared with 29% for LingBot-World 2.0 and 4% for SCOPE, and higher EB

than both baselines. With the generator fixed, FSA falls to 39% with

motion-only guidance, 35% with semantic prompting, 64% with post-hoc

updates, and 76% without reconciliation. These results support predicting

interaction consequences before generation, executing state updates, and

reconciling them with visual feedback. Visual metrics remain nearly unchanged

across ablations. Lower AQ than LingBot-World 2.0 may reflect our smaller

training dataset. The appendix provides further details and analysis.

6.2

Combat responses.

Figure  compares visible combat responses

from the same initial image and attack requests. In this example, RIGen produces a hit reaction followed by a fall and a sustained downed state,

while the baseline opponents remain active under repeated fire despite

receiving text guidance specifying the correct combat outcomes.

State-dependent interactions.

Figure  varies initial enemy health, player

ammunition, and state-dependent opponent strategy from a shared starting

scene under the same player input requests.

The low-health opponent falls, depleted ammunition suppresses the third

shot, and an injured opponent switches from hold to retreat, moving left

and crouching at cover. These examples illustrate how explicit state and

strategy affect visible gameplay.

7

We presented RIGen, a framework for reciprocal interaction in generative

gameplay. Player actions change persistent world state, while world rules

and actor decisions affect the player. Quantitative comparisons demonstrate

more reliable combat outcomes, and qualitative results illustrate

state-dependent interactions and autonomous enemy behavior.

Limitations and future work.

RIGen is not yet real-time, supports only single-opponent FPS gameplay,

and relies on VLM perception and reasoning for interaction decisions and

state verification. Future work will optimize generation and agent inference,

extend to multiple opponents and broader action spaces and game genres,

and improve visual grounding and reasoning reliability.

Appendix A

A.1

We build on the LTX  audiovisual architecture, using

the LTX-2.3 22B dev backbone . Separate video and audio

autoencoders produce latent sequences processed by coupled transformer

streams. Each stream uses self-attention and text cross-attention, with

cross-modal attention connecting video and audio. At 20 video frames per

second, each generated chunk contains two video latent steps, corresponding

to 16 new frames, and 20 audio latent steps, corresponding to 0.8 seconds.

Generation is causal between chunks. Tokens within a chunk are denoised

jointly.()

()

Lightricks, 2026

The action interface provides four continuous movement/camera channels

and supports fire, jump, and reload inputs. For each generated video latent step, the eight aligned raw-frame vectors

are concatenated into a 32-dimensional continuous-action vector $J_{t}$ and broadcast

over spatial locations. After projection, per-layer networks produce feature

scale and shift through FiLM ()

Perez et al., 2018

$h^{\prime}_{\ell,t}=\bigl(1+\gamma_{\ell}(J_{t})\bigr)\odot h_{\ell,t}+\beta_{\ell}(J_{t}).$ (6)

Buttons remain at the raw-frame rate and enter through an additional

cross-attention residual. Each generated video latent attends to its eight

aligned action frames and earlier retained actions, with future actions masked. Temporal rotary embeddings

align these queries and keys. Continuous

scale/shift outputs and button-attention output projections are initialized

to zero. The action branches act on the video stream, while cross-modal

attention connects the resulting dynamics to audio.()

Su et al., 2024

Writing $z_{j}$ for the audiovisual latents of generated chunk $j$ , the causal

model uses a compact context

$[\text{first-frame anchor}\mid z_{k-4:k-1}\mid T_{k}\mid r].$ (7)

Here $r$ denotes the encoded character reference. At steady state, four

previous chunks are clean context and only the target

chunk $T_{k}$ is denoised. Tokens in each generated chunk attend to tokens in

that chunk and earlier chunks.

Reference-image tokens attend only to one another and are readable directly by

the target video chunk. Direct cross-modal attention excludes the reference.

The anchor and reference receive no action or text updates. As the window

advances, old history is removed and temporal positions are rebased locally.

The same layout supports zero to three history chunks during startup.

An optional cache reuses clean-context keys and values within a chunk’s

denoising steps. It is rebuilt when the window advances.

A.2

The generator’s prompt does not encode numerical health, hit counters, or internal

generation identifiers. High-frequency player controls remain in the action

tensors, while text specifies the actor behavior and consequences those

controls should realize.

Each chunk has its own text condition $c_{j}=(g,p_{j})$ . The global description

covers the environment, weapon, and character appearance. Local guidance

describes the current actor behavior, visibility, and observable interaction

outcomes. Each chunk’s combined text condition is encoded independently,

and the resulting context tokens are concatenated. The text attention mask routes both video

and audio queries to the corresponding prompt, with padding

excluded and anchor/reference queries receiving no text-attention update

in the causal model. In bidirectional adaptation,

the initial frame instead shares the first generated chunk’s prompt.

Historical chunks use their corresponding prompts, while the target

directly attends only to its current prompt. Historical context remains

available through audiovisual attention, which is causal across chunks

during autoregressive training and generation.

At inference, a deterministic text renderer converts the controller’s

structured predictions and rule-updated state into local guidance.

A.3

Generator training optimizes the audiovisual backbone and action branches

while freezing the text encoder and autoencoders.

The Interaction Agent uses InternVL3-8B  without

task-specific fine-tuning, while the rule engine and prompt compiler are

programmed. The loader aligns video, audio, player controls,

reference images, and chunk text conditions at shared temporal boundaries.()

Zhu et al., 2025

Training hyperparameters.

We train on 16 NVIDIA GB300 GPUs with a global batch size of 16 and

BF16 mixed precision. Table  lists the

generator learning rates. Consistency distillation and distribution matching

use AdamW with $\beta=(0,0.999)$ , weight decay $0.01$ , and 100 warmup steps.

The learned score model uses a learning rate of $10^{-5}$ .

Both refiner stages use 8-bit AdamW with a learning rate of $10^{-5}$ ,

$\beta=(0.9,0.999)$ , weight decay $0.01$ , and 100 warmup steps.

The domain LoRA has rank 384 and scaling parameter $\alpha=384$ .

Basic Dynamics data teach control-conditioned local dynamics, while the

Bidirectional adaptation uses chunk-specific text conditions and a linear-path

flow-matching objective .

Consistency distillation and startup coverage.

For few-step generation, the implementation follows the teacher-forcing

consistency initialization in Causal-rCM .

This recipe builds on Consistency Models ,

sCM , and rCM .

A frozen autoregressive teacher advances a noisy sample between nearby noise

levels. At the advanced point, the current student produces a clean estimate

without gradients, which serves as the consistency target for its prediction

at the starting point. Video and audio both contribute to this loss.

Checkpoint EMA is maintained separately.()

Startup and continued generation use the same sliding-window context layout. The

training recipe alternates an update with four history chunks and an update

with zero, one, two, or three history chunks.

The final Arena recipe further distills text classifier-free

guidance  into the student. The teacher combines conditional and text-unconditional

predictions while retaining player actions and visual context. The student

uses a single conditional forward pass per denoising step.()

Ho & Salimans, 2022

Self-forcing distribution matching.

After consistency distillation, we apply self-forcing distribution

matching  as the second stage of the

Causal-rCM  recipe. The objective follows

DMD  and DMD2 , with bidirectional-teacher

supervision of an autoregressive student as in CausVid .

One student starts from

the initial frame, generates four startup chunks, and continues for five

additional chunks using the same reference, chunk-wise prompt routing, and sliding

context. No ground-truth history is inserted into this rollout. Both the

startup chunks and the later chunks receive distribution-matching supervision.()

semantic conditions. These score models receive no reference-image tokens,

so their text conditions describe character appearance explicitly.

The final Arena recipe applies text guidance to the

frozen score model, while the learned score model and student remain

conditional. Their normalized difference in denoised predictions

defines a stop-gradient target. The generator then replays the recorded final

denoising step of each chunk to optimize a masked video–audio regression

loss against that target. Rollout generation runs without gradients, avoiding storage of its full

computation graph.

Video refiner training.

We construct temporally aligned training pairs from the same arena clip.

Its original VAE encoding serves as the target. To construct the degraded

input, we spatially downsample the RGB frames, encode them, and apply a

frozen LTX-2.3 $2\times$ spatial upscaler v1.1

to restore the target spatial size.

We train a domain LoRA  on the refiner with truncated

flow matching  between

the original target and a noise-perturbed upsampled latent.

The refiner is first trained bidirectionally. Causal adaptation starts from

this checkpoint, conditions on the first frame, character reference, and

up to four clean history chunks, and applies loss only to the current

chunk. Training uses ground-truth history, while deployment uses previously

refined outputs. Both stages optimize only the domain LoRA, keeping the upsampler and

backbone frozen. The official LTX-2.3 distilled LoRA

v1.1  is disabled for this training loss and enabled

for few-step refinement at inference.()

Lightricks, 2026

()

Hu et al., 2022

()

Lipman et al., 2023

()

Lightricks, 2026

Inference settings.

The distilled Arena generator uses four denoising steps with noise levels

$(1,0.9375,0.8333,0.625,0)$ .

Refinement uses two denoising steps with noise levels

$(0.725,0.421875,0)$ , a classifier-free guidance scale of 1, and no

spatiotemporal guidance.

A.4

Prediction and state commitment.

At a chunk boundary, the controller retains the corrected state and uses

predicted events to compute provisional outcomes and local guidance.

Generation does not commit those predictions to the persistent ledger.

After decoding, verification produces the feedback used to obtain the next

retained state in Equation . The implementation

recomputes this state from the saved pre-generation state and observed

events, preventing predicted and verified damage from being counted twice.

The first chunk uses the initial frame and configured state without a

preceding verification step.

The retained gameplay state is stored independently of the generator’s

sliding visual context. When earlier frames leave that context, their

recorded interaction consequences remain available to subsequent rule

updates and enter generation through the current guidance.

2

Observation selection and shot prediction.

The online Arena implementation uses decoded RGB frames directly, without

an observation refiner. Within each chunk, it selects the first frame of

each uninterrupted firing interval and every fourth frame thereafter

(5 Hz at 20 FPS). Before generation, the latest available frame is the

preceding chunk’s last frame, or the initial image at startup. For each

selected firing time, a calibrated control-to-pixel mapping estimates the

image displacement from the intervening controls. We translate the latest

frame accordingly, take a $320\times 320$ crop centered on the screen, and

overlay a hollow green aiming ring. The Interaction Agent receives this

projected crop and a separate enemy appearance reference, and predicts

whether the enemy’s body overlaps the marked aiming region.

Visual verification.

After generation, we decode the corresponding actual firing frames,

the chunk’s final frame, and the frame three positions before it.

Together with the pre-generation frame, these form the sampled observations

$\mathcal{I}_{k-1}$ . A firing-frame audit receives the selected firing

frames in temporal order, with the same ring overlay, alongside the

pre-generation and two late frames. Unlike prediction, verification uses

full frames rather than center crops. The ring radius is 5% of the shorter

image dimension and leaves its interior unobstructed.

A separate state query places the final frame first and uses the

pre-generation and earlier late frame only as temporal context. It

classifies the enemy as alive, dead, or not visible in the final frame.

Both queries receive an appearance reference for identity only. Full

frames are padded to a $2{:}1$ canvas and the reference to a square,

without cropping their contents. Aim markers appear only in the VLM

inputs. The requested outcome is the condition being checked, not visual

evidence, and verification uses separate calls from prediction.

The rule engine specifies intended transitions, while committed visual

outcomes ground the state used for subsequent interaction. When an observed

outcome contradicts a prediction, the controller revises the affected state

and derives subsequent guidance from that revision. Numerical attributes

remain rule-maintained rather than directly estimated from images, and

occlusion alone is not treated as death.

Action constraints and opponent behavior.

Ammunition gates the executed fire commands and is consumed when a shot is

permitted, independently of whether it hits. Before an enemy can attack,

the Interaction Agent checks visual preconditions, including whether the

enemy is visible and facing the player. When these conditions hold, attacks

are sampled at a configured rate, and each attack hits with a preset

probability. Successful hits subtract a fixed

per-shot damage from player health. Reaching zero health disables player

controls and adds the corresponding terminal outcome to guidance.

For opponent behavior, the agent assesses movement feasibility from the

current scene. The behavior policy combines this assessment with retained

state and the configured strategy to select a movement description.

Attack rules and strategy-transition conditions can be edited in the rule layer.

Numerical state remains in the controller, while the generator receives

observable behavior and outcome descriptions. World-side events thus

combine visual assessment of the current scene with executable game rules

that update player state and constrain subsequent controls.

A.5

Reciprocal interaction concerns the causal effects of player actions on the

world and of world events on the player. It does not require every game

mechanic to be learned. Executable rules make damage, ammunition, and

termination conditions explicit and configurable, while scene-conditioned

behavior reasoning determines how actors act under those conditions.

Their combination connects world-side decisions to persistent consequences

for the player during continuous interaction.

Realizing these interactions also requires a generator that can express

their consequences. Explicit state specifies intended outcomes, and text

guidance communicates them, but the generator must learn to realize them

as visible behavior. We therefore develop interaction data, train the

conditioned generator, and connect event reasoning, executable updates,

and visual feedback in an online loop. The contribution is the reciprocal

generative gameplay enabled by this coordinated system, including its data

and training procedure. Reconciliation supplies feedback within this loop

by grounding subsequent decisions in committed observations.

Appendix B

All routes share the capture and alignment pipeline below. Counts refer to

accepted source recordings, excluding candidate jobs, prompt variants, and

overlapping training windows.

B.1

Execution and recording.

We specify the map, assets, initial conditions, actor policies, and player

controls before capture. The engine records gameplay demos together with

applied inputs, frame timing, state, and interaction events.

Requested controls and realized events are retained separately, with damage

labels taken from realized engine events. Offline replay renders the recorded

trajectory and game audio under a fixed client configuration. Presentation

settings, including HUD, crosshair, and effect suppression, are versioned

per route.

Renderer telemetry records camera position and orientation, transforms,

and projection parameters, synchronized with simulation ticks.

Time and action interface.

The capture pipelines use a 64 Hz simulation/control clock. Warm-up is

removed using the recorded capture boundary before aligning model time

zero. The model-facing stream uses 20 video frames per second, with four

continuous movement/camera channels and fire, jump, and reload inputs

under the shared action contract. Camera and movement values follow the recorded

applied controls. Button resampling preserves short active runs that might

otherwise disappear between sampled frames. In the long Interaction release,

the action profiles explicitly remove 64 warm-up ticks and align row zero

with the first video frame.

Native media differ across routes. Basic Dynamics stores 320 frames at 64 fps

and $1280\times 720$ resolution. Short and long Interaction sequences store 81 and 1,201

frames at 20 fps and $1280\times 720$ . Arena stores 1,201 frames at 20 fps

and $1664\times 960$ . Representative files in all four subsets contain

48 kHz stereo game audio. The model loader resizes video and resamples audio

according to the training configuration. The generator training configuration uses

$832\times 480$ video and 16 kHz stereo audio.

The 81-frame layout comprises an initial frame and five 16-frame chunks.

The 1,201-frame layout similarly supports 75 chunks.

Semantic labels and packaging.

We use Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite

() to separately annotate map style, weapon

appearance and operation, and player and enemy appearance.

Interaction releases add chunk-local motion,

visibility, damage, and death descriptions derived from telemetry.

Prompts distinguish no damage, nonlethal damage, a new death event, and an

already-dead actor. Off-screen intervals are described using visibility

records rather than invented visible motion. Player controls remain in

action tensors. Enemy movement and jumping belong to semantic conditions.

Where reference images are used, the manifest binds them to the appropriate

actor and time interval.()

Google DeepMind, 2026

gemini-3.1-flash-lite

B.2

Basic Dynamics contains 50,140 five-second clips across 28 maps and nine

weapons, including 39,539 without an enemy and 10,601 with a non-damaging

enemy distractor.

Movement, camera changes, firing, and local collision responses provide

the principal supervision. The supplement emphasizes pure idle,

idle-to-action, action-to-idle, interrupted action, smooth routes, and

wall impacts.

Route validation and camera filtering remove unsuitable trajectories.

B.3

Short interactions.

The short Interaction subset contains 42,000 recordings across five maps,

nine weapons, and 42 model–skin–color appearances.

Capture varies distance, opponent movement,

direction changes, stopping, jumping, visibility transitions, and firing.

Firing times are sampled deterministically from the scenario seed.

Weapon-specific schedules include isolated shots, repeated taps, and

bounded bursts. Opponent motion and jump programs are specified separately

from player controls.

Outcome labels follow the realized engine events, yielding 6,535 no-fire examples,

16,666 misses, 14,496 nonlethal-hit examples, and 4,303 kills.

The visibility allocation is 37,800 continuously visible examples,

2,100 exit-and-hold examples, and 2,100 exit-and-return examples.

The annotation identifies visibility transitions within each

0.8-second chunk. The underlying timestamped records also support

constructing annotations over windows of arbitrary duration within each

recording. This release describes view-frustum transitions, not

geometric occlusion behind arbitrary cover. Crosshair and casing effects are

disabled in its capture configuration.

Each recording has one

81-frame bidirectional view and one five-chunk autoregressive view.

Long interaction sequences.

Interaction-Long contains 1,791 accepted recordings with blood-hit effects

disabled during capture.

Each episode contains four actor slots, arranged either as distinct actors

or a controlled-return sequence, and zero, one, or two scheduled kills.

The accepted collection contains 900 controlled-return and 891

distinct-actor episodes.

The maps are Bromine, Courtfun, Geoplanetary, and Stormkeep. The weapons

are MachineGun, Rifle, and Shotgun. Scripted trajectories undergo collision

and ground-support checks. Camera schedules use frozen calibration traces,

with scan and aiming phases, rather than live feedback that tracks the

current enemy.

The reference bank contains 42 appearances with five clean views each.

Bindings expose the current actor reference, retain the outgoing reference

through its despawn transition, and mask intervals without an actor.

Each source episode provides fifteen 81-frame bidirectional windows.

The autoregressive view keeps each full sequence and its 75 chunk prompts.

B.4

Arena contains 1,800 one-minute

bot-versus-bot recordings in a compact arena, using MachineGun combat and

a fixed opponent appearance. Independent bot controls produce ongoing

movement and exchanges instead of prescribing a short outcome sequence.

The capture configuration bounds locomotion and camera motion and removes

crosshair and pickup clutter.

The release constructs the action stream from authoritative gameplay

records. Chunk descriptions summarize opponent motion, attacks, visibility,

nonlethal damage, kills, and player death from telemetry aligned with the

rendered camera. Fully off-screen chunks suppress visible-motion claims.

The manifest provides 75 prompts per episode and a fixed opponent

reference binding.

Arena trains RIGen-Arena.

B.5

Capture validation checks route geometry, camera behavior, and consistency

between scheduled interactions and recorded events. Manifest validation

checks media metadata, finite and aligned controls, complete prompt

schedules, and reference bindings.

Test set construction.

We reserve 100 Interaction recordings for quantitative evaluation. Their

maps and enemy appearances are excluded from all task-specific training

subsets, including Basic Dynamics, Interaction, Interaction-Long, and Arena,

and are not used in subsequent adaptation or distillation.

Appendix C

C.1

The 100 Xonotic scenarios comprise 50 survival targets and 50 death targets.

All RIGen variants in Table  use the same

Interaction-trained generator after sliding-window autoregressive training

on Interaction-Long, without Arena post-training or distillation.

SCOPE and LingBot-World 2.0 receive the prescribed

combat outcomes directly as text guidance.

Enemy motion is supplied by source annotations in place of online behavior

selection. The interaction agent handles hit, injury, and death reasoning

and correction of predicted state.

All variants use their own generated video history. Online interaction

variants compute guidance from that history, while RIGen (w/ Reference guidance)

uses frozen reference guidance.

Fixing enemy motion gives methods common behavior requirements and focuses

the comparison on motion adherence and combat-outcome realization, separating

behavior selection from its execution in generated video.

We combine controlled experiments, state-dependent branching examples, and

continuous closed-loop gameplay. Controlled experiments compare the

realization of specified interaction outcomes. Branch comparisons show how

state and strategy affect generated behavior, while RIGen-Arena demonstrates

the mutual effects of player actions and world events during continued play.

Together, these complementary evaluations examine outcome realization,

state dependence, and reciprocal interaction in the implemented system.

The external comparisons evaluate complete systems, including their data

and training recipes. Learning to realize interaction outcomes is part of

the proposed method. Specifying an outcome in text alone does not ensure

that a generator can express it. We therefore assess the resulting system

capability against external models and use fixed-generator ablations to

examine the online interaction mechanisms separately.

Evaluating generated trajectories.

Once a generated trajectory diverges from its source recording, source-engine

hit and visibility labels cannot automatically serve as ground truth for the

generated scene. Rule execution can be checked against configured transitions,

while judging whether a generated attack hits requires independent evidence

from the generated video itself. Autonomous behavior also admits multiple

valid choices under the same state, calling for task-based criteria that

accommodate alternative behaviors. Our benchmark uses prescribed motion and outcome

targets with video-based assessment. Event-level visual correctness and

autonomous decision quality require annotations or task criteria for the

generated trajectories, rather than direct reuse of source-engine labels.

C.2

Qwen3.8-27B  judges complete generated videos offline.()

Qwen Team, 2026

Enemy Behavior.

Enemy Behavior averages

satisfaction of directional motion checks within predefined time windows,

first within each video and then equally across the 100 scenarios. A check

receives credit only when the judge reports it as satisfied and cites visual

evidence within its time window. Lateral and depth motion are checked

separately, relative to the environment rather than camera-induced image

motion. For death-target cases, the prescribed lethal chunk and subsequent motion

requirements are excluded for all methods using the same fixed windows.

Final-state Agreement.

Final-state Agreement compares the enemy’s visible state in the final

0.8 seconds with its preassigned survival or death target. The target is

withheld from the judge. Unreadable outcomes and failures remain in the

denominator and receive no agreement credit.

Overall FSA uses all 100 cases. Survival-target and death-target success

rates each use the corresponding 50 cases, so overall FSA is their mean.

FSA tests whether the prescribed final combat outcome is actually realized.

Locally plausible motion and high visual quality do not establish that an

opponent survives or dies as required, making outcome agreement a distinct

interaction criterion. EB measures motion adherence, while qualitative

sequences illustrate intermediate combat responses.

Visual quality and dynamics.

The five visual metrics use the official dimension-specific VBench

pipelines on complete generated videos. Each reported score is the mean

per-video normalized score multiplied by 100. Dynamic Degree is the

percentage of videos meeting the official motion threshold.

The system also generates audio jointly with video.

C.3

The ablation rows in Table  compare inference-time variants using the

same video checkpoint, initial conditions, player inputs, and sampling settings.

1.

Predict interaction consequences before

generation, apply executable rules, and guide the current chunk.

Observe the generated chunk and reconcile predicted state with its

visible outcome before the next decision.Full RIGen.

2.

Retain player inputs, scene,

appearance, and source motion annotations. Remove hit, injury, and death

guidance and the online interaction VLM.Motion guidance only.

3.

The VLM maintains persistent textual

state and selects the next chunk’s combat outcome. Rules are supplied

as text, without an executable rule engine or an independent

verification-and-correction module. This variant compares agent-managed

state updates with executable rules and separate visual reconciliation.Semantic prompting.

4.

Generate first, observe events,

apply rules, and pass consequence guidance to the following chunk.

There is no pre-generation prediction of current-chunk consequences.Post-hoc event updates.

5.

Retain pre-generation prediction

and executable state updates, but do not correct the planned state from

post-generation verification. The next reasoning step still sees the

newly generated frames.Without reconciliation.

6.

Freeze reference event

guidance in advance and remove online VLM calls. Death instructions are

derived from source hit annotations combined with configured health and

damage rules. They specify a counterfactual task answer, not ground-truth

death in the source recording. The guidance is not revised from generated

observations, but autoregressive video context uses this variant’s own

outputs.RIGen (w/ Reference guidance).

C.4

Generation throughput at $832\times 480$ .

Parameters count the generation backbone.

Both RIGen settings include refinement.Table 2:

Runtime is measured on a single NVIDIA GB300 GPU.

In Table , Replay disables online VLM calls and

reuses the same guidance, while Online runs the interaction loop. Both

include refinement and remain below the target playback rate of 20 FPS.

item.title: WorldSolver：LLM 智能体能靠生成求解器模拟物理吗 ｜ WorldSolver: Can LLM Agents Simulate the Physical Dynamics via Solver Generation?
item.description:
一句话：不让模型直接预测画面，而是让它写求解器代码来模拟物理——这条路能走多远？

要点：

  • 把物理模拟转化成「让 LLM 生成求解器代码」
  • 避免端到端预测长程漂移问题
  • 给出这类方法在精度与稳定性上的边界评估

为什么值得看：给「AI 原生引擎」提供了另一条技术路线：不学物理，而是让 AI 写物理。对引擎开发者特别亲切。

中文摘要：WorldSolver 提出一个有意思的问题：与其让模型端到端预测物理演化（容易长程漂移），不如让它生成可执行的求解器代码，用数值方法得到稳定结果。作者系统评估了 LLM 智能体在这条路线上的表现——包括代码正确性、数值稳定性与长程一致性。这条「AI 写求解器」的思路对引擎开发者格外友好，因为产出是可直接跑在现有管线里的代码，而不是黑盒预测。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·智能体+游戏（English）

License: CC BY 4.0

arXiv:2610.08720v1 [cs.AI] 06 Oct 2026

WorldSolver: Can LLM Agents Simulate the Physical Dynamics via Solver Generation?

Siru Jiang   Yongzhe Lyu   Shuo Lu   Yubin Wang   Yuxiang Zhang

NLPR & MAIS, CASIA

Affiliation: PKU

Affiliation: Huawei Noah’s Ark LabCorresponding author.Project lead.

Affiliation: ‡†Yue Liao   Bin Wang   Jian Liang   Tieniu Tan

NLPR & MAIS, CASIA

Affiliation: Huawei Noah’s Ark LabCorresponding author.Project lead.

Affiliation: ‡†

Abstract

LLM-based agents are increasingly advancing scientific and engineering problem solving, with physics simulation emerging as a challenging yet practical testbed for reproducing complex physical phenomena with application in embodied AI, games and films.

As the workhorse of such simulation, a solver computes how the state of a dynamic system evolves over time.

Building such solvers requires physical understanding to identify appropriate models, mathematical reasoning to formulate the underlying dynamics, and software engineering to implement them as executable code, yet this capability of LLM agents remains underexplored.

To this end, we introduce , a benchmark of 168 simulation tasks derived from physical phenomena in 61 classic computer graphics papers, spanning 7 physical domains.

Each task contains a code scaffold that provides a fixed simulation environment for the scene, with the solver implementation left for the agent to complete.

Specifically, we evaluate them along three dimensions: for successful execution, for reproducing the intended dynamic behavior in the rendered simulation, and for physics-grounded verification of the generated dynamics.

Experiments on frontier agents reveal that producing executable solvers is difficult itself, and satisfying visual and physical correctness is even harder.

GPT-5.6-Sol and Claude-Opus-5 perform comparatively better than the other evaluated agents, yet achieve overall scores of only 48.7% and 46.7%, respectively.

WorldSolver is an early step toward agentic solver generation, and we hope it helps drive progress toward agents that can faithfully simulate the dynamic physical world.

Code is available at .WorldSolverExecution ChecksVisual FidelityPhysical Plausibility

https://github.com/sirujiang/WorldSolver

1

Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly capable of tackling complex real-world tasks , spanning from software engineering  to scientific discovery .

Recent studies have shown growing interest in physically realistic simulation of 3D worlds, with broad applications in embodied AI, games, and films .

A line of work focuses on static scene construction through asset composition and spatial layout .

Another explores dynamic scene generation to reproduce physical phenomena and their temporal evolution .(; )

to identify appropriate models, mathematical reasoning to formulate the underlying dynamics, and software engineering to implement them as executable code .

For example, cloth solver handles stiff elastic dynamics and frictional contact at high degrees of freedom , while fluid solver instead focuses on incompressibility enforcement and free-surface tracking .solver translates the governing equations of a physical model into a numerical procedure that evolves the simulated system over time(; )

However, existing works target dynamics scene generation either produce animations in a solver-free manner  or rely on existing simulation engine .

In contrast, scientific-computing benchmarks evaluate numerical solver generation for prescribed governing equations, where the physical model to be solved is given in advance .

Neither setting evaluates the full capability required for physical dynamics simulation, spanning physical understanding for model selection, mathematical reasoning for numerical formulation, and software engineering for executable implementation.

Together, they motivate our question:()
