The following cases show how a policy changes across episodes. They use recorded actions, visible narration, and saved notes, not private reasoning. They illustrate possible mechanisms rather than their frequency. These supplementary cases draw on interactions beyond the scoring windows and do not enter the reported scores.

In OpenCode–Opus 5 trial 1, a failed fusion is followed by the statement “never combine tier-3 gems.” The agent then treats its recipe map as complete and repeats a plan scoring 426. This illustrates how an incomplete belief can stop further tests.Stopping exploration in GemForge.

OpenCode–Opus 5 trial 1 records both the actor–scholar adjacency taboo and the mirror-room restriction on lantern carriers. Greedy placement leaves no safe room for the last actor. The agent then says “I need to reserve buffer positions proactively” and changes its allocation plan. The scores are 100 and 115, but the guest lists also change: the evidence is the revised allocation policy, not a controlled score improvement.Knowing taboos without reserving rooms.

B.1.3

EvoTest–Opus 5 trial 3 scores 46, 81, 83, 83, and 83 in GemForge’s scoring window. An earlier prompt records that the only fusion tried, jade with opal, produced slag. The episode-5 prompt then instructs the agent never to attempt tier-2 or tier-3 fusion, ruling out combinations it has not tested. This case shows how a processed prompt can generalize beyond the observed failure. It does not establish that compression causes the aggregate difference from Memory.One failed fusion becomes a broad rule.

B.1.4

In , OpenCode–GPT-5 Mini trial 3 (seed 2) serves dish 0 at all three banquets in episodes 2, 3, and 5, even though dishes at that position are both accepted and rejected. Its saved notes describe a policy of always serving the same index. By contrast, OpenCode–Kimi K3 trial 1 (seed 2) compares accepted dishes across episodes 1 and 2 and identifies sourness as irrelevant. In episode 3, an accepted non-hot dish leads it to rule out temperature and then test saltiness. These cases use recorded actions and visible narration within the first five episodes. Appendix D

Each entry brings together a game’s learning task, raw-score curves, a single performance table with trial variability, and archived rule-discovery annotations. Scores and supporting evidence can therefore be checked in one place.

Curves show episode-wise mean raw scores across trials. Their left, center, and right panels compare backbones, self-evolving methods, and harnesses. Each method curve averages its Kimi K3, Opus 5, and GPT-5 Mini curves.Reading the curves.

No rule-discovery labels are assigned to Opus 5.5 or GPT-6 Astra; score validation alone does not establish rule discovery.

All four metrics use normalized scores, with agent results reported as point estimates $\pm$ trial SD (Appendix ). Max averages individual trial peaks. Mean averages the episode-wise trial mean. First is the mean episode at which each trial first reaches its peak. The selected Human Top-1 record retains Max, Mean, and First. The symbol – marks quantities not reported for this selected record, not zero. Curves remain in raw units, and each entry gives the reference score needed to convert between scales.Reading the performance tables.

C

Each game defines local targets T1–Tk. S means at least one available trial provides evidence for the whole listed criterion, P means partial evidence without a complete trial, and – means insufficient evidence. S does not mean that all trials satisfy the target. We report these labels only within each game. The different archived criteria are not aggregated into overall percentages.Reading the rule-discovery labels.

The labels provide supplementary qualitative evidence from interaction records. They do not measure rule discovery within the scoring window. The first five games use complete-rule criteria. Criteria for the other games also include successful execution supported by observed performance. Terse logs, especially for GPT-5.6-SOL, can leave a target unverified even when a successful policy uses it.Scope of the rule annotations.

These annotations describe evidence in interaction records, not additional score measurements. A high score alone does not establish every hidden rule. For Haunted Inn and Poisoner, the entries identify which seed-dependent rule and policy labels use the same seed as the scored trials.

item.content:encoded:
一句话：用游戏当试验场，测 LLM 智能体能否从经验中学习而不是死记硬背。

要点：

  • 构造陌生游戏环境，隔离「预训练记忆」的干扰
  • 评估智能体跨回合的经验积累能力
  • 揭示当前模型更多是检索而非学习

为什么值得看：做 AI 驱动的 NPC 或玩法代理，最怕的是「换个关卡就废」。这个基准直接量化了这个风险。

中文摘要：Learn2Play Bench 用一组智能体不熟悉的游戏环境来测试一个关键能力：LLM 智能体能否真正从经验中学习，而不是依赖预训练里见过的模式。作者设计了多回合、可迁移的评测任务，并对比了不同策略下智能体的表现。结果显示多数模型在陌生环境中的经验积累能力有限，更多表现为模式检索。对想做「会成长的 NPC」的团队，这是一份必要的冷水。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·智能体+游戏（English）

License: CC BY 4.0

arXiv:2610.08215v2 [cs.AI] 08 Oct 2026

Learn2Play Bench: How Well Do LLM Agents Learn from Experience in Unfamiliar Environments?

Yibo LiJinhang QiuZhi ZhengQianyun GuoJiaying WuShuo JiBryan HooiNational University of Singaporeliyibo@u.nus.edu, bhooi@comp.nus.edu.sg

Abstract

Learning from experience is essential for LLM agents to adapt to unfamiliar and dynamic environments.

Evaluating this ability is therefore important for understanding how effectively agents acquire and use new knowledge.

Existing benchmarks have sought to evaluate this ability, but they primarily evaluate tasks whose rules are provided in the instructions or already familiar to pretrained models, making it difficult to distinguish learning from interactions from reasoning with existing knowledge.

To address this, we introduce , a benchmark of newly designed text-based games, whose rules are novel or counterintuitive, requiring agents to acquire knowledge through interaction rather than rely solely on pretrained knowledge.

These games provide reproducible feedback and automatic scoring, enabling controlled evaluation of learning across repeated attempts.

We also vary game instances to test whether agents can apply what they have learned to new situations.

Therefore, we evaluate how backbone models, self-evolving methods, and agent harnesses affect agents’ learning ability, revealing three findings: (1) Retaining complete records of actions and feedback can support more effective learning than summarizing these experiences into rules or strategies.

(2) Top-performing human players achieve higher peak scores than the evaluated agents. Humans explore more varied strategies, and repeat actions less.

(3) With the backbone fixed, changing the harness can improve performance while reducing estimated inference cost.

Together, these findings provide insights into how LLM agents learn from experience and suggest directions for future work to improve their learning ability.

Project website: .Learn2Play BenchExperience retention:Human–agent gap:Harness matters:

https://liushiliushi.github.io/learn2play-bench-website/

1

The ability of LLM agents to acquire new knowledge through interaction and use it to improve behavior is central to artificial general intelligence (AGI) . While the extensive knowledge acquired during pretraining enables agents to perform complex tasks (e.g., fixing software issues , completing web tasks , and operating desktop applications ), in realistic deployment,

agents often encounter whose rules are not covered by the pretrained knowledge.

For example, an agent struggles to control a robot through an unfamiliar command interface.

It must therefore try commands and observe the resulting motion to learn which joints each command activates.

Agents can then apply what they have learned to make better decisions in subsequent interactions.()

Hendrycks et al., 2025

()

Yang et al., 2024

()

Zhou et al., 2024

()

Xie et al., 2024

unfamiliar environments

Recent work has therefore developed self-evolving agents that reuse interaction feedback through memories, extracted rules, reasoning patterns, or evolving agent configurations .

However, evaluating whether these systems actually learn remains difficult.

Existing methods are often studied with different models, tasks, and evaluation protocols, making their learning behavior hard to compare directly.

More fundamentally, .

If an agent improves on a familiar task, we do not know whether it learned a new rule from interaction or merely recovered knowledge already encoded during pretraining.(; ; )

Zhang et al., 2025b

He et al., 2025

Ouyang et al., 2025

better task performance does not necessarily mean that an agent learns more effectively

This distinction is often overlooked in existing evaluations of continual or self-evolving agents.

Benchmarks often measure improvement over repeated attempts or task sequences , but many tasks are based on familiar real-world settings whose underlying rules may already be represented in pretraining, leaving agents’ learning ability insufficiently tested.

We therefore ask:(; ; ; ; ; )

He et al., 2025

Zheng et al., 2025

Wei et al., 2025

Yan et al., 2026

Yang et al., 2026a

Zhang et al., 2025a

How effectively can LLM agents learn from experience in unfamiliar environments?

To answer this question, we introduce , a benchmark of newly designed text-based games with unfamiliar or counterintuitive hidden rules.

For example, in one game, stealing a colleague’s lunch helps the player get promoted, while working hard does not.

Agents are not given these rules.

They must discover them by acting, observing textual feedback, and carrying useful experience into later episodes, without updating model weights.

Each game provides deterministic feedback and automatic scoring, allowing learning trajectories to be measured reproducibly.

In half of the games, characters, objects, or layouts change across episodes while the underlying rules remain fixed.

This setting tests whether agents can apply knowledge to new situations.Learn2Play Bench

Using this controlled setting, we compare different backbone models, self-evolving methods, and deployed agent harnesses, and contrast their behavior with human players.

Our experiments reveal five main findings:

Raw interaction histories can support stronger learning than methods that summarize experience into rules or strategies, because the original evidence remains available when earlier conclusions need revision (§4.2).

Top-performing human players reach higher peak scores than the evaluated agents, while exploring more varied action sequences and recovering more often after setbacks (§4.4).

With the backbone fixed, changing the harness can substantially improve both performance and learning.

In some cases, it also reduces inference cost through fewer model calls and less repeated context (§4.3, §4.6).

, even when the underlying rules stay the same. The drop in learning slope tends to be larger for weaker backbones under the same harness (§4.5).

For example, in , an agent learns how to assign guests to safe rooms but fails to plan ahead, leaving a later guest with nowhere safe to stay (§4.2).(1) Preserving evidence can matter more than compressing it.(2) Top-performing human players outperform the best agent.(3) Better harnesses can improve agent performance and learning while reducing inference cost.(4) Agents can learn more slowly in changing environments(5) Agents can learn rules from experience but still struggle to use them to develop effective strategies.Haunted Inn

Our contributions are threefold:

•

We introduce , a controlled benchmark of newly designed games with hidden rules, deterministic feedback, and automatic scoring. We also design re-shuffled games to evaluate whether agents could transfer the knowledge to new instances.Learn2Play Bench

•

We systematically compare backbone models, self-evolving methods, and agent harnesses, revealing factors that affect learning from experience and identifying directions for future research.

•

We conduct a human study on the same games and compare scores and interaction records to examine differences in performance and behavior between human players and LLM agents.

2

Recent work develops self-evolving agents to learn from experience at test time, adapting their behavior using feedback from earlier attempts .

Early methods reuse experience without updating model weights through verbal reflections in Reflexion , extracted insights and retrieved trajectories in ExpeL , or reusable executable skills in Voyager . Other methods organize experience into workflows and playbooks.

For example, AWM induces action workflows , Dynamic Cheatsheet curates compact strategies and code snippets , and ACE incrementally maintains structured playbooks rather than raw transcripts .

ReasoningBank and ERL distill trajectories into reusable reasoning patterns or heuristics  .

JitRL retrieves past trajectories to estimate action advantages and adjusts the model’s output logits at inference time without gradient updates .

Beyond constructing memories, GEPA evolves prompts through trajectory-level reflection , while Agents of Change revises both prompts and agent code through specialized collaborative roles .

EvoTest extends evolution to the broader agent configuration, including memory and tool-use routines  .

Meta-TTL further evolves the adaptation policy that determines how experience should update the agent .

Beyond context-level updates, TT-SI generates training examples from uncertain cases and fine-tunes the agent at test time .

Our goal is not to propose another adaptation method, but to assess how effectively existing methods learn under controlled conditions.

Our evaluation focuses on learning without weight updates: we compare backbones in a common harness and self-evolving methods with each backbone held fixed.Self-evolving agents.(; )

To assess whether these adaptation mechanisms improve later behavior, benchmarks evaluate agents over task sequences or repeated interactions.

StreamBench uses input–feedback streams , while MemoryBench studies learning from accumulated user feedback and Evo-Memory evaluates memory updates across task streams .

Related evaluations extend experience reuse to interactive tasks: LifelongAgentBench tests skill accumulation across related tasks , SWE-Bench-CL evaluates learning across successive coding issues , and MemoryArena tests memory use across interdependent sessions .

These benchmarks test whether experience improves later performance. On familiar tasks, however, it is unclear whether agents improve by learning something new or by using what they already know.

Other benchmarks study learning directly through interaction with environments. AutoEnv  also creates new environments to evaluate learning across diverse settings.

Closer to our setting, J-TTL  measures repeated improvement on Jericho games, but their public content may already be represented in model pretraining. ARC-AGI-3 tests interaction with unfamiliar visual environments, but performance also depends on visual capabilities .

We use newly designed text-based games with hidden rules to examine whether agents can discover previously unknown rules through actions and feedback.

We also compare fixed and changing instances of the same game to test whether agents can reuse experience when the visible situation changes.Benchmarks for self-evolving agents.()

To measure whether agents improve through experience in unfamiliar environments, we design games that satisfy the following principles:

•

We design games with novel hidden rules not found in existing games, including deliberately counterintuitive rules that conflict with common game knowledge.

For example, in one of our games, instead of hard work, stealing a colleague’s lunch helps the player get promoted. The agent must therefore learn which actions lead to promotion from the game’s feedback, rather than rely on expectations about real workplaces.Rule novelty.

•

Each game automatically assigns a score, enabling large-scale evaluation without human grading.Automatic scoring.

•

Deterministic outcomes allow us to replay interactions, compare agents under the same conditions, and inspect mistakes.Reproducibility.

•

To test whether agents transfer learned knowledge, we vary the visible situation across episodes while preserving the core rule.Controlled variation across episodes.

Based on the four principles above, we manually design Learn2Play Bench with 20 game templates, each of which can generate multiple instances that differ in layout, characters, or hidden-rule parameters. Figure  illustrates the game suite and an example interaction. Agents receive a goal and a set of available actions, interact through text to discover the hidden rules, and receive a final score at the end of each episode. They play repeated episodes and can use experience from earlier attempts. We divide the games along two dimensions. First, ten games repeat the same instance across episodes, whereas ten games change the visible instance while preserving the core rule. Second, we conduct pilot evaluations with several agents to estimate game difficulty and identify five games. We use a ten-episode scoring window for these games and a five-episode window for the remaining games. Appendix  explains what players must learn in each game, and appendix  provides the corresponding results and archived rule-discovery evidence.

4.1

We evaluate all agents on the same 20 game instances from Learn2Play Bench, using one fixed seed per game template.Datasets.

We evaluate each agent through a black-box command interface. The agent issues actions and observes textual feedback but cannot access the game source code or oracle solvers. We evaluate each game $g$ for $T_{g}$ episodes: $T_{g}=5$ for normal games and $T_{g}=10$ for challenge games, which are harder and therefore require more episodes to learn. The protocol requires three independent trials per game. Each trial starts with no memory of previous trials. Within a trial, the information retained from earlier episodes depends on the harness.Protocol.

We use four metrics to evaluate two complementary aspects of agent behavior across episodes: achieved performance and improvement through experience. Max and Mean measure achieved performance, while Learning Gain (LG) and Learning Slope (LS) measure improvement across episodes. Because score ranges differ across games, we compute these metrics using normalized scores. Appendix  explains normalization, trial aggregation, and game weighting. Let $z_{g,r,t}$ be a normalized terminal score for game $g$ , trial $r$ , and episode $t$ , and let $y_{g,t}$ denote the mean of these scores at episode $t$ . We define the four metrics as follows:Metrics.

A.2

•

averages the peak terminal scores $m_{g,r}$ of the $R_{g}$ scored trial trajectories within the evaluation window: $\mathrm{Max}_{g}=R_{g}^{-1}\sum_{r=1}^{R_{g}}m_{g,r}$ . It measures the best performance an agent demonstrates during evaluation.Max

•

averages performance across all evaluated episodes: $\mathrm{Mean}_{g}=T_{g}^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^{T_{g}}y_{g,t}$ . It measures how consistently the agent performs throughout evaluation.Mean

•

compares average performance in the first and last $k_{g}=\min(3,\lfloor T_{g}/2\rfloor)$ episodes: $\mathrm{LG}_{g}=k_{g}^{-1}(\sum_{t=T_{g}-k_{g}+1}^{T_{g}}y_{g,t}-\sum_{t=1}^{k_{g}}y_{g,t})$ . It measures the net improvement from the beginning to the end of evaluation.Learning Gain (LG)

•

fits $y_{g,t}=\beta_{0,g}+\beta_{1,g}t+\epsilon_{g,t}$ over all evaluated episodes and reports $\mathrm{LS}_{g}=\hat{\beta}_{1,g}$ . It measures the overall direction and rate of change across the full learning trajectory.Learning Slope (LS)

We first compute each metric separately for each game and then aggregate it across games as $\sum_{g}w_{g}M_{g}/\sum_{g}w_{g}$ , assigning weight 3 to challenge games and weight 1 to normal games. The five challenge games and fifteen normal games therefore each receive 50% of the total weight. To aggregate learning curves from games with different numbers of episodes, we map each game’s episodes onto a common 0–100% progress scale and use linear interpolation only for visualization.

To examine how different ways of retaining and reusing experience affect learning, we compare self-evolving methods separately for Kimi K3, Claude Opus 5, and GPT-5 Mini, holding the backbone fixed within each comparison.

We evaluate the following methods:

retains the dialogue within the current episode but discards it before the next, providing no cross-episode experience.

cumulatively adds the complete, unmodified interaction histories from preceding episodes to each new episode’s prompt, dropping the oldest episodes only when the history exceeds the context budget.

reflects on each completed episode to derive concise lessons about discovered rules, successful and failed actions, and next steps, then adds the accumulated lessons to the prompt for later episodes.

uses earlier interaction histories and outcomes to evolve a guiding prompt and a state-extraction program that steer action selection in subsequent episodes.

turns each successful or failed episode into a small set of reusable reasoning lessons and adds the accumulated bank to the prompt in later episodes.

induces reusable multi-step workflows from successful interaction histories and includes the resulting workflows in later episode prompts. Failed episodes are not used.Methods.NaiveMemoryReflexion()

We inspected the interaction logs to understand how models use experience.

Opus 5 and Qwen 3.8 Max test their understanding of the hidden rules and update it when new observations do not match their expectations.

In contrast, weaker models sometimes repeat actions that worked before, even when they no longer work.

They may also change several factors at once, making it hard to tell which factor affects the outcome.

For example, in , agents choose dishes for a king and learn about his food preferences from whether he accepts or rejects them.

In one GPT-5 Mini run, the agent keeps choosing dishes by their position on the menu, without using feedback from earlier choices.

Kimi K3 instead uses that feedback to choose which food attribute to test next.Stronger models use feedback to adjust their decisions, whereas weaker models may repeat the same actions despite new observations.Poisoner

4.2.2

retains raw histories without reflection, rule extraction, or workflow induction, yet leads all four metrics with Kimi K3.

This is because reflection and memory processing can turn an incomplete understanding into rules or workflows that later episodes continue to follow, while raw histories keep the original evidence available for revising those interpretations.

For example, in , agents combine ingredients to make gems. After one combination fails, an EvoTest–Opus 5 run adds a rule to its prompt telling it to avoid many other combinations, including one that would succeed.Simply using past interaction histories can outperform more elaborate self-evolving methods.MemoryGemForge

OpenCode is more flexible during play.

OpenCode lets the model decide when to review earlier feedback, run calculations, or check a plan before taking an action.

By contrast, the evaluated self-evolving methods follow preset steps for choosing actions and updating experience.

When an unexpected result occurs, OpenCode gives the model room to investigate and revise its plan before continuing, rather than only updating its memory for later episodes.OpenCode achieves better performance than the evaluated self-evolving methods when using the same backbone.

4.2.3

The game-specific audit shows agents repeating known strategies instead of testing alternatives.

For example, in , players combine ingredients to make increasingly valuable gems.

After several failed attempts, one Opus 5 run concludes that higher-value gems cannot be made and keeps repeating known recipes, limiting further improvement.Agents may stop exploring better strategies after finding one that partly works.GemForge

In an Opus 5 run, the agent states the relevant taboos but assigns rooms greedily, leaving no safe room for a later guest.

In the next episode, it reserves rooms for guests with fewer safe options.

The failure lies in choosing an action that works now without considering what it prevents later.Agents may know the rules but fail to plan ahead.Haunted Inn

To examine this behavioral difference beyond the single best record, we compare observed episodes from Human Top-3 with the models and self-evolving methods. Building on our findings, we discuss open questions in how to improve the learning ability of LLM agents and outline directions for future research.

In our comparison of human players and agents, Human Top-1 achieves a higher Max score than every agent configuration we evaluate, as shown in Tables  and . This is because humans try more varied strategies across episodes, while agents more often reuse strategies that have worked before (Appendix ). Future work should better balance exploration and exploitation, allowing agents to test new strategies even when their current strategy already earns high scores.How should agents balance exploration and exploitation?

B.3.3

With Kimi K3, outperforms the other self-evolving methods overall, as shown in Table . Unlike those methods, it retains full interaction histories rather than first distilling them into rules. This distinction matters when agents draw rules from limited evidence. In , EvoTest tried one gem combination and failed, but its later prompt instructed the agent not to test other combinations it had never tried (Appendix ). The prompt thus turned incomplete evidence into a definitive rule. Future work can explore ways to store experience, such as linking each learned rule to the original interactions behind it so agents can revisit the evidence and revise the rule when new feedback arrives.How should agents store learned rules?Memory

B.1.3

Our transfer evaluation shows that changing surface details, such as layouts or characters, can reduce agents’ learning slopes even when the underlying rules remain the same (Table ). In real-world tasks, agents also regularly encounter changes in their surroundings, available resources, and the people they interact with. This raises a broader question: how can agents adapt to these changes in their environments? Future methods could help agents compare experiences across different situations, distinguish shared rules from instance-specific details, and check when those rules still apply.How can agents learn what stays constant as environments change?

4.5

6

In this study, we investigate how effectively LLM agents learn from experience in unfamiliar environments.

Existing evaluations make it difficult to distinguish newly acquired knowledge from prior knowledge. To address this issue, we introduce Learn2Play Bench, a benchmark of newly designed text-based games with hidden rules that agents discover through interaction without updating their model weights.

We conducted comprehensive experiments comparing backbone models, self-evolving methods, deployed agent harnesses, and human players.

Our findings show that more elaborate self-evolving methods do not always improve learning, human players explore more varied strategies, with top-performing humans achieving higher peak scores than the models and self-evolving methods we evaluate, and agent harnesses can improve performance while reducing task costs.

We hope this work provides a foundation for evaluating and improving how agents learn from experience.

Let $x_{g,r,t}$ be the raw score for game $g$ , trial $r$ , and episode $t$ , and let $C_{g}$ be that game’s reference score. We convert it to $z_{g,r,t}=100x_{g,r,t}/C_{g}$ . This puts different games on a common scale.

Max first takes the peak normalized terminal score $m_{g,r}$ in each trial’s scoring window and then averages those peaks across the $R_{g}$ scored trial trajectories: $\mathrm{Max}_{g}=R_{g}^{-1}\sum_{r=1}^{R_{g}}m_{g,r}$ . For example, trial peaks of 40, 60, and 80 give Max $=60$ , not 80. The other metrics use the episode-wise mean of terminal scores, $y_{g,t}$ : Mean averages its scores, LG compares its late and early scores, and LS measures its linear trend per episode. The following cases show how a policy changes across episodes. They use recorded actions, visible narration, and saved notes, not private reasoning. They illustrate possible mechanisms rather than their frequency. These supplementary cases draw on interactions beyond the scoring windows and do not enter the reported scores.

In OpenCode–Opus 5 trial 1, a failed fusion is followed by the statement “never combine tier-3 gems.” The agent then treats its recipe map as complete and repeats a plan scoring 426. This illustrates how an incomplete belief can stop further tests.Stopping exploration in GemForge.

OpenCode–Opus 5 trial 1 records both the actor–scholar adjacency taboo and the mirror-room restriction on lantern carriers. Greedy placement leaves no safe room for the last actor. The agent then says “I need to reserve buffer positions proactively” and changes its allocation plan. The scores are 100 and 115, but the guest lists also change: the evidence is the revised allocation policy, not a controlled score improvement.Knowing taboos without reserving rooms.

B.1.3

EvoTest–Opus 5 trial 3 scores 46, 81, 83, 83, and 83 in GemForge’s scoring window. An earlier prompt records that the only fusion tried, jade with opal, produced slag. The episode-5 prompt then instructs the agent never to attempt tier-2 or tier-3 fusion, ruling out combinations it has not tested. This case shows how a processed prompt can generalize beyond the observed failure. It does not establish that compression causes the aggregate difference from Memory.One failed fusion becomes a broad rule.

B.1.4

In , OpenCode–GPT-5 Mini trial 3 (seed 2) serves dish 0 at all three banquets in episodes 2, 3, and 5, even though dishes at that position are both accepted and rejected. Its saved notes describe a policy of always serving the same index. By contrast, OpenCode–Kimi K3 trial 1 (seed 2) compares accepted dishes across episodes 1 and 2 and identifies sourness as irrelevant. In episode 3, an accepted non-hot dish leads it to rule out temperature and then test saltiness. These cases use recorded actions and visible narration within the first five episodes. Appendix C

Tables – give the weighted results over all games and separately over fixed and re-shuffled games. Per-game results appear alongside each game’s curves and rule evidence in Appendix . Point estimates retain the normalization, scoring windows, and aggregation used elsewhere in the paper. The standard deviations (SDs) describe variation across independent trials, not variation across episodes or game difficulty.We report trial variability for all 31 agent configurations and all four metrics.

13

15

D

Max takes that trial’s highest score, Mean averages its scores, LG compares its first and last $k_{g}$ episodes, and LS fits its score trend against the original episode indices. For trial-level metric values $M_{g,r}$ , the sample variance is $s_{g}^{2}=(n_{g}-1)^{-1}\sum_{r=1}^{n_{g}}(M_{g,r}-\bar{M}_{g})^{2}$ , and the tables report $\pm s_{g}$ . With complete trajectories, averaging these trial-level metrics reproduces the paper’s point estimates, apart from rounding of archived episode means.Within each game, we compute each metric separately for each complete trial.

Writing $a_{g}=w_{g}/\sum_{h}w_{h}$ , the reported aggregate SD is $s_{\mathrm{agg}}=\sqrt{\sum_{g}a_{g}^{2}s_{g}^{2}}$ . Under independent runs across games, this estimates the variability of a benchmark score formed from one trial per game. It does not pair arbitrary trial indices across games or treat differences between games as trial noise. This is an SD, not the standard error or a confidence interval of the reported multi-trial mean. The instance panel and reference scores are held fixed.Across games, we propagate within-game variation using the paper’s weights.

Appendix D

Each entry brings together a game’s learning task, raw-score curves, a single performance table with trial variability, and archived rule-discovery annotations. Scores and supporting evidence can therefore be checked in one place.

Curves show episode-wise mean raw scores across trials. Their left, center, and right panels compare backbones, self-evolving methods, and harnesses. Each method curve averages its Kimi K3, Opus 5, and GPT-5 Mini curves.Reading the curves.

No rule-discovery labels are assigned to Opus 5.5 or GPT-6 Astra; score validation alone does not establish rule discovery.

All four metrics use normalized scores, with agent results reported as point estimates $\pm$ trial SD (Appendix ). Max averages individual trial peaks. Mean averages the episode-wise trial mean. First is the mean episode at which each trial first reaches its peak. The selected Human Top-1 record retains Max, Mean, and First. The symbol – marks quantities not reported for this selected record, not zero. Curves remain in raw units, and each entry gives the reference score needed to convert between scales.Reading the performance tables.

C

Each game defines local targets T1–Tk. S means at least one available trial provides evidence for the whole listed criterion, P means partial evidence without a complete trial, and – means insufficient evidence. S does not mean that all trials satisfy the target. We report these labels only within each game. The different archived criteria are not aggregated into overall percentages.Reading the rule-discovery labels.

The labels provide supplementary qualitative evidence from interaction records. They do not measure rule discovery within the scoring window. The first five games use complete-rule criteria. Criteria for the other games also include successful execution supported by observed performance. Terse logs, especially for GPT-5.6-SOL, can leave a target unverified even when a successful policy uses it.Scope of the rule annotations.

These annotations describe evidence in interaction records, not additional score measurements. A high score alone does not establish every hidden rule. For Haunted Inn and Poisoner, the entries identify which seed-dependent rule and policy labels use the same seed as the scored trials.

item.title: SpeedrunBench：用速通任务考察 LLM 智能体的长程规划 ｜ SpeedrunBench: Challenging LLM Agents with Video Game Speedrunning
item.description:
一句话：把速通当作评测任务：智能体要自己找路线、抠帧、压缩步骤。

要点：

  • 速通天然要求长程规划与技巧性操作
  • 任务可量化（用时）且难以作弊
  • 暴露智能体在探索与执行上的短板

为什么值得看：AI 代理要驱动游戏玩法，执行精度与长程规划是硬指标；速通是现成的高难度标尺。

Abstract

Frontier LLM agents have been shown to be capable of solving increasingly complex tasks for which humans have measurable solutions. This begs the pertinent question of whether LLM agents can go beyond what humans have already solved. The ability to develop sophisticated strategies to tackle consequential problems becomes paramount as well-trodden, human-developed solutions become insufficient for problems for which we lack context or enough training data. We study agents’ capability of such strategy formation through the communal practice of video game speedrunning. In speedrunning, practitioners compete to find the fastest way to complete a video game under certain conditions, and in so doing uncovering interesting unorthodox play styles that require a thorough understanding and mastery of the underlying game mechanics. We introduce , a benchmark that evaluates frontier LLM agents across 9 different games. To perform well in this benchmark, agents must repeatedly improve their strategy, reflect on their performance, exploit their gained knowledge, and reason across a long-horizon of actions to improve on an increasingly difficult problem: being faster than themselves and everyone else. Our experiments show that while frontier agents approach human world records in simple platformer games, they remain behind human performance on longer, more complex games under practical budgets. These results suggest that is a useful testbed for studying agents’ strategy formation capabilities as well as being a saturation-resistant evaluation measure, as there is almost always a faster completion time waiting to be discovered.SpeedrunBenchSpeedrunBench1

Through the rich history of AI research, games have served as a common testbed for developing , testing and measuring various techniques, from search to state representation , and reinforcement learning . Games serve multiple desiderata for AI researchers: they are cheap, reproducible simulations with a clear ground truth , have human baselines , require multiple different skills across various modalities , and many games require long-horizon reasoning under partial observability . In being such a fruitful playground for AI development, games have been a driver of progress in their own right: developing AI to outplay humans in complex games has produced techniques that found uses elsewhere in AI research .(; )

It is no surprise, then, that games are once again an epicenter of AI evaluation. Their desirable qualities still hold as the landscape has shifted towards LLM agents, and prior work has leveraged many game genres , and purpose-built game environments in assessing model performance. However, benchmarking for game-playing agents has so far focused on : progress toward, or attainment of, the end of the game . While this remains a difficult task and, at the time of writing, a challenging one for frontier models , it does not provide researchers with an evergreen lens by which to continue to push and analyze model capabilities. No finite benchmark is immune to saturation, but some are more resistant, and we posit that is a better fit for the current landscape of LLM agents evaluation. It is one thing for an agent to finish a complex game; it is another to be the fastest in the world to do so. Speedrunning is a community practice whereby players attempt to complete a game under specified criteria (e.g., with or without glitches) in the fastest possible time . Players compete to beat the record, and discover strategies the game’s designers never anticipated (e.g., Figure ). These strategies arise from the underlying dynamics of the game systems and speedrunners develop a more complete model of a game’s mechanics than the people that built it . Game developers have responded in the past to speedrun records by patching their games, by deliberately preserving exploits, and by consulting speedrunners during development, with several studios reporting that speedrun analysis shaped design decisions . Thus, speedrunning is a proven mechanism by which humans have developed a cooperative culture of strategy formulation to optimize a shared goal (finding the fastest possible route to the end) that had downstream consequences for other objectives.(; ; ; ; ; ; )

As prior work has noted , games require long-horizon reasoning. Speedrunning stresses this further, as one must reason beyond what constitutes an acceptable solution to finding the fastest one. The state and action space of a game, even if held to be deterministic under a fixed seed, is finite but exponential in the machine’s memory , and it grows with every frame a run requires. If we take Super Mario Bros. for instance it has been shown to be NP-hard to complete, and speedrunning requires an additional optimality constraint, which makes it a more complex problem . Proving optimality in this context practically requires either a structural lower bound (e.g., the run must contain at least $n$ unavoidable frames) or exhaustion of the reachable space. This the source of speedrunning’s resistance to saturation, a game can be observed to be unsaturated whenever a new run exceeds the known best time, but saturation itself cannot be proven without solving the optimization problem outright. Thus, in practical terms, we should expect LLM agents to find speedrunning substantially harder than completion, as the task does not saturate when the agent does a successful valid run, every new record is an upper bound upon which to improve, and this improvement requires counterfactual reasoning about alternative routes and mechanics that no single episode reveals.

In the same way that beating the world’s experts at Go and Chess led to ground-breaking research in reinforcement learning , we believe speedrunning can invoke similar innovation in LLM agents.(; )

In this paper we introduce , a benchmark for evaluating LLM agents on speedrunning games, covering 10+ frontier agents and 9 different games.

We evaluate agents in three settings: an computer-use setting and two new offline settings. In , an agent observes the current frame and selects the next action or short sequence of actions while the game runs. In both offline settings, the agent repeatedly edits and replays a complete frame-indexed action trace for a fixed number of iterations.

begins with a goal-reaching reference trajectory and focuses on improving it, whereas requires the agent to first construct a successful trajectory. Each setting highlights a different capability: requires multimodal real-time perception, requires route discovery, as the agent begins without a successful trajectory, and focuses on improving an existing solution, as the agent begins with a successful reference trajectory. All settings demand long-horizon coherence, since the agent has to keep improving a route it already holds, over many turns, without breaking it.

Our experiments (Figure ) show that while recent frontier agents approach human world records on simpler platformer games, they remain slower on long, complex games such as role-playing, racing, and strategy games, given a fixed budget. Even when given a successful trace as a starting point, agents achieve only marginal improvements, showing a gap between finding a valid solution and improving it.SpeedrunBenchonlineonlineoffline-seedoffline-scratchonlineoffline-scratchoffline-seed

We define a game as a deterministic environment with state space $\mathcal{S}$

and a finite action space $\mathcal{A}$ , the set of controller inputs available on that console.

Play begins from a fixed initial state $s_{0}\in\mathcal{S}$ , and each action

advances the game by one frame, so a sequence of actions in $\mathcal{A}$ fully determines a run.

We explore three settings per game: , , for measuring different capabilities of each model (Figure ).

We further explain these three different setups in the following paragraphs.OnlineOffline-ScratchOffline-Seed

Online (Action prediction from screenshots)

Following prior work , given a current state $s$ of a game, the agent decides the next action $a\in\mathcal{A}$ .

A limited subset of frontier models (Opus 5, GPT-5.6-Sol, Grok 4.6) are capable of completing the game, but this setup only measures one aspect agent’s capability such as multimodal understanding. Since this setup can produce a baseline seed reference trajectory, we optimize it in the offline or trajectory editing setting.(; )

Hu et al., 2026

Zhang et al., 2025

Offline (Trace Editing)

This setting mimics human speedrunning by playing the game over and over again throughout the decades.

A run is represented as a frame-indexed action trace: a sequence of $n$ actions

$\{a_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}\in\mathcal{A}$ covering an entire action sequence, from start to goal.

On each turn the agent submits an edited trace, evaluated, and the agent receives the final state $s_{\text{final}}$ of the trace such as 1) outcome $o\in\{\text{true},\text{false}\}$ on whether it reached the goal, 2) the number of frames $f$ to reach the goal if $o=\text{true}$ , or the maximum progress the trace made if $o=\text{false}$ i.e., the edited trace no longer reached the goal.

The agent repeats this for a fixed number of turns (200 unless specified).

This can be regarded as action chunking i.e., predicting next $k$ actions  with an extremely long chunk.

3.3

For setup, we use a self-improving loop inspired by auto-research  to mimic humans speedrunning by playing the game multiple times, see where time was lost, change one thing, and run it again, for as long as the route keeps giving. The

settings reproduce that structure. At each iteration the agent selects its current best trace and the record of what it has already tried, proposes an edit, and receives a verdict.

We fix both the number of iterations and how many candidate traces the agent may evaluate within one iteration before committing to the edit it submits. These hyperparameters are left fixed across models.

That famous titles are memorized in model parameters is well known:

reports game content memorised during pretraining, and

Gemini 2.5 Pro has been observed confusing items across Pokémon versions, expecting tea where the game requires soda .

Hence, we add a controlled pair: Pokémon and Tuxemon holding genre and setting fixed while varying how much a title is likely to appear in a pretraining corpus. Both are turn-based RPGs, run under with the same iteration budget and scored on frames to the first gym.

Figure  shows that lower popularity does not make the open-source title harder to improve on when compared to the Pokémon run is the one in Figure . No model improves on the Pokémon seed by more than 1%, whereas GLM 5.3 and Grok 4.6 improve on the Tuxemon seed by 6.9% and 5.9%. Tuxemon is harder to make any progress on since every model on Pokémon submits at least one trace faster than the seed, while four of ten never submit a trace that reaches the Tuxemon gym.

Across ten models run on both titles, the rank correlation observed b/w titles is slightly negative at $-0.18$ . Hence, we see that results on a popular title are not predictive of performance on an unfamiliar one, which is consistent with popular titles being present in pretraining corpora.

We introduce , a benchmark that measures agents’ capability by assessing how fast an agent can finish a game and comparing it with the best known completion time. evaluates agents across three settings: an setting where agents get frame by frame screen shots and must take an action, and two settings where agents must optimize their game plan for the run either with a seeded trace or without.

We show that our benchmark remains challenging for current models (RQ1), as no agent reaches human world record on any game under a practical budget, with the best performing agent being on average as slow as the world record set by human players. Additionally we show that agents can improve their gameplay in an autoresearch-like loop (RQ2), even when the start seed is a near-optimal tool-assisted speedrun trace. However, giving the agents a slow seed as a starting point holds them back.

Agents perform better when they can construct the routes of their own accord, and expanding the agents’ ability to evaluate a candidate with a larger per-turn budget, as seen with how close the platformer games came to the world records.

We hope that inspires others to consider speedrunning as an avenue for pushing model abilities such as strategic thinking and long horizon coherence.SpeedrunBenchSpeedrunBenchonlineofflinemore than twiceSpeedrunBench

一句话：把速通当作评测任务：智能体要自己找路线、抠帧、压缩步骤。

要点：

  • 速通天然要求长程规划与技巧性操作
  • 任务可量化（用时）且难以作弊
  • 暴露智能体在探索与执行上的短板

为什么值得看：AI 代理要驱动游戏玩法，执行精度与长程规划是硬指标；速通是现成的高难度标尺。

中文摘要：SpeedrunBench 把速通（Speedrunning）引入智能体评测：跟普通通关不同，速通要求智能体找出最优路线、利用游戏机制漏洞、并在执行上做到近乎精确。这类任务天然可量化（完成时间），也很难通过背答案作弊。论文构建了相应的评测环境与基线，并分析了当前 LLM 智能体在该任务上的失败模式，为「AI 驱动玩法」的执行层能力提供了压力测试。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·智能体+游戏（English）

SpeedrunBench: Challenging LLM Agents with Video Game Speedrunning

Yoshinari Fujinuma

Keisuke Kamahori

Ryuto Koike

Abdelrahman Madkour

Affiliation: Varun Prashant Gangal, Monty Bichouna, Martyna Markiewicz, Shivani Jain,Affiliation: Duncan Curtis, Rebecca Qian, Anand Kannappan Patronus AI   University of Washington   Institute of Science Tokyo

Affiliation: Email:

{yoshinari.fujinuma,varun.gangal,abdelrahman.madkour,anand}@patronus.ai

Affiliation: kamahori@cs.washington.eduryuto.koike@nlp.comp.isct.ac.jp

Abstract

Frontier LLM agents have been shown to be capable of solving increasingly complex tasks for which humans have measurable solutions. This begs the pertinent question of whether LLM agents can go beyond what humans have already solved. The ability to develop sophisticated strategies to tackle consequential problems becomes paramount as well-trodden, human-developed solutions become insufficient for problems for which we lack context or enough training data. We study agents’ capability of such strategy formation through the communal practice of video game speedrunning. In speedrunning, practitioners compete to find the fastest way to complete a video game under certain conditions, and in so doing uncovering interesting unorthodox play styles that require a thorough understanding and mastery of the underlying game mechanics. We introduce , a benchmark that evaluates frontier LLM agents across 9 different games. To perform well in this benchmark, agents must repeatedly improve their strategy, reflect on their performance, exploit their gained knowledge, and reason across a long-horizon of actions to improve on an increasingly difficult problem: being faster than themselves and everyone else. Our experiments show that while frontier agents approach human world records in simple platformer games, they remain behind human performance on longer, more complex games under practical budgets. These results suggest that is a useful testbed for studying agents’ strategy formation capabilities as well as being a saturation-resistant evaluation measure, as there is almost always a faster completion time waiting to be discovered.SpeedrunBenchSpeedrunBench1

Through the rich history of AI research, games have served as a common testbed for developing , testing and measuring various techniques, from search to state representation , and reinforcement learning . Games serve multiple desiderata for AI researchers: they are cheap, reproducible simulations with a clear ground truth , have human baselines , require multiple different skills across various modalities , and many games require long-horizon reasoning under partial observability . In being such a fruitful playground for AI development, games have been a driver of progress in their own right: developing AI to outplay humans in complex games has produced techniques that found uses elsewhere in AI research .(; )

It is no surprise, then, that games are once again an epicenter of AI evaluation. Their desirable qualities still hold as the landscape has shifted towards LLM agents, and prior work has leveraged many game genres , and purpose-built game environments in assessing model performance. However, benchmarking for game-playing agents has so far focused on : progress toward, or attainment of, the end of the game . While this remains a difficult task and, at the time of writing, a challenging one for frontier models , it does not provide researchers with an evergreen lens by which to continue to push and analyze model capabilities. No finite benchmark is immune to saturation, but some are more resistant, and we posit that is a better fit for the current landscape of LLM agents evaluation. It is one thing for an agent to finish a complex game; it is another to be the fastest in the world to do so. Speedrunning is a community practice whereby players attempt to complete a game under specified criteria (e.g., with or without glitches) in the fastest possible time . Players compete to beat the record, and discover strategies the game’s designers never anticipated (e.g., Figure ). These strategies arise from the underlying dynamics of the game systems and speedrunners develop a more complete model of a game’s mechanics than the people that built it . Game developers have responded in the past to speedrun records by patching their games, by deliberately preserving exploits, and by consulting speedrunners during development, with several studios reporting that speedrun analysis shaped design decisions . Thus, speedrunning is a proven mechanism by which humans have developed a cooperative culture of strategy formulation to optimize a shared goal (finding the fastest possible route to the end) that had downstream consequences for other objectives.(; ; ; ; ; ; )

As prior work has noted , games require long-horizon reasoning. Speedrunning stresses this further, as one must reason beyond what constitutes an acceptable solution to finding the fastest one. The state and action space of a game, even if held to be deterministic under a fixed seed, is finite but exponential in the machine’s memory , and it grows with every frame a run requires. If we take Super Mario Bros. for instance it has been shown to be NP-hard to complete, and speedrunning requires an additional optimality constraint, which makes it a more complex problem . Proving optimality in this context practically requires either a structural lower bound (e.g., the run must contain at least $n$ unavoidable frames) or exhaustion of the reachable space. This the source of speedrunning’s resistance to saturation, a game can be observed to be unsaturated whenever a new run exceeds the known best time, but saturation itself cannot be proven without solving the optimization problem outright. Thus, in practical terms, we should expect LLM agents to find speedrunning substantially harder than completion, as the task does not saturate when the agent does a successful valid run, every new record is an upper bound upon which to improve, and this improvement requires counterfactual reasoning about alternative routes and mechanics that no single episode reveals.

In the same way that beating the world’s experts at Go and Chess led to ground-breaking research in reinforcement learning , we believe speedrunning can invoke similar innovation in LLM agents.(; )

In this paper we introduce , a benchmark for evaluating LLM agents on speedrunning games, covering 10+ frontier agents and 9 different games.

We evaluate agents in three settings: an computer-use setting and two new offline settings. In , an agent observes the current frame and selects the next action or short sequence of actions while the game runs. In both offline settings, the agent repeatedly edits and replays a complete frame-indexed action trace for a fixed number of iterations.

begins with a goal-reaching reference trajectory and focuses on improving it, whereas requires the agent to first construct a successful trajectory. Each setting highlights a different capability: requires multimodal real-time perception, requires route discovery, as the agent begins without a successful trajectory, and focuses on improving an existing solution, as the agent begins with a successful reference trajectory. All settings demand long-horizon coherence, since the agent has to keep improving a route it already holds, over many turns, without breaking it.

Our experiments (Figure ) show that while recent frontier agents approach human world records on simpler platformer games, they remain slower on long, complex games such as role-playing, racing, and strategy games, given a fixed budget. Even when given a successful trace as a starting point, agents achieve only marginal improvements, showing a gap between finding a valid solution and improving it.SpeedrunBenchonlineonlineoffline-seedoffline-scratchonlineoffline-scratchoffline-seed

Games have been serving as evaluation benchmarks for machine learning (ML) models well before LLMs became popular, from text adventures  to 2D

navigation  and abstract reasoning

tasks . Games were also the setting for some of

the field’s most visible results before LLMs, from Atari from

StarCraft II .

Recent benchmarks extend the setting to let frontier LLMs play games

directly. LMGame-Bench  supplies perception and memory scaffolds,

standardizes prompting, and screens for training data contamination, while

VideoGameBench  asks whether

vision-language models (VLMs) can complete popular titles at all.

pairs images with

questions to evaluate whether a VLM can identify what is wrong in a rendered screen. Individual

titles have also served as milestones in their own right, with Gemini 2.5 Pro clearing Pokémon

in 406.5 hours over two attempts , and

testing LLM capability on Pokémon battles

specifically.

Minecraft is the main setting where the objective is not merely completing something:

MineDojo  and Voyager  score an agent on how much it

acquires in an open world, by items obtained and skills learned.

In contrast, scores how

quickly it was completed, which continues to separate models after completion is reached by

challenging them to learn and discover speedrun-related skills.()

3.2

We define a game as a deterministic environment with state space $\mathcal{S}$

and a finite action space $\mathcal{A}$ , the set of controller inputs available on that console.

Play begins from a fixed initial state $s_{0}\in\mathcal{S}$ , and each action

advances the game by one frame, so a sequence of actions in $\mathcal{A}$ fully determines a run.

We explore three settings per game: , , for measuring different capabilities of each model (Figure ).

We further explain these three different setups in the following paragraphs.OnlineOffline-ScratchOffline-Seed

3

Online (Action prediction from screenshots)

Following prior work , given a current state $s$ of a game, the agent decides the next action $a\in\mathcal{A}$ .

A limited subset of frontier models (Opus 5, GPT-5.6-Sol, Grok 4.6) are capable of completing the game, but this setup only measures one aspect agent’s capability such as multimodal understanding. Since this setup can produce a baseline seed reference trajectory, we optimize it in the offline or trajectory editing setting.(; )

Hu et al., 2026

Zhang et al., 2025

Offline (Trace Editing)

This setting mimics human speedrunning by playing the game over and over again throughout the decades.

A run is represented as a frame-indexed action trace: a sequence of $n$ actions

$\{a_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}\in\mathcal{A}$ covering an entire action sequence, from start to goal.

On each turn the agent submits an edited trace, evaluated, and the agent receives the final state $s_{\text{final}}$ of the trace such as 1) outcome $o\in\{\text{true},\text{false}\}$ on whether it reached the goal, 2) the number of frames $f$ to reach the goal if $o=\text{true}$ , or the maximum progress the trace made if $o=\text{false}$ i.e., the edited trace no longer reached the goal.

The agent repeats this for a fixed number of turns (200 unless specified).

This can be regarded as action chunking i.e., predicting next $k$ actions  with an extremely long chunk.

5.2

Note that vision inputs are not required under settings, and therefore, more open-weight models can be evaluated under these settings. This is because, especially for simple games, no vision inputs are needed, smaller open-weight models can optimize.offline

3.3

For setup, we use a self-improving loop inspired by auto-research  to mimic humans speedrunning by playing the game multiple times, see where time was lost, change one thing, and run it again, for as long as the route keeps giving. The

settings reproduce that structure. At each iteration the agent selects its current best trace and the record of what it has already tried, proposes an edit, and receives a verdict.

We fix both the number of iterations and how many candidate traces the agent may evaluate within one iteration before committing to the edit it submits. These hyperparameters are left fixed across models.

5.1

In the experiments so far, the agent holds no in-turn scorer: it submits one trace per turn and gets one verdict. Here, we instead let the agent evaluate its own candidates, up to 200 per turn, and hold all else fixed. On SuperTux 1-1 this gives a controlled comparison, since the same models start from the same 9,498-frame seed and run for the same 200 turns in both settings

(Table ). With the scorer, every model escapes the seed and ends 4.0–5.1 $\times$

below where it ended without it. DeepSeek-V4-Pro reaches 1,847 frames, within 7% of the world

record and about two seconds slower, while DeepSeek-V4-Flash and GLM 5.2 remain 16% and 29% above

it (Figure ). On Super Mario Land 1-1, GLM 5.2 with the scorer

comes within 3% of the record after 220K evaluated traces over $\sim$ 114 hours

(Figure ), against 5,643 frames from the same human seed without

it. For these models, access to a scorer decides whether an agent escapes a non-optimal seeded trace, and

given enough evaluations the strongest agent on each short 2D level comes close to its world record.

5.3

That famous titles are memorized in model parameters is well known:

reports game content memorised during pretraining, and

Gemini 2.5 Pro has been observed confusing items across Pokémon versions, expecting tea where the game requires soda .

Hence, we add a controlled pair: Pokémon and Tuxemon holding genre and setting fixed while varying how much a title is likely to appear in a pretraining corpus. Both are turn-based RPGs, run under with the same iteration budget and scored on frames to the first gym.

Figure  shows that lower popularity does not make the open-source title harder to improve on when compared to the Pokémon run is the one in Figure . No model improves on the Pokémon seed by more than 1%, whereas GLM 5.3 and Grok 4.6 improve on the Tuxemon seed by 6.9% and 5.9%. Tuxemon is harder to make any progress on since every model on Pokémon submits at least one trace faster than the seed, while four of ten never submit a trace that reaches the Tuxemon gym.

Across ten models run on both titles, the rank correlation observed b/w titles is slightly negative at $-0.18$ . Hence, we see that results on a popular title are not predictive of performance on an unfamiliar one, which is consistent with popular titles being present in pretraining corpora.

We introduce , a benchmark that measures agents’ capability by assessing how fast an agent can finish a game and comparing it with the best known completion time. evaluates agents across three settings: an setting where agents get frame by frame screen shots and must take an action, and two settings where agents must optimize their game plan for the run either with a seeded trace or without.

We show that our benchmark remains challenging for current models (RQ1), as no agent reaches human world record on any game under a practical budget, with the best performing agent being on average as slow as the world record set by human players. Additionally we show that agents can improve their gameplay in an autoresearch-like loop (RQ2), even when the start seed is a near-optimal tool-assisted speedrun trace. However, giving the agents a slow seed as a starting point holds them back.

Agents perform better when they can construct the routes of their own accord, and expanding the agents’ ability to evaluate a candidate with a larger per-turn budget, as seen with how close the platformer games came to the world records.

We hope that inspires others to consider speedrunning as an avenue for pushing model abilities such as strategic thinking and long horizon coherence.SpeedrunBenchSpeedrunBenchonlineofflinemore than twiceSpeedrunBench

item.title: AI 游戏生成正在打一场「向下竞价」的战争 ｜ #007 - AI Game Creation is an "aggressive race to the bottom"
item.description:
一句话：行业观察：AI 生成游戏正在陷入价格战，内容质量反而被牺牲。

要点：

  • 分析生成式游戏工具如何在成本维度互相绞杀
  • 讨论 RE Engine 与 PS5 QSSR 等引擎侧技术动态
  • Sega 对生成式 AI 的态度与公关敏感点

为什么值得看：做 AI 原生引擎不只是技术选型，还要判断这个市场的价值走向——这篇给了行业侧的现实判断。

中文摘要：本期 AI and Games 由 Tommy Thompson 主持，围绕三条线索：一是 AI 生成游戏正在陷入「向下竞价」的恶性循环，工具越便宜、内容越同质；二是引擎侧动态，包括 RE Engine 与 PS5 的 QSSR 技术；三是 Sega 对生成式 AI 的谨慎态度及其公关敏感点。对关注「AI 原生引擎」商业化路径的开发者，这是一份来自行业观察者的冷静判断。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：AI and Games（English）

item.title: Esports World Model Dataset：用电竞数据训世界模型 ｜ Esports World Model Dataset
item.description:
一句话：把电竞比赛数据整理成世界模型训练集，为可预测的智能体环境提供数据基础。

要点：

  • 电竞对局天然带完整状态与操作序列
  • 数据集覆盖多款游戏的状态转移样本
  • 可支撑世界模型与智能体的训练与评测

为什么值得看：世界模型缺的不是模型而是数据；电竞数据是少有的「状态完整、动作对齐」的现成来源。

中文摘要：Esports World Model Dataset 把电竞比赛数据整理成可用于世界模型训练的结构化数据集：每局对局都有完整的状态序列与玩家操作，天然满足「状态-动作-下一状态」的训练格式。作者说明了数据采集、清洗与标注流程，并给出了世界模型在该数据上的训练与评测基准。对想训练「可预测的游戏环境」的团队，这类数据是稀缺资源。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·世界模型+游戏（English）

License: CC BY 4.0

arXiv:2610.16166v1 [cs.CV] 12 Oct 2026

Esports World Model Dataset

Weiyu Ma

Zeyuan Gong

King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST)

Affiliation: Xuhui Liu

King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST)

Affiliation: Wenxuan Zhang

King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST)

Affiliation: Jian Ding

King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST)

Affiliation: Xinyu Cui

Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences

Affiliation: Jian Zhao

Beijing Zhongguancun Academy & Zhongguancun Institute of Artificial Intelligence

Affiliation: Mohamed Elhoseiny

King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST)

Affiliation:

Abstract

Interactive world models must capture how multiple participants jointly

change a shared environment while observing different parts of it.

Competitive games make this challenge concrete: players cooperate

and compete, while fog of war, team vision and camera placement

determine what each can see. Modeling these interactions requires

data that connect individual observations and actions to shared

state and events.

We introduce the Esports World Model Dataset (EWM), a collection

of human gameplay spanning StarCraft II, Dota 2 and Counter-Strike 2,

with 3,053 games and maps and approximately 4,880 player-view hours,

including estimated hours for the ongoing CS2 extension. It includes

4,628 completed StarCraft II views, all ten perspectives for 303 Dota 2

matches, and up to ten views per round in CS2. Across these views,

replay-clock alignment connects rendered video with game-native

actions, structured state and events from the same match.

The three games expose complementary observation conditions:

private fog of war, shared team vision and first-person viewpoints.

In StarCraft II, player-specific entity records further distinguish live

observations from remembered snapshots and link co-observed entities

across opposing views. Together with temporal alignment, these records

allow researchers to distinguish legitimate information differences

from disagreement about shared state. By connecting human decisions, shared dynamics and player-specific

information, EWM supports research toward jointly controlled

multiplayer world models and interactive environments populated

by teammates and opponents learned from human play.

Dataset

Documentation

Code

EWM records every player’s view of real competitive matches. Each column shows two players of one match at the same instant, at the native $1280\times 720$ resolution: both players of a StarCraft II game (Esports World Cup 2025), a Radiant and a Dire player during a Dota 2 team fight (Esports World Cup 2026), and a Terrorist and a Counter-Terrorist in a Counter-Strike 2 round (IEM Kraków 2026). Each view is paired with the player’s actions and the engine state on the replay clock of the match.Figure 1:

Thirty player views from EWM, ten each from StarCraft II, Dota 2 and Counter-Strike 2 matches.Figure 2:

1

World models learn how an environment changes as agents interact with it. Recent advances in video generation and action-conditioned prediction have made it possible to simulate increasingly complex visual environments, from Atari and DOOM to commercial games and physical-world scenarios . For interactive models, the training data must connect what an agent observes, the actions it takes and the subsequent changes in its environment. Multiplayer settings extend this requirement: several agents act in the same world, but each may observe a different part of it.[, , , , , ]

11

12

1

26

3

21

This extension concerns who changes the world as well as who observes it. In competitive human play, each participant pursues objectives, selects actions and adapts to others; their decisions jointly shape the trajectory. A single-player prediction interface can absorb other actors into the environment, even when those actors behave actively. To study their interaction explicitly, data should associate each participant’s actions with their observations and the subsequent shared outcome. Recent multiplayer world models already explore joint action conditioning . A broader direction is to learn worlds populated by , with human gameplay providing examples of both cooperation and competition.[, ]

13

4

multiple active participants

Competitive games provide a concrete setting for connecting this interaction to observation. In StarCraft II, two opponents can watch the same battle and observe the same units, positions and damage. An army elsewhere on the map may be visible only to its owner, while an enemy building seen earlier remains as a remembered snapshot under fog of war. Both opponents can nevertheless issue commands that change what happens next, including outside the other’s current view. Dota 2 players share vision with their teammates but control separate cameras; Counter-Strike 2 players experience the same round through different first-person views. The paired views in illustrate these differences. A multiplayer world model must preserve while producing observations that reflect .

Figure1

a common underlying stateeach player’s information

Studying this behavior requires more than collecting several videos of the same match. When two views differ, the data should allow a researcher to determine whether they refer to the same replay time and entity, and whether that entity is currently observable to both players. These distinctions are difficult to recover reliably from pixels alone. Structured replay datasets provide actions and state for strategy games , while recent Counter-Strike datasets pair synchronized player videos with state and action trajectories . Dota2-Vis further studies visibility from team-perspective video . Together, these resources motivate a more direct connection between rendered gameplay and the information available to individual players.[, ]

27

18

[, ]

29

9

[]

5

We introduce the Esports World Model Dataset (EWM) to provide this connection across three competitive game genres. Starting from human match replays, we use the game clients to render player views and extract game-native actions, structured state and events. Replay time associates these outputs within each match. The resulting collection includes StarCraft II, Dota 2 and Counter-Strike 2, covering private fog of war, shared team vision and first-person viewpoints. This choice provides complementary observation regimes while retaining the native controls and state representation of each game. The recorded matches involve two human competitors in StarCraft II and ten in Dota 2 and Counter-Strike 2; video availability varies with the collection and, in CS2, player survival. These are trajectories of several decision-makers acting in one environment, with player views exposing different parts of that interaction.

The most detailed observation supervision is available in StarCraft II. Its player-specific records identify units that are currently observable and distinguish them from remembered snapshots. Live units observed by both players can be associated through their engine identifiers and compared on common state fields. The paired example in shows both kinds of information: shared units whose state agrees across players, and hidden units that appear only in their owner’s observation. These records connect a visible scene to the player’s information state, while keeping engine visibility distinct from whether an entity falls inside the camera window. Dota 2 and Counter-Strike 2 complement this supervision with multi-player video, replay-state streams and event-level records.

Figure8

This organization motivates two complementary directions for future world models. One is a shared simulation driven by several participants’ action streams, enabling them to interact in the same evolving world. The other retains a single focal player while using policies learned from human trajectories to control teammates or opponents. In that setting, policies choose the other participants’ actions and a world model predicts their joint consequences. Both directions build on the same need to connect human decisions, shared dynamics and player-specific information, alongside the observation-prediction and hidden-state tasks described later. Complete ten-player examples in and  make this relationship concrete: the participants experience one event through distinct views, with their actions and state associated on the match timeline.

Figures10

12

Our contributions are threefold:

•

We release , pairing rendered player views with game-native actions, state and events. Private fog of war, shared team vision and first-person viewpoints provide complementary settings for studying how several participants jointly change a world under different information constraints ().a multiplayer, multi-genre dataset of human interaction

Section3

•

We provide that distinguish live visibility from remembered snapshots and associate co-observed entities across opposing views. This supervision makes it possible to separate legitimate information differences from disagreement about shared state ().StarCraft II player-observation records

Section3.4

•

We document , with game-specific joining rules and linked visual, action and state examples. These provide a reproducible basis for constructing cross-player samples and inspecting their timing and observation semantics ( and ).replay-clock alignment and initial consistency checks

Sections3.6

4

We organize the report around the sources, extraction procedures and semantics of the released data, followed by coverage statistics and initial quality checks. The final sections describe research uses, evaluation requirements and future directions.

2

World models and multiplayer consistency.

Single-observer world models learn dynamics for control or generate interactive gameplay . Multiplayer systems increasingly generate several views jointly or maintain a shared representation . In particular, MIRA conditions on multiple players’ actions using bot-collected Rocket League trajectories . COMBO reasons from partial views in cooperative environments , while MASS, WorldWeaver and ConsistWorld study explicit state, memory or evidence sharing . These methods motivate datasets that associate multiple observations and action streams with a shared environment. EWM contributes human competitive trajectories across three games and adds StarCraft II records that identify which live state is available to each player.[, , , , ]

11

12

1

26

3

[, , , , ]

24

31

13

[]

[]

33

[, , ]

20

32

Video and embodied interaction data.

HowTo100M pairs instructional video with transcribed narration , while InternVid builds video–text pairs using generated descriptions . For learning actions from online gameplay, VPT uses an inverse dynamics model trained on a smaller labeled collection to annotate previously unlabeled video . Robotic resources provide a complementary approach: DROID records manipulation demonstrations across diverse scenes , and Open X-Embodiment standardizes datasets from multiple robot platforms . These efforts connect observations to language or actions at scale. EWM focuses on game-native commands, replay state and player-observation semantics; its three games retain their own action and state representations.[]

19

[]

28

[]

2

[]

14

[]

22

Rendered gameplay and replay datasets.

The closest Counter-Strike resources pair multiple player views with structured trajectories. X-Ego-CS includes synchronized perspectives from professional matches and a teammate/opponent location-prediction evaluation ; EgoCS-400K provides a substantially larger Counter-Strike collection with action, state and language annotations . Dota2-Vis provides dual-team video and minimap annotations for visibility analysis . places these approaches within the broader gameplay-data landscape. EWM extends this coverage to complementary strategy-game observation regimes, with player-specific entity records in StarCraft II.[]

29

Table1

Engine state / events: game state or events from the engine. Multi-POV: synchronized views of several players in one match. Cross-genre: several game genres. ✓ yes, ❍ partial, – no.Table 1:
