Partial observation and hidden-state estimation.

Brood War and StarCraft II datasets have long supported learning from structured replays ; Defogger predicts hidden strategy-game state . EWM connects that problem to rendered multi-view gameplay and distinguishes observation labels from privileged state. This distinction is also complementary to synchronized real-world egocentric video, where a game engine is unavailable as a source of entity records .[, , , ]

15

30

27

18

[]

25

[, ]

7

8

3

EWM is organized around a match and its replay timeline. Each is rendered from one participant’s perspective and associated with actions, state and events through the game’s replay clock. The three games share this organization but differ in their observation rules, native controls and available structured records. We first describe the sources and extraction procedures, then use concrete examples to explain how the modalities should be read together.player view

3.1

The collection combines high-ranked ladder and professional play (). In StarCraft II, most games are high-ranked ladder matches; 88% of views with known rating are at least 5,000 MMR. The 190 professional games come from the Esports World Cup 2025, Kung Fu Cup 2026 and Rongyi Cup Season 3 (2026), on game versions 5.0.14 and 5.0.15. Dota 2 sources are The International 2025, Esports World Cup 2026 and regional qualifiers of the Road to ENC 2026. The CS2 core combines 30 professional and 20 matchmaking maps, while the extended collection contains additional professional series. gives the event-level counts and identifies sources that remain unlabelled.

Figure3

Table4

Where the matches come from. StarCraft II combines tournament games with high-MMR ranked games; all Dota 2 matches and the Counter-Strike 2 extended set are professional, from the events shown and their qualifiers.Figure 3:

The games provide different settings for multi-view modeling. StarCraft II pairs two opponents whose armies explore a shared map under private fog of war. Dota 2 provides ten player cameras with shared vision within each team. Counter-Strike 2 provides first-person views of short rounds in which the available views decrease as players die. These differences determine both what a model can observe and how a prediction should be evaluated.

Modalities per game. All streams of a match share one clock.Table 2:

StarCraft IIDota 2Views2 per game10 per matchVideo $\times$ $\times$ camera view without interface, 1280720; minimap, 256256; 22.4 fps $\times$ Player View with interface and minimap, 1280720, 30 fpsActionsunit commands (ability, target, queued flag) and camera movesunit orders of all ten players, attributed to the issuing playerStateobserved units per view (type, owner, alliance, visibility, position, health, shields, energy, orders, buffs), resources, score, upgrades, cameracomplete entity state as a lossless change streamEventsunit deaths; game resultall game messages, including the combat logClockgame loop, 22.4/sreplay tick, 30/sFrame alignmentone frame per game loopreplay tick of every frame

summarizes the native streams. They are associated by replay time, but the action spaces are game-specific. The CS2 core records button states and view angles; recovery of raw mouse movement is a feature of the extended pipeline. Likewise, the core uses a round-level frame/tick rule, while the extended pipeline supplies explicit per-frame alignment tables. The timing conventions are detailed below.

Table2

3.2

A replay stores information used by the game engine to reproduce a recorded match. We use the Windows game clients to render player views and associate them with structured records on the replay timeline. summarizes the common organization of these processes: obtain player views and native records, associate them by replay time, and package the paired outputs. The game-specific implementations differ in how they obtain observations, decode state and map frames to the replay clock.

Figure4

StarCraft II.

The replay is loaded in its matching game build and replayed once per player with fog of war enabled. At each game loop, the extraction records the camera image, minimap and player-specific observation, together with actions and camera metadata. Matching the build allows both views to traverse the same replay timeline and retain shared tags for live units.

Dota 2.

The replay is parsed into entity-property changes and game messages, including combat logs and orders attributed to their issuing players. Persistent clients render the ten player slots in Player View mode in 120-second segments. The per-frame alignment records associate each independently rendered video with replay ticks and with actions in its frame intervals.

Counter-Strike 2.

The parser extracts round boundaries, player states, inputs and events. A recording process follows each player in first-person spectator mode, with the playback controls hidden. Clips run from round start until two seconds after the player’s death or the end of the round. The extended pipeline also checks client-build compatibility and recorded-player identity.

Shared data-construction stages and game-specific implementations. Native clients render player views, while game-specific extraction supplies actions and records; SC2 observations come from the replaying engine. Streams are associated on each match’s replay clock and packaged as paired outputs. The CS2 core uses four-tick frame intervals; its extension uses explicit mappings. This schematic summarizes separately implemented processes, and its game images and record tables are illustrative.Figure 4:

3.3

The montage in illustrates the visual coverage of the collection. To understand what these videos provide to a model, it is useful to first inspect the individual observation interfaces (, and ), then compare players at a common replay time. The montage samples different matches; the paired and team-view examples below establish the within-match correspondence.

Figure2

Figures5

6

7

In StarCraft II, a player controls an economy and an army while the camera exposes a local region of the map. The camera video omits the interface, and the minimap is a separate stream. A player’s raw entity observation can contain units outside this camera window, which is why camera RGB and engine-visible state must be treated as distinct modalities.

Dota 2’s Player View includes the player’s camera, interface and minimap. Teammates share vision but can attend to different parts of the same encounter. The first-person CS2 view includes its HUD and radar and is tied to one player’s position and viewing direction. These differences affect the information budget of a prediction or policy-learning task even when all three games supply video, actions and state.

StarCraft II: current observations and remembered state.

The released raw observation is player-specific and camera-independent. It records the player’s own units, neutral units and enemy units exposed by the engine’s observation rules. An engine-visible enemy can therefore be outside the current RGB frame. An enemy record marked describes a live observation. When an observed enemy structure returns under fog, the engine may retain a of its last-seen type and position. This memory record carries no current health or orders and may persist after the structure has disappeared. Enemy units that are neither currently observed nor retained as snapshots are absent.visiblesnapshot

shows this distinction in a single encounter. Units A and B are observed by both players, with matching common state, while only the owner has their orders. The units marked C appear in the owner’s frame and are absent from the opponent’s observation.

For a precise cross-view join, let $L_{i}(t)$ denote the engine tags of live units marked visible in player $i$ ’s observation at replay time $t$ . The set of live co-observed entities for players $i$ and $j$ is

$C_{ij}(t)=L_{i}(t)\cap L_{j}(t).$ (1)

The join is scoped to one match and replay time. On $C_{ij}(t)$ , the audit in compares common fields such as type, position, health and shield. Owner-only orders are outside this comparison. Remembered snapshots are excluded from the live-state join and examined separately through their last-seen information.

Evaluating generated pixels additionally requires a validated association between image content and entities, including camera projection and rendering effects.Engine visibility, camera-window inclusion and rendered pixels are different quantities.

3.6

We distinguish replay time, trajectory row index and video frame index. Replay time is an integer game loop in StarCraft II or a replay tick in Dota 2 and Counter-Strike 2. A frame index is local to one rendered view and must not be treated as a shared clock without checking the alignment records.

StarCraft II stores one trajectory row and one frame per game loop. Using $n$ for the trajectory row index, the action in row $n$ is assigned to the interval between observations $n$ and $n+1$ ; the explicit game-loop field provides replay time. Dota 2 records each frame’s replay tick and orders issued in the frame interval. Cross-view joins must account for repeated or missing samples.

In the core CS2 set, frame $k$ covers ticks $t_{r}+4k$ through $t_{r}+4k+3$ , where $t_{r}$ is the recorded round-start tick. This identifies an interval rather than a single engine state. The extended pipeline records frame-to-tick alignment explicitly. Views should be aligned by replay time and available ticks rather than by their endpoints.

The audits address two prerequisites for using the collection: whether observations can be associated on a shared replay clock, and whether live entity records that refer to the same world state can be compared across views. states the scope of each available check and the inference it supports.

Clock alignment.

For StarCraft II, camera commands provide an internal timing check: across 5.6M moves, the stored camera position matches the command target without a step offset. Shuffling commands within the view increases the reported positional error to 53.4 map units. This check measures the temporal association between stored camera commands and observations.

Dota 2 provides a complementary failure case. Independently rendered views have monotonic frame-to-tick mappings, but the same frame index can refer to different replay times. The largest difference in the audited matches is 0.83 s (). Joining on stored replay ticks addresses this indexing mismatch. CS2 joins similarly use the round-start tick and the frame interval defined in ; aligning clips by their ends would introduce offsets caused by different death times.

Live state and remembered observations.

The SC2 audit compares 13 games at every game loop. It joins 5.2M visible-enemy records to the owner’s records by engine tag and compares the common fields identified after . Snapshots are audited separately using their last-seen type and position, because a remembered structure may persist after its live counterpart has disappeared.

Equation1

The same sample illustrates why multiple views are informative: roughly 10% of a player’s units are visible to the opponent at a time (). This statistic describes 26 views from 13 games. The paired observations expose both shared state and substantial private information.

Figure30

Share of a player’s units visible to the opponent over a game (StarCraft II, 26 views of 13 games). Visibility is the engine’s fog-of-war state, not camera-window inclusion.Figure 29:

Largest replay-time difference between the ten Dota 2 views at one frame index, per audited match. Joining on the replay tick removes this frame-index offset.Figure 30:

5

EWM connects the actions of multiple human participants to their

player-specific observations and the evolution of a shared environment.

The full-team sequences in

and  illustrate this connection:

participants experience the same interaction through different views,

with their actions and event outcomes associated on a common replay

clock. This organization provides a data foundation for studying

world models with multiple active participants.

Figures19

23

Jointly controlled multiplayer worlds.

A central direction is to learn shared dynamics conditioned on several

participants’ actions while generating observations appropriate to

each player. Such a model could allow multiple users or agents to

cooperate and compete in one evolving world. EWM provides human

interaction trajectories across three complementary settings:

private fog of war, shared team vision and first-person viewpoints.

These settings connect visual prediction to coordination, opponent

adaptation and decisions made under partial information. Cross-view

state agreement and player-specific observation accuracy provide

complementary targets for evaluating the resulting simulations.

Human-data-driven teammates and opponents.

A complementary direction retains one focal player and learns policies

for the surrounding participants from human trajectories. In a

ten-player setting, one user could interact with nine learned teammates

and opponents, each choosing actions from its own observation history.

The policies determine how participants act, while the world model

predicts the consequences of their joint actions. EWM’s attributed

action streams and paired observations provide supervision for studying

both components. This combination could support characters that pursue

objectives, coordinate and initiate encounters, with held-out action

prediction, behavioral diversity and sustained cooperation or

competition providing useful evaluation targets.

Learning under partial observability.

The same data support predicting a player’s future observations and

estimating hidden state from observation history. SC2’s live entity

records, remembered snapshots and shared identifiers connect these

tasks to explicit observation semantics. A model can use historical

evidence to infer an unseen opponent’s likely state while generating

a view that respects the player’s current information. Remembered

snapshots provide historical observations; replay or owner-view

records provide reference state for fields available in those records.

The associated video and action sequences also support long-horizon

video understanding and imitation learning.

Experimental setup.

Each task should specify its observation modality and action inputs.

Camera RGB, minimap and camera-independent raw observations expose

different information. A focal-player task uses the player’s permitted

history and actions, whereas a joint simulator can condition on joint

actions. Dota 2 order tables therefore need to be filtered for

focal-player inputs. Full replay state and other players’ private

actions can serve as labels or explicitly privileged training

supervision. Structured evaluation can measure shared-state agreement

and observable-entity recovery; evaluation of video outputs additionally

requires an image-to-entity mapping.

Data should be split before sampling clips, keeping all players,

rounds and clips from a match together. CS2 maps should be grouped by

series when testing generalization across series. The SC2 release

provides the split in ; map-, patch- and player-disjoint

splits address further generalization questions.

Table3

6

The current release provides entity-level observation labels for SC2,

replay-rendered views with expert-heavy coverage, and initial audits

on selected matches. CS2 clips end shortly after player death, reducing

late-round view coverage. These characteristics guide the next stages

of dataset development.

Expanding coverage and observation labels.

The ongoing CS2 collection broadens the available match and participant

coverage. Extending player-specific visibility extraction to Dota 2

would connect its team-view videos to explicit observation labels.

Developing image-to-entity mappings would further link rendered

content to structured records, supporting visual evaluation across

different observation regimes.

Building reproducible benchmarks.

A next step is to establish fixed splits, input specifications and

baselines for observation prediction, hidden-state estimation and

cross-view consistency. SC2 provides a starting point through its live

observations, remembered snapshots and shared entity identifiers;

comparable protocols can then be developed for Dota 2 and CS2.

Broader data audits should report field-level errors, join failures

and event-to-image timing measurements. Versioned documentation

following datasheet principles can record

the collection, filtering and evaluation procedures, providing a

reproducible foundation for the research directions above.[]

6

7

Non-professional SC2 identities are redacted in the standard release;

identity handling is not uniform across all raw game files.

The project-authored structured data, alignment tables, metadata,

scripts and documentation are provided for non-commercial research

under CC BY-NC 4.0, as described in the release documentation.

Game footage, assets, replays and trademarks remain subject to their

owners’ rights and applicable source terms; the project license does

not cover that third-party content. Users should follow the release’s

access and reuse conditions. Inquiries may be sent to

.

sc2meisah@gmail.com

8

EWM pairs replay-rendered human competitive gameplay with actions and structured records across three observation regimes. These trajectories capture multiple participants whose decisions jointly change one world, with each player observing only part of it. Its central addition is the connection, in SC2, between synchronized player views and entity records that distinguish live shared information from remembered or unavailable observations. Paired encounters, full-team sequences and linked event records show how to construct samples at the level of a participant, an interaction or a shared match. The initial audits illustrate how to inspect these records and why views should be joined on replay time. These checks connect the data organization to the construction of temporally aligned, observation-aware samples. Looking ahead, such data can underpin research on both jointly controlled multiplayer worlds and single-player experiences populated by policies learned from human behavior. The dataset is intended to make those investigations, alongside observation prediction and hidden-state estimation, reproducible and easier to define.

一句话：把电竞比赛数据整理成世界模型训练集，为可预测的智能体环境提供数据基础。

要点：

  • 电竞对局天然带完整状态与操作序列
  • 数据集覆盖多款游戏的状态转移样本
  • 可支撑世界模型与智能体的训练与评测

为什么值得看：世界模型缺的不是模型而是数据；电竞数据是少有的「状态完整、动作对齐」的现成来源。

中文摘要：Esports World Model Dataset 把电竞比赛数据整理成可用于世界模型训练的结构化数据集：每局对局都有完整的状态序列与玩家操作，天然满足「状态-动作-下一状态」的训练格式。作者说明了数据采集、清洗与标注流程，并给出了世界模型在该数据上的训练与评测基准。对想训练「可预测的游戏环境」的团队，这类数据是稀缺资源。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·世界模型+游戏（English）

License: CC BY 4.0

arXiv:2610.16166v1 [cs.CV] 12 Oct 2026

Esports World Model Dataset

Weiyu Ma

Zeyuan Gong

King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST)

Affiliation: Xuhui Liu

Affiliation:

Abstract

Interactive world models must capture how multiple participants jointly

change a shared environment while observing different parts of it.

Competitive games make this challenge concrete: players cooperate

and compete, while fog of war, team vision and camera placement

determine what each can see. Modeling these interactions requires

data that connect individual observations and actions to shared

state and events.

We introduce the Esports World Model Dataset (EWM), a collection

of human gameplay spanning StarCraft II, Dota 2 and Counter-Strike 2,

with 3,053 games and maps and approximately 4,880 player-view hours,

including estimated hours for the ongoing CS2 extension. It includes

4,628 completed StarCraft II views, all ten perspectives for 303 Dota 2

matches, and up to ten views per round in CS2. Across these views,

replay-clock alignment connects rendered video with game-native

actions, structured state and events from the same match.

The three games expose complementary observation conditions:

private fog of war, shared team vision and first-person viewpoints.

In StarCraft II, player-specific entity records further distinguish live

observations from remembered snapshots and link co-observed entities

across opposing views. Together with temporal alignment, these records

allow researchers to distinguish legitimate information differences

from disagreement about shared state. By connecting human decisions, shared dynamics and player-specific

information, EWM supports research toward jointly controlled

multiplayer world models and interactive environments populated

by teammates and opponents learned from human play.

Dataset

Documentation

Code

EWM records every player’s view of real competitive matches. Each column shows two players of one match at the same instant, at the native $1280\times 720$ resolution: both players of a StarCraft II game (Esports World Cup 2025), a Radiant and a Dire player during a Dota 2 team fight (Esports World Cup 2026), and a Terrorist and a Counter-Terrorist in a Counter-Strike 2 round (IEM Kraków 2026). Each view is paired with the player’s actions and the engine state on the replay clock of the match.Figure 1:

Thirty player views from EWM, ten each from StarCraft II, Dota 2 and Counter-Strike 2 matches.Figure 2:

1

World models learn how an environment changes as agents interact with it. Recent advances in video generation and action-conditioned prediction have made it possible to simulate increasingly complex visual environments, from Atari and DOOM to commercial games and physical-world scenarios . For interactive models, the training data must connect what an agent observes, the actions it takes and the subsequent changes in its environment. Multiplayer settings extend this requirement: several agents act in the same world, but each may observe a different part of it.[, , , , , ]

11

12

1

26

3

21

This extension concerns who changes the world as well as who observes it. In competitive human play, each participant pursues objectives, selects actions and adapts to others; their decisions jointly shape the trajectory. A single-player prediction interface can absorb other actors into the environment, even when those actors behave actively. To study their interaction explicitly, data should associate each participant’s actions with their observations and the subsequent shared outcome. Recent multiplayer world models already explore joint action conditioning . A broader direction is to learn worlds populated by , with human gameplay providing examples of both cooperation and competition.[, ]

13

4

multiple active participants

Competitive games provide a concrete setting for connecting this interaction to observation. In StarCraft II, two opponents can watch the same battle and observe the same units, positions and damage. An army elsewhere on the map may be visible only to its owner, while an enemy building seen earlier remains as a remembered snapshot under fog of war. Both opponents can nevertheless issue commands that change what happens next, including outside the other’s current view. Dota 2 players share vision with their teammates but control separate cameras; Counter-Strike 2 players experience the same round through different first-person views. The paired views in illustrate these differences. A multiplayer world model must preserve while producing observations that reflect .

Figure1

a common underlying stateeach player’s information

Studying this behavior requires more than collecting several videos of the same match. When two views differ, the data should allow a researcher to determine whether they refer to the same replay time and entity, and whether that entity is currently observable to both players. These distinctions are difficult to recover reliably from pixels alone. Structured replay datasets provide actions and state for strategy games , while recent Counter-Strike datasets pair synchronized player videos with state and action trajectories . Dota2-Vis further studies visibility from team-perspective video . Together, these resources motivate a more direct connection between rendered gameplay and the information available to individual players.[, ]

27

18

[, ]

29

9

[]

5

We introduce the Esports World Model Dataset (EWM) to provide this connection across three competitive game genres. Starting from human match replays, we use the game clients to render player views and extract game-native actions, structured state and events. Replay time associates these outputs within each match. The resulting collection includes StarCraft II, Dota 2 and Counter-Strike 2, covering private fog of war, shared team vision and first-person viewpoints. This choice provides complementary observation regimes while retaining the native controls and state representation of each game. The recorded matches involve two human competitors in StarCraft II and ten in Dota 2 and Counter-Strike 2; video availability varies with the collection and, in CS2, player survival. These are trajectories of several decision-makers acting in one environment, with player views exposing different parts of that interaction.

The most detailed observation supervision is available in StarCraft II. Its player-specific records identify units that are currently observable and distinguish them from remembered snapshots. Live units observed by both players can be associated through their engine identifiers and compared on common state fields. The paired example in shows both kinds of information: shared units whose state agrees across players, and hidden units that appear only in their owner’s observation. These records connect a visible scene to the player’s information state, while keeping engine visibility distinct from whether an entity falls inside the camera window. Dota 2 and Counter-Strike 2 complement this supervision with multi-player video, replay-state streams and event-level records.

Figure8

This organization motivates two complementary directions for future world models. One is a shared simulation driven by several participants’ action streams, enabling them to interact in the same evolving world. The other retains a single focal player while using policies learned from human trajectories to control teammates or opponents. In that setting, policies choose the other participants’ actions and a world model predicts their joint consequences. Both directions build on the same need to connect human decisions, shared dynamics and player-specific information, alongside the observation-prediction and hidden-state tasks described later. Complete ten-player examples in and  make this relationship concrete: the participants experience one event through distinct views, with their actions and state associated on the match timeline.

Figures10

12

Our contributions are threefold:

•

We release , pairing rendered player views with game-native actions, state and events. Private fog of war, shared team vision and first-person viewpoints provide complementary settings for studying how several participants jointly change a world under different information constraints ().a multiplayer, multi-genre dataset of human interaction

Section3

•

We provide that distinguish live visibility from remembered snapshots and associate co-observed entities across opposing views. This supervision makes it possible to separate legitimate information differences from disagreement about shared state ().StarCraft II player-observation records

Section3.4

•

We document , with game-specific joining rules and linked visual, action and state examples. These provide a reproducible basis for constructing cross-player samples and inspecting their timing and observation semantics ( and ).replay-clock alignment and initial consistency checks

Sections3.6

4

We organize the report around the sources, extraction procedures and semantics of the released data, followed by coverage statistics and initial quality checks. The final sections describe research uses, evaluation requirements and future directions.

2

World models and multiplayer consistency.

Single-observer world models learn dynamics for control or generate interactive gameplay . Multiplayer systems increasingly generate several views jointly or maintain a shared representation . In particular, MIRA conditions on multiple players’ actions using bot-collected Rocket League trajectories . COMBO reasons from partial views in cooperative environments , while MASS, WorldWeaver and ConsistWorld study explicit state, memory or evidence sharing . These methods motivate datasets that associate multiple observations and action streams with a shared environment. EWM contributes human competitive trajectories across three games and adds StarCraft II records that identify which live state is available to each player.[, , , , ]

Video and embodied interaction data.

HowTo100M pairs instructional video with transcribed narration , while InternVid builds video–text pairs using generated descriptions . For learning actions from online gameplay, VPT uses an inverse dynamics model trained on a smaller labeled collection to annotate previously unlabeled video . Robotic resources provide a complementary approach: DROID records manipulation demonstrations across diverse scenes , and Open X-Embodiment standardizes datasets from multiple robot platforms . These efforts connect observations to language or actions at scale. EWM focuses on game-native commands, replay state and player-observation semantics; its three games retain their own action and state representations.[]

Rendered gameplay and replay datasets.

The closest Counter-Strike resources pair multiple player views with structured trajectories. X-Ego-CS includes synchronized perspectives from professional matches and a teammate/opponent location-prediction evaluation ; EgoCS-400K provides a substantially larger Counter-Strike collection with action, state and language annotations . Dota2-Vis provides dual-team video and minimap annotations for visibility analysis . places these approaches within the broader gameplay-data landscape. EWM extends this coverage to complementary strategy-game observation regimes, with player-specific entity records in StarCraft II.[]

Partial observation and hidden-state estimation.

Brood War and StarCraft II datasets have long supported learning from structured replays ; Defogger predicts hidden strategy-game state . EWM connects that problem to rendered multi-view gameplay and distinguishes observation labels from privileged state. This distinction is also complementary to synchronized real-world egocentric video, where a game engine is unavailable as a source of entity records .[, , , ]

EWM is organized around a match and its replay timeline. Each is rendered from one participant’s perspective and associated with actions, state and events through the game’s replay clock. The three games share this organization but differ in their observation rules, native controls and available structured records. We first describe the sources and extraction procedures, then use concrete examples to explain how the modalities should be read together.player view

3.1

The collection combines high-ranked ladder and professional play (). In StarCraft II, most games are high-ranked ladder matches; 88% of views with known rating are at least 5,000 MMR. The 190 professional games come from the Esports World Cup 2025, Kung Fu Cup 2026 and Rongyi Cup Season 3 (2026), on game versions 5.0.14 and 5.0.15. Dota 2 sources are The International 2025, Esports World Cup 2026 and regional qualifiers of the Road to ENC 2026. The CS2 core combines 30 professional and 20 matchmaking maps, while the extended collection contains additional professional series. gives the event-level counts and identifies sources that remain unlabelled.

Where the matches come from. StarCraft II combines tournament games with high-MMR ranked games; all Dota 2 matches and the Counter-Strike 2 extended set are professional, from the events shown and their qualifiers.Figure 3:

The games provide different settings for multi-view modeling. StarCraft II pairs two opponents whose armies explore a shared map under private fog of war. Dota 2 provides ten player cameras with shared vision within each team. Counter-Strike 2 provides first-person views of short rounds in which the available views decrease as players die. These differences determine both what a model can observe and how a prediction should be evaluated.

3.2

A replay stores information used by the game engine to reproduce a recorded match. We use the Windows game clients to render player views and associate them with structured records on the replay timeline. summarizes the common organization of these processes: obtain player views and native records, associate them by replay time, and package the paired outputs. The game-specific implementations differ in how they obtain observations, decode state and map frames to the replay clock.

Figure4

StarCraft II.

The replay is loaded in its matching game build and replayed once per player with fog of war enabled. At each game loop, the extraction records the camera image, minimap and player-specific observation, together with actions and camera metadata. Matching the build allows both views to traverse the same replay timeline and retain shared tags for live units.

Dota 2.

The replay is parsed into entity-property changes and game messages, including combat logs and orders attributed to their issuing players. Persistent clients render the ten player slots in Player View mode in 120-second segments. The per-frame alignment records associate each independently rendered video with replay ticks and with actions in its frame intervals.

Counter-Strike 2.

The parser extracts round boundaries, player states, inputs and events. A recording process follows each player in first-person spectator mode, with the playback controls hidden. Clips run from round start until two seconds after the player’s death or the end of the round. The extended pipeline also checks client-build compatibility and recorded-player identity.

Shared data-construction stages and game-specific implementations. Native clients render player views, while game-specific extraction supplies actions and records; SC2 observations come from the replaying engine. Streams are associated on each match’s replay clock and packaged as paired outputs. The CS2 core uses four-tick frame intervals; its extension uses explicit mappings. This schematic summarizes separately implemented processes, and its game images and record tables are illustrative.Figure 4:

In StarCraft II, a player controls an economy and an army while the camera exposes a local region of the map. The camera video omits the interface, and the minimap is a separate stream. A player’s raw entity observation can contain units outside this camera window, which is why camera RGB and engine-visible state must be treated as distinct modalities.

Dota 2’s Player View includes the player’s camera, interface and minimap. Teammates share vision but can attend to different parts of the same encounter. The first-person CS2 view includes its HUD and radar and is tied to one player’s position and viewing direction. These differences affect the information budget of a prediction or policy-learning task even when all three games supply video, actions and state.

StarCraft II: current observations and remembered state.

The released raw observation is player-specific and camera-independent. It records the player’s own units, neutral units and enemy units exposed by the engine’s observation rules. An engine-visible enemy can therefore be outside the current RGB frame. An enemy record marked describes a live observation. When an observed enemy structure returns under fog, the engine may retain a of its last-seen type and position. This memory record carries no current health or orders and may persist after the structure has disappeared. Enemy units that are neither currently observed nor retained as snapshots are absent.visiblesnapshot

shows this distinction in a single encounter. Units A and B are observed by both players, with matching common state, while only the owner has their orders. The units marked C appear in the owner’s frame and are absent from the opponent’s observation.

For a precise cross-view join, let $L_{i}(t)$ denote the engine tags of live units marked visible in player $i$ ’s observation at replay time $t$ . The set of live co-observed entities for players $i$ and $j$ is

$C_{ij}(t)=L_{i}(t)\cap L_{j}(t).$ (1)

The join is scoped to one match and replay time. On $C_{ij}(t)$ , the audit in compares common fields such as type, position, health and shield. Owner-only orders are outside this comparison. Remembered snapshots are excluded from the live-state join and examined separately through their last-seen information.

The structured records identify the player’s observation state; camera metadata helps locate that observation in the view. Evaluating generated pixels additionally requires a validated association between image content and entities, including camera projection and rendering effects.Engine visibility, camera-window inclusion and rendered pixels are different quantities.

Dota 2: shared vision and independent cameras.

Five teammates share vision but move their cameras independently. The rendered Player View includes the interface and minimap, while the parsed state stream contains information beyond a single player’s view. Per-entity player-visibility labels are not part of the current release. At the kill event in , the victim and killer reach replay tick 85,916 at different local frame indices. Their alignment records establish the correspondence between the views.

3.6

We distinguish replay time, trajectory row index and video frame index. Replay time is an integer game loop in StarCraft II or a replay tick in Dota 2 and Counter-Strike 2. A frame index is local to one rendered view and must not be treated as a shared clock without checking the alignment records.

StarCraft II stores one trajectory row and one frame per game loop. Using $n$ for the trajectory row index, the action in row $n$ is assigned to the interval between observations $n$ and $n+1$ ; the explicit game-loop field provides replay time. Dota 2 records each frame’s replay tick and orders issued in the frame interval. Cross-view joins must account for repeated or missing samples.

In the core CS2 set, frame $k$ covers ticks $t_{r}+4k$ through $t_{r}+4k+3$ , where $t_{r}$ is the recorded round-start tick. This identifies an interval rather than a single engine state. The extended pipeline records frame-to-tick alignment explicitly. Views should be aligned by replay time and available ticks rather than by their endpoints.

Clock alignment.

For StarCraft II, camera commands provide an internal timing check: across 5.6M moves, the stored camera position matches the command target without a step offset. Shuffling commands within the view increases the reported positional error to 53.4 map units. This check measures the temporal association between stored camera commands and observations.

Dota 2 provides a complementary failure case. Independently rendered views have monotonic frame-to-tick mappings, but the same frame index can refer to different replay times. The largest difference in the audited matches is 0.83 s (). Joining on stored replay ticks addresses this indexing mismatch. CS2 joins similarly use the round-start tick and the frame interval defined in ; aligning clips by their ends would introduce offsets caused by different death times.

Snapshots are audited separately using their last-seen type and position, because a remembered structure may persist after its live counterpart has disappeared.

5

EWM connects the actions of multiple human participants to their

player-specific observations and the evolution of a shared environment.

The full-team sequences in

and  illustrate this connection:

participants experience the same interaction through different views,

with their actions and event outcomes associated on a common replay

clock. This organization provides a data foundation for studying

world models with multiple active participants.

Figures19

23

Jointly controlled multiplayer worlds.

A central direction is to learn shared dynamics conditioned on several

participants’ actions while generating observations appropriate to

each player. Such a model could allow multiple users or agents to

cooperate and compete in one evolving world. EWM provides human

interaction trajectories across three complementary settings:

private fog of war, shared team vision and first-person viewpoints.

These settings connect visual prediction to coordination, opponent

adaptation and decisions made under partial information. Cross-view

state agreement and player-specific observation accuracy provide

complementary targets for evaluating the resulting simulations.

Human-data-driven teammates and opponents.

A complementary direction retains one focal player and learns policies

for the surrounding participants from human trajectories. In a

ten-player setting, one user could interact with nine learned teammates

and opponents, each choosing actions from its own observation history.

The policies determine how participants act, while the world model

predicts the consequences of their joint actions. EWM’s attributed

action streams and paired observations provide supervision for studying

both components. This combination could support characters that pursue

objectives, coordinate and initiate encounters, with held-out action

prediction, behavioral diversity and sustained cooperation or

competition providing useful evaluation targets.

Learning under partial observability.

The same data support predicting a player’s future observations and

estimating hidden state from observation history. SC2’s live entity

records, remembered snapshots and shared identifiers connect these

tasks to explicit observation semantics. A model can use historical

evidence to infer an unseen opponent’s likely state while generating

a view that respects the player’s current information. Remembered

snapshots provide historical observations; replay or owner-view

records provide reference state for fields available in those records.

The associated video and action sequences also support long-horizon

video understanding and imitation learning.

Experimental setup.

Each task should specify its observation modality and action inputs.

Camera RGB, minimap and camera-independent raw observations expose

different information. A focal-player task uses the player’s permitted

history and actions, whereas a joint simulator can condition on joint

actions. Dota 2 order tables therefore need to be filtered for

focal-player inputs. Full replay state and other players’ private

actions can serve as labels or explicitly privileged training

supervision. Structured evaluation can measure shared-state agreement

and observable-entity recovery; evaluation of video outputs additionally

requires an image-to-entity mapping.

Data should be split before sampling clips, keeping all players,

rounds and clips from a match together. CS2 maps should be grouped by

series when testing generalization across series. The SC2 release

provides the split in ; map-, patch- and player-disjoint

splits address further generalization questions.

Table3

6

The current release provides entity-level observation labels for SC2,

replay-rendered views with expert-heavy coverage, and initial audits

on selected matches. CS2 clips end shortly after player death, reducing

late-round view coverage. These characteristics guide the next stages

of dataset development.

Expanding coverage and observation labels.

The ongoing CS2 collection broadens the available match and participant

coverage. Extending player-specific visibility extraction to Dota 2

would connect its team-view videos to explicit observation labels.

Developing image-to-entity mappings would further link rendered

content to structured records, supporting visual evaluation across

different observation regimes.

Building reproducible benchmarks.

A next step is to establish fixed splits, input specifications and

baselines for observation prediction, hidden-state estimation and

cross-view consistency. SC2 provides a starting point through its live

observations, remembered snapshots and shared entity identifiers;

comparable protocols can then be developed for Dota 2 and CS2.

Broader data audits should report field-level errors, join failures

and event-to-image timing measurements. Versioned documentation

following datasheet principles can record

the collection, filtering and evaluation procedures, providing a

reproducible foundation for the research directions above.[]

8

EWM pairs replay-rendered human competitive gameplay with actions and structured records across three observation regimes. These trajectories capture multiple participants whose decisions jointly change one world, with each player observing only part of it. Its central addition is the connection, in SC2, between synchronized player views and entity records that distinguish live shared information from remembered or unavailable observations. Paired encounters, full-team sequences and linked event records show how to construct samples at the level of a participant, an interaction or a shared match. The initial audits illustrate how to inspect these records and why views should be joined on replay time. These checks connect the data organization to the construction of temporally aligned, observation-aware samples. Looking ahead, such data can underpin research on both jointly controlled multiplayer worlds and single-player experiences populated by policies learned from human behavior. The dataset is intended to make those investigations, alongside observation prediction and hidden-state estimation, reproducible and easier to define.

item.title: ActionRoPE：把动作当作坐标，换取世界模型的时空一致性 ｜ ActionRoPE: action as coordinates for spatially consistent control
item.description:
一句话：用旋转位置编码把动作信号编码成坐标，解决交互式世界模型的空间漂移。

要点：

  • 把动作当作空间坐标而非附加条件输入
  • 用 RoPE 式位置编码保证动作与画面的空间对齐
  • 明显缓解长时间交互后的场景漂移

为什么值得看：世界模型当引擎用时，玩家的移动会让画面越跑越歪；这是控制信号编码层面的根因级修复。

中文摘要：ActionRoPE 关注交互式世界模型里一个具体而致命的问题：随着交互步数增加，生成画面会逐渐偏离应有的空间关系。作者的做法是把动作信号当作空间坐标来处理，用类似旋转位置编码（RoPE）的方式注入模型，使控制与画面在空间上严格对齐。相比把动作当作额外条件向量，这种编码方式在长序列交互下显著减少了漂移。论文来自腾讯相关工作。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·世界模型+游戏（English）

Zhiyang Deng

Tencent

Affiliation: National University of Singapore

Affiliation: Yuzhe Wu

Affiliation: Zijun Lin

Affiliation: Yeying Jin

Affiliation: National University of Singapore

Affiliation:

Abstract

Game world models have made rapid progress toward real-time interactive generation. Yet action control is still predominantly implemented as feature conditioning, leaving the model to learn from training data how each action should move the visual world. This formulation is poorly matched to a broad class of , such as top-down and isometric games. In these worlds, player motion induces a geometrically well-defined planar camera displacement. We observe that the key to spatially consistent control in such worlds is to represent the effect of each action directly in world coordinates. To this end, we introduce , a parameter-free action interface that converts action-driven camera displacement into world-coordinate rotary positions. As a result, tokens corresponding to the same world location retain the same positional address across time. These world coordinates further expose a spatial asymmetry in generation: regions covered by the initial observation are geometrically known, while newly revealed regions remain to be synthesized. We therefore propose , which assigns token-wise denoising schedules according to this known–new structure. It allows observed regions to stabilize earlier, while new content is generated with reference to them. Compared with four representative action-conditioning mechanisms, our approach follows the commanded motion more faithfully and reduces the revisit drift by $66\%$ over the strongest baseline. The same interface transfers across video backbones from 1.3B to 33B parameters and to out-of-distribution scenes. Project Page: planar-camera worldsActionRoPECoordinate-Conditioned Noise Scheduling (CNS)

https://teawhite.cn/ActionRoPE/

1Corresponding author.1footnotetext: 2This work was completed during research internships at Tencent.2footnotetext: 3Project Lead.3footnotetext:

(a) In a planar-camera world, each action corresponds to a known translation of the scene.

(b) Standard RoPE re-addresses the same scene token after the camera moves, while ActionRoPE adds the camera displacement to each token’s position, keeping its index across frames.

(c) ActionRoPE enables precise motion and revisits, control in unseen scenes, and variable camera speed, without adding parameters to the control path.Figure 1: Action as world coordinates.

1

Game world models are emerging as a promising paradigm for interactive visual simulation . By conditioning video generation on user actions, they allow users to explore and manipulate generated worlds. Recent advances have substantially improved visual fidelity, temporal coherence, and generation efficiency, bringing these models closer to real-time playable environments . Yet realistic video alone is not enough for interaction. The generated world must also respond to user actions accurately and in a spatially consistent way.(; )

Bruce et al., 2024

Parker-Holder et al., 2024

(; ; )

Valevski et al., 2025

Decart and Etched, 2024

Parker-Holder and Fruchter, 2025

Existing game world models typically incorporate user actions as additional conditioning signals. Depending on the architecture, actions may be represented as discrete  or textual  tokens, or projected into the model as continuous features . They may also modulate intermediate activations through adaptive normalization  or enter through dedicated cross-attention modules . Despite their different implementations, these approaches share the same underlying formulation: an action is encoded as a feature, and the generative model is expected to learn how that feature should control the visual world. In other words, both the direction and magnitude of the resulting motion are learned from data rather than explicitly specified by the control interface. This raises a fundamental question: ()

Bruce et al., 2024

()

Zhu et al., 2026

()

Wang et al., 2026a

()

AlayaWorld Team et al., 2026

()

Wang et al., 2026b

How should action control be represented when its visual effect is governed by explicit geometry instead of being learned from conditioning features?

This question becomes particularly relevant in , such as top-down and isometric games. In these worlds, the player often stays near the screen center while the camera follows the player, causing the static scene to translate almost rigidly in the image plane. In this setting, the effect of an action is largely geometric. Once the action-to-camera scale is calibrated, the action directly determines both the direction and magnitude of the camera displacement. Yet existing interfaces still require the model to learn this geometric translation from data. As a result, the generated motion tends to regress toward motion patterns observed during training, failing to precisely follow the requested displacement. More fundamentally, feature-based action representations do not provide the model with an explicit world coordinate system. Without such coordinates, the model cannot directly tell whether a current token refers to a world location that has already been observed. When the camera returns to a previously seen location, the scene there may no longer look the same. The problem is therefore not merely insufficient conditioning capacity, but a mismatch between feature-based action representations and the geometric structure of planar-camera worlds.planar-camera worlds

To address this mismatch, we propose , a parameter-free action interface for planar-camera world models. Instead of encoding an action as an additional feature, ActionRoPE writes the resulting camera displacement directly into the positional coordinates of video tokens. Concretely, it converts screen-space RoPE  into action-aligned world-space RoPE, so that tokens corresponding to the same world location retain the same positional address across time (Figure ). In this way, the action directly specifies the direction and magnitude of the resulting motion, enabling precise and geometric control. At the same time, the world coordinates naturally reveal which tokens belong to the scene already determined by the first frame and which belong to newly exposed regions. Building on this structure, we further introduce . Unlike applying an undifferentiated denoising schedule to all spatial tokens, CNS assigns token-wise schedules  according to a known–new partition. Specifically, as the camera moves, tokens inside the first-frame region are denoised and stabilized earlier, while newly revealed tokens keep the original schedule. This allows newly revealed regions to be generated with reference to the already settled scene. Besides a $0.015$ M-parameter input channel that feeds the known–new partition to the network, both components add no learnable parameters and leave the underlying attention architecture unchanged.ActionRoPE()

We evaluate ActionRoPE against four representative action-conditioning strategies on the same backbone and under the same training setting. Across motion scaling, directional compliance, and closed-loop revisit, our method yields more precise and spatially consistent control, reducing the revisit drift by $66\%$ over the strongest baseline. CNS further improves world consistency by reducing the revisit error. The same interface also works on backbones of different sizes  and transfers to out-of-distribution scenes. This suggests that the coordinate-based control interface is not tied to a particular architecture or training visual domain. Together, our results show that representing action through world coordinates provides a simple yet effective alternative to conventional feature-based control.(; ; )

2.1

Game world models have evolved from passive gameplay generation toward interactive visual simulation, where future observations are generated in response to user actions . Genie  learns latent actions from unlabeled gameplay, while subsequent diffusion-based models adopt explicit controls , including keyboard inputs , cross-scene control , and real-time streaming generation . Recent work further incorporates richer states and interaction signals . Despite these differences, actions are typically injected as conditioning features, such as latent tokens, additive embeddings, language, adaptive normalization, or cross-attention . The resulting visual motion is therefore still learned from data.(; )

Our work studies a setting where the action-to-motion relation is explicitly geometric. In planar-camera worlds, calibrated player actions determine planar camera displacement, allowing us to represent control directly through world coordinates rather than learned action features.

2.2

Rotary positional embeddings (RoPE) are widely used to encode spatio-temporal token coordinates in video DiTs . Recent work has further incorporated camera geometry directly into positional representations rather than treating it only as an external condition . ReDirector , ReRoPE , SCoPE , and Matrix-Game 3.5  encode camera transformations, viewing rays, or projection geometry into RoPE-like coordinates, improving geometric consistency under viewpoint changes. These methods, however, are designed for viewpoint control in general 3D scenes and take the camera pose or trajectory as input.(; )

2.3

Standard diffusion models apply a shared noise level across all tokens at each denoising step. Several works instead assign different noise levels to different tokens. Diffusion Forcing , Rolling Diffusion , FIFO-Diffusion , and streaming generators  vary noise levels across temporal positions, and recent image-generation methods further explore spatially adaptive schedules . Related inpainting approaches exploit known regions through explicit resampling or content injection . These methods show that different regions can benefit from different denoising schedules, but the distinction is typically defined by time, an external mask, or explicit observed content.()

In contrast, our method uses the world coordinates provided by ActionRoPE to define this distinction directly. As shown in Figure , we propose ActionRoPE to turn a pretrained image-to-video diffusion transformer into an action-controlled world model without adding a control pathway.

We first formalize planar-camera worlds, in which the effect of an action is a camera displacement (Section ).

We then write this displacement into the rotary positions, so that a token is addressed by where it is in the world rather than where it is on the screen (Section ).

The same coordinates also separate known regions from newly revealed ones.

Building on this partition, we introduce Coordinate-Conditioned Noise Scheduling (CNS), which denoises known tokens earlier than newly revealed ones during both training and sampling (Section ).

Finally, Section  summarizes training and inference.

3.1

We consider a class of interactive game worlds in which the dominant camera motion is approximately planar, including top-down and isometric games. Given an initial frame and an action sequence, each action moves the player. The camera then follows the player and the static world translates approximately rigidly in the image plane. Once the action-to-camera scale is calibrated, the visual effect of an action is therefore largely determined by geometry.

Existing action-conditioning mechanisms, however, generally treat actions as additional feature signals, whether as tokens, added features, modulated activations, or cross-attention inputs. Despite their different implementations, these approaches share the same formulation:

$a_{k}\rightarrow\mathrm{Cond}(a_{k})\rightarrow\mathrm{Video\ Generator}\rightarrow\Delta_{k},$ (1)

where the model learns from data how an action should translate into the resulting visual motion. Consequently, both the direction and the magnitude of the motion are determined implicitly by the training distribution rather than explicitly by the control interface.

This formulation is unnecessarily indirect for planar-camera worlds. Here,

$\Delta_{k}=(\Delta x_{k},\Delta y_{k})$ denotes the cumulative camera displacement at temporal cell $k$ , i.e., the $k$ -th latent frame of the video model. For a static world point, its screen-space location changes with $\Delta_{k}$ , but its location in the underlying world remains unchanged. Thus, rather than learning the effect of an action as a feature transformation, we seek to represent action-induced motion directly through the positional coordinates used by the video model. Our main observation is simple: . This observation leads to ActionRoPE, which replaces screen-relative spatial positions with action-aligned world positions.in planar-camera worlds, action control can be formulated as coordinate alignment

The left panel shows the video DiT, where ActionRoPE replaces the screen-relative RoPE before self-attention and the known/new mask $\kappa$ is added to the patch embedding through a zero-initialized convolution. By binding camera motion to world coordinates, ActionRoPE keeps the same positional index for the same scene location across views, as illustrated in the upper-right panel. The same coordinates reveal which regions are known or newly revealed, and CNS assigns them different denoising schedules, as shown in the lower-right panel.Figure 2: Overview of ActionRoPE.

3.2

World-coordinate positional encoding.

Consider a video DiT operating on temporal cell $k$ and spatial token $(i,j)$ . Standard spatiotemporal RoPE assigns each token a position

$\mathbf{p}_{kij}=(k,i,j),$ (2)

where $(i,j)$ denotes the spatial token location in the current image plane. Since these spatial coordinates are reset for every individual frame, the same world location in the scene receives different positional addresses over time whenever the camera moves.

We instead define an action-aligned world coordinate for each token by explicitly compensating for the cumulative camera displacement $\Delta_{k}$ at temporal cell $k$ :

$\mathbf{p}^{\,w}_{kij}=\left(k,\;i+\frac{\Delta y_{k}}{s},\;j+\frac{\Delta x_{k}}{s}\right),$ (3)

where $s$ denotes the number of image pixels represented by one spatial token. In our Wan2.2 implementation, $s=32$ . The temporal coordinate remains unchanged.

We compute the rotary angles directly from the real-valued coordinates in Eq. . As RoPE naturally supports continuous positions, the camera displacement does not need to be quantized to the token grid. We refer to this parameter-free formulation as .

3

ActionRoPE

The key property of ActionRoPE is that tokens corresponding to the same world location share the same spatial positional address across time. Suppose a static object appears at screen coordinate $j$ in the first frame and shifts to $j-\delta$ after camera motion. Since the accumulated displacement $\Delta x_{k}/s$ increases by $\delta$ , both observations are assigned the same world coordinate, $(j-\delta)+\delta=j$ .

Cross-frame attention can therefore associate the two observations through positional alignment instead of inferring their relative displacement purely from visual appearance.

Known and newly revealed regions.

World coordinates also allow us to determine whether a token corresponds to a region already observed in the first frame. Let $\Omega_{0}$ denote the world-coordinate footprint covered by the first frame. We define a binary knownness field

$\kappa_{kij}=\mathbb{I}\left[\mathbf{p}^{\,w}_{kij}\in\Omega_{0}\right].$ (4)

Tokens with $\kappa_{kij}=1$ correspond to world locations already visible in the first frame, whereas tokens with $\kappa_{kij}=0$ correspond to newly exposed regions that remain to be synthesized.

This partition is entirely geometric and is determined by the given action trajectory itself. It is therefore computed in the same way during training and inference and does not require any auxiliary predictor.

Besides determining the noise schedule in Section , $\kappa$ is also given to the network as an input through a zero-initialized convolution added to the patch embedding.

This adds only $0.015$ M parameters, leaves the pretrained model unchanged at initialization, and lets each token directly identify whether it belongs to a known or a newly revealed region.

3.3

3.3

ActionRoPE aligns previously observed world locations across time, and also exposes an asymmetry that standard diffusion and flow-matching schedules ignore. Tokens inside the first-frame footprint $\Omega_{0}$ correspond to content that has already been observed, whereas tokens outside it correspond to genuinely unknown content. Standard schedules nevertheless apply the same noise level to every spatial location. We therefore propose , which adapts the denoising trajectory of each token according to its knownness $\kappa$ , so that known regions settle first and newly revealed content is generated with reference to them.Coordinate-Conditioned Noise Scheduling (CNS)

Shift-based token-wise schedule.

We build CNS on the shifted schedule of the underlying flow-matching model, $\sigma(u;S)=Su/\bigl(1+(S-1)u\bigr)$ , where $u\in[0,1]$ is linear time and $S$ the global shift. Given a global noise level $\sigma$ , we recover its linear time $u=\sigma/\bigl(S-(S-1)\sigma\bigr)$ and assign every token its own shift and noise level,

$S_{kij}=S\left(\frac{S_{\mathrm{known}}}{S}\right)^{\kappa_{kij}},\qquad\sigma_{kij}=\sigma(u;S_{kij})=\frac{S_{kij}\,u}{1+(S_{kij}-1)\,u},$ (5)

with $S_{\mathrm{known}}

Training with spatially varying noise.

For a sampled global noise level $\sigma$ , we noise each spatial location $(k,i,j)$ with its own $\sigma_{kij}$ , keeping the standard rectified-flow target and making the timestep embedding token-dependent:

$\mathbf{x}_{\sigma}=\left(1-\sigma_{kij}\right)\mathbf{x}_{0}+\sigma_{kij}\,\bm{\epsilon},\qquad\mathbf{v}^{*}=\bm{\epsilon}-\mathbf{x}_{0},\qquad t_{kij}=1000\,\sigma_{kij}.$ (6)

Following the standard image-to-video setup, the first temporal cell remains a clean anchor and is excluded from the loss. We additionally up-weight the loss on newly revealed regions, since their content is generated rather than retrieved through coordinate alignment.

Token-wise sampling.

At inference, CNS requires no additional model evaluations. At step $n$ the model is queried once with the token-wise timesteps, $\mathbf{v}_{n}=f_{\theta}\bigl(\mathbf{x}_{n},\,t^{(n)}_{kij},\,\mathbf{p}^{\,w}_{kij},\,\kappa_{kij}\bigr)$ , and each token advances along its own schedule,

$\mathbf{x}_{n+1}(k,i,j)=\mathbf{x}_{n}(k,i,j)+\mathbf{v}_{n}(k,i,j)\,\bigl(\sigma^{(n+1)}_{kij}-\sigma^{(n)}_{kij}\bigr).$ (7)

CNS thus changes only each spatial token is denoised during sampling. It does not warp, copy, or paste any content from the first frame. The content of the known regions is still recovered through the world-coordinate correspondence that is established by ActionRoPE.when

3.4

During training, we fine-tune the backbone transformer with Eq. , taking $\Delta_{k}$ from the logged player positions and up-weighting the loss on newly revealed tokens by a factor of $2$ . Fine-tuning adapts the pretrained model to world-coordinate positions, while the action-to-motion mapping itself is given by geometry. At inference, the user’s actions are integrated into $\Delta_{k}$ , which determines the world coordinates and $\kappa$ , and the video is sampled with Eq. . For real-time use, we also distill it into a four-step causal student with a key–value cache. Since RoPE attention depends only on the relative positions of tokens, ActionRoPE carries over to this streaming setting.

4.1

Dataset.

We build both training and evaluation on , a 2.5D action game rendered from a fixed top-down perspective.

The camera follows the player, so the scene translates almost rigidly in the image plane.

We record $50.9$ hours of automated exploration and cut it into $22{,}782$ clips of $81$ frames at $16$  fps and $832{\times}480$ resolution.

Of these, $18{,}528$ clips are used for training, and $982$ held-out clips form the evaluation set.

At test time, each model receives only the first frame of an evaluation clip and never its ground-truth continuation.No Rest for the Wicked

On the same Wan backbone, our method achieves the best motion fidelity, directional compliance and revisit consistency. It adds no parameters to the control path and only $0.015$ M parameters for the known/new mask channel.Table 1: Quantitative comparison results with baselines.

Backbones and training.

We use Wan2.2-TI2V-5B  as our main backbone and implement ActionRoPE, CNS and all four baselines on it.

All Wan models are fully fine-tuned from the same pretrained weights for $5{,}000$ steps with AdamW, a learning rate of $10^{-5}$ and a batch size of $16$ .

To examine whether our interface generalizes across architectures, we further change the backbone to SkyReels-V2-DF 1.3B , LTX-2.5 22B  and MiniMax-H3 33B  and evaluate under the same setting.()

Generalization across backbones.

Table  reports the results of our full model on four backbones that differ by more than an order of magnitude in size, and Figure  shows the same first frame and command on three of these backbones.

5

We presented ActionRoPE, a parameter-free action interface for planar-camera game world models.

It writes action-driven camera motion directly into the rotary positions of video tokens, turning action control from a learned mapping into coordinate alignment.

Building on the world coordinates, CNS lets known regions settle earlier, so that newly revealed content is generated with reference to them.

Experiments show that our method follows the commanded motion more precisely and keeps the world more consistent on revisits than representative action-injection mechanisms.

The same interface also transfers across backbones ranging from 1.3B to 33B parameters.

Appendix C

C.1

Table  summarizes the settings of each backbone.

The displacement $\Delta_{k}$ is averaged over the video frames that form latent frame $k$ , and $s$ is the number of pixels covered by one spatial token after the VAE and the patch embedding.

The world coordinates of Eq.  are added to the spatial RoPE positions of each backbone, and for MiniMax-H3, whose spatial positions are not spaced by one, $\Delta_{k}/s$ is scaled by the same spacing.

The knownness $\kappa$ is computed on the latent grid; for the token-wise timesteps, it is averaged over the latent positions of each token, so tokens on the footprint boundary receive intermediate values.

The mask channel is a zero-initialized layer that maps $\kappa$ to the hidden width and adds it to the patch embedding, i.e., a single-channel convolution with the patch-embedding kernel on Wan2.2 and SkyReels-V2, and a linear layer on LTX-2.5 and MiniMax-H3.

For CNS, $S$ is the default sampling shift of each backbone, and we keep the ratio $S_{\mathrm{known}}/S=0.4$ found on Wan2.2 for the other backbones.

All models start from the public pretrained weights and are trained for $5{,}000$ steps with AdamW, a weight decay of $0.01$ , a linear warm-up followed by a constant learning rate, bf16 precision and gradient clipping at $1.0$ .

The flow-matching loss excludes the first latent frame, and for our models, newly revealed tokens receive a weight of $2$ .

Text prompts describe only the scene, using one of $18$ scene descriptions of the game, and the scene description is dropped with probability $0.1$ .

At evaluation, all models use this scene-free prompt, the same first frames and commands, and a fixed random seed.

Sampling uses the number of steps and guidance scale in Table , with one model evaluation per step except for the guided LTX-2.5.

All of them are driven by the same per-frame camera displacement as our model (Section ), which each baseline converts into its own action format; Prompt and Cross-Attn quantize it into discrete direction labels and therefore keep the direction but not the speed.

Since they have no known/new partition, they use a uniform loss weight.

Newly added layers are zero-initialized, so each model starts from the pretrained backbone.

Appendix D

The recordings consist of $50.9$ hours of automated exploration in two sessions, one with the in-game day–night cycle and weather ( $34.55$  h) and one with fixed daytime and clear weather ( $16.39$  h).

The engine logs the player position at $20$  Hz, and we map it to screen displacement with a calibrated linear map that also accounts for terrain height.

We fit the scale of this map against the background motion measured in the videos ( $R^{2}$ of $0.99$ horizontally and $0.89$ vertically).

As a check on the action labels, the eight-way movement direction predicted from the logs agrees with that measured by optical flow on $87.7\%$ of $42{,}456$ samples, and on $98.0\%$ within one neighboring direction.

We remove corrupted segments, teleport windows, periods in which the player is stuck for at least $2$  s, and low-light frames, leaving $33.35$ usable hours.

These are cut into $20{,}882$ clips of $81$ frames with a stride of $84$ frames and resized to $832{\times}480$ .

The dataset further contains $1{,}900$ transition clips that splice two scenes.

Since adjacent clips overlap heavily, we split training and evaluation by entire exploration segments, and exclude $16$ buffer segments from both.

From the $20{,}983$ clips of the training split, we remove one clip with invalid labels, $257$ transition clips whose source clips lie in the evaluation split, and $2{,}197$ clips in which the game world runs slower than $0.8{\times}$ real time, which leaves $18{,}528$ training clips.

The evaluation set contains the $982$ held-out clips with valid labels that run at least at $0.9{\times}$ real time.

Appendix E

Commands.

The nominal speed ( $1.0{\times}$ ) is the median walking speed in the training data, $4.33$  px per frame horizontally.

Motion fidelity uses the first $100$ evaluation first frames and commands a straight walk to the right for $80$ frames at $0.5$ , $0.75$ , $1.0$ , $1.25$ and $1.5{\times}$ this speed.

Directional compliance commands the same walk at $1.0{\times}$ on all $982$ first frames.

Revisit consistency commands a walk to the right for $40$ frames followed by a walk to the left for $40$ frames, so that the commanded camera position at the final frame equals the initial one.

Measuring motion.

We detect SIFT features on contrast-enhanced grayscale frames, excluding a $160{\times}160$ -pixel box at the screen center where the player stays, and fit an affine motion with RANSAC.

The displacement between the first and the last frame is measured directly, and through intermediate frames when direct matching fails.

Clips whose motion cannot be measured, mostly very dark first frames, are excluded from the medians.

Metrics.

For motion fidelity, we regress the measured displacement on the commanded one through the origin and report the slope.

$R^{2}$ is computed around the mean of the measured displacement, so it becomes negative when the measured displacement does not vary with the command.

For directional compliance, we report the median absolute angle between the measured and commanded displacement.

For revisit consistency, we compare the final frame with the first frame outside the central box.

Before computing PSNR, we match the mean and standard deviation of each color channel of the final frame to the first frame, so that global brightness changes are not counted.

SSIM uses an $11{\times}11$ Gaussian window with $\sigma{=}1.5$ on grayscale frames, and NCC is computed on grayscale frames.

DINO is the cosine similarity between the DINOv2-base class tokens of the two frames, with the central box filled with gray.

The residual drift is the magnitude of the measured displacement between the first and the final frame.

Out-of-distribution first frames.

The $50$ out-of-distribution first frames depict scenes and art styles that do not appear in the game, such as cyberpunk cities, deserts, oil paintings and pixel art, each with the player at the screen center.

They are evaluated with the same commands and metrics, with motion fidelity on the first $10$ of them.

Appendix F

ActionRoPE assumes that the static world translates approximately rigidly in the image plane, which holds for top-down and isometric cameras that follow the player.

It does not model zoom or strong parallax, and moving objects do not follow the world coordinates.

The knownness $\kappa$ covers only the first-frame footprint, so regions that become visible later are not treated as known when the camera returns to them.

一句话：用旋转位置编码把动作信号编码成坐标，解决交互式世界模型的空间漂移。

要点：

  • 把动作当作空间坐标而非附加条件输入
  • 用 RoPE 式位置编码保证动作与画面的空间对齐
  • 明显缓解长时间交互后的场景漂移

为什么值得看：世界模型当引擎用时，玩家的移动会让画面越跑越歪；这是控制信号编码层面的根因级修复。

中文摘要：ActionRoPE 关注交互式世界模型里一个具体而致命的问题：随着交互步数增加，生成画面会逐渐偏离应有的空间关系。作者的做法是把动作信号当作空间坐标来处理，用类似旋转位置编码（RoPE）的方式注入模型，使控制与画面在空间上严格对齐。相比把动作当作额外条件向量，这种编码方式在长序列交互下显著减少了漂移。论文来自腾讯相关工作。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·世界模型+游戏（English）

Zhiyang Deng
