Abstract

Game world models have made rapid progress toward real-time interactive generation. Yet action control is still predominantly implemented as feature conditioning, leaving the model to learn from training data how each action should move the visual world. This formulation is poorly matched to a broad class of , such as top-down and isometric games. In these worlds, player motion induces a geometrically well-defined planar camera displacement. We observe that the key to spatially consistent control in such worlds is to represent the effect of each action directly in world coordinates. To this end, we introduce , a parameter-free action interface that converts action-driven camera displacement into world-coordinate rotary positions. As a result, tokens corresponding to the same world location retain the same positional address across time. These world coordinates further expose a spatial asymmetry in generation: regions covered by the initial observation are geometrically known, while newly revealed regions remain to be synthesized. We therefore propose , which assigns token-wise denoising schedules according to this known–new structure. It allows observed regions to stabilize earlier, while new content is generated with reference to them. Compared with four representative action-conditioning mechanisms, our approach follows the commanded motion more faithfully and reduces the revisit drift by $66\%$ over the strongest baseline. The same interface transfers across video backbones from 1.3B to 33B parameters and to out-of-distribution scenes. Project Page: planar-camera worldsActionRoPECoordinate-Conditioned Noise Scheduling (CNS)

https://teawhite.cn/ActionRoPE/

1Corresponding author.1footnotetext: 2This work was completed during research internships at Tencent.2footnotetext: 3Project Lead.3footnotetext:

(a) In a planar-camera world, each action corresponds to a known translation of the scene.

(b) Standard RoPE re-addresses the same scene token after the camera moves, while ActionRoPE adds the camera displacement to each token’s position, keeping its index across frames.

(c) ActionRoPE enables precise motion and revisits, control in unseen scenes, and variable camera speed, without adding parameters to the control path.Figure 1: Action as world coordinates.

1

Game world models are emerging as a promising paradigm for interactive visual simulation . By conditioning video generation on user actions, they allow users to explore and manipulate generated worlds. Recent advances have substantially improved visual fidelity, temporal coherence, and generation efficiency, bringing these models closer to real-time playable environments . Yet realistic video alone is not enough for interaction. The generated world must also respond to user actions accurately and in a spatially consistent way.(; )

Bruce et al., 2024

Parker-Holder et al., 2024

(; ; )

Valevski et al., 2025

Decart and Etched, 2024

Parker-Holder and Fruchter, 2025

Existing game world models typically incorporate user actions as additional conditioning signals. Depending on the architecture, actions may be represented as discrete  or textual  tokens, or projected into the model as continuous features . They may also modulate intermediate activations through adaptive normalization  or enter through dedicated cross-attention modules . Despite their different implementations, these approaches share the same underlying formulation: an action is encoded as a feature, and the generative model is expected to learn how that feature should control the visual world. In other words, both the direction and magnitude of the resulting motion are learned from data rather than explicitly specified by the control interface. This raises a fundamental question: ()

Bruce et al., 2024

()

Zhu et al., 2026

()

Wang et al., 2026a

()

AlayaWorld Team et al., 2026

()

Wang et al., 2026b

How should action control be represented when its visual effect is governed by explicit geometry instead of being learned from conditioning features?

This question becomes particularly relevant in , such as top-down and isometric games. In these worlds, the player often stays near the screen center while the camera follows the player, causing the static scene to translate almost rigidly in the image plane. In this setting, the effect of an action is largely geometric. Once the action-to-camera scale is calibrated, the action directly determines both the direction and magnitude of the camera displacement. Yet existing interfaces still require the model to learn this geometric translation from data. As a result, the generated motion tends to regress toward motion patterns observed during training, failing to precisely follow the requested displacement. More fundamentally, feature-based action representations do not provide the model with an explicit world coordinate system. Without such coordinates, the model cannot directly tell whether a current token refers to a world location that has already been observed. When the camera returns to a previously seen location, the scene there may no longer look the same. The problem is therefore not merely insufficient conditioning capacity, but a mismatch between feature-based action representations and the geometric structure of planar-camera worlds.planar-camera worlds

To address this mismatch, we propose , a parameter-free action interface for planar-camera world models. Instead of encoding an action as an additional feature, ActionRoPE writes the resulting camera displacement directly into the positional coordinates of video tokens. Concretely, it converts screen-space RoPE  into action-aligned world-space RoPE, so that tokens corresponding to the same world location retain the same positional address across time (Figure ). In this way, the action directly specifies the direction and magnitude of the resulting motion, enabling precise and geometric control. At the same time, the world coordinates naturally reveal which tokens belong to the scene already determined by the first frame and which belong to newly exposed regions. Building on this structure, we further introduce . Unlike applying an undifferentiated denoising schedule to all spatial tokens, CNS assigns token-wise schedules  according to a known–new partition. Specifically, as the camera moves, tokens inside the first-frame region are denoised and stabilized earlier, while newly revealed tokens keep the original schedule. This allows newly revealed regions to be generated with reference to the already settled scene. Besides a $0.015$ M-parameter input channel that feeds the known–new partition to the network, both components add no learnable parameters and leave the underlying attention architecture unchanged.ActionRoPE()

Su et al., 2024

1

Coordinate-Conditioned Noise Scheduling (CNS)(; ; )

Chen et al., 2024

Ruhe et al., 2024

Kim et al., 2024

We evaluate ActionRoPE against four representative action-conditioning strategies on the same backbone and under the same training setting. Across motion scaling, directional compliance, and closed-loop revisit, our method yields more precise and spatially consistent control, reducing the revisit drift by $66\%$ over the strongest baseline. CNS further improves world consistency by reducing the revisit error. The same interface also works on backbones of different sizes  and transfers to out-of-distribution scenes. This suggests that the coordinate-based control interface is not tied to a particular architecture or training visual domain. Together, our results show that representing action through world coordinates provides a simple yet effective alternative to conventional feature-based control.(; ; )

Team Wan, 2025

Chen et al., 2025

HaCohen et al., 2024

To sum up, our contributions are as follows:

•

We introduce , a parameter-free action-control formulation for planar-camera world models that represents camera motion directly in world-coordinate rotary positions. It turns action control from learned feature conditioning into explicit coordinate alignment.ActionRoPE

Building on the coordinates exposed by ActionRoPE, we propose , which distinguishes geometrically known and newly revealed regions. 2.1

Game world models have evolved from passive gameplay generation toward interactive visual simulation, where future observations are generated in response to user actions . Genie  learns latent actions from unlabeled gameplay, while subsequent diffusion-based models adopt explicit controls , including keyboard inputs , cross-scene control , and real-time streaming generation . Recent work further incorporates richer states and interaction signals . Despite these differences, actions are typically injected as conditioning features, such as latent tokens, additive embeddings, language, adaptive normalization, or cross-attention . The resulting visual motion is therefore still learned from data.(; )

Our work studies a setting where the action-to-motion relation is explicitly geometric. In planar-camera worlds, calibrated player actions determine planar camera displacement, allowing us to represent control directly through world coordinates rather than learned action features.

2.2

Rotary positional embeddings (RoPE) are widely used to encode spatio-temporal token coordinates in video DiTs . Recent work has further incorporated camera geometry directly into positional representations rather than treating it only as an external condition . ReDirector , ReRoPE , SCoPE , and Matrix-Game 3.5  encode camera transformations, viewing rays, or projection geometry into RoPE-like coordinates, improving geometric consistency under viewpoint changes. These methods, however, are designed for viewpoint control in general 3D scenes and take the camera pose or trajectory as input.(; )

Our method adopts the same geometric view of positional encoding but applies it specifically to action control. Instead of encoding an external 3D camera pose, ActionRoPE directly converts the action-driven planar displacement into world coordinates, so that the same world location retains the same positional address throughout the camera motion.

2.3

Standard diffusion models apply a shared noise level across all tokens at each denoising step. Several works instead assign different noise levels to different tokens. Diffusion Forcing , Rolling Diffusion , FIFO-Diffusion , and streaming generators  vary noise levels across temporal positions, and recent image-generation methods further explore spatially adaptive schedules . Related inpainting approaches exploit known regions through explicit resampling or content injection . These methods show that different regions can benefit from different denoising schedules, but the distinction is typically defined by time, an external mask, or explicit observed content.()

In contrast, our method uses the world coordinates provided by ActionRoPE to define this distinction directly. Locations that are already covered by the initial observation are treated as geometrically known, while newly revealed locations still remain uncertain. CNS then uses this known–new structure to assign token-wise denoising schedules, allowing known regions to stabilize earlier without explicitly copying or reinserting any observed content.

3

As shown in Figure , we propose ActionRoPE to turn a pretrained image-to-video diffusion transformer into an action-controlled world model without adding a control pathway.

We first formalize planar-camera worlds, in which the effect of an action is a camera displacement (Section ).

We then write this displacement into the rotary positions, so that a token is addressed by where it is in the world rather than where it is on the screen (Section ).

The same coordinates also separate known regions from newly revealed ones.

Building on this partition, we introduce Coordinate-Conditioned Noise Scheduling (CNS), which denoises known tokens earlier than newly revealed ones during both training and sampling (Section ).

Finally, Section  summarizes training and inference.

3.1

We consider a class of interactive game worlds in which the dominant camera motion is approximately planar, including top-down and isometric games. Given an initial frame and an action sequence, each action moves the player. The camera then follows the player and the static world translates approximately rigidly in the image plane. Once the action-to-camera scale is calibrated, the visual effect of an action is therefore largely determined by geometry.

Existing action-conditioning mechanisms, however, generally treat actions as additional feature signals, whether as tokens, added features, modulated activations, or cross-attention inputs. Despite their different implementations, these approaches share the same formulation:

$a_{k}\rightarrow\mathrm{Cond}(a_{k})\rightarrow\mathrm{Video\ Generator}\rightarrow\Delta_{k},$ (1)

where the model learns from data how an action should translate into the resulting visual motion. Consequently, both the direction and the magnitude of the motion are determined implicitly by the training distribution rather than explicitly by the control interface.

This formulation is unnecessarily indirect for planar-camera worlds. Here,

$\Delta_{k}=(\Delta x_{k},\Delta y_{k})$ denotes the cumulative camera displacement at temporal cell $k$ , i.e., the $k$ -th latent frame of the video model. For a static world point, its screen-space location changes with $\Delta_{k}$ , but its location in the underlying world remains unchanged. Thus, rather than learning the effect of an action as a feature transformation, we seek to represent action-induced motion directly through the positional coordinates used by the video model. Our main observation is simple: . This observation leads to ActionRoPE, which replaces screen-relative spatial positions with action-aligned world positions.in planar-camera worlds, action control can be formulated as coordinate alignment

The left panel shows the video DiT, where ActionRoPE replaces the screen-relative RoPE before self-attention and the known/new mask $\kappa$ is added to the patch embedding through a zero-initialized convolution. By binding camera motion to world coordinates, ActionRoPE keeps the same positional index for the same scene location across views, as illustrated in the upper-right panel. The same coordinates reveal which regions are known or newly revealed, and CNS assigns them different denoising schedules, as shown in the lower-right panel.Figure 2: Overview of ActionRoPE.

3.2

World-coordinate positional encoding.

Consider a video DiT operating on temporal cell $k$ and spatial token $(i,j)$ . Standard spatiotemporal RoPE assigns each token a position

$\mathbf{p}_{kij}=(k,i,j),$ (2)

where $(i,j)$ denotes the spatial token location in the current image plane. Since these spatial coordinates are reset for every individual frame, the same world location in the scene receives different positional addresses over time whenever the camera moves.

We instead define an action-aligned world coordinate for each token by explicitly compensating for the cumulative camera displacement $\Delta_{k}$ at temporal cell $k$ :

$\mathbf{p}^{\,w}_{kij}=\left(k,\;i+\frac{\Delta y_{k}}{s},\;j+\frac{\Delta x_{k}}{s}\right),$ (3)

where $s$ denotes the number of image pixels represented by one spatial token. In our Wan2.2 implementation, $s=32$ . The temporal coordinate remains unchanged.

We compute the rotary angles directly from the real-valued coordinates in Eq. . As RoPE naturally supports continuous positions, the camera displacement does not need to be quantized to the token grid. We refer to this parameter-free formulation as .

3

ActionRoPE

The key property of ActionRoPE is that tokens corresponding to the same world location share the same spatial positional address across time. Suppose a static object appears at screen coordinate $j$ in the first frame and shifts to $j-\delta$ after camera motion. Since the accumulated displacement $\Delta x_{k}/s$ increases by $\delta$ , both observations are assigned the same world coordinate, $(j-\delta)+\delta=j$ .

Cross-frame attention can therefore associate the two observations through positional alignment instead of inferring their relative displacement purely from visual appearance.

Known and newly revealed regions.

World coordinates also allow us to determine whether a token corresponds to a region already observed in the first frame. Let $\Omega_{0}$ denote the world-coordinate footprint covered by the first frame. We define a binary knownness field

$\kappa_{kij}=\mathbb{I}\left[\mathbf{p}^{\,w}_{kij}\in\Omega_{0}\right].$ (4)

Tokens with $\kappa_{kij}=1$ correspond to world locations already visible in the first frame, whereas tokens with $\kappa_{kij}=0$ correspond to newly exposed regions that remain to be synthesized.

This partition is entirely geometric and is determined by the given action trajectory itself. It is therefore computed in the same way during training and inference and does not require any auxiliary predictor.

Besides determining the noise schedule in Section , $\kappa$ is also given to the network as an input through a zero-initialized convolution added to the patch embedding.

This adds only $0.015$ M parameters, leaves the pretrained model unchanged at initialization, and lets each token directly identify whether it belongs to a known or a newly revealed region.

3.3

3.3

ActionRoPE aligns previously observed world locations across time, and also exposes an asymmetry that standard diffusion and flow-matching schedules ignore. Tokens inside the first-frame footprint $\Omega_{0}$ correspond to content that has already been observed, whereas tokens outside it correspond to genuinely unknown content. Standard schedules nevertheless apply the same noise level to every spatial location. We therefore propose , which adapts the denoising trajectory of each token according to its knownness $\kappa$ , so that known regions settle first and newly revealed content is generated with reference to them.Coordinate-Conditioned Noise Scheduling (CNS)

Shift-based token-wise schedule.

We build CNS on the shifted schedule of the underlying flow-matching model, $\sigma(u;S)=Su/\bigl(1+(S-1)u\bigr)$ , where $u\in[0,1]$ is linear time and $S$ the global shift. Given a global noise level $\sigma$ , we recover its linear time $u=\sigma/\bigl(S-(S-1)\sigma\bigr)$ and assign every token its own shift and noise level,

$S_{kij}=S\left(\frac{S_{\mathrm{known}}}{S}\right)^{\kappa_{kij}},\qquad\sigma_{kij}=\sigma(u;S_{kij})=\frac{S_{kij}\,u}{1+(S_{kij}-1)\,u},$ (5)

with $S_{\mathrm{known}}

Training with spatially varying noise.

For a sampled global noise level $\sigma$ , we noise each spatial location $(k,i,j)$ with its own $\sigma_{kij}$ , keeping the standard rectified-flow target and making the timestep embedding token-dependent:

$\mathbf{x}_{\sigma}=\left(1-\sigma_{kij}\right)\mathbf{x}_{0}+\sigma_{kij}\,\bm{\epsilon},\qquad\mathbf{v}^{*}=\bm{\epsilon}-\mathbf{x}_{0},\qquad t_{kij}=1000\,\sigma_{kij}.$ (6)

Following the standard image-to-video setup, the first temporal cell remains a clean anchor and is excluded from the loss. We additionally up-weight the loss on newly revealed regions, since their content is generated rather than retrieved through coordinate alignment.

Token-wise sampling.

At inference, CNS requires no additional model evaluations. At step $n$ the model is queried once with the token-wise timesteps, $\mathbf{v}_{n}=f_{\theta}\bigl(\mathbf{x}_{n},\,t^{(n)}_{kij},\,\mathbf{p}^{\,w}_{kij},\,\kappa_{kij}\bigr)$ , and each token advances along its own schedule,

$\mathbf{x}_{n+1}(k,i,j)=\mathbf{x}_{n}(k,i,j)+\mathbf{v}_{n}(k,i,j)\,\bigl(\sigma^{(n+1)}_{kij}-\sigma^{(n)}_{kij}\bigr).$ (7)

CNS thus changes only each spatial token is denoised during sampling. It does not warp, copy, or paste any content from the first frame. The content of the known regions is still recovered through the world-coordinate correspondence that is established by ActionRoPE.when

3.4

During training, we fine-tune the backbone transformer with Eq. , taking $\Delta_{k}$ from the logged player positions and up-weighting the loss on newly revealed tokens by a factor of $2$ . Fine-tuning adapts the pretrained model to world-coordinate positions, while the action-to-motion mapping itself is given by geometry. At inference, the user’s actions are integrated into $\Delta_{k}$ , which determines the world coordinates and $\kappa$ , and the video is sampled with Eq. . For real-time use, we also distill it into a four-step causal student with a key–value cache. Since RoPE attention depends only on the relative positions of tokens, ActionRoPE carries over to this streaming setting.

4.1

Dataset.

We build both training and evaluation on , a 2.5D action game rendered from a fixed top-down perspective.

The camera follows the player, so the scene translates almost rigidly in the image plane.

We record $50.9$ hours of automated exploration and cut it into $22{,}782$ clips of $81$ frames at $16$  fps and $832{\times}480$ resolution.

Of these, $18{,}528$ clips are used for training, and $982$ held-out clips form the evaluation set.

At test time, each model receives only the first frame of an evaluation clip and never its ground-truth continuation.No Rest for the Wicked

On the same Wan backbone, our method achieves the best motion fidelity, directional compliance and revisit consistency. It adds no parameters to the control path and only $0.015$ M parameters for the known/new mask channel.Table 1: Quantitative comparison results with baselines.

Backbones and training.

We use Wan2.2-TI2V-5B  as our main backbone and implement ActionRoPE, CNS and all four baselines on it.

All Wan models are fully fine-tuned from the same pretrained weights for $5{,}000$ steps with AdamW, a learning rate of $10^{-5}$ and a batch size of $16$ .

To examine whether our interface generalizes across architectures, we further change the backbone to SkyReels-V2-DF 1.3B , LTX-2.5 22B  and MiniMax-H3 33B  and evaluate under the same setting.()

Metrics.

For each evaluation clip, the model generates $81$ frames from the first frame under a scripted action sequence. We measure the camera motion by matching SIFT features on the background, excluding a $160$ -pixel box around the player.

tests whether the camera moves by the commanded amount: on $100$ first frames, we command straight walks at $0.5$ – $1.5{\times}$ the nominal speed, and we regress the measured displacement on the commanded one and report the slope and $R^{2}$ , both ideally $1$ .

tests whether it moves in the commanded direction: on all $982$ first frames, we command a $5$ -second straight walk, and we report the median angular error.

tests whether the world stays fixed over time: we command a $2.5$ -second walk away followed by a return along the same path back to the start, and we compare the final frame with the first frame by PSNR, SSIM, normalized cross-correlation (NCC), DINOv2 feature similarity  and residual geometric drift in pixels.Motion fidelityDirectional complianceRevisit consistency()

Comparison with baselines.

Table  compares our full model with the four baselines on the same backbone.

Our model outperforms all baselines on every metric without adding any parameters to the control path.

On revisit consistency, it improves over the strongest baseline on each metric by $2.8$  dB in PSNR, $13\%$ in SSIM and $21\%$ in NCC, and reduces the residual drift by $66\%$ .

Generalization across backbones.

Table  reports the results of our full model on four backbones that differ by more than an order of magnitude in size, and Figure  shows the same first frame and command on three of these backbones.

On all four backbones, the measured motion closely follows the commanded speed within $10\%$ and the commanded direction within $2^{\circ}$ , and the median revisit PSNR stays between $22.0$ and $23.9$  dB.

This indicates that the control comes from the coordinate interface itself rather than from a particular choice of backbone.

5

We presented ActionRoPE, a parameter-free action interface for planar-camera game world models.

It writes action-driven camera motion directly into the rotary positions of video tokens, turning action control from a learned mapping into coordinate alignment.

Building on the world coordinates, CNS lets known regions settle earlier, so that newly revealed content is generated with reference to them.

Experiments show that our method follows the commanded motion more precisely and keeps the world more consistent on revisits than representative action-injection mechanisms.

The same interface also transfers across backbones ranging from 1.3B to 33B parameters.

Appendix C

C.1

Table  summarizes the settings of each backbone.

The displacement $\Delta_{k}$ is averaged over the video frames that form latent frame $k$ , and $s$ is the number of pixels covered by one spatial token after the VAE and the patch embedding.

The world coordinates of Eq.  are added to the spatial RoPE positions of each backbone, and for MiniMax-H3, whose spatial positions are not spaced by one, $\Delta_{k}/s$ is scaled by the same spacing.

The knownness $\kappa$ is computed on the latent grid; for the token-wise timesteps, it is averaged over the latent positions of each token, so tokens on the footprint boundary receive intermediate values.

The mask channel is a zero-initialized layer that maps $\kappa$ to the hidden width and adds it to the patch embedding, i.e., a single-channel convolution with the patch-embedding kernel on Wan2.2 and SkyReels-V2, and a linear layer on LTX-2.5 and MiniMax-H3.

All models start from the public pretrained weights and are trained for $5{,}000$ steps with AdamW, a weight decay of $0.01$ , a linear warm-up followed by a constant learning rate, bf16 precision and gradient clipping at $1.0$ .

The flow-matching loss excludes the first latent frame, and for our models, newly revealed tokens receive a weight of $2$ .

Text prompts describe only the scene, using one of $18$ scene descriptions of the game, and the scene description is dropped with probability $0.1$ .

At evaluation, all models use this scene-free prompt, the same first frames and commands, and a fixed random seed.

Sampling uses the number of steps and guidance scale in Table , with one model evaluation per step except for the guided LTX-2.5.

All of them are driven by the same per-frame camera displacement as our model (Section ), which each baseline converts into its own action format; Prompt and Cross-Attn quantize it into discrete direction labels and therefore keep the direction but not the speed.

Since they have no known/new partition, they use a uniform loss weight.

Newly added layers are zero-initialized, so each model starts from the pretrained backbone.

Like Prompt, it receives the direction but not the speed.Cross-Attn()

Wang et al., 2026b

Appendix D

The recordings consist of $50.9$ hours of automated exploration in two sessions, one with the in-game day–night cycle and weather ( $34.55$  h) and one with fixed daytime and clear weather ( $16.39$  h).

The engine logs the player position at $20$  Hz, and we map it to screen displacement with a calibrated linear map that also accounts for terrain height.

We fit the scale of this map against the background motion measured in the videos ( $R^{2}$ of $0.99$ horizontally and $0.89$ vertically).

As a check on the action labels, the eight-way movement direction predicted from the logs agrees with that measured by optical flow on $87.7\%$ of $42{,}456$ samples, and on $98.0\%$ within one neighboring direction.

We remove corrupted segments, teleport windows, periods in which the player is stuck for at least $2$  s, and low-light frames, leaving $33.35$ usable hours.

These are cut into $20{,}882$ clips of $81$ frames with a stride of $84$ frames and resized to $832{\times}480$ .

The dataset further contains $1{,}900$ transition clips that splice two scenes.

Since adjacent clips overlap heavily, we split training and evaluation by entire exploration segments, and exclude $16$ buffer segments from both.

From the $20{,}983$ clips of the training split, we remove one clip with invalid labels, $257$ transition clips whose source clips lie in the evaluation split, and $2{,}197$ clips in which the game world runs slower than $0.8{\times}$ real time, which leaves $18{,}528$ training clips.

The evaluation set contains the $982$ held-out clips with valid labels that run at least at $0.9{\times}$ real time.

Appendix E

Commands.

The nominal speed ( $1.0{\times}$ ) is the median walking speed in the training data, $4.33$  px per frame horizontally.

Motion fidelity uses the first $100$ evaluation first frames and commands a straight walk to the right for $80$ frames at $0.5$ , $0.75$ , $1.0$ , $1.25$ and $1.5{\times}$ this speed.

Directional compliance commands the same walk at $1.0{\times}$ on all $982$ first frames.

Revisit consistency commands a walk to the right for $40$ frames followed by a walk to the left for $40$ frames, so that the commanded camera position at the final frame equals the initial one.

Measuring motion.

We detect SIFT features on contrast-enhanced grayscale frames, excluding a $160{\times}160$ -pixel box at the screen center where the player stays, and fit an affine motion with RANSAC.

The displacement between the first and the last frame is measured directly, and through intermediate frames when direct matching fails.

Clips whose motion cannot be measured, mostly very dark first frames, are excluded from the medians.

Metrics.

For motion fidelity, we regress the measured displacement on the commanded one through the origin and report the slope.

$R^{2}$ is computed around the mean of the measured displacement, so it becomes negative when the measured displacement does not vary with the command.

For directional compliance, we report the median absolute angle between the measured and commanded displacement.

For revisit consistency, we compare the final frame with the first frame outside the central box.

Before computing PSNR, we match the mean and standard deviation of each color channel of the final frame to the first frame, so that global brightness changes are not counted.

SSIM uses an $11{\times}11$ Gaussian window with $\sigma{=}1.5$ on grayscale frames, and NCC is computed on grayscale frames.

DINO is the cosine similarity between the DINOv2-base class tokens of the two frames, with the central box filled with gray.

The residual drift is the magnitude of the measured displacement between the first and the final frame.

Out-of-distribution first frames.

The $50$ out-of-distribution first frames depict scenes and art styles that do not appear in the game, such as cyberpunk cities, deserts, oil paintings and pixel art, each with the player at the screen center.

They are evaluated with the same commands and metrics, with motion fidelity on the first $10$ of them.

Appendix F

ActionRoPE assumes that the static world translates approximately rigidly in the image plane, which holds for top-down and isometric cameras that follow the player.

It does not model zoom or strong parallax, and moving objects do not follow the world coordinates.

The knownness $\kappa$ covers only the first-frame footprint, so regions that become visible later are not treated as known when the camera returns to them.

item.title: Recursive Game Creator：面向产品级体验的智能体游戏生成 ｜ Recursive Game Creator: An Agentic Product-Level Experience-Oriented Game Harness
item.description:
一句话：把「做一款能玩的产品级游戏」改成多智能体递归协作的流程，而不是一次性生成。

要点：

  • 以产品级体验为目标，而非单点素材生成
  • 用递归的智能体框架分解设计、实现与迭代
  • 港大 MMLab 工作，含完整游戏产物验证

为什么值得看：这是「AI 原生引擎」最接近真实生产的一种形态：AI 不只生成资产，而是驱动整个游戏构建闭环。

中文摘要：Recursive Game Creator 提出一套智能体框架，目标不是生成单张图或单个关卡，而是端到端产出一款「产品级、可玩」的游戏。它把任务递归分解：设计、实现、验证、迭代由不同角色的智能体接力完成，形成可自纠正的构建闭环。作者来自港大 MMLab，并给出了完整游戏产物的验证。对思考「AI 原生引擎该长什么样」的团队，这是一个颇具参考价值的范式。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·生成式玩法（English）

Recursive Game Creator:

An Agentic Product-Level

Experience-Oriented Game Harness

Jiajun Chen

HKU MMLab

Abstract

Recent game design agents have made substantial progress in generating playable games. However, program correctness does not ensure an enjoyable experience for players. We present Recursive Game Creator, an experience-oriented harness to advance agentic game development from rough game prototypes into entertaining games. Recursive Game Creator organizes recursive development around four components: Designer, Builder, Player, and Reviewer. The Designer translates user instructions and Reviewer’s feedback into detailed plans. The Builder turns these plans into candidate games. The coding-native Player creates and executes reusable policies through programmatic interfaces to efficiently collect diverse gameplay trajectories, mitigating evaluation bias caused by slow GUI-based collection. The Reviewer uses carefully designed trajectory-based metrics to induce player preferences, integrating with visual evidence and explicit textual preferences to evaluate games against game-specific criteria. Finally, the Reviewer accepts the better version and provides improvement reviews for the next round, closing the recursive loop. Our method achieves state-of-the-art overall performance of 77.89 on GameCraft-Bench. On GameASG-Bench, it achieves a strict task success rate of 53.2%, a 34.1% improvement over the same-model baseline, and the highest mean runtime-check pass rate at 93.4% among compared methods. A user study shows longer playtime and higher ratings. Project page is at: .

imbaldy.github.io/recursive-game-creator

2Equal contribution.2footnotetext: 1Corresponding author.1footnotetext:

Game examples from Recursive Game Creator. Rows show MOBA, racing, and visual-novel games, each with two paired views. Arrows link the paired panels. Version labels identify earlier-to-later examples from V1 to V2 and V3.Figure 1:

1

Coding agents can rapidly build runnable games, but successful execution does not establish the quality of play. Engaging mechanics, appropriate difficulty, coherent presentation, and responsive feedback shape player experience. Recent agentic workflows support iterative game development , yet translating gameplay into experience-oriented revision remains challenging. Progress toward product-level games requires a harness that connects development with repeated playtesting and adapts the game to its intended players.(; )

Yan et al., 2026

Hu et al., 2026

We introduce , an experience-oriented recursive harness to iteratively refine games. The harness mirrors a real game studio of four typical roles: Designer, Builder, Player, and Reviewer, as shown in Fig. . Starting from a user instruction, the Designer expands into a comprehensive design graph that includes gameplay mechanisms, storylines, feedback systems, and visual asset requirements. The Builder calls proper external tools, implementing the game backend, organizing audiovisual assets, and managing the project. Unlike previous work  with a GUI agent to test the game, we propose a Coding-Native Player that writes executable policies to collect gameplay trajectories efficiently and effectively. The Experience-Oriented Reviewer leverages diverse gameplay trajectories to conduct a thorough, game-specific diagnosis, including difficulty assessment, corner-bug discovery, and time-in-game recording. The Reviewer also leverages screenshots to evaluate game appearance. Finally, the Reviewer provides feedback to the Designer for next-round refinement.Recursive Game Creator

2

;

Huang et al. (2026)

Hu et al. (2026)

Although coding agents can interact with games through graphical user interfaces (GUIs) , screenshot-driven testing may omit structured state, legal actions, events, and progress signals available through programmatic interfaces. Requiring visual interpretation and a model decision for each action adds latency and limits frequent, fine-grained rollouts. Coding agents are primarily optimized for code generation and reasoning, rather than fine-grained visual game-state interpretation. To better align gameplay with these strengths, our Coding-Native Player provides frequent, repeatable, and diverse interaction through programmatic interfaces. Player constructs reusable policies with different strategies and capabilities. We execute policies to collect trajectories. This separates fast gameplay control from policy construction and the Reviewer’s visual assessment. It also preserves directly exposed state and event information for subsequent analysis. The Coding-Native Player offers several distinct advantages, including: high-frequency control, efficient trajectory collection, diverse capability simulation, and reproducible results.(; )

Huang et al., 2026

Zhang et al., 2026a

The Reviewer provides comprehensive feedback from collected trajectories. The Experience-Oriented Reviewer combines general standards such as playtime, success rate, and game-specific rubric evaluations to identify problems. Different types of games matter in different aspects. Beyond general evaluation, the Reviewer further analyzes suitable specific features of each game. For example, Responsive steering matters in racing, whereas a meaningful storyline and coherent dialogue matter in a visual novel. The Reviewer actively figures out these specific analysis criteria. The Reviewer expresses inferred preferences as structured text describing the desired experience, supporting observations, and revision priorities. Users can also supply explicit textual preferences during play. These inputs guide the next design plan, allowing refinement to address both game quality and a player’s taste.

The recursive loop connects these stages across versions. Policy execution produces trajectories. Trajectory and visual analysis produce experience and preference feedback. The Designer translates feedback into a plan. The Builder implements a new candidate for further testing. We evaluate the games on GameCraft-Bench  and GameASG-Bench . In our GameCraft-Bench evaluation, three refinement rounds raise the overall score from 72.70 to 77.89 (+5.19), with improvements in every reported category. On GameASG-Bench, the harness raises the success rate from 9.47 to 25/47 tasks and achieves a highest mean runtime check pass rate of 93.4%.()

Luo et al., 2026

()

Zhang et al., 2026c

We make three contributions.

•

We connect a multi-round closed-loop game design harness, Recursive Game Creator, that supports product-level game evolution and user-directed customization.Product-level game recursive harness.

•

We introduce coding-native player collects diverse gameplay trajectories for comprehensive evaluation. The experience-oriented Reviewer combines general and game-specific rubrics to support preference-informed feedback.Coding-native and experience-oriented game evolution.

•

Recursive Game Creator achieves the highest overall score on GameCraft-Bench and GameASG-Bench among all baselines. Our user study further proves the customized game evolution ability guided by preferences inferred from human play.State-of-the-art game design capability.

2

Applications of coding agents.

Code generation allows agents to work beyond software development, including video creation and embodied tasks. For educational videos, Code2Video combines planning, Python code generation, and visual review to improve the rendered layout . VideoAgent uses generated code to create animations and combines them with slides and narration for scientific videos . VideoCoCo uses a coding agent to write Blender programs that produce dynamic scene drafts. A video generation model then turns these drafts into realistic videos . In embodied control, Code as Policies turns language instructions into robot policy code that connects perception with control APIs . ProgPrompt uses program-like descriptions of available actions and objects to generate robot task plans . Voyager builds a library of reusable Minecraft skills and revises their code using environment feedback and execution errors . Eureka extends code generation to reward design, using feedback from policy training to revise reward functions . Across these applications, code gives agents a way to express, execute, and reuse structured behavior. These works motivate our use of executable policies for gameplay testing. Our focus is on connecting executable play, experience and preference analysis, and continued game evolution within a recursive harness aimed at product-level games.()

Chen et al., 2025b

()

Liang et al., 2026

()

Li et al., 2026

()

Liang et al., 2023

()

Singh et al., 2022

()

Wang et al., 2023

()

Ma et al., 2024

Game development with coding agents.

Coding agents generate and edit game programs within an explicit runtime. General software-agent systems such as MetaGPT and ChatDev organize planning, implementation, and testing . GameGPT applies role-based collaboration to game development . AutoUE targets Unreal Engine workflows, while OpenGame combines reusable project templates with debugging knowledge . Beyond initial generation, AVR-Agent iterates JavaScript content using audio-visual recordings and multimodal comparisons, and Harness-of-Harness supports persistent development with independent assessment .

Concurrent work RSIGame explores recursive self-improvement for agentic game development, using iterative evaluation feedback to refine generated games .

GameDevBench and GameCraft-Bench evaluate engine-grounded development and interactive artifacts. GameXpert-Bench extends evaluation across generation, repair, and cumulative optimization . However, generating runnable artifacts and repairing functional bugs do not by themselves establish an engaging player experience. We go further by connecting policy generation, trajectory collection, experience and preference analysis, and multi-round game revision, making the quality of play and continued customization explicit refinement targets.(; )

Feedback refinement and preference alignment.

Self-Refine and Reflexion use feedback to revise outputs or subsequent attempts . AFlow, EvoMAC, and the Darwin Gödel Machine instead optimize workflows, collaboration, or agent code . A related line makes the optimization objective sensitive to human preferences. Trajectory comparisons can train reward models, while RLHF and direct preference optimization align language-model behavior with preferred outputs . VideoDPO extends preference optimization to video diffusion using automatically scored pairs, which should be distinguished from direct human judgments . In games, experience-driven procedural content generation connects player modeling to content adaptation, and experience-driven RL generates racetracks toward target affective patterns . These works motivate feedback tied to the intended experience, while differing in what is optimized and who supplies the feedback. Our harness uses structured preference feedback to revise the game artifact while keeping the underlying model parameters fixed. Explicit user requests and preferences inferred from play inform subsequent design and implementation rounds.(; )

Recursive Game Creator’s multi-round refinement workflow. The Designer plans revisions and the Builder implements code and assets. The coding-native Player collects gameplay trajectories. The Reviewer combines behavioral and visual evidence with shared and game-specific criteria to produce preference-informed revision feedback. The central circular arrow denotes repeated refinement with a configurable number of rounds. Agentic-player refinement improves game quality across rounds, while human-involved refinement improves the play experience and its alignment with inferred player preferences.Figure 2:

Recursive Game Creator organizes game development as a closed loop involving the Designer, Builder, Player, and Reviewer. The Designer translates user requirements and evaluation feedback into a structured plan specifying intended experience, concrete changes, acceptance goals, and asset needs. The Builder implements this plan through draft and integrate stages, incorporates required assets, and performs targeted checks to produce a playable candidate.

The Player writes and executes code policies through the game’s programmatic interface, collecting behavioral trajectories and available visual records. These trajectories capture states, actions, events, progress, elapsed time, and termination outcomes, providing inspectable evidence of play. The Reviewer combines Player reports with behavioral and visual evidence to assess the experience against shared and game-specific criteria, and compares anonymized evidence from the candidate and retained versions. These evidence-based judgments inform version retention, while the Reviewer’s findings guide the Designer’s next plan. This loop connects game construction, policy-based play, experience assessment, and iterative refinement.

3.1

The Designer expands the user brief into the core play loop, mechanics, progression and difficulty, visual direction, and production priorities. It combines the available game state and recent feedback with user requirements to form a plan:

$P_{t}=\operatorname{Design}(U,G_{t},\mathcal{H}_{t-1})=(h_{t},\Delta_{t},A_{t},X_{t}),$

where $U$ , $G_{t}$ , and $\mathcal{H}_{t-1}$ denote the user brief, current game, and recent feedback when available. The hypothesis $h_{t}$ states the intended experiential improvement and its basis; $\Delta_{t}$ specifies concrete changes and strengths to preserve; $A_{t}$ defines acceptance goals in terms of scenes, player inputs, and observable outcomes; and $X_{t}$ lists asset requests. This representation turns experience goals into implementation decisions and testable objectives.

Subsequently, the Builder inherits the implementation plans from the Designer and selects implementation tools according to the game’s mechanics, interaction requirements, visual direction, and asset needs. Implementation proceeds from a playable draft to an integrated candidate:

$Z_{t}=\operatorname{Draft}(G_{t},\Delta_{t}),\qquad X_{t}^{*}=\operatorname{Generate}(X_{t};Z_{t}),\qquad C_{t}=\operatorname{Integrate}(Z_{t},X_{t}^{*}),$

where $Z_{t}$ is the draft, $X_{t}$ denotes requested assets, $X_{t}^{*}$ contains assets actually generated by the framework, and $C_{t}$ is the integrated candidate.

During drafting, the Builder implements the core loop and planned changes, using placeholders when needed. The framework executes asset requests and makes generated files available for integration. The Builder then checks their presentation in gameplay scenes and their interaction with collision, animation, and interaction regions. Targeted self-checks and configured project checks complement the Player’s broader play evidence. This staged workflow links asset production to its in-game integration and validation; generating an asset alone does not establish an improvement to play.

3.2

The Player constructs executable gameplay policies, separating policy generation from repeated interaction. Each policy uses the game’s exposed state to choose valid actions and collect a trajectory. This enables state-based control without requiring a language-model response or visual interpretation at every action. For candidate version $C_{t}$ at round $t$ , policy $\pi_{t,k}$ produces trajectory $\tau_{t,k}$ :

$\tau_{t,k}=\operatorname{Rollout}(C_{t},\pi_{t,k}),\qquad\mathcal{E}_{t}=\{(\tau_{t,k},V_{t,k})\}_{k=1}^{K}.$

Here, $C_{t}$ is the candidate game version, $\pi_{t,k}$ is an executable policy, $\tau_{t,k}$ is its trajectory, and $V_{t,k}$ denotes visual records when available. The evidence set $\mathcal{E}_{t}$ contains records from $K$ rollouts.

The Player reads the state schema, available actions, and testing objectives, then writes a policy that observes states, chooses actions, and repeats until the task ends or the rollout budget is reached. Policies run through the game’s programmatic or command-line interface. Rollout requests are dispatched as execution jobs, allowing repeated trials and separate game instances. The Player inspects outcomes and execution failures and revises policy code when needed. It does not use a conversational response as a substitute for executing the rollout.Policy construction and execution.

Policies vary in strategy, skill, exploration, and risk tolerance. For example, one favors fast progress while another explores optional content. Their rollouts record exposed states, actions, events, progress, elapsed time, and termination outcomes. Parallel or repeated execution supplies multiple attempts and failure cases under known policy settings. These records are passed to the Reviewer. Visual capture and presentation assessment belong to the review stage. Policy and observation settings are recorded with each trajectory to support comparisons across game versions.Diverse policies and trajectory records.

The trajectories support estimates of completion, difficulty, explored content, and points of failure or stagnation. Direct state and event access avoids reconstructing these variables from every rendered frame. Lightweight execution and parallel sampling make repeated trials practical, while policies with different strategies can expose failures that one strategy misses. The resulting records connect gameplay behavior to the Reviewer’s diagnosis and the next design revision. Total testing cost includes policy generation, repair, execution, and review. Proxy strategies provide varied test behavior, but do not establish that they represent the full human player population. Human trajectories and explicit feedback supply additional evidence about individual preferences.Behavioral evidence and testing cost.

3.3

The Reviewer combines behavioral trajectories, visual observations, and user input into an experience assessment and actionable revision feedback. Its inputs are associated with the evaluated game version and policy or player session. The assessment preserves the distinction between observed behavior, inferred preference, and explicit user requests.

The coding-native Player supplies many trajectories from policies with different skills and strategies. The Reviewer uses this evidence to estimate success rates and examine where play ends or gets stuck. Success that comes too easily may offer little challenge, while repeated failure may cause frustration. The goal is therefore a suitable level of difficulty for the intended players, not the highest possible success rate. Comparing outcomes across policies helps assess whether progress is achievable and whether stronger play is rewarded. For version comparisons, policy settings and observation access must remain consistent.Shared signals, success rate and playtime.

The same trajectories record playtime. The Reviewer examines run times together with progress, explored content, and reasons for stopping. This helps distinguish a long run with varied activity from one spent stuck at the same point. Success rate and playtime therefore support a broader assessment of difficulty and playability. Both remain measures of the tested policies. Proxy playtime alone does not show human interest or enjoyment.

The Reviewer starts from shared assessment dimensions, including control responsiveness, content richness, narrative or progression pacing, visual coherence, and support for exploration or replay. It instantiates these dimensions as criteria suited to the game’s genre and intended experience. For example, a racing game may require clear track guidance, responsive steering, and visible collision feedback, while a visual novel may require coherent dialogue and choices with discernible consequences. The Reviewer checks consistency between rules, visual cues, and observed play, and explains strengths, weaknesses, and tradeoffs rather than averaging unrelated criteria.Game-specific rubric.

The Reviewer obtains sampled screenshots and available recordings from rendered gameplay, and examines them alongside play reports without seeing source code or version order. Trajectories show where a policy succeeds, fails, or stops progressing. Rendered views show what a player could see at those moments. The Reviewer uses them to assess text readability, visual style, and action feedback. Visual review is separate from the fast control loop, so collecting a trajectory does not require interpreting an image at every step. Brief effects or missing feedback may still require a recording rather than a few frames.Visual evidence and diagnosis.

Each observation is tied to its game version, policy, and replay. The Reviewer separates what happened from why it may have happened. A failed turn could reflect poor controls, an unclear cue, or a weak policy. When the cause is uncertain, the feedback specifies what further evidence would help resolve it.

The Reviewer translates trajectory patterns, visual findings, and explicit user input into a textual preference record. The record describes the desired experience, supporting evidence, whether a preference is inferred or user-stated, and the corresponding revision priority. A tendency to explore optional areas, for example, may suggest interest in discovery. A user’s request for less demanding combat supplies an explicit difficulty target. These observations inform design hypotheses rather than establishing preferences from playtime alone. The Designer receives this record alongside concrete changes and follow-up checks for the next revision.Structured experience and preference feedback.

The Reviewer compares a candidate with the retained game using the same shared signals and game-specific criteria. It checks whether the changes address the earlier revision goals and introduce new problems. The output is an A/B preference, a tie, or an unavailable judgment, with reasons and evidence paths. Feedback states the problem, its possible cause, its effect on play, and a revision goal with a follow-up check. The harness maps the Reviewer’s judgment back to the game versions and selects which artifact to retain.Version comparison and retention.

4

We evaluate Recursive Game Creator on GameCraft-Bench and GameASG-Bench. These benchmarks test game quality and whether generated games meet their requirements. We then examine rollout coverage, representative development examples, and expert assessments of experience-oriented refinement.

The GPT-6 Astra baseline scores 71.26 overall. Recursive Game Creator improves overall quality from 72.70 in the first round to 77.89 in the third, a gain of 5.19 points across rounds and 6.63 points over the same-model baseline. The final score exceeds the strongest reported baseline by 6.37 points, and all five categories improve across our three rounds. Action shows the largest increase, from 67.96 to 77.62 (+9.66). Its first two rounds remain below the same-model baseline Action score of 73.33, before reaching 77.62 in the third. One possible explanation is that action-game quality depends on coordinated changes to controls, collision handling, combat feedback, and progression, whose interactions can require several playtest and revision cycles. The larger late-stage gain is consistent with this interpretation, although the category scores alone do not identify its cause.

5

Recursive Game Creator is an experience-oriented recursive harness that connects design, tool-assisted implementation, executable play, and preference-informed review. Its coding-native Player collects reusable gameplay trajectories through programmatic interfaces, while the Reviewer combines behavioral evidence, visual observations, and user input to guide version selection and subsequent revisions. This policy-to-trajectory-to-feedback loop enables continued game evolution with fixed model parameters. Across our evaluations, Recursive Game Creator achieves state-of-the-art overall performance on GameCraft-Bench and the highest mean runtime-check pass rate among compared methods on GameASG-Bench. Development examples and expert assessments characterize improvements in controls, content, and presentation. The harness provides a foundation for advancing functional prototypes toward product-level games and evaluating continued adaptation to individual players.

一句话：把「做一款能玩的产品级游戏」改成多智能体递归协作的流程，而不是一次性生成。

要点：

  • 以产品级体验为目标，而非单点素材生成
  • 用递归的智能体框架分解设计、实现与迭代
  • 港大 MMLab 工作，含完整游戏产物验证

为什么值得看：这是「AI 原生引擎」最接近真实生产的一种形态：AI 不只生成资产，而是驱动整个游戏构建闭环。

中文摘要：Recursive Game Creator 提出一套智能体框架，目标不是生成单张图或单个关卡，而是端到端产出一款「产品级、可玩」的游戏。它把任务递归分解：设计、实现、验证、迭代由不同角色的智能体接力完成，形成可自纠正的构建闭环。作者来自港大 MMLab，并给出了完整游戏产物的验证。对思考「AI 原生引擎该长什么样」的团队，这是一个颇具参考价值的范式。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·生成式玩法（English）

Recursive Game Creator:

An Agentic Product-Level

Experience-Oriented Game Harness

Jiajun Chen

HKU MMLab

Abstract

Recent game design agents have made substantial progress in generating playable games. However, program correctness does not ensure an enjoyable experience for players. We present Recursive Game Creator, an experience-oriented harness to advance agentic game development from rough game prototypes into entertaining games. Recursive Game Creator organizes recursive development around four components: Designer, Builder, Player, and Reviewer. The Designer translates user instructions and Reviewer’s feedback into detailed plans. The Builder turns these plans into candidate games. The coding-native Player creates and executes reusable policies through programmatic interfaces to efficiently collect diverse gameplay trajectories, mitigating evaluation bias caused by slow GUI-based collection. The Reviewer uses carefully designed trajectory-based metrics to induce player preferences, integrating with visual evidence and explicit textual preferences to evaluate games against game-specific criteria. Finally, the Reviewer accepts the better version and provides improvement reviews for the next round, closing the recursive loop. Our method achieves state-of-the-art overall performance of 77.89 on GameCraft-Bench. On GameASG-Bench, it achieves a strict task success rate of 53.2%, a 34.1% improvement over the same-model baseline, and the highest mean runtime-check pass rate at 93.4% among compared methods. A user study shows longer playtime and higher ratings. Project page is at: .

imbaldy.github.io/recursive-game-creator

Game examples from Recursive Game Creator. Rows show MOBA, racing, and visual-novel games, each with two paired views. Arrows link the paired panels. Version labels identify earlier-to-later examples from V1 to V2 and V3.Figure 1:

1

Coding agents can rapidly build runnable games, but successful execution does not establish the quality of play. Engaging mechanics, appropriate difficulty, coherent presentation, and responsive feedback shape player experience. Recent agentic workflows support iterative game development , yet translating gameplay into experience-oriented revision remains challenging. Progress toward product-level games requires a harness that connects development with repeated playtesting and adapts the game to its intended players.(; )

Yan et al., 2026

Hu et al., 2026

We introduce , an experience-oriented recursive harness to iteratively refine games. The harness mirrors a real game studio of four typical roles: Designer, Builder, Player, and Reviewer, as shown in Fig. . Starting from a user instruction, the Designer expands into a comprehensive design graph that includes gameplay mechanisms, storylines, feedback systems, and visual asset requirements. The Builder calls proper external tools, implementing the game backend, organizing audiovisual assets, and managing the project. Unlike previous work  with a GUI agent to test the game, we propose a Coding-Native Player that writes executable policies to collect gameplay trajectories efficiently and effectively. The Experience-Oriented Reviewer leverages diverse gameplay trajectories to conduct a thorough, game-specific diagnosis, including difficulty assessment, corner-bug discovery, and time-in-game recording. The Reviewer also leverages screenshots to evaluate game appearance. Finally, the Reviewer provides feedback to the Designer for next-round refinement.Recursive Game Creator

2

;

Huang et al. (2026)

Hu et al. (2026)

Although coding agents can interact with games through graphical user interfaces (GUIs) , screenshot-driven testing may omit structured state, legal actions, events, and progress signals available through programmatic interfaces. Requiring visual interpretation and a model decision for each action adds latency and limits frequent, fine-grained rollouts. Coding agents are primarily optimized for code generation and reasoning, rather than fine-grained visual game-state interpretation. To better align gameplay with these strengths, our Coding-Native Player provides frequent, repeatable, and diverse interaction through programmatic interfaces. Player constructs reusable policies with different strategies and capabilities. We execute policies to collect trajectories. This separates fast gameplay control from policy construction and the Reviewer’s visual assessment. It also preserves directly exposed state and event information for subsequent analysis. The Coding-Native Player offers several distinct advantages, including: high-frequency control, efficient trajectory collection, diverse capability simulation, and reproducible results.(; )

Huang et al., 2026

Zhang et al., 2026a

The Reviewer provides comprehensive feedback from collected trajectories. The Experience-Oriented Reviewer combines general standards such as playtime, success rate, and game-specific rubric evaluations to identify problems. Different types of games matter in different aspects. Beyond general evaluation, the Reviewer further analyzes suitable specific features of each game. For example, Responsive steering matters in racing, whereas a meaningful storyline and coherent dialogue matter in a visual novel. The Reviewer actively figures out these specific analysis criteria. The Reviewer expresses inferred preferences as structured text describing the desired experience, supporting observations, and revision priorities. Users can also supply explicit textual preferences during play. These inputs guide the next design plan, allowing refinement to address both game quality and a player’s taste.

The recursive loop connects these stages across versions. Policy execution produces trajectories. Trajectory and visual analysis produce experience and preference feedback. The Designer translates feedback into a plan. The Builder implements a new candidate for further testing. We evaluate the games on GameCraft-Bench  and GameASG-Bench . In our GameCraft-Bench evaluation, three refinement rounds raise the overall score from 72.70 to 77.89 (+5.19), with improvements in every reported category. On GameASG-Bench, the harness raises the success rate from 9.47 to 25/47 tasks and achieves a highest mean runtime check pass rate of 93.4%.()

Luo et al., 2026

()

Zhang et al., 2026c

We make three contributions.

•

We connect a multi-round closed-loop game design harness, Recursive Game Creator, that supports product-level game evolution and user-directed customization.Product-level game recursive harness.

•

We introduce coding-native player collects diverse gameplay trajectories for comprehensive evaluation. The experience-oriented Reviewer combines general and game-specific rubrics to support preference-informed feedback.Coding-native and experience-oriented game evolution.

•

Recursive Game Creator achieves the highest overall score on GameCraft-Bench and GameASG-Bench among all baselines. Our user study further proves the customized game evolution ability guided by preferences inferred from human play.State-of-the-art game design capability.

2

Applications of coding agents.

Code generation allows agents to work beyond software development, including video creation and embodied tasks. For educational videos, Code2Video combines planning, Python code generation, and visual review to improve the rendered layout . VideoAgent uses generated code to create animations and combines them with slides and narration for scientific videos . VideoCoCo uses a coding agent to write Blender programs that produce dynamic scene drafts. A video generation model then turns these drafts into realistic videos . In embodied control, Code as Policies turns language instructions into robot policy code that connects perception with control APIs . ProgPrompt uses program-like descriptions of available actions and objects to generate robot task plans . Voyager builds a library of reusable Minecraft skills and revises their code using environment feedback and execution errors . Eureka extends code generation to reward design, using feedback from policy training to revise reward functions . Across these applications, code gives agents a way to express, execute, and reuse structured behavior. These works motivate our use of executable policies for gameplay testing. Our focus is on connecting executable play, experience and preference analysis, and continued game evolution within a recursive harness aimed at product-level games.()

Chen et al., 2025b

Game development with coding agents.

Coding agents generate and edit game programs within an explicit runtime. General software-agent systems such as MetaGPT and ChatDev organize planning, implementation, and testing . GameGPT applies role-based collaboration to game development . AutoUE targets Unreal Engine workflows, while OpenGame combines reusable project templates with debugging knowledge . Beyond initial generation, AVR-Agent iterates JavaScript content using audio-visual recordings and multimodal comparisons, and Harness-of-Harness supports persistent development with independent assessment .

Concurrent work RSIGame explores recursive self-improvement for agentic game development, using iterative evaluation feedback to refine generated games .

GameDevBench and GameCraft-Bench evaluate engine-grounded development and interactive artifacts. GameXpert-Bench extends evaluation across generation, repair, and cumulative optimization . However, generating runnable artifacts and repairing functional bugs do not by themselves establish an engaging player experience. We go further by connecting policy generation, trajectory collection, experience and preference analysis, and multi-round game revision, making the quality of play and continued customization explicit refinement targets.(; )

Feedback refinement and preference alignment.

Self-Refine and Reflexion use feedback to revise outputs or subsequent attempts . AFlow, EvoMAC, and the Darwin Gödel Machine instead optimize workflows, collaboration, or agent code . A related line makes the optimization objective sensitive to human preferences. Trajectory comparisons can train reward models, while RLHF and direct preference optimization align language-model behavior with preferred outputs . VideoDPO extends preference optimization to video diffusion using automatically scored pairs, which should be distinguished from direct human judgments . In games, experience-driven procedural content generation connects player modeling to content adaptation, and experience-driven RL generates racetracks toward target affective patterns . These works motivate feedback tied to the intended experience, while differing in what is optimized and who supplies the feedback. Our harness uses structured preference feedback to revise the game artifact while keeping the underlying model parameters fixed. Explicit user requests and preferences inferred from play inform subsequent design and implementation rounds.(; )
