learns a state-aware scene representation from a casual capture (: input video frames showing the user interacting with the car).

The scene is decomposed into a static base and a set of independently switchable slots, one per interactable object (here: right door, hood, trunk).

Each slot models two binary states, enabling SwitchSplat to render any combination of object configurations from novel viewpoints at inference time (: four of the $2^{3}=8$ possible slot configurations, labeled by their on/off state vector).

Figure 1. SwitchSplattopbottomThe top row is a filmstrip of a camera moving around a blue car while a person successively opens its side door, hood, and trunk. The bottom row contains four novel-view renderings of the car, each paired with labeled switches for the trunk, door, and hood. The examples show all three parts closed, only the hood open, only the trunk open, and both the trunk and hood open, illustrating independent composition of the three binary object states.

Abstract.

3D Gaussian Splatting has made high-fidelity 3D reconstruction fast and accessible, yet existing representations assume a static world.

This assumption breaks down in casual captures, where a user naturally interacts with the environment – opening doors, toggling switches, or moving objects – introducing discrete state changes that no current framework can model.

Time-conditioned dynamic methods such as 4DGS conflate a state was observed with state the scene is in, limiting them to replaying seen sequences rather than composing arbitrary object configurations.

We present SwitchSplat, the first 3DGS representation to address this gap via a base $+$ slot decomposition: a shared static base captures the invariant scene, while each slot independently holds the two binary states (on/off) of one interactable object.

Because the assignment of Gaussians to slots is fully differentiable, the model discovers the geometry of each state directly from video, without manual annotation.

At inference, the user can freely combine slot states and render the resulting scene from any viewpoint.

We validate SwitchSplat on a new casual-capture dataset and show that it outperforms static and dynamic baselines in novel-view synthesis quality, while uniquely supporting rendering of state combinations never seen during capture.

Project page: .whenwhat

https://switchsplat.github.io

Novel View Synthesis, Gaussian Splatting, State-aware Rendering, $360^{\circ}$ Capture

Keywords:

†by†cc-license:

1.

In inverse rendering, Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)  has emerged as the leading representation for real-time, high-fidelity novel-view synthesis, enabling a new generation of interactive applications.

Its combination of fast training and efficient rendering has driven broad adoption across academia as well as industry, from Matterport’s digital twins and Niantic Scaniverse’s mobile reconstruction to Meta’s Hyperscape.()

Kerbl et al., 2023

111

https://www.meta.com/experiences/meta-horizon-hyperscape-capture-beta/8798130056953686/

While early 3DGS pipelines required meticulous data acquisition (fixed exposure and white balance, controlled lighting, and a perfectly static scene), recent works like 3DGRT  and FullCircle  have unlocked capture: viewpoints need not be carefully curated – made possible by $360^{\circ}$ cameras held in a single hand – and the capturer’s pixels are automatically masked out to satisfy the static-scene assumption.

This freedom naturally invites users to with the environment during capture – opening doors, toggling switches, or repositioning objects – turning the operator into both an active agent a dynamic distractor within the scene.()

Moenne-Loccoz et al., 2024

()

Foroutan et al., 2026

casualinteractand

Yet no existing reconstruction framework is equipped to handle these interactions.

Many contemporary 3D representations enforce a strict static-world assumption: when an operator triggers a discrete state change – opening a door, flipping a switch, relocating an object – the model has no mechanism to account for the resulting geometric variation.

As a result, even state-of-the-art pipelines can only represent a single, frozen scene configuration, and capturing multiple stable states requires re-recording the scene from scratch.

One could argue that the natural candidate to address this limitation is the family of 4D Gaussian Splatting methods , which extend 3DGS to dynamic scenes by conditioning the scene representation on time.

However, this design choice fundamentally conflates a state was observed with state the scene is in: the model learns to replay a specific sequence of observations, not to understand independent object configurations.()

Yang et al., 2024b

whenwhat

As a result, 4D methods are largely limited to novel-viewpoint synthesis of seen sequences; composing an unseen combination of object states—e.g., door open and light on—is not directly supported, since no single timestamp in the training data corresponds to that configuration.

What is needed instead is a representation that scene state from time, allowing the user to freely specify both the viewpoint and the desired configuration of each object independently.de-correlates

To address these challenges, we propose , a method that learns “state-aware” representations from casual captures featuring human-object interactions; see .

SwitchSplat organizes the scene into a – the parts that never change throughout the capture – and a set of , one per interactable object.

Each slot holds two 3D representations corresponding to the binary states of that object (“on” and “off”).

For example, if a room was captured while a closet door was closed for part of the recording and open for another, a single slot would hold both the “off” state (door closed, interior hidden) and the “on” state (door open, interior visible), while the walls, floor, and furniture – unchanged throughout – are handled by the static base.

To assign each Gaussian primitive to the right part of the scene, we attach a small learnable score vector that controls how strongly the primitive belongs to the base, or to either state of each slot.SwitchSplat

Figure1

static baseslots

This decomposition avoids data redundancy: without a shared static base, one would need to duplicate the full scene geometry for every slot, with no reusable structure across states.

Instead, SwitchSplat shares the base across all configurations and only stores the geometry that actually differs per state.

Because the full pipeline is differentiable end-to-end, the model learns simultaneously which Gaussians belong to which slot and when each slot is active – directly from the input video, without any manual annotation.

At inference, the user can query any combination of slot states independently – e.g., closet door open and desk lamp on – and render the resulting scene from any viewpoint.2

This is structurally analogous to PCA-based morphable models : the static base plays the role of the mean face, each slot’s on/off representations correspond to the eigenvectors, and the state activations act as the blend-shape coefficients.22()

Blanz and Vetter, 2023

To summarize our contributions:

(1) We in the 3DGS literature: existing representations cannot model scenes with discrete, user-triggered state changes (e.g., objects that can be opened, switched, or moved), and we show that naïvely applying dynamic methods such as 4DGS fails to address this.

(2) We propose SwitchSplat, the first 3DGS representation to address this problem via a , where a shared static base captures the invariant scene and each slot independently models the binary states of one interactable object.

(3) We demonstrate on a that SwitchSplat improves novel-view synthesis quality over static and dynamic baselines, and uniquely supports rendering arbitrary combinations of object states from unseen viewpoints.identify a novel problembase $+$ slot decompositionnew casual-capture dataset

2.

3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)  has become the dominant representation for novel-view synthesis, optimizing a set of anisotropic Gaussian primitives that render at real-time rates.

Extensions beyond the standard perspective-camera model are particularly relevant to our setting: 3DGRT  reformulates rendering via ray tracing, and 3DGUT  adds support for highly distorted cameras and secondary rays, enabling casual capture with wide field-of-view sensors.

FullCircle  further shows that raw dual-fisheye $360^{\circ}$ video suffices for high-quality reconstruction, automatically masking the camera operator.

Despite these advances, all of these pipelines represent the scene as a single, fixed configuration.

When multiple object states are present in the capture—a door open in some frames and closed in others—the model either conflates them into averaged geometry and ghosting artifacts, or learns to discard the minority state as a distractor .

Either way, only one configuration survives in the final model; there is no mechanism to retain, switch between, or compose multiple stable states at inference time.()

Kerbl et al., 2023

()

Moenne-Loccoz et al., 2024

()

Wu et al., 2025a

()

Foroutan et al., 2026

()

Sabour et al., 2025

From a casual capture in which the operator interacts with objects (a), we fit a differentiable (b) whose learnable endpoints $(t_{l},t_{r})$ and temperature ${rgb(0bp)=(0,0,0);rgb(25bp)=(0,0,0);rgb(75bp)=(0.5,0.5,0.5);rgb(100bp)=(0.5,0.5,0.5)}_{k}$ define a per-frame interaction probability $\pi_{k}(t)$ for each object.

Each 3D Gaussian primitive carries a state-logit vector $\ell$ over a static channel together with an and an channel per slot, yielding per-state probabilities (c).

At render time (d), these probabilities are fused with $\pi_{k}(t)$ into a frame-conditional opacity $\tilde{\alpha}(t)$ that drives standard volumetric composition.

All Gaussians, state logits, and slot-table parameters are optimized end-to-end under photometric losses, producing a state-aware scene that renders arbitrary object configurations from novel viewpoints.

Figure 2. Pipeline –slot tablebaseoffonFrom left to right, the diagram shows filmstrips from a casual kitchen capture; four colored temporal slot windows aligned with icons for different interactable objects; Gaussian ellipses separated into dark-blue off, gray base, and light-blue on groups; projected Gaussian layers selected by the requested state; and kitchen renderings with an appliance closed or open. Arrows indicate that the slot probabilities and categorical Gaussian assignments determine state-conditioned opacity and the final rendering.

Dynamic Gaussian Splatting

A large family of methods extends 3DGS to dynamic scenes by conditioning the representation on time.

Dynamic 3D Gaussians  tracks persistent primitives across frames, while Deformable 3D Gaussians  and 4DGS  deform a canonical scene over time, with 4DGS using a learned space-time encoding.

Spacetime Gaussians  further augments primitives with temporal opacity and parametric motion.

Subsequent work improves efficiency, temporal consistency, or geometric accuracy via depth priors .

Differently from our method, all of these methods are parameterized by time, not by object state: recovering a specific scene configuration requires locating the right moment in the recording, and rendering a novel combination of states—e.g., two objects in configurations never co-observed—is not supported.()

Luiten et al., 2024

()

Yang et al., 2024a

()

Wu et al., 2024

()

Li et al., 2024a

(; ; ; ; )

Yang et al., 2024b

Sun et al., 2024

Duan et al., 2024

Li et al., 2024b

Liu et al., 2025b

Decomposed Gaussian Splatting

More recent dynamic Gaussian methods, such as SDD-4DGS , observe that applying deformation models to the entire scene is often inefficient, since most real-world scenes are largely static.

This motivates methods that decompose scenes into static and dynamic components: GauFRe  combines a static Gaussian component with deformable dynamic Gaussians, while Swift4D  improves efficiency by passing only dynamic Gaussians through the deformation model.

DeGauss  further uses dynamic-static decomposition to improve robustness to transient distractors.

This observation is closely aligned with our setting, since object interactions usually affect only a small part of a $360^{\circ}$ environment.

In contrast to our method, existing decomposition methods still treat the dynamic component as a temporally varying foreground: they separate dynamic regions from a static background, but provide no mechanism to independently switch or compose object states at inference time.()

Sun et al., 2025

()

Liang et al., 2025

()

Wu et al., 2025b

()

Wang et al., 2025a

Controllable Scene Representation

A parallel line of work studies controllable and articulated 3D representations.

Pre-Gaussian methods such as Watch It Move  discover articulated structure from object motion; PARIS  goes further by decoupling static and movable parts from two multi-view captures of the same scene.

Gaussian-based approaches extend this to photorealistic settings: SC-GS  enables motion editing via sparse control points, Template-free Articulated Gaussian Splatting  supports re-posing with super-points, and RigGS  adds rig-based editing and interpolation.

ArtGS  and ArticulatedGS  further focus on part-level modeling of individual objects.

Crucially, all of these methods aim to object motion or articulation—they model how parts move, rather than discarding motion entirely to focus on the discrete stable configurations of the scene.

In contrast, our method treats object interactions as a nuisance to be factored out, retaining only the clean on/off states and ignoring the transient motion between them.()

Noguchi et al., 2022

()

Liu et al., 2023

()

Huang et al., 2024

()

Wan et al., 2024

()

Yao et al., 2025

()

Liu et al., 2025a

()

Guo et al., 2025

encode

State-aware Scene Reconstruction

Closest to our setting are methods that reconstruct scenes across discrete object states.

IGFuse  and RecurGS  address this by using semantic cues to detect state changes and aligning them via rigid transformations.

GaussianCut  and DecoupledGaussian  contribute related tools for object segmentation and scene decomposition.

However, all of these methods assume that state changes can be described as rigid motions of segmented object entities—an assumption that breaks down for casual capture, where interaction boundaries are fuzzy and deformations are non-rigid.

In contrast, SwitchSplat learns which Gaussians belong to each state directly from photometric supervision, without requiring object masks, or rigid-body assumptions.()

Hu et al., 2026

()

Hu et al., 2025

()

Jain et al., 2024

()

Wang et al., 2025b

3.

SwitchSplat learns a state-aware 3D representation from casual captures by decomposing the scene into controllable, state-conditioned components.

In the following subsections, we detail our methodology by first formulating our state-conditioned Gaussian primitives and describing their integration within volume rendering ().

We then introduce the parameterization of the differentiable slot-table (), followed by our slot initialization procedure ().

Finally, we describe our training pipeline and objectives that facilitate granular, state-controlled visualization during inference ( and ).

Sec.3.1

Sec.3.2

Sec.3.3

Secs.3.4

3.5

Terminology

A corresponds to one interactable object and holds two 3D representations for its binary states: “off” (e.g., door closed) and “on” (e.g., door open).

A is a per-frame binary variable indicating which state is currently observed.

All parts of the scene that remain constant throughout the capture are handled by the , which is shared across all configurations.slotslot activationstatic base

3.1.

Each 3D Gaussian primitive in our model is defined by its standard geometric and appearance attributes: mean $\mu$ , covariance $\Sigma$ , opacity $\alpha$ , and view-dependent appearance  $\mathbf{c}$ .

To make our representation state-aware, we augment every Gaussian with a learnable categorical state distribution $\mathbf{p}=\operatorname{softmax}(\ell)$ over $1+2K$ channels, where $K$ is the total number of object slots.

These channels comprise a single static channel $\ell[0]$ , together with a pair of ( $\ell[2k{-}1]$ ) and ( $\ell[2k]$ ) channels for each slot $k\in\{1,\dots,K\}$ .

The two channels per slot — rather than one — let the softmax assign each Gaussian to a single configuration, so that disjoint subsets of primitives can independently model the geometry and appearance of an object in each of its two states (see ).

This separation is essential because the on/off configurations of an object generally differ not just in appearance, but also in spatial extent — a closed door and an open door, for instance, occupy different parts of the scene — which a single shared primitive simply cannot represent.baseoffon

Figure3

Each Gaussian carries a learnable logit vector  $\boldsymbol{\ell}$ that defines a categorical distribution  $\mathbf{p}$ that softly assigns each primitive to the static base or “on”/“off” object states.  At render time, user specifies list of states that are active

or inactive

, and the probability of each gaussian being present in the scene  $\omega(\tilde{\mathbf{p}})$ is computed via Eq. ().

Figure 3. State-aware Gaussian – (left)(right)

1

An image of an open refrigerator is decomposed into three soft Gaussian-assignment layers representing the static base, the refrigerator's off state, and its on state. State-dependent binary weights of one, zero, and one retain the base and on-state layers while suppressing the off-state layer. The retained layers are summed to render the refrigerator in its open state.

Test-time rendering

Assume we have trained our representation, and that we want to render an image corresponding to the slot configuration $\tilde{\mathbf{p}}\in\{0,1\}^{K}$ .

This is achieved by computing the probability of each gaussian being present in the scene to be rendered:

(1) $\omega(\tilde{\mathbf{p}})=\mathbf{p}[0]+\sum_{k=1}^{K}\Big(\tilde{\mathbf{p}}[k]\cdot\mathbf{p}[2k]+(1-\tilde{\mathbf{p}}[k])\cdot\mathbf{p}[2k-1]\Big)$

This formulation ensures that “base” Gaussians remain present across all frames, while the presence of the on/off state Gaussians is gated by the probability of the corresponding slot being on.

We then gate the opacity of the gaussian by this probability:

(2) $\tilde{\alpha}=\alpha\cdot\omega(\tilde{\mathbf{p}}),$

which is then used to compute the final RGB color for a ray $\mathbf{r}$ via classical volume rendering :()

Tagliasacchi and Mildenhall, 2022

$\hat{I}(\mathbf{r})=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{H}(\mathbf{r})}T_{i}(\mathbf{r})\cdot\tilde{\alpha}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{c}_{i}(\mathbf{r}),\quad T_{i}(\mathbf{r})=\prod_{j

where $\mathcal{H}(r)$ represents the set of Gaussians intersected by the ray in depth order and $\mathbf{c}_{i}(r)$ denotes the view-dependent color.

While $\tilde{\mathbf{p}}$ will be selected by the user at test-time, the key question in training our representation lies in how to propagate the gradients from image $\hat{I}_{t}$ at time $t$ to the (per-Gaussian) state distribution  $\mathbf{p}$ .

3.2.

To achieve this, we exploit the key assumption that, within the video, the activation state of a slot is .

Let us denotes with the per-slot scalar $\pi_{k}(t)\in[0,1]$ the probability of slot $k$ being in its state at time $t$ .

Then, $\forall k\neq 0$ we have that $\pi_{k}(t)$ is zero everywhere outside some bounded, closed region.

Without loss of generality, let us drop the indexing $k$ , and focus on a single entry $\pi(t)$ .

We can satisfy our compact support assumption by explicitly parameterizing $\pi(t)$ as a defined by its temporal endpoints $(t_{l},t_{r})$ , and a temperature parameter ${rgb(0bp)=(0,0,0);rgb(25bp)=(0,0,0);rgb(75bp)=(0.5,0.5,0.5);rgb(100bp)=(0.5,0.5,0.5)}$ that controls the smoothness of transition; see .compactly supported in timeonsmooth window function3

To ensure $t_{l}\leq t_{r}$ in practice we optimize auxiliary free variables $u$ and $v$ , and then remap them to $t_{l}=\min(u,v)$ and $t_{r}=\max(u,v)$ .33

Sweeping ${rgb(0bp)=(0,0,0);rgb(25bp)=(0,0,0);rgb(75bp)=(0.5,0.5,0.5);rgb(100bp)=(0.5,0.5,0.5)}$ interpolates between sharp rectangular windows (low ${rgb(0bp)=(0,0,0);rgb(25bp)=(0,0,0);rgb(75bp)=(0.5,0.5,0.5);rgb(100bp)=(0.5,0.5,0.5)}$ ) and broad, soft transitions (high ${rgb(0bp)=(0,0,0);rgb(25bp)=(0,0,0);rgb(75bp)=(0.5,0.5,0.5);rgb(100bp)=(0.5,0.5,0.5)}$ ).

The left plot overlays slot-window curves for temperatures 0.7, 2, and 6: the lowest temperature produces nearly rectangular transitions, while higher temperatures produce progressively broader, smoother shoulders. The right plot shows complementary Bernoulli probabilities, with the active-state probability near one inside the endpoints and the dashed inactive-state probability near one outside. (3) $\displaystyle\pi(t)=\frac{\sigma_{rgb(0bp)=(0,0,0);rgb(25bp)=(0,0,0);rgb(75bp)=(0.5,0.5,0.5);rgb(100bp)=(0.5,0.5,0.5)}(t-t_{l})\cdot\sigma_{rgb(0bp)=(0,0,0);rgb(25bp)=(0,0,0);rgb(75bp)=(0.5,0.5,0.5);rgb(100bp)=(0.5,0.5,0.5)}(t_{r}-t)}{\sigma_{rgb(0bp)=(0,0,0);rgb(25bp)=(0,0,0);rgb(75bp)=(0.5,0.5,0.5);rgb(100bp)=(0.5,0.5,0.5)}(t_{m}-t_{l})\cdot\sigma_{rgb(0bp)=(0,0,0);rgb(25bp)=(0,0,0);rgb(75bp)=(0.5,0.5,0.5);rgb(100bp)=(0.5,0.5,0.5)}(t_{r}-t_{m})}$

Therefore, to model the time window of each object interaction, we treat the state of the $k$ -th slot at time $t$ as a Bernoulli random variable $\mathcal{S}_{k,t}\in\{0,1\}$ , where $\mathcal{S}_{k,t}=1$ denotes the slot being in its state and $\mathcal{S}_{k,t}=0$ its state, whose probability mass function (PMF) for a specific state $s\in\{0,1\}$ is given by:onoff

(4) $\displaystyle P(\mathcal{S}_{k,t}=s)=\pi_{k}(t)^{s}(1-\pi_{k}(t))^{1-s}$

Train-time rendering

The quantity $\pi_{k}(t)$ defined above is our , which we use to compute the probability of each Gaussian being present in the scene at time $t$ :slot table

(5) $\displaystyle\omega(t)=\mathbf{p}[0]+\sum_{k=1}^{K}\Big(\pi_{k}(t)\cdot\mathbf{p}[2k]+(1-\pi_{k}(t))\cdot\mathbf{p}[2k-1]\Big)$

from which, like before, we can compute a time-dependent effective opacity for volume rendering the predicted image $\hat{I}_{t}$ :

(6) $\displaystyle\tilde{\alpha}(t)=\alpha\cdot\omega(t)$

This differentiable rendering framework ensures that gradients propagate seamlessly to the slot activation probabilities, Gaussian state memberships, and geometric parameters, enabling stable and efficient joint optimization of the entire scene representation.

3.3.

In a casual capture setting, neither the total number of slots $K$ , nor the precise slot transition timestamps are known a priori.

Requiring the user to annotate them would defeat the very premise of a “casual” capture.

To address this, we leverage the reasoning capabilities of Vision-Language Models (VLMs), and in particular GPT $5.6$ , to provide an approximate initialization for the slot-table.

By prompting GPT $5.6$ with a sequence of frames, we extract semantically grounded start and end timestamps for each distinct object interaction.

These timestamps serve as the initial values for the endpoint parameters $(t_{l},t_{r})$ in our slot-table.

This VLM-informed initialization allows the system to bypass exhaustive temporal searches or complex diagnostics, providing a clean and efficient configuration for final full-resolution training.

To facilitate a robust optimization process, we initialize each interaction slot with a high temperature value ${rgb(0bp)=(0,0,0);rgb(25bp)=(0,0,0);rgb(75bp)=(0.5,0.5,0.5);rgb(100bp)=(0.5,0.5,0.5)}$ .

This high-temperature initialization ensures that the Bernoulli random variable $\mathcal{S}_{k,t}$ begins with smooth transitions at the boundaries, allowing the gradients to flow more effectively over a wider temporal range during the initial stages of optimization.

3.4.

Leveraging the initial parameters derived from the VLM-based slot discovery phase, we proceed to optimize our final state-aware scene representation.

We build our state-aware framework upon the 3D Gaussian Unscented Transform (3DGUT) architecture .

Following the 3DGUT pipeline, we initialize the 3D Gaussian primitives using COLMAP-derived point clouds and augment each primitive with the learnable state logits $\ell$ .

To provide an unbiased starting point for optimization, these logits are initialized such that the base/on/off state channels are assigned equal membership probabilities.

Throughout this stage, we jointly optimize the geometric attributes of the Gaussians, their state logits, and the temporal parameters of the slot-table $(t_{l},t_{r},{rgb(0bp)=(0,0,0);rgb(25bp)=(0,0,0);rgb(75bp)=(0.5,0.5,0.5);rgb(100bp)=(0.5,0.5,0.5)})$ .

We strictly adhere to the optimization schedule established by 3DGUT, including its specialized densification and pruning protocols.

To ensure consistent state behavior during optimization, we modify the standard densification process: whenever a Gaussian primitive is cloned or split, its state logits are inherited by the resultant primitives.

This inheritance mechanism ensures that state-aware attributes remain spatially coherent even as the underlying scene geometry increases in complexity.()

Wu et al., 2025a

3.5.

Beyond the standard $L_{1}$ photometric and SSIM losses used to preserve perceptual fidelity, we employ two additional regularizers to mitigate floater artifacts, and prevent the emergence of redundant Gaussian primitives by supervising the optimization process via:

(7) $\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{}}=\mathcal{L}_{\text{rgb}}+\lambda_{1}\mathcal{L}_{\text{SSIM}}+\lambda_{2}\mathcal{L}_{\text{sparsity}}+\lambda_{3}\mathcal{L}_{\text{compactness}}$

Sparsity loss

To ensure a parsimonious partitioning of the scene, we regularize the Gaussian primitives to favor the static base state, thereby preventing unnecessary scene regions from being categorized as interactive.

This is achieved by applying a negative log-likelihood penalty on the base state probability for all $N$ Gaussians:

(8) $\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{sparsity}}=-\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n}\log\mathbf{p}_{n}[0]$

Compactness loss

To encourage Gaussians within slots to form spatially cohesive clusters, we first compute the opacity-weighted center of mass for primitives assigned to the on state of slot $k$ :

(9) $\displaystyle\overline{\mu}_{k}=\frac{\sum_{n}\alpha_{n}\cdot\mathbf{p}_{n}[2k]\cdot\mu_{n}}{\sum_{n}\alpha_{n}\cdot\mathbf{p}_{n}[2k]+\epsilon}$

and then penalize the weighted variance  for both the off and on states to encourage local clustering:()

Sun et al., 2021

(10) $\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{compactness}}$ $\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2K}\sum_{j=\{0,1\}}\frac{\sum_{n}\alpha_{n}\cdot\mathbf{p}_{n}[2k-j]\cdot||\mu_{n}-\overline{\mu}_{k}||^{2}}{\sum_{n}\alpha_{n}\cdot\mathbf{p}_{n}[2k-j]+\epsilon}$

To validate the effectiveness of our proposed algorithm in the absence of an existing dataset with variable object interactions, we collected a custom dataset using a consumer-grade Insta360 X4 dual-fisheye $360^{\circ}$ camera.

This hardware choice reflects the typical setup of casual users.

During capture, we emulated non-expert behaviors, moving through the scene and interacting with objects—transitioning them from resting to active states and back.

Our dataset comprises $12$ scenes organized into two groups.

The contains $10$ casually captured scenes ( $8$ indoor and $2$ outdoor), each featuring $3$ – $9$ object interactions.

The contains $2$ additional scenes for which we acquire controlled test sequences with novel camera trajectories and object-state combinations.

4.4.

Beyond the standard held-out evaluation on the original trajectories, we evaluate SwitchSplat on two additional generalization settings: novel camera frames and novel state-combination frames.

For two representative scenes, we acquire dedicated test trajectories containing previously unseen camera viewpoints and object-state combinations, and compare against 4DGS and DeGauss. Because 4DGS and DeGauss parameterize scene variation by continuous time rather than a discrete state code, we evaluate both dynamic baselines on the novel-camera and novel state-combination splits using a per-image oracle over time. For each target image, we select the rendering with the highest PSNR for both methods; these results therefore constitute upper bounds.

As shown in , SwitchSplat consistently outperforms the dynamic baselines on novel camera frames and produces sharper reconstructions with fewer structural artifacts.

We further evaluate novel state-combination frames, where multiple independently controlled interactions are composed into configurations not observed during training. Quantitative results in demonstrate that SwitchSplat maintains high reconstruction quality under these unseen configurations, highlighting the compositional generalization enabled by our state-conditioned representation.

Slot representation

We first evaluate the importance of the slot representation.

When interaction slots are removed, the model reduces to a scene representation without any of our slot-specific components, including slot optimization and the associated regularization terms.

We next assess the importance of optimizing the initialized slot parameters.

For this ablation, slots are initialized normally via VLM outputs but their parameters are kept fixed throughout training.

Compactness regularization

The compactness loss encourages state-conditioned Gaussians associated with the same interaction to remain spatially localized, preventing them from dispersing across unrelated regions of the scene.

This spatial prior therefore plays an important role in learning coherent state-dependent representations.

Sparsity regularization

Removing the sparsity regularization has a modest effect on average reconstruction quality.

The regularizer nevertheless discourages unnecessary assignment of otherwise static Gaussians to interactive states, promoting a more parsimonious state decomposition and reducing spurious state-dependent changes.

5.

We presented SwitchSplat, a 3D Gaussian Splatting framework that learns state-aware scene representations directly from casual video captures.

By decomposing the scene into a shared static base and a set of independently controllable slots, each modeling the binary “on”/“off” states of one interactable object, SwitchSplat decouples scene state from time – enabling a capability that time-conditioned dynamic methods fundamentally cannot provide: free composition of object configurations at inference, including combinations never observed during capture.

The slot table is initialized via a VLM and jointly refined end-to-end through differentiable rendering, requiring no manual annotation.

Experiments on our new casual-capture dataset show that SwitchSplat outperforms static and dynamic baselines in novel-view synthesis quality, and uniquely generalizes to out-of-distribution camera paths and unseen state combinations.

Limitations and future work

The current model assumes binary object states with the constraints of single-operator capture with one free hand.

Extending to continuous or multi-valued states by multiple operators – would broaden the applicability of the framework.

The slot count and approximate interaction windows are currently seeded by a VLM; a fully unsupervised discovery of both the number and timing of interactions from raw video remains an open problem.

Finally, SwitchSplat focuses on novel-view synthesis; combining our state-aware decomposition with physics-based priors or generative models could enable downstream applications such as scene editing and simulation.

A.1.

We captured twelve real-world scenes using an Insta360 X4 dual-fisheye 360 camera, comprising ten standard scenes and two golden scenes. Video frames were extracted at 4 FPS. We use the raw fisheye frames for reconstruction to avoid propagating stitching artifacts into the scene representation. Camera-holder masks are automatically obtained using the FullCircle masking pipeline. These masks, together with the fisheye frames, are passed to COLMAP for camera pose estimation and subsequent image undistortion. Input images are downsampled by a factor of two. An overview of the object-interaction intervals and temporal structure of all twelve scenes is provided in .

Figure15

A.2.

We evaluate reconstruction and generalization using four evaluation splits.

This split contains held-out frames in which all objects remain in their initial base state. It evaluates reconstruction of the canonical scene configuration and provides a natural comparison point for static reconstruction methods.Base-state test frames.

For each scene, we hold out every eight frame from the original capture sequence. Frames occurring during object transitions are excluded, such that evaluation is performed only on stable object configurations. The remaining frames constitute our standard test set and cover the object states observed throughout the original capture.All standard test frames.

For the two golden scenes, Kitchen 2 and Oslo, we additionally perform controlled recaptures under prescribed binary object states and new camera trajectories, as illustrated in . These recaptures define two additional evaluation splits.

Figure8

We recapture object-state configurations observed during the original training sequence using new camera trajectories. This split evaluates generalization to novel viewpoints while keeping the scene configuration within the set observed during training.Novel camera frames.

We additionally recapture joint object-state configurations that never occurred during the training sequence, again using new camera trajectories. This split evaluates whether the learned representation can compose individually observed object states into previously unseen scene configurations.Novel state-combination frames.

Dynamic-baseline evaluation.

DeGauss and 4DGS represent scene variation using a continuous timestamp and cannot directly condition on the prescribed state code of a Golden-set test image. For the novel-camera and novel state-combination splits, we therefore evaluate both methods using the same per-image oracle-over-time protocol. We first evaluate 30 uniformly spaced timestamps over $[0,1]$ , then evaluate 8 additional timestamps within a $\pm 0.03$ neighborhood of the best coarse prediction. The rendering with the highest PSNR across both stages is retained. PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS are computed from this same selected rendering; SSIM and LPIPS are not independently optimized. Since the ground-truth image is used to select the timestamp, these results should be interpreted as oracle upper bounds.

The training sequence contains one interaction at a time, repeatedly returning to the base state.

We additionally recapture the scene under controlled object states using new camera trajectories.

States observed during training evaluate novel camera trajectories, while previously unseen joint states evaluate novel state combinations.

Figure 8. Golden-set benchmark construction.(a)(b)

A.3.

For fair comparison, all methods use corresponding undistorted pinhole images for both training and rendering, with the camera-holder exclusion masks mapped into the respective undistorted image representation.

We initialize our Gaussians from the COLMAP SfM point cloud and use the same densification and pruning schedule as 3DGUT. Gaussian parameters and state logits are optimized with fused Adam, while the slot-window endpoints and temperatures use a separate Adam optimizer; both optimizers are stepped jointly. SwitchSplat, FullCircle, and 4DGS are trained for 30,000 iterations with batch size 4. DeGauss uses batch size 4 with a 1,000-iteration coarse stage followed by a 30,000-iteration fine stage. The learning rates for opacity and state logits are both $5\times 10^{-2}$ .

The state-sparsity loss has weight $10^{-4}$ , starts at iteration 18,000, and ramps linearly over 1,000 iterations. The compactness loss has weight $5\times 10^{-4}$ , starts at iteration 21,000, and also ramps linearly over 1,000 iterations. For each slot, both states are measured relative to the opacity- and assignment-weighted centroid of the active state. After iterations 18,000 and 21,000, we mean-center the state logits and scale them by $0.3$ , reducing assignment confidence as the corresponding regularizer becomes active.

Different movable parts or controls of the same larger object are separate events and must not be merged merely because they belong to the same object.¨- The sequence may begin with a setup or base-capture traversal in which the camera circles or surveys the scene. Do not count that traversal unless a specific part or control is manipulated and changes state.¨- When the manipulated part is obscured, repeated approach-manipulate-withdraw cycles, separated by clear disengagement or repositioning, may establish separate episodes.¨- Estimate the midpoint of the user’s state-changing action, not only the first frame where the object is perfectly stable or unobstructed.¨- Use the rendered t=FRAME labels for transition timing.¨- If a transition is uncertain, still give the best approximate frame and lower confidence.¨- Keep events in chronological order.¨- Do not invent events with no visual support, but missing an event is worse than reporting a plausible low-confidence one.¨- Valid frame range is {N_FRAME}¨¨Timestamp convention:¨- The attached images are in chronological order.¨- They are sampled every 8 frames, with the first and final frames included.¨- Each image has its exact frame number rendered on its pixels as t=FRAME.¨- The rendered t=FRAME label is authoritative; use the stride only as a consistency check.¨¨Analyze only the attached images. A.7.

Our outdoor scenes contain substantial temporal variation unrelated to the discrete object-state changes targeted by SwitchSplat, including wind-driven vegetation, changing sky and clouds, and distant street activity. Such variation can disproportionately affect full-frame image metrics and partially obscure differences in the reconstruction quality of the interactive scene content. We therefore additionally evaluate all methods after excluding these moving-background regions, while otherwise retaining the same evaluation protocol. As shown in , under the original evaluation, SwitchSplat (3DGUT) achieves $29.03$  dB compared with $29.14$  dB for 4DGS, despite producing visibly cleaner reconstructions. After excluding the moving background, SwitchSplat improves to $32.87$  dB, compared with $31.87$  dB for 4DGS, while also achieving the best SSIM and LPIPS. A similar trend is observed on Balcony, where SwitchSplat remains the strongest method. These results suggest that the apparent discrepancy between quantitative and qualitative performance on the outdoor scenes is largely attributable to unrelated background dynamics.

一句话：用随手拍摄的素材，让 3DGS 场景学会物体的离散状态切换（开/关、有/无）。

要点：

  • 从非受控拍摄中自动发现物体的离散状态变化
  • 把状态建模进高斯泼溅表示，支持切换
  • SIGGRAPH Asia 2026 会议论文

为什么值得看：可交互的数字资产需要「状态」而不是静态重建；这套把离散状态塞进 3DGS 的做法，直接对应引擎里的资产表达。

中文摘要：SwitchSplat 研究如何从随手拍摄（非受控）的场景数据中学习物体的离散状态——例如灯的开与关、物体的有与无——并把状态建模进 3D 高斯泼溅表示里，使得重建结果可以被切换，而不是只能回放原始拍摄状态。论文被 SIGGRAPH Asia 2026 接收。对需要「可交互重建资产」的引擎流程，这是一种更贴近实际需求的表示方式。

learns a state-aware scene representation from a casual capture (: input video frames showing the user interacting with the car).

The scene is decomposed into a static base and a set of independently switchable slots, one per interactable object (here: right door, hood, trunk).

Each slot models two binary states, enabling SwitchSplat to render any combination of object configurations from novel viewpoints at inference time (: four of the $2^{3}=8$ possible slot configurations, labeled by their on/off state vector).

Figure 1. SwitchSplattopbottomThe top row is a filmstrip of a camera moving around a blue car while a person successively opens its side door, hood, and trunk. The bottom row contains four novel-view renderings of the car, each paired with labeled switches for the trunk, door, and hood. The examples show all three parts closed, only the hood open, only the trunk open, and both the trunk and hood open, illustrating independent composition of the three binary object states.

Abstract.

3D Gaussian Splatting has made high-fidelity 3D reconstruction fast and accessible, yet existing representations assume a static world.

This assumption breaks down in casual captures, where a user naturally interacts with the environment – opening doors, toggling switches, or moving objects – introducing discrete state changes that no current framework can model.

Time-conditioned dynamic methods such as 4DGS conflate a state was observed with state the scene is in, limiting them to replaying seen sequences rather than composing arbitrary object configurations.

We present SwitchSplat, the first 3DGS representation to address this gap via a base $+$ slot decomposition: a shared static base captures the invariant scene, while each slot independently holds the two binary states (on/off) of one interactable object.

Because the assignment of Gaussians to slots is fully differentiable, the model discovers the geometry of each state directly from video, without manual annotation.

At inference, the user can freely combine slot states and render the resulting scene from any viewpoint.

We validate SwitchSplat on a new casual-capture dataset and show that it outperforms static and dynamic baselines in novel-view synthesis quality, while uniquely supporting rendering of state combinations never seen during capture.

Project page: .whenwhat

https://switchsplat.github.io

Novel View Synthesis, Gaussian Splatting, State-aware Rendering, $360^{\circ}$ Capture

Keywords:

†by†cc-license:

1.

In inverse rendering, Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)  has emerged as the leading representation for real-time, high-fidelity novel-view synthesis, enabling a new generation of interactive applications.

Its combination of fast training and efficient rendering has driven broad adoption across academia as well as industry, from Matterport’s digital twins and Niantic Scaniverse’s mobile reconstruction to Meta’s Hyperscape.()

Kerbl et al., 2023

111

https://www.meta.com/experiences/meta-horizon-hyperscape-capture-beta/8798130056953686/

While early 3DGS pipelines required meticulous data acquisition (fixed exposure and white balance, controlled lighting, and a perfectly static scene), recent works like 3DGRT  and FullCircle  have unlocked capture: viewpoints need not be carefully curated – made possible by $360^{\circ}$ cameras held in a single hand – and the capturer’s pixels are automatically masked out to satisfy the static-scene assumption.

This freedom naturally invites users to with the environment during capture – opening doors, toggling switches, or repositioning objects – turning the operator into both an active agent a dynamic distractor within the scene.()

Moenne-Loccoz et al., 2024

()

Foroutan et al., 2026

casualinteractand

Yet no existing reconstruction framework is equipped to handle these interactions.

Many contemporary 3D representations enforce a strict static-world assumption: when an operator triggers a discrete state change – opening a door, flipping a switch, relocating an object – the model has no mechanism to account for the resulting geometric variation.

As a result, even state-of-the-art pipelines can only represent a single, frozen scene configuration, and capturing multiple stable states requires re-recording the scene from scratch.

One could argue that the natural candidate to address this limitation is the family of 4D Gaussian Splatting methods , which extend 3DGS to dynamic scenes by conditioning the scene representation on time.

However, this design choice fundamentally conflates a state was observed with state the scene is in: the model learns to replay a specific sequence of observations, not to understand independent object configurations.()

Yang et al., 2024b

whenwhat

As a result, 4D methods are largely limited to novel-viewpoint synthesis of seen sequences; composing an unseen combination of object states—e.g., door open and light on—is not directly supported, since no single timestamp in the training data corresponds to that configuration.

What is needed instead is a representation that scene state from time, allowing the user to freely specify both the viewpoint and the desired configuration of each object independently.de-correlates

To address these challenges, we propose , a method that learns “state-aware” representations from casual captures featuring human-object interactions; see .

SwitchSplat organizes the scene into a – the parts that never change throughout the capture – and a set of , one per interactable object.

Each slot holds two 3D representations corresponding to the binary states of that object (“on” and “off”).

For example, if a room was captured while a closet door was closed for part of the recording and open for another, a single slot would hold both the “off” state (door closed, interior hidden) and the “on” state (door open, interior visible), while the walls, floor, and furniture – unchanged throughout – are handled by the static base.

To assign each Gaussian primitive to the right part of the scene, we attach a small learnable score vector that controls how strongly the primitive belongs to the base, or to either state of each slot.SwitchSplat

Figure1

static baseslots

This decomposition avoids data redundancy: without a shared static base, one would need to duplicate the full scene geometry for every slot, with no reusable structure across states.

Instead, SwitchSplat shares the base across all configurations and only stores the geometry that actually differs per state.

Because the full pipeline is differentiable end-to-end, the model learns simultaneously which Gaussians belong to which slot and when each slot is active – directly from the input video, without any manual annotation.

At inference, the user can query any combination of slot states independently – e.g., closet door open and desk lamp on – and render the resulting scene from any viewpoint.2

This is structurally analogous to PCA-based morphable models : the static base plays the role of the mean face, each slot’s on/off representations correspond to the eigenvectors, and the state activations act as the blend-shape coefficients.22()

Blanz and Vetter, 2023

To summarize our contributions:

(1) We in the 3DGS literature: existing representations cannot model scenes with discrete, user-triggered state changes (e.g., objects that can be opened, switched, or moved), and we show that naïvely applying dynamic methods such as 4DGS fails to address this.

(2) We propose SwitchSplat, the first 3DGS representation to address this problem via a , where a shared static base captures the invariant scene and each slot independently models the binary states of one interactable object.

(3) We demonstrate on a that SwitchSplat improves novel-view synthesis quality over static and dynamic baselines, and uniquely supports rendering arbitrary combinations of object states from unseen viewpoints.identify a novel problembase $+$ slot decompositionnew casual-capture dataset

2.

3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)  has become the dominant representation for novel-view synthesis, optimizing a set of anisotropic Gaussian primitives that render at real-time rates.

Extensions beyond the standard perspective-camera model are particularly relevant to our setting: 3DGRT  reformulates rendering via ray tracing, and 3DGUT  adds support for highly distorted cameras and secondary rays, enabling casual capture with wide field-of-view sensors.

FullCircle  further shows that raw dual-fisheye $360^{\circ}$ video suffices for high-quality reconstruction, automatically masking the camera operator.

Despite these advances, all of these pipelines represent the scene as a single, fixed configuration.

When multiple object states are present in the capture—a door open in some frames and closed in others—the model either conflates them into averaged geometry and ghosting artifacts, or learns to discard the minority state as a distractor .

Either way, only one configuration survives in the final model; there is no mechanism to retain, switch between, or compose multiple stable states at inference time.()

Dynamic Gaussian Splatting

A large family of methods extends 3DGS to dynamic scenes by conditioning the representation on time.

Dynamic 3D Gaussians  tracks persistent primitives across frames, while Deformable 3D Gaussians  and 4DGS  deform a canonical scene over time, with 4DGS using a learned space-time encoding.

Spacetime Gaussians  further augments primitives with temporal opacity and parametric motion.

Subsequent work improves efficiency, temporal consistency, or geometric accuracy via depth priors .

Differently from our method, all of these methods are parameterized by time, not by object state: recovering a specific scene configuration requires locating the right moment in the recording, and rendering a novel combination of states—e.g., two objects in configurations never co-observed—is not supported.()

Decomposed Gaussian Splatting

More recent dynamic Gaussian methods, such as SDD-4DGS , observe that applying deformation models to the entire scene is often inefficient, since most real-world scenes are largely static.

This motivates methods that decompose scenes into static and dynamic components: GauFRe  combines a static Gaussian component with deformable dynamic Gaussians, while Swift4D  improves efficiency by passing only dynamic Gaussians through the deformation model.

DeGauss  further uses dynamic-static decomposition to improve robustness to transient distractors.

This observation is closely aligned with our setting, since object interactions usually affect only a small part of a $360^{\circ}$ environment.

In contrast to our method, existing decomposition methods still treat the dynamic component as a temporally varying foreground: they separate dynamic regions from a static background, but provide no mechanism to independently switch or compose object states at inference time.()

Controllable Scene Representation

A parallel line of work studies controllable and articulated 3D representations.

Pre-Gaussian methods such as Watch It Move  discover articulated structure from object motion; PARIS  goes further by decoupling static and movable parts from two multi-view captures of the same scene.

Gaussian-based approaches extend this to photorealistic settings: SC-GS  enables motion editing via sparse control points, Template-free Articulated Gaussian Splatting  supports re-posing with super-points, and RigGS  adds rig-based editing and interpolation.

ArtGS  and ArticulatedGS  further focus on part-level modeling of individual objects.

Crucially, all of these methods aim to object motion or articulation—they model how parts move, rather than discarding motion entirely to focus on the discrete stable configurations of the scene.

In contrast, our method treats object interactions as a nuisance to be factored out, retaining only the clean on/off states and ignoring the transient motion between them.()

State-aware Scene Reconstruction

Closest to our setting are methods that reconstruct scenes across discrete object states.

IGFuse  and RecurGS  address this by using semantic cues to detect state changes and aligning them via rigid transformations.

GaussianCut  and DecoupledGaussian  contribute related tools for object segmentation and scene decomposition.

However, all of these methods assume that state changes can be described as rigid motions of segmented object entities—an assumption that breaks down for casual capture, where interaction boundaries are fuzzy and deformations are non-rigid.

In contrast, SwitchSplat learns which Gaussians belong to each state directly from photometric supervision, without requiring object masks, or rigid-body assumptions.()

3.

SwitchSplat learns a state-aware 3D representation from casual captures by decomposing the scene into controllable, state-conditioned components.

In the following subsections, we detail our methodology by first formulating our state-conditioned Gaussian primitives and describing their integration within volume rendering ().

We then introduce the parameterization of the differentiable slot-table (), followed by our slot initialization procedure ().

Finally, we describe our training pipeline and objectives that facilitate granular, state-controlled visualization during inference ( and ).

Terminology

A corresponds to one interactable object and holds two 3D representations for its binary states: “off” (e.g., door closed) and “on” (e.g., door open).

A is a per-frame binary variable indicating which state is currently observed.

All parts of the scene that remain constant throughout the capture are handled by the , which is shared across all configurations.slotslot activationstatic base

3.1.

Each 3D Gaussian primitive in our model is defined by its standard geometric and appearance attributes: mean $\mu$ , covariance $\Sigma$ , opacity $\alpha$ , and view-dependent appearance  $\mathbf{c}$ .

To make our representation state-aware, we augment every Gaussian with a learnable categorical state distribution $\mathbf{p}=\operatorname{softmax}(\ell)$ over $1+2K$ channels, where $K$ is the total number of object slots.

These channels comprise a single static channel $\ell[0]$ , together with a pair of ( $\ell[2k{-}1]$ ) and ( $\ell[2k]$ ) channels for each slot $k\in\{1,\dots,K\}$ .

The two channels per slot — rather than one — let the softmax assign each Gaussian to a single configuration, so that disjoint subsets of primitives can independently model the geometry and appearance of an object in each of its two states (see ).

This separation is essential because the on/off configurations of an object generally differ not just in appearance, but also in spatial extent — a closed door and an open door, for instance, occupy different parts of the scene — which a single shared primitive simply cannot represent.baseoffon

Test-time rendering

Assume we have trained our representation, and that we want to render an image corresponding to the slot configuration $\tilde{\mathbf{p}}\in\{0,1\}^{K}$ .

This is achieved by computing the probability of each gaussian being present in the scene to be rendered:

(1) $\omega(\tilde{\mathbf{p}})=\mathbf{p}[0]+\sum_{k=1}^{K}\Big(\tilde{\mathbf{p}}[k]\cdot\mathbf{p}[2k]+(1-\tilde{\mathbf{p}}[k])\cdot\mathbf{p}[2k-1]\Big)$

This formulation ensures that “base” Gaussians remain present across all frames, while the presence of the on/off state Gaussians is gated by the probability of the corresponding slot being on.

We then gate the opacity of the gaussian by this probability:

(2) $\tilde{\alpha}=\alpha\cdot\omega(\tilde{\mathbf{p}}),$

which is then used to compute the final RGB color for a ray $\mathbf{r}$ via classical volume rendering :()

where $\mathcal{H}(r)$ represents the set of Gaussians intersected by the ray in depth order and $\mathbf{c}_{i}(r)$ denotes the view-dependent color.

While $\tilde{\mathbf{p}}$ will be selected by the user at test-time, the key question in training our representation lies in how to propagate the gradients from image $\hat{I}_{t}$ at time $t$ to the (per-Gaussian) state distribution  $\mathbf{p}$ .

Train-time rendering

The quantity $\pi_{k}(t)$ defined above is our , which we use to compute the probability of each Gaussian being present in the scene at time $t$ :slot table

This differentiable rendering framework ensures that gradients propagate seamlessly to the slot activation probabilities, Gaussian state memberships, and geometric parameters, enabling stable and efficient joint optimization of the entire scene representation.

3.3.

In a casual capture setting, neither the total number of slots $K$ , nor the precise slot transition timestamps are known a priori.

Requiring the user to annotate them would defeat the very premise of a “casual” capture.

To address this, we leverage the reasoning capabilities of Vision-Language Models (VLMs), and in particular GPT $5.6$ , to provide an approximate initialization for the slot-table.

By prompting GPT $5.6$ with a sequence of frames, we extract semantically grounded start and end timestamps for each distinct object interaction.

These timestamps serve as the initial values for the endpoint parameters $(t_{l},t_{r})$ in our slot-table.

This VLM-informed initialization allows the system to bypass exhaustive temporal searches or complex diagnostics, providing a clean and efficient configuration for final full-resolution training.

To facilitate a robust optimization process, we initialize each interaction slot with a high temperature value ${rgb(0bp)=(0,0,0);rgb(25bp)=(0,0,0);rgb(75bp)=(0.5,0.5,0.5);rgb(100bp)=(0.5,0.5,0.5)}$ .

This high-temperature initialization ensures that the Bernoulli random variable $\mathcal{S}_{k,t}$ begins with smooth transitions at the boundaries, allowing the gradients to flow more effectively over a wider temporal range during the initial stages of optimization.

3.4.

Leveraging the initial parameters derived from the VLM-based slot discovery phase, we proceed to optimize our final state-aware scene representation.

We build our state-aware framework upon the 3D Gaussian Unscented Transform (3DGUT) architecture .

Following the 3DGUT pipeline, we initialize the 3D Gaussian primitives using COLMAP-derived point clouds and augment each primitive with the learnable state logits $\ell$ .

To provide an unbiased starting point for optimization, these logits are initialized such that the base/on/off state channels are assigned equal membership probabilities.

Throughout this stage, we jointly optimize the geometric attributes of the Gaussians, their state logits, and the temporal parameters of the slot-table $(t_{l},t_{r},{rgb(0bp)=(0,0,0);rgb(25bp)=(0,0,0);rgb(75bp)=(0.5,0.5,0.5);rgb(100bp)=(0.5,0.5,0.5)})$ .

We strictly adhere to the optimization schedule established by 3DGUT, including its specialized densification and pruning protocols.

To ensure consistent state behavior during optimization, we modify the standard densification process: whenever a Gaussian primitive is cloned or split, its state logits are inherited by the resultant primitives.

This inheritance mechanism ensures that state-aware attributes remain spatially coherent even as the underlying scene geometry increases in complexity.()

Beyond the standard $L_{1}$ photometric and SSIM losses used to preserve perceptual fidelity, we employ two additional regularizers to mitigate floater artifacts, and prevent the emergence of redundant Gaussian primitives by supervising the optimization process via:

Sparsity loss

To ensure a parsimonious partitioning of the scene, we regularize the Gaussian primitives to favor the static base state, thereby preventing unnecessary scene regions from being categorized as interactive.

This is achieved by applying a negative log-likelihood penalty on the base state probability for all $N$ Gaussians:

(8) $\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{sparsity}}=-\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n}\log\mathbf{p}_{n}[0]$

Compactness loss

To encourage Gaussians within slots to form spatially cohesive clusters, we first compute the opacity-weighted center of mass for primitives assigned to the on state of slot $k$ :

and then penalize the weighted variance  for both the off and on states to encourage local clustering:()

4.

To validate the effectiveness of our proposed algorithm in the absence of an existing dataset with variable object interactions, we collected a custom dataset using a consumer-grade Insta360 X4 dual-fisheye $360^{\circ}$ camera.

This hardware choice reflects the typical setup of casual users.

During capture, we emulated non-expert behaviors, moving through the scene and interacting with objects—transitioning them from resting to active states and back.

Our dataset comprises $12$ scenes organized into two groups.

The contains $10$ casually captured scenes ( $8$ indoor and $2$ outdoor), each featuring $3$ – $9$ object interactions.

The contains $2$ additional scenes for which we acquire controlled test sequences with novel camera trajectories and object-state combinations.

We preprocess the raw dual-fisheye data following FullCircle  to mask the capturer.

The calibration is performed in COLMAP using the masked fisheye frames, and then the fisheye images are undistorted into standard pinhole images.standard setgolden set()

4.4.

Beyond the standard held-out evaluation on the original trajectories, we evaluate SwitchSplat on two additional generalization settings: novel camera frames and novel state-combination frames.

For two representative scenes, we acquire dedicated test trajectories containing previously unseen camera viewpoints and object-state combinations, and compare against 4DGS and DeGauss. Because 4DGS and DeGauss parameterize scene variation by continuous time rather than a discrete state code, we evaluate both dynamic baselines on the novel-camera and novel state-combination splits using a per-image oracle over time. For each target image, we select the rendering with the highest PSNR for both methods; these results therefore constitute upper bounds.

As shown in , SwitchSplat consistently outperforms the dynamic baselines on novel camera frames and produces sharper reconstructions with fewer structural artifacts.

We further evaluate novel state-combination frames, where multiple independently controlled interactions are composed into configurations not observed during training. Quantitative results in demonstrate that SwitchSplat maintains high reconstruction quality under these unseen configurations, highlighting the compositional generalization enabled by our state-conditioned representation.

Slot representation

We first evaluate the importance of the slot representation.

When interaction slots are removed, the model reduces to a scene representation without any of our slot-specific components, including slot optimization and the associated regularization terms.

We next assess the importance of optimizing the initialized slot parameters.

Compactness regularization

The compactness loss encourages state-conditioned Gaussians associated with the same interaction to remain spatially localized, preventing them from dispersing across unrelated regions of the scene.

This spatial prior therefore plays an important role in learning coherent state-dependent representations.

Sparsity regularization

Removing the sparsity regularization has a modest effect on average reconstruction quality.

The regularizer nevertheless discourages unnecessary assignment of otherwise static Gaussians to interactive states, promoting a more parsimonious state decomposition and reducing spurious state-dependent changes.

We evaluate the impact of various components in our method by systematically excluding them and analyzing the reconstruction quality (PSNR) on the “Kitchen 2” scene.

5.

We presented SwitchSplat, a 3D Gaussian Splatting framework that learns state-aware scene representations directly from casual video captures.

By decomposing the scene into a shared static base and a set of independently controllable slots, each modeling the binary “on”/“off” states of one interactable object, SwitchSplat decouples scene state from time – enabling a capability that time-conditioned dynamic methods fundamentally cannot provide: free composition of object configurations at inference, including combinations never observed during capture.

The slot table is initialized via a VLM and jointly refined end-to-end through differentiable rendering, requiring no manual annotation.

Experiments on our new casual-capture dataset show that SwitchSplat outperforms static and dynamic baselines in novel-view synthesis quality, and uniquely generalizes to out-of-distribution camera paths and unseen state combinations.

Limitations and future work

The current model assumes binary object states with the constraints of single-operator capture with one free hand.

Extending to continuous or multi-valued states by multiple operators – would broaden the applicability of the framework.

The slot count and approximate interaction windows are currently seeded by a VLM; a fully unsupervised discovery of both the number and timing of interactions from raw video remains an open problem.

Finally, SwitchSplat focuses on novel-view synthesis; combining our state-aware decomposition with physics-based priors or generative models could enable downstream applications such as scene editing and simulation.

A.1.

We captured twelve real-world scenes using an Insta360 X4 dual-fisheye 360 camera, comprising ten standard scenes and two golden scenes. Video frames were extracted at 4 FPS. We use the raw fisheye frames for reconstruction to avoid propagating stitching artifacts into the scene representation. Camera-holder masks are automatically obtained using the FullCircle masking pipeline. These masks, together with the fisheye frames, are passed to COLMAP for camera pose estimation and subsequent image undistortion. Input images are downsampled by a factor of two. An overview of the object-interaction intervals and temporal structure of all twelve scenes is provided in .

Figure15

A.2.

We evaluate reconstruction and generalization using four evaluation splits.

This split contains held-out frames in which all objects remain in their initial base state. It evaluates reconstruction of the canonical scene configuration and provides a natural comparison point for static reconstruction methods.Base-state test frames.

For each scene, we hold out every eight frame from the original capture sequence. Frames occurring during object transitions are excluded, such that evaluation is performed only on stable object configurations. The remaining frames constitute our standard test set and cover the object states observed throughout the original capture.All standard test frames.

For the two golden scenes, Kitchen 2 and Oslo, we additionally perform controlled recaptures under prescribed binary object states and new camera trajectories, as illustrated in . These recaptures define two additional evaluation splits.

Figure8

We recapture object-state configurations observed during the original training sequence using new camera trajectories. This split evaluates generalization to novel viewpoints while keeping the scene configuration within the set observed during training.Novel camera frames.

We additionally recapture joint object-state configurations that never occurred during the training sequence, again using new camera trajectories. This split evaluates whether the learned representation can compose individually observed object states into previously unseen scene configurations.Novel state-combination frames.

Dynamic-baseline evaluation.

DeGauss and 4DGS represent scene variation using a continuous timestamp and cannot directly condition on the prescribed state code of a Golden-set test image. For the novel-camera and novel state-combination splits, we therefore evaluate both methods using the same per-image oracle-over-time protocol. We first evaluate 30 uniformly spaced timestamps over $[0,1]$ , then evaluate 8 additional timestamps within a $\pm 0.03$ neighborhood of the best coarse prediction. The rendering with the highest PSNR across both stages is retained. PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS are computed from this same selected rendering; SSIM and LPIPS are not independently optimized. Since the ground-truth image is used to select the timestamp, these results should be interpreted as oracle upper bounds.

The training sequence contains one interaction at a time, repeatedly returning to the base state.

We additionally recapture the scene under controlled object states using new camera trajectories.

States observed during training evaluate novel camera trajectories, while previously unseen joint states evaluate novel state combinations.

Figure 8. Golden-set benchmark construction.(a)(b)

A.3.

For fair comparison, all methods use corresponding undistorted pinhole images for both training and rendering, with the camera-holder exclusion masks mapped into the respective undistorted image representation.

We initialize our Gaussians from the COLMAP SfM point cloud and use the same densification and pruning schedule as 3DGUT. Gaussian parameters and state logits are optimized with fused Adam, while the slot-window endpoints and temperatures use a separate Adam optimizer; both optimizers are stepped jointly. SwitchSplat, FullCircle, and 4DGS are trained for 30,000 iterations with batch size 4. DeGauss uses batch size 4 with a 1,000-iteration coarse stage followed by a 30,000-iteration fine stage. The learning rates for opacity and state logits are both $5\times 10^{-2}$ .

The state-sparsity loss has weight $10^{-4}$ , starts at iteration 18,000, and ramps linearly over 1,000 iterations. The compactness loss has weight $5\times 10^{-4}$ , starts at iteration 21,000, and also ramps linearly over 1,000 iterations. For each slot, both states are measured relative to the opacity- and assignment-weighted centroid of the active state. After iterations 18,000 and 21,000, we mean-center the state logits and scale them by $0.3$ , reducing assignment confidence as the corresponding regularizer becomes active.

For completeness, we report the full per-scene evaluation in terms of PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS. reports results on the 10 standard benchmark scenes for both the base-state subset and all standard test frames, while reports results on the two Golden scenes across the base-state, standard-test, novel-camera, and novel state-combination splits. We use GPT-5.6 Sol to automatically initialize both the number of interaction

slots and their approximate temporal extents. We uniformly sample the camera

stream every 8 frames, resize each frame to $480\times 480$ , and render its

identify distinct object-state episodes and return approximate on/off

transition timestamps together with a confidence score. We discard predicted

intervals shorter than 20 frames and apply confidence-ranked temporal

non-maximum suppression with an IoU threshold of $0.8$ .

Within this region, both the final temporal IoU and test PSNR remain high despite large errors in the initial center or duration; cases A–C illustrate several such trajectories. Only for sufficiently extreme perturbations does optimization converge to an incorrect temporal interval, as illustrated by cases D–F.

A.7.

Our outdoor scenes contain substantial temporal variation unrelated to the discrete object-state changes targeted by SwitchSplat, including wind-driven vegetation, changing sky and clouds, and distant street activity. Such variation can disproportionately affect full-frame image metrics and partially obscure differences in the reconstruction quality of the interactive scene content. We therefore additionally evaluate all methods after excluding these moving-background regions, while otherwise retaining the same evaluation protocol. As shown in , under the original evaluation, SwitchSplat (3DGUT) achieves $29.03$  dB compared with $29.14$  dB for 4DGS, despite producing visibly cleaner reconstructions. After excluding the moving background, SwitchSplat improves to $32.87$  dB, compared with $31.87$  dB for 4DGS, while also achieving the best SSIM and LPIPS. A similar trend is observed on Balcony, where SwitchSplat remains the strongest method. These results suggest that the apparent discrepancy between quantitative and qualitative performance on the outdoor scenes is largely attributable to unrelated background dynamics.

item.title: OUGS：3DGS 里按物体感知不确定性挑下一个视角 ｜ OUGS: Active View Selection via Object-aware Uncertainty Estimation in 3DGS
item.description:
一句话：用物体级不确定性给 3DGS 重建做主动视角选择，用更少的拍摄补全场景。

要点：

  • 把不确定性拆到物体粒度，而不是全图像素级
  • 据此决定下一次拍摄/采样应该对准哪里
  • 在 3DGS 重建质量与采集成本之间取得更优折中

为什么值得看：扫描式资产采集与数字孪生都会遇到「拍哪里」的问题；物体级不确定性比全图指标更实用。

中文摘要：OUGS 研究 3D 高斯泼溅重建中的主动视角选择问题：与其均匀采样，不如先估计哪些区域重建质量差，再针对性补拍。作者把不确定性建模到物体粒度，并以此驱动下一次视角选择，从而在相同采集预算下获得更好的重建质量。对需要现场采集资产的团队，这套「先估不确定、再决定拍哪」的流程可以直接借用。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

\ConferencePaper\CGFStandardLicense

OUGS: Active View Selection via Object-aware Uncertainty Estimation in 3DGS

45Volume: 2Issue: Haiyi Li,

Qi Chen,

Denis Kalkofen,

and Hsiang-Ting Chen1121University of Adelaide, Australia1Graz University of Technology2

Abstract

Recent advances in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) have achieved state-of-the-art results for novel view synthesis. However, efficiently capturing high-fidelity reconstructions of specific objects within complex scenes remains a significant challenge. A key limitation of existing active reconstruction methods is their reliance on scene-level uncertainty metrics, which are often biased by irrelevant background clutter and lead to inefficient view selection for object-centric tasks.

We present OUGS, a novel framework that addresses this challenge with a more principled, physically-grounded uncertainty formulation for 3DGS. Our core innovation is to derive uncertainty directly from the of the 3D Gaussian primitives (e.g., position, scale, rotation). By propagating the covariance of these parameters through the rendering Jacobian, we establish a highly interpretable uncertainty model. This foundation allows us to then seamlessly integrate semantic segmentation masks to produce a targeted, uncertainty score that effectively disentangles the object from its environment. This allows for a more effective active view selection strategy that prioritizes views critical to improving object fidelity.

Experimental evaluations on public datasets demonstrate that our approach significantly improves the efficiency of the 3DGS reconstruction process and achieves higher quality for targeted objects compared to existing state-of-the-art methods, while also serving as a robust uncertainty estimator for the global scene.explicit physical parametersobject-aware

1

Efficient 3D scene reconstruction is a foundational goal in computer vision and robotics. The advent of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF)  marked a breakthrough, enabling photorealistic novel view synthesis by learning implicit volumetric representations. More recently, 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)  has emerged as a compelling alternative. By modeling scenes with explicit 3D Gaussian primitives and leveraging a fast, differentiable rasterization pipeline, 3DGS achieves real-time rendering speeds without compromising visual fidelity, addressing the high computational cost that limits NeRF’s practicality.[]

MST∗20

[]

KKLD23

Despite these advances, both NeRF and 3DGS remain highly data-intensive, typically requiring dense image captures to produce high-quality reconstructions . This motivates the need for active reconstruction , where a human  or robotic agent actively selects a minimal subset of views that maximally reduces uncertainty. Achieving this requires models to estimate their own information needs in real-time—a capability that hinges on accurate uncertainty estimation.[, ]

NBM∗22

CKD∗25

[]

CLK11

[, ]

STC∗25

MZC∗25

: Figure 1A complex background can inflate image-level uncertainty.This can mislead active view selection away from the object.

: Figure 2Objectaware uncertainty guides 3DGS view planning for precise object reconstruction.-Our physically-grounded uncertainty model, derived from the explicit parameters of the 3D Gaussians, is combined with a semantic mask to generate an object-level uncertainty score. This score effectively guides the active view selection to improve object fidelity, as shown for 5, 10, and 20 selected views.

In this context, recent work has explored incorporating uncertainty into both NeRFs  and 3DGS. For the latter, emerging research has methods based on ensemble variance  or Fisher Information approximations . However, these pioneering methods share a fundamental limitation: they typically estimate uncertainty at the scene level. As illustrated in figure , a global uncertainty score is often dominated by complex but irrelevant background clutter, misleading the view selection process. This is particularly problematic for applications where the primary goal is to capture a with the highest possible fidelity, such as in cultural heritage preservation, industrial inspection, and AR . These scenarios demand object-centric planning, where background noise can distort the focus.[, ]

GRS∗24

KMKS24

HD25
