Physics-based Lagrangian simulation has a rich history in computer graphics, evolving from early elastic models to finite element methods (FEM) , contact handling , and others . Recently, barrier-based methods such as incremental potential contact (IPC) provide strict intersection-free guarantees, but incur high computational costs . Conversely, real-time solvers achieve interactive rates at the expense of physical fidelity, and they cannot learn the behavior of high-accuracy solvers . Differentiable simulators restore gradients, but either require tedious hand-derived formulations or need to backpropagate through every integration step . In contrast, PhysLDM serves as a fast, end-to-end differentiable neural surrogate learned directly from high-accuracy solvers.Physics-based deformable simulation.()

Neural simulators provide a fast, fully differentiable alternative to traditional solvers. The dominant paradigm of neural simulators is the AR rollout, which predicts the next state frame-by-frame. This paradigm has been adopted across diverse physical simulation fields . However, AR methods lack the global temporal context necessary for long-horizon consistency, potentially leading to temporal incoherence or trajectory drift. The concurrent work of performs one-shot multi-frame prediction, but is restricted to low-resolution surface meshes (training on about $356$ vertices per scene) from a limited set of templates ( $35$ different meshes). However, spatiotemporal autoencoders remain largely unexplored for high-fidelity, volumetric-mesh deformable-body physical simulation. In fact, existing autoencoders for physical simulation typically compress only the domain , with concurrent neural simulators following a similar . While spatiotemporal autoencoders have been successfully deployed in other domains, their architectures are tailored to their respective tasks, such as video generation and other fields . Unfortunately, these designs do not transfer directly to deformable physics. For deformable-body physical simulation, deterministic regression and generative diffusion have never been systematically compared. In practice, most work in neural simulation uses regression . Meanwhile, diffusion has instead been adopted where output distributions matter, such as image and video synthesis and human motion . Although the concurrent work of claims that diffusion is superior to deterministic regression, motivated by the diversity of futures under unobserved initial conditions, it never compares one-shot regression with diffusion. 3.1

We formulate the physical simulation of volumetric objects as a trajectory prediction task. Let a scene be represented as a tetrahedral mesh with rest vertices $\mathbf{r}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times 3}$ . The initial state of the system is defined as $\mathbf{s}_{0}=(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{R}_{0},\mathbf{c}_{0},\mathbf{v}_{0},\boldsymbol{\omega}_{0},E)$ , which encompasses the rest geometry, the frame- $0$ pose, linear velocity, and angular velocity, together with the Young’s modulus $E$ of the material. Our goal is to model the distribution $p(\mathbf{X}\mid\mathbf{s}_{0})$ of future vertex trajectories $\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times N\times 3}$ over a horizon of $T$ frames. Rather than modeling the raw world coordinates directly, we factor each frame into a global rigid transform acting on a canonical deformation:

$\mathbf{x}_{t}=\mathbf{R}_{t}\,(\mathbf{r}+\mathbf{d}_{t})+\mathbf{c}_{t},$ (1)

where $\mathbf{R}_{t}\in\mathrm{SO}(3)$ and $\mathbf{c}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{3}$ denote the per-frame rigid rotation and centroid translation, and $\mathbf{d}_{t}$ represents the residual canonical (rigid-free) deformation field. $\mathbf{R}_{t}$ and $\mathbf{c}_{t}$ are extracted from each ground-truth frame in closed form by a per-frame Procrustes (Kabsch) fit of the rest shape . This factoring separates the large-scale rigid motion from the small-scale deformation. The rigid transform $(\mathbf{R}_{t},\mathbf{c}_{t})$ carries the global motion in six degrees of freedom per frame. The canonical deformation field $\mathbf{d}_{t}$ then only has to capture the local deformation, which is independent of the object’s pose.()

Umeyama, 1991

3.2

As shown in Figure , PhysLDM has three main modules: a Spatial VAE, an ST-VAE, and an LDM.

2

The framework consists of three main components:

(1) A (top left) that encodes the per-frame canonical mesh into a compact set of resolution-independent latent tokens.

(2) An (bottom) that compresses the temporal trajectory into a single joint latent $\mathbf{Z}$ , which serves as the training target of the LDM.

(3) An (top right) that predicts the entire latent trajectory from the initial state in a single diffusion pass.   $\ast$ denotes the frozen decoders, which decode the latent into the final full trajectory.Figure 2: Overview of PhysLDM.Spatial VAEST-VAELDMDec

To efficiently process high-resolution volumetric meshes of varying vertex counts, we compress individual frames using a Spatial VAE. Following the representation of , a set of $K$ learnable query tokens cross-attends the canonical mesh vertices to extract a fixed-size set of $K$ latent tokens $\mathbf{z}_{t}$ , which remains independent of the vertex count $N$ . The decoder mirrors the encoder: each rest vertex, embedded with its position, cross-attends the latent tokens and is decoded to its displacement. This module ensures that the latent representation is resolution-independent.Spatial VAE.

Zhang et al. (2026)

The ST-VAE compresses the input $T$ -frame trajectory by a factor of $T/M$ into a compact latent $\mathbf{Z}$ . Each frame is represented by $K{+}1$ tokens: the $K$ deformation tokens from the spatial VAE and one additional rigid token that embeds the pose ( $\mathbf{R}_{t}$ and $\mathbf{c}_{t}$ ) in its channels. This token sequence first passes through axial blocks that alternate self-attention across tokens within a frame and along the temporal axis , after which it is decoupled into a deformation track and a rigid track. For the deformation track, the standard choice (as in video VAEs) would merge every $T/M$ frames into one latent frame and then decode it with a local temporal upsampler. However, this standard design introduces the staircase artifacts analyzed in Sec.  (Staircase analysis). We instead employ a holistic temporal representation where time is summarized by factorized self-attention: for each of the $K$ spatial tokens separately, $M$ learnable queries are prepended to its temporal sequence, attended along the time axis, and kept as the only temporal outputs, giving $K\times M$ tokens in total, which we call holistic temporal tokens. For the rigid track, sharing the holistic tokens with the deformation causes capacity competition and degrades the reconstruction (see ablation in Sec. ). The rigid token therefore takes a dedicated linear temporal pathway and recombines with the canonical shape per frame during decoding. Ultimately, the two tracks merge into the single joint latent $\mathbf{Z}$ that serves as the training target of the LDM. The ST-VAE decoder is kept frozen during the LDM stage to decode latents back into full trajectories.ST-VAE.(; ; )

Conditioned on the initial state, the LDM predicts the latent of the full $T$ -frame trajectory in one pass. The frame- $0$ mesh is injected via cross-attention on its spatial latent, while the pose, the initial velocity, and the stiffness condition the network via adaptive layer normalization (AdaLN) alongside the flow timestep. The mesh topology enters only through the frozen decoder, whose graph neural network (GNN) refines the decoded vertices over the tetrahedral mesh. We employ a flow-matching diffusion transformer (DiT) utilizing rectified flow to model the probability path. Architecture details are in Appendix .LDM.()

3.3

Our model is trained in three stages. The first stage trains the spatial VAE with a Charbonnier (smoothed $L_{1}$ ) position-reconstruction loss and a Kullback–Leibler (KL) loss (see the spatial-VAE-pretraining ablation in Appendix ). The second stage trains the ST-VAE on top of the pretrained spatial VAE. Its loss consists mainly of deformation and rigid reconstruction losses over all $T$ frames and a KL loss, together with a latent-anchor loss to the spatial manifold. The third stage trains the LDM on the pretrained, frozen ST-VAE, with a flow-matching velocity mean-squared error (MSE) loss. Complete loss forms, weights, and training details are given in Appendix .

Notably, our framework relies entirely on kinematic supervision. Every reconstruction loss is computed directly from geometry, namely vertex positions, velocities, and rigid poses. No constitutive models are used during training or inference. This purely data-driven approach makes PhysLDM agnostic to the underlying simulator’s energy model, allowing it to seamlessly scale across diverse materials, and giving it the potential to learn from real-world captured trajectories where explicit energy models are unavailable (Appendix ).Constitutive-Model-Free Supervision.

Data and setup.

We generate high-accuracy physical simulation data with a GPU FEM solver based on IPC . For each scene, we randomly select $n$ objects ( $n\leq 3$ ) from more than $30{,}000$ Objaverse objects, tetrahedralize them with fTetWild into volumetric meshes, and assign each object a random initial velocity ( $v_{0}$ ) and a random stiffness (Young’s modulus, $E$ ). The simulation time step is $1/60$  s and each trajectory has $64$ frames. The Objaverse scenes ( $63{,}397$ single-object and $16{,}078$ multi-body trajectories) are split into training, validation, and held-out test sets at a ratio of $90\%:5\%:5\%$ . For OOD evaluation, we generate scenes in the same way from the objects of two other datasets, GSO and Toys4K. The ST-VAE and the LDM are trained on scenes with $N\in[500,5{,}000]$ vertices. The ST-VAE and LDM results in this paper are trained on single-object scenes ( $n{=}1$ ). Our extended model is trained on multi-object scenes ( $n\leq 3$ ; see the multi-body extension in Appendix ). In the controlled ST-VAE comparisons, we use ST-VAE Small ( $K{=}512$ , $T{=}32$ , $M{=}4$ , $95$ M parameters). In the LDM experiments, we use ST-VAE Base ( $K{=}512$ , $T{=}64$ , $M{=}8$ , $124$ M parameters; Table ). Both configurations compress a trajectory by $8N/513$ in token count, which reaches $78\times$ at the $5{,}000$ -vertex cap. Training details are in Appendix . Full data details, evaluation setup, and metric definitions are in Appendix .(; )

B

Staircase analysis.

Standard temporal compression methods (such as video VAEs) uniformly compress consecutive frames into fixed latent blocks along the time axis and decode them with a local temporal upsampler, but this approach is not suitable for 3D volumetric deformable dynamics trajectory reconstruction: it causes the object’s deformation to hold and then snap to the next state, creating an unnatural “staircase” artifact that severely degrades visual fidelity. While this timing error is easily perceptible in video playback, it is difficult to identify from static multi-frame snapshots alone; therefore, we quantify it via the deformation-change correlation (DCC), defined in Appendix . Although DCC does not solely measure overall reconstruction quality on its own, it plays a decisive role in evaluating the physical plausibility of the motion when reconstruction precision is comparable. A detailed analysis of the staircase artifact is given in Appendix .

B.3

C

Chaos analysis.

Although physics simulators are commonly assumed to produce deterministic trajectories once initial states and parameters are fully specified, this is not guaranteed for GPU solvers. As shown in Fig. , running the same scene five times from byte-identical inputs yields visibly different final poses, with corresponding vertices landing up to $442$  mm apart. This divergence stems from two factors: first, the underlying hardware non-determinism of GPU solvers introduces negligible initial variations; second, the inherently chaotic nature of complex deformable dynamics can rapidly amplify these microscopic errors into macroscopic trajectory divergence. Consequently, training data is not a deterministic function of initial conditions. We also verify this at scale on the $300$ Objaverse held-out scenes: running each scene twice from identical initial conditions, the final-frame vertex trajectories of $23.7\%$ of these meter-scale scenes differ by more than $1\%$ of the object size (about $1$  cm), and those of $7.7\%$ differ by more than $5\%$ (about $5$  cm) (Table ). This chaotic nature suggests why regression models struggle: faced with multiple branching futures, a squared-error loss would drive the model toward the conditional mean, collapsing incompatible outcomes into a damped and non-physical average. A generative approach like our LDM naturally avoids this by sampling plausible trajectories. A more detailed chaos analysis is given in Appendix .

ST-VAE Reconstruction Results.

Table  and Fig.  evaluate our holistic ST-VAE against two alternative designs: standard temporal compression (the design of video VAEs) and a direct world-coordinate baseline (which applies holistic compression without the factoring of Eq. ()). All models share a matched compression rate and are assessed across the same three evaluation sets (Appendix ). The results yield three primary observations. First, holistic temporal compression eliminates staircase artifacts. Standard compression suffers from the staircase artifact (Sec. , Staircase analysis), which shows up as its clearly lower DCC. Our holistic ST-VAE preserves accurate motion timing, achieving a DCC exceeding $0.93$ across all evaluation sets. Furthermore, augmenting the standard baseline with auxiliary velocity or spectral losses, or placing the latent frames adaptively in time, does not mitigate this limitation (Table ). Second, decoupling rigid motion from deformation enhances precision. The direct world-coordinate baseline underperforms the holistic ST-VAE across all deformation and rigid motion metrics, and shows noisy and cluttered geometric detail in the visual comparison (Fig. ). Third, the holistic ST-VAE achieves superior precision across diverse scenarios. Under up to $78\times$ compression, the ST-VAE yields a mean geometric reconstruction error of just $2.48$  mm on held-out scenes, representing about half the error of the standard baseline, with a median vertex error below $2$  mm. It achieves the best performance across nearly all metrics and datasets, except for one rigid-rotation entry where it is a close second. This performance holds robustly zero-shot on OOD sets like GSO and Toys4K, where its errors stay at the same level as in distribution, and on high-resolution meshes exceeding the $5{,}000$ -vertex training cap, where its mean error is still only a few millimeters. The least accurate held-out cases, geometries with many long, thin features, are analyzed in Appendix .

Prediction Results.

Table  and Fig.  compare three models predicting a $64$ -frame trajectory from the same initial state: our LDM, a capacity-matched deterministic regression model (both using one-shot prediction and the same ST-VAE), and a frame-by-frame AR graph network based on MeshGraphNets (MGN) (Appendix ). Because complex deformable dynamics are inherently chaotic, world-space error alone is insufficient to evaluate prediction quality, as the ground truth represents only one of many valid outcomes. Therefore, Table  primarily relies on physics-consistency checks (Appendix ; the full set of checks is in Table ). Across all metrics and datasets, the LDM significantly outperforms both baselines. We highlight three observations from the results. First, the LDM consistently outperforms deterministic regression in generating physically plausible trajectories. The regression model produces damped outputs with geometric artifacts and jitter (e.g., $22.7\%$ volume violations versus $7.9\%$ for the LDM on held-out scenes). In contrast, the LDM reduces these artifacts and better preserves the deformation-to-rigid energy ratio. Second, one-shot prediction provides the global temporal context necessary to prevent the compounding errors typically seen in autoregressive models. Consequently, the AR baseline drifts over time and accumulates nearly three times the world-space error of the LDM ( $80.6$ against $28.2$  mm). Third, this strong performance transfers zero-shot to OOD datasets (GSO and Toys4K), demonstrating the robust generalization of our approach. Finally, the LDM remains highly efficient, running at $40$ to $80$ frames per second on a single GPU, even for high-resolution meshes exceeding the training cap (Appendix ).

bestsecond-best

The diffusion results in Table  use a single sample per scene, which cannot show whether diffusion captures the several possible outcomes of a chaotic scene. To test whether diffusion benefits from modeling several outcomes, we compare the two models separately on chaotic and non-chaotic held-out scenes and draw eight diffusion samples per scene (Appendix ). Diffusion outperforms regression on both subsets. One may worry that this only reflects a stronger model. However, the diffusion samples spread much more widely on the chaotic scenes, and this spread follows the difference between two runs of the solver. Since the model is the same on both subsets, this effect comes from the generative paradigm and not from a stronger model. A soft key dropped onto the ground illustrates it (Fig. ). Run twice, the solver lets the key fall over in two different directions. Every diffusion sample faithfully falls toward one of the two correct directions, while regression predicts a non-physical average that matches neither run.

4.1

ST-VAE.

We remove the ST-VAE and let a DiT of the same capacity as our LDM denoise the vertex $\times$ frame tokens directly (Table ). Without the latent, one-shot diffusion at native resolution is computationally prohibitive. Memory per sample grows with the vertex count. Even on a $140$  GiB H200, the model at batch  $1$ runs out of memory at $2{,}600$ vertices. With the latent, the LDM works on a fixed number of tokens and its cost is independent of the vertex count. The vertex-dependent cost moves to the ST-VAE stage, whose training memory grows linearly with $N$ (Table ), so on the same GPU the training cap rises from about $2{,}500$ vertices without the latent to about $14{,}000$ for ST-VAE Base. The latent also improves the quality of the generated geometry. A raw-coordinate model predicts every vertex directly, so any noise left by the sampler shows up as per-vertex jitter. Our model decodes all vertices from the latent, so the same noise only shifts the shape slightly and coherently (illustrated in Appendix ).

9

9

L

The dedicated rigid pathway in ST-VAE.

In the ST-VAE (Sec. ), the rigid token bypasses the holistic temporal compression and takes its own linear temporal pathway. To test this design, we route the rigid token through the shared holistic temporal compression instead. In our experiments, this one change causes two failures: the translation error explodes, and the reconstructed deformation shrinks drastically (detailed diagnostics in Appendix ). Further ablations (spatial-VAE pretraining and the decoder GNN) are reported in Appendix .

K

Material Estimation.

The bottom-right block of Fig.  shows a material estimation task. Given a single simulated trajectory of a body with unknown stiffness, we recover its Young’s modulus $E$ by gradient descent through the model, since the mismatch to the observed trajectory is differentiable in $E$ end to end. Because Young’s modulus is usually measured on a logarithmic scale, we optimize $E$ in $\log_{10}$ space, where an error of $1$  dex means a factor of $10$ . To cover a wide range of stiffness, we repeat the task on seven bodies with moduli from $3\times 10^{4}$ to $3\times 10^{6}$  Pa, each starting from an initial guess up to $1.1$  dex away. In all seven cases, our model recovers $E$ within $0.06$  dex in $40$ Adam steps, which takes about $40$ seconds per run. DiffIPC solves the task only after its solver parameters are tuned by hand, and then needs $26$ minutes on $48$ threads. Newton/Warp fails in the backward pass, because backpropagating through its enormous number of substeps explodes the gradient.

1

Beyond Material Estimation: Designing the Throw.

Based on the first task, we may ask a further question: which throw reveals the stiffness best, so that the estimation above becomes easier? Easier means that a change of $E$ produces a larger change of the trajectory, so the trajectory carries more information about the stiffness. We therefore maximize the sensitivity of the predicted trajectory to $E$ over the release velocity by gradient ascent through the model. The objective is a derivative, so its gradient is a second-order quantity. Our model supports higher-order derivatives through the automatic differentiation of PyTorch, so it provides this gradient directly, and $30$ Adam steps finish the design in $7$ minutes. Replayed in the ground-truth simulator, the optimized throw makes the rigid motion $13\times$ more sensitive to the stiffness. DiffIPC offers only first-order derivatives and cannot be applied directly to this second-order task. A workaround is to obtain the second-order gradient by nested finite differences, but then DiffIPC is about $635\times$ slower than our model per gradient step. The whole design would take several days, which is not acceptable in practice. Newton/Warp does not produce a usable first-order gradient on this scene, so a second-order one is out of reach.

5

We introduce PhysLDM, a latent diffusion paradigm for predicting the dynamics of high-fidelity volumetric deformable bodies. To overcome the computational limits of processing high-resolution meshes, we developed a novel holistic ST-VAE that explicitly disentangles global rigid motion from local deformations. This architecture eliminates the staircase artifacts inherent to standard temporal compression, ensuring highly accurate trajectory reconstruction even for high-resolution, out-of-distribution meshes. Operating on this compact latent representation, we demonstrate that while deterministic regression produces damped, non-physical averages in this chaotic regime, our generative approach predicts physically consistent trajectories in a single diffusion pass. Finally, trained purely kinematically, PhysLDM delivers robust zero-shot generalization and provides end-to-end differentiability, unlocking complex inverse design optimizations that remain intractable for traditional solvers.

Currently, our model focuses on predicting $64$ -frame trajectories in a single diffusion pass. Extending this one-shot approach into an autoregressive framework presents a promising direction for future research.Limitations and Future Work.

§A specifies the architecture, losses, and training of all three stages. §B gives the data, evaluation setup, and metric definitions. §C details the staircase analysis of standard temporal compression. §D the chaos experiment on a traditional GPU simulator. §E describes the baselines. §F collects further ablations. §G reports inference runtime. §H shows additional qualitative results. §I analyzes the extreme cases. §J the multi-body extension. §K the setup and results of the differentiable applications. §L the comparison with concurrent work. §M tests the constitutive-model-agnostic property on a second energy model and on real captured trajectories.

Appendix A

Our model is trained in three stages, one per component: the spatial VAE for $183$ k iterations, ST-VAE Base for $150$ k iterations, and the LDM for $278$ k iterations. The three stages together take about $7$ days on $8$ H200 GPUs.

A.1

The spatial VAE is an $8$ -layer transformer of hidden width $512$ ( $44$ M parameters). Its input is one frame in canonical coordinates, i.e. the rest shape plus the deformation $\mathbf{d}_{t}$ of Eq. () with the rigid motion removed. The encoder cross-attends $K{=}512$ learned query tokens against the $N$ vertex tokens of the frame and outputs $K$ latent tokens of width $D{=}48$ , independent of $N$ . We denote the latent of frame $t$ by $\mathbf{z}_{t}$ . The decoder mirrors the encoder: the $N$ rest vertices, embedded with their positions, cross-attend the latent tokens and are decoded back to their $N$ displacements. The decoder additionally takes the mesh topology as input, because a shallow GNN over the tetrahedral mesh then refines the decoded displacements. The spatial VAE is trained first with a Charbonnier position loss and a KL term.

1

A.2

The per-frame latents $\{\mathbf{z}_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T}$ are processed by a stack of factorized space–time attention blocks . The holistic temporal compression then summarizes the time axis: $M$ learned query tokens attend over each spatial token’s $T$ -frame sequence, and only these $M$ outputs are kept as the temporal representation, while the $T$ per-frame outputs are discarded. The rigid-motion token bypasses this attention compression and is compressed by a separate linear temporal path. The two are kept apart because the rigid signal is orders of magnitude larger than the deformation and, when the two share one compression path, takes over the shared latent and starves the deformation track (Sec. , Appendix ). The two tracks then merge: the joint latent is $\mathbf{Z}\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times(K+1)\times D}$ of Sec. , i.e. $M$ temporal tokens for each of the $K$ deformation tokens and the rigid token, each of width $D{=}48$ . The decoder mirrors the encoder: per-frame queries attend over the $M$ temporal tokens to recover a latent for every frame, which the spatial VAE decoder turns into vertex positions. Table  lists the two ST-VAE configurations used in this paper, ST-VAE Small for the controlled comparisons of Table  and ST-VAE Base for the LDM experiments (Sec. ). Both configurations compress a trajectory by the same factor, counted in tokens. The input has one token per vertex per frame, $T\times N$ tokens in total, and the latent has $M\times(K{+}1)$ tokens. Since $T/M{=}8$ and $K{+}1{=}513$ in both configurations, the token compression ratio is $8N/513$ , which reaches $78\times$ at the $5{,}000$ -vertex cap.(; ; )

A.3

The LDM and the regression model receive the same conditioning: the frame- $0$ spatial latent through cross-attention, and the initial pose, the initial velocity $v_{0}$ , and the Young’s modulus $E$ through adaptive layer normalization. The LDM is a DiT with $12$ blocks of width $768$ ( $170$ M parameters) operating on the $4{,}104$ latent tokens of ST-VAE Base ( $M\times(K{+}1)=8\times 513$ tokens of width $D{=}48$ ). It is trained with rectified flow and sampled by Euler integration. The regression model is a capacity-matched transformer that emits the full latent trajectory in one pass. Training the spatial VAE, ST-VAE Base, and the LDM takes about $7$ days in total on $8$ H200 GPUs.

A.4

All position losses use a Charbonnier penalty on the per-vertex error norm,

$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{charb}}(\hat{\mathbf{x}},\mathbf{x})\;=\;\frac{1}{|V|}\sum_{i\in V}\sqrt{\lVert\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{i}-\mathbf{x}_{i}\rVert^{2}+\epsilon^{2}},\qquad\epsilon=10^{-3}\ (=1\,\mathrm{mm}),$ (2)

$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{S1}}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{charb}}+\beta_{1}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{KL}}$ with a standard Gaussian KL term and $\beta_{1}=10^{-5}$ .Stage 1: Spatial VAE.

The objective combines the deformation reconstruction of all $T$ frames, the rigid track, and a KL term:Stage 2: ST-VAE.

$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{S2}}=\sum_{j\in\{\mathrm{deform},R,c\}}\Big(\tfrac{1}{2}e^{-s_{j}}\mathcal{L}_{j}+\tfrac{1}{2}s_{j}\Big)+\beta_{2}\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{KL}}^{\mathrm{fb}},$ (3)

where $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{deform}}$ is $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{charb}}$ averaged over the $T$ decoded frames, $\mathcal{L}_{R}$ and $\mathcal{L}_{c}$ are mean-squared errors on the rigid token’s rotation and translation, and the three are balanced by the learned uncertainty weights $s_{j}$ of . $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{KL}}^{\mathrm{fb}}$ is the KL term with per-channel free bits .

The latent is standardized per modality (rigid and deformation channels separately). With flow time $\tau$ , noise $\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{I})$ and the straight path $\mathbf{x}_{\tau}=(1{-}\tau)\mathbf{z}+\tau\boldsymbol{\epsilon}$ , the LDM minimizes a token-weighted velocity regressionStage 3: LDM.

$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DiT}}=\mathbb{E}_{\tau,\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\Big[\big\langle w_{k}\,\lVert\hat{\mathbf{v}}_{k}-(\boldsymbol{\epsilon}-\mathbf{z})_{k}\rVert^{2}\big\rangle_{k}\Big],\qquad w_{k}=\begin{cases}\lambda_{\mathrm{rigid}}&k\ \text{a rigid token}\\

\lambda_{\mathrm{deform}}&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}$ (4)

where $k$ indexes the $(K{+}1)\times M$ latent tokens and $\lambda_{\mathrm{rigid}}$ is a hand-tuned weight that up-weights the rigid token relative to the deformation tokens ( $\lambda_{\mathrm{deform}}{=}1$ ). The regression model minimizes the same token-weighted mean-squared error directly on the latent.

Appendix B

B.1

All simulation data are generated with StiffGIPC , a GPU IPC solver. IPC solvers are widely adopted in scenarios that demand high simulation accuracy, such as embodied AI . Such a solver runs offline. Learning its behavior and turning it into a fast, fully differentiable neural simulator is therefore of practical importance. All 3D meshes used for training come from the Objaverse dataset . Each asset is voxel-remeshed to a watertight surface, tetrahedralized with fTetWild , reduced to its largest connected component, and rescaled to a unit bounding box. Meshes with more than $10{,}000$ vertices are discarded, and the ST-VAE and the LDM are trained on scenes with $500$ – $5{,}000$ vertices. Every scene drops one meter-scale solid onto a ground plane. The object is released with its lowest point $0.85$ to $1.65$  m above the ground. Each object receives a random initial velocity $v_{0}$ and a random stiffness $E$ (a horizontal $v_{0}\sim U(0,2)$  m/s and a Young’s modulus $E$ log-uniform in $[3\times 10^{4},3\times 10^{6}]$  Pa) under a Stable Neo-Hookean material. Multi-body scenes follow the same setting with two or three objects, each with its own $E$ and $v_{0}$ , thrown toward each other so that they collide in mid-air before reaching the ground. In total, the dataset contains $63{,}397$ single-object and $16{,}078$ multi-body simulated trajectories. The simulation time step is $1/60$  s, and each trajectory has $64$ frames. Held-out scenes are excluded from all three training stages, and every reported number is computed on these held-out scenes or on the OOD sets. For OOD evaluation we generate $1{,}015$ GSO and $3{,}814$ Toys4K scenes under the identical simulation setting. They never appear in training.()

(deformation-change correlation): the deformation change of a trajectory at frame $t$ is the mean vertex displacement between two consecutive frames in canonical (rigid-free) coordinates, $v(t)=\mathrm{mean}_{v}\lVert\mathbf{d}_{t+1,v}-\mathbf{d}_{t,v}\rVert$ , where $\mathbf{d}_{t,v}$ is the position of vertex $v$ in the deformation field $\mathbf{d}_{t}$ . The deformation-change curve is $v(t)$ over the trajectory. DCC is the Pearson correlation between the deformation-change curves of the reconstruction and of the ground truth. It is reported as the mean across scenes. It detects the staircase artifact directly, since holds suppress the speed and snaps spike it. This metric is amplitude-invariant, so it does not reflect reconstruction quality on its own and should be considered together with the other metrics.DCC

2

All of these metrics are computed from the predicted and ground-truth trajectories alone and do not require knowledge of the underlying constitutive model. The violation rates are defined as follows. A physical quantity (speed or acceleration) is computed for every vertex at every frame, once from the prediction and once from the ground truth. Each such vertex-frame pair is one sample. A sample is counted as a violation if the predicted value is more than twice, or less than half, the ground-truth value. The violation rate is the fraction of violated samples. Samples whose ground-truth value is too small to be meaningful are excluded by a magnitude threshold.

•

(volume violation rate): this measures whether the prediction preserves volume where the ground truth does. For every tetrahedron at every frame, we compute how much its volume differs from its rest volume, once in the ground truth and once in the prediction. We look only at the cases where the ground truth changes the volume by less than $3\%$ , because there the ground truth preserves volume. Among these cases, a violation is one where the prediction changes the volume by more than $10\%$ . The rate is the fraction of violations.Volume viol.

•

(self-intersection rate): the percentage of surface triangles of the tetrahedral mesh that cross another surface triangle, averaged over frames and reported as the median across scenes. The ground truth has no self-intersection in any frame, so its value is $0$ .Self-int.

•

and (velocity and acceleration violation rates): the violation rate of the per-vertex speed and acceleration magnitudes. The acceleration threshold excludes free fall and settled frames.Vel. viol.Acc. viol.

•

$KE_{\mathrm{def}}/KE_{\mathrm{rig}}$ (deformation-to-rigid kinetic energy ratio): a rigid transform $(\mathbf{R}_{t},\mathbf{c}_{t})$ is fitted to every frame by the Kabsch algorithm, which gives the rigid trajectory $\mathbf{r}_{t,v}=\mathbf{R}_{t}\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{v}+\mathbf{c}_{t}$ of the rest shape $\bar{\mathbf{x}}$ . The vertex velocity $\mathbf{v}_{t,v}$ (central difference of $\mathbf{x}_{t,v}$ ) is split into the rigid velocity $\mathbf{v}^{\mathrm{rig}}_{t,v}$ (central difference of $\mathbf{r}_{t,v}$ ) and the deformation residual $\mathbf{v}^{\mathrm{def}}_{t,v}=\mathbf{v}_{t,v}-\mathbf{v}^{\mathrm{rig}}_{t,v}$ . With lumped vertex masses $m_{v}$ and the impact window $W$ ( $\pm 10$ frames around first contact), the two kinetic energies are

$KE_{\mathrm{def}}=\tfrac{1}{2}\sum_{t\in W}\sum_{v}m_{v}\lVert\mathbf{v}^{\mathrm{def}}_{t,v}\rVert^{2},\qquad KE_{\mathrm{rig}}=\tfrac{1}{2}\sum_{t\in W}\sum_{v}m_{v}\lVert\mathbf{v}^{\mathrm{rig}}_{t,v}\rVert^{2},$

and the reported value is $(KE_{\mathrm{def}}/KE_{\mathrm{rig}})_{\mathrm{pred}}\,/\,(KE_{\mathrm{def}}/KE_{\mathrm{rig}})_{\mathrm{GT}}$ , taken as the median across scenes. Scenes where the ground truth barely deforms (deformation below $1\%$ of the kinetic energy) are skipped. At impact, the kinetic energy of the object is divided between the motion of the object as a whole and the internal motion that deforms it. How much goes into deformation depends on how soft the object is and how hard it hits. The ground truth gives the correct proportion for the same object and the same impact, so comparing the two ratios shows whether the prediction moves energy into deformation the way the GPU solver does. A value below $1$ means the prediction deforms less than the ground truth and moves more rigidly. A value above $1$ would mean unphysical deformation or jitter. In Table  every model is below $1$ , and the regression model is the lowest on all three evaluation sets, consistent with the damped averages discussed in Sec. .

The symptom is wrong timing of rapid motion. Where the ground truth changes quickly, for instance at impact, the reconstruction holds its shape for several frames and then jumps to catch up, so the motion arrives late and all at once. We diagnose it in three ways. Fig.  plots the deformation-change curve on five scenes. The curves of the standard baseline, its two variants, and adaptive compression stay below ground truth for several frames and then overshoot it in one frame. The holistic ST-VAE follows the ground truth, and so does the direct world-coordinate baseline, which uses the same holistic temporal compression. Fig.  shows the same behavior directly on the silhouettes of one scene. The silhouettes of the standard baseline and its variants change less than the ground truth for three frames and then more than it in the last one or two frames. Adaptive compression changes less than the ground truth over all five frame pairs and releases the motion even later. The direct world-coordinate baseline follows the ground truth until the last pair. Table  scores the five scenes with DCC. The holistic ST-VAE is the best or tied on every scene.

C.2

In the standard baseline, the decoded frames at the latent-frame positions are accurate, and the frames between them carry the error. The most likely cause is that standard compression summarizes every $k$ frames into one latent frame and loses the high-frequency temporal information that says when, within those $k$ frames, the rapid change happens. One might think that the problem is a mismatch between neighboring blocks. This is not the case. Two observations show that the error builds up inside each block. First, the standard baseline moves too little during the early frames of every block and then catches up in the last frames, whereas the ground truth moves at a steady pace throughout the block. Second, smoothing the reconstruction across block boundaries does not remove the artifact.

C.3

The two variants of the standard baseline and the adaptive-compression baseline all keep the approach of standard temporal compression: they compress the trajectory into a fixed number of latent frames and then reconstruct the frames by local temporal upsampling, so they leave the artifact in place. The velocity loss and the spectral loss change the training signal only. The standard baseline still cannot place the rapid change at the right instant between two latent frames. Adaptive compression moves the latent frames toward the impact, which makes the steps fewer but steeper. A likely reason is that the rebound and settling phases are left with one or two latent frames, so their motion is released in a late snap. The direct world-coordinate baseline uses the holistic temporal compression and shows almost no staircase. Its high DCC in Table  together with its lower precision in Table  shows that its weakness is precision rather than timing.

Appendix D

This section gives the details of the chaos experiment in Sec.  (Chaos analysis). A common assumption is that a physics simulator produces a deterministic trajectory once the initial state and parameters are fully specified. In practice, this is not guaranteed for modern GPU solvers. Because of their speed, GPU solvers are increasingly used to generate physical simulation data at scale, so the consequences of this non-determinism for learning deserve a closer look. Two separate facts are involved. First, a GPU solver is not bit-reproducible: its parallel reductions add floating-point numbers in a different order on every run, which perturbs the state at the level of rounding error. On its own this would be harmless. Second, the complex dynamics of deformable bodies are chaotic: it can amplify such a perturbation into a macroscopic difference in the outcome. The experiment below separates the two.

4

D.1

We take one held-out scene, a soft tennis racket dropped onto the ground, and run the GPU solver five times on the same GPU from inputs: the same tetrahedral mesh, initial state, material parameters, and solver configuration. To measure how far two runs drift apart at a given frame, we compute the displacement of every vertex between the two runs and report the largest one as a fraction of the object’s extent.byte-identical

D.2

The non-determinism of the solver is real but minute. After the first simulation step the five runs differ by at most $0.02$  mm, two hundred-thousandths of the object size. Before the racket reaches the ground, the runs still differ by at most $3\%$ of the object size, mostly in the strings of the net, and their centres of mass by less than $1$  mm. Until the racket reaches the ground, the five runs are therefore practically identical.

D.3

The behavior changes qualitatively at impact. After the racket hits the ground, the runs diverge rapidly and settle into visibly different poses (Fig. ). Over the ten pairs of runs, the final divergence ranges from $10\%$ to $51\%$ of the object size, with a median of $21\%$ . The same vertex can land up to $442$  mm apart in two runs.

7

To check that this is chaos and not a peculiarity of the reduction order, we replace the rounding noise by a controlled perturbation: a deterministic initial rotation of the racket between $10^{-8}$ and $10^{-2}$  rad. The final divergence is of the same order for every magnitude and does not grow with it. A perturbation a million times larger does not produce a larger difference. This is the signature of chaotic dynamics. The racket has several possible resting poses. Even the smallest perturbation is already enough to change which one it ends in, so making the perturbation larger does not make the difference larger. It only changes which resting pose the racket lands in.

D.4

The sensitivity comes from complex dynamics involving contact. When the racket hits the ground, the solver makes a discrete decision about which edge or corner touches first, and a microscopic perturbation can flip this decision. From then on the bounce and the final pose follow different paths. In our experiments, soft objects that are thin, branchy, or non-convex are more prone to amplifying this chaotic effect.

We measure their difference relative to the object size, defined as the diagonal of the bounding box at frame $0$ . Most scenes are reproduced closely. The median difference between the two runs is $0.5$  mm over the trajectory and $1.0$  mm at the last frame. A substantial minority of scenes, however, diverge. At the last frame, about a quarter of the scenes end more than $1\%$ of the object size apart, and the most divergent scene ends $35\%$ apart. In all of these scenes, the two runs agree to sub-millimeter precision until ground contact and separate afterwards, as in the racket example. A difference of $1\%$ of the object size means that the two runs end more than $1$  cm apart on a meter-scale object, which is already a large error for high-precision physical simulation. A regression model can only learn the mean of such diverging outcomes, so high precision is difficult to reach on these scenes.

D.6

In a chaotic scene, the same initial state can lead to several different outcomes. A regression model gives one prediction per initial state, while a diffusion model can draw several. This section tests whether, on chaotic scenes, the samples of the LDM actually cover the different outcomes that the solver produces. We split the $300$ held-out scenes of Table  by how far the two solver runs end apart: $71$ chaotic scenes, whose runs end more than $1\%$ of the object size apart, and $229$ non-chaotic scenes. For every scene we draw eight samples from the LDM and report two numbers: the error of a single sample, and the error of the best of the eight samples. Choosing the best sample needs the ground truth, so the best-of-eight result is an upper bound on sample selection, not a usable predictor. All other settings follow Table .

B.4

Table  shows that a single diffusion sample already improves on the regression model in every metric, on both subsets. It has a lower error than the regression model in $79\%$ of the non-chaotic scenes and $65\%$ of the chaotic scenes. The advantage of diffusion is therefore not limited to chaotic scenes.Diffusion outperforms regression on both subsets.

6

What differs between the two subsets is how much the eight samples add over a single one. Picking the best of the eight lowers the median error by $3.4$  mm on the non-chaotic scenes and by $9.3$  mm on the chaotic scenes. The samples also spread further apart under chaos: the gap between the best and the worst sample of a scene is $7$  mm on the non-chaotic scenes and $25$  mm on the chaotic scenes (medians over scenes). On the chaotic scenes, this spread follows the physics. It grows with the distance between the two solver runs (Spearman $\rho=0.38$ , $p=0.001$ ), and the second solver run lies inside the spread of the eight samples in $99\%$ of the scenes. The benefit does not depend on picking the best sample: averaged over the eight samples, the median final-frame error on the chaotic scenes is $138$  mm, below the $162$  mm of the regression model. The diffusion model is thus more uncertain where the physics is less predictable, and this uncertainty covers outcomes that the solver itself produces.Multiple samples matter more under chaos.

In a scene with several possible outcomes, diffusion can learn these outcomes, whereas regression can only learn a non-physical average that matches none of them. Fig.  shows such a scene, a soft key. When the solver is run twice, the key falls over in two different directions. The regression model predicts a single pose that lies between the two runs and resembles neither. The eight diffusion samples instead fall on both sides, and the closest of them come close to each of the two runs. Other scenes behave similarly. Among the six scenes whose two runs end more than $30^{\circ}$ apart, at least one diffusion sample ends within $30^{\circ}$ of a solver run in five scenes, while the regression model does so in only one.An example: a falling soft key.

8

One may worry that the diffusion model is simply the stronger model (the LDM uses $50$ sampling steps, the regression model a single pass), and that the results above reflect this difference. Three observations show that on chaotic scenes the advantage comes from the paradigm. First, the diffusion samples differ from each other in a way that follows the physics: their spread grows with the distance between the two solver runs and contains the second run in $99\%$ of the chaotic scenes. A deterministic model, however strong, gives a single prediction per initial state and has no such spread. Second, where the solver itself produces clearly different outcomes, the diffusion samples reach them, while the regression prediction is a non-physical average between them, as in the key example. Third, the benefit of drawing several samples depends on the scenes, not on the model. With the same model on both subsets, it is almost three times larger on the chaotic scenes ( $9.3$ against $3.4$  mm), whereas a difference in model strength would affect both subsets alike.An advantage of the paradigm, not of a stronger model.

In summary, diffusion predicts more accurately than regression on both chaotic and non-chaotic scenes. On chaotic scenes it also produces several plausible outcomes, while regression gives a single non-physical average result. These results show that diffusion is better suited to chaotic deformable dynamics.

F.1

This section gives the measurements behind the ST-VAE ablation of Sec. , which asks what happens to the training cost when the ST-VAE is removed and the LDM denoises the raw vertex $\times$ frame tokens directly. We compare two options on the same GPU at increasing vertex counts $N$ . The first is our LDM architecture applied to the raw tokens, without any latent. The second is our pipeline with the ST-VAE, where the LDM works on a fixed set of $4{,}104$ latent tokens and the ST-VAE is the stage with the largest memory footprint. Table  lists the peak training memory of both.

4.1

9

Without the ST-VAE the number of tokens is $T\times N$ , so memory grows with $N$ . The raw-token model fits at batch  $1$ up to $2{,}500$ vertices and runs out of memory at $2{,}600$ , below the median resolution of our dataset ( ${\sim}3{,}400$ vertices). More than half of the training scenes therefore cannot be processed at all. With the ST-VAE, the LDM costs about $4.4$  GiB per trajectory at any $N$ . The ST-VAE stage grows linearly with $N$ , by about $8$  GiB per $1{,}000$ vertices, and ST-VAE Base trains up to about $14{,}000$ vertices on the same card. The latent therefore does not remove the vertex-dependent cost, but moves it to a stage that scales far more gently.

F.2

Sec.  shows that routing the rigid token through the shared holistic temporal compression makes the translation error explode and starves the deformation track: on a small held-out diagnostic set, the translation error grows from $1.8$ to $887$  mm, and the reconstructed deformation shrinks to $28\%$ of its true magnitude ( $97\%$ with the dedicated pathway). In addition, the failure is not a matter of numerical scale. Normalizing the rigid signal to unit variance before the shared compression barely helps ( $52.8\!\rightarrow\!49.6$  mm world error), whereas the dedicated linear pathway reaches $8.3$  mm. The rigid and the deformation signals compete for the capacity of the shared latent, and the dedicated pathway removes this competition.

4.1

F.3

This section explains why the spatial VAE needs to be pretrained first rather than trained directly together with the ST-VAE. We compare two training schemes at a matched budget. The first pretrains the spatial VAE and then trains the ST-VAE on top of it with an additional latent-anchor loss (Sec. ), which ties the per-frame latents reconstructed by the ST-VAE to those of the pretrained spatial VAE. The second trains both stages jointly from scratch, with a randomly initialized spatial VAE.

3.3

We find that joint training works poorly. At the standard learning rate, training diverges within a few thousand steps. At a reduced learning rate, it converges to a much worse model: the geometric reconstruction error is about $5\times$ that of the pretrained scheme, the deformation is much weaker than the ground truth, and volume is lost. The likely reason is that the two stages chase each other. The latent that the ST-VAE learns to reproduce keeps moving while the spatial VAE is still changing, so the temporal model has no fixed target. Pretraining fixes the target first. Once pretrained, the spatial VAE can either be kept frozen during ST-VAE training or fine-tuned with a smaller learning rate, and the two options give similar results. We keep it frozen for ST-VAE Small and fine-tune it for ST-VAE Base.

F.4

We use a GNN component in the spatial VAE decoder because the field decoder places every vertex independently, so nothing ties neighboring vertices together, and the GNN over the tetrahedral mesh adds this coupling. We compare three placements of the GNN: in the decoder, as in our model; removed; and moved to the encoder instead. Without the GNN, reconstruction degrades and many mesh edges end up stretched far from their rest length. With the GNN in the encoder, the result is worse on every metric, because smoothing the mesh before encoding removes detail before it reaches the latent, whereas smoothing after decoding only regularizes the output.

Appendix I

This section analyzes extreme cases. The accuracy of the LDM is fundamentally bounded by the reconstruction performance of the ST-VAE, meaning that the most challenging cases for the ST-VAE set the limits of the entire pipeline. Across the held-out scenes, the largest reconstruction errors mostly occur on geometries with many long, thin features.

Fig.  illustrates a representative extreme case, a soft birdcage comprising $9{,}021$ nodes, which is $1.8$ times the $5{,}000$ -vertex training cap and contains dozens of thin bars only a few tetrahedra thick. Its mean reconstruction error over the trajectory is $9.9$  mm, about twice the held-out mean for meshes above the training cap (Table ). This error is localized to the thin bars, which exhibit distorted and tangled reconstructions. Nevertheless, the overall shape of the collapsed cage, its pose, and its motion over the trajectory are all recovered.

12

1

Furthermore, node count alone is not the primary performance bottleneck. For instance, the teaser mug shown in Fig.  represents a compact solid with $11{,}621$ nodes ( $2.3$ times the training cap) yet achieves a lower reconstruction error of $5.3$  mm. What distinguishes the birdcage is the density of thin features that deform independently of each other. The folding of every bar is a high-frequency deformation, and the fixed-size latent has to carry it for dozens of bars at once. The latent has enough capacity for the global shape, but not for the fine detail of every bar.

Appendix J

This section describes the multi-body extension of our method and presents its qualitative results. Our approach generalizes effectively to multi-object scenes. The factorization defined in Eq. () is applied at the scene level: a single global rigid transform $(\mathbf{R}_{t},\mathbf{c}_{t})$ is fitted across the vertices of all bodies, while the relative motion among bodies is captured by the canonical deformation field $\mathbf{d}_{t}$ . Because the spatial VAE encodes all vertices within a scene through a shared set of $K$ query tokens, multi-body scenes are encoded, compressed, and predicted in the same manner as single-body objects, requiring no architectural modifications to the ST-VAE or the LDM.

Comparison of our model with two differentiable simulators on downstream applications. Our approach supports higher-order derivatives, enabling complex optimization tasks that are either computationally infeasible or numerically unstable for existing solvers.Table 13:

K.1

The first task is to recover the Young’s modulus $E^{\star}$ of a body from a single observed trajectory. Because $E$ enters our model through the scalar material channel, the mismatch between the predicted rollout and the observation is end-to-end differentiable with respect to $\log E$ . Starting from initial guesses up to 1.1 dex away from seven ground-truth moduli $E^{\star}\in[3{\cdot}10^{4},3{\cdot}10^{6}]$ , our model successfully recovers all seven within $0.06$  dex in just 40 Adam steps ( $\sim$ 40 seconds).

Figure  compares the observed, initial, and recovered trajectories and shows the estimation error across all seven moduli.

15

(a) Four matched time samples of the observed trajectory ( $E^{\star}=60$  kPa), the initial model prediction ( $E_{0}=250$  kPa), and the prediction after 40 Adam steps ( $\hat{E}=52.4$  kPa). All views share the same camera and scale.

(b) Absolute log-stiffness error for seven ground-truth moduli, with the illustrated case highlighted in blue. All seven final estimates are within $0.06$  dex; each optimization takes approximately 40 seconds. Curves show the recorded iterates without smoothing.Figure 15: Basic material estimation.

Existing differentiable simulators already have difficulty with this first-order task. DiffIPC does not converge under default settings and only runs stably after manual tuning of the solver parameters, and then needs about 26 minutes. Newton/Warp, meanwhile, fails on this task: it consumes massive memory (49 GB tape for 131k substeps) before its gradients explode through the complex dynamics simulation, resulting in random gradient signs and total optimization failure.

K.2

Building on the first task, we ask a further question: which throw makes the stiffness easiest to estimate? A throw is informative when a small change in $E$ produces a large change in the resulting trajectory.

Task Setup.

Crucially, how large this trajectory change is depends on the stiffness of the body itself. Therefore, the trajectory sensitivity must be evaluated at a specific value of $E$ , which we set to $E^{\star}$ ( $6{\cdot}10^{4}$  Pa). The design is thus local: it finds the most informative throw for a body of roughly this stiffness, assuming a rough estimate of the stiffness is already available. To ensure robustness against launch errors, we maximize the sensitivity of the predicted rigid motion to $\log_{10}E$ , averaged over eight small perturbations of the release velocity $v_{0}$ . Because the objective itself is a derivative, maximizing it via gradient ascent fundamentally requires a .second-order gradient

Optimization Results.

Our model supports higher-order derivatives and provides this second-order gradient directly via reverse-mode automatic differentiation. In just 30 Adam steps (7 minutes), our model successfully optimizes the throw. Replaying this designed throw in the ground-truth solver confirms its effectiveness: the sensitivity of the rigid motion to $E$ increases by $13\times$ , and per-vertex sensitivity by $1.85\times$ . This highly informative trajectory significantly widens the basin of attraction, enabling successful $E$ recovery even from a distant initial guess ( $E_{0}=10^{6}$ ) where the original throw stalls.

Figure  visualizes the ground-truth trajectories of the initial and the optimized throw, the sensitivity gain, and the subsequent material-estimation runs from this distant initial guess.

The first three columns show true motion at matched times and a shared camera scale. In the final column, rigid translation and rotation offsets from the nominal trajectory are magnified by $5\times$ , using equal magnification in both rows.

(b) Cumulative rigid-pose sensitivity, normalized by the initial throw’s final score, increases by $13.4\times$ . This score is computed from the unamplified GT trajectories.

Comparison with Differentiable Simulators.

If the first-order task is already this challenging for existing solvers, this second-order throw design becomes infeasible for them. DiffIPC is inherently limited to first-order analytic adjoints; forcing it to approximate the necessary second-order gradient requires nested finite differences ( $64$ forward solves per step). As a result, a single gradient step takes 2.4 hours, about $635\times$ slower than our model. The whole design would therefore take about three days, which is not acceptable in practice. For Newton/Warp, which already fails to produce a usable first-order gradient, such higher-order applications are insurmountable. In contrast, PhysLDM effortlessly scales to these advanced demands, acting as a fast, stable surrogate that natively supports higher-order derivatives. L.3

Fig.  compares the predictions of the two models on four held-out scenes at this resolution, shown at the last frame of the trajectory. Both models place the object roughly where the ground truth places it. The difference is in the geometric detail. The concurrent model produces surfaces that are visibly noisy: the block bends and its faces ripple, the spoon and the shaft of the screwdriver are corrugated, and the bottle is lumpy. The zoom-in views show this noise on every surface. Our model keeps the shape of every object and its surfaces stay smooth.

17

The reason lies in where each model generates geometry. Our ST-VAE is pretrained to reconstruct shapes, so the decoder maps any latent it receives to a clean shape on the learned manifold. A small error in the latent predicted by the LDM therefore becomes a small, coherent change of the shape, and the geometric detail is preserved. The concurrent model predicts every vertex coordinate directly, so there is nothing between its prediction and the geometry. A small error in any coordinate appears on the surface as is, and the many small errors of a diffusion model add up to noisy geometric detail.

This problem is not visible in the concurrent work’s own demonstrations because meshes in their training data are simple and coarse, with at most a few hundred vertices, and the whole dataset is built from only a few dozen mesh templates. A model can learn these few simple shapes accurately with much less difficulty. On our data, with thousands of distinct objects at native resolution, learning the geometry itself becomes much harder.

L.4

Our model is also much faster at inference. The concurrent model denoises $N\times 64$ vertex tokens, so its latency grows with the mesh, whereas our LDM denoises the fixed $4{,}104$ latent tokens. On a scene of about $1{,}000$ vertices, our model predicts a $64$ -frame trajectory in about $1.5$  s at $50$ sampling steps and $0.8$  s at $20$ , while the concurrent model needs about $12.9$  s and $5.1$  s, so ours is roughly $9\times$ and $6\times$ faster.

The two models on four held-out scenes (a block, a spoon, a screwdriver and a bottle; all $\leq 1{,}000$ vertices) at the last frame of the trajectory. For each scene the full object is followed by a zoom-in view of the boxed region. Rows: ground truth (rose), our three-stage pipeline trained on the same scenes with the same budget (Table ), and the concurrent DiT-B model. Our model preserves the geometric detail of every object. The concurrent model places the objects correctly, but its geometric detail is visibly noisy: the block bends and its faces ripple, the spoon and the shaft of the screwdriver are corrugated, and the bottle is lumpy. The zoom-in views show this noise on every surface.Figure 17:

Appendix M

PhysLDM is trained with kinematic supervision only (Sec. ). No energy model or material law enters the data format, the losses, or the architecture. This design gives PhysLDM three practical advantages, which we test in this section.

3.3

1.

Because the constitutive model never enters training, the same pipeline can learn from simulations with any energy model.Diverse energy models.

2.

For the same reason, PhysLDM can learn from trajectories with only an implicit energy model, such as trajectories captured in the real world.Data without an explicit energy model.

3.

Our training data are tetrahedral meshes, but PhysLDM does not depend on the tetrahedra themselves. The spatial VAE only takes vertex positions and a graph over the vertices. For a tetrahedral mesh, the graph is given by the tetrahedral edges. A surface mesh fits this structure naturally, with its triangle edges as the graph. For a point cloud, we can use a $k$ -nearest-neighbor graph or no edges at all. PhysLDM therefore runs on these formats without any change to the model or the training code. Because our input does not need to be a tetrahedral mesh, PhysLDM also supports object types beyond volumetric solids, such as cloth and rope, which are usually not represented with tetrahedra.Seamless support for other data formats, such as surface meshes and point clouds.

We test these advantages in two steps. First, we apply the pretrained PhysLDM, trained only on Stable Neo-Hookean simulations of Objaverse meshes, to new data without any adaptation. Second, we fine-tune it on the new data with the unchanged training code.

M.1

We take $40$ held-out Objaverse scenes and simulate each scene twice with StiffGIPC from the same initial state. The first run uses the Stable Neo-Hookean energy of the training data . The second run uses an as-rigid-as-possible (ARAP) energy with the same shear stiffness and no volume term, so the objects are softer and more compressible. The two energies move the trajectories $28$  mm apart (median over scenes). We exclude the chaotic scenes of Appendix , so this difference comes from the energy model and not from solver noise.Diverse energy models.()

Smith et al., 2018

()

Sorkine and Alexa, 2007

D

We use $22$ real captured sequences from : $9$ soft volumetric objects (plush toys and a package), $8$ pieces of cloth, and $5$ ropes, each lifted, pushed, or stretched by a human hand on a table. The data are 3D points tracked over time with three RGB-D cameras, with $616$ to $7{,}826$ points per object. There is no mesh and no explicit energy model, and the forces of the human hand are not observed. The setting of these scenes is also very different from that of our training data. In our simulations, every object is released in the air with an initial velocity and falls onto the ground. In the captured sequences, the object rests on a table and is manipulated by a human hand. The real data are therefore out of domain for PhysLDM. We store the tracked points as the vertices and a $k$ -nearest-neighbor graph ( $k=8$ ) as the topology, in the same file format as our simulated data. PhysLDM is thus seamlessly compatible with these data, without any change to our code.Real captured point clouds.

Jiang et al. (2025)

We use the metrics of Table  (Appendix ): the volume violation rate, the deformation-to-rigid kinetic energy ratio, and the world-coordinate error, each reported as the median over scenes. The first two need tetrahedra and are not defined on the point clouds.Evaluation.

On the simulated scenes, the reconstruction error is $4.5$  mm with Stable Neo-Hookean and $4.6$  mm with ARAP. On the real point clouds it is $6.0$  mm. This is the most demanding test: the scenes show manipulation by a human hand instead of objects thrown onto the ground, the data are real captures instead of simulations, the input is a point cloud instead of a tetrahedral mesh, and cloth and rope never appear in training. Even on this out-of-domain data, the ST-VAE reconstructs the motion accurately without any adaptation. Although the ST-VAE was trained only on Stable Neo-Hookean simulations, it represents motion under an unseen energy model (ARAP) and real motion without an explicit energy model almost as accurately (Fig. ). This shows that its latent space is not tied to the energy model of the training data.The ST-VAE generalizes zero-shot across energy models and to real point clouds.

On the simulated scenes with Stable Neo-Hookean, the prediction error is $23.9$  mm, in line with Table . With ARAP, the error grows to $37.5$  mm and the kinetic energy ratio drops to $0.79$ : the LDM predicts the deformation of the material it was trained on, while the ARAP objects deform more. On the real sequences, the zero-shot prediction fails ( $875$  mm) because of the domain gap, not the energy model. The LDM has only learned objects thrown onto the ground, while the real object stays on the table until the human hand moves it.The LDM prediction depends on the training data.

M.3

To adapt PhysLDM to new data, we only replace the training data with the new trajectories and fine-tune the LDM from the pretrained weights with the same trainer. The ST-VAE stays frozen. The same procedure applies to both energy models and to the real point clouds. Table  reports the results on the fine-tuning subsets, so the values before fine-tuning differ slightly from Table . For both explicit energy models, the prediction error drops by about two thirds, to $7.6$  mm and $8.8$  mm. For ARAP, the kinetic energy ratio moves from $0.80$ to $0.92$ , so the LDM learns the softer material from the trajectories alone. On the real point clouds, the error drops from $921$ to $6.2$  mm: the LDM learns from the tracked points that a resting object stays on the table and how the points move (Fig. ).

In summary, the same PhysLDM, with the same code and losses, handles simulations with different energy models, real captured trajectories without an explicit energy model, and other data formats such as point clouds. Its ST-VAE transfers to all of them zero-shot, and its LDM adapts to them by fine-tuning. Visual results of PhysLDM on the real captured data are shown in Fig. .

item.title: FluidGen：物理感知的流体视频生成 ｜ FluidGen: Physics-Aware Fluid Video Generation via Motion-Guided Post-Training
item.description:
一句话：在通用视频模型上做运动引导的后训练，让生成的水花符合流体物理。

要点：

  • 通用视频模型生成流体时常常违背物理规律
  • 用运动引导的后训练把物理约束注入模型
  • 生成结果在流动形态与交互响应上更可信

为什么值得看：流体是引擎里最难模拟也最常被要求「看起来对」的东西；这类方法给实时特效提供了新的素材来源。

中文摘要：FluidGen 针对通用视频生成模型在流体场景下的物理失真问题：水花、烟雾这类介质的运动规律一旦学错，画面立刻露馅。作者采用运动引导的后训练策略，在预训练视频模型上注入流体运动的物理约束，使生成结果在流动形态、惯性响应与交互反应上更接近真实模拟。论文来自 Stanford，对需要大量流体特效素材的团队有实际价值。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

FluidGen: Physics-Aware Fluid Video Generation via Motion-Guided Post-Training

Yang Zheng*Zizhang Li*Boyang Deng*Jan Ackermann

Lei Shu

Affiliation: Yinghao Xu   Jiajun Wu   Gordon Wetzstein   Leonidas GuibasStanford University

Affiliation: Equal contribution

Affiliation: *

Abstract

Video generation models produce visually compelling motion but systematically fail on fluid phenomena, including smoke, fire, and explosion debris, where outputs lack coherent vortical structure and collapse to bland dynamics that violate the physics of real fluids. Classical solvers achieve high physical fidelity but require detailed 3D scenes and carefully tuned parameters, making them impractical for in-the-wild imagery and video generation. We address this gap by injecting a data-driven fluid prior into a pre-trained video model, trained on a mixture of high-fidelity Houdini simulation data with paired velocity-field ground truth and curated in-the-wild fluid video data for appearance diversity. The core of our approach is a dual stream architecture that predicts per-frame velocity fields alongside RGB, supervised by simulation ground truth. This auxiliary signal regularizes generation toward physically consistent motion and exposes an interpretable physical quantity that we further leverage as a reward for velocity-aware direct preference optimization. Our model produces substantially more realistic fluid dynamics sequences than strong video baselines and optimization-based methods. Our data, code, and model will be publicly released. Project page: .

https://y-zheng18.github.io/FluidGen/

We introduce , a physics-aware video diffusion model for realistic fluid dynamics. FluidGen jointly predicts per-frame velocity fields (insets) that regularize generation toward physically consistent motion.

Figure 1: FluidGen

1

Realistic fluid phenomena, including billowing smoke, rolling fire, and the dust and ash of an explosion, are among the most important visual elements in film, games, and immersive media, and also among the hardest to make look right. Their motion is driven by complex, turbulent physical dynamics, and humans can notice errors in problematic fluid dynamics immediately: for example a plume that rises too uniformly, a flame that moves in an unnatural direction, or a debris cloud without proper swirling structure. Synthesizing fluid content that holds up under this realism has been a long-standing goal in computer graphics, and despite decades of progress, it still typically requires expert artists, expensive simulation tools, and large amounts of manual effort.

One family of approaches treats fluid dynamics synthesis as a simulation problem. Classical physical solvers solve the Navier–Stokes equations  on grids , particles , or hybrid representations , and produce physically faithful results when the scene parameters and boundary conditions are carefully defined. To extend simulation to single- or multi-view videos captured in the wild, more recent works reconstruct a 3D fluid representation from videos with regularization derived from physical priors and re-simulating with the reconstructed representation. Another line of work uses neural networks as replacements to accelerate explicit solvers . A shared fundamental component of these works is the reliance on manually designed simulation rules (e.g., Navier–Stokes equations) that are themselves only approximations of the highly complex fluid dynamics process. As a result, they remain brittle: small reconstruction errors build up, fluid parameters must be tuned per scene, and the state-of-the-art methods still struggle on the casual images that dominate real-world content.()

A new family of approaches turns to large-scale generative models, which now carry remarkably strong priors over both motion and appearance from internet-scale training . A natural way to use them in physical content creation is as a learned renderer on top of an explicit simulator, leaning on the generator’s appearance prior while leaving the dynamics to the solver. Yet on fluid phenomena specifically, this combination still falls short. On their own, modern video models consistently violate basic physical rules in scenes with complex fluid dynamics . Earlier physics-aware generation efforts have focused mostly on rigid  or elastic  objects rather than on volumetric, turbulent fluids. To close this gap on fluid dynamics, very recent works explicitly couple a video generator with an underlying simulator that provides fluid dynamics guidance. However, all aforementioned pipelines still depend on the heavy machinery of an authored 3D scene and a configured simulator, which limits their applicability to in-the-wild fluid content synthesis.(; ; ; )

We argue that video model itself can learn complex fluid dynamics directly, but RGB supervision alone provides an insufficient training signal: appearance errors dominate the convergence while subtle physical errors are easily ignored. We therefore introduce an internal motion representation, jointly predicted with RGB, that explicitly exposes fluid dynamics to the model. Specifically, we predict a 3D velocity field describing fluid motion over time, providing a more physically meaningful representation than optical flow or trajectories .(; )

Wang et al., 2024

Zhang et al., 2025b

This representation enables a clean two-stage post-training pipeline for a pretrained video diffusion model . First, we jointly supervise RGB and velocity prediction using high-fidelity Houdini simulations with ground-truth velocity fields, together with in-the-wild fluid videos for appearance diversity and gives the model the generalization ability for in-the-wild content. Second, we perform velocity-aware DPO , using the model’s own predicted velocity field together with appearance signals to rank samples by physical plausibility. The resulting model produces more coherent vortices, natural advection, and fine-scale turbulent structure and clearly outperforms state-of-the-art strong video-generation and simulation-based baselines.()

Wan et al., 2025

(; )

Rafailov et al., 2023

Liu et al., 2025a

In summary, our contributions are:

•

We propose a dual-head video model architecture that jointly predicts an internal fluid velocity field alongside RGB pixels, providing an explicit and interpretable physical signal that guides dynamics learning.

•

We curate a fluid training corpus that pairs high-quality Houdini simulations with collected in-the-wild smoke, fire, and explosion footage, combining dense physical supervision with the appearance variety needed for real-world generalization.

•

We design a two-stage training pipeline that first jointly supervises RGB and velocity prediction and then aligns the model outputs with a post-training stage using its own predicted velocity field as the reward.

2

Realistic fluid visual effect synthesis in graphics has long been driven by analytical physical simulation. Classical Eulerian solvers discretize the Navier–Stokes equations on regular grids , while particle-based formulations  represent fluids as collections of moving particles, and hybrid representations such as PBF  balance accuracy with interactivity from both sides. To reduce simulation cost, neural networks have been used as accelerating components for the traditional solvers . Built on top of existing fluid simulation formulations, a complementary line of work aims to recover fluid representations directly from captured video and re-simulates them . Combined with differentiable rendering, these works directly build fluid assets from real-world captures instead of requiring manual construction in the simulator. However all of these methods rely on human-defined simulation rules and are bounded by the approximation accuracy. Our work takes the opposite path: we treat fluid dynamics as the learnable property of a video model itself, without the explicit solver at inference time.Fluid Simulation and Reconstruction.(; )

Recent video diffusion models exhibit strong motion priors but are not necessarily physically faithful, and even frontier models still violate basic physical principles in scenes with complex dynamics . A line of work combines traditional simulation with video generation. PhysGen  couples video generation with rigid-body physics through SDEdit , PhysMotion  extends this into the elastic domain, and PhysDreamer  distills physical parameters using a video model as prior. These methods focus on solid materials and cannot naturally extend to volumetric, turbulent fluids. A second family  instead steers diffusion sampling with LLM-derived physical context. Another line of work fine-tunes video models on labeled synthetic data to emit auxiliary channels alongside RGB, though these channels are appearance properties, e.g., intrinsics  or weather , rather than the dynamical state we predict.Physics-Aware Video Synthesis.(; )

To accommodate fluid effect synthesis, a recent line of work  built the system on top of the multi-physics simulator , conditioning the video generation model through bi-modal control. Although these hybrid systems improve physical plausibility for fluids and also other materials, they still require an authored 3D scene and a configured simulator, limiting their applicability to generation from in-the-wild content. We share their goal but bake the physics directly into the video model through our model design and the training pipeline, with no manual effort on explicit simulators.(; ; )

Preference optimization, as a post-training stage, has become a standard recipe for aligning generative models with human-defined high-dimensional quality. DPO  provides a simple offline formulation for the optimization target, and Diffusion-DPO  further adapts it to training with diffusion models. VideoDPO  extends preference alignment to the video diffusion domain with a multi-aspect scoring system, and DenseDPO  introduces fine-grained temporal preference labels to better target motion quality. EpipolarDPO  employs epipolar constraints to enhance geometry consistency of video generation. Inspired by these, we further treat physical quality, especially complex fluid effects, as another signal that can be used for preference optimization. In detail, we leverage our model’s native velocity field prediction as part of the reward signal, turning an auxiliary physical output into a physics-grounded preference indicator at the alignment stage.Preference Optimization Post-Training.()
