Our pipeline augments a pretrained video diffusion model with a velocity prediction stream and train it in two stages: joint supervised fine-tuning on simulated and in-the-wild fluid videos, followed by velocity-aware DPO using physics-informed rewards.

Figure 2: Overview of FluidGen

3.1

Our model is trained to jointly generate a fluid video and a pixel-aligned 3D velocity field video using a single video diffusion model, and subsequently trained with the reward metric computed directly from its own velocity field output. Therefore, velocity and RGB predictions serve two key roles. First, as an auxiliary motion signal that regularizes the appearance stream toward more coherent and consistent dynamics through this joint prediction .

More importantly, it transforms every generated sample into the physical dynamics that can be evaluated directly, thereby enabling a velocity-based preference optimization stage without requiring any external motion estimator or simulator.()

Chefer et al., 2025

Concretely, our architecture is a dual-head extension of a pretrained video diffusion transformer (DiT ) (§) that produces both an RGB stream and a velocity stream from a shared latent. The model is trained in two stages: 1) Joint supervised fine-tuning (§): a flow-matching  objective over the joint latent trained on a mixed corpus of Houdini simulations with paired ground-truth velocity, and in-the-wild fluid videos. 2) Velocity-aware DPO post-training (§): a DPO objective driven by a velocity-informed reward that evaluates each generated trajectory using its predicted velocity field.

Both stages share the same model and output velocity representation, which we introduce first in §.()

Peebles and Xie, 2023

3.3

3.4

()

Lipman et al., 2022

3.5

3.2

3.2

At every pixel of each generated frame, we represent the 3D motion of the underlying fluid particles as a velocity vector $\mathbf{v}=(v_{x},v_{y},v_{z})\in\mathbb{R}^{3}$ , expressed in the camera coordinate system. To remain compatible with the standard video model latent space and preserve the pretrained VAE encoder without modification, we do not regress $\mathbf{v}$ directly. Instead, we encode $\mathbf{v}$ into a three-channel color $\mathbf{c}\in[0,1]^{3}$ via a spherical decomposition, as illustrated in Fig. , and have the velocity head predict $\mathbf{c}$ as an auxiliary RGB-like stream. Let $\rho=\|\mathbf{v}\|$ , $\theta=\arccos(v_{z}/\rho)\in[0,\pi]$ , and $\phi=\mathrm{atan2}(v_{y},v_{x})\in[-\pi,\pi]$ . The encoding is defined as

3

$\mathbf{c}=\Big(\tfrac{\rho}{S},\;\tfrac{\theta}{\pi},\;\tfrac{\phi+\pi}{2\pi}\Big)\in[0,1]^{3},\quad S=\sigma\sqrt{H^{2}+W^{2}},$ (1)

where $(H,W)$ is the image resolution and the global scale $\sigma=10^{-2}$ is chosen such that typical advection magnitudes occupy the middle of the $[0,1]$ range. At inference, the predicted $\mathbf{c}$ is decoded back to $\mathbf{v}$ by inverting Eq. .

1

3.3

Our model builds upon a pretrained 14B image-to-video Diffusion Transformer , whose VAE encodes a video into a $16$ -channel spatiotemporal latent $\mathbf{z}^{\mathrm{rgb}}\in\mathbb{R}^{16\times T\times h\times w}$ .

We extend the backbone with a parallel operating on a velocity latent of identical shape, and concatenate the two along the channel dimension to form a joint latent, following VideoJam :()

Wan et al., 2025

velocity head()

Chefer et al., 2025

$\tilde{\mathbf{z}}=[\mathbf{z}^{\mathrm{rgb}};\,\mathbf{z}^{\mathrm{vel}}]\in\mathbb{R}^{32\times T\times h\times w}.$ (2)

The velocity latent is encoded and decoded using the same VAE as the RGB stream: we simply treat the encoded velocity image (Eq. ) as an additional RGB clip. This preserves the pretrained perceptual capability of the backbone while avoiding the need to train a separate encoder-decoder latent space.

Two transformer components are widened to support the joint latent (Fig. ):

1

2

The initial patchify projection is expanded so that its input depth grows from $16+K$ to $16+16+K$ , where $K$ denotes the number of conditioning channels (conditional image and binary mask latent). The first $16+K$ channels reuse the pretrained weights directly, while the additional $16$ corresponding to the velocity latent are zero-initialized. So the model can start the training stage without losing the base prediction ability.Patch Embedding Input.

The final projection layer mapping tokens back to patch space is widened from an output dimension of $16$ to $32$ . The RGB channels reuse the pretrained weights, while the velocity channels are initialized to zero.

This zero initialization scheme preserves the pretrained model behavior at initialization: the RGB branch is initially identical to the original pretrained model, while the velocity branch remains inactive at the beginning of the joint supervised fine-tuning. We empirically explored architectures with separate denoisers and explicit cross-attention bridges, but found that a single shared denoiser sampled along one trajectory already maintains strong causal consistency between RGB and velocity while being substantially simpler for training and inference.Output Head.

3.4

The dual-head model is fine-tuned on two complementary datasets.

1) High-fidelity Houdini simulations of smoke, fire, and explosion scenes rendered together with dense ground-truth Eulerian velocity fields, which provide clean $(\text{RGB},\mathbf{v})$ supervision as illustrated in Fig.  and anchor the velocity head to physically plausible fluid behavior. Please refer to § and Appendix  for more details on the dataset construction.

2) A curated collection of in-the-wild fluid videos supplies appearance diversity, including lighting, materials, scales, and camera motion, which is difficult to produce in simulation and is critical for generalization to real-world inputs.Training Data.

3

4

B.2

Here we show two examples of simulated scenes: the rendered RGB frames, velocity field frames and visualized velocity directions in our Houdini-constructed dataset.

Figure 3: Data visualization.

Both heads are trained jointly with a single flow-matching objective  over the combined $32$ -channel latent. Let $\mathbf{z}_{1}=[\mathbf{z}_{1}^{\mathrm{rgb}};\mathbf{z}_{1}^{\mathrm{vel}}]$ denote the encoded clean target, let $\mathbf{z}_{0}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{I})$ be the noise sampled from a standard Gaussian distribution, and let $\mathbf{z}_{t}=(1-t)\mathbf{z}_{0}+t\mathbf{z}_{1}$ be the linear interpolation. The denoiser $\mathbf{v}_{\Theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t,\mathbf{c},\mathbf{y})$ is trained to predict the conditional flow $\mathbf{z}_{1}-\mathbf{z}_{0}$ viaJoint Flow-Matching Objective.(; )

Lipman et al., 2022

Wan et al., 2025

$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SFT}}=\mathbb{E}_{t,\,\mathbf{z}_{0},\,\mathbf{z}_{1}}\Big[m\,\big\|\mathbf{v}_{\Theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t,\mathbf{c},\mathbf{y})-(\mathbf{z}_{1}-\mathbf{z}_{0})\big\|^{2}\Big],$ (3)

where $\mathbf{c}$ denotes the image-conditioning input and $\mathbf{y}$ the text prompt. The per-channel mask $m$ equals $1$ for all channels on samples with velocity supervision (the Houdini subset), and equals $0$ only on RGB channels for samples without velocity targets (the in-the-wild subset). Consequently, the velocity head is trained exclusively on simulation data, while the RGB head benefits from the full appearance distribution. In practice, the two datasets are interleaved at a fixed mixing ratio during training.

3.5

First stage fine-tuning yields a model capable of jointly generating an RGB stream and a plausible velocity field stream in a single forward pass. However, the physical quality of generated samples still exhibits suboptimal performance. Many samples will remain visibly degenerate, as it is hard for the model to simply learn the physical process  – especially for highly unconstrained and complex fluid dynamics.

Consequently, we employ a post-training stage to reduce this variability by aligning the generator with the physics-informed reward, through the preference optimization.()

Bansal et al., 2025

We assign each generated sample a scalar reward

$R(\tilde{\mathbf{z}})\in[0,1]$ , defined as a convex combination of thirteen component rewards. Each component acts as a soft indicator of physical plausibility. Eleven components are computed directly from the decoded velocity field and fall into three categories:Physics-Informed Reward.

terms: including direction diversity, temporal coherence, and multi-scale gradient detail, which encourage non-trivial and temporally stable flow structure;Structural

terms: including activity naturalness, temporal dynamics balance, life-cycle envelope, and radial outflow, which encourage agreement with the empirical distribution of Houdini simulations;Statistical

terms: including advection self-consistency, Q-criterion diversity, direction-field enstrophy , and Kolmogorov inertial range compliance , which encourage classical properties of turbulent flow.Physical()

Hunt et al., 1988

()

Kraichnan, 1974

As illustrated in Fig. , this composite reward reliably separates faithful fluid dynamics from unrealistic ones, and serves as the criterion for preference pairs in the post-training stage.

4

For each conditioning pair $(\mathbf{c}_{i},\mathbf{y}_{i})$ drawn from the first stage training corpus, we sample $N{=}4$ candidates using independent random seeds. Since each sample is itself a $32$ -channel video latent containing both RGB and velocity streams generated by the same denoiser, the aforementioned reward can be evaluated directly on the model output without any additional motion estimator. Within each candidate set, we construct a preference pair $(\tilde{\mathbf{z}}^{+},\tilde{\mathbf{z}}^{-})$ using the highest and lowest reward samples, respectively, and discard pairs whose reward gap is below a threshold $\delta$ .Preference Pairs and Flow-DPO Objective.

distinguishes plausible from implausible fluid dynamics. Four samples (left: RGB frame; right: visualized velocity field) from the same input annotated with their reward values. High reward samples exhibit organized, turbulent flow structure with rich directional diversity and coherent vortical motion, while low reward samples show collapsed velocity fields that do not correspond to realistic fluid behavior.Figure 4: Physics-informed reward

Given a pair at diffusion time $t$ , let $\mathbf{u}^{\star}_{t}$ denote the flow-matching target from Eq. , and let $\mathbf{v}_{\Theta}$ and $\mathbf{v}_{\Theta_{\mathrm{ref}}}$ denote the trainable and reference denoisers, respectively. Following the MSE-based Diffusion-DPO formulation  adapted to flow matching , we define the per-sample preference residual as:

3

()

Wallace et al., 2024

(; )

Rafailov et al., 2023

Liu et al., 2025a

$\Delta(\tilde{\mathbf{z}})=\big\|\mathbf{v}_{\Theta}(\tilde{\mathbf{z}},t)-\mathbf{u}^{\star}_{t}\big\|^{2}-\big\|\mathbf{v}_{\Theta_{\mathrm{ref}}}(\tilde{\mathbf{z}},t)-\mathbf{u}^{\star}_{t}\big\|^{2},$ (4)

and optimize

$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DPO}}=-\mathbb{E}_{(\tilde{\mathbf{z}}^{+},\tilde{\mathbf{z}}^{-}),\,t}\;\log\sigma\ \Big(-\tfrac{1}{2}\beta\big(\Delta(\tilde{\mathbf{z}}^{+})-\Delta(\tilde{\mathbf{z}}^{-})\big)\Big),$ (5)

where $\sigma(\cdot)$ denotes the logistic sigmoid function and $\beta$ is a temperature parameter. The objective decreases when the trainable model improves its prediction error on preferred samples more than on dispreferred samples, relative to the reference model. During this stage, we optimize $\mathbf{v}_{\Theta}$ using low-rank adaptation (LoRA ) applied to attention and FFN linear layers while freezing the backbone parameters. The reference model $\mathbf{v}_{\Theta_{\mathrm{ref}}}$ is obtained implicitly by disabling the LoRA adapters during inference.()

As aforementioned in §, our training dataset is consist of two sources. In detail, we constructed $13125$ videos from Houdini simulation, 15570 real-world videos from FluidNexus dataset , and curated $6521$ videos from the real-world footage. In total resulting in a training set of more than $35$ K videos. Each video is resized to the desired $480\times 832$ resolution, for portrait videos we equally pad black pixels on left and right to match the size ratio. Each video has $81$ frames for training.Datasets.

Our model is initialized from the pretrained Wan-2.1-14B image-to-video diffusion model . During the joint Supervised Fine-Tuning (FT) stage, we train the widened transformer blocks for 7000 iterations with a batch size of 1 and a learning rate of 1e-5. For the Velocity-Aware DPO stage, we freeze the backbone and train LoRA adapters (rank $r=64$ ) for 500 iterations using a preference margin threshold $\delta=0.05$ and temperature $\beta=500$ . Training was conducted on 8 NVIDIA H100 GPUs. The codebase is built on DiffSynth  and Epipolar-DPO .Implementation Details.()

We evaluate along two axes using two benchmarks. The benchmark  provides multiview captures of real fluids with ground-truth reference frames; on $15$ randomly selected sequences, we report PSNR and SSIM for per-frame reconstruction fidelity, LPIPS  for perceptual similarity, and FVD  for distributional distance over spatiotemporal features. To evaluate general video quality on in-the-wild image inputs, we additionally report VBench  scores on $20$ selected images along three dimensions relevant to fluid synthesis: Imaging Quality (per-frame visual fidelity), Aesthetic Quality (perceptual appeal), and Subject Consistency (temporal stability of foreground content, critical for coherent advection without flickering).Metrics.FluidNexus()

4.2

Tab.  reports results on the FluidNexus benchmark. We note that the FluidNexus baseline used here is an upgraded multi-view variant of the original method, which consumes multiple synchronized views as input and requires several hours of per-scene optimization to reconstruct the underlying fluid representation. Despite this substantially heavier setup, it still fails to recover some fine level turbulent details such as small scale eddies and high-frequency boundary roll-ups, which is reflected in its lower SSIM and notably higher LPIPS and FVD compared to our method. Wan2.1-I2V-14B, on the other hand, struggles to produce faithful fluid dynamics from a single image and frequently introduces appearance artifacts such as color shifting and texture drift over time. In contrast, our model, conditioned on only a single image and run in a single forward pass, achieves the best or on par metrics with the multi-view FluidNexus baseline, indicating that our generated complex fluid dynamics closely match the ground-truth captures.

2

To verify that our training stages do not compromise general generative capability on in-the-wild content, we evaluate our method using VBench metrics in Tab. . Our final model matches or surpasses the Wan2.1-I2V-14B base model on all three reported dimensions, with clear gains in Imaging Quality and Subject Consistency. The improvement in Subject Consistency is particularly meaningful for fluid scenes: it indicates that the auxiliary velocity stream regularizes the RGB stream toward temporally coherent advection, mitigating the flickering and shifting artifacts observed in the base model. Together, the two benchmarks show that our method substantially improves physical fidelity.

Fig.  shows visual comparisons against ground-truth captures from the FluidNexus benchmark. The upgraded FluidNexus baseline recovers the coarse shape and trajectory of the smoke plume, but its reconstructions after several hours of optimization still appear overly smooth and lose some fine-scale wisps and turbulent filaments visible in the ground truth, indicating the disadvantage of relying only on the manually defined physical approximation laws.

Wan2.1-I2V-14B produces motion that diverges from the reference dynamics and exhibits noticeable color drift and appearance inconsistency over time. In contrast, our method reproduces both the global rising trajectory and fine turbulent structures, including thin tendrils at the plume boundary, while requiring only a single forward pass from a single input image.

We further compare against Wan2.1-I2V-14B on in-the-wild inputs in Fig. , where our full model produces more vivid and physically realistic fluid dynamics. Finally, our model supports several downstream applications, including fluid-related visual effects (Fig. ) via keyframe control (images are generated by NanoBanana 2 ), velocity field prediction (Fig. ) from input videos using RePaint-style  conditional sampling, and fluid simulation driven by the generated 3D velocity fields (Fig. ). More results are provided in Appendix  and on our project page.

The stage I fine-tuning achieves significant gain compared to the basemodel: FluidGen w/o DPO improves PSNR from $22.50$ to $31.52$ and reduces FVD from $569.7$ to $192.1$ over the base model, while improving Subject Consistency on VBench ( $0.8929\rightarrow 0.9383$ ).

We attribute this improvement to our curated training corpus of high-fidelity Houdini simulations and in-the-wild fluid videos, which exposes the model to the turbulent dynamics largely absent from the base model’s pretraining distribution.Joint Supervised Fine-Tuning.

DPO trades a small amount of reconstruction fidelity for noticeably better perceptual quality. FluidNexus metrics remain on par with the FT-only model, while VBench Imaging Quality improves significantly and Aesthetic Quality slightly. The slight drop in Subject Consistency ( $0.9383\rightarrow 0.9350$ ) is expected: the preference signal favors higher-energy, more turbulent motion. Qualitatively (Fig. ), the FT+DPO model (FluidGen) produces richer fine-scale details and more vivid fire and smoke motion than FluidGen w/o DPO. 5

5

We present FluidGen, a framework for synthesizing physically plausible fluid dynamics directly within a video diffusion model, bridging the gap between the rich appearance priors of generative models and the dynamic constraints of classical fluid solvers. By augmenting a pretrained video diffusion transformer with a dual-head architecture, our model jointly predicts RGB pixels and an underlying 3D velocity field, capturing complex fluid dynamics without authored 3D scenes or explicit simulators at inference.

Our two-stage training pipeline first jointly fine-tunes the model with dense physical supervision from high-fidelity Houdini simulations alongside the visual diversity of in-the-wild videos, then applies a velocity-aware preference optimization stage that uses the model’s native velocity predictions to compute a physics-informed reward over structural, statistical, and fluid properties, aligning the generator toward turbulent, coherent, and physically sound motion.

While our method focuses on volumetric fluids such as smoke, fire, and explosions, the core idea of embedding interpretable physical representations into generative latents points toward a broader paradigm for physics-aware synthesis. Future work could extend the dual-head approach to other physical systems such as liquids or elastic materials, or expose the predicted velocity fields as a direct control handle for artists. Our results demonstrate that with the right internal representations and alignment strategies, large-scale video models can natively master complex physical dynamics.

Appendix B

B.1

Let $\mathbf{v}_{t}(x,y)=(v_{x},v_{y},v_{z})$ denote the per-pixel 3D velocity field at frame $t$ decoded from the velocity stream of a generated sample $\tilde{\mathbf{z}}$ via the inverse transformation of Eq. . We write $\rho_{t}=\|\mathbf{v}_{t}\|$ for the speed magnitude and $\hat{\mathbf{u}}_{t}=\mathbf{v}_{t}/\rho_{t}$ for the unit-direction field, and set it to zero when $\rho_{t}$ falls below a small numerical floor value. At each frame we define an active region $\mathcal{A}_{t}=\{(x,y):\rho_{t}(x,y)>\tau_{\rho}\}$ that filters out near static background pixels, where $\tau_{\rho}=\alpha_{a}S$ with $S$ the encoding scale of Eq.  and $\alpha_{a}$ a fixed fraction.

We also use the normalized R-channel $R_{t}\in[0,1]$ of the encoded velocity image directly for temporal-difference statistics. The symbols $\kappa_{\bullet}$ , $\mu_{\bullet}$ , and $\sigma_{\bullet}$ denote scalar hyper-parameters; their values are calibrated once on a small held-out set of Houdini-simulated and curated in-the-wild clips, and are listed at the end of this section.Notation.

1

1

In total, we compute eleven reward components (Tab. ), which act on the velocity stream and fall into three groups.Reward components.

3

Structural terms target the spatial and temporal organization of the direction field:

•

$R_{\mathrm{div}}$ penalizes direction collapse via the per-component variance of $\hat{\mathbf{u}}$ ,

•

$R_{\mathrm{tc}}$ measures the temporal Pearson correlation of the spatial gradients of $\hat{\mathbf{u}}$ ,

•

$R_{\mathrm{msd}}$ rewards consistent gradient richness at scales $s\in\{1,2,4\}$ so that the flow shows structured detail at all scales rather than blur or pure noise.

Statistical terms match the empirical distribution of Houdini simulations:

•

$R_{\mathrm{act}}$ on the mean active-pixel fraction $\bar{f}_{a}=\mathbb{E}_{t}[|\mathcal{A}_{t}|/HW]$ ,

•

$R_{\mathrm{tdb}}$ on the mean temporal change of $R_{t}$ ,

•

$R_{\mathrm{ro}}$ on the speed weighted cosine alignment between the image plane velocity $(v_{x},v_{z})$ and the radial direction $\mathbf{r}$ from an automatically estimated source, averaged over early frames.

Physical terms encode classical criterions of turbulent flow:

We synthesize the training set in SideFX Houdini using its Pyro solver, covering three asset families: rising , ambient , and bursting . 一句话：在通用视频模型上做运动引导的后训练，让生成的水花符合流体物理。

要点：

  • 通用视频模型生成流体时常常违背物理规律
  • 用运动引导的后训练把物理约束注入模型
  • 生成结果在流动形态与交互响应上更可信

为什么值得看：流体是引擎里最难模拟也最常被要求「看起来对」的东西；这类方法给实时特效提供了新的素材来源。

中文摘要：FluidGen 针对通用视频生成模型在流体场景下的物理失真问题：水花、烟雾这类介质的运动规律一旦学错，画面立刻露馅。作者采用运动引导的后训练策略，在预训练视频模型上注入流体运动的物理约束，使生成结果在流动形态、惯性响应与交互反应上更接近真实模拟。论文来自 Stanford，对需要大量流体特效素材的团队有实际价值。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

FluidGen: Physics-Aware Fluid Video Generation via Motion-Guided Post-Training

Yang Zheng*Zizhang Li*Boyang Deng*Jan Ackermann

Lei Shu

Affiliation: Yinghao Xu   Jiajun Wu   Gordon Wetzstein   Leonidas GuibasStanford University

Affiliation: Equal contribution

Affiliation: *

Abstract

Video generation models produce visually compelling motion but systematically fail on fluid phenomena, including smoke, fire, and explosion debris, where outputs lack coherent vortical structure and collapse to bland dynamics that violate the physics of real fluids. Classical solvers achieve high physical fidelity but require detailed 3D scenes and carefully tuned parameters, making them impractical for in-the-wild imagery and video generation. We address this gap by injecting a data-driven fluid prior into a pre-trained video model, trained on a mixture of high-fidelity Houdini simulation data with paired velocity-field ground truth and curated in-the-wild fluid video data for appearance diversity. The core of our approach is a dual stream architecture that predicts per-frame velocity fields alongside RGB, supervised by simulation ground truth. This auxiliary signal regularizes generation toward physically consistent motion and exposes an interpretable physical quantity that we further leverage as a reward for velocity-aware direct preference optimization. Our model produces substantially more realistic fluid dynamics sequences than strong video baselines and optimization-based methods. Our data, code, and model will be publicly released. Project page: .

https://y-zheng18.github.io/FluidGen/

We introduce , a physics-aware video diffusion model for realistic fluid dynamics. FluidGen jointly predicts per-frame velocity fields (insets) that regularize generation toward physically consistent motion.

Figure 1: FluidGen

1

Realistic fluid phenomena, including billowing smoke, rolling fire, and the dust and ash of an explosion, are among the most important visual elements in film, games, and immersive media, and also among the hardest to make look right. Their motion is driven by complex, turbulent physical dynamics, and humans can notice errors in problematic fluid dynamics immediately: for example a plume that rises too uniformly, a flame that moves in an unnatural direction, or a debris cloud without proper swirling structure. Synthesizing fluid content that holds up under this realism has been a long-standing goal in computer graphics, and despite decades of progress, it still typically requires expert artists, expensive simulation tools, and large amounts of manual effort.

One family of approaches treats fluid dynamics synthesis as a simulation problem. Classical physical solvers solve the Navier–Stokes equations  on grids , particles , or hybrid representations , and produce physically faithful results when the scene parameters and boundary conditions are carefully defined. To extend simulation to single- or multi-view videos captured in the wild, more recent works reconstruct a 3D fluid representation from videos with regularization derived from physical priors and re-simulating with the reconstructed representation. Another line of work uses neural networks as replacements to accelerate explicit solvers . A shared fundamental component of these works is the reliance on manually designed simulation rules (e.g., Navier–Stokes equations) that are themselves only approximations of the highly complex fluid dynamics process. As a result, they remain brittle: small reconstruction errors build up, fluid parameters must be tuned per scene, and the state-of-the-art methods still struggle on the casual images that dominate real-world content.()

Constantin and Foiaş, 1988

(; )

Stam, 2023

Bridson, 2015

(; )

Müller et al., 2003

Zhu and Bridson, 2005

()

Macklin and Müller, 2013

(; ; ; )

Eckert et al., 2019

Chu et al., 2022

Yu et al., 2023

Gao et al., 2025

(; ; ; )

Kim et al., 2019

Sanchez-Gonzalez et al., 2020

Ummenhofer et al., 2019

Cai et al., 2021

A new family of approaches turns to large-scale generative models, which now carry remarkably strong priors over both motion and appearance from internet-scale training . A natural way to use them in physical content creation is as a learned renderer on top of an explicit simulator, leaning on the generator’s appearance prior while leaving the dynamics to the solver. Yet on fluid phenomena specifically, this combination still falls short. On their own, modern video models consistently violate basic physical rules in scenes with complex fluid dynamics . Earlier physics-aware generation efforts have focused mostly on rigid  or elastic  objects rather than on volumetric, turbulent fluids. To close this gap on fluid dynamics, very recent works explicitly couple a video generator with an underlying simulator that provides fluid dynamics guidance. However, all aforementioned pipelines still depend on the heavy machinery of an authored 3D scene and a configured simulator, which limits their applicability to in-the-wild fluid content synthesis.(; ; ; )

Wan et al., 2025

Brooks et al., 2024

Polyak et al., 2024

Bar-Tal et al., 2024

()

Zhan et al., 2026

We argue that video model itself can learn complex fluid dynamics directly, but RGB supervision alone provides an insufficient training signal: appearance errors dominate the convergence while subtle physical errors are easily ignored. We therefore introduce an internal motion representation, jointly predicted with RGB, that explicitly exposes fluid dynamics to the model. Specifically, we predict a 3D velocity field describing fluid motion over time, providing a more physically meaningful representation than optical flow or trajectories .(; )

Wang et al., 2024

Zhang et al., 2025b

This representation enables a clean two-stage post-training pipeline for a pretrained video diffusion model . First, we jointly supervise RGB and velocity prediction using high-fidelity Houdini simulations with ground-truth velocity fields, together with in-the-wild fluid videos for appearance diversity and gives the model the generalization ability for in-the-wild content. Second, we perform velocity-aware DPO , using the model’s own predicted velocity field together with appearance signals to rank samples by physical plausibility. The resulting model produces more coherent vortices, natural advection, and fine-scale turbulent structure and clearly outperforms state-of-the-art strong video-generation and simulation-based baselines.()

Wan et al., 2025

(; )

Rafailov et al., 2023

Liu et al., 2025a

In summary, our contributions are:

•

We propose a dual-head video model architecture that jointly predicts an internal fluid velocity field alongside RGB pixels, providing an explicit and interpretable physical signal that guides dynamics learning.

•

We curate a fluid training corpus that pairs high-quality Houdini simulations with collected in-the-wild smoke, fire, and explosion footage, combining dense physical supervision with the appearance variety needed for real-world generalization.

•

We design a two-stage training pipeline that first jointly supervises RGB and velocity prediction and then aligns the model outputs with a post-training stage using its own predicted velocity field as the reward.

2

Realistic fluid visual effect synthesis in graphics has long been driven by analytical physical simulation. Classical Eulerian solvers discretize the Navier–Stokes equations on regular grids , while particle-based formulations  represent fluids as collections of moving particles, and hybrid representations such as PBF  balance accuracy with interactivity from both sides. To reduce simulation cost, neural networks have been used as accelerating components for the traditional solvers . Built on top of existing fluid simulation formulations, a complementary line of work aims to recover fluid representations directly from captured video and re-simulates them . Combined with differentiable rendering, these works directly build fluid assets from real-world captures instead of requiring manual construction in the simulator. However all of these methods rely on human-defined simulation rules and are bounded by the approximation accuracy. Our work takes the opposite path: we treat fluid dynamics as the learnable property of a video model itself, without the explicit solver at inference time.Fluid Simulation and Reconstruction.(; )

Stam, 2023

Bridson, 2015

(; )

Recent video diffusion models exhibit strong motion priors but are not necessarily physically faithful, and even frontier models still violate basic physical principles in scenes with complex dynamics . A line of work combines traditional simulation with video generation. PhysGen  couples video generation with rigid-body physics through SDEdit , PhysMotion  extends this into the elastic domain, and PhysDreamer  distills physical parameters using a video model as prior. These methods focus on solid materials and cannot naturally extend to volumetric, turbulent fluids. A second family  instead steers diffusion sampling with LLM-derived physical context. Another line of work fine-tunes video models on labeled synthetic data to emit auxiliary channels alongside RGB, though these channels are appearance properties, e.g., intrinsics  or weather , rather than the dynamical state we predict.Physics-Aware Video Synthesis.(; )

Motamed et al., 2025

Bansal et al., 2025

Lin et al., 2025

To accommodate fluid effect synthesis, a recent line of work  built the system on top of the multi-physics simulator , conditioning the video generation model through bi-modal control. Although these hybrid systems improve physical plausibility for fluids and also other materials, they still require an authored 3D scene and a configured simulator, limiting their applicability to generation from in-the-wild content. We share their goal but bake the physics directly into the video model through our model design and the training pipeline, with no manual effort on explicit simulators.(; ; )

Li et al., 2025b

Zhan et al., 2026

Liu et al., 2026

()

Authors, 2024

Preference optimization, as a post-training stage, has become a standard recipe for aligning generative models with human-defined high-dimensional quality. DPO  provides a simple offline formulation for the optimization target, and Diffusion-DPO  further adapts it to training with diffusion models. VideoDPO  extends preference alignment to the video diffusion domain with a multi-aspect scoring system, and DenseDPO  introduces fine-grained temporal preference labels to better target motion quality. EpipolarDPO  employs epipolar constraints to enhance geometry consistency of video generation. Inspired by these, we further treat physical quality, especially complex fluid effects, as another signal that can be used for preference optimization. In detail, we leverage our model’s native velocity field prediction as part of the reward signal, turning an auxiliary physical output into a physics-grounded preference indicator at the alignment stage.Preference Optimization Post-Training.()

Rafailov et al., 2023

()

Wallace et al., 2024

3

.

Our pipeline augments a pretrained video diffusion model with a velocity prediction stream and train it in two stages: joint supervised fine-tuning on simulated and in-the-wild fluid videos, followed by velocity-aware DPO using physics-informed rewards.

Figure 2: Overview of FluidGen

3.1

Our model is trained to jointly generate a fluid video and a pixel-aligned 3D velocity field video using a single video diffusion model, and subsequently trained with the reward metric computed directly from its own velocity field output. Therefore, velocity and RGB predictions serve two key roles. First, as an auxiliary motion signal that regularizes the appearance stream toward more coherent and consistent dynamics through this joint prediction .

More importantly, it transforms every generated sample into the physical dynamics that can be evaluated directly, thereby enabling a velocity-based preference optimization stage without requiring any external motion estimator or simulator.()

Chefer et al., 2025

Concretely, our architecture is a dual-head extension of a pretrained video diffusion transformer (DiT ) (§) that produces both an RGB stream and a velocity stream from a shared latent. The model is trained in two stages: 1) Joint supervised fine-tuning (§): a flow-matching  objective over the joint latent trained on a mixed corpus of Houdini simulations with paired ground-truth velocity, and in-the-wild fluid videos. 2) Velocity-aware DPO post-training (§): a DPO objective driven by a velocity-informed reward that evaluates each generated trajectory using its predicted velocity field.

Both stages share the same model and output velocity representation, which we introduce first in §.()

Peebles and Xie, 2023

3.3

3.4

()

Lipman et al., 2022

3.5

3.2

3.2

At every pixel of each generated frame, we represent the 3D motion of the underlying fluid particles as a velocity vector $\mathbf{v}=(v_{x},v_{y},v_{z})\in\mathbb{R}^{3}$ , expressed in the camera coordinate system. To remain compatible with the standard video model latent space and preserve the pretrained VAE encoder without modification, we do not regress $\mathbf{v}$ directly. Instead, we encode $\mathbf{v}$ into a three-channel color $\mathbf{c}\in[0,1]^{3}$ via a spherical decomposition, as illustrated in Fig. , and have the velocity head predict $\mathbf{c}$ as an auxiliary RGB-like stream. Let $\rho=\|\mathbf{v}\|$ , $\theta=\arccos(v_{z}/\rho)\in[0,\pi]$ , and $\phi=\mathrm{atan2}(v_{y},v_{x})\in[-\pi,\pi]$ . The encoding is defined as

3

$\mathbf{c}=\Big(\tfrac{\rho}{S},\;\tfrac{\theta}{\pi},\;\tfrac{\phi+\pi}{2\pi}\Big)\in[0,1]^{3},\quad S=\sigma\sqrt{H^{2}+W^{2}},$ (1)

where $(H,W)$ is the image resolution and the global scale $\sigma=10^{-2}$ is chosen such that typical advection magnitudes occupy the middle of the $[0,1]$ range. At inference, the predicted $\mathbf{c}$ is decoded back to $\mathbf{v}$ by inverting Eq. .

1

3.3

Our model builds upon a pretrained 14B image-to-video Diffusion Transformer , whose VAE encodes a video into a $16$ -channel spatiotemporal latent $\mathbf{z}^{\mathrm{rgb}}\in\mathbb{R}^{16\times T\times h\times w}$ .

We extend the backbone with a parallel operating on a velocity latent of identical shape, and concatenate the two along the channel dimension to form a joint latent, following VideoJam :()

Wan et al., 2025

velocity head()

Chefer et al., 2025

$\tilde{\mathbf{z}}=[\mathbf{z}^{\mathrm{rgb}};\,\mathbf{z}^{\mathrm{vel}}]\in\mathbb{R}^{32\times T\times h\times w}.$ (2)

The velocity latent is encoded and decoded using the same VAE as the RGB stream: we simply treat the encoded velocity image (Eq. ) as an additional RGB clip. This preserves the pretrained perceptual capability of the backbone while avoiding the need to train a separate encoder-decoder latent space.

Two transformer components are widened to support the joint latent (Fig. ):

1

2

The initial patchify projection is expanded so that its input depth grows from $16+K$ to $16+16+K$ , where $K$ denotes the number of conditioning channels (conditional image and binary mask latent). The first $16+K$ channels reuse the pretrained weights directly, while the additional $16$ corresponding to the velocity latent are zero-initialized. So the model can start the training stage without losing the base prediction ability.Patch Embedding Input.

The final projection layer mapping tokens back to patch space is widened from an output dimension of $16$ to $32$ . The RGB channels reuse the pretrained weights, while the velocity channels are initialized to zero.

This zero initialization scheme preserves the pretrained model behavior at initialization: the RGB branch is initially identical to the original pretrained model, while the velocity branch remains inactive at the beginning of the joint supervised fine-tuning. We empirically explored architectures with separate denoisers and explicit cross-attention bridges, but found that a single shared denoiser sampled along one trajectory already maintains strong causal consistency between RGB and velocity while being substantially simpler for training and inference.Output Head.

3.4

The dual-head model is fine-tuned on two complementary datasets.

1) High-fidelity Houdini simulations of smoke, fire, and explosion scenes rendered together with dense ground-truth Eulerian velocity fields, which provide clean $(\text{RGB},\mathbf{v})$ supervision as illustrated in Fig.  and anchor the velocity head to physically plausible fluid behavior. Please refer to § and Appendix  for more details on the dataset construction.

2) A curated collection of in-the-wild fluid videos supplies appearance diversity, including lighting, materials, scales, and camera motion, which is difficult to produce in simulation and is critical for generalization to real-world inputs.Training Data.

3

4

B.2

Here we show two examples of simulated scenes: the rendered RGB frames, velocity field frames and visualized velocity directions in our Houdini-constructed dataset.

Figure 3: Data visualization.

Both heads are trained jointly with a single flow-matching objective  over the combined $32$ -channel latent. Let $\mathbf{z}_{1}=[\mathbf{z}_{1}^{\mathrm{rgb}};\mathbf{z}_{1}^{\mathrm{vel}}]$ denote the encoded clean target, let $\mathbf{z}_{0}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{I})$ be the noise sampled from a standard Gaussian distribution, and let $\mathbf{z}_{t}=(1-t)\mathbf{z}_{0}+t\mathbf{z}_{1}$ be the linear interpolation. The denoiser $\mathbf{v}_{\Theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t,\mathbf{c},\mathbf{y})$ is trained to predict the conditional flow $\mathbf{z}_{1}-\mathbf{z}_{0}$ viaJoint Flow-Matching Objective.(; )

Lipman et al., 2022

Wan et al., 2025

$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SFT}}=\mathbb{E}_{t,\,\mathbf{z}_{0},\,\mathbf{z}_{1}}\Big[m\,\big\|\mathbf{v}_{\Theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t,\mathbf{c},\mathbf{y})-(\mathbf{z}_{1}-\mathbf{z}_{0})\big\|^{2}\Big],$ (3)

where $\mathbf{c}$ denotes the image-conditioning input and $\mathbf{y}$ the text prompt. The per-channel mask $m$ equals $1$ for all channels on samples with velocity supervision (the Houdini subset), and equals $0$ only on RGB channels for samples without velocity targets (the in-the-wild subset). Consequently, the velocity head is trained exclusively on simulation data, while the RGB head benefits from the full appearance distribution. In practice, the two datasets are interleaved at a fixed mixing ratio during training.

3.5

First stage fine-tuning yields a model capable of jointly generating an RGB stream and a plausible velocity field stream in a single forward pass. However, the physical quality of generated samples still exhibits suboptimal performance. Many samples will remain visibly degenerate, as it is hard for the model to simply learn the physical process  – especially for highly unconstrained and complex fluid dynamics.

Consequently, we employ a post-training stage to reduce this variability by aligning the generator with the physics-informed reward, through the preference optimization.()

Bansal et al., 2025

We assign each generated sample a scalar reward

$R(\tilde{\mathbf{z}})\in[0,1]$ , defined as a convex combination of thirteen component rewards. Each component acts as a soft indicator of physical plausibility. Eleven components are computed directly from the decoded velocity field and fall into three categories:Physics-Informed Reward.

terms: including direction diversity, temporal coherence, and multi-scale gradient detail, which encourage non-trivial and temporally stable flow structure;Structural

terms: including activity naturalness, temporal dynamics balance, life-cycle envelope, and radial outflow, which encourage agreement with the empirical distribution of Houdini simulations;Statistical

terms: including advection self-consistency, Q-criterion diversity, direction-field enstrophy , and Kolmogorov inertial range compliance , which encourage classical properties of turbulent flow.Physical()

Hunt et al., 1988

()

Kraichnan, 1974

As illustrated in Fig. , this composite reward reliably separates faithful fluid dynamics from unrealistic ones, and serves as the criterion for preference pairs in the post-training stage.

4

For each conditioning pair $(\mathbf{c}_{i},\mathbf{y}_{i})$ drawn from the first stage training corpus, we sample $N{=}4$ candidates using independent random seeds. Since each sample is itself a $32$ -channel video latent containing both RGB and velocity streams generated by the same denoiser, the aforementioned reward can be evaluated directly on the model output without any additional motion estimator. Within each candidate set, we construct a preference pair $(\tilde{\mathbf{z}}^{+},\tilde{\mathbf{z}}^{-})$ using the highest and lowest reward samples, respectively, and discard pairs whose reward gap is below a threshold $\delta$ .Preference Pairs and Flow-DPO Objective.

distinguishes plausible from implausible fluid dynamics. Four samples (left: RGB frame; right: visualized velocity field) from the same input annotated with their reward values. High reward samples exhibit organized, turbulent flow structure with rich directional diversity and coherent vortical motion, while low reward samples show collapsed velocity fields that do not correspond to realistic fluid behavior.Figure 4: Physics-informed reward

Given a pair at diffusion time $t$ , let $\mathbf{u}^{\star}_{t}$ denote the flow-matching target from Eq. , and let $\mathbf{v}_{\Theta}$ and $\mathbf{v}_{\Theta_{\mathrm{ref}}}$ denote the trainable and reference denoisers, respectively. Following the MSE-based Diffusion-DPO formulation  adapted to flow matching , we define the per-sample preference residual as:

3

()

Wallace et al., 2024

(; )

Rafailov et al., 2023

Liu et al., 2025a

$\Delta(\tilde{\mathbf{z}})=\big\|\mathbf{v}_{\Theta}(\tilde{\mathbf{z}},t)-\mathbf{u}^{\star}_{t}\big\|^{2}-\big\|\mathbf{v}_{\Theta_{\mathrm{ref}}}(\tilde{\mathbf{z}},t)-\mathbf{u}^{\star}_{t}\big\|^{2},$ (4)

and optimize

$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DPO}}=-\mathbb{E}_{(\tilde{\mathbf{z}}^{+},\tilde{\mathbf{z}}^{-}),\,t}\;\log\sigma\ \Big(-\tfrac{1}{2}\beta\big(\Delta(\tilde{\mathbf{z}}^{+})-\Delta(\tilde{\mathbf{z}}^{-})\big)\Big),$ (5)

where $\sigma(\cdot)$ denotes the logistic sigmoid function and $\beta$ is a temperature parameter. The objective decreases when the trainable model improves its prediction error on preferred samples more than on dispreferred samples, relative to the reference model. During this stage, we optimize $\mathbf{v}_{\Theta}$ using low-rank adaptation (LoRA ) applied to attention and FFN linear layers while freezing the backbone parameters. The reference model $\mathbf{v}_{\Theta_{\mathrm{ref}}}$ is obtained implicitly by disabling the LoRA adapters during inference.()

Hu et al., 2022

4

We evaluate our method’s ability to generate visually compelling and physically plausible fluid phenomena. Our experiments are designed to answer three key questions: 1) Does our dual-head architecture and training pipeline improve the physical fidelity of generated fluids compared to state-of-the-art video models? 2) How do the joint velocity prediction and the subsequent DPO post-training individually contribute to the final performance? Please refer to our project page for more video results and comparisons.

while the model after the Joint Supervised Fine-tuning (FluidGen w/o DPO) generates physically coherent dynamics.

4.1

As aforementioned in §, our training dataset is consist of two sources. In detail, we constructed $13125$ videos from Houdini simulation, 15570 real-world videos from FluidNexus dataset , and curated $6521$ videos from the real-world footage. In total resulting in a training set of more than $35$ K videos. Each video is resized to the desired $480\times 832$ resolution, for portrait videos we equally pad black pixels on left and right to match the size ratio. Each video has $81$ frames for training.Datasets.

Our model is initialized from the pretrained Wan-2.1-14B image-to-video diffusion model . During the joint Supervised Fine-Tuning (FT) stage, we train the widened transformer blocks for 7000 iterations with a batch size of 1 and a learning rate of 1e-5. For the Velocity-Aware DPO stage, we freeze the backbone and train LoRA adapters (rank $r=64$ ) for 500 iterations using a preference margin threshold $\delta=0.05$ and temperature $\beta=500$ . Training was conducted on 8 NVIDIA H100 GPUs. The codebase is built on DiffSynth  and Epipolar-DPO .Implementation Details.()

We evaluate along two axes using two benchmarks. The benchmark  provides multiview captures of real fluids with ground-truth reference frames; on $15$ randomly selected sequences, we report PSNR and SSIM for per-frame reconstruction fidelity, LPIPS  for perceptual similarity, and FVD  for distributional distance over spatiotemporal features. To evaluate general video quality on in-the-wild image inputs, we additionally report VBench  scores on $20$ selected images along three dimensions relevant to fluid synthesis: Imaging Quality (per-frame visual fidelity), Aesthetic Quality (perceptual appeal), and Subject Consistency (temporal stability of foreground content, critical for coherent advection without flickering).Metrics.FluidNexus()

4.2

Tab.  reports results on the FluidNexus benchmark. We note that the FluidNexus baseline used here is an upgraded multi-view variant of the original method, which consumes multiple synchronized views as input and requires several hours of per-scene optimization to reconstruct the underlying fluid representation. Despite this substantially heavier setup, it still fails to recover some fine level turbulent details such as small scale eddies and high-frequency boundary roll-ups, which is reflected in its lower SSIM and notably higher LPIPS and FVD compared to our method. Wan2.1-I2V-14B, on the other hand, struggles to produce faithful fluid dynamics from a single image and frequently introduces appearance artifacts such as color shifting and texture drift over time. In contrast, our model, conditioned on only a single image and run in a single forward pass, achieves the best or on par metrics with the multi-view FluidNexus baseline, indicating that our generated complex fluid dynamics closely match the ground-truth captures.

2

To verify that our training stages do not compromise general generative capability on in-the-wild content, we evaluate our method using VBench metrics in Tab. . Our final model matches or surpasses the Wan2.1-I2V-14B base model on all three reported dimensions, with clear gains in Imaging Quality and Subject Consistency. The improvement in Subject Consistency is particularly meaningful for fluid scenes: it indicates that the auxiliary velocity stream regularizes the RGB stream toward temporally coherent advection, mitigating the flickering and shifting artifacts observed in the base model. Together, the two benchmarks show that our method substantially improves physical fidelity.

4.3

Fig.  shows visual comparisons against ground-truth captures from the FluidNexus benchmark. The upgraded FluidNexus baseline recovers the coarse shape and trajectory of the smoke plume, but its reconstructions after several hours of optimization still appear overly smooth and lose some fine-scale wisps and turbulent filaments visible in the ground truth, indicating the disadvantage of relying only on the manually defined physical approximation laws.

Wan2.1-I2V-14B produces motion that diverges from the reference dynamics and exhibits noticeable color drift and appearance inconsistency over time. In contrast, our method reproduces both the global rising trajectory and fine turbulent structures, including thin tendrils at the plume boundary, while requiring only a single forward pass from a single input image.

We further compare against Wan2.1-I2V-14B on in-the-wild inputs in Fig. , where our full model produces more vivid and physically realistic fluid dynamics. Finally, our model supports several downstream applications, including fluid-related visual effects (Fig. ) via keyframe control (images are generated by NanoBanana 2 ), velocity field prediction (Fig. ) from input videos using RePaint-style  conditional sampling, and fluid simulation driven by the generated 3D velocity fields (Fig. ). More results are provided in Appendix  and on our project page.

The stage I fine-tuning achieves significant gain compared to the basemodel: FluidGen w/o DPO improves PSNR from $22.50$ to $31.52$ and reduces FVD from $569.7$ to $192.1$ over the base model, while improving Subject Consistency on VBench ( $0.8929\rightarrow 0.9383$ ).

We attribute this improvement to our curated training corpus of high-fidelity Houdini simulations and in-the-wild fluid videos, which exposes the model to the turbulent dynamics largely absent from the base model’s pretraining distribution.Joint Supervised Fine-Tuning.

DPO trades a small amount of reconstruction fidelity for noticeably better perceptual quality. FluidNexus metrics remain on par with the FT-only model, while VBench Imaging Quality improves significantly and Aesthetic Quality slightly. The slight drop in Subject Consistency ( $0.9383\rightarrow 0.9350$ ) is expected: the preference signal favors higher-energy, more turbulent motion. Qualitatively (Fig. ), the FT+DPO model (FluidGen) produces richer fine-scale details and more vivid fire and smoke motion than FluidGen w/o DPO. Please refer to our project page for better visualization.Velocity-Aware DPO.

5

5

We present FluidGen, a framework for synthesizing physically plausible fluid dynamics directly within a video diffusion model, bridging the gap between the rich appearance priors of generative models and the dynamic constraints of classical fluid solvers. By augmenting a pretrained video diffusion transformer with a dual-head architecture, our model jointly predicts RGB pixels and an underlying 3D velocity field, capturing complex fluid dynamics without authored 3D scenes or explicit simulators at inference.

Our two-stage training pipeline first jointly fine-tunes the model with dense physical supervision from high-fidelity Houdini simulations alongside the visual diversity of in-the-wild videos, then applies a velocity-aware preference optimization stage that uses the model’s native velocity predictions to compute a physics-informed reward over structural, statistical, and fluid properties, aligning the generator toward turbulent, coherent, and physically sound motion.

While our method focuses on volumetric fluids such as smoke, fire, and explosions, the core idea of embedding interpretable physical representations into generative latents points toward a broader paradigm for physics-aware synthesis. Future work could extend the dual-head approach to other physical systems such as liquids or elastic materials, or expose the predicted velocity fields as a direct control handle for artists. Our results demonstrate that with the right internal representations and alignment strategies, large-scale video models can natively master complex physical dynamics.

Appendix B

B.1

Let $\mathbf{v}_{t}(x,y)=(v_{x},v_{y},v_{z})$ denote the per-pixel 3D velocity field at frame $t$ decoded from the velocity stream of a generated sample $\tilde{\mathbf{z}}$ via the inverse transformation of Eq. . We write $\rho_{t}=\|\mathbf{v}_{t}\|$ for the speed magnitude and $\hat{\mathbf{u}}_{t}=\mathbf{v}_{t}/\rho_{t}$ for the unit-direction field, and set it to zero when $\rho_{t}$ falls below a small numerical floor value. At each frame we define an active region $\mathcal{A}_{t}=\{(x,y):\rho_{t}(x,y)>\tau_{\rho}\}$ that filters out near static background pixels, where $\tau_{\rho}=\alpha_{a}S$ with $S$ the encoding scale of Eq.  and $\alpha_{a}$ a fixed fraction.

We also use the normalized R-channel $R_{t}\in[0,1]$ of the encoded velocity image directly for temporal-difference statistics. The symbols $\kappa_{\bullet}$ , $\mu_{\bullet}$ , and $\sigma_{\bullet}$ denote scalar hyper-parameters; their values are calibrated once on a small held-out set of Houdini-simulated and curated in-the-wild clips, and are listed at the end of this section.Notation.

1

1

In total, we compute eleven reward components (Tab. ), which act on the velocity stream and fall into three groups.Reward components.

3

Structural terms target the spatial and temporal organization of the direction field:

•

$R_{\mathrm{div}}$ penalizes direction collapse via the per-component variance of $\hat{\mathbf{u}}$ ,

•

$R_{\mathrm{tc}}$ measures the temporal Pearson correlation of the spatial gradients of $\hat{\mathbf{u}}$ ,

•

$R_{\mathrm{msd}}$ rewards consistent gradient richness at scales $s\in\{1,2,4\}$ so that the flow shows structured detail at all scales rather than blur or pure noise.

Statistical terms match the empirical distribution of Houdini simulations:

•

$R_{\mathrm{act}}$ on the mean active-pixel fraction $\bar{f}_{a}=\mathbb{E}_{t}[|\mathcal{A}_{t}|/HW]$ ,

•

$R_{\mathrm{tdb}}$ on the mean temporal change of $R_{t}$ ,

•

$R_{\mathrm{lc}}$ on the global rise-peak-decay envelope of per-frame energy $e_{t}=\mathbb{E}_{x,y}[\rho_{t}]$ via a weighted combination of peak position, monotone rise, monotone decay, second-derivative smoothness, and contrast sub-scores $\{s_{k}\}$ ,

•

$R_{\mathrm{ro}}$ on the speed weighted cosine alignment between the image plane velocity $(v_{x},v_{z})$ and the radial direction $\mathbf{r}$ from an automatically estimated source, averaged over early frames.

Physical terms encode classical criterions of turbulent flow:

•

$R_{\mathrm{adv}}$ checks one-step advection self-consistency through a bilinear warp $\mathcal{W}$ of $\mathbf{v}_{t}$ along $(v_{x},v_{z})$ ,

•

$R_{Q}$ rewards a spread of the Q-criterion of $\hat{\mathbf{u}}$ , $Q_{\hat{u}}=\Omega_{12}^{2}-(S_{11}^{2}+S_{22}^{2}+2S_{12}^{2})$ , where $S$ and $\Omega$ are the symmetric and antisymmetric parts of $\nabla\hat{\mathbf{u}}$  ,()

Hunt et al., 1988

•

$R_{\mathrm{ens}}$ rewards the enstrophy of the directional field vorticity $\omega_{\hat{u}}=\partial_{x}\hat{u}_{z}-\partial_{z}\hat{u}_{x}$ on $\mathcal{A}_{t}$ ,

•

item.title: DLSS 5 与 3D 引导神经渲染：NVIDIA 给游戏开发者的新工具 ｜ What's New for Game Developers: DLSS 5 with 3D-Guided Neural Rendering, NVIDIA ACE Updates, and New RTX Kit Capabilities
item.description:
一句话：DLSS 5 引入 3D 引导的神经渲染，ACE 与 RTX Kit 同步更新。

要点：

  • DLSS 5 用 3D 场景信息引导超分，而不仅依赖 2D 帧
  • ACE 更新带来更强的端侧角色 AI 能力
  • RTX Kit 新增若干渲染与工具链特性

为什么值得看：厂商一手资料，直接对应引擎集成工作——超分与 AI 角色是当前最先落地到产线的两项 AI 能力。

中文摘要：NVIDIA 开发者博客汇总了面向游戏开发者的最新更新：DLSS 5 引入「3D 引导的神经渲染」，用场景几何信息而不只是 2D 帧特征来引导超分，从而在边缘与细节上更稳定；同时更新了 NVIDIA ACE（端侧角色 AI 框架）与 RTX Kit 的多项能力。这篇是官方一手技术说明，适合直接拿去评估引擎侧的集成成本。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：NVIDIA Developer（English）

Content Creation / Rendering

What’s New for Game Developers: DLSS 5 with 3D-Guided Neural Rendering, NVIDIA ACE Updates, and New RTX Kit Capabilities

Sep 22, 2026

By

Phillip Singh

L

T

F

R

E

NVIDIA DLSS 5

The technology operates on a strict one-frame-in, one-frame-out model with game-engine motion vectors for deterministic, temporally stable output running locally on GeForce RTX 50 Series GPUs at up to 4K.

Developers gain granular controls including model selection, Structure Intensity and Tone Intensity adjustments, semantic AI masking, and engine-level masking to direct the neural rendering effect across scenes.

NVIDIA ACE

The NVIDIA In-Game Inferencing SDK adds RTX Spark support, Gemma4 integration, a Stable Diffusion plugin, and llama.cpp performance enhancements for local AI deployment alongside graphics.

RTX Mega Geometry 2.0

Next Steps

DLSS 5 article

NVIDIA In-Game Inference SDK

RTX Mega Geometry SDK

Powered by NVIDIA Nemotron. AI-generated content may summarize information incompletely. Verify important information.

Learn more

introduces DLSS 3D-Guided Neural Rendering and granular controls that help game developers add lifelike lighting and material detail while preserving their artistic intent. We also look at updates to , RTX Mega Geometry 2.0, and RTX Kit across character AI, high-density geometry, and rendering workflows.

NVIDIA DLSS 5

NVIDIA ACE

This post covers:

How DLSS 5 uses the game engine’s rendered frame as the foundation for 3D-Guided Neural Rendering and how NBA 2K27’s developer, Visual Concepts, uses DLSS 5 to enhance materials and lighting while preserving scanned facial geometry

New NVIDIA ACE speech and inferencing capabilities

RTX Kit SDK updates including RTX Mega Geometry 2.0 support for streaming continuous level-of-detail clusters

Video 1. Edward Liu, director of applied deep learning research at NVIDIA, and Gabriele Leone, director of content technology, explain how the technology and its developer controls work, including how DLSS 5 is designed to remain grounded in game-engine data, maintain frame-to-frame stability, and give developers control over the final output

DLSS 5 with 3D-guided neural rendering extends the graphics pipeline as a final neural-rendering stage. It uses the game engine’s rendered frame, including its artist-authored geometry, textures, and lighting buffers as an unyielding foundation.

The engine frame defines what must remain, while developers direct what may change. Using frame color and motion vectors, the model is designed to add lifelike lighting and material detail while preserving scene structure, character identity, and artistic intent.

Figure 1. DLSS 5 is trained to preserve artistic intent by maintaining character identity, scene and lighting semantics, and camera composition

Built specifically for real-time 3D rendering, DLSS 5 delivers deterministic, temporally stable output. Operating on a strict one-frame-in, one-frame-out model with game-engine motion vectors keeps results consistent as players move. The compact, specialized model runs locally on a single GeForce RTX 50 Series GPU at up to 4K.

Figure 2. DLSS 5 processes a strict one-frame-in, one-frame-out sequence for real-time frame-by-frame stability, instead of processing multi-frame chunks like offline generative models

Controls and integration for developers

Art direction:

Targeted application:

Input quality:

Figure 3. DLSS 5 puts art-direction tools in developers’ hands, including model selection, Structure Intensity and Tone Intensity controls, semantic AI masking, and engine-level masking

DLSS 5 is available now in NBA 2K27, developed by Visual Concepts and published by 2K, for all GeForce RTX 50 Series desktop and laptop GPUs. GeForce NOW Ultimate members can also experience it when streaming from NVIDIA-operated GeForce RTX 5080-powered gaming rigs in the cloud. Visual Concepts uses overall tone and style controls plus a per-pixel uplift control mask to fine-tune character detail while respecting player likenesses.

Video 2. Hear from NBA2K developer, Visual Concepts, on how they tuned NVIDIA DLSS 5 to help achieve a more lifelike NBA experience in 2K27

In , DLSS 5 preserves scanned facial geometry while enhancing skin subsurface scattering, light transmission through hair and ears, and contact shadows.NBA 2K27

For more details about DLSS 5, check out our . Sign up to be notified for DLSS updates for developers .

DLSS 5 article

here

NVIDIA ACE offers ready-to-integrate AI models and tools for building knowledgeable, interactive, and conversational in-game characters. The latest updates expand the speech pipeline and inference framework, making it easier for developers to run AI in their games.

To run these models locally alongside game graphics, the NVIDIA In-Game Inferencing (NVIGI) SDK delivers a high-performance, streamlined path for deploying local AI models through in-process C++ execution.

Key Release Highlights

NVIDIA Nemotron Speech 3.5 Streaming

Qwen3 TTS

NVIDIA In-Game Inference SDK Updates

RTX Spark Support (Developer Preview)

Expanded Model Support

New Plugins & Samples

Performance Enhancements

llama.cpp

Access NVIDIA In-Game Inference SDK .

here

Figure 5. NVIDIA In-Game Inferencing provides a unified plugin architecture for running AI models locally alongside graphics workloads

NVIDIA RTX Kit is a suite of rendering technologies for training and deploying AI in shaders, path tracing detailed scenes at game-ready performance, and rendering lifelike digital characters. The latest SDK updates expand support for high-density geometry, neural texture workflows, lighting, and texture filtering.

Figure 6. Scene from the RTX Mega Geometry sample app using Zorah assets highlighting the impact of Mega Geometry

RTX Kit 2026.3 updates include:

RTX Character Rendering 1.4 improves far-field hair BCSDF sampling and energy conservation

RTX Dynamic Illumination 3.1 adds DLSS Ray Reconstruction integration and some improvements to ReSTIR PT

RTX Neural Texture Compression 0.10 beta adds support for the Microsoft DirectX 12 Agility SDK preview with Linear Algebra, enabling RTX Tensor Core acceleration for neural texture decompression in DirectX shaders. It also adds Windows ARM64 support.

RTX Neural Shading 1.4 adds support for the latest DirectX Linear Algebra preview toolchain and updates its shader and sample dependencies.

RTX Texture Filtering 1.3 introduces Collaborative Texture Filtering, a technique designed to improve magnification quality for stochastic texture filtering. It also adds Windows ARM64 support.

In addition to the RTX Kit updates, has been updated to 2.0 which adds support for streaming of continuous level-of-detail clusters for high-density meshes. The scale of detail is demonstrated in a newly released textured glTF version of Zorah.

RTX Mega Geometry SDK

Figure 7. NVIDIA RTX Mega Geometry organizes detailed meshes into clusters so ray-traced scenes can adapt geometric detail efficiently

RTX Mega Geometry is coming soon to Gears of War: E-Day, offering GeForce games higher frame rates, higher levels of image quality, and with even more responsive controls. We sat down with the Coalition’s Studio Technical Director, Kate Rayner, and Rendering Lead, Mike Perzel to learn more about Gears of War: E-Day’s integrations of RTX Mega Geometry and DLSS.

Video 3. RTX: Inside the Game | Gears of War: E-Day with DLSS 4.5 and RTX Mega Geometry

item.title: OrTeN：地形与线扫相机轨迹的联合神经逆渲染 ｜ OrTeN: Neural Inverse Graphics for Joint Terrain and Line-scan Camera Trajectory Reconstruction
item.description:
一句话：用神经逆渲染同时恢复地形几何与线扫相机的运动轨迹。

要点：

  • 线扫相机数据缺少常规帧间对应关系
  • 把地形与相机轨迹放进同一优化框架联合求解
  • MIT 团队，面向测绘与重建场景

为什么值得看：逆渲染从「恢复物体」走向「恢复场景 + 相机」，对扫描式资产与地形管线有参考价值。

中文摘要：OrTeN 来自 MIT，处理的是线扫相机（line-scan）采集场景下的逆渲染问题：这类数据没有传统相机的帧间几何一致性，常规 SfM 与 NeRF 流程难以直接套用。作者把地形几何与相机轨迹放进同一个神经逆渲染框架里联合优化，从而在缺少显式对应的条件下同时恢复场景结构与采集轨迹。对测绘、扫描与地形重建类管线有直接参考意义。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

License: CC BY 4.0

arXiv:2610.24075v1 [cs.CV] 16 Oct 2026

OrTeN: Neural Inverse Graphics for Joint Terrain and Line-scan Camera Trajectory Reconstruction

Josef Biberstein

Massachusetts Institute of Technology

Affiliation: Email:

jxb@mit.edu

Sertac Karaman

Massachusetts Institute of Technology

Affiliation: Email:

sertac@mit.edu

Abstract

Digital terrain maps (DTMs) are used for landing site selection, terrain-relative navigation, and geological analysis in planetary exploration.

Existing state-of-practice reconstruction techniques for creating DTMs from satellite imagery use multi-view stereo, requiring complex pipelines for dealing with camera error, changing illumination, and images with limited disparity.

This work introduces Orbital Terrain Networks (OrTeN), a DTM construction method that uses neural inverse rendering to jointly optimize a textured height map and orbital camera corrections from line-scan satellite images.

OrTeN operates directly on calibrated line-scan images with pixel values expressed as radiance factor (I/F) and corrects both broad trajectory pose inconsistencies and high-frequency pointing jitter jointly with surface reconstruction during training.

Surface-projected patch normalized cross-correlation (NCC) enforces consistency between observations of the same terrain, refining an initial rough reconstruction.

A semi-empirical reflectance model and shadow rendering are used to fit surface appearance from multi-date imagery with differing solar illumination.

OrTeN requires only calibrated line-scan images and initial camera poses and does not use any structural priors including ranging/depth measurements or initial rough DTMs.

OrTeN is evaluated on four planetary imagery datasets.

Aligned terrain RMSEs are 2.35 m at Jezero Crater, 2.82 m at Gale Crater, 16.18 m at Olympus Mons, and 0.43 m at McGetchin Crater.

: Figure 1Summary of OrTeN DTM reconstructions.

OrTeN produces high-quality digital terrain maps (DTMs) from multi-view imagery without structural priors.

Combining bundle adjustment, normalized cross-correlation, a semi-empirical photometric model, and geometric shadows allows OrTeN to reconstruct terrain reliably across multiple different instruments, planetary bodies, and lighting conditions.

1

Digital terrain maps (DTMs) are an important supporting data product in space exploration.

Accurate DTMs enable landing site selection and terrain-relative navigation (TRN) during entry, descent, and landing for modern autonomous space exploration missions such as Mars 2020 .

They also provide the topographic context needed to interpret planetary landforms and their geological history .[, ]

11

21

[]

29

Current pipelines for orbital DTM production used in the space science community rely on classical multi-view stereo (MVS) techniques to infer terrain structure—features are detected and matched between radiometrically calibrated images, bundle adjustment (BA) is performed to refine camera poses, and stereo correspondences are triangulated to produce a 3D terrain model .

MVS can produce high-quality maps suitable for mission operations, but a number of challenges inherent to both MVS itself and its application to satellite datasets complicate the process.

These challenges include the difficulty of getting reliable feature matches in the presence of shadows or low-texture regions, the line-scan geometry of most satellite images not admitting the epipolar constraints assumed by traditional MVS, and transients like dust storms or seasonal changes that alter the appearance of the terrain.

Correcting for these effects can require labor-intensive preprocessing and careful manual intervention, making MVS pipelines cumbersome to use.[, ]

22

7

Neural inverse graphics provides a methodology for scene reconstruction that can address many of the challenges faced by classical MVS pipelines.

For instance, satellite adaptations of neural radiance fields (NeRFs) model changing illumination and acquisition appearance while recovering scene geometry .

However, full 3D volumetric representations admit degenerate solutions—for instance, all scene density concentrated in front of cameras, explaining the observed images without recovering the true geometry—which can be particularly problematic when working with low-disparity orbital imagery where depth cues are weak.

While structural priors can help mitigate these degeneracies , these measurements are not always available or reliable.[, , ]

15

26

27

[, ]

38

36

OrTeN mitigates the shortcomings of classical MVS and volumetric neural reconstruction by optimizing a textured height map directly.

Critically, OrTeN requires no structural priors to achieve accurate terrain reconstruction from images and approximate camera poses.

It builds on Neural Terrain Maps (NTM) , adding direct bundle adjustment of line-scan camera extrinsics jointly with training, a semi-empirical photometric model, and geometric shadow modeling.

The contributions of this work are:[]

8

1.

A pipeline for creating accurate DTMs through differentiable volume rendering of textured height maps including a first-order approximation of distance to the height map along the ray to improve performance at oblique angles.

2.

Joint terrain and line-scan camera optimization, including smooth trajectory adjustment and high-frequency jitter removal, and a semi-empirical, spatially varying photometric model including geometric shadow modeling with an image-space prior.

3.

An evaluation on four Mars and Moon scenes with varied relief and illumination, using the Context Camera (CTX) and Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera (LROC) Narrow Angle Camera (NAC).

OrTeN achieves aligned height errors below the ground sampling distance (GSD) in three scenes and improves on the tested Ames Stereo Pipeline (ASP) reconstruction in those scenes.

2

DTM creation with MVS.

A number of well-established pipelines exist for creating DTMs from orbital imagery using MVS, including the Ames Stereo Pipeline (ASP), satellite stereo pipeline (s2p), and COLMAP .

All of these methods use feature extraction and matching to constrain camera alignment before performing dense stereo matching to triangulate terrain.

Orbital imagery is often taken by linescan cameras, and therefore integration into standard MVS pipelines requires particular care because each detector line is acquired at a different pose.

This precludes the standard epipolar geometry assumptions used in perspective-camera MVS to make searching for correspondences straightforward.

Linescan epipolar loci are generally curved, so the global rectification used for ideal perspective cameras must be replaced by local or sensor-specific constructions .

ASP can also refine time-varying camera states to correct high-frequency jitter .[, , , ]

4

Illumination changes, common in multi-date satellite data acquisitions, create an additional challenge for traditional MVS approaches.

Shadows and surface reflectance can change between acquisitions even when terrain is static and make feature selection and matching more difficult.

Therefore, masking shadows and other illumination-dependent artifacts is often necessary to improve the robustness of MVS matching.

Shadows can also provide important geometric information which can be exploited in reconstruction, and shape-from-shading methods exploit this to further refine existing DTMs .

OrTeN performs trajectory bundle adjustment, including jitter removal, jointly with training, and uses a semi-empirical photometric model with explicit geometric shadow handling to improve terrain reconstruction.[]

3

Neural reconstruction of orbital imagery.

S-NeRF introduced illumination-aware neural rendering for satellite photogrammetry, and Sat-NeRF added rational polynomial coefficient (RPC) camera support and transient appearance modeling.

EO-NeRF built on these previous methods to establish a baseline framework for general-purpose scenes on Earth by incorporating geometrically consistent shadows with learned radiometric and camera corrections and transient appearance embeddings .

Season-NeRF separated seasonal appearance from Sun and viewing geometry , while a semi-empirical bidirectional reflectance distribution function (BRDF) was incorporated into BRDF-NeRF .

Other methods address the geometry directly through depth supervision, surface constraints, or gravity-aligned and coarse-to-fine regularization .

Gaussian splatting for satellite imagery has also emerged as an alternative to methods utilizing volume rendering, offering efficient, high-quality neural scene representations .[, , ]

More recent works have begun to focus on large-scale terrain reconstruction using neural inverse graphics.

Both NTM and LNEM introduce direct rendering of linescan imagery for terrain reconstruction .

For descent imagery, de Almeida . incorporate a neural height field into reconstruction from wide-angle cameras .

OrTeN eschews structural priors and retains the explicitly parameterized terrain representation, as is done in NTM, and adds ray-distance-based opacity and improved regularization with normalized cross-correlation (NCC).

Its coarse-to-fine optimization follows the principle established by BARF: low-frequency structure should stabilize camera alignment before fine appearance is exposed .[, ]
