Key elements of the OrTeN pipeline.

OrTeN represents the scene with a height field $h_{\theta}:\mathbb{R}^{2}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ in a local east–north–up (ENU) frame and learned surface appearance ().

The surface is $\mathbf{x}=(x,y,h_{\theta}(x,y))$ , and unit-direction camera rays are given by $\mathbf{r}(t)=\mathbf{o}+t\mathbf{d}$ .

The origin is constructed as the common look point of all cameras, the horizontal bounds are set by the image footprints on the horizontal plane, enlarged by a factor of 1.5, and the vertical bounds are set by global planetary height limits.

Fig.2

3.1

OrTeN follows the lineage of NeuS, which derives opacity from the decrease of a logistic cumulative distribution function (CDF) along a ray through an implicit surface .

Applying this construction to distance along the ray rather than vertical height residual gives[]

37

$\displaystyle\alpha_{j}$ $\displaystyle=\left[1-\frac{\Phi_{\beta}(q(t_{j+1}))}{\Phi_{\beta}(q(t_{j}))}\right]_{+},$ (1) $\displaystyle T_{j}$ $\displaystyle=\prod_{k(2)

Here $\Phi_{\beta}(q)=(1+e^{-q/\beta})^{-1}$ , $[z]_{+}=\max(z,0)$ , $\alpha_{j}$ is interval opacity, $T_{j}$ is transmittance to that interval, and $w_{j}$ is its rendering weight.

The CDF ratio is evaluated on a log scale to improve numerical stability.

Sampling locations are chosen with a proposal network as is done in Nerfacto .[]

35

To obtain $q$ , the effect of terrain slope and viewing direction on the height residual is considered:

$\displaystyle f(t)$ $\displaystyle=r_{z}(t)-h_{\theta}(\mathbf{r}_{xy}(t)),$ (3) $\displaystyle f^{\prime}(t)$ $\displaystyle=d_{z}-\nabla h_{\theta}(\mathbf{r}_{xy}(t))^{\top}\mathbf{d}_{xy},$ (4) $\displaystyle q(t)$ $\displaystyle=\frac{f(t)}{\max(-f^{\prime}(t),10^{-3})}.$ (5)

Subscripts $xy$ and $z$ select horizontal and vertical components.

For a plane, $q(t)=t_{\star}-t$ when the denominator clamp is inactive, where $t_{\star}$ is the intersection distance.

This formulation ensures the learned width $\beta>0$ has the same metric meaning across terrain slopes and viewing angles.

Height derivatives are calculated by finite differences using a first-order formulation.

3.2

Training uses calibrated scalar radiance factor $I/F=\pi L/F_{\odot}$ images, where $L$ is observed radiance and $F_{\odot}$ is solar irradiance at the body .

Albedo $a_{\psi}$ is aggregated over the ray samples:[, ]

6

32

$A=\sum_{j}w_{j},\qquad\bar{a}=\frac{\sum_{j}w_{j}a_{\psi}(\mathbf{r}_{xy}(\bar{t}_{j}))}{\max(A,10^{-8})},$ (6)

where $\bar{t}_{j}$ is the interval midpoint.

A second network head predicts the spatial Lunar–Lambert mixture $m_{\phi}(x,y)$ , integrated in the same way to give $\bar{m}$ .

The normalized, weighted terrain normal $\mathbf{n}$ is used to compute positive incidence and emission cosines $\mu_{0}=[\mathbf{n}^{\top}\mathbf{s}]_{+}$ and $\mu=[\mathbf{n}^{\top}(-\mathbf{d})]_{+}$ , with $\mathbf{s}$ pointing toward the Sun.

The direct-light factor is

$\displaystyle F(\mu_{0},\mu,m)$ $\displaystyle=(1-m)\mu_{0}+\frac{2m\mu_{0}}{\max(\mu_{0}+\mu,10^{-6})},$ (7) $\displaystyle D$ $\displaystyle=\frac{F(\mu_{0},\mu,\bar{m})}{F(\cos 30^{\circ},1,\bar{m})}.$ (8)

This interpolates between Lambert and Lommel–Seeliger responses .[]

28

Geometric shadows.

Starting from the weighted camera-ray depth, a surface intersection is refined and traced toward the Sun until the ray leaves the scene bounds.

Solar interval opacities $\alpha_{k}^{\odot}$ are converted to visibility using

$V=V_{\rm att}\prod_{k}(1-\alpha_{k}^{\odot}),\qquad V_{\eta}=(1-\eta)V_{\rm att}+\eta V.$ (9)

Here $V_{\rm att}$ smoothly suppresses light on back-facing slopes and is zero when the Sun is below the local horizon.

The startup factor $\eta$ ramps cast shadows in over 500 updates.

Terrain outside the bounds cannot cast shadows in this model.

OrTeN uses a semi-empirical image formation model inspired by EO-NeRF’s shadow-fill and affine brightness approach .

The predicted image for acquisition $i$ is[]

27

$\widehat{y}_{i}=g_{i}\bigl[V_{\eta}D+(1-V_{\eta})a_{\rm amb}(\mathbf{s})\bigr]\bar{a}+b_{i}.$ (10)

The Sun-dependent ambient factor $a_{\rm amb}\in(0,1)$ fills shadows without inheriting the direct-light angular response.

Scalar gains $g_{i}=e^{u_{i}-\bar{u}}$ and offsets absorb acquisition-wide brightness differences, with $\bar{u}=M^{-1}\sum_{i}u_{i}$ fixing the geometric mean gain to one across $M$ acquisitions.

The same image model is used throughout training.

Histogram-valley shadow detection  is adopted to provide an initial image-space shadow estimate at startup.

Only sufficiently dark, distinct pixels are accepted, and mask erosion is applied to remove boundary transients.

For an ordinary rendering batch $\mathcal{B}$ , a regularizer is applied:[]

1

$\mathcal{L}_{\rm shadow}=|\mathcal{B}|^{-1}\sum_{p\in\mathcal{B}}z_{p}V_{p}^{2},$ (11)

where $z_{p}=1$ marks a detected core and $z_{p}=0$ means unknown.

This loss is one-sided, so unlabeled pixels are not treated as either shadow or sunlit.

3.3

A linescan pixel $(\ell,s)$ has nominal origin $\mathbf{o}_{i}^{0}(\ell)$ and direction $\mathbf{d}_{i}^{0}(\ell,s)$ .

Intrinsics and distortion are retained, and corrections are optimized in the local scene frame:

$\displaystyle\mathbf{o}_{i}$ $\displaystyle=\mathbf{o}_{i}^{0}+\Delta\mathbf{p}_{i}(u),$ (12) $\displaystyle\mathbf{d}_{i}$ $\displaystyle=\exp([\Delta\boldsymbol{\omega}_{i}(u)]_{\times})\mathbf{d}_{i}^{0},$ (13) $\displaystyle\Delta\mathbf{p}_{i}(u)$ $\displaystyle=s_{p}\sum_{k=0}^{3}B_{k}(u)\mathbf{P}_{ik},$ (14) $\displaystyle\Delta\boldsymbol{\omega}_{i}(u)$ $\displaystyle=s_{\omega}\left[\sum_{k=0}^{3}B_{k}(u)\mathbf{W}_{ik}+r\mathbf{J}_{i}(u)\right].$ (15)

Here $u\in[0,1]$ is normalized acquisition time and $B_{k}$ are cubic Bernstein functions.

The matrix $[\boldsymbol{\omega}]_{\times}$ implements the cross product with $\boldsymbol{\omega}$ , and its exponential gives the corresponding rotation.

The learned controls $\mathbf{P}_{ik},\mathbf{W}_{ik}$ use physical scales $s_{p},s_{\omega}$ which are constrained by soft priors based on expected trajectory error .

During the refinement phase (), the ramp $r$ introduces angular jitter $\mathbf{J}_{i}$ , represented by a cubic B-spline with 64 intervals per acquisition.

Its global cubic component is removed so it cannot duplicate the smooth trajectory correction.[]

11

3.4

In addition to uniformly sampled rays, at each training iteration $5\times 5$ patches are sampled in source images and projected onto the current height field through the refined cameras.

Each patch point is then projected from the surface into other acquisitions, where bilinear interpolation is used to calculate observed intensities.

For accepted source–neighbor pairs, the normalized cross-correlation loss is

$\mathcal{L}_{\rm NCC}=\mathbb{E}_{P,i,j}\left[1-\frac{\langle P_{i}-\bar{P}_{i},P_{j}-\bar{P}_{j}\rangle}{\|P_{i}-\bar{P}_{i}\|_{2}\,\|P_{j}-\bar{P}_{j}\|_{2}}\right].$ (16)

Here $P_{i},P_{j}$ contain the observed patch intensities and $\bar{P}_{i},\bar{P}_{j}$ are their means.

$\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ is the inner product.

Invalid, occluded, low-contrast, and nearly parallel view pairs are rejected, and up to three of the best eligible neighbors are retained per source patch.

NCC is active in both roughing and refinement ().

Training progresses from images downsampled by $4\times$ to $2\times$ , then to native resolution.

Active encoding levels are adjusted to approximately match the current image resolution.

There are two training stages: roughing and refinement.

Roughing ends when terrain and camera motion stabilize or the roughing update limit is reached.

Let $s_{y}=\sqrt{\mathbb{E}_{\rm train}[y^{2}]}$ be the RMS brightness of all training pixels.

The rendering loss is

$\mathcal{L}_{I/F}=\mathbb{E}_{p\in\mathcal{B}}\left[(\widehat{y}_{p}-y_{p})^{2}/s_{y}^{2}\right].$ (17)

Albedo starts exactly at $s_{y}$ , ambient at 0.2, and gains and offsets at one and zero.

The remaining surface and appearance penalties are

$\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\rm bend}$ $\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}}\left[s_{h}^{2}\|\mathbf{H}_{s_{h}}h_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})\|_{F}^{2}\right],$ (18) $\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\rm width}$ $\displaystyle=\log\bigl(1+(\beta/g_{0})^{2}\bigr),$ (19) $\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\rm radio}$ $\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{i}\left[((u_{i}-\bar{u})/0.1)^{2}+(b_{i}/0.01)^{2}\right],$ (20) $\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\rm amb}$ $\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{s}}\left[\bigl[\operatorname{logit}a_{\rm amb}(\mathbf{s})-\log 9\bigr]_{+}^{2}\right].$ (21)

Here $\mathbf{H}_{s_{h}}$ is the finite-difference Hessian.

In order, these losses regularize surface bending, control the rendering width, enforce radiometric calibration, and constrain the ambient illumination.

The fixed scale $g_{0}$ is the initial training-image GSD.

The optional ambient penalty acts only when the ambient factor exceeds 0.9.

Camera regularization penalizes the dimensionless trajectory controls and, in refinement, the sampled jitter motion.

Let $\mathbf{c}_{i}(u)$ concatenate the trajectory position and rotation corrections divided by $s_{p}$ and $s_{\omega}$ .

Its second derivative penalizes trajectory curvature:

$\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\rm camera}={}$ $\displaystyle\lambda_{C}\mathbb{E}_{i,k}(\|\mathbf{P}_{ik}\|_{2}^{2}+\|\mathbf{W}_{ik}\|_{2}^{2})$ $\displaystyle+\lambda_{C}\mathbf{1}_{r>0}\mathbb{E}_{i,u}\|\mathbf{J}_{i}(u)\|_{2}^{2}$ $\displaystyle+\lambda_{K}\mathbb{E}_{i}\int_{0}^{1}\|\mathbf{c}_{i}^{\prime\prime}(u)\|_{2}^{2}du.$ (22)

Here $W_{lj}$ is proposal level $l$ ’s total mass in bins overlapping final interval $j$ .

Four lunar and Martian datasets were selected for their varied terrain and illumination and the availability of reference DTMs.

Jezero Crater, Gale Crater, and Olympus Mons each contain fifteen $1024\times 1024$ CTX crops.

McGetchin Crater contains ten LROC NAC crops of the same size.

Images are calibrated to I/F using the Integrated Software for Imagers and Spectrometers (ISIS) and paired with initial line-scan camera states.

4.2

Metrics for each scene are calculated over a fixed reference footprint that is covered by at least five initial cameras.

To resolve the gauge freedom inherent in the bundle adjustment process, reconstructed DTMs are aligned to the reference DTM using a six-degree-of-freedom rigid transformation.

No scale change, local warping, or separate alignment for different metrics is applied.

For aligned height errors $e_{p}=\widehat{h}_{a}(p)-h_{\rm ref}(p)$ on $N$ valid posts, the metrics are

$\mathrm{RMSE}_{a}=\sqrt{N^{-1}\sum_{p}e_{p}^{2}},\qquad\mathrm{MAE}_{a}=N^{-1}\sum_{p}|e_{p}|.$ (25)

The subscript $a$ denotes metrics applied to rigidly aligned DTMs, so these scores measure relative shape rather than absolute geolocation.

Slope is evaluated using a local quadratic surface fit calculated over a $9\times 9$ sliding window.

This follows established practices in terrain analysis  and reduces sensitivity to reference DTM artifacts.

Slope RMSE is the RMS difference between slope angles in degrees, under the same rigid alignment.

Although OrTeN permits direct network differentiation, the reported comparison differentiates polynomial fits to every method’s raster export to match spatial scale.

Height RMSE and MAE use unsmoothed elevations.[]

18

a

One $64\times 64$ block per acquisition, at the full image resolution, is held out during training for perceptural metric calculation.

This is necessary because of learned image-dependent radiometric calibration.

PSNR is $10\log_{10}(R^{2}/\mathrm{MSE})$ where $R$ is the 99th minus 1st percentile of the pooled held-out observations per scene.

SSIM uses the same range and $11\times 11$ Gaussian windows ( $\sigma=1.5$ pixels), averaged over valid window centers.

4.3

All training runs use a single seed, are limited to 15,000 iterations, and use a batch size of 8,192 rays.

The same configuration for OrTeN is used across all four scenes.

This includes enabling trajectory BA, jitter adjustment, and the detected-shadow prior with weight 0.01.

The roughing stage iteration cap is set to 8,000 updates.

Comparisons with depth-supervised EO-NeRF  and ASP  are reported.

EO-NeRF uses the same camera-derived scene bounds as OrTeN, 8,192 rays per update, 128 depth samples per ray, and fixed cameras.

Its depth targets come from the unaligned ASP stereo mosaics, without reference-terrain supervision or registration.

ASP uses image-based BA, dense stereo, and jitter refinement anchored to its own stereo terrain estimates.

The same ASP pipeline is used for all scenes.[]

5

OrTeN jointly reconstructs terrain and refines line-scan cameras from calibrated orbital images without depth supervision or stereo initialization.

Across four Mars and Moon scenes, it achieves sub-GSD aligned terrain RMSE in three and improves on the tested ASP reconstruction in those same three scenes.

The ablations demonstrate the importance of camera refinement and surface-patch NCC for achieving high geometric accuracy.

They also show that an accurate image reconstruction can coexist with an incorrect surface.

Comparison with EO-NeRF with depth supervision also demonstrates that structural priors are not sufficient to achieve accurate terrain reconstruction efficiently.

However, a number of limitations remain.

Without structural priors such as ranging measurements or known control points, absolute geolocation is not possible.

Furthermore, it is possible that integrating structural priors into OrTeN could improve reconstruction accuracy and efficiency and should be tested.

While the height map representation is an effective structural prior for the datasets considered here, when detail becomes sufficient, this representation becomes more limiting.

For instance, height maps cannot represent overhangs or complex 3D structures like caves.

Future work should work on mitigating these shortcomings to allow ground level imagery to be integrated into the terrain reconstruction process.

一句话：用神经逆渲染同时恢复地形几何与线扫相机的运动轨迹。

要点：

  • 线扫相机数据缺少常规帧间对应关系
  • 把地形与相机轨迹放进同一优化框架联合求解
  • MIT 团队，面向测绘与重建场景

为什么值得看：逆渲染从「恢复物体」走向「恢复场景 + 相机」，对扫描式资产与地形管线有参考价值。

中文摘要：OrTeN 来自 MIT，处理的是线扫相机（line-scan）采集场景下的逆渲染问题：这类数据没有传统相机的帧间几何一致性，常规 SfM 与 NeRF 流程难以直接套用。作者把地形几何与相机轨迹放进同一个神经逆渲染框架里联合优化，从而在缺少显式对应的条件下同时恢复场景结构与采集轨迹。对测绘、扫描与地形重建类管线有直接参考意义。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

License: CC BY 4.0

arXiv:2610.24075v1 [cs.CV] 16 Oct 2026

OrTeN: Neural Inverse Graphics for Joint Terrain and Line-scan Camera Trajectory Reconstruction

Josef Biberstein

Massachusetts Institute of Technology

Affiliation: Email:

jxb@mit.edu

Sertac Karaman

Massachusetts Institute of Technology

Affiliation: Email:

sertac@mit.edu

Abstract

Digital terrain maps (DTMs) are used for landing site selection, terrain-relative navigation, and geological analysis in planetary exploration.

Existing state-of-practice reconstruction techniques for creating DTMs from satellite imagery use multi-view stereo, requiring complex pipelines for dealing with camera error, changing illumination, and images with limited disparity.

This work introduces Orbital Terrain Networks (OrTeN), a DTM construction method that uses neural inverse rendering to jointly optimize a textured height map and orbital camera corrections from line-scan satellite images.

OrTeN operates directly on calibrated line-scan images with pixel values expressed as radiance factor (I/F) and corrects both broad trajectory pose inconsistencies and high-frequency pointing jitter jointly with surface reconstruction during training.

Surface-projected patch normalized cross-correlation (NCC) enforces consistency between observations of the same terrain, refining an initial rough reconstruction.

A semi-empirical reflectance model and shadow rendering are used to fit surface appearance from multi-date imagery with differing solar illumination.

OrTeN requires only calibrated line-scan images and initial camera poses and does not use any structural priors including ranging/depth measurements or initial rough DTMs.

OrTeN is evaluated on four planetary imagery datasets.

Aligned terrain RMSEs are 2.35 m at Jezero Crater, 2.82 m at Gale Crater, 16.18 m at Olympus Mons, and 0.43 m at McGetchin Crater.

: Figure 1Summary of OrTeN DTM reconstructions.

OrTeN produces high-quality digital terrain maps (DTMs) from multi-view imagery without structural priors.

Combining bundle adjustment, normalized cross-correlation, a semi-empirical photometric model, and geometric shadows allows OrTeN to reconstruct terrain reliably across multiple different instruments, planetary bodies, and lighting conditions.

1

Digital terrain maps (DTMs) are an important supporting data product in space exploration.

Accurate DTMs enable landing site selection and terrain-relative navigation (TRN) during entry, descent, and landing for modern autonomous space exploration missions such as Mars 2020 .

They also provide the topographic context needed to interpret planetary landforms and their geological history .[, ]

11

21

[]

29

Current pipelines for orbital DTM production used in the space science community rely on classical multi-view stereo (MVS) techniques to infer terrain structure—features are detected and matched between radiometrically calibrated images, bundle adjustment (BA) is performed to refine camera poses, and stereo correspondences are triangulated to produce a 3D terrain model .

MVS can produce high-quality maps suitable for mission operations, but a number of challenges inherent to both MVS itself and its application to satellite datasets complicate the process.

These challenges include the difficulty of getting reliable feature matches in the presence of shadows or low-texture regions, the line-scan geometry of most satellite images not admitting the epipolar constraints assumed by traditional MVS, and transients like dust storms or seasonal changes that alter the appearance of the terrain.

Correcting for these effects can require labor-intensive preprocessing and careful manual intervention, making MVS pipelines cumbersome to use.[, ]

22

7

Neural inverse graphics provides a methodology for scene reconstruction that can address many of the challenges faced by classical MVS pipelines.

For instance, satellite adaptations of neural radiance fields (NeRFs) model changing illumination and acquisition appearance while recovering scene geometry .

However, full 3D volumetric representations admit degenerate solutions—for instance, all scene density concentrated in front of cameras, explaining the observed images without recovering the true geometry—which can be particularly problematic when working with low-disparity orbital imagery where depth cues are weak.

While structural priors can help mitigate these degeneracies , these measurements are not always available or reliable.[, , ]

15

26

27

[, ]

38

36

OrTeN mitigates the shortcomings of classical MVS and volumetric neural reconstruction by optimizing a textured height map directly.

Critically, OrTeN requires no structural priors to achieve accurate terrain reconstruction from images and approximate camera poses.

It builds on Neural Terrain Maps (NTM) , adding direct bundle adjustment of line-scan camera extrinsics jointly with training, a semi-empirical photometric model, and geometric shadow modeling.

The contributions of this work are:[]

8

1.

A pipeline for creating accurate DTMs through differentiable volume rendering of textured height maps including a first-order approximation of distance to the height map along the ray to improve performance at oblique angles.

2.

Joint terrain and line-scan camera optimization, including smooth trajectory adjustment and high-frequency jitter removal, and a semi-empirical, spatially varying photometric model including geometric shadow modeling with an image-space prior.

3.

An evaluation on four Mars and Moon scenes with varied relief and illumination, using the Context Camera (CTX) and Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera (LROC) Narrow Angle Camera (NAC).

OrTeN achieves aligned height errors below the ground sampling distance (GSD) in three scenes and improves on the tested Ames Stereo Pipeline (ASP) reconstruction in those scenes.

2

DTM creation with MVS.

A number of well-established pipelines exist for creating DTMs from orbital imagery using MVS, including the Ames Stereo Pipeline (ASP), satellite stereo pipeline (s2p), and COLMAP .

All of these methods use feature extraction and matching to constrain camera alignment before performing dense stereo matching to triangulate terrain.

Orbital imagery is often taken by linescan cameras, and therefore integration into standard MVS pipelines requires particular care because each detector line is acquired at a different pose.

This precludes the standard epipolar geometry assumptions used in perspective-camera MVS to make searching for correspondences straightforward.

Linescan epipolar loci are generally curved, so the global rectification used for ideal perspective cameras must be replaced by local or sensor-specific constructions .

ASP can also refine time-varying camera states to correct high-frequency jitter .[, , , ]

7

13

33

34

[, ]

14

19

[]

4

Illumination changes, common in multi-date satellite data acquisitions, create an additional challenge for traditional MVS approaches.

Shadows and surface reflectance can change between acquisitions even when terrain is static and make feature selection and matching more difficult.

Therefore, masking shadows and other illumination-dependent artifacts is often necessary to improve the robustness of MVS matching.

Shadows can also provide important geometric information which can be exploited in reconstruction, and shape-from-shading methods exploit this to further refine existing DTMs .

OrTeN performs trajectory bundle adjustment, including jitter removal, jointly with training, and uses a semi-empirical photometric model with explicit geometric shadow handling to improve terrain reconstruction.[]

3

Neural reconstruction of orbital imagery.

S-NeRF introduced illumination-aware neural rendering for satellite photogrammetry, and Sat-NeRF added rational polynomial coefficient (RPC) camera support and transient appearance modeling.

EO-NeRF built on these previous methods to establish a baseline framework for general-purpose scenes on Earth by incorporating geometrically consistent shadows with learned radiometric and camera corrections and transient appearance embeddings .

Season-NeRF separated seasonal appearance from Sun and viewing geometry , while a semi-empirical bidirectional reflectance distribution function (BRDF) was incorporated into BRDF-NeRF .

Other methods address the geometry directly through depth supervision, surface constraints, or gravity-aligned and coarse-to-fine regularization .

Gaussian splatting for satellite imagery has also emerged as an alternative to methods utilizing volume rendering, offering efficient, high-quality neural scene representations .[, , ]

15

26

27

[]

17

[]

39

[, , ]

38

31

36

[, ]

2

9

More recent works have begun to focus on large-scale terrain reconstruction using neural inverse graphics.

Both NTM and LNEM introduce direct rendering of linescan imagery for terrain reconstruction .

For descent imagery, de Almeida . incorporate a neural height field into reconstruction from wide-angle cameras .

OrTeN eschews structural priors and retains the explicitly parameterized terrain representation, as is done in NTM, and adds ray-distance-based opacity and improved regularization with normalized cross-correlation (NCC).

Its coarse-to-fine optimization follows the principle established by BARF: low-frequency structure should stabilize camera alignment before fine appearance is exposed .[, ]

8

23

et al[]

12

[]

24

3

: Figure 2

Two linescan acquisitions $i,j$ observe overlapping terrain swaths.

The dashed trajectory indicates the original extrinsics, which are corrected during bundle adjustment.

Bundle adjustment refines position and attitude, including angular jitter.

Terrain networks predict height, albedo, material mixture, and a Sun-dependent ambient factor.

Gray-to-red camera-ray samples illustrate interval opacity $\alpha_{j}$ , with transition width controlled by $\beta$ .

Sun-directed opacity integration determines visibility $V$ .

Source image patches are lifted onto the current height field and compared with neighbor observations through normalized cross-correlation $\rho$ , constraining terrain and cameras jointly.

Key elements of the OrTeN pipeline.

OrTeN represents the scene with a height field $h_{\theta}:\mathbb{R}^{2}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ in a local east–north–up (ENU) frame and learned surface appearance ().

The surface is $\mathbf{x}=(x,y,h_{\theta}(x,y))$ , and unit-direction camera rays are given by $\mathbf{r}(t)=\mathbf{o}+t\mathbf{d}$ .

The origin is constructed as the common look point of all cameras, the horizontal bounds are set by the image footprints on the horizontal plane, enlarged by a factor of 1.5, and the vertical bounds are set by global planetary height limits.

Fig.2

3.1

OrTeN follows the lineage of NeuS, which derives opacity from the decrease of a logistic cumulative distribution function (CDF) along a ray through an implicit surface .

Applying this construction to distance along the ray rather than vertical height residual gives[]

37

$\displaystyle\alpha_{j}$ $\displaystyle=\left[1-\frac{\Phi_{\beta}(q(t_{j+1}))}{\Phi_{\beta}(q(t_{j}))}\right]_{+},$ (1) $\displaystyle T_{j}$ $\displaystyle=\prod_{k(2)

Here $\Phi_{\beta}(q)=(1+e^{-q/\beta})^{-1}$ , $[z]_{+}=\max(z,0)$ , $\alpha_{j}$ is interval opacity, $T_{j}$ is transmittance to that interval, and $w_{j}$ is its rendering weight.

The CDF ratio is evaluated on a log scale to improve numerical stability.

Sampling locations are chosen with a proposal network as is done in Nerfacto .[]

35

To obtain $q$ , the effect of terrain slope and viewing direction on the height residual is considered:

$\displaystyle f(t)$ $\displaystyle=r_{z}(t)-h_{\theta}(\mathbf{r}_{xy}(t)),$ (3) $\displaystyle f^{\prime}(t)$ $\displaystyle=d_{z}-\nabla h_{\theta}(\mathbf{r}_{xy}(t))^{\top}\mathbf{d}_{xy},$ (4) $\displaystyle q(t)$ $\displaystyle=\frac{f(t)}{\max(-f^{\prime}(t),10^{-3})}.$ (5)

Subscripts $xy$ and $z$ select horizontal and vertical components.

For a plane, $q(t)=t_{\star}-t$ when the denominator clamp is inactive, where $t_{\star}$ is the intersection distance.

This formulation ensures the learned width $\beta>0$ has the same metric meaning across terrain slopes and viewing angles.

Height derivatives are calculated by finite differences using a first-order formulation.

3.2

Training uses calibrated scalar radiance factor $I/F=\pi L/F_{\odot}$ images, where $L$ is observed radiance and $F_{\odot}$ is solar irradiance at the body .

Albedo $a_{\psi}$ is aggregated over the ray samples:[, ]

6

32

$A=\sum_{j}w_{j},\qquad\bar{a}=\frac{\sum_{j}w_{j}a_{\psi}(\mathbf{r}_{xy}(\bar{t}_{j}))}{\max(A,10^{-8})},$ (6)

where $\bar{t}_{j}$ is the interval midpoint.

A second network head predicts the spatial Lunar–Lambert mixture $m_{\phi}(x,y)$ , integrated in the same way to give $\bar{m}$ .

The normalized, weighted terrain normal $\mathbf{n}$ is used to compute positive incidence and emission cosines $\mu_{0}=[\mathbf{n}^{\top}\mathbf{s}]_{+}$ and $\mu=[\mathbf{n}^{\top}(-\mathbf{d})]_{+}$ , with $\mathbf{s}$ pointing toward the Sun.

The direct-light factor is

$\displaystyle F(\mu_{0},\mu,m)$ $\displaystyle=(1-m)\mu_{0}+\frac{2m\mu_{0}}{\max(\mu_{0}+\mu,10^{-6})},$ (7) $\displaystyle D$ $\displaystyle=\frac{F(\mu_{0},\mu,\bar{m})}{F(\cos 30^{\circ},1,\bar{m})}.$ (8)

This interpolates between Lambert and Lommel–Seeliger responses .[]

28

Geometric shadows.

Starting from the weighted camera-ray depth, a surface intersection is refined and traced toward the Sun until the ray leaves the scene bounds.

Solar interval opacities $\alpha_{k}^{\odot}$ are converted to visibility using

$V=V_{\rm att}\prod_{k}(1-\alpha_{k}^{\odot}),\qquad V_{\eta}=(1-\eta)V_{\rm att}+\eta V.$ (9)

Here $V_{\rm att}$ smoothly suppresses light on back-facing slopes and is zero when the Sun is below the local horizon.

The startup factor $\eta$ ramps cast shadows in over 500 updates.

Terrain outside the bounds cannot cast shadows in this model.

OrTeN uses a semi-empirical image formation model inspired by EO-NeRF’s shadow-fill and affine brightness approach .

The predicted image for acquisition $i$ is[]

27

$\widehat{y}_{i}=g_{i}\bigl[V_{\eta}D+(1-V_{\eta})a_{\rm amb}(\mathbf{s})\bigr]\bar{a}+b_{i}.$ (10)

The Sun-dependent ambient factor $a_{\rm amb}\in(0,1)$ fills shadows without inheriting the direct-light angular response.

Scalar gains $g_{i}=e^{u_{i}-\bar{u}}$ and offsets absorb acquisition-wide brightness differences, with $\bar{u}=M^{-1}\sum_{i}u_{i}$ fixing the geometric mean gain to one across $M$ acquisitions.

The same image model is used throughout training.

Histogram-valley shadow detection  is adopted to provide an initial image-space shadow estimate at startup.

Only sufficiently dark, distinct pixels are accepted, and mask erosion is applied to remove boundary transients.

For an ordinary rendering batch $\mathcal{B}$ , a regularizer is applied:[]

1

$\mathcal{L}_{\rm shadow}=|\mathcal{B}|^{-1}\sum_{p\in\mathcal{B}}z_{p}V_{p}^{2},$ (11)

where $z_{p}=1$ marks a detected core and $z_{p}=0$ means unknown.

This loss is one-sided, so unlabeled pixels are not treated as either shadow or sunlit.

3.3

A linescan pixel $(\ell,s)$ has nominal origin $\mathbf{o}_{i}^{0}(\ell)$ and direction $\mathbf{d}_{i}^{0}(\ell,s)$ .

Intrinsics and distortion are retained, and corrections are optimized in the local scene frame:

$\displaystyle\mathbf{o}_{i}$ $\displaystyle=\mathbf{o}_{i}^{0}+\Delta\mathbf{p}_{i}(u),$ (12) $\displaystyle\mathbf{d}_{i}$ $\displaystyle=\exp([\Delta\boldsymbol{\omega}_{i}(u)]_{\times})\mathbf{d}_{i}^{0},$ (13) $\displaystyle\Delta\mathbf{p}_{i}(u)$ $\displaystyle=s_{p}\sum_{k=0}^{3}B_{k}(u)\mathbf{P}_{ik},$ (14) $\displaystyle\Delta\boldsymbol{\omega}_{i}(u)$ $\displaystyle=s_{\omega}\left[\sum_{k=0}^{3}B_{k}(u)\mathbf{W}_{ik}+r\mathbf{J}_{i}(u)\right].$ (15)

Here $u\in[0,1]$ is normalized acquisition time and $B_{k}$ are cubic Bernstein functions.

The matrix $[\boldsymbol{\omega}]_{\times}$ implements the cross product with $\boldsymbol{\omega}$ , and its exponential gives the corresponding rotation.

The learned controls $\mathbf{P}_{ik},\mathbf{W}_{ik}$ use physical scales $s_{p},s_{\omega}$ which are constrained by soft priors based on expected trajectory error .

During the refinement phase (), the ramp $r$ introduces angular jitter $\mathbf{J}_{i}$ , represented by a cubic B-spline with 64 intervals per acquisition.

Its global cubic component is removed so it cannot duplicate the smooth trajectory correction.[]

11

Sec.3.5

3.4

In addition to uniformly sampled rays, at each training iteration $5\times 5$ patches are sampled in source images and projected onto the current height field through the refined cameras.

Each patch point is then projected from the surface into other acquisitions, where bilinear interpolation is used to calculate observed intensities.

For accepted source–neighbor pairs, the normalized cross-correlation loss is

$\mathcal{L}_{\rm NCC}=\mathbb{E}_{P,i,j}\left[1-\frac{\langle P_{i}-\bar{P}_{i},P_{j}-\bar{P}_{j}\rangle}{\|P_{i}-\bar{P}_{i}\|_{2}\,\|P_{j}-\bar{P}_{j}\|_{2}}\right].$ (16)

Here $P_{i},P_{j}$ contain the observed patch intensities and $\bar{P}_{i},\bar{P}_{j}$ are their means.

$\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ is the inner product.

Invalid, occluded, low-contrast, and nearly parallel view pairs are rejected, and up to three of the best eligible neighbors are retained per source patch.

NCC is active in both roughing and refinement ().

Sec.3.5

3.5

: Figure 3OrTeN’s architecture.

Learned networks are blue, optimized parameters are red, and analytic operations are gray.

Layer boxes give output dimensions, and arrow colors indicate activations.

One spatial encoding  feeds the height, albedo, and Lunar–Lambert material outputs.

The ambient network uses a fourth-order spherical harmonic (SH) encoding of the Sun direction.

Height also supplies normals and solar visibility $V_{\eta}$ .

Proposal sampling is omitted for clarity.[]

30

shows the overall network architecture.

Training progresses from images downsampled by $4\times$ to $2\times$ , then to native resolution.

Active encoding levels are adjusted to approximately match the current image resolution.

There are two training stages: roughing and refinement.

Roughing ends when terrain and camera motion stabilize or the roughing update limit is reached.

Refinement lowers the geometry learning rate, increases NCC sampling, and introduces jitter and local regularization.

Fig.3

Let $s_{y}=\sqrt{\mathbb{E}_{\rm train}[y^{2}]}$ be the RMS brightness of all training pixels.

The rendering loss is

$\mathcal{L}_{I/F}=\mathbb{E}_{p\in\mathcal{B}}\left[(\widehat{y}_{p}-y_{p})^{2}/s_{y}^{2}\right].$ (17)

Albedo starts exactly at $s_{y}$ , ambient at 0.2, and gains and offsets at one and zero.

The remaining surface and appearance penalties are

$\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\rm bend}$ $\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}}\left[s_{h}^{2}\|\mathbf{H}_{s_{h}}h_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})\|_{F}^{2}\right],$ (18) $\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\rm width}$ $\displaystyle=\log\bigl(1+(\beta/g_{0})^{2}\bigr),$ (19) $\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\rm radio}$ $\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{i}\left[((u_{i}-\bar{u})/0.1)^{2}+(b_{i}/0.01)^{2}\right],$ (20) $\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\rm amb}$ $\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{s}}\left[\bigl[\operatorname{logit}a_{\rm amb}(\mathbf{s})-\log 9\bigr]_{+}^{2}\right].$ (21)

Here $\mathbf{H}_{s_{h}}$ is the finite-difference Hessian.

In order, these losses regularize surface bending, control the rendering width, enforce radiometric calibration, and constrain the ambient illumination.

The fixed scale $g_{0}$ is the initial training-image GSD.

The optional ambient penalty acts only when the ambient factor exceeds 0.9.

Camera regularization penalizes the dimensionless trajectory controls and, in refinement, the sampled jitter motion.

Let $\mathbf{c}_{i}(u)$ concatenate the trajectory position and rotation corrections divided by $s_{p}$ and $s_{\omega}$ .

Its second derivative penalizes trajectory curvature:

$\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\rm camera}={}$ $\displaystyle\lambda_{C}\mathbb{E}_{i,k}(\|\mathbf{P}_{ik}\|_{2}^{2}+\|\mathbf{W}_{ik}\|_{2}^{2})$ $\displaystyle+\lambda_{C}\mathbf{1}_{r>0}\mathbb{E}_{i,u}\|\mathbf{J}_{i}(u)\|_{2}^{2}$ $\displaystyle+\lambda_{K}\mathbb{E}_{i}\int_{0}^{1}\|\mathbf{c}_{i}^{\prime\prime}(u)\|_{2}^{2}du.$ (22)

For each camera or solar ray, the proposal loss is the histogram-envelope objective used by Nerfstudio :[]

35

$\mathcal{L}_{\rm env}=\sum_{l}\mathbb{E}_{j}\frac{[w_{j}-W_{lj}]_{+}^{2}}{w_{j}+10^{-7}}.$ (23)

Here $W_{lj}$ is proposal level $l$ ’s total mass in bins overlapping final interval $j$ .

The camera and solar proposal losses are summed as $\mathcal{L}_{\rm proposal}$ .

The complete objective is

$\displaystyle\mathcal{L}={}$ $\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{I/F}+\eta\lambda_{N}\mathcal{L}_{\rm NCC}+\lambda_{W}\mathcal{L}_{\rm width}+\lambda_{R}\mathcal{L}_{\rm radio}$ $\displaystyle+\mathcal{L}_{\rm camera}+\mathcal{L}_{\rm proposal}$ $\displaystyle+r\left(\lambda_{B}\mathcal{L}_{\rm bend}+\lambda_{S}\mathcal{L}_{\rm shadow}+\lambda_{A}\mathcal{L}_{\rm amb}\right).$ (24)

The refinement ramp $r$ is zero during roughing and rises over 500 updates after transition.

4

4.1

Four lunar and Martian datasets were selected for their varied terrain and illumination and the availability of reference DTMs.

Jezero Crater, Gale Crater, and Olympus Mons each contain fifteen $1024\times 1024$ CTX crops.

McGetchin Crater contains ten LROC NAC crops of the same size.

Images are calibrated to I/F using the Integrated Software for Imagers and Spectrometers (ISIS) and paired with initial line-scan camera states.

gives additional details on the instruments and reference DTM quality for each dataset.

The Olympus dataset reference uses a DTM separately reconstructed from the same image collection because a high-quality engineering DTM was unavailable.

Table1

: Table 1

Instruments are CTX  and LROC NAC .

Acc. / prec. denotes vertical accuracy / precision.

GSD is estimated by intersecting adjacent pixel rays from initial cameras with the local ENU $xy$ plane.

For Olympus Mons, precision was estimated from the RMS elevation difference between two stereo DTMs generated from image pairs with no cameras in common during construction of the ASP reference used to evaluate OrTeN.

Dataset instrument and DTM reference overview.a[]

25

b[]

32

‡

4.2

Metrics for each scene are calculated over a fixed reference footprint that is covered by at least five initial cameras.

To resolve the gauge freedom inherent in the bundle adjustment process, reconstructed DTMs are aligned to the reference DTM using a six-degree-of-freedom rigid transformation.

No scale change, local warping, or separate alignment for different metrics is applied.

For aligned height errors $e_{p}=\widehat{h}_{a}(p)-h_{\rm ref}(p)$ on $N$ valid posts, the metrics are

$\mathrm{RMSE}_{a}=\sqrt{N^{-1}\sum_{p}e_{p}^{2}},\qquad\mathrm{MAE}_{a}=N^{-1}\sum_{p}|e_{p}|.$ (25)

The subscript $a$ denotes metrics applied to rigidly aligned DTMs, so these scores measure relative shape rather than absolute geolocation.

Slope is evaluated using a local quadratic surface fit calculated over a $9\times 9$ sliding window.

This follows established practices in terrain analysis  and reduces sensitivity to reference DTM artifacts.

Slope RMSE is the RMS difference between slope angles in degrees, under the same rigid alignment.

Although OrTeN permits direct network differentiation, the reported comparison differentiates polynomial fits to every method’s raster export to match spatial scale.

Height RMSE and MAE use unsmoothed elevations.[]

18

a

One $64\times 64$ block per acquisition, at the full image resolution, is held out during training for perceptural metric calculation.

This is necessary because of learned image-dependent radiometric calibration.

PSNR is $10\log_{10}(R^{2}/\mathrm{MSE})$ where $R$ is the 99th minus 1st percentile of the pooled held-out observations per scene.

SSIM uses the same range and $11\times 11$ Gaussian windows ( $\sigma=1.5$ pixels), averaged over valid window centers.

4.3

All training runs use a single seed, are limited to 15,000 iterations, and use a batch size of 8,192 rays.

The same configuration for OrTeN is used across all four scenes.

This includes enabling trajectory BA, jitter adjustment, and the detected-shadow prior with weight 0.01.

The roughing stage iteration cap is set to 8,000 updates.

Comparisons with depth-supervised EO-NeRF  and ASP  are reported.

EO-NeRF uses the same camera-derived scene bounds as OrTeN, 8,192 rays per update, 128 depth samples per ray, and fixed cameras.

Its depth targets come from the unaligned ASP stereo mosaics, without reference-terrain supervision or registration.

ASP uses image-based BA, dense stereo, and jitter refinement anchored to its own stereo terrain estimates.

The same ASP pipeline is used for all scenes.[]

Mean setup-plus-training times are 52.7/41.2 minutes for OrTeN on NVIDIA RTX 6000 Ada Generation/RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs, respectively.

These include periodic evaluation and checkpointing, exclude final evaluation, and average different scene/configuration mixes across GPUs.

OrTeN uses Adam with a 500-step warmup to learning rates of $3\times 10^{-3}$ for geometry and appearance, $10^{-3}$ for cameras, and $10^{-2}$ for proposal networks.

Geometry decays during roughing, then starts refinement at most $1.5\times 10^{-4}$ and decays to $5\times 10^{-5}$ .

Appearance and camera rates finish at $3\times 10^{-4}$ and $10^{-5}$ .

On the Olympus Mons scene, the RMSE remains at 2.91 $\times$ GSD.

Its large relief (almost 3 km) and substantial cast shadows make reconstruction challenging.

Tab.2

Depth-supervised EO-NeRF fails to reconstruct accurate DTMs in any of the scenes despite access to structural supervision.

It falls short of OrTeN both visually and in structural accuracy.

Noting that the default EO-NeRF configuration trains for much longer (300,000 iterations) and takes 10-20 hours to converge, this comparison demonstrates that OrTeN’s approach achieves meaningful improvement in both efficiency and accuracy.

The results of the ablation are summarized in .

Tab.3

Removing BA significantly degrades the quality of the reconstructed DTMs across all scenes, highlighting the importance of joint optimization of camera parameters and scene geometry.

shows baseline and no-BA renderings of the same acquisition for the McGetchin Crater scene.

The no-BA ablation shows clearly degraded visual reconstruction quality with a drop of more than 10 dB in reserved-pixel PSNR.

The DTM is similarly impacted with RMSE increasing from 0.43 to 10.36 m and the quality of the reconstruction visibly degrading, especially in the fine detail around the central crater region.

OrTeN jointly reconstructs terrain and refines line-scan cameras from calibrated orbital images without depth supervision or stereo initialization.

Across four Mars and Moon scenes, it achieves sub-GSD aligned terrain RMSE in three and improves on the tested ASP reconstruction in those same three scenes.

The ablations demonstrate the importance of camera refinement and surface-patch NCC for achieving high geometric accuracy.

They also show that an accurate image reconstruction can coexist with an incorrect surface.

Comparison with EO-NeRF with depth supervision also demonstrates that structural priors are not sufficient to achieve accurate terrain reconstruction efficiently.

However, a number of limitations remain.

Without structural priors such as ranging measurements or known control points, absolute geolocation is not possible.

Furthermore, it is possible that integrating structural priors into OrTeN could improve reconstruction accuracy and efficiency and should be tested.

While the height map representation is an effective structural prior for the datasets considered here, when detail becomes sufficient, this representation becomes more limiting.

For instance, height maps cannot represent overhangs or complex 3D structures like caves.

Future work should work on mitigating these shortcomings to allow ground level imagery to be integrated into the terrain reconstruction process.

item.title: PhysSkin++：自监督神经蒙皮实现实时且可泛化的物理动画 ｜ PhysSkin++: Real-Time and Generalizable Physics-Based Animation via Self-Supervised Neural Skinning
item.description:
一句话：从静态几何学出连续的神经蒙皮场，构建紧凑形变子空间，让实时物理动画跨形状泛化。

要点：

  • 跨不同 3D 形状与空间离散方式泛化，是实时物理解算的老大难
  • 神经蒙皮场自编码器预测与形状相关的形变子空间
  • 在未见过的形状上保持稳定，并维持实时性能

为什么值得看：角色与布料实时解算的提速路线，直接对应引擎里的蒙皮与形变管线。

中文摘要：实时物理动画要在各种 3D 形状与不同空间离散方式上泛化仍然困难。PhysSkin++ 的做法是从静态几何学习连续的神经蒙皮场，用它构建紧凑的形变子空间；核心是神经蒙皮场自编码器（NSFA），能够预测与形状相关的子空间，从而在未见形状上也保持稳定与实时。相比逐模型训练的传统方案，泛化与成本都更优。

主题：游戏引擎

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

License: CC BY 4.0

arXiv:2610.26067v1 [cs.CV] 19 Oct 2026

PhysSkin++: Real-Time and Generalizable Physics-Based Animation via Self-Supervised Neural Skinning

Yuanhang Lei

Baofei Liu

Xingxuan Li

Tao Cheng

Zixuan Wang

Boming Zhao

Yujun Shen

Siyuan Huang

Ruizhen Hu

Peter Yichen Chen

Hujun Bao

and Zhaopeng Cui

†$†$ Corresponding author.†thanks: †Yuanhang Lei, Baofei Liu, Xingxuan Li, Tao Cheng, Zixuan Wang, Boming Zhao, Hujun Bao, and Zhaopeng Cui are with the State Key Laboratory of CAD&CG, Zhejiang University.†thanks: †Yujun Shen is with Ant Group, Hangzhou 310000, China.†thanks: †Siyuan Huang is with the Beijing Institute for General Artificial Intelligence (BIGAI).†thanks: †Ruizhen Hu is with Shenzhen University.†thanks: †Peter Yichen Chen is with the University of British Columbia.†thanks:

Abstract

Generalizing real-time physics-based animation across diverse 3D shapes and spatial discretizations remains challenging. In this paper, we introduce PhysSkin++, a physics-informed framework that learns continuous neural skinning fields from static geometries to construct compact deformation subspaces. Specifically, we propose a Neural Skinning Fields Autoencoder that predicts shape-dependent deformation subspaces without per-object network training. To learn these subspaces without simulation trajectories, we develop a Physics-Informed Self-Supervised Learning strategy that combines skinning-field normalization with conflict-aware gradient correction, stabilizing joint optimization under physical and orthogonality constraints. The learned representation supports efficient reduced dynamics with user control and contact interactions, together with direct animation binding to meshes, point clouds, and 3D Gaussians. For prescribed rig animation, we further introduce a self-supervised complementarity objective to learn complementary elastic responses without enforcing complementarity constraints at runtime. Experiments demonstrate cross-shape generalization of the learned skinning fields, real-time reduced simulation, and applications to controllable, collision-aware, and rig-complementary animation. Project page: .

https://zju3dv.github.io/PhysSkin_plus/

Physics-based animation, geometric deep learning, reduced-order modeling, self-supervised learning.

Index Terms:

PhysSkin++ is a generalizable physics-informed neural skinning framework for object animation. The framework is learned directly from static 3D geometries via physics-informed self-supervision without any annotated data. Once trained, PhysSkin++ can be applied in a feed-forward manner to perform neural skinning for diverse 3D shapes and discretizations, enabling real-time physics-based animation. It further supports interactive control, collision-aware multi-object interaction, and rig-complementary animation.Fig. 1:

I Introduction

Real-time physics-based animation is a long-standing goal in computer vision and graphics, underpinning applications in VR/AR authoring, character animation, and interactive digital content creation. To support such applications, an animation system must provide a compact yet expressive motion representation that captures physically plausible deformations, accommodates user control and interactions, and remains computationally efficient for real-time animation.

Subspace physics-based animation  addresses this by learning a low-dimensional motion subspace for efficient computation, and then lifting the result back to the full space using a subspace mapping. However, classical methods  optimize a single linear subspace mapping matrix tied to a particular mesh topology and resolution, which prevents generalization across different spatial discretizations. Recently, neural methods  have emerged as promising alternatives by using neural networks to learn subspace mappings that naturally handle arbitrary spatial discretizations. These approaches, however, must still train a separate network per object and fail to generalize to different 3D shapes. In parallel, recent transformer-based approaches learn physical dynamics directly from simulation trajectories across diverse objects and physical systems . Although this data-driven route enables generalizable neural simulation, it requires extensive trajectory supervision and does not explicitly construct a low-dimensional deformation subspace for reduced-order animation. These limitations motivate a central question: [, ]

2

10

[, ]

2

51

[, ]

10

49

[, ]

15

58

How can we learn a physics-consistent deformation subspace mapping that generalizes across diverse 3D shapes and discretizations directly from static geometries, without relying on supervised training data?

In this work, we introduce PhysSkin++ (Fig. ), a generalizable physics-informed framework for real-time physics-based animation across diverse 3D shapes and discretizations. In the spirit of Linear Blend Skinning (LBS) , we use continuous skinning fields to define a deformation subspace mapping, with handle transformations serving as the reduced coordinates for full-space 3D object deformation. To construct this representation directly from static geometries, we introduce a Neural Skinning Fields Autoencoder. Specifically, PhysSkin++ employs a transformer-based point cloud encoder to extract latent shape features from surface samples, while a cross-attention decoder predicts continuous neural skinning fields at arbitrary spatial locations. PhysSkin++ requires no simulation trajectories, skinning annotations, or category-specific priors. This mesh-free, discretization-agnostic representation generalizes across object categories, topologies, and resolutions.

1

[]

43

Learning such a deformation subspace mapping purely from geometry is highly non-trivial. A physically meaningful subspace must exhibit low potential energy, reflecting deformation modes compatible with physically plausible behavior; spatial smoothness, ensuring coherent deformations; and orthogonality, promoting independence among the deformation modes. We therefore formulate a self-supervised objective consisting of potential-energy, smoothness, and orthogonality terms. However, jointly optimizing these terms often leads to conflicts in gradient magnitude and direction, making naive joint optimization unstable. To overcome this optimization challenge, we introduce a Physics-Informed Self-Supervised Learning (PISSL) strategy. First, we apply on-the-fly skinning-field normalization, which regulates the scale of the learned skinning weights and prevents numerical drift during training. Second, we incorporate a conflict-aware gradient correction mechanism  to resolve destructive interference among gradients of the loss terms, enabling balanced optimization and stable convergence. Together, these mechanisms enable PhysSkin++ to learn a physically consistent deformation subspace mapping directly from static geometries, with spatially smooth and approximately orthogonal skinning fields.[]

37

At runtime, we advance the reduced coordinates through implicit reduced dynamics and map them to full-space deformations through the learned skinning-based subspace mapping. To support controllable and collision-aware animation, we incorporate Dirichlet boundary conditions, interactive control, environmental interaction, and multi-object contact into this formulation. Prescribed boundary displacements are enforced through a boundary-compatible deformation map, while external forces and contact interactions are incorporated through their corresponding energy terms. This formulation supports both rigid–deformable and deformable–deformable interactions within the learned deformation subspaces. Moreover, the continuous deformation map can be directly bound to different spatial discretizations, including 3D Gaussian representations , enabling physics-based animation of diverse object representations within the same reduced dynamics framework.[]

28

Beyond purely physics-driven animation, PhysSkin++ also supports rig-complementary animation when an artist-authored LBS rig is available. Artist-authored rigs provide intuitive low-dimensional control, but their kinematic deformations alone cannot reproduce physical elastic responses, while increasing the complexity of a rig places a greater burden on animation authoring. Complementary dynamics  addresses this tension by augmenting a prescribed rig animation with complementary physical deformations. Following this principle, PhysSkin++ treats the user-authored rig-based animation as the primary animation and learns neural skinning fields for complementary elastic response. We augment the self-supervised objective with a rig-space complementarity term defined by the rig Jacobian, encouraging the learned deformation subspace to be complementary to the prescribed rig animation space. At runtime, the resulting reduced dynamics enriches the prescribed animation with physics-based complementary displacement without enforcing the rig-space complementarity constraint at every step. Both animation settings share the continuous skinning representation and reduced dynamics framework.[, ]

65

6

Experiments on various datasets evaluate the learned skinning fields and demonstrate real-time physics-based animation across diverse shapes, controls, interactions, and spatial discretizations. Our contributions are:

•

We present , a generalizable physics-informed framework for real-time physics-based animation across diverse 3D shapes and discretizations by learning neural skinning fields directly from static geometries. Its Neural Skinning Fields Autoencoder employs a transformer-based shape encoder and a cross-attention decoder to predict continuous skinning fields.PhysSkin++

•

We develop a that incorporates on-the-fly skinning-field normalization and conflict-aware gradient correction, enabling stable joint optimization of multiple self-supervised loss terms.Physics-Informed Self-Supervised Learning (PISSL) strategy

•

We develop a that supports Dirichlet boundary conditions, interactive control, environmental interaction, and multi-object contact, together with discretization-agnostic binding of the continuous deformation map to meshes, point clouds, and 3D Gaussian representations.controllable and collision-aware reduced dynamics formulation

•

We support by extending the self-supervised objective with a rig-space complementarity term defined by the rig Jacobian. This enables physics-based complementary elastic responses under interactive rig control and user-authored animation sequences without enforcing the rig-space complementarity constraint at runtime.rig-complementary animation

A preliminary version of this work has been published as PhysSkin . The present article extends the conference version in four aspects. First, we develop a reduced dynamics formulation for controllable and collision-aware animation, supporting prescribed boundary displacements, interactive control, environmental interaction, and multi-object contact. Second, we provide a discretization-agnostic binding formulation for 3D Gaussian representations, updating both Gaussian centers and anisotropic covariances through local affine transformations determined by the learned skinning fields and current reduced coordinates. Third, we extend the deformation representation with prescribed rig displacement and the self-supervised objective with a rig-space complementarity term. These extensions support complementary elastic deformation for prescribed rig animations without enforcing the complementarity constraint at runtime. Finally, we expand the experimental evaluation to cover controllable and collision-aware animation, 3D Gaussian animation, and self-supervised rig-complementarity learning, including rig-complementary animation under interactive rig control and user-authored animation sequences.[]

30

II Related Work

Neural Physics-Based Animation.

Subspace physics-based animation  is an effective method for accelerating animation computations. Its core idea is to learn a low-dimensional motion subspace for efficient computation, and then lift the result back to the full space using a subspace mapping. Recently, fully neural approaches have been proposed to directly learn subspace mapping by neural networks. Data-driven methods  represented by CROM  learn the mapping for a single object by fitting neural networks to motion sequences from physical simulators, but they have limited generalization ability to unseen motion patterns. Data-free methods  learn a low-energy subspace mapping by physics-informed learning without requiring motion sequences, but pure neural network approaches often struggle to converge to high-quality subspace representations. Recently, Simplicits  learns neural skinning weight functions as a physics-informed subspace mapping by minimizing a quadratic energy subject to orthogonality constraints, which stabilizes training compared to purely neural models but limits generalization due to its per-object network design. Our method overcomes these limitations with a neural skinning fields autoencoder that outputs skinning weights generalizing across diverse 3D shapes, enabling real-time subspace physics-based animation. Our physics-informed neural subspace formulation retains explicit reduced-order dynamics and complements approaches that learn dynamics directly from simulation trajectories.

Another classical reduced deformation representation is skeletal rigging-based animation . Recently, based on 3D shape VAEs , many works  have performed supervised learning from expert-annotated 3D object rigging and skinning datasets to infer objects’ joints, bones, and skinning weights through a feed-forward network. However, some methods are limited to specific categories of 3D shapes such as characters  or animals , as they incorporate category-specific priors  such as predefined skeletal structures or semantic constraints, making it difficult to generalize to other object categories. Works represented by Anymate  learn from annotated 3D object rigging and skinning datasets and design category-agnostic network architectures, thereby enabling the ability to generalize across diverse object categories and demonstrating stronger generalization capabilities. However, these methods heavily rely on expert-annotated data , which are costly and difficult to scale. In contrast, our work employs self-supervised learning to train neural skinning fields directly from static 3D geometries without any annotated data.Neural Rigging and Skinning Representations.[, , ]

III Method

III-AFramework Overview and Problem Formulation

PhysSkin++ is a generalizable physics-informed framework for real-time physics-based animation across diverse 3D shapes and discretizations. As illustrated in Fig. , our neural skinning fields autoencoder predicts continuous skinning fields from static geometry to define a deformation subspace mapping. The autoencoder is trained through Physics-Informed Self-Supervised Learning (PISSL) under physical and numerical constraints. At runtime, we advance reduced coordinates to animate objects with boundary conditions, interactive control, and contact. Beyond purely physics-driven animation, PhysSkin++ also supports rig-complementary animation by learning complementary deformation subspaces for prescribed rigs. Moreover, the continuous deformation map supports binding to mesh vertices, sampled points, and 3D Gaussians.

2

Given a static 3D shape, we first sample volumetric cubature points for animation and surface points for shape encoding. A shape encoder processes the surface points to produce shape latents, from which a set of learnable queries extract handle latents via cross-attention. Subsequently, spatial queries attend to the handle latents through another cross-attention block to derive point-wise features, which are decoded into neural skinning fields. A geometry-only, physics-informed learning strategy optimizes the network in a self-supervised manner under physical and orthogonality constraints, enabling the learned skinning fields to support real-time, physics-based animation.Fig. 2:

Classical full-space physics-based animation methods  typically use explicit or implicit time integrators to update the object’s motion state. Explicit time integrators are often constrained by stability conditions , while implicit time integrators require solving a large nonlinear optimization problem in the high-dimensional full space. PhysSkin++ instead represents the deformation using continuous neural skinning fields and advances only the corresponding reduced-order subspace coordinates through implicit time integration. This lower-dimensional optimization reduces computational cost , enabling real-time physics-based animation.[, , , , , ]

To model full-space 3D object deformations within a reduced-order subspace, in the spirit of Linear Blend Skinning (LBS) , we represent the deformation map $\bm{x}=\phi(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{z}(t))$ using a weighted sum of $m$ affine displacement transformations:Continuous Skinning-Based Deformation Representation.[]

43

$\phi(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{z})=\mathbf{X}+\sum_{i=1}^{m}\bm{W}_{\!i}(\mathbf{X})\mathbf{Z}_{i}\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{X}\\

1\end{bmatrix}.$ (1)

Here, $\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{3}$ is a point in undeformed space and $\bm{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{3}$ is its deformed position, $m$ is the number of , $\bm{W}_{\!i}:\mathbb{R}^{3}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ is the continuous skinning weight function associated with handle $i$ , and $\mathbf{Z}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{3\times 4}$ parameterizes its affine displacement. The vector $\mathbf{z}=\text{flat}(\mathbf{Z})\in\mathbb{R}^{12m}$ stacks all handle parameters and serves as the reduced-order subspace coordinates, compactly representing the full-space deformation of $n$ spatial sample points, where $m\ll n$ . We first describe the representation and learning procedure for purely physics-driven animation, and then introduce the prescribed rig displacement and rig-space complementarity objective in Sec. .skinning handles

III-E

III-BNeural Skinning Fields Autoencoder

We train a neural skinning fields autoencoder to predict spatially continuous skinning weights across diverse 3D shapes and discretizations. The resulting mesh-free representation supports the skinning-based real-time animation described in Sec. . Unlike existing neural subspace methods  that train a separate neural network for each object, our single feed-forward network generalizes across diverse objects, improving scalability and practicality.

III-D

[, ]

44

10

We use the transformer-based point cloud encoder Michelangelo  to extract a highly compressed latent set $\mathbf{F}_{s}\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times d}$ for a given 3D shape via a cross-attention block and several self-attention blocks:Neural 3D Shape Encoding.[]

67

$\mathbf{F}_{s}=\mathrm{SelfAttn}^{(1:L)}(\mathrm{CrossAttn}(\mathbf{Q}_{s},\gamma(\mathbf{P}))),$ (2)

where $\mathbf{Q}_{s}\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times d}$ is a set of learnable shape latent tokens, $\mathbf{P}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times 6}$ is the sampled surface point cloud with $N$ points, each point consisting of 3D coordinates and normals, $\gamma(\cdot)$ is point-wise positional encoding, $\mathrm{SelfAttn}^{(1:L)}(\cdot)$ indicates a stack of $L$ self-attention layers that iteratively improve the shape latent representation, $M$ is the number of latents, and $d$ is the dimension of each latent.

In practice, the shape encoder is pretrained on the ShapeNet dataset  via a signed distance field (SDF) reconstruction task  to learn generalizable geometric priors. We then freeze the encoder parameters during training to enhance efficiency.[]

7

[]

47

To obtain spatially continuous skinning fields, we decode the shape latent set $\mathbf{F}_{s}$ obtained from Eq. () into spatially varying skinning weights.

We first assign $m$ learnable skinning handle tokens $\mathbf{Q}_{h}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times d}$ , and then use a cross-attention block to extract a skinning handle latent set $\mathbf{F}_{h}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times d}$ from the shape latent set $\mathbf{F}_{s}$ :Neural Skinning Fields Decoding.

2

$\mathbf{F}_{h}=\mathrm{CrossAttn}(\mathbf{Q}_{h},\mathrm{SelfAttn}(\mathbf{F}_{s})).\vskip 3.00003pt$ (3)

Next, for any spatial query point $\mathbf{X}$ , we use another cross-attention block to extract a point-wise skinning feature $\mathbf{F}_{p}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ from the skinning handle latent set $\mathbf{F}_{h}$ :

$\mathbf{F}_{p}=\mathrm{CrossAttn}(\gamma(\mathbf{X}),\mathbf{F}_{h}).\vskip 3.00003pt$ (4)

Finally, we concatenate the point-wise skinning feature $\mathbf{F}_{p}$ with the positional encoding of the query point, and use a ResNet-style MLP to compute the skinning fields:

$\bm{W}(\mathbf{X})=\mathrm{MLP}(\mathbf{F}_{p}\oplus\gamma(\mathbf{X})),\vskip 1.99997pt$ (5)

where $\bm{W}(\mathbf{X})\in\mathbb{R}^{m}$ is the skinning weight vector at point $\mathbf{X}$ , and $\oplus$ denotes the concatenation operator. To promote orthogonality among different skinning modes, we apply an Orthogonalization by Newton’s Iteration (ONI) module  at the final layer of the MLP, and we adopt ELU as the activation function in the MLP, which allows learning flexible and expressive skinning-based deformation subspaces without enforcing non-negativity on the learned skinning modes. We denote the full autoencoder by $\Phi_{\theta}$ and its skinning weight output at $\mathbf{X}$ by $\Phi_{\theta}(\mathbf{X})$ . The continuous fields can be queried throughout the object, while cubature points specify locations for physics-informed training and numerical integration.[]

26

In the classical Finite Element Method (FEM) , the object’s volume is typically discretized into a tetrahedral mesh  to facilitate numerical solutions of physical equations. Unlike triangle surface meshes commonly used for rendering, which only contain surface points, tetrahedral meshes include interior volumetric elements that better capture the object’s spatial structure. To train the neural skinning fields autoencoder, we sample cubature points both on the object’s surface and inside its volume, with each cubature point serving as a spatial query point $\mathbf{X}$ for computing the potential energy $E_{\textrm{pot}}$ during subspace learning and skinning-based real-time animation. This sampling captures volumetric deformation behavior that surface-only sampling cannot, in contrast to popular 3D Shape VAEs  that only sample surface points. To sample interior cubature points, we first convert the object’s surface mesh into a watertight mesh , then uniformly sample points in the voxelized spatial grid using ray tracing , and classify points as being outside the object if the ray intersects the surface mesh and the dot product with the normal is negative. For surface cubature points, we employ Sharp Edge Sampling (SES)  to better capture geometric details.Cubature Points Sampling.[]

III-CPhysics-Informed Self-Supervised Learning

To learn a deformation subspace mapping directly from static geometry without annotated skinning data or precomputed simulation trajectories, we train the neural skinning fields autoencoder with a Physics-Informed Self-Supervised Learning (PISSL) strategy. The learned skinning fields should be spatially smooth and mutually independent, while inducing low-energy deformations. We therefore formulate a self-supervised objective consisting of potential-energy, smoothness, and orthogonality terms:

$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{subspace}}(\theta)=\mathcal{L}_{\text{smooth}}(\theta)+\lambda_{\text{pot}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{pot}}(\theta)+\lambda_{\text{orth}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{orth}}(\theta),$ (6)

where $\lambda_{\text{pot}}$ and $\lambda_{\text{orth}}$ weight the potential-energy and orthogonality losses, respectively. The additional objective for rig-complementary learning is introduced in Sec. .

III-E

Evolution of neural skinning fields during optimization. Starting from disordered initial representations, our physics-informed self-supervised learning progressively organizes them into physically consistent, approximately orthogonal, and spatially smooth skinning results. For visualization, each skinning weight function $\bm{W}_{i}$ is divided by $\max|\bm{W}_{i}|$ to fall within $[-1,1]$ .Fig. 3:

To encourage physically plausible deformations, we construct a low-energy subspace  by minimizing the expected potential energy of deformations induced by randomly sampled subspace coordinates $\mathbf{z}\in\mathbb{R}^{12m}$ :Physical Constraints.[]

49

$\mathcal{L}_{\text{pot}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z}\sim\mathcal{N}}[E_{\textrm{pot}}^{\theta}(\phi(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{z}))],\vskip 3.99994pt$ (7)

where $\mathbf{z}$ is defined in Sec. , and $\mathcal{N}=\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mu^{2}\mathbf{I}_{12m})$ denotes a Gaussian distribution over $\mathbb{R}^{12m}$ with $\mu=0.2$ . The expectation is estimated by averaging the potential energy over sampled subspace coordinates within a training batch. Here, $E_{\textrm{pot}}^{\theta}(\phi(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{z}))$ denotes the object’s potential energy evaluated using the deformation map induced by $\mathbf{z}$ under the current network parameters $\theta$ , with spatial integration approximated using cubature points. During training, we linearly interpolate the potential energy computation from the linear elasticity  model to the Neo-Hookean  model to enhance training stability . Besides the low-energy constraint imposed by $\mathcal{L}_{\text{pot}}$ , we also expect $\Phi_{\theta}(\mathbf{X})$ to be spatially smooth, so we introduce a spatial smoothness loss:

44

$\mathcal{L}_{\text{smooth}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{X}\sim\mathcal{S}}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\|\nabla\Phi_{\theta}^{i}(\mathbf{X})\|^{2},$ (8)

where $\mathcal{S}$ denotes the set of sampled cubature points introduced in Sec. , and $\nabla\Phi_{\theta}^{i}$ is the spatial gradient of the $i$ -th skinning weight function at point $\mathbf{X}$ under the current network parameters $\theta$ .

III-B

To enhance subspace expressiveness, we introduce a loss that promotes orthogonality among the learned skinning weight functions:Orthogonality Constraint.

$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{orth}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}\sim\mathcal{S}}\left[\sum_{i=1}^{m}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}j=1\\

j\neq i\end{subarray}}^{m}\Big(\Phi_{\theta}^{i}(\mathbf{X}_{\mathcal{D}})^{\top}\Phi_{\theta}^{j}(\mathbf{X}_{\mathcal{D}})\Big)^{2}\right],$ (9)

where $\mathcal{D}$ denotes a training batch of cubature points sampled from the overall set $\mathcal{S}$ , and $\mathbf{X}_{\mathcal{D}}$ represents the corresponding point matrix within the batch.

Simplicits  jointly penalizes deviations from orthogonality and unit magnitude. We instead $\ell_{2}$ -normalize each column of the skinning weight matrix evaluated at the batch points on the fly. This normalization regulates the scale of the learned modes and prevents numerical drift during training, thereby facilitating optimization of the orthogonality objective and promoting more independent neural skinning fields. However, gradients of the self-supervised loss terms can differ substantially in magnitude and conflict in direction, making naive joint optimization unstable. To overcome this challenge, we complement our on-the-fly skinning-field normalization with ConFIG  to correct conflicting gradients and stabilize joint optimization.

In Fig. , we visualize the evolution of different skinning modes during optimization, demonstrating that our physics-informed self-supervised framework progressively organizes the initially unstructured skinning representations into low-energy, approximately orthogonal, and spatially smooth skinning results, which are then used for real-time physics-based animation as detailed in Sec. .Stable Joint Optimization.[]

III-D

III-DSkinning-Based Real-Time Animation

The learned neural skinning fields define a continuous subspace mapping through which reduced coordinates determine full-space deformations for physics-based animation. We first describe the basic reduced dynamics, and then incorporate boundary conditions, external control, and contact energies. Rig-complementary dynamics is introduced separately in Sec. .

III-E

With the skinning-based subspace representation, we can create motions with physically plausible deformations directly in the reduced-order subspace. We discretize the governing Newtonian physical equations using standard implicit time integration and update the subspace coordinates $\mathbf{z}$ over time as:Subspace Dynamics.

$\mathbf{z}_{t+1}=\underset{\mathbf{z}}{\arg\min}\;\frac{1}{2h^{2}}\|\mathbf{z}-2\mathbf{z}_{t}+\mathbf{z}_{t-1}\|_{\mathbf{M}}^{2}+E_{\textrm{pot}}(\phi(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{z})),$ (10)

where $h$ is the time step size, $\|\cdot\|_{\mathbf{M}}$ is the norm induced by the reduced mass matrix $\mathbf{M}$ , and $E_{\textrm{pot}}$ is the potential energy that induces the internal force, with $E_{\textrm{pot}}$ supporting general hyperelastic material models. This formulation can be solved using standard Newton-based methods . The much lower subspace dimensionality allows efficient optimization of Eq. () , enabling real-time physics-based animation.[]

46

10

[]

6
