We first evaluate neural skinning on unseen objects from the test set of the RigNet  dataset to assess generalization. The RigNet dataset provides annotated skinning data; we fine-tune the pretrained feed-forward neural skinning baselines using these annotations, whereas our model is trained only on the 3D meshes. Table  reports the quantitative comparison on unseen objects. Our method significantly outperforms the baselines across all three evaluation metrics, demonstrating its generalization ability.

We further evaluate our method on the ShapeNet dataset , which provides clearly defined object categories. Our model is trained jointly across all categories, and all baselines are evaluated on the corresponding test sets. Because Simplicits can only be trained on a single object at a time, we train an individual Simplicits model for each object. The quantitative results in Table  show that our method consistently outperforms all baselines.

In Fig.  and Fig. , we compare the qualitative skinning results with the baselines. Our method produces more physically consistent, geometrically orthogonal, and spatially smooth skinning results. Fig.  and Fig.  further show that our method generalizes to unseen objects and produces high-quality skinning results. For additional results, please refer to the supplementary material.Results.[]

Rig-Complementary Neural Skinning Fields.

We evaluate the neural skinning fields learned with our self-supervised rig-complementarity objective on characters from the RigNet dataset [

62

], which provides the skeletal rigs and associated LBS skinning weights. Fig.

shows the learned fields across diverse character geometries and rig structures, with spatially varying patterns over the body and appendages. We further examine the resulting complementary elastic responses under interactive rig control and user-authored animation sequences in Sec.

IV-D

IV-CAblation Studies

To validate our design choices, we conduct ablation studies covering both the key components of the proposed Physics-Informed Self-Supervised Learning (PISSL) strategy and the rig-space complementarity term in the rig-complementary setting, using the RigNet  dataset. As shown in Table , we remove or modify the PISSL components to assess their individual effects on model performance. Specifically, we evaluate the smoothness loss $\mathcal{L}_{\text{smooth}}$ , the orthogonality constraint $\mathcal{L}_{\text{orth}}$ , the skinning normalization process, the ONI  layer, and conflict-aware gradient correction using ConFIG . The quantitative results demonstrate that these components maintain the numerical stability and orthogonality of the learned neural skinning fields, which are essential for well-conditioned and physically consistent deformation behavior. In Fig. , we visualize the skinning results obtained without the potential energy loss $\mathcal{L}_{\text{pot}}$ , where the model fails to produce physically interpretable skinning fields. Fig.  further compares neural skinning fields learned with and without $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{comp}}$ . Without this term, the visualized fields form broad regions across the head, torso, and limbs. Incorporating $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{comp}}$ changes these distributions, with visible differences in the ears, wings, and limb regions across multiple characters. These comparisons illustrate the effect of rig-space complementarity learning on the spatial organization of the skinning fields.[]

IV-DDiverse Real-Time Physics-Based Animation

We next examine the broader animation scope enabled by PhysSkin++. Its discretization-agnostic neural skinning fields support efficient reduced dynamics for controllable and collision-aware animation, rig-complementary animation, and direct binding to 3D Gaussian representations.

Time Efficiency. We first evaluate the time efficiency of our skinning-based subspace animation. We compare it with a classical FEM method using implicit time integration and an MPM method using explicit time integration. For these two full-space physical simulators, we use open-source high-performance GPU implementations , [

9

68

]. All methods are evaluated on the same CPU and GPU hardware. As shown in Table , our method demonstrates excellent time efficiency.

Controllable and Collision-Aware Animation.

Beyond unconstrained deformation, we qualitatively examine how the learned neural skinning subspaces respond to prescribed controls and environmental contact. As shown in Fig.

4

(a), the Dirichlet boundary conditions enforce zero displacement over the prescribed upper regions, while the unconstrained geometry deforms under gravity. In the interactive sequences of Fig.

4

(b), the lower region of each object is fixed by Dirichlet boundary conditions, while Gaussian-kernel-weighted dragging provides localized control over the remaining deformable domain. Fig.

4

(c) further demonstrates contact with planar environments across diverse shapes and boundary orientations, with the contact response modeled by the boundary-penalty energy in Eq. (

14

).

We further evaluate collision-aware animation involving multiple objects. In the rigid–deformable sequences of Fig.

5

(a), a rigid body is released from an elevated position and falls under gravity onto a deformable object. Contact between the two objects is modeled by the point-pair IPC-style barrier in Eq. (

15

), while contact with the supporting floor is handled by the boundary-penalty energy in Eq. (

14

). In the deformable–deformable sequences of Fig.

5

(b), multiple deformable objects are released from elevated positions and fall under gravity. Contacts among the falling objects are resolved using the point-pair IPC-style barrier in Eq. (

15

), while their contact with the supporting floor is modeled by the boundary-penalty energy in Eq. (

14

). These results demonstrate controllable deformation and multi-object interaction within the PhysSkin++ skinning-based reduced representation.

Rig-Complementary Animation.

We evaluate the resulting rig-complementary animation under both interactive control and user-authored animation sequences, as shown in Fig.

7

. For interactive rig control, we implement a Polyscope-based graphical interface [

48

] that allows users to manipulate bone poses at runtime. The resulting rig motion defines the primary animation, while PhysSkin++ computes the corresponding complementary elastic response. For user-authored rig animation, we obtain source skeletal animation sequences from Mixamo [

1

] and retarget them to the target character rigs using Auto-Rig Pro [

3

]. In both settings, PhysSkin++ augments the primary rig animation with temporally evolving, physics-based complementary deformation.

Animation results on 3DGS models .Fig. 15: []

42

Discretization-Agnostic 3D Gaussian Animation. Owing to the discretization-agnostic nature of our neural skinning formulation, the learned deformation fields can be evaluated directly on 3D Gaussian primitives without introducing an underlying mesh discretization. Following the 3D Gaussian binding formulation in Sec.

III-F

, we evaluate PhysSkin++ on the ShapeSplat dataset [

42

], which contains 3D Gaussian reconstructions of objects from ShapeNet [

7

]. As shown in Fig.

15

, the learned fields are queried at the Gaussian rest centers, and the induced local affine deformation updates both the centers and anisotropic covariances to produce coherent physics-based animation. We encourage readers to visit our project page for additional animation videos.

V Conclusion

In this paper, we present PhysSkin++, a generalizable physics-informed framework for real-time physics-based animation across diverse 3D shapes and discretizations. A neural skinning fields autoencoder learns continuous skinning fields directly from static geometries to define a skinning-based subspace mapping. Our Physics-Informed Self-Supervised Learning (PISSL) strategy promotes physically plausible deformations through a self-supervised objective and stabilizes joint optimization through on-the-fly skinning-field normalization and conflict-aware gradient correction. At runtime, a reduced dynamics formulation advances the reduced coordinates and supports Dirichlet boundary conditions, interactive control, environmental interaction, and both rigid–deformable and deformable–deformable contact. Beyond purely physics-driven animation, we extend the deformation representation with prescribed rig displacement and the self-supervised objective with a rig-space complementarity term, enabling complementary elastic responses for prescribed rig animations without enforcing the complementarity constraint at runtime. The continuous deformation map also enables discretization-agnostic binding to meshes, point clouds, and 3D Gaussian representations. Experiments demonstrate that PhysSkin++ achieves outstanding performance on generalizable neural skinning while enabling real-time physics-based animation. As a limitation, our current formulation does not incorporate semantic priors for modeling complex geometries. Future work will explore such priors to improve the expressiveness of the learned skinning-based subspace mapping.

item.title: 图形编程周报 #458：四元数 log/exp 的 SIMD 实现与本周精选 ｜ Graphics Programming Weekly - Issue 458 - October 11th, 2026
item.description:
一句话：本周图形论文与博客精选，头条是针对单位四元数的 SIMD 友好 log/exp 实现。

要点：

  • 单位四元数 log/exp 的可向量化实现，误差与吞吐都做了量化对比
  • 汇集本周新出的图形论文、引擎技术博客与工具更新
  • 每期按主题分组，是跟进图形前沿成本最低的一份周报

为什么值得看：动画与姿态系统里四元数插值无处不在，SIMD 化能直接吃到 CPU 端性能。

中文摘要：本期周报汇集了 2026 年 10 月中旬的图形学论文与工程博客。头条是一份针对单位四元数 log/exp 的专用实现，采用 SIMD 友好写法，给出了误差与性能数据，适合动画、IK、姿态混合等高频插值场景直接采用。其余条目按渲染、几何、工具链分组，覆盖本周新论文与引擎侧技术分享。

主题：游戏引擎

来源：Graphics Programming Weekly（English）

Graphics Programming Weekly 458

Sun, Oct 11, 2026

weekly

presents specialized SIMD-friendly log and exp functions for unit quaternions

achieves error bounds comparable to standard-library implementations while avoiding full-turn angle ambiguity

introduces Reservoir Light Replay Backpropagation (ResLRB) for reverse-mode differentiable light tracing

compresses the adjoint graph during the primal pass with a streaming weighted reservoir

yields an unbiased gradient estimator whose peak memory is independent of path length

analyzes a frame of Hitman World of Assassination

covers G-buffer generation, tiled deferred lighting, cascaded shadows, screen-space ambient occlusion/reflections, volumetric fog and post-processing

maps GPU optimization instincts from graphics to large-language-model inference

benchmarks Qwen3 models on an RTX 3090 across quantization, Flash Attention, KV-cache compression and speculative decoding

shows optimization targeting the different bottlenecks

provides a self-study roadmap for learning graphics programming from free online resources

recommends C++, CMake, SDL alongside linear algebra, projective geometry and data structures

summarizes recent WebGPU and WGSL additions shipping in Chrome 155-156

highlights the fragment_depth extension, unaligned compressed textures, new linear color spaces and the snorm10-10-10-2 vertex format

introduces the upcoming bindless texture sampling support in WebGPU via GPUResourceTable

demonstrates a projected-decal emoji demo

compares bindless allocation against texture-array fallbacks and notes future heterogeneous resource tables

presents a real-time collision-detection framework for SDF-encoded geometry

combines temporal coherence caching with curvature-guided importance sampling to form sparse contact manifolds

runs complex scenes with thousands of rigid bodies

explains Metal dual-source blending, where a fragment shader emits a primary and secondary color for the blend unit

walks through using the technique to approximate sRGB-correct blending for Dear ImGui

concludes that programmable blending provides a more exact match on supported Apple Silicon GPUs

presents a plug-in acceleration suite for order-independent transparency

exploits spatial and temporal coherence through adaptive tiled sampling or variable-rate shading plus temporal reprojection

covers the development of a custom 2D lighting system in Unity for the cyberpunk game Glitch Hunt

applies data-oriented design principles to support hundreds of concurrent dynamic lights with minimal CPU overhead

details hand-drawn specular and bloom maps alongside reactive fog and rain systems

releases DxTimingCaptureLibrary, an open-source C++ helper for DirectX ETW events

exposes GPU timings, object lifetime, residency/paging, DirectStorage, pipeline compiles and PIX markers

provides samples for console logging, Perfetto tracing, D3D12 journal entries and memory visualization

updates meshoptimizer support for hierarchical clustered LOD using NVIDIA’s vk_lod_clusters sample

discusses meshopt compression, simplification improvements, error clamping and a new meshlet topology codec

shows the Zorah scene processing pipeline and foliage area-preservation heuristics

explains how Blender’s move from OpenGL to Vulkan and Metal exposed shader portability, compilation-time and legacy GLSL maintenance challenges

introduces Blender Shading Language (BSL), a C++ subset for sharing code between CPU and GPU

outlines plans to migrate more legacy shaders, expand C++ syntax support and consider binary formats as graphics standards evolve

explains how bgfx’s shaderc translates a GLSL dialect to many backend languages without its own AST

relies on the C preprocessor, textual patching and real target compilers such as FXC, DXC, Glslang and Tint

compares the approach with modern alternatives

presents a method that combines standard triangle mesh representations with per-pixel local raymarching to render displacement maps, volumetric effects, and self-shadowing on bone-animated meshes

preserves exisitng workflows and fallback to normal mapping

Thanks to for support of this series.

Nia Bickford

item.title: Capcom 的 AI 布局为何「翻译失灵」 ｜ Capcom's New AI Venture Gets Lost in Translation
item.description:
一句话：复盘 Capcom 的 AI 尝试：技术没问题，问题出在表达与定位。

要点：

  • 分析 Capcom 对外发布的 AI 计划引发的争议
  • 讨论日系厂商在 AI 叙事上的沟通难题
  • 对照其他工作室更成功的 AI 落地方式

为什么值得看：引擎与工具团队常要面对「怎么向制作人和玩家解释 AI」这个问题，这是一份现实案例。

中文摘要：AI and Games 本周以 Capcom 的 AI 举措为切入点，讨论一个常被忽视的维度：技术本体并不是问题，真正让项目受阻的是对外表达与定位。作者复盘了 Capcom 相关发布引发的争议，对照其他工作室更平稳的 AI 落地路径，指出日系厂商在「AI 叙事」上的沟通结构性问题。对需要向非技术同事解释 AI 方案的团队有借鉴价值。

主题：游戏引擎

来源：AI and Games（English）

Hello and welcome to this week’s edition of AI and Games. I’m feeling pretty under the weather this week sadly as some plague has descended upon our house somehow.

This week will be a little shorter than usual given I am propped up on a variety of drugs but still wanted to get something out to you. With a focus on the Capcom’s comments last week on their planned updates to their proprietary RE engine that were misrepresented by a lot of the gaming press and social media.

Follow AI and Games on:

BlueSky

|

YouTube

|

LinkedIn

|

TikTok

Couple of quick announcements for you, including another Tommy sighting in the wild next week. Provided I shake off this horrid cough…

Very excited to say that this time next week myself and fellow AI and Games Conference founders Duygu Cakmak and Matthias Siemonsmeier will be at Game Republic New Horizons! Running from 14th-16th October in sunny Middlesborough, we’re doing something we’ve never actually tried before: speaking together on stage! We promise a fun panel as we dig into the current state of AI in the games industry in 2026. Expect some strong opinions, and a friendly bit of banter among friends.

Oh good grief we’re only five weeks out: five weeks! It’s all systems go here at AI and Games HQ as myself, Shraddha, Sally, and the rest of the team are all chipping away at the 101 things we need to do to get ready for this years event. Don’t forget to

grab your tickets

if you haven’t already. But for now, here’s more talk announcements!

Cheat Codes and Compliance CodesThe Legal Playbook for AI and Games in 2026Rupam Davé / Lewis Silkin

We’re pleased to welcome back Rupam Davé to talk once again about the ever-evolving legal landscape surrounding Machine Learning and Generative AI and its adoption in the video games industry. Rupam’s presentations have continued to prove popular each year at the conference, and he now holds the record as the longest-serving speaker at the AI and Games Conference having presented in 2024 and 2025.

From Multiplayer to Single Player: Shipping Generative AI Temps in Dimensional Double ShiftBrian Tanner and Alex Kearney / Artificial Agency

Dimensional Double Shift is a co-op VR title released for the Meta Quest where players have to work together and coordinate around complex tasks. However, what would the circumstances need to look like for this to ship AI teammates? Alex and Brian from Artificial Agency dig into how this was achieved using small-scale Generative AI agents in the cloud, albeit capped to operate within a hard two-second window. With insight into how to operate three concurrent agents all while ensuring they run at significantly smaller inference costs than your typical GenAI models.

Perception and reaction systems for large amounts of NPCsAlejandro Moya / Grip Studios

Last but most certainly not least for this week’s announcements we welcome Alejandro Moya from Grip Studios who in recent years have been co-developers on titles such as Subnautica, Mafia: The Old Country, and Marvel’s Midnight Suns. Moya will be sharing their insights into building perception systems for large numbers of NPCs in ways that scale in practical and sensible ways. Something of a spiritual sequel to the

fantastic perception talk

from Vadim Petrov of Warhorse Studios in 2025.

Some headlines in brief:

SEGA is insistent that they’re being

“very cautious”

around the use of AI in creative works.

Call of Duty creators Activision discuss how

cheating is now an $8.5 billion industry

and AI is certainly contributing to that issue. A point we need to discuss on our case study series in the future.

Base PS5’s are now getting

their own version of AI upscaling

courtesy of Quick Spectral Super Resolution (QSSR) rolling out for Wolverine and Ghost of Yotei.

Micron

celebrates

higher prices for customers and record profits as RAM supply expected to worsen in 2027.

Google announces

their new Playground platform

, essentially their own AI game engine creator.

Thanks for reading AI and Games! This post is public so feel free to share it.

Share

Capcom’s inhouse games platform: the RE Engine

Last week was Capcom’s own in-house tech conference Capcom Open Conference RE: 2026, and a big part of that event was discussions around the future of the RE engine. However, while the games industry has been enthralled by their releases in recent years ranging from Resident Evil: Requiem to Street Fighter 6, Pragmata, Monster Hunter: Wilds and more recently Onimusha: Way of the Sword, folks were up in arms about the suggestion that they’re transforming the engine into a system built for Generative AI games. An issue that stemmed both from again misunderstandings of how AI works in games, but also a fundamental issue of translation.

Image Credit:

GameBiz.jp

The ‘REach for the moon’ Engine - that’s right kids, it doesn’t stand for Resident Evil - is the successor to the MT Framework and has been used in production since Resident Evil 7: Biohazard released in 2017. It’s since been used for virtually all of Capcom’s titles in recent years, including all of the titles mentioned above as well as the modern reboots of classic Resident Evil games. During the conference there was a presentation by programmer Satoshi Ishida entitled “The Outlook and Future of the ‘REX’ Project”. REX is the codename given to the next generation version of the RE engine (dubbed ‘RE neXt Engine’) which has been in development since at least 2023.

During the presentation Ishida gave a brief discussion of some of the major challenges faced by developers at the studio. Notably that many simple tasks can prove time consuming and onerous, and that the engine needs to become easier to use as the number of devs on a given project increases. Hence their solution is to integrate AI tooling into future workflows. The intention being to update the engine to allow for more effective integration of AI models for areas such as editor tools, development support, and quality assurance.

The new modules being built as part of REX

This has led to the creation of new components to the RE engine, all of which integrating AI in some form or another. Note that none of these components are AI modules in themselves, but are described as potentially integrating AI models in their efforts to be more efficient. Now this all makes sense. Both given there are a variety of machine learning models already used in some aspects of game development, but there is also potential for them to integrate LLMs to support in specific tasks. Ishida gave some examples in the talk such as translating data from various file formats and syntaxes, to performant code generation based off visual editing workflows.

While Capcom remain cagey about embracing Generative AI for assets, the integration of machine learning and potential generative models to support common tasks of the dev team sounds like a much more reasonable and sensible approach - even compared to some of the more egregious examples of public engines

like Unreal Engine 6

. This strikes me as a more sensible adoption of AI into workflows given it appears to be driven by their own experiences of actually shipping content with their engine.

Now I first caught wind of this while on a short vacation and seeing the IGN story being bounced around with a lot of sensational rhetoric around this being how Capcom now embraces GenAI in their games. Though I really read this as far removed from such an assessment. What Ishida describes is changing parts of a workflow to now integrate AI tools to support an existing process, rather than merely supplant it - and the humans involved - with AI tooling.

But perhaps the other key aspect of what drove this misunderstanding outside of the most folks lack of understanding of AI’s use in games, is a sentence in the report by GameBiz which when machine-translated into English reads like this:

Ishida commented that these technological advancements will ultimately lead to the larger goal of evolving into an "AI-generation game engine."

This appears to be where many a headline such as those by

Eurogamer

and

IGN

emerged from, but I think this has been misread as ‘an engine that generates games with AI’ rather than simply ‘an engine updated to reflect the current era of AI technologies’.

This was later corroborated by folks more fluent in Japanese than I am. Notably John Linneman over at Digital Foundry who pointed out that the term ‘generation’ in this translation is in reference to an epoch. This is an ‘age of AI’ - a generation if you will - and not referring to the use of AI as a means to generate content.

Note: Eurogamer has since amended the story and removed the original social media post implying that the engine is focussed on AI-generation.

So what this means in the future we’ll still waiting to see. But I do believe that this is a headline that’s been blown out of proportion once again as a result of a lack of understanding of AI integration. Though admittedly there was a language barrier this time around!

Okay, yup… that’ll do. I need more drugs. Catch you next week!

Discussion about this post

No posts

Ready for more?

item.title: CrossTL：跨语言 GPU 程序翻译如何保留源语言语义 ｜ CrossTL: Hub-Based Translation of GPU Programs and the Preservation of Source-Language Rules
item.description:
一句话：用中枢式中间表示把一种着色器语言翻译成另一种，同时保住源语言的语义规则。

要点：

  • 跨图形 API 的着色器移植长期靠人工重写
  • 采用 hub 式中转结构而非两两直译
  • 重点解决源语言特有语义在翻译中丢失的问题

为什么值得看：多平台引擎的着色器维护成本极高；这类自动翻译方案直接对应「一次编写多端运行」的工程诉求。

Abstract.

GPU programs are written in vendor languages that share a syntax but disagree on what operations mean: on integer overflow, division by zero, NaN handling, floating-point contraction, data layout and dispatch. A translated program can therefore compile on its target and still compute something else.

We study what a hub language that connects many GPU languages must record to preserve meaning, using CrossTL, a source-to-source translator that routes ten languages to eleven targets.

We define faithful translation as refinement up to rejection under a compile configuration and a recorded state encoding. In a model of operation rules, recording each operation’s rule and lowering it through one table per target preserves meaning when annotation is sound and complete and the table is sound; given an exact frame, every target construct must refine the source’s rule, and a hub that does not refuse must record an operation’s source exactly where defined rules conflict.

We ran 66 hazard kernels in six languages, 44 of them registered by hash before they ran, on one Apple GPU and on Mesa’s CPU drivers: SPIRV-Cross, naga, Tint, Slang and CrossTL each lose some source rule, and outcomes change with the compile configuration and the Vulkan implementation.

Carrying the rules removes 32 of 37 divergences on the carried rules, and none of 462 held-out executions diverges; the five that remain are MoltenVK wrap-around failures, three of which a conformant Vulkan driver for Metal reproduces. An SMT check of the rule table finds 13 of 131 entries unsound as recorded.

On 2,585 third-party programs, established translators produce valid graphics code more often than CrossTL in 31 of 39 comparisons, and carrying the rules changes validity by at most 0.2 points per target.

1.

GPU programs are written in vendor languages: game engines keep their shaders in GLSL or HLSL, machine-learning frameworks for Apple silicon write their kernels in the Metal Shading Language (MSL), and scientific codes for NVIDIA hardware use CUDA.

Moving such code to another platform means translating it, and the established tools each cover part of the space: compilers and decompilers around SPIR-V , translators with their own intermediate representations, such as naga, Tint and Slang , and one-directional translators for compute code .(; ; )

Getting the syntax right is the easy part.

shows a one-line GLSL kernel and what ten translation routes make of it on seven runtime configurations.

GLSL defines signed addition to wrap around, so is false for the largest integer; MSL inherits C++’s rule that signed overflow is undefined, and Apple’s compiler folds the comparison to true.

Every route that copies the operator into MSL, including SPIRV-Cross and CrossTL, the hub-based translator that this paper studies, yields a program that compiles and computes the wrong answer, and so does HLSL compiled by DXC, which marks signed arithmetic as non-wrapping.

naga and Tint succeed, because their intermediate representations give signed arithmetic wrap-around semantics and their back ends polyfill it , while MoltenVK, a Vulkan layer over Metal, miscompiles even correct SPIR-V, and so, for addition, does KosmicKrisp, a conformant Vulkan driver for the same GPU.

The languages also disagree on unsigned division by zero, NaN operands of , contraction of $a\cdot b+c$ , buffer layouts and partial work-groups (), and none of these rules is visible in a program’s text.

The difficulty is sharpest for translators built around a hub language, which need one importer per source and one emitter per target instead of one translator per pair .

A hub that records only an operator cannot tell whether the operation follows GLSL’s rule or MSL’s.

Compiler intermediate representations avoid the problem by fixing one semantics per operation and recording deviations from it, as LLVM does with flags, poison values and fast-math flags and SPIR-V with decorations and float-control modes ; shader translators inherit the semantics of one language, WGSL for naga and Tint, SPIR-V for SPIRV-Cross.

A hub that accepts many source languages has no single semantics to inherit. We ask what such a hub must record to preserve the meaning of the programs it translates.()

This paper.

We study CrossTL, an open-source translator that imports ten GPU languages (GLSL, HLSL, Metal with its C++ templates, SPIR-V assembly, CUDA, HIP, OpenCL C, Rust-GPU, Mojo and Slang) into CrossGL, a textual hub language, and emits eleven, WGSL and GLSL ES among them. We define faithful translation, show that carrying each operation’s source-language rule through the hub suffices for it and when it is necessary, implement rule carrying in CrossTL as CrossTL-R, and evaluate both, with a suite of hazard kernels, an analysis plan and three hypotheses registered by hash before CrossTL-R ran. Our contributions are:

•

a semantic account of GPU program translation ( and ): a specification-derived catalogue of 18 classes of operations on which eight GPU languages disagree, faithfulness as refinement up to rejection, obligations and their treatments, and the bases on which a passing test can rest;

Results.

SPIRV-Cross, naga, Tint, Slang and CrossTL each lose some source rule, and outcomes change with Metal’s math mode and the Vulkan implementation. Carrying the rules removes 32 of the 37 divergences on the carried rules, 24 of them failures of CrossTL’s own SPIR-V output, against 14 for local fixes to that emitter, and on the held-out kernels CrossTL-R diverged in none of 462 executions; the five that remain are MoltenVK wrap-around failures, three of which KosmicKrisp, a conformant driver for the same GPU, reproduces in an exploratory run. A mechanical check finds 13 of the table’s 131 operator entries unsound as recorded; the suite’s matches on them hold only by implementation. A single strongest semantics would keep the same rules with about nine times as many rewrites (exploratory). On third-party code, 31 % of CrossTL’s translations are usable, established translators produce valid output more often in 31 of 39 comparisons, and carrying the rules changes no target’s accepted share by more than 0.2 points.

2.

GPU languages share a vocabulary of vectors, buffers, barriers and stage entry points, but they give the same operations different meanings.

From the specifications of GLSL, HLSL, MSL, WGSL, SPIR-V, CUDA and OpenCL C we derived a catalogue of 18 classes of such differences (H1–H18) .

gives the rules on values, and in those on the floating-point environment, memory and execution. Each cell rests on a clause of the language’s specification, quoted in the artifact, with one exception.

HLSL’s specification is a draft that is silent on most rows , so we state HLSL’s rules twice: the legacy rules of the Direct3D bytecode (DXBC) that the FXC compiler emits , against which many shaders were written, and the rules under which DXC, the current compiler, translates them to DXIL , which we established by inspecting and executing the code it emits. The evaluation uses the current rules; repeats it under the legacy ones.(; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; )

Values.

On signed overflow the languages fall into three groups. GLSL, WGSL and SPIR-V define signed arithmetic to wrap around. CUDA and OpenCL C inherit from C and C++ the rule that signed overflow is undefined, and MSL restates it; Apple’s Metal compiler uses the rule (). MSL departs from C++ elsewhere: it masks shift counts and leaves with a negative operand undefined. HLSL falls between: DXBC’s wraps, but DXC marks signed additions and multiplications and folds to true even without optimisation.

Shift counts, unsigned division by zero, float-to-integer conversion and with a NaN operand each have three or more answers.

The floating-point environment.

By default every language lets a compiler contract $a\cdot b+c$ into a fused multiply-add, and most defaults let it assume that NaNs and infinities do not occur.

The opt-outs differ in kind: per operation ( in GLSL and HLSL, in SPIR-V), per scope ( in MSL, in OpenCL C), per entry point, instruction or type (SPIR-V’s float-control execution modes and its per-instruction fast-math flags, core since Vulkan 1.4 ), per compilation (Metal’s compile options), or not at all (WGSL).

Some opt-outs are optional device features, and some are partial: MSL’s safe mode still allows contraction within a statement . A program’s meaning therefore depends on a configuration that its text does not contain, and the effect can be large: compiled for an Apple M2 Max with the API default of fast math and fast functions, MSL’s for $|a|\leq 10^{4}$ has a median error of 40 units in the last place (ULP) and a 99th percentile of 80,263 ULP, against 0 and 2 ULP with precise functions.preciseNoContraction#pragma METAL fpFP_CONTRACT(; )

Memory and execution.

A Metal occupies 16 bytes in a buffer, whereas an HLSL structured buffer of has a 12-byte stride, so a translation that copies the type changes the layout that the host must upload.

Metal can launch a partial work-group, which most other APIs cannot, so a Metal kernel that omits its bounds check is correct only on Metal; and MSL leaves the SIMD-group width implementation-defined, whereas Direct3D wave sizes range from 4 to 128.float3float3

3.

CrossTL has four layers ( in ). print native programs as CrossGL text, one parses CrossGL into a syntax tree, eleven walk the tree, and a turns a repository into a planned translation whose artifacts carry contracts that loaders check. Ten importers and eleven emitters cover 110 directed language pairs. CrossTL is written in Python and is open source; statements about it refer to the implementation archived in our artifact.

3.1.

CrossGL is a C-family language with extensions from Rust and WGSL: declarations, bindings, expressions, generics with trait bounds, WGSL-style address spaces, and for sixteen canonical stages, from vertex to ray-tracing callable; in shows a kernel in CrossGL. Two design decisions shape the system.

First, . Each importer builds its own native syntax tree and prints CrossGL, which the front end parses again. The hub is therefore inspectable, but in practice it is a family of dialects: the front end accepts variant spellings of the same metadata and treats unknown type names as named types, so that importers can stay close to their sources, and every emitter must accept every dialect.

Second, , and languages are registered by binding them to an importer or an emitter. There is no typed or lowered representation; the front end validates metadata, stage layouts and stage interfaces but does not check types, and each emitter infers types itself, recursively over tables of declarations, struct members and swizzles, resolving overloads by argument types. The hub therefore cannot tell which language’s rule an operation follows ().fnletmatchstage blocks

3.2.

An importer maps its language’s resource model onto CrossGL resources, keeping the source’s binding attributes (descriptor sets and bindings, registers and spaces, buffer indices, specialisation constants) for the emitters to map into their targets’ index spaces, explicit bindings first.

MSL is a C++ dialect, and production Metal libraries use templates heavily: the 49 files of Apple’s MLX framework  instantiate templates into 17,832 host-visible kernel entries. Since no target has the same templates, the Metal importer the program before parsing it, in a sequence of source-to-source steps (); an argument that cannot be deduced is reported, not guessed.

The SPIR-V importer reads assembly and decompiles it: it rebuilds one structured construct per function from the merge instructions, turns two-way $\phi$ -nodes into conditional expressions, and flattens other control flow, a source of silent defects ().

Some rules are discharged in the hub itself. For , , , and seven other Metal functions, the importer writes an explicit CrossGL implementation into the program, adapted from Arm’s optimized-routines, so that an emitter has to translate only integer arithmetic, bit reinterpretation and binary32 operations faithfully, without reassociating or contracting them..metal()

The eleven emitters are hand-written tree walkers. The SPIR-V emitter prints assembly, producing structured control flow by construction and keeping locals in function-scope variables rather than $\phi$ -nodes. The GLSL and HLSL emitters carry most of the semantic machinery: a C-family conversion model for integer promotion and narrowing, binary16 emulated in binary32 with re-rounding after every operation , lowering of device pointers to (resource, offset) pairs, emulation of 32-lane subgroups through shared memory, which they refuse outside provably uniform control flow, and narrowing of indices that a constant, an interval analysis or a declared range bounds.

When an emitter meets a construct it cannot lower, it with a typed diagnostic, to a default value, type or padding while leaving a comment, or an identifier it does not know and leaves the failure to the target compiler. A fallback is a silent loss that only a comment marks, and formatting can strip comments, so our evaluation reads the raw emitter output.()

3.3.

A project file supplies the facts that single-file translation cannot know, such as work-group sizes, subgroup widths, specialisation constants and ranges of scalar inputs, and the run records a hash of every source and artifact.

Obligations () that concern the host travel in the artifact as JSON contract lines: the exact grid that a kernel written for Metal’s partial thread-groups assumes, ranges of scalar inputs, folded specialisation constants, and the encoding of a buffer whose element type the target lacks, such as binary16 values stored as 16-bit integers for Direct3D without native 16-bit types. That record is an $R$ in the sense of ; for other buffers the host reads the layout from the artifact by reflection, and the encoding is the identity. Caller-trusted index ranges are assumptions, and the run report lists them instead.

Before each dispatch, the loader checks the artifact’s hash and contracts against its package record, the dispatch geometry, the sizes and aliasing of the bound views, and the scalar preconditions on the bytes actually uploaded; a violation rejects the dispatch rather than converting or clamping a value. This implements the check treatment of , which tests.

Programs, configurations and states.

Let $p$ be a program in a source language $S$ , built under a configuration $\kappa$ that comprises compiler options, execution modes and device features.

An input state $\sigma\in\Sigma_{S}$ comprises the buffer contents, the launch geometry and any scalar inputs that the host passes.

We write $\llbracket p\rrbracket_{S,\kappa}(\sigma)$ for the set of outcomes that the specification of $S$ allows, each outcome being final buffer contents or non-termination, to which a deadlock also counts.

The set is never empty: it is a singleton for a fully specified computation, larger for unspecified or implementation-defined results, and contains every outcome when $p$ has undefined behaviour on $\sigma$ .

An is any value of its type, and the program stays defined; a value, as in SPIR-V and LLVM, becomes undefined behaviour only when an operation needs a valid value, such as a branch condition, an address or a divisor .unspecified valuepoison(; ; )

Artifacts, encodings and loaders.

A translator produces an artifact $a$ in a target language $T$ , the configuration $\kappa_{T}$ that the artifact requires, and an encoding $R$ that relates source input states to target input states and target outcomes to source outcomes; under $R$ , for example, a launch may be rounded up to whole work-groups. $R$ must relate every input state that satisfies the assumption $\Phi$ below to some target state; on outcomes it must be the converse of a function, the host’s decoding, which the buffers’ declared types fix independently of $p$ and which maps non-termination to itself; and, like $\kappa_{T}$ , it must be recorded with the artifact in a form that the host or the loader applies. Otherwise an encoding that relates every outcome to every other would make any artifact faithful.

A layout that the module declares in the target’s own terms, such as a SPIR-V or a std430 block, fixes the target’s encoding but does not record $R$ , because it does not say how the source’s data map onto it. An artifact that records no $R$ is read with the identity on host-visible data.

We write $\llbracket a\rrbracket_{T,\kappa_{T},\Psi}$ for the outcomes that $T$ ’s specification allows under $\kappa_{T}$ to the implementations that satisfy an assumption $\Psi$ , such as support for NaN. The artifact’s loader $\mathcal{L}$ may check a predicate on the target state before it dispatches the artifact: $\llbracket\mathcal{L}\circ a\rrbracket_{T,\kappa_{T},\Psi}(\sigma^{\prime})$ is $\{\bot_{\mathit{rej}}\}$ if the check fails on $\sigma^{\prime}$ , and $\llbracket a\rrbracket_{T,\kappa_{T},\Psi}(\sigma^{\prime})$ otherwise. An artifact that $T$ ’s compiler rejects counts as a refusal.ArrayStride

Definition 4.1 (Faithful translation).

The artifact $(a,\kappa_{T},R)$ is to $(p,\kappa)$ under an assumption $\Phi$ on input states and an assumption $\Psi$ on implementations if, for every $\sigma\models\Phi$ and every $\sigma^{\prime}$ with $R(\sigma,\sigma^{\prime})$ , every outcome of $\llbracket\mathcal{L}\circ a\rrbracket_{T,\kappa_{T},\Psi}(\sigma^{\prime})$ is $\bot_{\mathit{rej}}$ , or $p$ has undefined behaviour on $\sigma$ , or the outcome decodes under $R$ to an outcome in $\llbracket p\rrbracket_{S,\kappa}(\sigma)$ .faithful

Faithfulness is refinement up to rejection and encoding; execution can only refute it, because the definition quantifies over every implementation of $T$ that conforms under $\kappa_{T}$ and satisfies $\Psi$ . A checked predicate is enforced by $\mathcal{L}$ , so the states that violate it end in $\bot_{\mathit{rej}}$ , whereas an assumed predicate enters $\Phi$ or $\Psi$ and removes those states or implementations from the quantifier.

Definition 4.2 (Obligation).

Let $\mu$ be a translator’s mapping from source constructs to target constructs, under the configuration $\kappa_{T}$ that the artifact records. A construct $c$ , an operator occurrence whose operands its context supplies, carries an under $\mu$ if, for some program context $C$ , some translation of $C[c]$ that maps $c$ to $\mu(c)$ and is otherwise faithful () is unfaithful to $C[c]$ under $(\mathit{true},\mathit{true})$ .obligation

Obligations depend on the mapping: for MSL’s , emitting SPIR-V’s instead of removes the obligation for non-zero remainders but leaves one for zero remainders, whose sign SPIR-V does not specify. The catalogue of lists the rule pairs for which mapping an operator to its namesake is unfaithful.

A translator can treat an obligation in five ways. It can it, by emitting a construct or a configuration under which the target’s rule refines the source’s; it, by having the loader reject the states for which it cannot; it, by restricting $\Phi$ or $\Psi$ and recording the restriction; , by stopping with a diagnostic; or it, by doing none of these.fmodOpFRemOpFMod

Definition 4.3 (Drop-free translation).

A translator is for a class of obligations if it never drops an obligation of that class.

It is for the class if, in addition, it never relies on an assumption in $\Phi$ or $\Psi$ : every obligation of the class is discharged, checked or refused.drop-freefail-closed

Both properties are relative to a class of obligations: every translator is drop-free for the empty class, and our verdicts are only as complete as the catalogue that defines the classes.

Why a passing test passed.

A run whose result equals the oracle has one of four . The match is when the target’s rule refines the source’s under $\kappa_{T}$ ; it holds when the artifact discharges the obligation, possibly under a configuration or an assumption that it records; it holds when the run matched only under a configuration that the artifact does not record, such as Metal’s safe math mode; and it holds when neither the target’s rule nor the artifact guarantees it.

Only the first two bases support faithfulness; they are the per-occurrence condition of , read off the artifact. A match on either of the other two, for an obligation that the artifact neither discharges nor records, is a : the obligation was dropped, but the runtime that executed the artifact did not expose it.basesdefined by the targetby constructionby configurationby implementation

5.

CrossGL records the syntax of an operation, not which language’s rule it follows: an printed by the GLSL importer wraps on overflow, the same text printed by the Metal importer does not, and an emitter that sees only the hub cannot tell the two apart. This section models the rules, states when carrying them through the hub preserves them, and describes and checks CrossTL-R, which implements rule carrying in CrossTL.x + 1

5.1.

Fix a set of operators, such as signed 32-bit addition, left shift, unsigned division, remainder, narrowing conversion, float-to-integer conversion and , each with an arity and operand types, and let $V$ be the set of values.

A $\rho$ for an $n$ -ary operator maps each argument tuple $v\in V^{n}$ either to a non-empty set $\rho(v)\subseteq V$ of permitted results or to $\top$ , which stands for undefined behaviour; $\rho_{\top}$ is the rule that is undefined everywhere.

A language $L$ gives each operator $\mathit{op}$ a rule $\rho_{L,\kappa}(\mathit{op})$ under each configuration $\kappa$ ; we write $\rho_{L}(\mathit{op})$ for its reference configuration (). For signed addition, $\rho_{\mathrm{GLSL}}(+)(x,y)=\{\mathrm{wrap}_{32}(x+y)\}$ , whereas $\rho_{\mathrm{MSL}}(+)(x,y)=\top$ whenever $x+y$ overflows.

We read the catalogue as follows: an unspecified result is the set of all values of its type; a result that may be poison or LLVM is that set for a source and $\top$ for a target; is unspecified and is $\top$ . This over-approximates what a target may do and under-approximates what a source permits, except that and are read permissively in a source; the guarantees below are relative to this reading.minrule

Definition 5.1 (Refinement of rules).

A rule $\rho^{\prime}$ a rule $\rho$ , written $\rho^{\prime}\sqsubseteq\rho$ , if for every argument tuple $v$ , either $\rho(v)=\top$ , or $\rho^{\prime}(v)\neq\top$ and $\rho^{\prime}(v)\subseteq\rho(v)$ .refines

A refinement may resolve nondeterminism and may define what was undefined, but it may not add a result or make undefined what was defined. The relation $\sqsubseteq$ is a partial order with greatest element $\rho_{\top}$ .

Under the identity encoding, mapping $\mathit{op}$ from $S$ to its namesake in $T$ creates an obligation () only if $\rho_{T,\kappa_{T}}(\mathit{op})\not\sqsubseteq\rho_{S,\kappa}(\mathit{op})$ , and exactly then when $S$ ’s rule is exact at a conflicting tuple that a kernel can load ( in ). GLSL’s wrapping addition is thus an obligation for MSL, whereas MSL’s undefined overflow is refined by every rule and is an obligation for no target.

Theorem5.2

Proposition 5.4 (Recording the source).

Let $D(\mathit{op})$ be the set of rules $\rho_{S,\kappa}(\mathit{op})$ , other than $\rho_{\top}$ , that the sources give $\mathit{op}$ under the configurations of the programs translated.

(a) The rules in $D(\mathit{op})$ have a common refinement iff, for every tuple $v$ , the sets $\rho(v)$ of the rules $\rho\in D(\mathit{op})$ that are defined at $v$ share an element; their weakest common refinement is then the pointwise meet $\sqcap D(\mathit{op})$ , which is the least element of $D(\mathit{op})$ when there is one. Annotating every occurrence of $\mathit{op}$ , from every source, with one rule $\rho^{\circ}$ makes (P1)’s first half hold iff $\rho^{\circ}\sqsubseteq\sqcap D(\mathit{op})$ .

(b) If there is no common refinement, witnessed by a tuple $v$ at which the conflicting sources’ rules are exact, then for any hub whose importers map the witness kernels of the conflicting sources (load $v$ , apply $\mathit{op}$ , store the result) to one hub program, the artifact that any emitter produces for it is refused, rejects the witness state, or is unfaithful under $(\mathit{true},\mathit{true})$ to one of the kernels.

(c) A construct of $T$ that refines $\sqcap D(\mathit{op})$ also refines each $\rho_{S,\kappa}(\mathit{op})$ , but not conversely; so a hub that carries only $\sqcap D(\mathit{op})$ must refuse wherever one that carries each source’s rule must, and possibly elsewhere.

For every rule that CrossTL-R carries, $D(\mathit{op})$ has a least element over CrossTL’s sources: wrapping arithmetic, masked shifts, Direct3D’s division by zero, the truncated remainder, truncating narrowing, saturating conversion with NaN to zero, the NaN-ignoring , an exact , and unsigned mixed comparison. A hub that gives every operation this rule, as naga and Tint do for wrap-around, would keep the carried rules too (a), but must refuse wherever a target cannot implement the strongest rule, even for sources that do not ask for it (c); measures that price.

Elsewhere, defined rules conflict: with a WGSL importer, WGSL’s $x/0=x$ would meet legacy Direct3D’s , an instance of (b); Direct3D 11’s flushing of binary32 subnormals against CUDA’s preservation, and the 12- against the 16-byte stride, are analogues of (b) for the floating-point environment and for encodings. There a hub that does not refuse must record the source’s rule, or the artifact an encoding; CrossTL-R does neither. Records must be per operation when one hub program mixes provenance, as CrossTL’s do: importers insert CrossGL implementations of Metal’s precise functions, and the lowering inserts polyfills written against the hub’s rules.minisnan

Annotation.

The annotation pass knows the source language and infers operand types from a table of declarations, struct members and function results. It rewrites each operation whose source rule it carries into a call to a reserved intrinsic: signed $+$ , $-$ and $\times$ from GLSL, SPIR-V and HLSL become and its siblings, shifts from MSL, OpenCL C and HLSL and its siblings, unsigned division from HLSL , and a NaN-sensitive ; mixed signed-unsigned comparisons and stores into 8- and 16-bit variables become explicit conversions. For HLSL it carries the legacy rules, which refine the current ones for every operator it annotates.

The annotation is incomplete in known ways, each a failure of (P1): it covers scalar operations only, so vector and 64-bit integer arithmetic keeps its namesake; Rust-GPU, Mojo and Slang programs pass through unannotated; an operation whose operand types the pass cannot infer is left unchanged (); and neither GLSL’s and SPIR-V’s oversized shifts, which give some value where CUDA has undefined behaviour, nor HLSL’s truncated under the current rules is carried.__cgl_wrap_add__cgl_shl_u__cgl_udiv_d3dfmin__cgl_fmin_num

Lowering.

The rule table is data: a set of (rule, target) pairs lowered natively, refusals of the NaN-dependent rules for WGSL, and a polyfill for every other pair (); of its $9\times 11=99$ entries, 15 are native, 80 are polyfill entries and 4 refusals, and 4 also record a configuration and 8 an assumption. The 80 entries use 17 polyfills, 35 statements of CrossGL in all, under reserved names; the lowering injects those that a program uses, and the ordinary emitters translate them, so each polyfill is only as faithful as each emitter’s lowering of the trusted base: unsigned 32-bit arithmetic and , bit reinterpretation, select, signed and unsigned comparisons, binary32 comparisons and , and conversions of in-range values (). Wrapping addition, for example, becomes .

A +C record is self-enforcing, because the Metal compiler applies the pragma; a +A record is a comment line that no loader checks. The passes do not run for units that the project layer specialises or equips with contracts.

Floating-point rules.

The NaN-aware rules test for NaN on the bit pattern rather than with , which a target that may assume NaNs absent can fold; the test is exact wherever bit reinterpretation is. The Metal artifact requests safe math with the scoped pragma that MSL defines (+C); WGSL lets an implementation assume that NaNs are absent and offers no opt-out, so the table refuses these rules for WGSL; and for GLSL, whose implementations need not support NaN, the artifact records the assumption that they do (+A).

Two targets defeat these entries through their trusted base, so (P2) fails there. Unless a SPIR-V entry point declares (or, under Vulkan 1.4, states its floating-point environment), Vulkan lets an implementation assume that no floating-point operation sees a NaN or an infinity; the mode lifts this only for bit-preserving operations and a listed set, such as and the comparisons, and , through which the polyfill reads the bits, is in neither . A sound entry would test with under the mode, or clear NotNaN with per-instruction flags under Vulkan 1.4; both need the device property , and without it the rule must be refused. DXC, in turn, marks every non-precise floating-point comparison with LLVM’s fast-math flags , so the HLSL polyfills that compare a possibly infinite value are sound only with on the compared values or under , and the artifacts have neither.

Platform.

All experiments ran on one Apple M2 Max. Of our seven runtime configurations, four compile through Apple’s GPU compiler: Metal under safe math and under the API default of fast math (for the hazard suite also relaxed math), MoltenVK, which translates SPIR-V to MSL with SPIRV-Cross and compiles it with fast math, and wgpu, which translates WGSL to MSL. Three execute on Mesa’s LLVM-based CPU drivers: lavapipe for Vulkan, llvmpipe for OpenGL, and lavapipe for DXIL, which dxil-spirv converts to SPIR-V as vkd3d-proton does, in place of Direct3D 12 . Apple’s Metal Shader Converter turned the same DXIL into Metal libraries . After the registered runs, we also executed every SPIR-V artifact on KosmicKrisp, a Vulkan driver for Apple GPUs certified conformant to Vulkan 1.4 (exploratory) . CUDA and HIP outputs were compiled by nvcc but not executed. The validators were each target’s reference tools, with naga for WGSL; Rust and Mojo outputs had none ().(; )

AppendixQ

Corpus.

The corpus has 22 slices from 12 permissively licensed projects (). A is a translation unit that declares an entry point, with its include closure resolved as the project’s build resolves it. Of 2,713 units in ten languages, 2,404 compiled, 128 did not, and 181 Rust-GPU and Mojo units have no native check, so the experiments use 2,585 units in 719 of units that share code or authorship. Two slices, the MLX kernels and the Mojo puzzles, were used during CrossTL’s development ().

Each unit was translated to every target with a 300-second limit, and a stage-support matrix fixed in advance marks each (unit, target) cell feasible, partial or infeasible. A feasible cell is if the target’s validator accepts the output, the raw output carries no fallback marker, and it declares an entry point; if it is accepted but carries a fallback or declares no entry point; if the validator rejects it; and if CrossTL stopped with a diagnostic, crashed or timed out.

Hazard suite.

The suite has one compute kernel for every catalogue class and every source language that the class’s behaviour under its reference configuration (safe math for MSL, as MLX, PyTorch and ggml build it); where a language leaves the behaviour undefined or unspecified, there is no case, and weaker no-UB obligations are not tested. This gives 66 cases in six source languages, of which 56 carry an obligation. Each kernel processes 64 inputs with critical values ( $2^{31}-1$ , zero divisors, NaN, $\pm\infty$ , $\pm 0$ , subnormals, oversized shifts) at fixed positions, and each oracle is a Python model of the cited rule. Every case went through CrossTL and CrossTL-R to seven targets, and through every third-party chain that accepts its source language: glslang or DXC to SPIR-V followed by SPIRV-Cross, naga or Tint; naga’s GLSL front end; Slang; DXC followed by the Metal Shader Converter; and HIPIFY.defines

Registration, amendments and codings.

Before CrossTL-R or any of the 44 new cases ran, we fixed the suite’s selection rule, routes, oracles, analysis plan and three hypotheses in a document whose SHA-256 we recorded; the other 22 cases come from an earlier suite whose outcomes we knew. : every CrossTL-R output that its validator accepts preserves the source rule on every executed runtime, on the target’s rule or by construction except where the table records an assumption. : unmodified CrossTL’s outcomes depend on the source language for a fixed rule and target. : CrossTL-R changes no target’s accepted share on the corpus by more than one point. Thirteen dated amendments record later changes; two correct the catalogue (A12, from an internal review: MSL’s and SPIR-V’s ; A13, from the table check: DXC’s comparisons), and and  report each registered item as registered and as corrected.

We coded the basis of every preserved (case, route) artifact () and, as registered, the mechanism of every failure: a to a default, a , a , or a divergence of an artifact that is correct by its target’s specification. Each artifact was coded twice under written codebooks, once with the translator’s identity visible and once blind, by separate instances of a large language model (Claude Opus 5.5), so agreement measures consistency between instances, not human agreement; the blind packets still revealed CrossTL-R through its polyfill names in 75 of its 225 packets. Statistics.

RQ1, RQ2 and the sign-flip test were not registered. Corpus results are proportions with cluster-bootstrap intervals over program families (2,000 resamples). Paired comparisons with CrossTL-R use exact McNemar tests, and comparisons with other translators a sign-flip test over families, both with Holm’s correction. 6.2.

The 2,585 units give 27,671 attempted (unit, target) cells, of which 6,986 ask a target for a stage it cannot express; they serve RQ5. Of the 20,583 feasible cells, 17,567 are for the nine targets that have a validator ( in breaks them down by source, target and slice).

Of these, 31.1 % of the translations are usable, 3.9 % degraded and 35.0 % rejected by the target’s validator, and in 30.0 % CrossTL stops.

The share depends on the source language and on the corpus’s composition. From the four graphics languages, 35 to 57 % of the translations are usable; from Metal, CUDA, HIP, OpenCL C and Mojo, below 5 %, mostly because their imports fail or hub type names and source built-ins pass through unchanged (). Two collections of Vulkan samples, one with its Rust-GPU ports, supply 71 % of the feasible validated cells and 98 % of the usable translations: averaged over projects instead of cells, the usable share is 11.6 % (19.8 % over source languages), and leaving out one project at a time gives 21.8 to 33.7 %. Removing the two seen slices changes it from 31.1 to 32.0 %.

Even a round trip through the hub loses programs: translated back into its own language, a program yields usable output in 75 % of the feasible GLSL cells but only 8 % of the Metal ones. Some losses are silent: 603 of the 1,489 SPIR-V outputs that accepts (40 %) contain a fallback marker.

Across all 20,583 feasible cells, CrossTL stopped on 6,113, 171 of them with a crash or time-out and the rest with a diagnostic. Two blind model codings of a stratified sample of 706 diagnostics agreed on 95 % of it ( $\kappa=0.92$ ); reweighted, they attribute 53 to 57 % of the diagnostics to unsupported constructs, 24 to 26 % to inconsistencies in CrossTL’s own state, 17 % to parse failures, and 1.4 to 3.6 % to a meaning-preservation reason, which a rule-based classification of the messages, with which they agree only moderately ( $\kappa\leq 0.57$ ), puts at 21 %.

About a third of CrossTL’s translations of third-party programs are usable, a share that two collections of Vulkan samples dominate. Invalid outputs outnumber stops, most stops report unsupported constructs, and 40 % of the SPIR-V outputs that validate have silently lost a construct.Answer to RQ1.

6.3.

We ran every third-party chain on every graphics unit of each source language it accepts, under the same validators: SPIRV-Cross, naga and Tint on SPIR-V that glslang or DXC produced, or that the corpus supplies; naga’s GLSL front end; and Slang. A chain succeeds when the validator accepts its output and the output declares an entry point that compiles with its stage’s profile; CrossTL’s output must also carry no fallback marker, a requirement that changes no comparison’s direction.

The established chains produce valid output significantly more often than CrossTL in 31 of the 39 comparisons ( in ). SPIRV-Cross succeeds on 81 to 89 % of the units for every pair it offers, against 16 to 69 % for CrossTL; its largest lead, from SPIR-V to HLSL, is 66 percentage points (interval 59–73). CrossTL is significantly ahead in six comparisons: against naga, through either front end, from GLSL to Metal and HLSL and from SPIR-V to WGSL, and against Slang from Slang to HLSL (66 against 12 %), where Slang’s entry points lack the semantics that DXC requires of a stage’s interface; compiled as libraries, 88 % of Slang’s HLSL outputs are accepted ().

Overflow.

Every route whose intermediate representation carries the wrap rule keeps it on every registered runtime except MoltenVK, where every SPIR-V route fails (): naga, through either front end, Tint, and CrossTL-R. Routes that copy the operator, SPIRV-Cross and CrossTL, lose the rule on Metal, because the Metal compiler folds the comparison.

In the exploratory run on KosmicKrisp, every SPIR-V route of the three addition cases with an obligation diverges, glslang’s output and the suite’s reference SPIR-V included (): the driver’s MSL printer emits the addition as a signed addition, which Apple’s compiler folds, and multiplication by two survives only because Mesa’s NIR first rewrites it into a shift.

Compiling the Metal overflow artifacts with Apple’s (exploratory) kept the rule in all 10 overflow artifacts that diverged on Metal and changed none of the 18 that matched; an MSL file cannot request the flag, and CrossTL’s artifacts do not record it.

DXC emits for HLSL’s signed arithmetic and folds even at , so a translation into HLSL that copies a GLSL or SPIR-V addition, such as CrossTL’s or SPIRV-Cross’s, can compute a different result without a diagnostic, whereas naga’s and Tint’s polyfills survive.

Other rules, configuration and the runtime stack.

Every translator whose outputs ran loses some rule except two: glslang, whose only divergences arise on the Vulkan drivers for Metal, and the Metal Shader Converter. naga and Tint drop SPIR-V’s on the way to MSL and WGSL, and Slang drops HLSL’s . DXC’s SPIR-V back end gives HLSL structured buffers of a 16-byte stride unless is given; the module declares the stride but records no encoding (), so a host that keeps Direct3D’s 12-byte elements reads the wrong data. CrossTL also loses contraction control, signed zeros and the sign of C’s on several targets, and subgroup reductions on SPIR-V and Direct3D ().

On Metal, 12 of the 191 (case, route) cells with an obligation change outcome between the three configurations, every change separating safe mode from the other two; CrossTL’s Metal output for CUDA’s , for example, meets the source’s error bound only in safe mode, which it does not request. Between lavapipe and MoltenVK, 33 of the 130 cells with an obligation differ (15 in the wrap rule, 10 in contraction), so that 19 of 95 distinct SPIR-V binaries behave differently on the two implementations.

On the suite’s NaN cases, no runtime exploited the latitude for NaN: every one matched on Metal under fast math, CrossTL’s unannotated outputs included, and CrossTL’s SPIR-V failures on NaN are translator defects. Divergences.

Of the 37 divergences, 29 are on SPIR-V, 24 of them failures of CrossTL’s own SPIR-V output and 5 MoltenVK wrap failures, and 8 are wrap losses on Metal and Direct3D 12. Fixing the SPIR-V emitter locally removes 14 of the 37, all on SPIR-V. Carrying the rules removes 32, the 8 cross-language losses included; on Direct3D 12 the wrap polyfill survives DXC’s folding. Source-agnostic emitter changes, as in naga and Tint, could remove the control’s other 18, so the contrast measures the scope of the fixes, not where an obligation must be discharged. Where the target cannot express a rule, CrossTL-R refuses: it refuses the seven NaN-dependent cases on WGSL, for which CrossTL had produced five invalid outputs and two that matched only because wgpu’s Metal back end happens to honour NaN.

Combining the two arms adds two divergences: the SPIR-V emitter types the remainder polyfill’s literal as unsigned, and the control’s unsigned-promotion fix then lowers its signed test as , which is always false. This is a failure of (P2) in a base operator, which no check of the table alone can reveal.0x < 0OpULessThan

Theorem5.2

All five remaining divergences are wrap-around on MoltenVK: the emitted is correct by the SPIR-V specification, but MoltenVK’s translation to MSL turns it into signed arithmetic that Apple’s compiler may assume does not overflow . MoltenVK implements Vulkan’s portability subset and is not a conformant implementation ; but KosmicKrisp, which is certified conformant, fails the three addition cases by the same mechanism, so conformance testing does not exercise this fold, and on this point KosmicKrisp does not conform to the specification (). In the theorem’s terms, both drivers implement a weaker target whose signed addition does not wrap. An exploratory table keyed by the runtime stack, which polyfills SPIR-V bound for MoltenVK, preserved all 10 overflow runs on MoltenVK and lavapipe; on KosmicKrisp the same polyfill fails the three additions, because the driver prints its unsigned addition as a signed one. The divergences falsify the registered H-R1, which quantifies over the runtimes we executed; CrossTL-R’s first run, before amendment A1, also diverged on .

H-R1’s basis clause fails for 18 of CrossTL-R’s 102 matches on the carried rules. Thirteen trace to (P2), at entries that the mechanical check finds unsound: the 7 NaN tests on SPIR-V and 5 comparisons of infinite values on HLSL hold only by implementation, and so does CUDA’s remainder through Metal’s native . The other 5 are wrap matches on lavapipe that rest on the target’s rule, which the registered basis rule counts as implementation-dependent because MoltenVK did not keep them.OpIAdd()

Held-out kernels.

Because CrossTL-R was debugged on the suite, we froze it and tested it on 102 random kernels in five source languages, generated from a fixed seed, each a random expression over carried operations; under the corrected catalogue, 84 carry an obligation. CrossTL diverged in 120 of 444 executions, all on SPIR-V, in 10 of the 14 (rule, source) cells; CrossTL-R diverged in none of 462. The kernels test less severely than the suite, since none compares an overflowing expression, and the registered prediction that CrossTL would diverge on every target where the suite shows a loss failed.

For a fixed carried rule and target, CrossTL’s outcome differs between source languages in only 2 of 26 cells, both caused by one SPIR-V emitter defect, and in none for CrossTL-R: H-R2 holds, narrowly, and most of CrossTL’s losses depend on the target alone.

6.6.

Checks.

We tested the loader by fault injection, independently of CrossTL’s own tests (). In runtime packages for Metal, OpenGL and Direct3D around a kernel with a checked scalar precondition, package inspection rejected all 315 mutations of the contract lines, including 52 well-formed contracts with another meaning, and the host-side dispatch checks rejected every request outside the precondition and accepted every request inside it. The checks guard only what a contract records: none of the value-level obligations of RQ3 is a contract.

Refusals.

On the suite, CrossTL refused 9 outputs and CrossTL-R 16, adding the seven NaN-dependent cases on WGSL. Combining outcomes and codings per (class, target) cell (), and leaving out the 5 cells for partial work-groups, which single-file translation never exercises, CrossTL is drop-free in 30 of the remaining 100 cells, refuses in 5 and drops in 51, 22 of them latently; CrossTL-R is drop-free in 42, refuses in 8 and drops in 39, 17 latently. Neither is fail-closed: both rely on assumptions, such as caller-trusted index ranges, and both drop obligations, CrossTL in 16 of the 21 classes and CrossTL-R in 14.

On the corpus, CrossTL refused only 2,147 (31 %) of the 6,986 cells that ask a target for a stage it cannot express, unevenly across targets ().

7.

Implications for hub design.

A record of the rule helps only if it is complete, and type inference over CrossTL’s untyped tree leaves about half of the relevant operations in graphics programs unannotated, so a rule-carrying hub needs a typed intermediate representation. The configuration belongs to the artifact: CrossTL’s Metal and HLSL outputs depend on a math mode or a that they do not request, and a sound SPIR-V NaN rule on a device property. A rule table is small enough to check mechanically, but the defect that broke the combined arm lies in an emitter’s lowering of a base operator, which only a per-emitter test would catch. And a translator should lower for the stack that will execute the artifact: correct SPIR-V diverged on two Vulkan drivers for Metal, one certified conformant.precise

Scope of the claims.

holds in a model of operation rules, relative to the reading of the catalogue in ; the implementation is not verified, divergence counts are lower bounds for the inputs and stacks tested, and the experiment varies one hub. Recording operation rules is not new (); what is new is a source-to-source hub with many source languages, in which provenance is per source and some rules can be honoured only by configuring or refusing the target, and the account of when it must be recorded.

Threats to validity.

All executions ran through two code generators, Apple’s and Mesa’s: Direct3D 12 was emulated, no NVIDIA, AMD, Intel or mobile driver ran anything, and CUDA and HIP outputs were only compiled; the NaN entries rest on the specifications, not on observed failures. Validity is measured by proxies, two collections of Vulkan samples dominate the corpus, no strongest-semantics arm ran on the suite, and , matrix and layouts and barrier scope are untested.

The catalogue, cases, oracles, rule table and codings were all prepared with one model under the authors’ direction, so an error in the catalogue propagates to all of them; an internal review found four, two of which removed obligations (A12), and encoding the table for the mechanical check a fifth (A13). We corrected seven errors in our harness and one in the analysis of Slang’s HLSL, none changing a conclusion ( and ); the held-out kernels, none of which compares an overflowing value, only partly offset the debugging of CrossTL-R on the suite.INT_MIN/-1bool

8.

Intermediate languages and their semantics.

Routing $M$ source languages and $N$ targets through one intermediate language is as old as UNCOL  and underlies the Amsterdam Compiler Kit, GCC, LLVM, MLIR and WebAssembly . These IRs record the rules that source operators leave implicit: LLVM marks additions or , models their violation as poison and attaches fast-math flags , some of which (, , ) Alive-FP formalises ; MLIR’s dialect has overflow attributes and distinct and ; SPIR-V has and , separate and , float-control execution modes and, with the float-controls extension that Vulkan 1.4 makes core, per-instruction fast-math flags ; TDF and the CLI give arithmetic operations explicit error treatments ; WebAssembly instead defines integer arithmetic completely, and C2Rust emits for C’s unsigned arithmetic .

Per-target lowering of a recorded rule is established too: MLIR’s conversion from to SPIR-V emulates the signed remainder for Vulkan and guards the NaN-propagating with unless fast-math flags allow otherwise . In these IRs each operator variant has one fixed rule, and each front end picks the variant; a source-to-source hub must pick it per source for targets that are themselves languages with undefined behaviour and scoped configurations, and states when the pick must name the source. Undefined behaviour, studied for C , reaches GPUs through MSL, CUDA, OpenCL C and DXC.(; ; )

Shader and compute translators.

glslang and DXC compile GLSL and HLSL to SPIR-V ; SPIRV-Cross decompiles SPIR-V to GLSL, HLSL and MSL , and MoltenVK and IREE’s Metal back end use it to run SPIR-V on Metal ; vkd3d-proton and the Metal Shader Converter run DXIL on Vulkan and Metal . naga, a bidirectional hub around a validated module with configurable bounds-check policies, and Tint, which compiles WGSL through its own IR with configurable polyfills for division, remainder and shifts , give their IRs WGSL’s wrap-around semantics and polyfill it where the back end’s language leaves overflow undefined : a single fixed semantics, which keeps a source rule only where it refines that rule. Slang compiles an HLSL-derived language through its own IR, with target legalisation and direct SPIR-V emission , and has an open proposal to define integer semantics across targets . clspv and clvk bring OpenCL C to Vulkan , and so face the OpenCL-to-Vulkan rows of .

Compute translation has mostly started from CUDA ; binary and IR-level approaches  and portability layers and domain-specific languages  avoid source translation, and learned translators can produce code that compiles but behaves differently .

Earlier work described CrossTL’s hub-and-spoke design and evaluated it on small sets of programs ; and  qualify its statement that CrossGL captures the essential semantics of all supported languages.(; ; )

Correctness of translators and GPU programs.

Translation validation checks each translation instead of the translator , CompCert proves a compiler correct , and Alive2 checks LLVM optimisations as refinement queries to an SMT solver , as we check the rule table; our definitions borrow their refinement view.

Differential testing, random program generation and equivalence modulo inputs  have GPU descendants ; conformance suites check an implementation against one specification , yet a certified driver can still fold a wrapping addition (); our suite checks translations against the source’s rules. 9.

A hub that records only syntax loses the rules that GPU languages give the same operations. Recording each operation’s rule and lowering it through one table per target keeps them when annotation is sound and complete and the table is sound; given an exact frame each target construct must refine the source’s rule, and a hub that does not refuse must record the source where defined rules conflict. In CrossTL, every remaining failure traced to an unsound table entry, an emitter’s lowering of the trusted base, or a runtime that miscompiles correct code, a certified-conformant driver included; a faithful translator must record its configuration and be tested on its users’ stacks.

Data-Availability Statement

The artifact is released with this preprint as arXiv ancillary files, and CrossTL is available at .

The artifact contains the hazard suite with its registration and amendments, the held-out kernel generator, the experiment harness and container files, the CrossTL-R passes as a patch against the evaluated implementation of CrossTL, the mechanical check of the rule table, manifests and scripts that rebuild the corpus from pinned upstream revisions, the raw results of every experiment, the coding packets, codebooks and codes, and the scripts that regenerate every table, figure and number in this paper from those results.

The raw translator outputs and run records (about 3.8 GB) exceed the size limit for supplementary material; they will be deposited in an archive with a persistent identifier for artifact evaluation, and the scripts regenerate them.

Regenerating the analyses needs only Python. Re-running the experiments needs an Apple-silicon Mac for the Metal, MoltenVK, KosmicKrisp, wgpu and OpenCL runs and a container runtime for Mesa, DXC, dxil-spirv and nvcc; the artifact cannot execute CUDA or HIP outputs, which this study only compiled.

The corpus files are not redistributed and remain under their original licences.

We will submit the artifact to Artifact Evaluation.
