Two conclusions follow. First, the FSQ reconstruction — trained without any smoothness reward — already preserves most of the Ground Truth smoothness ( $96.4\%$ / $87.3\%$ on Truebones Zoo/Articulation 2.0 at $T_{D}{=}4$ ), improving with the token budget ( $97.6\%$ / $92.4\%$ at $T_{D}{=}8$ ); discretization thus incurs only a modest cost that shrinks with more tokens, confirming that a low $L_{1}$ /IoU error does not conceal non-smooth artifacts. Second, the larger drop stems from autoregressive sampling ( $91.8\%$ / $73.7\%$ before GRPO), which GRPO substantially recovers ( $95.3\%$ / $80.6\%$ )—as expected, since $R_{mo}$ is one of its objectives—compensating for this generation-induced gap rather than for tokenization loss.

5.4.4.

Finally, we verify the importance of our robustness-oriented data augmentation pipeline. We performed an ablation by selectively disabling specific augmentation modules, such as non-uniform scaling, sub-tree dropping, and random joint deletion, and retraining the autoregressive model. As reported in Table , removing any single module results in a consistent degradation of skeletal prediction accuracy across all datasets. For example, omitting non-uniform scaling increases the J2J error on ModelsResource from $2.857$ to $3.030$ . The most significant drop occurs when removing joint deletion strategies, confirming that simulating topological imperfections during training is vital for handling the diverse and often noisy geometry found in production environments.

6.

In this work, we introduced , an automated framework for skeletal rigging and skinning weight prediction that approaches the fidelity of professional artist workflows. Our core insight is that the longstanding bottleneck in automatic skinning is a representation problem. By proposing , i.e., a compact, discrete representation learned via an FSQ-CVAE, we successfully transformed the ill-posed regression of sparse skinning matrices into a robust token prediction task. This design enabled us to train a unified autoregressive model that jointly synthesizes skeletal structures and skinning weights, capturing the intrinsic dependencies between articulation and deformation that prior decoupled methods ignore. Our experiments demonstrate that this unified approach, combined with a novel GRPO-based reinforcement learning stage, significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. The integration of geometric and semantic reward functions proves particularly effective for generalization, allowing the model to generate coherent rigs for complex, out-of-distribution assets that defy standard supervised learning.TokenRigSkinTokens

Despite these advancements, several avenues for improvement remain. We illustrate representative failure cases in Figure , which predominantly stem from extremely thin or topologically ambiguous geometry that is under-represented in training. First, while our FSQ-CVAE offers high compression efficiency, a comparative analysis suggests a residual performance gap remains compared to continuous-latent VAEs in extremely challenging skinning scenarios. As quantified in Table , discretization does incur a measurable reconstruction loss relative to a continuous CVAE, so our use of discrete tokens is a deliberate trade-off: it enables a autoregressive model (skeletal parameters are inherently discrete) and fast sampling without iterative denoising. We expect continuous representations to eventually close this gap as mainstream generative paradigms mature, while the underlying idea of skinning weights should remain central regardless of whether the tokens are discrete or continuous. Recent developments in continuous token representations  may offer a path to bridge this gap, potentially enhancing predictive precision without sacrificing the benefits of sequence modeling. Second, our current framework generates rigs autonomously based on learned priors. However, professional production often requires adherence to specific topological standards. Extending our autoregressive model to accept user-specified topological templates or interactive guidance would be a valuable direction, effectively transforming TokenRig from an automatic generator into a flexible, artist-directed co-pilot. Finally, while our RL stage improves geometric validity, future work could explore physics-based rewards to further ensure the dynamic plausibility of the generated deformations during animation.Limitations and Discussions.

item.title: MOMO：从移动声源还原人体动作 ｜ MOMO: Human Motion from Moving Sounds
item.description:
一句话：不止从声音生成动作，还考虑声源本身在移动——更贴近真实空间关系。

要点：

  • 现有音生动作方法假设声源固定，脱离实际
  • 把声源运动轨迹纳入条件，生成与之匹配的动作
  • 华南理工与港大合作，含多模态数据标注

为什么值得看：空间音频与动作驱动结合，对引擎里的「声源-角色」联动系统（如 VR、过场动画）有直接启发。

中文摘要：MOMO 处理一个被忽略的细节：以往「从声音生成人体动作」的方法都假设声源是静止的，但现实中声源（脚步、乐器、车辆）往往在移动。作者把声源的运动轨迹作为额外条件引入生成模型，使产出的动作在方向、速度与空间关系上与声音一致。论文来自华南理工与香港大学，对空间音频驱动动画、VR 过场等场景有直接价值。

主题：游戏引擎

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

MOMO: Human Motion from Moving Sounds

Deli Cai

Abstract

Human responses to sound depend not only on its semantic content, but also on the evolving spatial relationship between source and listener, conveyed through spatial audio and its temporal dynamics. Modeling human reactions to such dynamic spatial audio is important for character animation, human behavior analysis, and robotics. As of yet, existing audio-driven motion generation methods primarily focus on non-spatial or static acoustic conditions, leaving this important problem largely underexplored. To bridge this gap, we formulate the novel task of dynamic spatial-audio-driven human motion generation and introduce two motion-captured datasets. We introduce the namic patial udio and otion dataset (DySAM) as the first dataset and benchmark for this task, providing synchronized binaural audio, 3D human motions, and moving sound source trajectories. Given the importance of dynamic spatial cues of sound sources, we further provide the namic patial udio ocalization dataset (DySAL), an auxiliary binaural localization dataset that pairs diverse acoustic events with head poses and moving source trajectories to support spatial audio perception.

For benchmarking, we propose MOMO for human tion generation from ving Sounds, a diffusion-based framework guided by three coupled principles: localization, understanding, and generation.

MOMO performs localization by estimating head-centric spatial direction cues of the moving source directly from raw binaural audio, avoiding reliance on ground-truth source coordinates. It performs understanding by extracting frame-wise audio-content representations, and performs generation by conditioning motion diffusion on both semantic features and dynamic spatial cues. Moreover, MOMO incorporates frame-wise motion correction during denoising, enabling temporally adaptive motion synthesis under evolving audio-spatial cues.

Experiments show that MOMO outperforms existing baselines in motion fidelity, audio-motion alignment, and physical plausibility, demonstrating the potential of dynamic spatial audio for embodied motion generation.

Project page: DySAMDySALMoMo

https://cdlchoi.github.io/projects/MOMO

This paper proposes a novel task for synthesizing 3D human motions in response to . To support this new task, we collect DySAM, the first dataset comprising synchronized dynamic spatial audio, corresponding sound source trajectories, and high-quality 3D human motion. In this figure, the model generates diverse and realistic human reactions to various moving acoustic events.Figure 1: dynamicspatialaudio

1

Diverse Reactions to Moving Sounds.Figure 2:

Human responses to sound arise from integrating semantic meaning with cues and the . A barking dog approaching from behind may elicit avoidance, whereas a speeding car approaching may prompt reorientation. Crucially, the same sound can evoke different actions depending on its source’s location and motion relative to the listener. Modeling this perception–action coupling supports context-aware virtual humans and embodied agents in character animation, virtual reality, human–computer interaction, and embodied intelligence.spatial audiotemporal dynamics of sound sources

Existing human motion datasets and methods have mainly focused on conditions such as action labels , text descriptions , music , and speech . Recently, to the best of our knowledge, MOSPA introduced the first spatial-audio-driven human motion dataset, SAM, along with a corresponding motion generation method, showing that spatial audio cues are crucial for generating realistic human motions. However, the SAM dataset mainly focuses on a static sound source, where the sound source position remains fixed within each sequence. Moreover, MOSPA requires the ground-truth absolute position of the sound source as a condition for motion generation, which is difficult to obtain in real-world scenarios and limits its applicability to embodied agents. Therefore, dynamic spatial-audio-driven human motion generation, which models human motion responses to time-varying spatial audio from moving sound sources, remains largely underexplored, especially in practical settings without access to ground-truth sound source positions.()

To address this gap, we introduce DySAM, a dataset for dynamic spatial-audio-driven human motion generation. DySAM contains synchronized binaural audio, 3D human motion, and dynamic sound source trajectories captured in an indoor environment. Human motion and sound source trajectories are recorded using a Vicon motion capture system , while binaural audio is captured by high-sensitivity microphones near the actors’ ears, approximating the audio perceived by the actors. The main dataset contains 2,336 ten-second audio-motion sequences, totaling 23,360 seconds (approximately 6.5 hours), with motion at 30 FPS and audio at 48 kHz. It covers 42 audio types and 109 unique audio sources, including human sounds, animal sounds, vehicles, and environmental sounds, with 8 subjects and a binary genre label indicating sensitive or insensitive reactions. In addition, we provide DySAL, an auxiliary sound source localization dataset of 11,730 seconds, pairing binaural audio of diverse acoustic events with listener head 6DoF poses and frame-wise moving sound source annotations to support dynamic spatial audio perception.()

Vicon, 2026

Motivated by the fact that human reactions to spatial sound depend on both where the sound comes from and what the sound is, we formulate spatial-audio-driven motion generation around three coupled functional components: , , and . Guided by this design principle, we propose MOMO, a diffusion-based framework for generating human motion conditioned on dynamic spatial audio. For localization, MOMO estimates frame-wise head-centric spatial cues of sound source from raw binaural audio using a sound source localization network, eliminating the reliance on privileged ground-truth source coordinates. For understanding, a pretrained CLAP audio encoder encodes the binaural audio to obtain frame-wise audio-content features. For generation, MOMO employs a diffusion-based motion generator conditioned on the predicted spatial cues, CLAP audio features, and genre label.

Since human motion needs to continuously adapt to the evolving spatial cues of the sound source, while self-attention only provides implicit interactions between motion tokens and condition tokens, we further introduce a module in the Transformer denoiser to explicitly refine motion tokens with frame-wise conditions, along with a that adaptively controls the correction magnitude for each frame.localizationunderstandinggeneration()

Wu et al., 2023

Frame-wise Motion CorrectionCorrection Strength Predictor

By using head-centric DoA estimated directly from binaural audio, MOMO provides a more practical formulation for spatial-audio-driven motion generation in embodied robot settings. Compared with MOSPA , which relies on ground-truth global sound source coordinates, our egocentric formulation avoids privileged source-location annotations and better reflects how embodied agents infer dynamic sound direction from their own auditory observations. Extensive quantitative and qualitative experiments show that MOMO outperforms existing baselines, producing more realistic motions that respond to dynamic spatial-audio cues.()

Xu et al., 2025

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

•

We introduce two datasets: DySAM, to the best of our knowledge the first dataset for dynamic spatial-audio-driven human motion generation, and DySAL, an auxiliary sound source localization dataset collected in indoor reverberant environments.

•

We propose MOMO, a practical framework for generating human motion from binaural audio without requiring ground-truth source coordinates. It integrates sound source localization, CLAP-based audio content encoding, and diffusion-based motion generation to model human responses to moving sound sources.

•

Extensive quantitative and qualitative experiments show that MOMO generates natural, plausible, and spatially consistent human motion, better aligning with real motion and outperforming existing baselines.

2

Conditional Human Motion Generation.

Conditional human motion generation has been extensively studied under various conditions, such as action labels , textual descriptions , trajectories , and motion language models that treat human motion as a foreign language . These methods generate diverse and natural motions from semantic conditions, but they generally do not consider audio, let alone its spatial attributes. In contrast, our work focuses on audio-driven conditions with explicit spatial information.()

Audio-Driven Human Motion Generation.

Audio-driven human motion generation has been studied mainly in two directions. The first is music-driven dance generation , which generates choreography that matches the rhythm and style of the music. The second is speech-driven gesture synthesis , which generates co-speech gestures from speech content and prosody. Most of these methods use monaural or stereo audio and ignore the spatial attributes of the sound source. MOSPA is the first to study spatial-audio-driven human motion generation with binaural audio, but it assumes a static sound source position. Different from MOSPA, we consider dynamic spatial audio, where the source moves over time, and the DoA changes accordingly.(; ; ; ; ; ; ; )

Spatial Sound Understanding.

Estimating the direction of a sound source from binaural signals is a classic problem in acoustic scene analysis, for instance using binaural cues combined with deep learning .

Recent works also model room acoustics and room impulse responses to support sound source localization in complex indoor scenes .

In this paper, we adopt a sound source localization network to predict the head-centric DoA from binaural audio, which serves as the spatial condition for motion generation. This makes our framework practical in real-world scenarios where ground-truth source coordinates are unavailable.(; )

This section presents two newly collected motion-capture datasets for dynamic spatial-audio-driven human motion generation.

The Dynamic Spatial Audio and Motion dataset (DySAM) serves as the main benchmark for this task, providing synchronized binaural audio, 3D human motions, and moving sound source trajectories.

To support broader research on dynamic spatial audio perception, we introduce the Dynamic Spatial Audio Localization dataset (DySAL) that pairs diverse acoustic events with listener head poses and mocap-recorded moving source trajectories.

Data Capture Setup.

Data Collection Setup. Figure 3:

We collect the data in an indoor environment with natural reverberation using a Vicon motion capture system , which records both human motion and the trajectory of a moving sound source (as shown in Fig. ). We use an omnidirectional speaker to play the dynamic audio. We choose binaural audio as the audio modality, following the SAM dataset , as it is a common form of spatial audio that aligns with human auditory perception and can be readily applied to virtual characters and robotic platforms. Binaural audio is recorded using two microphones placed near the actor’s ears, allowing the signals to approximate the auditory input the actor perceives during capture. Specifically, we use Sound Professionals MS-TFB-2 microphones  and a Deity PR-2 recorder for binaural audio recording. The audio recorder is synchronized with the mocap system using timecode, ensuring temporal alignment among binaural audio, human motion, and sound source trajectories.()

DySAM is the first dataset for dynamic spatial-audio-driven human motion generation, containing synchronized binaural audio, 3D human motion, and dynamic sound source trajectories (Dyn. SS). We also provide DySAL, an auxiliary sound source localization dataset containing dynamic binaural recordings of diverse acoustic events with frame-wise source annotations.Table 1: Statistics of the DySAM dataset.

3.1

Our main dataset, DySAM, is collected for dynamic spatial-audio-driven human motion generation, with visualization snapshots provided in Fig. . Each sequence consists of a 10-second binaural audio clip, the corresponding 3D human motion stored in the SMPL-X format , and the trajectory of a moving sound source in the world coordinate system. As summarized in Tab. , DySAM contains 2,336 synchronized audio-motion sequences, amounting to 23,360 seconds (approximately 6.5 hours) of paired data. The captured motions are represented as SMPL-X model . The audio’s sampling rate is 48,000 Hz, while the motion is represented at 30 FPS for network training. DySAM covers 42 audio types and 109 unique audio sources, spanning diverse daily-life acoustic events such as animal sounds, vehicles, alarms, music, and human speech. It was collected with 8 actors, including 5 female and 3 male. Each sequence is annotated with one of two reaction genres, sensitive or insensitive, with an approximately balanced 1:1 ratio.

3.2

We additionally collect DySAL, an auxiliary sound source localization dataset, using the same motion capture setup. It provides abundant spatial supervision for training the SSL network, enabling robust estimation of dynamic head-centric DoA cues from binaural audio. It contains 11,730 seconds, approximately 3.3 hours, of binaural audio paired with frame-wise sound source positions and the listener’s head 6DoF pose in the world coordinate system. These spatial cues can facilitate broader studies of spatial audio perception, such as absolute source localization and direction-of-arrival estimation. To ensure the diversity of acoustic events, we collect raw audio from AIST , ESC-50 , and UrbanSound8K , covering a wide range of music, environmental, human, animal, mechanical, and urban sounds.

Further details on the data collection and data processing pipeline for the two datasets are provided in Appendix .()

4

We propose MOMO, a diffusion-based framework for dynamic-spatial-audio-driven human motion generation. In real world, human reactions to spatial sound depend on both spatial direction and audio content.

Accordingly, MOMO consists of three coupled functional components: , , and , as illustrated in Fig. . For localization, a sound source localization (SSL) network estimates a frame-wise head-centric direction-of-arrival (DoA) sequence $\bm{D}=\{d_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{3}\}_{t=1}^{T}$ from raw binaural audio, T is the max length of motion (Sec. ). For understanding, a pretrained CLAP audio encoder extracts temporally aligned audio content representations $\bm{A}=\{a_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T}$ from the mono audio. For generation, a transformer-encoder-based conditional diffusion model synthesizes motion through frame-wise correction conditioned on $\bm{D}$ , $\bm{A}$ , the genre label $g$ , and the diffusion timestep $\tau$ . Rather than relying solely on attention mechanism, it incorporates and , allowing the denoiser to adaptively determine the correction magnitude for each frame under dynamic spatial-audio conditions (Sec. ). For network training, we adopt a 272-dimensional motion representation following .localizationunderstandinggeneration

5

4.1

Frame-wise Motion CorrectionCorrection Strength Predictor

4.2

()

Xiao et al., 2025

4.1

In real-world scenes, ground-truth absolute global coordinates of sound sources are often unavailable. To obtain a motion-relevant and coordinate-invariant spatial cue, we represent the sound source at each frame as a head-centric direction-of-arrival (DoA) unit vector, transformed from the source position in the world coordinate system to the head coordinate system using the 6DoF head pose. Specifically, the SSL network predicts a sequence of frame-wise DoA vectors $\hat{\bm{D}}=\{\hat{d}_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T}$ , where each $\hat{d}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{3}$ is a unit vector. This head-centric representation avoids the need for absolute global source coordinates.

Our SSL network is inspired by the binaural sound localization framework of Garcia et al. , which employs STFT-based binaural cues with a cascaded CNN-GRU architecture. We follow their use of STFT-based binaural spatial features and a CNN front-end for extracting local spectro-temporal patterns, but replace the GRU-based temporal modeling module with a Transformer encoder to better capture long-range temporal dependencies under reverberant environments. The SSL network is trained to predict the frame-wise head-centric DoA unit vector using a cosine-distance loss:

$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ssl}}=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left(1-\hat{d}_{t}\cdot d_{t}\right),$

where $\hat{d}_{t}$ and $d_{t}$ denote the predicted and ground-truth DoA unit vectors, respectively, both normalized in the head coordinate system. Once trained, the SSL network is frozen and used to predict the spatial condition sequence $\hat{\bm{D}}$ . Please refer to Appendix for more details on the SSL architecture and training setup.()

García-Barrios et al., 2022

B

MOMO comprises three coupled functional components: a sound source localization (SSL) network predicts a frame-wise head-centric DoA sequence $\hat{\bm{D}}$ from binaural audio (); a CLAP audio encoder extracts frame-wise audio content features $\bm{A}$ from mono audio (); and a conditional diffusion model that iteratively denoise the Gaussian noise to generated motion, integrating Frame-wise Motion Correction to adaptively correct each motion according to frame-wise conditions ().

Figure 5: Overview of MOMO framework.localizationunderstandinggeneration

4.2

We formulate motion generation as conditional denoising diffusion . Given noisy motion $\mathbf{x}_{\tau}$ at diffusion step $\tau$ , the denoising network predicts the clean motion sequence $\mathbf{x}_{0}$ conditioned on audio content, DoA, genre, and timestep embeddings. For audio content, we average the binaural signal into a mono waveform and feed it into a pretrained CLAP encoder . The extracted hidden features are pooled over channel and frequency dimensions and temporally aligned with the motion sequence, producing frame-wise audio features $\bm{A}=\{a_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T}$ .()

Ho et al., 2020

Wu et al., 2023

Building on the Transformer encoder of , we project $\mathbf{x}_{\tau}$ into motion tokens $\bm{m}=\{\mathbf{m}_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T}$ and concatenate them with condition tokens derived from audio features, DoA features, genre, and the diffusion-step embedding. The concatenated tokens are fed into the Transformer encoder for conditional denoising. Since the attention mechanism only provides implicit interactions between motion tokens and the frame-wise condition tokens, we further introduce a module to explicitly correct motion tokens based on frame-wise conditions, together with a that adaptively determines the correction strength.

Xu et al. (2025)

Frame-wise Motion CorrectionCorrection Strength Predictor

To explicitly leverage both global and frame-wise conditions, we apply a residual correction module based on Adaptive Layer Normalization (AdaLN) on after each Transformer encoder layer to refine the intermediate motion token, which is formulated asFrame-wise Motion Correction.

$\bm{m}^{\prime}=\bm{m}+\bm{\alpha}\odot\bm{\delta},$ (1)

where $\bm{\delta}=\{\delta_{i}\}_{i=1}^{T}$ denotes the frame-wise correction, and $\bm{\alpha}=\{\alpha_{i}\}_{i=1}^{T}$ is an frame-wise correction strength.

The modulation condition $\bm{c}=\{c_{i}\}_{i=1}^{T}$ consists of four components: the timestep embedding $t$ , the genre embedding $g$ , the frame-wise audio feature $\bm{A}$ , and the frame-wise DoA feature $\bm{D}$ . The unified condition sequence is obtained by summing these components at each frame, with the global timestep and genre embeddings broadcast to all $T$ frames: $c_{i}=e_{t}+e_{g}+a_{i}+d_{i}$ . This condition sequence is then used to modulate the motion tokens.

An MLP then estimates scale and shift sequences $(\bm{\gamma},\bm{\beta})=\mathrm{MLP}(\mathbf{c}_{i})$ for AdaLN , yielding the correction:()

Peebles and Xie, 2023

$\bm{\delta}=\mathrm{FFN}\left(\mathrm{LN}(\bm{m})\odot(1+\bm{\gamma})+\bm{\beta}\right),$ (2)

The correction strength should not be a fixed parameter tied to a specific layer or frame position. Instead, the strength of motion correction should depend on the audio content, spatial DoA cues, genre, and the current denoising step. We therefore predict $\bm{\alpha}$ dynamically from the interaction between motion tokens and frame-wise conditions.Correction Strength Predictor.

Specifically, we use motion tokens as queries $\bm{Q}=\bm{m}$ and modulation condition as keys and values $\bm{K}=\bm{V}=\bm{c}$ . Considering that human responses to sounds may exhibit temporal delays, we apply a causal attention mask to prevent the token at frame $t$ from attending to future condition frames. The correct strength is bounded by

$\bm{\alpha}=\alpha_{\max}\cdot\mathrm{Sigmoid}(\mathrm{MLP}_{\alpha}(\mathrm{CrossAttn}(\bm{m},\bm{c}_{\leq t},\bm{c}_{\leq t}))).$ (3)

This design decouples the estimation of the condition-dependent correction and its strength: the AdaLN modulation module predicts the correction term, while the cross-attention predictor dynamically determines how strongly this correction is applied.

4.3

We train MOMO a reconstruction loss:

$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{diff}}=\left\|\bm{x_{0}}-\bm{\hat{x_{0}}}(\mathbf{x}_{\tau},\tau,\mathbf{c})\right\|_{2}^{2}.$

To ensure temporal continuity and reduce foot-sliding artifacts, we further use a delta loss

$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{del}}=\left\|\hat{\bm{x_{0}}}-\bm{x_{0}}\right\|_{2}^{2}$

and a foot contact loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{foot}}$ . The overall objective is:()

Xu et al., 2025

$\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{diff}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{del}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{del}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{foot}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{foot}}.$ (4)

Experimental Setup.

We split the main DySAM dataset into train/validation/test sets with a ratio of 8:1:1. For training the sound source localization network, we transform the global sound source position into head-centric unit direction vector using the head 6DoF pose, and use it as the ground-truth DoA. Regarding metrics, we use FID, R-precision, Diversity , Average Pairwise Distance (APD) , and a physics-based skating ratio, as detailed in Appendix . We introduce a multi-branch motion-audio-source evaluator for feature extraction, aiming to better measure the spatial alignment between the generated motion and the moving sound source; details are provided in Appendix .

We compare with diffusion-based and VQ-based baselines, including EDGE , POPDG , MOSPA , and MoMask++ . All baselines are trained on the same DySAM split, with their original input conditions replaced by traditional acoustic features for fair comparison.()

Ablation Study on Sound Source Localization Network.

We evaluate the architectural design of the SSL network, focusing on the DoA representation and temporal modeling module. All variants follow the same training schedule and are evaluated by frame-wise angular error on the DySAM validation set. As shown in Table , unit direction vectors outperform spherical coordinates, while the Transformer encoder further improves localization accuracy over Bi-GRU, supporting its effectiveness in temporal spatial-audio modeling. In addition, Table  shows that incorporating the DySAL training split reduces the angular error on the DySAL validation set, indicating that its frame-wise annotations provide useful spatial supervision for the diverse acoustic events covered by the dataset. The SSL network used in MOMO adopts the unit-direction-vector representation, the Transformer encoder, and joint training on DySAM and DySAL.

6

This paper introduces the task of dynamic spatial-audio-driven human motion generation. We present DySAM, the first dataset and benchmark for this task containing synchronized binaural audio, 3D human motion, and moving sound source trajectories, together with DySAL, an auxiliary dataset that provides diverse acoustic events and frame-wise spatial annotations for dynamic spatial audio perception.

We further propose MOMO, a diffusion-based framework that explicitly leverages frame-wise audio-spatial conditions to generate high-quality human motions in response to dynamic spatial audio.

Extensive experiments demonstrate that MOMO produces natural and physically plausible motions with improved alignment to dynamic spatial audio.

Our current setting considers a single prominent moving sound source. Extending the framework to multiple simultaneous sources would require jointly reasoning about source separation, localization, and their potentially different behavioral relevance. We leave this challenging setting for future research and evaluation.Limitations and Future Work:

Appendix A

A.1

At the beginning of each clip, the dynamic sound source, i.e., a speaker, starts from one of four azimuthal regions relative to the actor: front-left, rear-left, rear-right, and front-right. This design enables us to capture diverse human reactions to sounds arriving from different directions. The trajectory of the sound source is designed to be either straight or curved. Moreover, the sound source either moves toward the actor and reaches the actor’s position, or passes by without contact. These two movement patterns elicit fundamentally different responses. For example, an actor may react differently when a dog or a car rushes toward them than when it merely passes by.

We further define two reaction styles: insensitive and sensitive, to represent different levels of responsiveness to the same acoustic event. For instance, when hearing an explosion, an insensitive actor may remain largely unreactive, whereas a sensitive actor may immediately move away from the sound source. The two reaction styles are approximately balanced in the dataset.

A.2

The data are collected in a typical indoor environment with natural room reverberation. The motion capture system consists of 20 Vicon cameras installed around the capture space, recording both the human body motion and the sound source trajectory at 120 Hz.

For the moving sound source, we use a cylindrical omni-directional speaker to play the audio, ensuring stable sound radiation in different directions as the speaker moves. For binaural audio recording, a high-sensitivity microphone is placed near each ear of the actor to capture the audio perceived by the actor as faithfully as possible. The two microphones are connected to a Deity PR-2 recorder , which is synchronized with the Vicon system in advance using timecode. This setup ensures accurate temporal alignment between the recorded binaural audio and the corresponding motion capture data.()

Deity Microphones, 2026

A.3

The DySAM dataset covers 42 distinct audio types, corresponding to 109 unique audio sources, as listed in Tab. . Each audio type comprises one to six audio sources, and for each audio source 8 to 32 ten-second motion sequences are collected, yielding 2,336 (binaural audio, motion) pairs in total. These audio types span daily-life sounds including animal vocalizations, vehicles, environmental noises, alarms, musical instruments, and human speech.

A1

The 42 distinct audio types covered in DySAM, corresponding to 109 unique audio sources. Each audio source is accompanied by 8 to 32 ten-second motion sequences, and the dataset contains 2,336 (binaural audio, motion) pairs in total.Table A1:

A.4

To ensure broad audio diversity, we collect raw audio materials from AIST , ESC-50 , and UrbanSound8K . AIST mainly contains music and dance-related audio with diverse rhythms, styles, and structures. ESC-50 provides environmental sounds from natural scenes, human activities, animal sounds, indoor and outdoor daily scenes, and mechanical devices, such as rain, sea waves, bird calls, coughing, footsteps, keyboard typing, bells, and vacuum cleaners. UrbanSound8K contains typical urban sounds, including air conditioners, car horns, children playing, dog barks, drilling, engine idling, gunshots, jackhammers, sirens, and street music.()

By combining these sources, DySAL covers music, human activities, natural environments, animals, indoor and outdoor daily activities, transportation, mechanical construction, alarms, and urban public spaces. This diversity broadens the range of acoustic events available for training and evaluating sound source localization models under dynamic spatial-audio conditions.

A.5

For intuitively understand our data processing pipeline, we provide four visualization examples of the DySAM dataset in Fig. .

A1

During capture, the actor wears a motion capture suit with multiple reflective markers attached to the body, represented by the in Fig.  The Vicon system exports the captured data as C3D files, where each file stores the world coordinates of all body markers for every frame. We use Mosh++ to fit each C3D sequence into the SMPL-X parameters. The fitted SMPL-X motion is then canonicalized by rotating the human body in the initial frame to face the positive $y$ -axis and move the center of the body to the origin. For training the motion generation model, we further convert the SMPL-X motion into the 272-dimensional motion representation following .Motion processing.green points

To track the position of the sound source, i.e., the speaker, we attach eight reflective markers around the speaker ( in Fig. ), which approximately correspond to the eight vertices of a cuboid. For each C3D sequence, we use the speaker markers in the initial frame as reference markers. We then estimate the speaker translation in each subsequent frame by solving the rigid alignment between the reference markers and the current-frame markers using singular value decomposition (SVD). The estimated translation is used as the global sound source location in our dataset, represented by the in Fig. . In practice, some speaker markers may be missing in certain frames due to occlusion or tracking failure, making SVD-based estimation unreliable or infeasible. For these frames, we use Kalman filtering to smoothly interpolate and complete the missing sound source locations.Sound source location processing.orange points

To train the sound source localization network, we further compute the head-centric sound source location. Specifically, for each frame, we perform forward kinematics on the fitted SMPL-X body model to obtain the translation and rotation of the head joint, i.e., joint 15. We then transform the global sound source location into the head coordinate system using the estimated head pose, yielding the head-centric sound source location as the direction-related supervision signal.Head-centric DoA processing.

Appendix B

We provide additional implementation details of the sound source localization network used in Sec. . The SSL network estimates a head-centric direction of arrival from binaural audio. For every frame, it predicts a unit vector

$\mathbf{d}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{3},$

which points from the listener’s head toward the sound source and is expressed in the listener’s head coordinate system.

4.1

Binaural feature extraction.

We compute the short-time Fourier transform (STFT) of the left and right binaural signals using a $40\,\mathrm{ms}$ Hamming window, zero-padded to an FFT size of $2048$ , and a hop size of $33.3\,\mathrm{ms}$ , yielding a frame rate of $30\,\mathrm{Hz}$ aligned with the motion sequence. We keep the lowest $256$ frequency bins, corresponding to frequencies up to approximately $6\,\mathrm{kHz}$ .

Let $L_{t,f}$ and $R_{t,f}$ denote the complex STFT coefficients of the left and right channels at time frame $t$ and frequency bin $f$ . The SSL input contains four channels: (1) the average magnitude spectrum, (2-3) the sine and cosine of the interaural phase difference (IPD), and (4) the interaural level difference (ILD). The first channel encodes the overall spectral magnitude, the second and third channels encode the IPD without phase-wrapping discontinuities, and the fourth channel provides the relative loudness between the two ears. The resulting binaural feature is a tensor $\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{4\times 300\times 256}$ , where every sequence is represented by $300$ frames at $30\,\mathrm{Hz}$ to match the motion sequences. The extraction procedure is summarized in the Python pseudo-code below.

⬇

1defextract_binaural_features(audio):234S_L=librosa.stft(audio[0])5S_R=librosa.stft(audio[1])678A_L,phi_L=np.abs(S_L),np.angle(S_L)9A_R,phi_R=np.abs(S_R),np.angle(S_R)101112X1=(A_L+A_R)/213X2=np.sin(phi_L-phi_R)14X3=np.cos(phi_L-phi_R)15eps=1e-1016X4=20*np.log10((A_L+eps)/(A_R+eps))171819X=np.stack([X1,X2,X3,X4])20X=X[:,:256,:]21returnX

Network architecture.

The SSL network consists of a convolutional spectral encoder followed by a Transformer-based temporal encoder. The convolutional front-end contains three convolutional blocks. Each block applies a $3\times 3$ convolution followed by a ReLU activation and max pooling along the frequency axis with stride $4$ . This progressively reduces the frequency dimension from $256$ to $64$ , $16$ , and $4$ , while preserving the temporal resolution.

After the convolutional blocks, the feature map is flattened at each time frame and projected into a $C$ -dimensional latent space, where $C=128$ . We add a learnable absolute positional encoding to the frame-wise tokens before feeding them into the temporal encoder.

Different from , which adopts a GRU for temporal modeling, we use a Transformer encoder. The encoder has $L=4$ layers, $8$ attention heads, and a feed-forward hidden dimension of $256$ . We use pre-normalization Transformer blocks for stable training. The self-attention mechanism enables each frame to aggregate binaural evidence from the entire sequence, which helps resolve ambiguous localization cues caused by reverberation or transient source motion.()

García-Barrios et al., 2022

The Transformer outputs one token per frame. Each token is passed through two fully connected layers to regress a three-dimensional vector, which is then L2-normalized to obtain the predicted DoA:

$\mathbf{d}_{t}=\frac{\mathbf{o}_{t}}{\|\mathbf{o}_{t}\|_{2}},$

where $\mathbf{o}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{3}$ is the raw output vector before normalization.

Training objective.

The SSL network is trained using head-relative source direction labels from DySAM and DySAL. The ground-truth direction vector at frame $t$ is normalized to unit length and denoted as $\bar{\mathbf{d}}_{t}$ . We optimize the cosine-distance loss:

$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ssl}}=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left(1-\mathbf{d}_{t}\cdot\bar{\mathbf{d}}_{t}\right).$

This objective is monotonically related to the angular error between the predicted and ground-truth DoA vectors and directly supervises the directional information used by the downstream motion generator.

During motion generation, the SSL network parameters are frozen. Given only binaural audio, the network produces the frame-wise DoA sequence

$\mathbf{D}=\{\mathbf{d}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{d}_{T}\},$

which is used as the spatial condition of the diffusion model.

Appendix C

The evaluator framework consists of a motion autoencoder co-trained with Bi-GRU feature extractors. A reconstruction loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{recon}}$ is applied between the ground-truth motion $\mathbf{x}$ and the decoded motion $\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ produced by the motion autoencoder. Two Bi-GRU encoders extract the audio feature and the sound source feature from the binaural audio and the sound source trajectory, respectively, and the concatenation of the two features forms the condition latent. Additionally, an InfoNCE loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{InfoNCE}}$ operates on the extracted condition features and motion features.Figure C2:

Inspired by the evaluator design from , our evaluator is a motion–condition matching network , which measures how well a motion sequence corresponds to a given spatial audio condition. It maps both modalities into a shared latent space, in which the R-precision metrics are computed by nearest-neighbor retrieval and the FID is computed between the feature distributions of the ground-truth and the generated motions. Different from , whose condition only contains the acoustic content, our condition additionally involves the trajectory of the sound source, so that the evaluator is sensitive to the spatial correspondence between the moving sound source and the human reaction.()

Xu et al., 2025

()

Xu et al., 2025

Network architecture.

As illustrated in Fig. , the evaluator consists of a motion autoencoder and three bidirectional GRUs (Bi-GRUs), each with 4 layers and a hidden size of 512. The feature of a Bi-GRU is obtained by concatenating its last forward and backward hidden states, which yields a 1024-dimensional feature vector.

C2

The motion autoencoder follows a transformer encoder–decoder structure. The input motion sequence $\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times 272}$ is first projected to a 512-dimensional latent space and added with a positional encoding, and is then encoded by a 4-layer transformer encoder with 4 attention heads and a 1024-dimensional feed-forward layer. The encoder output is averaged over time into a single latent vector and replicated along the temporal axis, which serves as the query of a transformer decoder of the same configuration attending to the encoder output. A final linear layer maps the decoder output back to the 272-dimensional motion space to produce the reconstructed motion $\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ . The output of the motion encoder is further encoded by a Bi-GRU to obtain the motion feature.

The condition branch consists of an audio encoder and a sound source encoder. The audio encoder takes the traditional features described in Appendix . The sound source encoder takes the absolute position of the sound source in the world coordinate system $\mathbf{s}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times 3}$ , projects it to 64 dimensions and encodes it with a Bi-GRU. The resulting audio and sound source features are concatenated and projected by a linear layer into the condition feature, whose dimension matches that of the motion feature.

E

Training objective and details.

The evaluator is optimized with two objectives. The motion autoencoder is supervised by a reconstruction loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{recon}}$ , which encourages the latent space to preserve the motion content. The condition and motion representations are aligned through contrastive learning using the InfoNCE loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{InfoNCE}}$ . During training, we randomly zero the sound source feature of an entire sequence with a probability of 0.3, producing audio-only conditions. This enables the evaluator to also apply to settings where the sound source trajectory is unavailable, while the audio condition is always retained.

We train the evaluator for up to 1,000 epochs using the Adam optimizer  with a learning rate of $5\times 10^{-5}$ and a batch size of 32. The evaluator is trained on all sequences of DySAM.()

van den Oord et al., 2018

()

Kingma and Ba, 2014

Appendix D

The FID is computed between the motion features of the ground-truth motions in the test set and those of the generated motions, where both sets of features are extracted by the frozen motion encoder of the evaluator. Gaussian distributions are fitted to the two feature sets, and the Fréchet distance between them serves as a metric for assessing the quality and fidelity of the synthesized motions.Fréchet Inception Distance (FID).

We compute the R-precision within batches of 32 sequences of the test set, following the protocol of . For each batch, the conditions and the motion features are L2-normalized, and the cosine similarities between all condition–motion pairs are ranked, where the pool of each condition consists of its matched motion together with the other 31 in-batch motions as distractors. The R-precision is then obtained by determining the probability that the matched motion appears among the top-1, top-2 and top-3 ranked positions, and is averaged over all the batches. The metric is computed in both the condition-to-motion and the motion-to-condition retrieval directions. The query condition used in our experiments consists of the ground-truth binaural audio and the ground-truth sound source trajectory, independently of the condition adopted by each generator, so that all compared methods are evaluated against the same query set. The Real Motion row in the main tables corresponds to using the ground-truth motions as the retrieval target.R-precision.()

Guo et al., 2022

We compute the skating ratio from recovered world-space foot joints, using the left and right foot joints indexed as 10 and 11 in the 22-joint SMPL protocol. For each foot, we compute its horizontal velocity on the ground plane at 30 Hz and smooth it with a 5-frame window. A foot is considered if it remains within 5 cm above the floor in adjacent frames and its smoothed horizontal speed is below 0.30 m/s. We count a valid contact frame as skating only when neither foot is planted. Airborne frames, where both feet are above 5 cm, and penetration frames, where any foot is below the floor plane, are excluded from the skating ratio and reported separately as float and penetration ratios. The procedure is summarized as follows.Skating Ratio.planted

Our skating ratio formulation is modified from GMD , which marks a frame as skating when either foot is close to the ground and moves faster than $0.50$  m/s. This can falsely flag frames where one foot is stably planted while the other foot briefly moves or drags near the floor, since the original metric evaluates each foot independently and ignores whether the body has a valid support foot. In contrast, our metric detects the absence of any stable support foot. This support-foot criterion avoids counting normal swing-foot motion as skating when the other foot stably supports the body.()

Karunratanakul et al., 2023

To verify the metric behavior, we evaluate both definitions on the ground-truth motions of DySAM. As shown in Tab. , the original formulation reports a skating ratio of 13.9% on ground-truth data, which is inconsistent with the fact that these motions are captured from real humans and should contain little foot skating. In contrast, our formulation gives a much lower ratio of 1.26%, indicating that the revised metric better reflects actual foot skating artifacts rather than false positives caused by normal foot motion or representation noise.

Appendix F

To evaluate the controllability of MOMO with respect to the reaction genre, we compare generated motions under two genre labels, where label 1 denotes a sensitive reaction and label 0 denotes an insensitive reaction. As shown in Fig. , for three representative audio examples, we keep the binaural audio input unchanged and only switch the genre label during generation.

F3

MOMO produces clearly different responses for the two labels. Motions generated with label 1 show larger amplitudes and stronger avoidance reactions, whereas those with label 0 are more restrained and subtle. These results demonstrate that MOMO can effectively control the reaction intensity and expressiveness through the genre condition.

Appendix G

To investigate the applicability of dynamic spatial-audio-driven motion generation to embodied agents, we provide both simulated and real-world robot demonstrations. These demonstrations serve as preliminary evidence that the generated motions can be transferred to robotic platforms, suggesting the potential of our task formulation for future embodied deployment.

For the simulated robot demonstration, we retarget the generated SMPL-X motion parameters to a humanoid robot using GMR . A pretrained TWIST controller is then used to track the retargeted motion and drive the robot in the MuJoCo environment , as shown in Fig. .()

We conduct a user study to evaluate the perceptual quality of generated motions. The study focuses on two aspects:

(1) , which measures whether the generated motion looks natural, realistic, and temporally smooth; and

(2) , which measures whether the motion response is consistent with the audio content and the movement of the sound source.motion realism and fluencyalignment with dynamic spatial audio

A total of 30 participants take part in the study. We provide 10 audio cases for evaluation. For each case, participants are shown six videos: one ground-truth motion video as the reference, and five generated motion videos from different methods, including MOMO(Ours), MOSPA , MoMask++ , POPDG , and EDGE . 一句话：不止从声音生成动作，还考虑声源本身在移动——更贴近真实空间关系。

要点：

  • 现有音生动作方法假设声源固定，脱离实际
  • 把声源运动轨迹纳入条件，生成与之匹配的动作
  • 华南理工与港大合作，含多模态数据标注

为什么值得看：空间音频与动作驱动结合，对引擎里的「声源-角色」联动系统（如 VR、过场动画）有直接启发。

中文摘要：MOMO 处理一个被忽略的细节：以往「从声音生成人体动作」的方法都假设声源是静止的，但现实中声源（脚步、乐器、车辆）往往在移动。作者把声源的运动轨迹作为额外条件引入生成模型，使产出的动作在方向、速度与空间关系上与声音一致。论文来自华南理工与香港大学，对空间音频驱动动画、VR 过场等场景有直接价值。

Abstract

Human responses to sound depend not only on its semantic content, but also on the evolving spatial relationship between source and listener, conveyed through spatial audio and its temporal dynamics. Modeling human reactions to such dynamic spatial audio is important for character animation, human behavior analysis, and robotics. As of yet, existing audio-driven motion generation methods primarily focus on non-spatial or static acoustic conditions, leaving this important problem largely underexplored. To bridge this gap, we formulate the novel task of dynamic spatial-audio-driven human motion generation and introduce two motion-captured datasets. We introduce the namic patial udio and otion dataset (DySAM) as the first dataset and benchmark for this task, providing synchronized binaural audio, 3D human motions, and moving sound source trajectories. Given the importance of dynamic spatial cues of sound sources, we further provide the namic patial udio ocalization dataset (DySAL), an auxiliary binaural localization dataset that pairs diverse acoustic events with head poses and moving source trajectories to support spatial audio perception.

For benchmarking, we propose MOMO for human tion generation from ving Sounds, a diffusion-based framework guided by three coupled principles: localization, understanding, and generation.

MOMO performs localization by estimating head-centric spatial direction cues of the moving source directly from raw binaural audio, avoiding reliance on ground-truth source coordinates. It performs understanding by extracting frame-wise audio-content representations, and performs generation by conditioning motion diffusion on both semantic features and dynamic spatial cues. Moreover, MOMO incorporates frame-wise motion correction during denoising, enabling temporally adaptive motion synthesis under evolving audio-spatial cues.

Experiments show that MOMO outperforms existing baselines in motion fidelity, audio-motion alignment, and physical plausibility, demonstrating the potential of dynamic spatial audio for embodied motion generation.

Project page: DySAMDySALMoMo

https://cdlchoi.github.io/projects/MOMO

This paper proposes a novel task for synthesizing 3D human motions in response to . To support this new task, we collect DySAM, the first dataset comprising synchronized dynamic spatial audio, corresponding sound source trajectories, and high-quality 3D human motion. In this figure, the model generates diverse and realistic human reactions to various moving acoustic events.Figure 1: dynamicspatialaudio

1

Diverse Reactions to Moving Sounds.Figure 2:

Human responses to sound arise from integrating semantic meaning with cues and the . A barking dog approaching from behind may elicit avoidance, whereas a speeding car approaching may prompt reorientation. Crucially, the same sound can evoke different actions depending on its source’s location and motion relative to the listener. Modeling this perception–action coupling supports context-aware virtual humans and embodied agents in character animation, virtual reality, human–computer interaction, and embodied intelligence.spatial audiotemporal dynamics of sound sources

Existing human motion datasets and methods have mainly focused on conditions such as action labels , text descriptions , music , and speech . Recently, to the best of our knowledge, MOSPA introduced the first spatial-audio-driven human motion dataset, SAM, along with a corresponding motion generation method, showing that spatial audio cues are crucial for generating realistic human motions. However, the SAM dataset mainly focuses on a static sound source, where the sound source position remains fixed within each sequence. Moreover, MOSPA requires the ground-truth absolute position of the sound source as a condition for motion generation, which is difficult to obtain in real-world scenarios and limits its applicability to embodied agents. Therefore, dynamic spatial-audio-driven human motion generation, which models human motion responses to time-varying spatial audio from moving sound sources, remains largely underexplored, especially in practical settings without access to ground-truth sound source positions.()

Guo et al., 2020

()

Guo et al., 2022

Zhuang et al., 2022

Tseng et al., 2023

Xu et al., 2025

To address this gap, we introduce DySAM, a dataset for dynamic spatial-audio-driven human motion generation. DySAM contains synchronized binaural audio, 3D human motion, and dynamic sound source trajectories captured in an indoor environment. Human motion and sound source trajectories are recorded using a Vicon motion capture system , while binaural audio is captured by high-sensitivity microphones near the actors’ ears, approximating the audio perceived by the actors. The main dataset contains 2,336 ten-second audio-motion sequences, totaling 23,360 seconds (approximately 6.5 hours), with motion at 30 FPS and audio at 48 kHz. It covers 42 audio types and 109 unique audio sources, including human sounds, animal sounds, vehicles, and environmental sounds, with 8 subjects and a binary genre label indicating sensitive or insensitive reactions. In addition, we provide DySAL, an auxiliary sound source localization dataset of 11,730 seconds, pairing binaural audio of diverse acoustic events with listener head 6DoF poses and frame-wise moving sound source annotations to support dynamic spatial audio perception.()

Motivated by the fact that human reactions to spatial sound depend on both where the sound comes from and what the sound is, we formulate spatial-audio-driven motion generation around three coupled functional components: , , and . Guided by this design principle, we propose MOMO, a diffusion-based framework for generating human motion conditioned on dynamic spatial audio. For localization, MOMO estimates frame-wise head-centric spatial cues of sound source from raw binaural audio using a sound source localization network, eliminating the reliance on privileged ground-truth source coordinates. For understanding, a pretrained CLAP audio encoder encodes the binaural audio to obtain frame-wise audio-content features. For generation, MOMO employs a diffusion-based motion generator conditioned on the predicted spatial cues, CLAP audio features, and genre label.

Since human motion needs to continuously adapt to the evolving spatial cues of the sound source, while self-attention only provides implicit interactions between motion tokens and condition tokens, we further introduce a module in the Transformer denoiser to explicitly refine motion tokens with frame-wise conditions, along with a that adaptively controls the correction magnitude for each frame.localizationunderstandinggeneration()

By using head-centric DoA estimated directly from binaural audio, MOMO provides a more practical formulation for spatial-audio-driven motion generation in embodied robot settings. Compared with MOSPA , which relies on ground-truth global sound source coordinates, our egocentric formulation avoids privileged source-location annotations and better reflects how embodied agents infer dynamic sound direction from their own auditory observations. Extensive quantitative and qualitative experiments show that MOMO outperforms existing baselines, producing more realistic motions that respond to dynamic spatial-audio cues.()

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

•

We introduce two datasets: DySAM, to the best of our knowledge the first dataset for dynamic spatial-audio-driven human motion generation, and DySAL, an auxiliary sound source localization dataset collected in indoor reverberant environments.

•

We propose MOMO, a practical framework for generating human motion from binaural audio without requiring ground-truth source coordinates. It integrates sound source localization, CLAP-based audio content encoding, and diffusion-based motion generation to model human responses to moving sound sources.

•

Extensive quantitative and qualitative experiments show that MOMO generates natural, plausible, and spatially consistent human motion, better aligning with real motion and outperforming existing baselines.

Conditional Human Motion Generation.

Conditional human motion generation has been extensively studied under various conditions, such as action labels , textual descriptions , trajectories , and motion language models that treat human motion as a foreign language . These methods generate diverse and natural motions from semantic conditions, but they generally do not consider audio, let alone its spatial attributes. In contrast, our work focuses on audio-driven conditions with explicit spatial information.()

Audio-Driven Human Motion Generation.

Audio-driven human motion generation has been studied mainly in two directions. The first is music-driven dance generation , which generates choreography that matches the rhythm and style of the music. The second is speech-driven gesture synthesis , which generates co-speech gestures from speech content and prosody. Most of these methods use monaural or stereo audio and ignore the spatial attributes of the sound source. MOSPA is the first to study spatial-audio-driven human motion generation with binaural audio, but it assumes a static sound source position. Different from MOSPA, we consider dynamic spatial audio, where the source moves over time, and the DoA changes accordingly.(; ; ; ; ; ; ; )

Spatial Sound Understanding.

Estimating the direction of a sound source from binaural signals is a classic problem in acoustic scene analysis, for instance using binaural cues combined with deep learning .

Recent works also model room acoustics and room impulse responses to support sound source localization in complex indoor scenes .

In this paper, we adopt a sound source localization network to predict the head-centric DoA from binaural audio, which serves as the spatial condition for motion generation. This makes our framework practical in real-world scenarios where ground-truth source coordinates are unavailable.(; )

This section presents two newly collected motion-capture datasets for dynamic spatial-audio-driven human motion generation.

The Dynamic Spatial Audio and Motion dataset (DySAM) serves as the main benchmark for this task, providing synchronized binaural audio, 3D human motions, and moving sound source trajectories.

To support broader research on dynamic spatial audio perception, we introduce the Dynamic Spatial Audio Localization dataset (DySAL) that pairs diverse acoustic events with listener head poses and mocap-recorded moving source trajectories.

Data Capture Setup.

Data Collection Setup. Figure 3:

We collect the data in an indoor environment with natural reverberation using a Vicon motion capture system , which records both human motion and the trajectory of a moving sound source (as shown in Fig. ). We use an omnidirectional speaker to play the dynamic audio. We choose binaural audio as the audio modality, following the SAM dataset , as it is a common form of spatial audio that aligns with human auditory perception and can be readily applied to virtual characters and robotic platforms. Binaural audio is recorded using two microphones placed near the actor’s ears, allowing the signals to approximate the auditory input the actor perceives during capture. Specifically, we use Sound Professionals MS-TFB-2 microphones  and a Deity PR-2 recorder for binaural audio recording. The audio recorder is synchronized with the mocap system using timecode, ensuring temporal alignment among binaural audio, human motion, and sound source trajectories.()

DySAM is the first dataset for dynamic spatial-audio-driven human motion generation, containing synchronized binaural audio, 3D human motion, and dynamic sound source trajectories (Dyn. SS). We also provide DySAL, an auxiliary sound source localization dataset containing dynamic binaural recordings of diverse acoustic events with frame-wise source annotations.Table 1: Statistics of the DySAM dataset.

3.1

Our main dataset, DySAM, is collected for dynamic spatial-audio-driven human motion generation, with visualization snapshots provided in Fig. . Each sequence consists of a 10-second binaural audio clip, the corresponding 3D human motion stored in the SMPL-X format , and the trajectory of a moving sound source in the world coordinate system. As summarized in Tab. , DySAM contains 2,336 synchronized audio-motion sequences, amounting to 23,360 seconds (approximately 6.5 hours) of paired data. The captured motions are represented as SMPL-X model . The audio’s sampling rate is 48,000 Hz, while the motion is represented at 30 FPS for network training. DySAM covers 42 audio types and 109 unique audio sources, spanning diverse daily-life acoustic events such as animal sounds, vehicles, alarms, music, and human speech. It was collected with 8 actors, including 5 female and 3 male. Each sequence is annotated with one of two reaction genres, sensitive or insensitive, with an approximately balanced 1:1 ratio.

We additionally collect DySAL, an auxiliary sound source localization dataset, using the same motion capture setup. It provides abundant spatial supervision for training the SSL network, enabling robust estimation of dynamic head-centric DoA cues from binaural audio. It contains 11,730 seconds, approximately 3.3 hours, of binaural audio paired with frame-wise sound source positions and the listener’s head 6DoF pose in the world coordinate system. These spatial cues can facilitate broader studies of spatial audio perception, such as absolute source localization and direction-of-arrival estimation. To ensure the diversity of acoustic events, we collect raw audio from AIST , ESC-50 , and UrbanSound8K , covering a wide range of music, environmental, human, animal, mechanical, and urban sounds.

We propose MOMO, a diffusion-based framework for dynamic-spatial-audio-driven human motion generation. In real world, human reactions to spatial sound depend on both spatial direction and audio content.

Accordingly, MOMO consists of three coupled functional components: , , and , as illustrated in Fig. . For localization, a sound source localization (SSL) network estimates a frame-wise head-centric direction-of-arrival (DoA) sequence $\bm{D}=\{d_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{3}\}_{t=1}^{T}$ from raw binaural audio, T is the max length of motion (Sec. ). For understanding, a pretrained CLAP audio encoder extracts temporally aligned audio content representations $\bm{A}=\{a_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T}$ from the mono audio. For generation, a transformer-encoder-based conditional diffusion model synthesizes motion through frame-wise correction conditioned on $\bm{D}$ , $\bm{A}$ , the genre label $g$ , and the diffusion timestep $\tau$ . Rather than relying solely on attention mechanism, it incorporates and , allowing the denoiser to adaptively determine the correction magnitude for each frame under dynamic spatial-audio conditions (Sec. ). For network training, we adopt a 272-dimensional motion representation following .localizationunderstandinggeneration

4.1

In real-world scenes, ground-truth absolute global coordinates of sound sources are often unavailable. To obtain a motion-relevant and coordinate-invariant spatial cue, we represent the sound source at each frame as a head-centric direction-of-arrival (DoA) unit vector, transformed from the source position in the world coordinate system to the head coordinate system using the 6DoF head pose. Specifically, the SSL network predicts a sequence of frame-wise DoA vectors $\hat{\bm{D}}=\{\hat{d}_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T}$ , where each $\hat{d}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{3}$ is a unit vector. This head-centric representation avoids the need for absolute global source coordinates.

Our SSL network is inspired by the binaural sound localization framework of Garcia et al. , which employs STFT-based binaural cues with a cascaded CNN-GRU architecture. We follow their use of STFT-based binaural spatial features and a CNN front-end for extracting local spectro-temporal patterns, but replace the GRU-based temporal modeling module with a Transformer encoder to better capture long-range temporal dependencies under reverberant environments. The SSL network is trained to predict the frame-wise head-centric DoA unit vector using a cosine-distance loss:

$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ssl}}=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left(1-\hat{d}_{t}\cdot d_{t}\right),$

where $\hat{d}_{t}$ and $d_{t}$ denote the predicted and ground-truth DoA unit vectors, respectively, both normalized in the head coordinate system. Once trained, the SSL network is frozen and used to predict the spatial condition sequence $\hat{\bm{D}}$ . Please refer to Appendix for more details on the SSL architecture and training setup.()

MOMO comprises three coupled functional components: a sound source localization (SSL) network predicts a frame-wise head-centric DoA sequence $\hat{\bm{D}}$ from binaural audio (); a CLAP audio encoder extracts frame-wise audio content features $\bm{A}$ from mono audio (); and a conditional diffusion model that iteratively denoise the Gaussian noise to generated motion, integrating Frame-wise Motion Correction to adaptively correct each motion according to frame-wise conditions ().

Figure 5: Overview of MOMO framework.localizationunderstandinggeneration

4.2

We formulate motion generation as conditional denoising diffusion . Given noisy motion $\mathbf{x}_{\tau}$ at diffusion step $\tau$ , the denoising network predicts the clean motion sequence $\mathbf{x}_{0}$ conditioned on audio content, DoA, genre, and timestep embeddings. For audio content, we average the binaural signal into a mono waveform and feed it into a pretrained CLAP encoder . The extracted hidden features are pooled over channel and frequency dimensions and temporally aligned with the motion sequence, producing frame-wise audio features $\bm{A}=\{a_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T}$ .()

Building on the Transformer encoder of , we project $\mathbf{x}_{\tau}$ into motion tokens $\bm{m}=\{\mathbf{m}_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T}$ and concatenate them with condition tokens derived from audio features, DoA features, genre, and the diffusion-step embedding. The concatenated tokens are fed into the Transformer encoder for conditional denoising. Since the attention mechanism only provides implicit interactions between motion tokens and the frame-wise condition tokens, we further introduce a module to explicitly correct motion tokens based on frame-wise conditions, together with a that adaptively determines the correction strength.

Xu et al. (2025)

Frame-wise Motion CorrectionCorrection Strength Predictor

To explicitly leverage both global and frame-wise conditions, we apply a residual correction module based on Adaptive Layer Normalization (AdaLN) on after each Transformer encoder layer to refine the intermediate motion token, which is formulated asFrame-wise Motion Correction.

$\bm{m}^{\prime}=\bm{m}+\bm{\alpha}\odot\bm{\delta},$ (1)

where $\bm{\delta}=\{\delta_{i}\}_{i=1}^{T}$ denotes the frame-wise correction, and $\bm{\alpha}=\{\alpha_{i}\}_{i=1}^{T}$ is an frame-wise correction strength.

The modulation condition $\bm{c}=\{c_{i}\}_{i=1}^{T}$ consists of four components: the timestep embedding $t$ , the genre embedding $g$ , the frame-wise audio feature $\bm{A}$ , and the frame-wise DoA feature $\bm{D}$ . The unified condition sequence is obtained by summing these components at each frame, with the global timestep and genre embeddings broadcast to all $T$ frames: $c_{i}=e_{t}+e_{g}+a_{i}+d_{i}$ . This condition sequence is then used to modulate the motion tokens.

An MLP then estimates scale and shift sequences $(\bm{\gamma},\bm{\beta})=\mathrm{MLP}(\mathbf{c}_{i})$ for AdaLN , yielding the correction:()

Peebles and Xie, 2023

$\bm{\delta}=\mathrm{FFN}\left(\mathrm{LN}(\bm{m})\odot(1+\bm{\gamma})+\bm{\beta}\right),$ (2)

The correction strength should not be a fixed parameter tied to a specific layer or frame position. Instead, the strength of motion correction should depend on the audio content, spatial DoA cues, genre, and the current denoising step. We therefore predict $\bm{\alpha}$ dynamically from the interaction between motion tokens and frame-wise conditions.Correction Strength Predictor.

Specifically, we use motion tokens as queries $\bm{Q}=\bm{m}$ and modulation condition as keys and values $\bm{K}=\bm{V}=\bm{c}$ . Considering that human responses to sounds may exhibit temporal delays, we apply a causal attention mask to prevent the token at frame $t$ from attending to future condition frames. The correct strength is bounded by

$\bm{\alpha}=\alpha_{\max}\cdot\mathrm{Sigmoid}(\mathrm{MLP}_{\alpha}(\mathrm{CrossAttn}(\bm{m},\bm{c}_{\leq t},\bm{c}_{\leq t}))).$ (3)

This design decouples the estimation of the condition-dependent correction and its strength: the AdaLN modulation module predicts the correction term, while the cross-attention predictor dynamically determines how strongly this correction is applied.

4.3

We train MOMO a reconstruction loss:

$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{diff}}=\left\|\bm{x_{0}}-\bm{\hat{x_{0}}}(\mathbf{x}_{\tau},\tau,\mathbf{c})\right\|_{2}^{2}.$

To ensure temporal continuity and reduce foot-sliding artifacts, we further use a delta loss

$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{del}}=\left\|\hat{\bm{x_{0}}}-\bm{x_{0}}\right\|_{2}^{2}$

and a foot contact loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{foot}}$ . The overall objective is:()

$\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{diff}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{del}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{del}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{foot}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{foot}}.$ (4)

Experimental Setup.

We split the main DySAM dataset into train/validation/test sets with a ratio of 8:1:1. For training the sound source localization network, we transform the global sound source position into head-centric unit direction vector using the head 6DoF pose, and use it as the ground-truth DoA. Regarding metrics, we use FID, R-precision, Diversity , Average Pairwise Distance (APD) , and a physics-based skating ratio, as detailed in Appendix . We introduce a multi-branch motion-audio-source evaluator for feature extraction, aiming to better measure the spatial alignment between the generated motion and the moving sound source; details are provided in Appendix .

We compare with diffusion-based and VQ-based baselines, including EDGE , POPDG , MOSPA , and MoMask++ . All baselines are trained on the same DySAM split, with their original input conditions replaced by traditional acoustic features for fair comparison.()

This paper introduces the task of dynamic spatial-audio-driven human motion generation. We present DySAM, the first dataset and benchmark for this task containing synchronized binaural audio, 3D human motion, and moving sound source trajectories, together with DySAL, an auxiliary dataset that provides diverse acoustic events and frame-wise spatial annotations for dynamic spatial audio perception.

We further propose MOMO, a diffusion-based framework that explicitly leverages frame-wise audio-spatial conditions to generate high-quality human motions in response to dynamic spatial audio.

Extensive experiments demonstrate that MOMO produces natural and physically plausible motions with improved alignment to dynamic spatial audio.

Our current setting considers a single prominent moving sound source. Extending the framework to multiple simultaneous sources would require jointly reasoning about source separation, localization, and their potentially different behavioral relevance. We leave this challenging setting for future research and evaluation.Limitations and Future Work:

Appendix A

A.1

At the beginning of each clip, the dynamic sound source, i.e., a speaker, starts from one of four azimuthal regions relative to the actor: front-left, rear-left, rear-right, and front-right. This design enables us to capture diverse human reactions to sounds arriving from different directions. The trajectory of the sound source is designed to be either straight or curved. Moreover, the sound source either moves toward the actor and reaches the actor’s position, or passes by without contact. These two movement patterns elicit fundamentally different responses. For example, an actor may react differently when a dog or a car rushes toward them than when it merely passes by.

We further define two reaction styles: insensitive and sensitive, to represent different levels of responsiveness to the same acoustic event. For instance, when hearing an explosion, an insensitive actor may remain largely unreactive, whereas a sensitive actor may immediately move away from the sound source. The two reaction styles are approximately balanced in the dataset.

A.2

The data are collected in a typical indoor environment with natural room reverberation. The motion capture system consists of 20 Vicon cameras installed around the capture space, recording both the human body motion and the sound source trajectory at 120 Hz.

For the moving sound source, we use a cylindrical omni-directional speaker to play the audio, ensuring stable sound radiation in different directions as the speaker moves. For binaural audio recording, a high-sensitivity microphone is placed near each ear of the actor to capture the audio perceived by the actor as faithfully as possible. The two microphones are connected to a Deity PR-2 recorder , which is synchronized with the Vicon system in advance using timecode. This setup ensures accurate temporal alignment between the recorded binaural audio and the corresponding motion capture data.()

Deity Microphones, 2026

A.3

The DySAM dataset covers 42 distinct audio types, corresponding to 109 unique audio sources, as listed in Tab. . Each audio type comprises one to six audio sources, and for each audio source 8 to 32 ten-second motion sequences are collected, yielding 2,336 (binaural audio, motion) pairs in total. These audio types span daily-life sounds including animal vocalizations, vehicles, environmental noises, alarms, musical instruments, and human speech.

A.4

To ensure broad audio diversity, we collect raw audio materials from AIST , ESC-50 , and UrbanSound8K . AIST mainly contains music and dance-related audio with diverse rhythms, styles, and structures. ESC-50 provides environmental sounds from natural scenes, human activities, animal sounds, indoor and outdoor daily scenes, and mechanical devices, such as rain, sea waves, bird calls, coughing, footsteps, keyboard typing, bells, and vacuum cleaners. UrbanSound8K contains typical urban sounds, including air conditioners, car horns, children playing, dog barks, drilling, engine idling, gunshots, jackhammers, sirens, and street music.()

By combining these sources, DySAL covers music, human activities, natural environments, animals, indoor and outdoor daily activities, transportation, mechanical construction, alarms, and urban public spaces. This diversity broadens the range of acoustic events available for training and evaluating sound source localization models under dynamic spatial-audio conditions.

A1

During capture, the actor wears a motion capture suit with multiple reflective markers attached to the body, represented by the in Fig.  The Vicon system exports the captured data as C3D files, where each file stores the world coordinates of all body markers for every frame. We use Mosh++ to fit each C3D sequence into the SMPL-X parameters. The fitted SMPL-X motion is then canonicalized by rotating the human body in the initial frame to face the positive $y$ -axis and move the center of the body to the origin. To track the position of the sound source, i.e., the speaker, we attach eight reflective markers around the speaker ( in Fig. ), which approximately correspond to the eight vertices of a cuboid. For each C3D sequence, we use the speaker markers in the initial frame as reference markers. We then estimate the speaker translation in each subsequent frame by solving the rigid alignment between the reference markers and the current-frame markers using singular value decomposition (SVD). The estimated translation is used as the global sound source location in our dataset, represented by the in Fig. . In practice, some speaker markers may be missing in certain frames due to occlusion or tracking failure, making SVD-based estimation unreliable or infeasible. For these frames, we use Kalman filtering to smoothly interpolate and complete the missing sound source locations.Sound source location processing.orange points

To train the sound source localization network, we further compute the head-centric sound source location. Specifically, for each frame, we perform forward kinematics on the fitted SMPL-X body model to obtain the translation and rotation of the head joint, i.e., joint 15. We then transform the global sound source location into the head coordinate system using the estimated head pose, yielding the head-centric sound source location as the direction-related supervision signal.Head-centric DoA processing.
