Appendix B

We provide additional implementation details of the sound source localization network used in Sec. . The SSL network estimates a head-centric direction of arrival from binaural audio. For every frame, it predicts a unit vector

$\mathbf{d}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{3},$

which points from the listener’s head toward the sound source and is expressed in the listener’s head coordinate system.

4.1

Binaural feature extraction.

We compute the short-time Fourier transform (STFT) of the left and right binaural signals using a $40\,\mathrm{ms}$ Hamming window, zero-padded to an FFT size of $2048$ , and a hop size of $33.3\,\mathrm{ms}$ , yielding a frame rate of $30\,\mathrm{Hz}$ aligned with the motion sequence. We keep the lowest $256$ frequency bins, corresponding to frequencies up to approximately $6\,\mathrm{kHz}$ .

Let $L_{t,f}$ and $R_{t,f}$ denote the complex STFT coefficients of the left and right channels at time frame $t$ and frequency bin $f$ . The SSL input contains four channels: (1) the average magnitude spectrum, (2-3) the sine and cosine of the interaural phase difference (IPD), and (4) the interaural level difference (ILD). The first channel encodes the overall spectral magnitude, the second and third channels encode the IPD without phase-wrapping discontinuities, and the fourth channel provides the relative loudness between the two ears. The resulting binaural feature is a tensor $\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{4\times 300\times 256}$ , where every sequence is represented by $300$ frames at $30\,\mathrm{Hz}$ to match the motion sequences. The extraction procedure is summarized in the Python pseudo-code below.

Network architecture.

The SSL network consists of a convolutional spectral encoder followed by a Transformer-based temporal encoder. The convolutional front-end contains three convolutional blocks. Each block applies a $3\times 3$ convolution followed by a ReLU activation and max pooling along the frequency axis with stride $4$ . This progressively reduces the frequency dimension from $256$ to $64$ , $16$ , and $4$ , while preserving the temporal resolution.

After the convolutional blocks, the feature map is flattened at each time frame and projected into a $C$ -dimensional latent space, where $C=128$ . We add a learnable absolute positional encoding to the frame-wise tokens before feeding them into the temporal encoder.

Different from , which adopts a GRU for temporal modeling, we use a Transformer encoder. The encoder has $L=4$ layers, $8$ attention heads, and a feed-forward hidden dimension of $256$ . We use pre-normalization Transformer blocks for stable training. The self-attention mechanism enables each frame to aggregate binaural evidence from the entire sequence, which helps resolve ambiguous localization cues caused by reverberation or transient source motion.()

García-Barrios et al., 2022

The Transformer outputs one token per frame. Each token is passed through two fully connected layers to regress a three-dimensional vector, which is then L2-normalized to obtain the predicted DoA:

$\mathbf{d}_{t}=\frac{\mathbf{o}_{t}}{\|\mathbf{o}_{t}\|_{2}},$

where $\mathbf{o}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{3}$ is the raw output vector before normalization.

Training objective.

The SSL network is trained using head-relative source direction labels from DySAM and DySAL. The ground-truth direction vector at frame $t$ is normalized to unit length and denoted as $\bar{\mathbf{d}}_{t}$ . We optimize the cosine-distance loss:

$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ssl}}=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left(1-\mathbf{d}_{t}\cdot\bar{\mathbf{d}}_{t}\right).$

This objective is monotonically related to the angular error between the predicted and ground-truth DoA vectors and directly supervises the directional information used by the downstream motion generator.

During motion generation, the SSL network parameters are frozen. Given only binaural audio, the network produces the frame-wise DoA sequence

$\mathbf{D}=\{\mathbf{d}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{d}_{T}\},$

which is used as the spatial condition of the diffusion model.

Appendix C

The evaluator framework consists of a motion autoencoder co-trained with Bi-GRU feature extractors. A reconstruction loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{recon}}$ is applied between the ground-truth motion $\mathbf{x}$ and the decoded motion $\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ produced by the motion autoencoder. Two Bi-GRU encoders extract the audio feature and the sound source feature from the binaural audio and the sound source trajectory, respectively, and the concatenation of the two features forms the condition latent. Additionally, an InfoNCE loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{InfoNCE}}$ operates on the extracted condition features and motion features.Figure C2:

Inspired by the evaluator design from , our evaluator is a motion–condition matching network , which measures how well a motion sequence corresponds to a given spatial audio condition. It maps both modalities into a shared latent space, in which the R-precision metrics are computed by nearest-neighbor retrieval and the FID is computed between the feature distributions of the ground-truth and the generated motions. Different from , whose condition only contains the acoustic content, our condition additionally involves the trajectory of the sound source, so that the evaluator is sensitive to the spatial correspondence between the moving sound source and the human reaction.()

Xu et al., 2025

()

Xu et al., 2025

Network architecture.

As illustrated in Fig. , the evaluator consists of a motion autoencoder and three bidirectional GRUs (Bi-GRUs), each with 4 layers and a hidden size of 512. The feature of a Bi-GRU is obtained by concatenating its last forward and backward hidden states, which yields a 1024-dimensional feature vector.

C2

The motion autoencoder follows a transformer encoder–decoder structure. The input motion sequence $\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times 272}$ is first projected to a 512-dimensional latent space and added with a positional encoding, and is then encoded by a 4-layer transformer encoder with 4 attention heads and a 1024-dimensional feed-forward layer. The encoder output is averaged over time into a single latent vector and replicated along the temporal axis, which serves as the query of a transformer decoder of the same configuration attending to the encoder output. A final linear layer maps the decoder output back to the 272-dimensional motion space to produce the reconstructed motion $\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ . The output of the motion encoder is further encoded by a Bi-GRU to obtain the motion feature.

The condition branch consists of an audio encoder and a sound source encoder. The audio encoder takes the traditional features described in Appendix . The sound source encoder takes the absolute position of the sound source in the world coordinate system $\mathbf{s}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times 3}$ , projects it to 64 dimensions and encodes it with a Bi-GRU. The resulting audio and sound source features are concatenated and projected by a linear layer into the condition feature, whose dimension matches that of the motion feature.

E

Training objective and details.

The evaluator is optimized with two objectives. The motion autoencoder is supervised by a reconstruction loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{recon}}$ , which encourages the latent space to preserve the motion content. The condition and motion representations are aligned through contrastive learning using the InfoNCE loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{InfoNCE}}$ . During training, we randomly zero the sound source feature of an entire sequence with a probability of 0.3, producing audio-only conditions. This enables the evaluator to also apply to settings where the sound source trajectory is unavailable, while the audio condition is always retained.

We train the evaluator for up to 1,000 epochs using the Adam optimizer  with a learning rate of $5\times 10^{-5}$ and a batch size of 32. The evaluator is trained on all sequences of DySAM.()

Appendix D

The FID is computed between the motion features of the ground-truth motions in the test set and those of the generated motions, where both sets of features are extracted by the frozen motion encoder of the evaluator. Gaussian distributions are fitted to the two feature sets, and the Fréchet distance between them serves as a metric for assessing the quality and fidelity of the synthesized motions.Fréchet Inception Distance (FID).

We compute the R-precision within batches of 32 sequences of the test set, following the protocol of . For each batch, the conditions and the motion features are L2-normalized, and the cosine similarities between all condition–motion pairs are ranked, where the pool of each condition consists of its matched motion together with the other 31 in-batch motions as distractors. The R-precision is then obtained by determining the probability that the matched motion appears among the top-1, top-2 and top-3 ranked positions, and is averaged over all the batches. The metric is computed in both the condition-to-motion and the motion-to-condition retrieval directions. The query condition used in our experiments consists of the ground-truth binaural audio and the ground-truth sound source trajectory, independently of the condition adopted by each generator, so that all compared methods are evaluated against the same query set. The Real Motion row in the main tables corresponds to using the ground-truth motions as the retrieval target.R-precision.()

Guo et al., 2022

We compute the skating ratio from recovered world-space foot joints, using the left and right foot joints indexed as 10 and 11 in the 22-joint SMPL protocol. For each foot, we compute its horizontal velocity on the ground plane at 30 Hz and smooth it with a 5-frame window. A foot is considered if it remains within 5 cm above the floor in adjacent frames and its smoothed horizontal speed is below 0.30 m/s. We count a valid contact frame as skating only when neither foot is planted. Our skating ratio formulation is modified from GMD , which marks a frame as skating when either foot is close to the ground and moves faster than $0.50$  m/s. This can falsely flag frames where one foot is stably planted while the other foot briefly moves or drags near the floor, since the original metric evaluates each foot independently and ignores whether the body has a valid support foot. In contrast, our metric detects the absence of any stable support foot. This support-foot criterion avoids counting normal swing-foot motion as skating when the other foot stably supports the body.()

To verify the metric behavior, we evaluate both definitions on the ground-truth motions of DySAM. As shown in Tab. , the original formulation reports a skating ratio of 13.9% on ground-truth data, which is inconsistent with the fact that these motions are captured from real humans and should contain little foot skating. In contrast, our formulation gives a much lower ratio of 1.26%, indicating that the revised metric better reflects actual foot skating artifacts rather than false positives caused by normal foot motion or representation noise.

item.title: 皮克斯《Hoppers》的制作幕后搬上 SIGGRAPH Asia 2026 ｜ Pixar Animation Studios Brings the Making of 'Hoppers' to SIGGRAPH Asia 2026
item.description:
一句话：皮克斯将在 SIGGRAPH Asia 2026 分享新片《Hoppers》的创意决策与技术实现。

要点：

  • 聚焦创意选择如何反向驱动技术方案，而非单列技术清单
  • 披露影片制作中动画与渲染管线的新增模块
  • SIGGRAPH Asia 2026 现场场次

为什么值得看：顶级动画工作室的管线演进往往会下沉到引擎，提前知道他们解决了什么问题可以少走弯路。

中文摘要：SIGGRAPH 官方博客预告了皮克斯在 SIGGRAPH Asia 2026 的场次：围绕新片《Hoppers》讲述制作过程中的创意决策、技术创新与团队协作。文章强调创意需求如何倒逼技术选型，而不是罗列工具。对关注动画管线、角色渲染与制作流程的开发者来说，这是少有的能直接听到一线工作室复盘的机会。

主题：图形学

来源：SIGGRAPH Blog（English）

Pixar Animation Studios Brings the Making of ‘Hoppers’ to SIGGRAPH Asia 2026

by | | ,

SIGGRAPH Asia

15 October 2026

Animation

Conferences

Image credit: Leading image provided by SIGGRAPH Asia 2026

This December, the creative minds behind Disney and Pixar’s “Hoppers” are heading to Kuala Lumpur!

SIGGRAPH Asia 2026 is excited to welcome Pixar Animation Studios for a Featured Speakers session, “We’re All In This Together: The Making Of Disney and Pixar’s ‘Hoppers,’” offering a behind-the-scenes look at the artistry, technology, and collaboration that brought the film to life.

Creating the world of “Hoppers” came with a unique challenge: Bringing together three distinct visual styles, from the graphic clarity of comedy and the carefully controlled lighting and staging of suspense to the rich, observational beauty of nature photography.

To bring these elements together, the filmmakers developed a collaborative approach that balanced stylization with realism, combining physical simulation and artistic design to create the film’s distinctive visual world.

At SIGGRAPH Asia 2026, the Pixar team will share insights into the creative decisions, technical innovations, and collaborative processes behind the film, highlighting how artists and technologists across different disciplines worked together to bring their vision to the screen.

Meet the Pixar Team at SIGGRAPH Asia 2026

Layout lead, Pixar Animation Studios VFX supervisor, Pixar Animation Studios Tailoring and simulation supervisor, Pixar Animation StudiosAndrea Goh,Beth Albright,Lyon Liew,

And that’s not all! More exciting sessions, industry-leading speakers, and program highlights are still to be announced as we count down to SIGGRAPH Asia 2026.

item.title: 量化的高阶矩编码 LBM：更快的格子玻尔兹曼流体模拟 ｜ Quantized High-Performance High-Order Moment-Encoded LBM
item.description:
一句话：用量化与高阶矩编码把格子玻尔兹曼方法（LBM）跑到更高性能。

要点：

  • LBM 的矩表示在高阶时需要大量存储与带宽
  • 用量化压缩矩数据，降低内存占用
  • 保持数值稳定性与模拟精度

为什么值得看：流体模拟的内存带宽瓶颈是老问题；量化是引擎侧常用的手段，这篇给出了在 LBM 上的系统做法。

中文摘要：这篇 TOG 论文研究如何让格子玻尔兹曼方法（LBM）在高阶矩编码下跑得更快。LBM 把分布函数转成矩表示后，高阶项会带来显著的存储与带宽压力。作者引入量化手段压缩矩数据，并系统分析了精度损失与数值稳定性的边界，在不牺牲模拟可信度的前提下显著降低了内存占用与带宽需求。

主题：图形学

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

Quantized High-Performance High-Order Moment-Encoded LBM

TOGJournal: Computing methodologies Physical simulationCCS: Yixin Chen

email:

yixinc.chen@mail.utoronto.ca

, , Affiliation: University of TorontoTorontoCanada, Wei Li

Corresponding author.

Note: email:

1104720604wei@gmail.com

, , Affiliation: Shanghai Jiao Tong UniversityShanghaiChina, David I.W. Levin

diwlevin@cs.toronto.edu

and Kui Wu

email:

walker.kui.wu@gmail.com

, , Affiliation: LIGHTSPEEDLos AngelesUSA

. Figure 1

Turbulent smoke interacting with a Ducati motorcycle model with intricate geometry on a $1000\times 400\times 400$ grid using our GPU-optimized, 16-bit quantized LBM solver. The simulation preserves rich fine-scale vortical structures and remains numerically stable under highly complex boundary conditions. For this scene, our method achieves a $9.0\times$ speedup over the original FP32 HOME-LBM  implementation, while reducing memory usage by $25\%$ .()

Li et al., 2023

Abstract.

Lattice Boltzmann methods (LBM) are widely used for visually rich fluid simulation, but their high memory bandwidth and storage requirements limit GPU performance and scalability, especially when coupled with complex geometry. Recent high-order moment-encoded LBM (HOME-LBM) reduces memory cost by storing compact velocity moments and performing collision directly in moment space, but its tightly coupled boundary treatment introduces divergent control flow. We present a high-performance, quantized HOME-LBM framework for large-scale turbulent fluid–solid simulations on a single GPU. Our geometry-decoupled computation scheme separates the regular fluid update from a sparse solid-correction stage, isolating geometry-dependent computations to improve GPU efficiency. To further reduce storage and memory traffic, we develop a reduced-precision representation for HOME-LBM by combining von Neumann stability analysis, empirical moment-range estimation, and runtime decomposition of second-order moments to control quantization error. We evaluate our approach on real-time demonstrations and large-scale examples using both D3Q19 and D3Q27 lattices, with additional 2D and 3D numerical experiments assessing accuracy and stability. Across the tested benchmarks, our framework substantially accelerates the original FP32 HOME-LBM implementation, with a maximum speedup of $32.5\times$ on the Hilbert-curve geometry.

Moment storage is reduced by $50\%$ in fluid-only simulations and $25\%$ in fluid–solid coupling examples, while maintaining numerical stability, fidelity, and high visual quality.

In the static delta-wing benchmark, our solver achieves a $5.2\times$ speedup over Leapfrog Flow Maps (LFM) under the tested configuration.

fluid simulation; lattice Boltzmann method; GPU computing; quantization; fluid–solid coupling

Keywords:

1.

. Figure 2Smoke around an F1 car on a $1000\times 400\times 400$ grid (left: frame 80; right: frame 160) highlights a complex, multi-scale wake: strong shear layers from the wheels, rear wing, and diffuser roll up into coherent vortices near the vehicle, then stretch and break down into a turbulent, filamentary plume downstream.

Fluid simulation plays a central role in computer graphics, enabling the realistic synthesis of natural phenomena such as wind, smoke, and fire. Beyond visual fidelity, high-performance fluid simulation has become increasingly important for downstream applications, including shape design , robotic control in virtual environments , and inverse optimization problems .()

Ma et al., 2021

(; ; ; ; )

Ma et al., 2018

Xian et al., 2023

Hu et al., 2026

Song et al., 2025

Liu et al., 2022b

(; ; )

Du et al., 2020

Li et al., 2022b

Chen et al., 2024

Stable Fluids , which solves the Navier–Stokes (NS) equations on Eulerian grids, remains widely used in real-time applications because of its simplicity, efficiency, and stability. While subsequent work has improved computational efficiency and better preserved fine-scale details, achieving stable, high-resolution simulations under strict real-time constraints remains challenging in practice. Grid-based solvers typically rely on global pressure solves and therefore can incur substantial synchronization and communication overhead across the grid. Particle-based methods, by contrast, often require expensive neighbor searches, irregular memory access patterns, and dynamic data structures, all of which reduce throughput and GPU utilization. Together, these bottlenecks limit scalability on modern GPUs and worsen as simulation resolution and geometric complexity grow.

In contrast to these macroscopic solvers, the lattice Boltzmann method (LBM) has emerged as a compelling alternative for turbulent, weakly compressible flows because of its massive parallelism and strong vortex-preserving properties. By operating locally on discretized lattice nodes at the mesoscopic scale, LBM is well suited to GPU acceleration. However, standard LBM schemes impose substantial memory overhead: a conventional double-buffered D3Q27 implementation stores two sets of $27$ floating-point distribution functions per node, leading to heavy memory traffic and limited scalability.()

Stam, 1999

To address this limitation, proposed the high-order moment-encoded LBM (HOME-LBM), which stores a compact set of velocity moments instead of the full lattice distribution functions and performs a lightweight collision operator directly in moment space. This formulation reduces memory and bandwidth requirements and has been shown to improve robustness in turbulent-flow simulations. Nevertheless, several practical bottlenecks remain. Its fluid–solid boundary treatment still relies on costly link–solid intersection tests tightly coupled with the streaming operation, leading to irregular control flow and reduced GPU utilization. Furthermore, although quantization has proven effective in reducing memory footprint and bandwidth in large-scale simulations , designing a robust reduced-precision representation for LBM remains nontrivial due to its stability constraints.

Li et al. (2023)

(; )

Hu et al., 2021

Liu et al., 2022a

To accelerate HOME-LBM with complex fluid–solid interactions and reduce memory consumption for large-scale simulations on a single GPU, we propose a high-performance quantized HOME-LBM framework. Our approach consists of two main components. First, we analyze the computational bottlenecks of the original HOME-LBM on GPUs when handling interactions with solid objects, and then present a geometry-decoupled computation scheme for efficient GPU parallelization. Second, to further reduce memory cost, we develop a 16-bit fixed-point quantization for moment storage (). We characterize the linear stability of the unquantized moment-encoded updates on D2Q9 and D3Q27 lattices through von Neumann analysis and combine these results with empirical moment statistics to guide quantization-range selection. For second-order moments, we store and quantize only the non-equilibrium components and reconstruct the equilibrium contributions analytically, narrowing the storage dynamic range.

Sec. 5

We validate our approach through real-time demonstrations and large-scale benchmarks under both D3Q19 and D3Q27 configurations, as well as 2D and 3D numerical experiments assessing accuracy and stability.

At a fixed fluid-grid resolution, mesh-complexity experiments isolate the performance contributions of geometry decoupling and moment quantization. Compared with the original FP32 HOME-LBM, our method achieves $4.1\times$ to $32.5\times$ speedups across the tested configurations (), with the maximum on the Hilbert-curve benchmark (). Moment-buffer storage is reduced by $50\%$ in fluid-only simulations and $25\%$ in fluid–solid coupling, where one buffer remains in FP32 for boundary-correction accumulation. On the static delta-wing benchmark, our solver achieves a $5.2\times$ speedup over Leapfrog Flow Maps (LFM)  under the tested configuration (). Large-scale examples, including $1024^{3}$ fluid-only simulations and fluid–solid interactions involving multimillion-triangle geometries, demonstrate improved scalability on a single GPU while preserving numerical stability, fidelity, and high visual quality.

Table 2

. Figure 3Fluid-only plume simulations (frame 180) using our 16-bit quantized kinetic solver at a grid resolution of $1024^{3}$ . Left: Reynolds number $\mathrm{Re}=$ 40,960. Right: $\mathrm{Re}=$ 2,048,000.

Navier–Stokes Solvers

Macroscopic Navier–Stokes solvers have long been the backbone of graphics fluid simulation. As a seminal work, introduces Stable Fluids to solve the NS equations on Eulerian grids using an unconditionally stable semi-Lagrangian advection scheme. This approach enables fluid simulations with large time steps, significantly improving efficiency for computer graphics applications, but it suffers from excessive numerical diffusion. To mitigate this issue, a variety of improved advection schemes have been proposed, including BFECC , the modified MacCormack scheme , MacCormack with reflection (MC+R) , bidirectional flow maps , covector advection , neural flow maps , the Eulerian vortex method on flow maps  and Leapfrog Flow Maps , all of which aim to better preserve vortical details over time. Recent work has also explored alternatives to conventional grid-based pressure solvers, including stochastic approaches such as velocity-based Monte Carlo fluids , neural Monte Carlo fluid simulation , and adaptive mesh-free representations such as Gaussian Fluids . These methods offer promising trade-offs in adaptivity, stochastic estimation, and learned acceleration, whereas our work focuses on dense, geometry-rich fluid simulation with highly regular local updates on GPUs.

Beyond Eulerian methods, Lagrangian approaches, such as smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH) , provide particle-based alternatives to Eulerian discretizations. However, these methods struggle to capture turbulence with few particles. Hybrid Eulerian–Lagrangian approaches combine grid-based computations with particle-based transport to improve accuracy, including FLIP and its extensions , and recent particle-flow-map formulations designed to improve long-range advection and preserve vortical structures . ST-FLIP  extends particle-to-grid transfer into space–time to support larger time steps in free-surface and two-phase simulations. Vortex methods, including vortex particles , vortex filaments , and vortex sheets , as well as grid-based vorticity correction , can preserve vortical structures more effectively and provide scalable strategies for maintaining fine-scale flow details.

Alongside advances in flow representation, the computational power of modern GPUs has substantially accelerated fluid solvers through multigrid methods , fixed-point iterations , and compact Poisson filters , as well as multi-GPU parallelization for large-scale simulations . Fast VEM  addresses complex boundaries using a virtual-element discretization on body-fitted cut-cell grids and a specialized geometric multigrid solver. Despite these advances, hybrid Eulerian–Lagrangian approaches , while offering improved fidelity and accuracy, still incur significant memory overhead because they must maintain both grids and particles. Moreover, grid-based Poisson solvers typically rely on iterative methods that require many GPU kernel launches, limiting overall performance.(; )

Boltzmann-based Solvers

The lattice Boltzmann method, a mesoscopic numerical approach, has recently emerged as a compelling alternative to traditional incompressible NS solvers for both single-phase  and multiphase  flows. Unlike the macroscopic formulations above, LBM evolves distribution functions through purely local collision and streaming operations, avoiding global pressure projection and making it particularly attractive for massively parallel GPU architectures. Early graphics applications  primarily rely on the low-order Bhatnagar–Gross–Krook (BGK) collision model , motivating higher-order collision schemes such as central-moment multiple-relaxation-time (CM-MRT) models , which reduce both dispersion and dissipation errors. Coupling fluids with solids in the LBM framework has also been extensively investigated, with approaches including the immersed boundary (IB) method , a variety of bounce-back schemes , and hybrid macroscopic–mesoscopic boundary models , enabling applications such as underwater swimming and UAV training . Recent work also couples two-phase LBM with the material point method (MPM) to simulate volume-preserving air–water–sand mixtures .

Because LBM operates locally at the mesoscopic scale on lattice nodes, it is well suited for GPU acceleration and large-scale simulations . improve GPU efficiency through optimized data layouts, load-balanced immersed-boundary processing, and a multi-kernel execution strategy, while introduces in-place streaming schemes that reduce distribution-buffer storage through direction-dependent read/write scheduling.

To further reduce memory overhead, HOME-LBM  compresses per-node storage to 10 moment variables for D3Q27 and reconstructs 27 distribution functions on the fly.

However, its original solid-coupling implementation still requires expensive link–solid intersection tests and exhibits divergent branching during solid coupling, reducing parallel efficiency and scalability. For a broader overview of recent advances in LBM and its applications in computer graphics, we refer readers to the SIGGRAPH course by .(; ; )

Von Neumann Stability Analysis of LBM

Von Neumann (VN) stability analysis  has been widely used to characterize numerical stability, dispersion, and dissipation in LBM. Early studies apply it to the BGK model  and demonstrate the superior stability of the MRT model . Subsequent work further analyzed high-order and regularized schemes , as well as cascaded and central-moment MRT schemes . While VN stability analysis has been widely used in LBM, a corresponding VN analysis for moment-encoded formulations remains largely unexplored.()

Quantization in Graphics

Data quantization offers a complementary strategy to reduce storage and memory traffic. In graphics, researchers have explored custom numerical formats and automatic bit-width search , but these approaches often rely on heuristic optimization or learning-based search, which are computationally intractable for the chaotic dynamics of turbulent LBM flows. Neural compression methods such as NeuralVDB  and ACORN  achieve impressive compression ratios but incur significant inference overhead, hindering high-frequency real-time updates. Reduced precision has also been studied in LBM , but directly applying reduced-precision schemes to LBM is particularly challenging because small perturbations may accumulate through repeated collision–streaming updates and destabilize long-horizon simulations. This motivates stability-constrained quantization strategies specifically tailored to the dynamics of moment-encoded LBM.(; )

3.1.

In the context of single-phase fluid dynamics, the governing kinetic equation for the evolution of the particle distribution function is the Boltzmann equation :()

Shan et al., 2006

(1) $\frac{\partial\bm{f}}{\partial t}+\bm{v}\cdot\nabla\bm{f}=\Omega(\bm{f})+\bm{F}\cdot\nabla_{\bm{v}}\bm{f}\;,$

where $\bm{f}(\bm{x},\bm{v},t)$ denotes the distribution function, $\bm{F}$ represents external forces, and $\Omega$ is the collision operator that relaxes $\bm{f}$ towards the local thermodynamic equilibrium $\bm{f}^{\text{eq}}$  . The collision operator $\Omega$ models local relaxation of the distribution toward equilibrium and determines the viscosity and dissipative behavior of the scheme. In discrete LBM, choices such as BGK  and central-moment MRT  specify different collision models, while HOME-LBM  evaluates collision

directly in its stored moment representation.

By discretizing time $t$ into uniform time steps, space $\bm{x}$ into a regular lattice grid, and velocity $\bm{v}$ into a finite set of $q$ discrete directions, the continuous Boltzmann equation ( ) becomes the lattice Boltzmann equation (LBE) in dimensionless units:()

3.2.

To reduce the memory footprint and bandwidth cost of standard LBM while preserving physical accuracy, proposed the high-order moment-encoded LBM.

The key idea of HOME-LBM is to store velocity moments $\rho,\rho\bm{u}$ , and $\rho\bm{S}$ in memory and reconstruct distribution functions on the fly using a third-order Hermite basis, balancing accuracy and computational efficiency.

Solid Coupling

HOME-LBM performs fluid–solid coupling by reconstructing boundary distribution functions at solid intersection points and replacing the corresponding streamed distributions on lattice links. Specifically, when a lattice link originating from a grid node $\bm{x}$ intersects a solid boundary at point $\bm{p}$ , it reconstructs a boundary distribution at $\bm{p}$ and streams it to the grid node. Under the assumption of a homogeneous weakly compressible fluid, $\rho^{\bm{p}}\!=\!\rho^{\bm{x}}$ .

Velocity $\bm{u}^{\bm{p}}$ can be computed based on the linear velocity and angular velocity of the solid at $\bm{p}$ . The second-order tensor $\bm{S}^{\bm{p}}$ is approximated as:

(12) $\smash{{S}^{\bm{p},\text{eq}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\alpha\beta}={u}^{\bm{p}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\alpha}{u}^{\bm{p}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\beta}}\;,\quad{S}^{\bm{p}}_{\alpha\beta}={u}^{\bm{p}}_{\alpha}{u}^{\bm{p}}_{\beta}+\bigl({S}^{\bm{x}}_{\alpha\beta}-{u}^{\bm{x}}_{\alpha}{u}^{\bm{x}}_{\beta}\bigr).$

Given velocity moments at $\bm{p}$ , the boundary distribution $f^{\bm{p}}_{i}$ is reconstructed using and then streamed to $\bm{x}$ . Finally, the force and torque exerted by the fluid on the solid are obtained by summing the momentum exchange over all nodes $\bm{x}$ whose links intersect the solid.

In this section, we first analyze why solid coupling slows down the original HOME-LBM kernel (), and then present our geometry-decoupled computation scheme for efficient GPU parallelization ().

4.1.

HOME-LBM  achieves substantial speedups over earlier GPU-based LBM implementations  through several key design choices. First, for D3Q27, it reduces per-node storage from $27$ distribution functions to $10$ moment variables, thereby significantly lowering both the memory footprint and memory traffic. Second, by reconstructing distribution functions on the fly from stored moments, the streaming step can be executed more efficiently within each thread block using shared memory.

In addition, HOME-LBM fuses collision, streaming, and boundary handling into a single GPU kernel, eliminating the overhead of multiple kernel launches and improving overall throughput.()

()

However, with complex solid geometries, this fused formulation introduces a critical GPU bottleneck. In the original update procedure (), each lattice thread must determine whether its incoming lattice links intersect the solid surface. For intersecting links, the thread must further reconstruct the boundary distribution function and perform momentum-exchange computations. As a result, the main fluid-update kernel directly incorporates geometric complexity. For high-resolution meshes, the per-step runtime can increase substantially compared with fluid-only simulations ().

Although spatial data structures such as bounding volume hierarchies (BVHs) can accelerate these intersection tests, their traversal introduces data-dependent execution paths. 4.2.

To alleviate the solid-coupling bottleneck, we restructure the original HOME-LBM pipeline into two GPU stages: fluid update and solid boundary correction, separated by an intermediate buffer copy.

Rather than embedding boundary processing into every lattice-node update, our method first advances the fluid field uniformly over the entire lattice and then applies only the boundary-induced discrepancies as localized corrections. As a result, the main fluid kernel runtime becomes much less sensitive to solid-geometry complexity.

However, in conventional fluid–solid coupled LBM formulations, boundary processing is mathematically intertwined with streaming. Post-streaming distributions near solid boundaries depend directly on boundary reconstruction or bounce-back updates, so a naive separation of boundary handling is generally inconsistent with the original numerical scheme. A key enabler of this decomposition is a reordering of the update sequence. Instead of the classical formulation, in which boundary handling is tightly coupled with streaming, we adopt a scheme. This allows solid effects to be applied afterward as additive moment corrections in a separate sparse stage.streaming $\rightarrow$ collisioncollision $\rightarrow$ streaming

Consequently, the resulting decomposition is not a straightforward kernel split; instead, a reformulation enables it by approximately preserving the effect of boundary processing on the original update while decoupling geometry-dependent operations from the fluid update. We state where the two differ below and evaluate the quantitative impact of this reformulation on boundary accuracy in .

In the first kernel (), all lattice nodes are processed uniformly to advance the fluid dynamics, independent of the presence of solid boundaries.

The kernel begins by fetching the stored moment variables $\rho$ , $\rho\bm{u}$ , and $\rho\bm{S}$ , after which the moment-based collision operator ( – ) is applied to obtain the post-collision moments $\rho^{+}$ , $(\rho\bm{u})^{+}$ , and $(\rho\bm{S})^{+}$ .

The streamed values are subsequently converted back into updated moments at $t+1$ using  and written to the output buffer in global memory. By integrating moment-based collision, distribution reconstruction, and streaming into a single regular kernel, this stage removes solid-intersection tests and boundary handling from the main fluid update, avoiding branch-heavy, geometry-related control flow and irregular memory accesses. After the fluid update, a separate kernel () copies the post-streaming moments at time $t+1$ into a read-only buffer. The solid-correction kernel then reconstructs its inputs from this fixed copy and accumulates moment increments into the output buffer. The copy is required because several triangles may add corrections to the same lattice node through AtomicAdd while other triangles read that node to reconstruct distribution functions; reading from the output buffer would make each reconstruction depend on how many corrections had already been applied,

whereas the fixed copy gives every triangle the same input. The pseudocode describes the FP32 variant, and the reduced-precision storage is introduced in .

Sec. 6.1

Relation to the Original Update.

Stage I streams distributions reconstructed from post-collision moments at time $t$ , whereas Stage II reconstructs $f_{i}^{\mathrm{II}}(\bm{x})$ from a fixed copy of the post-streaming moments at time $t+1$ . Although both distributions refer to the same target time $t+1$ , the boundary treatment uses the updated, post-streaming density $\rho^{t+1}$ , so the two reconstructions rely on states from different stages of the time step.

Consequently, the correction does not generally reproduce the direct boundary replacement in the original HOME-LBM implementation exactly, even without quantization.

A second, geometric source of discrepancy is that the correction stage treats every triangle independently and assumes a single-layer surface: where a lattice link crosses more than one surface layer within one lattice spacing, as between the upper and lower faces of a thin shell, each intersecting triangle contributes its own correction, whereas the original fused kernel replaces such a link once, at its nearest intersection (see also the

limitations in ).

In , we evaluate the resulting discrepancy.

Sec. 6.3

Pre-stage.

As in prior work , moving solids require an additional preprocessing stage to update the acceleration structure. Without this preprocessing, each GPU thread would need to iterate over all lattice nodes within a triangle’s bounding box and perform link–triangle intersection tests, resulting in many redundant evaluations.()

Li et al., 2023

To reduce this overhead while keeping kernel launches minimal, we voxelize the solid surface and mark the lattice nodes that contain surface triangles. During traversal of a triangle bounding box, empty lattice nodes can then be efficiently skipped using this occupancy mask. Because this preprocessing is required only when the solid geometry changes, it is negligible for static scenes, where it runs once. For moving solids, the corresponding revoxelization overhead is included in the reported simulation timings ().

5.

To further reduce the memory footprint of HOME-LBM, we introduce a quantization scheme for moment-based representations. Since quantization errors can accumulate over long simulation horizons and potentially destabilize the simulation,

rather than selecting numerical ranges purely through empirical tuning, we perform a von Neumann analysis of the moment-encoded LBM to characterize the stable operating regime (). More details on the von Neumann analysis can be found

in . We then combine three complementary sources of constraints to design our quantization scheme (). First, we identify admissible velocity ranges under which perturbations remain bounded. Second, within this regime, we collect conservative runtime statistics from representative simulations to determine practical bounds for density, momentum, and stress-related variables. Third, for second-order moments, we store only their non-equilibrium components and reconstruct the equilibrium contributions analytically, reducing the dynamic range that must be quantized. Together, these ingredients yield a practical $16$ -bit fixed-point representation for the stored moments. The resulting format reduces both memory bandwidth and storage cost while preserving long-horizon stability and physical fidelity in challenging turbulent-flow scenarios.

5.1.

Mapping Reconstruction.

Unlike conventional distribution-based LBM, HOME-LBM does not explicitly store the post-collision distribution functions. Instead, it reconstructs them from a reduced set of velocity moments using a third-order Hermite expansion. As a result, the effective update mapping differs from that of standard distribution-based LBM. Specifically, perturbations evolve through a composite mapping that includes collision, moment extraction, and reconstruction, rather than through the standard collision operator alone. We express the HOME-LBM update as

(15) $\bm{g}^{\mathrm{HOME}}(\bm{f})=\bm{h}\!\left(\bm{m}(\bm{f}^{+})\right),$

where $\bm{h}(\cdot)$ denotes Hermite reconstruction of the distribution, $\bm{m}(\bm{f})\doteq(\rho,\bm{u},\bm{S})$ denotes the moment extraction defined in , and the intermediate post-collision state $\bm{f}^{+}$ is obtained by applying the underlying non-orthogonal central-moment multiple-relaxation-time (NOCM-MRT)  collision step (see  for more details) to $\bm{f}$ :

where $\bm{M}=\bm{M}^{\mathrm{NOCM}}(\bm{u})$ is the moment transformation matrix of the NOCM-MRT collision model, and $\bm{R}$ is a diagonal matrix of relaxation rates $\{r_{i}\}_{i=1,\dots,q}$  .()

Li et al., 2020

This “moment representation + reconstruction” procedure first converts the post-collision distribution into a set of moments and then reconstructs the distribution by projecting it onto a truncated third-order Hermite subspace. Although this reconstruction is algebraically equivalent at the macroscopic level, it alters the effective linearized update operator, thereby affecting numerical stability and error amplification.

Linearization of Composite Mapping.

Following the standard perturbation and linearization procedure introduced in , we linearize the composite mapping $\bm{g}^{\mathrm{HOME}}$ around a uniform equilibrium and analyze its Jacobian with respect to the distribution function. Since $\bm{g}^{\mathrm{HOME}}$ is a composition of moment extraction, collision, and reconstruction operators, the chain rule gives its Jacobian directly.

Experimental Range for Density.

In weakly compressible LBM, density fluctuations are expected to remain small around the reference value $\rho=1$ . Nevertheless, because the method is not strictly incompressible, we explicitly account for density variation. In an extreme-turbulence $3$ D flow-over-sphere experiment () with inlet velocity $0.256$ , viscosity $\nu=0$ , and grid resolution $512\times 256\times 256$ , we observe density values within the range $\rho\in[0.8,1.5]$ , even in highly vortical regions. We empirically select our fixed quantization ranges based on representative simulations shown in this paper and we clamp out-of-range values to the nearest endpoint.

Range Reduction of Second-Order Moments.

In the same flow-over-sphere experiment (), we observe

density-normalized second-order moment components $\bm{S}$ within the range $[-0.1,0.6]$ . We further reduce the quantization range by decomposing the stress tensor into equilibrium and non-equilibrium components. Specifically, following the definition in , the isotropic contribution has already been subtracted, so that the second-order moment tensor can be written as

Fig. 8

Eq. 5

(24) ${\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\rho S_{\alpha\alpha}=\rho S^{\mathrm{neq}}_{\alpha\alpha}+\rho u_{\alpha}^{2}},\quad\rho S_{\alpha\beta}=\rho S^{\mathrm{neq}}_{\alpha\beta}+\rho u_{\alpha}u_{\beta}\quad(\alpha\neq\beta),$

where the equilibrium contribution is determined analytically from the density and velocity fields. We store and quantize only the high-frequency non-equilibrium components, whose amplitudes are progressively smaller under multiscale perturbation analysis  and are therefore particularly amenable to quantization:()

Harris, 2004

(25) $\rho S^{\mathrm{neq}}_{\alpha\alpha}={\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\rho S_{\alpha\alpha}-\rho u_{\alpha}^{2}},\quad\rho S^{\mathrm{neq}}_{\alpha\beta}=\rho S_{\alpha\beta}-\rho u_{\alpha}u_{\beta}\quad(\alpha\neq\beta).$

This decomposition reduces the range of the second-order moment from $[-0.1,0.6]$ to $[-0.1,0.1]$ , decreasing the uniform

quantization step size by a factor of $3.5$ at the same bit width. Since the actual stored quantity is the stress density $\rho S^{\mathrm{neq}}$ rather than $S^{\mathrm{neq}}$ itself, so each of its components is quantized over $[-0.1\rho_{\max},0.1\rho_{\max}]=[-0.15,0.15]$ for $\rho_{\max}=1.5$ (). The factor 3.5 is unchanged because both intervals scale with $\rho_{\max}$ . This design is also consistent with the preceding stability analysis, which indicates that the dissipation and stability properties of HOME-LBM are governed primarily by non-equilibrium moments, whereas the equilibrium components mainly contribute to macroscopic transport and can therefore be reconstructed analytically without compromising stability.

Table 1

Normalization and Fixed-point Quantization.

Each moment component $m$ is normalized to the unit interval as

(26) $m^{\prime}=\frac{m-m_{\min}}{m_{\max}-m_{\min}},$

where $m_{\min}$ and $m_{\max}$ denote the predefined bounds obtained from the range analysis above. This normalization maps all stored moments to $[0,1]$ . Each normalized component is then quantized to a $b$ -bit unsigned integer using uniform quantization:

(27) $q(m)=\left\lfloor m^{\prime}\left(2^{b}-1\right)+\tfrac{1}{2}\right\rfloor.$

Dequantization is performed using the inverse mapping

(28) $\hat{m}=m_{\min}+q(m)\left(\frac{m_{\max}-m_{\min}}{2^{b}-1}\right),$

which reconstructs an approximation of the original value $m$ up to quantization error. In our implementation, most moment components are stored as $16$ -bit fixed-point integers ( $b=16$ ), allowing two moments to be packed into a single $32$ -bit word. Consequently, the moment buffer requires only five values per lattice node, rather than $10$ values, reducing both the memory footprint and the global memory write bandwidth by approximately $50\%$ .uint32float32

Data Layout.

To improve memory efficiency and access coherence, we store fluid nodes in a structure-of-arrays (SoA) layout  and organize them into fixed-size $8\times 8\times 8$ tiles. This layout improves spatial locality when accessing boundary-adjacent fluid nodes and enables coalesced memory access during solid correction.()

Chen et al., 2022

Dithering.

To reduce bias from deterministic rounding, we apply spatial dithering during quantization. Specifically, a small zero-mean noise, uniformly distributed in $[-\tfrac{1}{2},\tfrac{1}{2}]$ of one quantization unit , is added to the normalized value before rounding, drawn independently for every node and every time step, and the result is clamped to $[0,2^{b}-1]$ . This converts deterministic rounding error into zero-mean stochastic noise, thereby preventing systematic bias accumulation over long time integration.()

Liu et al., 2022a

Atomic Accumulation with Mixed Precision.

When solid coupling is present, multiple triangle faces may contribute moment corrections to the same lattice node, which requires atomic accumulation of moment updates in the solid-correction kernel. Performing atomic operations directly on quantized fixed-point values would introduce order-dependent rounding errors and may lead to noticeable bias accumulation over long simulations. To mitigate this issue, we adopt a mixed-precision strategy.

Specifically, we maintain two moment buffers: a full-precision buffer and a compact 16-bit quantized buffer. The fluid update kernel () reads the compact buffer and writes post-streaming moments to the FP32 buffer (the output buffer of ). The buffer copy kernel () then encodes these post-streaming moments into the compact buffer, overwriting the previous time step’s data. During solid correction (), the compact buffer remains read-only: the solid-correction kernel decodes its contents and accumulates

the resulting moment corrections into the FP32 buffer using . Once all solid corrections are complete, the corrected moments are encoded back into the compact buffer for the next fluid update. Since only one of the moment buffers is quantized, the overall memory reduction is about $25\%$ compared with the FP32 implementation, which we find is a favorable trade-off between accuracy and bandwidth savings in solid-coupled simulations.

2D Taylor Vortex

We first evaluate the long-term robustness of vortex evolution using the 2D Taylor vortex benchmark, following the setup in prior work . This benchmark is sensitive to numerical dissipation and perturbation growth, making it well suited for assessing the stability of our proposed quantized simulations. We compare against representative grid-based and particle-based fluid solvers, including Semi-Lagrangian , MacCormack , MC+R , PolyPIC , BiMocq, Covector Fluids (CF) , and the Eulerian vortex method on flow maps , as well as HOME-LBM  baselines using both double precision (64-bit) and single precision (32-bit). All methods use the same grid resolution, $256\times 256$ .

As shown in , classical semi-Lagrangian schemes show progressive vortex-core diffusion, while particle-based methods preserve sharper structures but introduce more high-frequency artifacts. In contrast, HOME-LBM preserves coherent vortex structures with limited dissipation. Our proposed 16-bit quantized solver remains visually consistent with the 64-bit and 32-bit HOME-LBM baselines and closely matches other high-quality advection methods, indicating that moment-space quantization preserves visual fidelity and numerical behavior while reducing memory usage by 50 $\%$ .(; )

2D Double-layer Vortex

We next evaluate the proposed quantized representation’s sensitivity to different bit allocations using the 2D double-layer vortex benchmark. We adopt an adaptive bit-allocation strategy to balance quantization error across different moment components. Since density and velocity variables exhibit similar normalized ranges and directly affect macroscopic transport, we assign the same bit width to $\rho$ and $\rho\bm{u}$ . In contrast, after the range reduction described in , the non-equilibrium stress moments $\rho\bm{S}^{\mathrm{neq}}$ have a much smaller dynamic range and can therefore be represented with fewer bits.

We denote each configuration as $b_{\rho,u}/b_{S}$ , where $b_{\rho,u}$ and $b_{S}$ are the bit widths for density–velocity and stress moments, respectively. For example, the configuration stores $\rho$ and $\rho\bm{u}$ using 16 bits and stores $\rho\bm{S}^{\mathrm{neq}}$ using 15 bits.

As shown in , where both the L2 relative error and the memory usage are measured against the 64-bit double-precision run, this allocation yields a smooth accuracy–memory trade-off. Reducing stress precision to 14–15 bits introduces only minor error increases, whereas more aggressive reduction rapidly degrades both numerical accuracy and visual quality.

3D Trefoil Knot.

To assess the ability of our 16-bit moment quantization to preserve 3D vortex structures, we adopt the trefoil-knot benchmark of .

We compare our 16-bit quantized solver against Semi-Lagrangian , MacCormack , MC+R , BiMocq, Covector Fluids (CF) and its extension with the method of characteristic mapping (MCM) , as well as the FP32 HOME-LBM baseline .

As shown in , the quantized solver produces vortex structures visually consistent with the FP32 baseline, with both retaining more kinetic energy than CF but less than CF+MCM.

Their kinetic-energy and enstrophy histories closely agree ( (a,b)), including the transient enstrophy increase during vortex reconnection.

After 5.5 s, the relative mass drifts remain small, at $3.5\times 10^{-5}$ for FP32 and $4\times 10^{-5}$ for the quantized solver ( (c)).

These results suggest that 16-bit moment quantization largely preserves vortex dynamics and mass conservation behavior while reducing storage requirements.

We compare the end-to-end simulation performance of our GPU-oriented geometry-decoupled implementation with the original single-kernel HOME-LBM algorithm . Both implementations use identical collision models, boundary conditions, and time step sizes.

In terms of memory footprint, the proposed solver reduces storage by approximately $50\%$ in fluid-only simulations and $25\%$ in fluid–solid coupling scenarios.

In terms of runtime, it is $4.1\times$ to $32.5\times$ faster than HOME-LBM on the thirteen configurations the original implementation supports (). The speedup comes from regular memory access patterns and reduced warp divergence in the fluid update, and from the sparse solid-correction stage, which restricts geometric execution to boundary-intersecting cells and significantly reduces unnecessary thread activity. For airflow over the thin-shell delta wing shown in , our method achieves a $4.1\times$ speedup, $2.8\times$ of which comes from geometry decoupling alone (), and reproduces the spiral vortices near the wing edges seen in the experiment of .()

In this setting, the solid geometry must be voxelized dynamically at each time step, introducing an average overhead of approximately $2.1\,\mathrm{ms}$ per LBM iteration in our implementation. Including this cost, our solver takes $5.16\,\mathrm{ms}$ per LBM iteration () and two LBM iterations advance the same physical time as one LFM step, taking approximately $10.3\,\mathrm{ms}$ in total. Compared to the $40.7\,\mathrm{ms}$ per step of , our solver achieves nearly a $4\times$ speedup.

7.

$1024^{3}$ Fluid Simulation.

To demonstrate the scalability and fidelity of our solver at extreme resolutions, we simulate two cases of a plume formed by obliquely impacting jets on a $1024^{3}$ grid at different Reynolds numbers, as shown in . The Reynolds number is defined as $\mathrm{Re}=UL/\nu$ with the inlet speed $U=0.2$ and the domain edge length $L=1024$ lattice units. At lower Reynolds numbers, the flow exhibits stable, coherent vortex structures, while at higher Reynolds numbers, the solver resolves fine-scale turbulent filaments and intermittent eddies across a wide range of spatial scales.

Our quantized formulation reduces the memory footprint by $50\%$ compared to FP32 baselines, enabling large-scale simulations that would otherwise exceed the GPU memory capacity of a single GPU. This demonstrates that our framework can efficiently support high-resolution fluid simulations while preserving rich small-scale flow details.

Fig. 3

Large-scale Fluid–solid Coupling.

We further demonstrate large-scale fluid–solid interaction using turbulent smoke simulations around a Ducati motorcycle and a Ferrari F1 racing car at a grid resolution of $1000\times 400\times 400$ , as shown in  and . Both simulations use a closed computational domain with stationary no-slip walls. The simulations use 16-bit quantization and incorporate highly detailed solid geometry with intricate boundary features. Despite the large simulation size and geometric complexity, the solver develops complex shear layers and coherent vortex structures while maintaining stable temporal evolution and consistent visual quality over long sequences, achieving an average performance of approximately 1 second per frame. This shows that the proposed framework efficiently supports high-resolution, geometry-rich fluid–solid simulations while preserving fine-scale flow details.

Real-time Simulation

We demonstrate real-time smoke simulations interacting with solids that exhibit a highly complex porous microgeometry, as shown in . The dense, irregular fluid–solid interfaces generate intense multi-scale turbulence while simultaneously imposing stringent stability and performance demands on the solver. Despite these challenges, our method remains numerically stable and consistently sustains real-time performance across all tested porous configurations. As reported in , the example run at a grid resolution of $256\times 128\times 128$ took $1.1\,\mathrm{ms}$ per iteration.

8.

We presented a stability-constrained GPU framework for memory-efficient, high-performance moment-based lattice Boltzmann simulation with complex fluid–solid interaction. The proposed geometry-decoupled computation scheme decouples dense fluid evolution from sparse boundary correction, substantially reducing warp divergence and improving GPU utilization in complex geometries. In addition, our von Neumann stability analysis provides moment-wise stability constraints that inform the design of a robust reduced-precision representation for HOME-LBM. Together, these techniques significantly reduce memory footprint without sacrificing numerical stability. Our experiments demonstrate moment-storage reductions of $50\%$ in fluid-only and $25\%$ in fluid–solid simulations, speedups of $4.1\times$ to $32.5\times$ over the original HOME-LBM across the configurations it supports, and a $5.2\times$ speedup over LFM on the static delta-wing benchmark under the tested configuration, enabling higher-resolution simulations within the constraints of a single GPU at approximately one second per frame for our largest fluid–solid scenes. More broadly, this work illustrates how theoretical stability analysis can directly inform practical GPU system design for scalable LBM simulation.

Limitations and Future Work

Our current implementation assumes single-layer surface meshes and does not yet support layered geometry or complex self-intersections, which would require more advanced inside–outside classification and intersection handling. In the current per-triangle correction, links that cross more than one surface layer within one lattice spacing are corrected more than once, which contributes to the boundary discrepancy measured in . Moreover, while our boundary treatment is optimized for robustness and throughput, we do not explicitly evaluate sub-cell geometric accuracy or boundary error convergence; incorporating wall-function models  is a natural next step.

Several promising directions remain, including extending the framework to fully coupled two-way interactions and integrating multi-resolution or adaptive discretization to further improve scalability for large-scale scenes. Our implementation retains two moment buffers, and the buffer copy between the fluid and solid-correction stages accounts for a substantial share of the per-step time in coupled scenes; adapting in-place streaming schemes , which remove the second distribution buffer in standard LBM, to moment-encoded storage provides a way to reduce this cost.

Appendix A

The standard von Neumann stability analysis for LBM  is a linear Fourier-mode analysis that studies whether small perturbations in the distribution functions grow or decay under the discrete streaming–collision update. By linearizing the dynamics about a uniform equilibrium state and introducing plane-wave perturbations, the method yields an amplification matrix $\mathbf{G}$ whose eigenvalues characterize linear stability, numerical dissipation, and dispersion across wavenumbers. Here, we briefly summarize the key elements of classical formulations required for extending the analysis to HOME-LBM in . A more detailed review of the classical VN formulation of LBM is provided in .()

Sterling and Chen, 1996

A.1.

Starting from the lattice Boltzmann equation () and following  to neglect the external force term for clarity, the discrete kinetic update can be written as:

Eq. 2

Sterling and Chen (1996)

(29) $f_{i}(\bm{x}+\bm{c}_{i},t+1)=f_{i}(\bm{x},t)+\Omega_{i}(\bm{f}),$

where $\Omega_{i}$ is the discrete collision term. We define the post-collision mapping

(30) $g_{i}(\bm{f})=f_{i}+\Omega_{i}(\bm{f}),$

so that the update becomes

(31) $f_{i}(\bm{x}+\bm{c}_{i},t+1)=g_{i}(\bm{f}(\bm{x},t)).$

A.2.

We introduce a small perturbation around a spatially uniform equilibrium distribution:

(32) $f_{i}(\bm{x},t)=\bar{f}_{i}+f_{i}^{\prime}(\bm{x},t),\quad\text{with}\quad|\bar{f}_{i}|\gg|f_{i}^{\prime}|,$

where $\bar{f}_{i}$ denotes the globally uniform equilibrium distribution that does not vary with time and space, and $f_{i}^{\prime}(\bm{x},t)$ at node $\bm{x}$ and time $t$ accounts for a small perturbation from $\bar{f}_{i}$ .

Performing the first-order Taylor expansion of $g_{i}$ around $\bar{f}_{i}$ with a small perturbation $f^{\prime}_{i}$ yields:

(33) $g_{i}(\bar{\bm{f}}+\bm{f}^{\prime})\approx g_{i}(\bar{\bm{f}})+\sum_{j}\left.\frac{\partial g_{i}}{\partial f_{j}}\right|_{\bar{\bm{f}}}f^{\prime}_{j}.$

To proceed, we note that most practical LBM collision models can be interpreted as linear relaxation of moments toward their equilibrium values . When expressed in distribution-function space, this relaxation admits the unified matrix representation:()

Higuera and Jiménez, 1989

(34) $\Omega(\bm{f})=\bm{K}(\bm{f}^{eq}-\bm{f}),$

where the collision matrix $\bm{K}$ characterizes how the distribution function relaxes toward its equilibrium state. Therefore, the corresponding linearized evolution becomes:

(35) $\bm{g}(\bar{\bm{f}}+\bm{f}^{\prime})=\bar{\bm{f}}+\bm{f}^{\prime}(\bm{x},t)+\bm{K}\bigl(\bm{\Lambda}-\bm{I}\bigr)\,\bm{f}^{\prime}(\bm{x},t),$

where $\bm{\Lambda}$ is the Jacobian of the equilibrium distribution with elements

(36) $\Lambda_{ij}=\frac{\partial f^{eq}_{i}}{\partial\rho}\frac{\partial\rho}{\partial f_{j}}+\sum_{\alpha}\frac{\partial f^{eq}_{i}}{\partial u_{\alpha}}\frac{\partial u_{\alpha}}{\partial f_{j}}.$

Without forcing, gives

$\partial\rho/\partial f_{j}=1$ and

$\partial u_{\alpha}/\partial f_{j}=(c_{j\alpha}-u_{\alpha})/\rho$ , and every equilibrium used in this paper is $\rho$ times a polynomial in $\bm{u}$ , so that $\partial\bm{f}^{\text{eq}}/\partial\rho=\bm{f}^{\text{eq}}/\rho$ . Hence

Eq. 5

(37) $\bm{\Lambda}=\frac{1}{\rho}\Bigl[\bm{f}^{\text{eq}}\,\bm{1}^{\!\top}+\sum_{\alpha}\frac{\partial\bm{f}^{\text{eq}}}{\partial u_{\alpha}}\,\bigl(\bm{c}_{\alpha}-u_{\alpha}\bm{1}\bigr)^{\!\top}\Bigr],$

where $\bm{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{q}$ is the vector of ones and $(\bm{c}_{\alpha})_{j}=c_{j\alpha}$ . The equilibrium $\bm{f}^{\text{eq}}$ and its derivatives $\partial\bm{f}^{\text{eq}}/\partial u_{\alpha}$ are given in Appendix  for D2Q9 and in Appendix  for D3Q27.

A.3.

Following the standard VN procedure, we substitute into  a plane-wave solution of the form :

Eq. 38

()

Wissocq et al., 2020

(39) $f_{i}^{\prime}(\bm{x},t)=\hat{f}_{i}e^{\mathrm{i}(\bm{k}\cdot\bm{x}-\omega t)},$

where $\hat{f}_{i}$ denotes the complex amplitude, and the exponential term represents a monochromatic plane wave with wave vector $\bm{k}$ and angular frequency $\omega$ . Combining the streaming phase factor with the Jacobian operator yields the amplification matrix $\bm{G}(\bm{k})$ :

(40) $\bm{G}(\bm{k})=\bm{D}(\bm{k})\left[\bm{I}+\bm{K}(\bm{\Lambda}-\bm{I})\right],$

where $\bm{D}(\bm{k})=\text{diag}(e^{-\mathrm{i}\bm{k}\cdot\bm{c}_{0}},\dots,e^{-\mathrm{i}\bm{k}\cdot\bm{c}_{q-1}})$ represents the advection operator in Fourier space. $\bm{K}$ and $\bm{\Lambda}$ denote the collision and Jacobian matrices, respectively. This matrix $\bm{G}(\bm{k})$ compactly encodes the linearized evolution of Fourier modes and provides a convenient basis for analyzing the stability, dispersion, and numerical properties of the scheme.

Appendix B

Collision modeling plays a central role in determining both the accuracy and the stability of lattice Boltzmann solvers. Each collision model considered in this work is specified by its collision matrix $\bm{K}$ in . This section gives $\bm{K}$ for the three reference models and refers to the original papers for their derivation. We list the moment bases and relaxation rates per lattice in  and , and we assemble the amplification matrices for all four models, including HOME-LBM. All moment-matrix inverses are computed numerically (), and the matrices are at most $27\times 27$ .

B.1.

The classical BGK formulation  applies a single relaxation time to relax each lattice population toward its local

equilibrium. The collision operator is written as()

Bhathnagor et al., 1954

(41) $\Omega_{i}^{\mathrm{BGK}}=\frac{1}{\tau}\left(f_{i}^{\mathrm{eq}}-f_{i}\right),\qquad{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\bm{K}^{\mathrm{BGK}}=\frac{1}{\tau}\,\bm{I},}$

where $\tau$ is the relaxation time determining the rate at which the distribution function approaches equilibrium. The BGK model yields the following relation between $\tau$ and the kinematic viscosity $\nu$ : $\tau=3\nu+\tfrac{1}{2}$ (equivalently $\nu=c_{s}^{2}(\tau-\tfrac{1}{2})$ ).

B.2.

To overcome the stability limitations of the BGK model, the MRT framework introduces a more stable collision operator that acts in moment space rather than directly on the distribution functions . In the RM-MRT formulation, the collision model is performed on polynomial moments constructed from the lattice velocities, $\bm{m}=\bm{M}^{\mathrm{RM}}\bm{f}$ and $\bm{m}^{\mathrm{eq}}=\bm{M}^{\mathrm{RM}}\bm{f}^{\mathrm{eq}}$ , where the rows of the raw-moment transformation matrix $\bm{M}^{\mathrm{RM}}$ are polynomials in the lattice velocities and do not depend on the local fluid velocity (Appendices  and ). Each moment is relaxed toward its equilibrium at its own rate, $\bm{\Omega}^{\mathrm{RM}}=(\bm{M}^{\mathrm{RM}})^{-1}\bm{R}\,(\bm{m}^{\mathrm{eq}}-\bm{m})$ , so that the RM-MRT collision operator is(; ; )

B.3.

While RM-MRT improves stability over BGK, its use of raw moments lacks Galilean invariance, which can degrade accuracy and cause instabilities at low viscosities. The non-orthogonal central moment multiple relaxation time model (NOCM-MRT) addresses this issue by defining moments relative to the local fluid velocity, thereby achieving significantly improved invariance properties and enhanced robustness and accuracy for turbulent flows .

Let $\bm{u}$ denote the local macroscopic velocity, and let $\mathbf{M}^{\mathrm{NOCM}}(\bm{u})$ be the central-moment transformation matrix, which shifts the velocity basis so that the resulting moments, $\bm{m}=\mathbf{M}^{\mathrm{NOCM}}(\bm{u})\,\bm{f}$ and $\bm{m}^{\mathrm{eq}}=\mathbf{M}^{\mathrm{NOCM}}(\bm{u})\,\bm{f}^{\mathrm{eq}}$ , are computed with respect to $\bm{c}_{i}-\bm{u}$ (Appendices  and ); $\bm{m}^{\mathrm{eq}}$ represents the central-moment equilibrium obtained from the Maxwellian equilibrium distribution. The NOCM-MRT collision operator is then expressed as(; )

De Rosis, 2017

De Rosis and Luo, 2019

D.3

(43) $\displaystyle\bm{\Omega}^{\mathrm{NOCM}}$ $\displaystyle=\mathbf{K}^{\mathrm{NOCM}}\left(\bm{f}^{\mathrm{eq}}-\bm{f}\right),$ $\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mathbf{K}^{\mathrm{NOCM}}}$ $\displaystyle}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{\displaystyle=\mathbf{M}^{\mathrm{NOCM}}(\bm{u})^{-1}\mathbf{R}\,\mathbf{M}^{\mathrm{NOCM}}(\bm{u}),}$

where $\mathbf{R}=\mathrm{diag}(\bm{r}^{\mathrm{NOCM}})$ is a diagonal relaxation matrix specifying independent relaxation rates for each central moment. Relaxing higher-order moments more aggressively provides strong damping

of non-hydrodynamic modes while preserving the correct recovery of Navier–Stokes dynamics .()

C.1.

For completeness, we list the discrete velocities, lattice weights, and the lattice speed of sound used throughout this work. The D2Q9 lattice consists of nine discrete velocity directions

$\bm{c}_{i}=(c_{x,i},c_{y,i}),\qquad i=0,\ldots,8,$

with components:

$c_{x}=\begin{pmatrix}0&1&0&-1&0&1&-1&-1&1\end{pmatrix}$ $c_{y}=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&1&0&-1&1&1&-1&-1\end{pmatrix}.$

The corresponding lattice weights are

$w=\begin{pmatrix}\frac{4}{9},\;\frac{1}{9},\;\frac{1}{9},\;\frac{1}{9},\;\frac{1}{9},\;\frac{1}{36},\;\frac{1}{36},\;\frac{1}{36},\;\frac{1}{36}\end{pmatrix}.$

The lattice speed of sound is $c_{s}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{3}}$ .

The above definitions are used for constructing the RM-MRT matrix $\mathbf{M}^{\mathrm{RM}}$ , the NOCM-MRT transformation matrix $\mathbf{M}^{\mathrm{NOCM}}(\bm{u})$ , and all Hermite-based reconstructions described in this appendix.

一句话：用量化与高阶矩编码把格子玻尔兹曼方法（LBM）跑到更高性能。

要点：

  • LBM 的矩表示在高阶时需要大量存储与带宽
  • 用量化压缩矩数据，降低内存占用
  • 保持数值稳定性与模拟精度

为什么值得看：流体模拟的内存带宽瓶颈是老问题；量化是引擎侧常用的手段，这篇给出了在 LBM 上的系统做法。

中文摘要：这篇 TOG 论文研究如何让格子玻尔兹曼方法（LBM）在高阶矩编码下跑得更快。LBM 把分布函数转成矩表示后，高阶项会带来显著的存储与带宽压力。作者引入量化手段压缩矩数据，并系统分析了精度损失与数值稳定性的边界，在不牺牲模拟可信度的前提下显著降低了内存占用与带宽需求。

主题：图形学

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

Quantized High-Performance High-Order Moment-Encoded LBM

. Figure 1

Turbulent smoke interacting with a Ducati motorcycle model with intricate geometry on a $1000\times 400\times 400$ grid using our GPU-optimized, 16-bit quantized LBM solver. The simulation preserves rich fine-scale vortical structures and remains numerically stable under highly complex boundary conditions. For this scene, our method achieves a $9.0\times$ speedup over the original FP32 HOME-LBM  implementation, while reducing memory usage by $25\%$ .()

Li et al., 2023

Abstract.

Lattice Boltzmann methods (LBM) are widely used for visually rich fluid simulation, but their high memory bandwidth and storage requirements limit GPU performance and scalability, especially when coupled with complex geometry. Recent high-order moment-encoded LBM (HOME-LBM) reduces memory cost by storing compact velocity moments and performing collision directly in moment space, but its tightly coupled boundary treatment introduces divergent control flow. We present a high-performance, quantized HOME-LBM framework for large-scale turbulent fluid–solid simulations on a single GPU. Our geometry-decoupled computation scheme separates the regular fluid update from a sparse solid-correction stage, isolating geometry-dependent computations to improve GPU efficiency. To further reduce storage and memory traffic, we develop a reduced-precision representation for HOME-LBM by combining von Neumann stability analysis, empirical moment-range estimation, and runtime decomposition of second-order moments to control quantization error. We evaluate our approach on real-time demonstrations and large-scale examples using both D3Q19 and D3Q27 lattices, with additional 2D and 3D numerical experiments assessing accuracy and stability. Across the tested benchmarks, our framework substantially accelerates the original FP32 HOME-LBM implementation, with a maximum speedup of $32.5\times$ on the Hilbert-curve geometry.

Moment storage is reduced by $50\%$ in fluid-only simulations and $25\%$ in fluid–solid coupling examples, while maintaining numerical stability, fidelity, and high visual quality.

In the static delta-wing benchmark, our solver achieves a $5.2\times$ speedup over Leapfrog Flow Maps (LFM) under the tested configuration.

fluid simulation; lattice Boltzmann method; GPU computing; quantization; fluid–solid coupling

Figure 2Smoke around an F1 car on a $1000\times 400\times 400$ grid (left: frame 80; right: frame 160) highlights a complex, multi-scale wake: strong shear layers from the wheels, rear wing, and diffuser roll up into coherent vortices near the vehicle, then stretch and break down into a turbulent, filamentary plume downstream.

Fluid simulation plays a central role in computer graphics, enabling the realistic synthesis of natural phenomena such as wind, smoke, and fire. Beyond visual fidelity, high-performance fluid simulation has become increasingly important for downstream applications, including shape design , robotic control in virtual environments , and inverse optimization problems .()

Stable Fluids , which solves the Navier–Stokes (NS) equations on Eulerian grids, remains widely used in real-time applications because of its simplicity, efficiency, and stability. While subsequent work has improved computational efficiency and better preserved fine-scale details, achieving stable, high-resolution simulations under strict real-time constraints remains challenging in practice. Grid-based solvers typically rely on global pressure solves and therefore can incur substantial synchronization and communication overhead across the grid. Particle-based methods, by contrast, often require expensive neighbor searches, irregular memory access patterns, and dynamic data structures, all of which reduce throughput and GPU utilization. Together, these bottlenecks limit scalability on modern GPUs and worsen as simulation resolution and geometric complexity grow.

In contrast to these macroscopic solvers, the lattice Boltzmann method (LBM) has emerged as a compelling alternative for turbulent, weakly compressible flows because of its massive parallelism and strong vortex-preserving properties. By operating locally on discretized lattice nodes at the mesoscopic scale, LBM is well suited to GPU acceleration. However, standard LBM schemes impose substantial memory overhead: a conventional double-buffered D3Q27 implementation stores two sets of $27$ floating-point distribution functions per node, leading to heavy memory traffic and limited scalability.()

Stam, 1999

To address this limitation, proposed the high-order moment-encoded LBM (HOME-LBM), which stores a compact set of velocity moments instead of the full lattice distribution functions and performs a lightweight collision operator directly in moment space. This formulation reduces memory and bandwidth requirements and has been shown to improve robustness in turbulent-flow simulations. Nevertheless, several practical bottlenecks remain. Its fluid–solid boundary treatment still relies on costly link–solid intersection tests tightly coupled with the streaming operation, leading to irregular control flow and reduced GPU utilization. Furthermore, although quantization has proven effective in reducing memory footprint and bandwidth in large-scale simulations , designing a robust reduced-precision representation for LBM remains nontrivial due to its stability constraints.

Li et al. (2023)

(; )

Hu et al., 2021

Liu et al., 2022a

To accelerate HOME-LBM with complex fluid–solid interactions and reduce memory consumption for large-scale simulations on a single GPU, we propose a high-performance quantized HOME-LBM framework. Our approach consists of two main components. First, we analyze the computational bottlenecks of the original HOME-LBM on GPUs when handling interactions with solid objects, and then present a geometry-decoupled computation scheme for efficient GPU parallelization. Second, to further reduce memory cost, we develop a 16-bit fixed-point quantization for moment storage (). We characterize the linear stability of the unquantized moment-encoded updates on D2Q9 and D3Q27 lattices through von Neumann analysis and combine these results with empirical moment statistics to guide quantization-range selection. For second-order moments, we store and quantize only the non-equilibrium components and reconstruct the equilibrium contributions analytically, narrowing the storage dynamic range.

Sec. 5

We validate our approach through real-time demonstrations and large-scale benchmarks under both D3Q19 and D3Q27 configurations, as well as 2D and 3D numerical experiments assessing accuracy and stability.

At a fixed fluid-grid resolution, mesh-complexity experiments isolate the performance contributions of geometry decoupling and moment quantization. Compared with the original FP32 HOME-LBM, our method achieves $4.1\times$ to $32.5\times$ speedups across the tested configurations (), with the maximum on the Hilbert-curve benchmark (). Moment-buffer storage is reduced by $50\%$ in fluid-only simulations and $25\%$ in fluid–solid coupling, where one buffer remains in FP32 for boundary-correction accumulation. On the static delta-wing benchmark, our solver achieves a $5.2\times$ speedup over Leapfrog Flow Maps (LFM)  under the tested configuration (). Large-scale examples, including $1024^{3}$ fluid-only simulations and fluid–solid interactions involving multimillion-triangle geometries, demonstrate improved scalability on a single GPU while preserving numerical stability, fidelity, and high visual quality.

Navier–Stokes Solvers

Macroscopic Navier–Stokes solvers have long been the backbone of graphics fluid simulation. As a seminal work, introduces Stable Fluids to solve the NS equations on Eulerian grids using an unconditionally stable semi-Lagrangian advection scheme. This approach enables fluid simulations with large time steps, significantly improving efficiency for computer graphics applications, but it suffers from excessive numerical diffusion. To mitigate this issue, a variety of improved advection schemes have been proposed, including BFECC , the modified MacCormack scheme , MacCormack with reflection (MC+R) , bidirectional flow maps , covector advection , neural flow maps , the Eulerian vortex method on flow maps  and Leapfrog Flow Maps , all of which aim to better preserve vortical details over time. Recent work has also explored alternatives to conventional grid-based pressure solvers, including stochastic approaches such as velocity-based Monte Carlo fluids , neural Monte Carlo fluid simulation , and adaptive mesh-free representations such as Gaussian Fluids . These methods offer promising trade-offs in adaptivity, stochastic estimation, and learned acceleration, whereas our work focuses on dense, geometry-rich fluid simulation with highly regular local updates on GPUs.

Beyond Eulerian methods, Lagrangian approaches, such as smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH) , provide particle-based alternatives to Eulerian discretizations. However, these methods struggle to capture turbulence with few particles. Hybrid Eulerian–Lagrangian approaches combine grid-based computations with particle-based transport to improve accuracy, including FLIP and its extensions , and recent particle-flow-map formulations designed to improve long-range advection and preserve vortical structures . ST-FLIP  extends particle-to-grid transfer into space–time to support larger time steps in free-surface and two-phase simulations. Vortex methods, including vortex particles , vortex filaments , and vortex sheets , as well as grid-based vorticity correction , can preserve vortical structures more effectively and provide scalable strategies for maintaining fine-scale flow details.

Alongside advances in flow representation, the computational power of modern GPUs has substantially accelerated fluid solvers through multigrid methods , fixed-point iterations , and compact Poisson filters , as well as multi-GPU parallelization for large-scale simulations . Fast VEM  addresses complex boundaries using a virtual-element discretization on body-fitted cut-cell grids and a specialized geometric multigrid solver. Despite these advances, hybrid Eulerian–Lagrangian approaches , while offering improved fidelity and accuracy, still incur significant memory overhead because they must maintain both grids and particles. Moreover, grid-based Poisson solvers typically rely on iterative methods that require many GPU kernel launches, limiting overall performance.(; )
