Boltzmann-based Solvers

The lattice Boltzmann method, a mesoscopic numerical approach, has recently emerged as a compelling alternative to traditional incompressible NS solvers for both single-phase  and multiphase  flows. Unlike the macroscopic formulations above, LBM evolves distribution functions through purely local collision and streaming operations, avoiding global pressure projection and making it particularly attractive for massively parallel GPU architectures. Early graphics applications  primarily rely on the low-order Bhatnagar–Gross–Krook (BGK) collision model , motivating higher-order collision schemes such as central-moment multiple-relaxation-time (CM-MRT) models , which reduce both dispersion and dissipation errors. Coupling fluids with solids in the LBM framework has also been extensively investigated, with approaches including the immersed boundary (IB) method , a variety of bounce-back schemes , and hybrid macroscopic–mesoscopic boundary models , enabling applications such as underwater swimming and UAV training . Recent work also couples two-phase LBM with the material point method (MPM) to simulate volume-preserving air–water–sand mixtures .

Because LBM operates locally at the mesoscopic scale on lattice nodes, it is well suited for GPU acceleration and large-scale simulations . improve GPU efficiency through optimized data layouts, load-balanced immersed-boundary processing, and a multi-kernel execution strategy, while introduces in-place streaming schemes that reduce distribution-buffer storage through direction-dependent read/write scheduling.

To further reduce memory overhead, HOME-LBM  compresses per-node storage to 10 moment variables for D3Q27 and reconstructs 27 distribution functions on the fly.

However, its original solid-coupling implementation still requires expensive link–solid intersection tests and exhibits divergent branching during solid coupling, reducing parallel efficiency and scalability. For a broader overview of recent advances in LBM and its applications in computer graphics, we refer readers to the SIGGRAPH course by .(; ; )

Von Neumann Stability Analysis of LBM

Von Neumann (VN) stability analysis  has been widely used to characterize numerical stability, dispersion, and dissipation in LBM. Early studies apply it to the BGK model  and demonstrate the superior stability of the MRT model . Subsequent work further analyzed high-order and regularized schemes , as well as cascaded and central-moment MRT schemes . While VN stability analysis has been widely used in LBM, a corresponding VN analysis for moment-encoded formulations remains largely unexplored.()

Quantization in Graphics

Data quantization offers a complementary strategy to reduce storage and memory traffic. In graphics, researchers have explored custom numerical formats and automatic bit-width search , but these approaches often rely on heuristic optimization or learning-based search, which are computationally intractable for the chaotic dynamics of turbulent LBM flows. Neural compression methods such as NeuralVDB  and ACORN  achieve impressive compression ratios but incur significant inference overhead, hindering high-frequency real-time updates. Reduced precision has also been studied in LBM , but directly applying reduced-precision schemes to LBM is particularly challenging because small perturbations may accumulate through repeated collision–streaming updates and destabilize long-horizon simulations. This motivates stability-constrained quantization strategies specifically tailored to the dynamics of moment-encoded LBM.(; )

Before introducing our method, we briefly review the fundamentals of LBM and high-order moment-encoded formulations, including distribution reconstruction, moment-space collision, and fluid–solid coupling. Bold symbols denote vectors, matrices, or tensors, while non-bold symbols denote scalars or individual components; Latin indices $i,j$ label discrete velocity directions, and Greek indices $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ label Cartesian components.

3.1.

In the context of single-phase fluid dynamics, the governing kinetic equation for the evolution of the particle distribution function is the Boltzmann equation :()

Shan et al., 2006

(1) $\frac{\partial\bm{f}}{\partial t}+\bm{v}\cdot\nabla\bm{f}=\Omega(\bm{f})+\bm{F}\cdot\nabla_{\bm{v}}\bm{f}\;,$

where $\bm{f}(\bm{x},\bm{v},t)$ denotes the distribution function, $\bm{F}$ represents external forces, and $\Omega$ is the collision operator that relaxes $\bm{f}$ towards the local thermodynamic equilibrium $\bm{f}^{\text{eq}}$  . The collision operator $\Omega$ models local relaxation of the distribution toward equilibrium and determines the viscosity and dissipative behavior of the scheme. In discrete LBM, choices such as BGK  and central-moment MRT  specify different collision models, while HOME-LBM  evaluates collision

directly in its stored moment representation.

By discretizing time $t$ into uniform time steps, space $\bm{x}$ into a regular lattice grid, and velocity $\bm{v}$ into a finite set of $q$ discrete directions, the continuous Boltzmann equation ( ) becomes the lattice Boltzmann equation (LBE) in dimensionless units:()

3.2.

To reduce the memory footprint and bandwidth cost of standard LBM while preserving physical accuracy, proposed the high-order moment-encoded LBM.

The key idea of HOME-LBM is to store velocity moments $\rho,\rho\bm{u}$ , and $\rho\bm{S}$ in memory and reconstruct distribution functions on the fly using a third-order Hermite basis, balancing accuracy and computational efficiency.

Solid Coupling

HOME-LBM performs fluid–solid coupling by reconstructing boundary distribution functions at solid intersection points and replacing the corresponding streamed distributions on lattice links. Specifically, when a lattice link originating from a grid node $\bm{x}$ intersects a solid boundary at point $\bm{p}$ , it reconstructs a boundary distribution at $\bm{p}$ and streams it to the grid node. Under the assumption of a homogeneous weakly compressible fluid, $\rho^{\bm{p}}\!=\!\rho^{\bm{x}}$ .

Velocity $\bm{u}^{\bm{p}}$ can be computed based on the linear velocity and angular velocity of the solid at $\bm{p}$ . The second-order tensor $\bm{S}^{\bm{p}}$ is approximated as:

Given velocity moments at $\bm{p}$ , the boundary distribution $f^{\bm{p}}_{i}$ is reconstructed using and then streamed to $\bm{x}$ . In this section, we first analyze why solid coupling slows down the original HOME-LBM kernel (), and then present our geometry-decoupled computation scheme for efficient GPU parallelization ().

Sec. 4.1

Sec. 4.2

4.1.

HOME-LBM  achieves substantial speedups over earlier GPU-based LBM implementations  through several key design choices. First, for D3Q27, it reduces per-node storage from $27$ distribution functions to $10$ moment variables, thereby significantly lowering both the memory footprint and memory traffic. Second, by reconstructing distribution functions on the fly from stored moments, the streaming step can be executed more efficiently within each thread block using shared memory.

In addition, HOME-LBM fuses collision, streaming, and boundary handling into a single GPU kernel, eliminating the overhead of multiple kernel launches and improving overall throughput.()

Li et al., 2023

()

Li et al., 2020

However, with complex solid geometries, this fused formulation introduces a critical GPU bottleneck. In the original update procedure (), each lattice thread must determine whether its incoming lattice links intersect the solid surface. For intersecting links, the thread must further reconstruct the boundary distribution function and perform momentum-exchange computations. As a result, the main fluid-update kernel directly incorporates geometric complexity. For high-resolution meshes, the per-step runtime can increase substantially compared with fluid-only simulations ().

4.2.

To alleviate the solid-coupling bottleneck, we restructure the original HOME-LBM pipeline into two GPU stages: fluid update and solid boundary correction, separated by an intermediate buffer copy.

Rather than embedding boundary processing into every lattice-node update, our method first advances the fluid field uniformly over the entire lattice and then applies only the boundary-induced discrepancies as localized corrections. As a result, the main fluid kernel runtime becomes much less sensitive to solid-geometry complexity.

However, in conventional fluid–solid coupled LBM formulations, boundary processing is mathematically intertwined with streaming. Post-streaming distributions near solid boundaries depend directly on boundary reconstruction or bounce-back updates, so a naive separation of boundary handling is generally inconsistent with the original numerical scheme. A key enabler of this decomposition is a reordering of the update sequence. Instead of the classical formulation, in which boundary handling is tightly coupled with streaming, we adopt a scheme. This allows solid effects to be applied afterward as additive moment corrections in a separate sparse stage.streaming $\rightarrow$ collisioncollision $\rightarrow$ streaming

Consequently, the resulting decomposition is not a straightforward kernel split; instead, a reformulation enables it by approximately preserving the effect of boundary processing on the original update while decoupling geometry-dependent operations from the fluid update. We state where the two differ below and evaluate the quantitative impact of this reformulation on boundary accuracy in .

Sec. 6.1

Relation to the Original Update.

Stage I streams distributions reconstructed from post-collision moments at time $t$ , whereas Stage II reconstructs $f_{i}^{\mathrm{II}}(\bm{x})$ from a fixed copy of the post-streaming moments at time $t+1$ . Although both distributions refer to the same target time $t+1$ , the boundary treatment uses the updated, post-streaming density $\rho^{t+1}$ , so the two reconstructions rely on states from different stages of the time step.

Consequently, the correction does not generally reproduce the direct boundary replacement in the original HOME-LBM implementation exactly, even without quantization.

A second, geometric source of discrepancy is that the correction stage treats every triangle independently and assumes a single-layer surface: where a lattice link crosses more than one surface layer within one lattice spacing, as between the upper and lower faces of a thin shell, each intersecting triangle contributes its own correction, whereas the original fused kernel replaces such a link once, at its nearest intersection (see also the

limitations in ).

In , we evaluate the resulting discrepancy.

Sec. 8

Sec. 6.3

Pre-stage.

As in prior work , moving solids require an additional preprocessing stage to update the acceleration structure. Without this preprocessing, each GPU thread would need to iterate over all lattice nodes within a triangle’s bounding box and perform link–triangle intersection tests, resulting in many redundant evaluations.()

Li et al., 2023

To reduce this overhead while keeping kernel launches minimal, we voxelize the solid surface and mark the lattice nodes that contain surface triangles. During traversal of a triangle bounding box, empty lattice nodes can then be efficiently skipped using this occupancy mask. Because this preprocessing is required only when the solid geometry changes, it is negligible for static scenes, where it runs once. For moving solids, the corresponding revoxelization overhead is included in the reported simulation timings ().

Table 2

5.

To further reduce the memory footprint of HOME-LBM, we introduce a quantization scheme for moment-based representations. Since quantization errors can accumulate over long simulation horizons and potentially destabilize the simulation,

rather than selecting numerical ranges purely through empirical tuning, we perform a von Neumann analysis of the moment-encoded LBM to characterize the stable operating regime (). More details on the von Neumann analysis can be found

in . We then combine three complementary sources of constraints to design our quantization scheme (). First, we identify admissible velocity ranges under which perturbations remain bounded. Second, within this regime, we collect conservative runtime statistics from representative simulations to determine practical bounds for density, momentum, and stress-related variables. Third, for second-order moments, we store only their non-equilibrium components and reconstruct the equilibrium contributions analytically, reducing the dynamic range that must be quantized. Together, these ingredients yield a practical $16$ -bit fixed-point representation for the stored moments. The resulting format reduces both memory bandwidth and storage cost while preserving long-horizon stability and physical fidelity in challenging turbulent-flow scenarios.

5.1.

Mapping Reconstruction.

Unlike conventional distribution-based LBM, HOME-LBM does not explicitly store the post-collision distribution functions. Instead, it reconstructs them from a reduced set of velocity moments using a third-order Hermite expansion. As a result, the effective update mapping differs from that of standard distribution-based LBM. Specifically, perturbations evolve through a composite mapping that includes collision, moment extraction, and reconstruction, rather than through the standard collision operator alone. We express the HOME-LBM update as

(15) $\bm{g}^{\mathrm{HOME}}(\bm{f})=\bm{h}\!\left(\bm{m}(\bm{f}^{+})\right),$

where $\bm{h}(\cdot)$ denotes Hermite reconstruction of the distribution, $\bm{m}(\bm{f})\doteq(\rho,\bm{u},\bm{S})$ denotes the moment extraction defined in , and the intermediate post-collision state $\bm{f}^{+}$ is obtained by applying the underlying non-orthogonal central-moment multiple-relaxation-time (NOCM-MRT)  collision step (see  for more details) to $\bm{f}$ :

Eq. 5

(; )

De Rosis, 2017

De Rosis and Luo, 2019

Appendix B

(16) $\bm{f}^{+}=\bm{f}+\bm{\Omega}^{\mathrm{NOCM}}(\bm{f})=\bm{f}-\bm{M}^{-1}\bm{R}\bm{M}\bigl(\bm{f}-\bm{f}^{\mathrm{eq}}\bigr),$

where $\bm{M}=\bm{M}^{\mathrm{NOCM}}(\bm{u})$ is the moment transformation matrix of the NOCM-MRT collision model, and $\bm{R}$ is a diagonal matrix of relaxation rates $\{r_{i}\}_{i=1,\dots,q}$  .()

Li et al., 2020

This “moment representation + reconstruction” procedure first converts the post-collision distribution into a set of moments and then reconstructs the distribution by projecting it onto a truncated third-order Hermite subspace. Although this reconstruction is algebraically equivalent at the macroscopic level, it alters the effective linearized update operator, thereby affecting numerical stability and error amplification.

Linearization of Composite Mapping.

Following the standard perturbation and linearization procedure introduced in , we linearize the composite mapping $\bm{g}^{\mathrm{HOME}}$ around a uniform equilibrium and analyze its Jacobian with respect to the distribution function. Since $\bm{g}^{\mathrm{HOME}}$ is a composition of moment extraction, collision, and reconstruction operators, the chain rule gives its Jacobian directly.

Experimental Range for Density.

In weakly compressible LBM, density fluctuations are expected to remain small around the reference value $\rho=1$ . Nevertheless, because the method is not strictly incompressible, we explicitly account for density variation. In an extreme-turbulence $3$ D flow-over-sphere experiment () with inlet velocity $0.256$ , viscosity $\nu=0$ , and grid resolution $512\times 256\times 256$ , we observe density values within the range $\rho\in[0.8,1.5]$ , even in highly vortical regions. We empirically select our fixed quantization ranges based on representative simulations shown in this paper and we clamp out-of-range values to the nearest endpoint.

Normalization and Fixed-point Quantization.

Each moment component $m$ is normalized to the unit interval as

(26) $m^{\prime}=\frac{m-m_{\min}}{m_{\max}-m_{\min}},$

where $m_{\min}$ and $m_{\max}$ denote the predefined bounds obtained from the range analysis above. This normalization maps all stored moments to $[0,1]$ . Each normalized component is then quantized to a $b$ -bit unsigned integer using uniform quantization:

(27) $q(m)=\left\lfloor m^{\prime}\left(2^{b}-1\right)+\tfrac{1}{2}\right\rfloor.$

Dequantization is performed using the inverse mapping

(28) $\hat{m}=m_{\min}+q(m)\left(\frac{m_{\max}-m_{\min}}{2^{b}-1}\right),$

which reconstructs an approximation of the original value $m$ up to quantization error. In our implementation, most moment components are stored as $16$ -bit fixed-point integers ( $b=16$ ), allowing two moments to be packed into a single $32$ -bit word. Consequently, the moment buffer requires only five values per lattice node, rather than $10$ values, reducing both the memory footprint and the global memory write bandwidth by approximately $50\%$ .uint32float32

Data Layout.

To improve memory efficiency and access coherence, we store fluid nodes in a structure-of-arrays (SoA) layout  and organize them into fixed-size $8\times 8\times 8$ tiles. This layout improves spatial locality when accessing boundary-adjacent fluid nodes and enables coalesced memory access during solid correction.()

Chen et al., 2022

Dithering.

To reduce bias from deterministic rounding, we apply spatial dithering during quantization. Specifically, a small zero-mean noise, uniformly distributed in $[-\tfrac{1}{2},\tfrac{1}{2}]$ of one quantization unit , is added to the normalized value before rounding, drawn independently for every node and every time step, and the result is clamped to $[0,2^{b}-1]$ . This converts deterministic rounding error into zero-mean stochastic noise, thereby preventing systematic bias accumulation over long time integration.()

Liu et al., 2022a

Atomic Accumulation with Mixed Precision.

When solid coupling is present, multiple triangle faces may contribute moment corrections to the same lattice node, which requires atomic accumulation of moment updates in the solid-correction kernel. Performing atomic operations directly on quantized fixed-point values would introduce order-dependent rounding errors and may lead to noticeable bias accumulation over long simulations. To mitigate this issue, we adopt a mixed-precision strategy.

Specifically, we maintain two moment buffers: a full-precision buffer and a compact 16-bit quantized buffer. The fluid update kernel () reads the compact buffer and writes post-streaming moments to the FP32 buffer (the output buffer of ). The buffer copy kernel () then encodes these post-streaming moments into the compact buffer, overwriting the previous time step’s data. During solid correction (), the compact buffer remains read-only: the solid-correction kernel decodes its contents and accumulates

the resulting moment corrections into the FP32 buffer using . Once all solid corrections are complete, the corrected moments are encoded back into the compact buffer for the next fluid update. Since only one of the moment buffers is quantized, the overall memory reduction is about $25\%$ compared with the FP32 implementation, which we find is a favorable trade-off between accuracy and bandwidth savings in solid-coupled simulations.

2D Taylor Vortex

We first evaluate the long-term robustness of vortex evolution using the 2D Taylor vortex benchmark, following the setup in prior work . This benchmark is sensitive to numerical dissipation and perturbation growth, making it well suited for assessing the stability of our proposed quantized simulations. We compare against representative grid-based and particle-based fluid solvers, including Semi-Lagrangian , MacCormack , MC+R , PolyPIC , BiMocq, Covector Fluids (CF) , and the Eulerian vortex method on flow maps , as well as HOME-LBM  baselines using both double precision (64-bit) and single precision (32-bit). All methods use the same grid resolution, $256\times 256$ .

As shown in , classical semi-Lagrangian schemes show progressive vortex-core diffusion, while particle-based methods preserve sharper structures but introduce more high-frequency artifacts. In contrast, HOME-LBM preserves coherent vortex structures with limited dissipation. Our proposed 16-bit quantized solver remains visually consistent with the 64-bit and 32-bit HOME-LBM baselines and closely matches other high-quality advection methods, indicating that moment-space quantization preserves visual fidelity and numerical behavior while reducing memory usage by 50 $\%$ .(; )

2D Double-layer Vortex

We next evaluate the proposed quantized representation’s sensitivity to different bit allocations using the 2D double-layer vortex benchmark. We adopt an adaptive bit-allocation strategy to balance quantization error across different moment components. Since density and velocity variables exhibit similar normalized ranges and directly affect macroscopic transport, we assign the same bit width to $\rho$ and $\rho\bm{u}$ . In contrast, after the range reduction described in , the non-equilibrium stress moments $\rho\bm{S}^{\mathrm{neq}}$ have a much smaller dynamic range and can therefore be represented with fewer bits.

We denote each configuration as $b_{\rho,u}/b_{S}$ , where $b_{\rho,u}$ and $b_{S}$ are the bit widths for density–velocity and stress moments, respectively. For example, the configuration stores $\rho$ and $\rho\bm{u}$ using 16 bits and stores $\rho\bm{S}^{\mathrm{neq}}$ using 15 bits.

As shown in , where both the L2 relative error and the memory usage are measured against the 64-bit double-precision run, this allocation yields a smooth accuracy–memory trade-off. Reducing stress precision to 14–15 bits introduces only minor error increases, whereas more aggressive reduction rapidly degrades both numerical accuracy and visual quality.

3D Trefoil Knot.

To assess the ability of our 16-bit moment quantization to preserve 3D vortex structures, we adopt the trefoil-knot benchmark of .

We compare our 16-bit quantized solver against Semi-Lagrangian , MacCormack , MC+R , BiMocq, Covector Fluids (CF) and its extension with the method of characteristic mapping (MCM) , as well as the FP32 HOME-LBM baseline .

As shown in , the quantized solver produces vortex structures visually consistent with the FP32 baseline, with both retaining more kinetic energy than CF but less than CF+MCM.

Their kinetic-energy and enstrophy histories closely agree ( (a,b)), including the transient enstrophy increase during vortex reconnection.

After 5.5 s, the relative mass drifts remain small, at $3.5\times 10^{-5}$ for FP32 and $4\times 10^{-5}$ for the quantized solver ( (c)).

These results suggest that 16-bit moment quantization largely preserves vortex dynamics and mass conservation behavior while reducing storage requirements.

As discussed in , the discrepancy has two sources, both present in 32-bit precision: the boundary correction is reconstructed from the post-streaming moments at $t+1$ , whereas the distribution it replaces was streamed from the post-collision moments at $t$ ; and the per-triangle correction cannot resolve multi-layer geometry, so links that cross both faces of the thin shell within one lattice spacing receive more than one correction, whereas the original kernel replaces them once at their nearest intersection. We compare the end-to-end simulation performance of our GPU-oriented geometry-decoupled implementation with the original single-kernel HOME-LBM algorithm . Both implementations use identical collision models, boundary conditions, and time step sizes.

7.

$1024^{3}$ Fluid Simulation.

To demonstrate the scalability and fidelity of our solver at extreme resolutions, we simulate two cases of a plume formed by obliquely impacting jets on a $1024^{3}$ grid at different Reynolds numbers, as shown in . The Reynolds number is defined as $\mathrm{Re}=UL/\nu$ with the inlet speed $U=0.2$ and the domain edge length $L=1024$ lattice units. At lower Reynolds numbers, the flow exhibits stable, coherent vortex structures, while at higher Reynolds numbers, the solver resolves fine-scale turbulent filaments and intermittent eddies across a wide range of spatial scales.

Our quantized formulation reduces the memory footprint by $50\%$ compared to FP32 baselines, enabling large-scale simulations that would otherwise exceed the GPU memory capacity of a single GPU. This demonstrates that our framework can efficiently support high-resolution fluid simulations while preserving rich small-scale flow details.

Large-scale Fluid–solid Coupling.

We further demonstrate large-scale fluid–solid interaction using turbulent smoke simulations around a Ducati motorcycle and a Ferrari F1 racing car at a grid resolution of $1000\times 400\times 400$ , as shown in  and . Both simulations use a closed computational domain with stationary no-slip walls. The simulations use 16-bit quantization and incorporate highly detailed solid geometry with intricate boundary features. This shows that the proposed framework efficiently supports high-resolution, geometry-rich fluid–solid simulations while preserving fine-scale flow details.

8.

We presented a stability-constrained GPU framework for memory-efficient, high-performance moment-based lattice Boltzmann simulation with complex fluid–solid interaction. The proposed geometry-decoupled computation scheme decouples dense fluid evolution from sparse boundary correction, substantially reducing warp divergence and improving GPU utilization in complex geometries. In addition, our von Neumann stability analysis provides moment-wise stability constraints that inform the design of a robust reduced-precision representation for HOME-LBM. Together, these techniques significantly reduce memory footprint without sacrificing numerical stability. Our experiments demonstrate moment-storage reductions of $50\%$ in fluid-only and $25\%$ in fluid–solid simulations, speedups of $4.1\times$ to $32.5\times$ over the original HOME-LBM across the configurations it supports, and a $5.2\times$ speedup over LFM on the static delta-wing benchmark under the tested configuration, enabling higher-resolution simulations within the constraints of a single GPU at approximately one second per frame for our largest fluid–solid scenes. More broadly, this work illustrates how theoretical stability analysis can directly inform practical GPU system design for scalable LBM simulation.

Limitations and Future Work

Our current implementation assumes single-layer surface meshes and does not yet support layered geometry or complex self-intersections, which would require more advanced inside–outside classification and intersection handling. In the current per-triangle correction, links that cross more than one surface layer within one lattice spacing are corrected more than once, which contributes to the boundary discrepancy measured in . Moreover, while our boundary treatment is optimized for robustness and throughput, we do not explicitly evaluate sub-cell geometric accuracy or boundary error convergence; incorporating wall-function models  is a natural next step.

Several promising directions remain, including extending the framework to fully coupled two-way interactions and integrating multi-resolution or adaptive discretization to further improve scalability for large-scale scenes. Our implementation retains two moment buffers, and the buffer copy between the fluid and solid-correction stages accounts for a substantial share of the per-step time in coupled scenes; adapting in-place streaming schemes , which remove the second distribution buffer in standard LBM, to moment-encoded storage provides a way to reduce this cost.

Appendix A

The standard von Neumann stability analysis for LBM  is a linear Fourier-mode analysis that studies whether small perturbations in the distribution functions grow or decay under the discrete streaming–collision update. By linearizing the dynamics about a uniform equilibrium state and introducing plane-wave perturbations, the method yields an amplification matrix $\mathbf{G}$ whose eigenvalues characterize linear stability, numerical dissipation, and dispersion across wavenumbers. Here, we briefly summarize the key elements of classical formulations required for extending the analysis to HOME-LBM in . A more detailed review of the classical VN formulation of LBM is provided in .()

Sterling and Chen, 1996

Sec. 5.1

()

Chávez-Modena et al., 2018

A.1.

Starting from the lattice Boltzmann equation () and following  to neglect the external force term for clarity, the discrete kinetic update can be written as:

Eq. 2

Sterling and Chen (1996)

(29) $f_{i}(\bm{x}+\bm{c}_{i},t+1)=f_{i}(\bm{x},t)+\Omega_{i}(\bm{f}),$

where $\Omega_{i}$ is the discrete collision term. We define the post-collision mapping

(30) $g_{i}(\bm{f})=f_{i}+\Omega_{i}(\bm{f}),$

so that the update becomes

(31) $f_{i}(\bm{x}+\bm{c}_{i},t+1)=g_{i}(\bm{f}(\bm{x},t)).$

A.2.

We introduce a small perturbation around a spatially uniform equilibrium distribution:

(32) $f_{i}(\bm{x},t)=\bar{f}_{i}+f_{i}^{\prime}(\bm{x},t),\quad\text{with}\quad|\bar{f}_{i}|\gg|f_{i}^{\prime}|,$

where $\bar{f}_{i}$ denotes the globally uniform equilibrium distribution that does not vary with time and space, and $f_{i}^{\prime}(\bm{x},t)$ at node $\bm{x}$ and time $t$ accounts for a small perturbation from $\bar{f}_{i}$ .

Performing the first-order Taylor expansion of $g_{i}$ around $\bar{f}_{i}$ with a small perturbation $f^{\prime}_{i}$ yields:

(33) $g_{i}(\bar{\bm{f}}+\bm{f}^{\prime})\approx g_{i}(\bar{\bm{f}})+\sum_{j}\left.\frac{\partial g_{i}}{\partial f_{j}}\right|_{\bar{\bm{f}}}f^{\prime}_{j}.$

To proceed, we note that most practical LBM collision models can be interpreted as linear relaxation of moments toward their equilibrium values . When expressed in distribution-function space, this relaxation admits the unified matrix representation:()

Higuera and Jiménez, 1989

(34) $\Omega(\bm{f})=\bm{K}(\bm{f}^{eq}-\bm{f}),$

where the collision matrix $\bm{K}$ characterizes how the distribution function relaxes toward its equilibrium state. Therefore, the corresponding linearized evolution becomes:

(35) $\bm{g}(\bar{\bm{f}}+\bm{f}^{\prime})=\bar{\bm{f}}+\bm{f}^{\prime}(\bm{x},t)+\bm{K}\bigl(\bm{\Lambda}-\bm{I}\bigr)\,\bm{f}^{\prime}(\bm{x},t),$

where $\bm{\Lambda}$ is the Jacobian of the equilibrium distribution with elements

(36) $\Lambda_{ij}=\frac{\partial f^{eq}_{i}}{\partial\rho}\frac{\partial\rho}{\partial f_{j}}+\sum_{\alpha}\frac{\partial f^{eq}_{i}}{\partial u_{\alpha}}\frac{\partial u_{\alpha}}{\partial f_{j}}.$

Without forcing, gives

$\partial\rho/\partial f_{j}=1$ and

$\partial u_{\alpha}/\partial f_{j}=(c_{j\alpha}-u_{\alpha})/\rho$ , and every equilibrium used in this paper is $\rho$ times a polynomial in $\bm{u}$ , so that $\partial\bm{f}^{\text{eq}}/\partial\rho=\bm{f}^{\text{eq}}/\rho$ . Hence

Eq. 5

(37) $\bm{\Lambda}=\frac{1}{\rho}\Bigl[\bm{f}^{\text{eq}}\,\bm{1}^{\!\top}+\sum_{\alpha}\frac{\partial\bm{f}^{\text{eq}}}{\partial u_{\alpha}}\,\bigl(\bm{c}_{\alpha}-u_{\alpha}\bm{1}\bigr)^{\!\top}\Bigr],$

where $\bm{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{q}$ is the vector of ones and $(\bm{c}_{\alpha})_{j}=c_{j\alpha}$ . The equilibrium $\bm{f}^{\text{eq}}$ and its derivatives $\partial\bm{f}^{\text{eq}}/\partial u_{\alpha}$ are given in Appendix  for D2Q9 and in Appendix  for D3Q27.

C.5

D.5

Combining   and , the evolution of the perturbation is given by:

Eq. 31

Eq. 35

(38) $f^{\prime}_{i}(\bm{x}+\bm{c}_{i},\,t+1)=\Bigl[\bm{I}+\bm{K}\bigl(\bm{\Lambda}-\bm{I}\bigr)\Bigr]_{ij}f^{\prime}_{j}(\bm{x},t).$

This equation defines a linear dynamical system and serves as the starting point for the subsequent Fourier (von Neumann) stability analysis.

A.3.

Following the standard VN procedure, we substitute into  a plane-wave solution of the form :

Eq. 38

()

Wissocq et al., 2020

(39) $f_{i}^{\prime}(\bm{x},t)=\hat{f}_{i}e^{\mathrm{i}(\bm{k}\cdot\bm{x}-\omega t)},$

where $\hat{f}_{i}$ denotes the complex amplitude, and the exponential term represents a monochromatic plane wave with wave vector $\bm{k}$ and angular frequency $\omega$ . Combining the streaming phase factor with the Jacobian operator yields the amplification matrix $\bm{G}(\bm{k})$ :

(40) $\bm{G}(\bm{k})=\bm{D}(\bm{k})\left[\bm{I}+\bm{K}(\bm{\Lambda}-\bm{I})\right],$

where $\bm{D}(\bm{k})=\text{diag}(e^{-\mathrm{i}\bm{k}\cdot\bm{c}_{0}},\dots,e^{-\mathrm{i}\bm{k}\cdot\bm{c}_{q-1}})$ represents the advection operator in Fourier space. $\bm{K}$ and $\bm{\Lambda}$ denote the collision and Jacobian matrices, respectively. This matrix $\bm{G}(\bm{k})$ compactly encodes the linearized evolution of Fourier modes and provides a convenient basis for analyzing the stability, dispersion, and numerical properties of the scheme.

Appendix B

Collision modeling plays a central role in determining both the accuracy and the stability of lattice Boltzmann solvers. Each collision model considered in this work is specified by its collision matrix $\bm{K}$ in . This section gives $\bm{K}$ for the three reference models and refers to the original papers for their derivation. We list the moment bases and relaxation rates per lattice in  and , and we assemble the amplification matrices for all four models, including HOME-LBM. All moment-matrix inverses are computed numerically (), and the matrices are at most $27\times 27$ .

B.1.

The classical BGK formulation  applies a single relaxation time to relax each lattice population toward its local

equilibrium. The collision operator is written as()

Bhathnagor et al., 1954

(41) $\Omega_{i}^{\mathrm{BGK}}=\frac{1}{\tau}\left(f_{i}^{\mathrm{eq}}-f_{i}\right),\qquad{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\bm{K}^{\mathrm{BGK}}=\frac{1}{\tau}\,\bm{I},}$

where $\tau$ is the relaxation time determining the rate at which the distribution function approaches equilibrium. The BGK model yields the following relation between $\tau$ and the kinematic viscosity $\nu$ : $\tau=3\nu+\tfrac{1}{2}$ (equivalently $\nu=c_{s}^{2}(\tau-\tfrac{1}{2})$ ).

B.2.

To overcome the stability limitations of the BGK model, the MRT framework introduces a more stable collision operator that acts in moment space rather than directly on the distribution functions . In the RM-MRT formulation, the collision model is performed on polynomial moments constructed from the lattice velocities, $\bm{m}=\bm{M}^{\mathrm{RM}}\bm{f}$ and $\bm{m}^{\mathrm{eq}}=\bm{M}^{\mathrm{RM}}\bm{f}^{\mathrm{eq}}$ , where the rows of the raw-moment transformation matrix $\bm{M}^{\mathrm{RM}}$ are polynomials in the lattice velocities and do not depend on the local fluid velocity (Appendices  and ). Each moment is relaxed toward its equilibrium at its own rate, $\bm{\Omega}^{\mathrm{RM}}=(\bm{M}^{\mathrm{RM}})^{-1}\bm{R}\,(\bm{m}^{\mathrm{eq}}-\bm{m})$ , so that the RM-MRT collision operator is(; ; )

d’Humières, 1992

where $\mathbf{R}=\mathrm{diag}(\bm{r}^{\mathrm{RM}})$ is a diagonal matrix of relaxation rates for each moment (Appendices  and ).

B.3.

While RM-MRT improves stability over BGK, its use of raw moments lacks Galilean invariance, which can degrade accuracy and cause instabilities at low viscosities. The non-orthogonal central moment multiple relaxation time model (NOCM-MRT) addresses this issue by defining moments relative to the local fluid velocity, thereby achieving significantly improved invariance properties and enhanced robustness and accuracy for turbulent flows .

Let $\bm{u}$ denote the local macroscopic velocity, and let $\mathbf{M}^{\mathrm{NOCM}}(\bm{u})$ be the central-moment transformation matrix, which shifts the velocity basis so that the resulting moments, $\bm{m}=\mathbf{M}^{\mathrm{NOCM}}(\bm{u})\,\bm{f}$ and $\bm{m}^{\mathrm{eq}}=\mathbf{M}^{\mathrm{NOCM}}(\bm{u})\,\bm{f}^{\mathrm{eq}}$ , are computed with respect to $\bm{c}_{i}-\bm{u}$ (Appendices  and ); $\bm{m}^{\mathrm{eq}}$ represents the central-moment equilibrium obtained from the Maxwellian equilibrium distribution. The NOCM-MRT collision operator is then expressed as(; )

where $\mathbf{R}=\mathrm{diag}(\bm{r}^{\mathrm{NOCM}})$ is a diagonal relaxation matrix specifying independent relaxation rates for each central moment. Relaxing higher-order moments more aggressively provides strong damping

of non-hydrodynamic modes while preserving the correct recovery of Navier–Stokes dynamics .()

For completeness, we list the discrete velocities, lattice weights, and the lattice speed of sound used throughout this work. The D2Q9 lattice consists of nine discrete velocity directions

item.title: Open-Form Geometric Style Transfer：开放形态的几何风格迁移 ｜ Open-Form Geometric Style Transfer
item.description:
一句话：不再局限于闭合网格，把几何风格迁移扩展到开放形态（片状、线状结构）。

要点：

  • 传统几何风格迁移假设输入是闭合流形网格
  • 扩展到开放形态：薄壳、条带、线框等结构
  • 特拉维夫大学与深圳大学合作

为什么值得看：资产生产里大量内容并非闭合网格（布料、植被、建筑构件）；这条线把风格迁移的适用范围扩大了一圈。

中文摘要：Open-Form Geometric Style Transfer 研究几何风格迁移的一个实际限制：以往方法大多假设输入是闭合的流形网格，但真实资产里充满开放形态——薄壳、条带、线框、植被片等。作者把风格迁移扩展到这类结构，重新定义了局部几何特征的对应与迁移方式，使风格化能覆盖更广的资产类型。论文来自特拉维夫大学与深圳大学合作，对批量资产风格化管线有直接价值。

主题：图形学

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

License: CC BY 4.0

arXiv:2610.26820v1 [cs.CV] 19 Oct 2026

Open-Form Geometric Style Transfer

Adar Elad

Email:

elad.research@gmail.com

Gal Metzer

Tel Aviv University

Tel Aviv University

Affiliation: Email:

Abstract

A geometric style learned from one family of shapes is typically applied to

new shapes from the same family. We consider a more challenging setting:

learning the geometric design language of a stylized Latin alphabet and

applying it to new forms, from Greek glyphs to entirely different structures

such as human poses. We introduce Open-Form Geometric Style Transfer,

where the forms to which a learned geometric style can be applied are not

restricted to the shape family in which that style was observed.

This setting is deceptively challenging: the difficulty is not merely learning

a style, but learning the style without learning the shape family in which it

was observed. We represent target forms by structural sketches and disentangle

structural adherence from style realization using a Geometry LoRA and a

style-specific LoRA. Critically, open-form transfer requires the Geometry LoRA

to be universal. To achieve this, we devise a geometry-enrichment

strategy that constructs a large and purposefully diverse collection of

synthetic structural sketches spanning a broad range of unfamiliar geometries.

Our experiments and ablations demonstrate the importance of both

disentanglement and this universal geometry prior, enabling geometric styles

learned from glyphs, pictograms, and other shape families to be transferred to

substantially different, unseen forms.

: Figure 1Open-Form Geometric Style Transfer.

Given a small set of examples sharing a geometric style (left), we learn their

common geometric design language and apply it to unseen structural sketches.

The resulting forms (right) span challenging and unrelated shape families,

illustrating open-form transfer beyond the family in which the style was

originally observed.

†Corresponding author†footnotetext: ∗

1

: Figure 2Open-Form Geometric Style Transfer.

Given a set of glyph examples sharing a geometric style (left), we learn to

apply that style to new structural sketches (right). The target forms are

unseen during style learning and may belong to entirely different shape

families.

Style transfer is a long-standing and intriguing problem in visual computing:

given examples that contain both content and style, the goal is to capture the

essence of the style, separate it from the particular content on which it is

observed, and apply it to new content. The separation of style from content has

been studied for decades , and has more

recently become central to neural style transfer and generative

modeling .

At the heart of the problem lies the ability to distinguish from .[, ]

8

7

[, , ]

13

27

15

what is

representedhow it is expressed

In this work, we focus on , where style governs how an

underlying structure is geometrically realized. A canonical example is a font:

different glyphs have different structures, yet their geometric realizations

follow a coherent design language that makes them immediately recognizable as

belonging to the same font. More generally, such geometric styles cannot be

inferred from a single example; it is revealed through a collection of different

shapes that share the same design language. Early work has considered related

notions of separating style from content and transferring geometric style across

shapes .geometric style[, ]

25

9

Existing approaches typically learn and apply such styles within a shared domain: a style observed on letters is transferred to other letters, and a style observed on human figures is applied to other human figures.

We remove this restriction and consider transferring a geometric style to an .

As illustrated in Figure , a style learned from a

Latin alphabet may be applied to Greek glyphs, or more radically, to human

poses; conversely, a geometric style learned from pictograms may be applied to

glyphs. We call this new setting ,

where the forms to which a learned geometric style can be applied are not

restricted to the shape family in which that style was observed. We focus on

forms whose underlying structure can be represented by a sparse structural

sketch, which serves as the geometry to be styled.[, , ]

22

29

26

open space of formsOpen-Form Geometric Style TransferOpen-Form Geometric Style Transfer

The open-form setting, illustrated in Figure , is deceptively challenging.

The difficulty is not simply learning a style, but .

Existing font-generation methods can transfer styles to unseen

glyphs , and some explicitly

separate character content from style. However, their structural component is

learned and evaluated largely within the glyph domain, often within a single

writing system. This distinction becomes critical when the target form leaves

the source domain.

A straightforward LoRA trained on a limited styled shape family learns an entangled

style with the geometries observed at training (Sec. ), causing it

to drift toward familiar source-domain shapes when presented with substantially

different target geometries.

2

learning the style

without learning the shape family in which that style was observed[, , , ]

29

26

32

18

4.2

Our approach addresses this entanglement by separating .

A Geometry LoRA is responsible for faithfully following the target structural sketch serving as a geometric-adherence prior, while a Style LoRA learns how that geometry should be realized in the desired style.

Accordingly, the Geometry LoRA must be : generalize across the vast universe of styles, responding to structure rather than shape identity or residual stylistic cues.

Acquiring such a universal geometry prior is itself non-trivial: a corpus of ordinary glyphs provides a limited and familiar geometry vocabulary, allowing the model to recognize known shapes rather than truly follow the input structure.

We therefore introduce a geometry-enrichment strategy (GEE Sec. ) that systematically leverages SVG font data to construct a large collection of unfamiliar synthetic geometries, untangled from their source style.

This strategy proves vital for successfully learning a universal geometry LoRA.structural adherence from style realizationuniversal

3.2

Our contributions are threefold:

•

We introduce , where a geometric style learned from one shape domain is applied to universally arbitrary forms.Open-Form Geometric Stylization

•

We show that open-form stylization requires separating structural adherence from style realization.

•

Finally, we introduce a geometry-enrichment strategy for constructing the broad and diverse structural training distribution needed to acquire this universal prior.

We evaluate these ideas through controlled ablations and increasingly challenging transfers, from held-out glyphs and cross-alphabet transfer to unrelated forms such as human poses, demonstrating that a geometric style can be extended well beyond the family of shapes on which it was observed.

2

Our work builds on three lines of research: the separation of style and

content, font and glyph style transfer, and structurally conditioned

generation. Below we review each line, clarify how our notion of

style relates to them, and how they relate to our approach.geometric

2.1

Our work is closely connected to the seminal work of Tenenbaum and

Freeman  on separating style and content.

Using bilinear models, they showed that a common style can be inferred from

multiple observations and applied to new content. Particularly relevant to

our setting is their treatment of fonts, where style is shared across

different letters and can be used to synthesize previously unseen characters.

This provides an early and elegant formulation of style as a factor that can

be learned across a family of shapes and separated from their individual

geometry. Our work builds on this perspective, but considers an open-form

setting in which the new content need not belong to the same family: a

geometric style learned from one alphabet may be applied to another alphabet,

or even to a different class of structures such as human poses.[]

25

More broadly, style transfer has a long history in computer vision and

graphics, with much of the literature focusing on style as visual appearance.

Early example-based methods  synthesized and transferred texture by sampling local neighborhoods or patches

from example images.

later introduced neural style transfer, demonstrating that content and artistic style can be represented separately within a deep network and recombined to render new content in the appearance of a reference image. Recent diffusion-based methods

such as StyleAligned , B-LoRA ,

InstantStyle , and ZipLoRA

substantially extend the quality and flexibility of reference-based style

transfer. Across these works, style is predominantly expressed through visual

appearance, including texture, color, material, brushwork, and shading.[, ]

Our notion of is different. Here, style determines how

an underlying structure is geometrically realized: how curves are formed,

junctions are connected, strokes vary in thickness, gaps are introduced, and

structural elements terminate or interact. Such a style is naturally revealed

by a of related shapes rather than by a single reference image.

Glyphs provide a particularly clean instance of this setting: individual

characters differ in structure, while together they reveal a consistent

geometric design language. Related notions of transferring geometric style

across shapes were also explored in early work by .

2.2

Modern font-generation methods provide the closest setting to our work, as

they explicitly transfer a common style across glyphs with different

structures. FontDiffuser  formulates one-shot

diffusion-based font generation, using multi-scale content aggregation to

preserve character structure and contrastive learning to capture style. It

generalizes to unseen characters and also demonstrates cross-lingual

generation. MX-Font  addresses few-shot font generation using multiple

localized experts that disentangle content and style while capturing different local style characteristics.

It also demonstrates cross-lingual generalization to unseen writing systems.

VecFusion  approaches font generation in the

vector domain, explicitly modeling glyph topology, paths, and Bézier control

points, and supports applications including glyph completion and few-shot

style transfer. Skeleton-Guided Diffusion  is particularly

related to our structural representation, using character skeletons to guide

diffusion and preserve structure during font generation. StrokeStyles  decomposes font glyphs into

meaningful stroke structures and uses this representation for consistent

geometric stylization across characters.[]

FLUX-Font  is particularly close to our work architecturally.

It adapts a pre-trained diffusion transformer using separate LoRA

modules  for glyph content and style, explicitly separating

the two factors rather than learning them through a single adapter. Our method

shares this general motivation, but separates structural adherence from style

realization hierarchically: a universal Geometry LoRA is first trained to

Despite their differences, these methods share an important restriction:

their structural representations and learned priors are designed for the

glyph domain. Their goal is to generalize from observed characters to other

characters, possibly across writing systems, but the target remains a glyph.

Open-form transfer removes this restriction. The target structural sketch may

describe a character, a pictogram, a human pose, or another unrelated form.

Consequently, separating content from style within the font domain is not

sufficient; the geometry-following component must itself generalize beyond

the shape family in which the style was observed.

Spatially conditioned diffusion models provide a complementary line of related

work. ControlNet  and

Our problem, however, is not spatial conditioning alone. The structural sketch

specifies a form whose geometric realization must change according to a style

learned from a separate set of examples. The challenge is therefore to preserve

the target structure while preventing the learned style from carrying with it

the shape distribution on which that style was observed. We use structural

conditioning as a means toward this goal, learning a universal geometry prior

that remains fixed while different geometric styles are acquired. At inference,

we treat structure and style as independent conditions and adopt the

dual-conditioning guidance of InstructPix2Pix , allowing

their strengths to be controlled separately.[]

3.1

The purpose of UGL is to fine-tune a text-to-image diffusion model to follow open-form geometries (i.e. sketches).

Starting from a pre-trained text-to-image diffusion transformer (DiT), we fit LoRA parameters on the DiT’s weights using sketch-glyph data pairs constructed by GEE.

The rich, diverse synthetic data produced by the GEE allows us to select a high LoRA rank without overfitting, giving the UGL significant learning capacity.

After this one-time training, we freeze UGL and share it across all Style LoRAs, providing a common geometry prior beyond each style’s specific training examples.

: Figure 4GEE overview.

(a) Geometry generation recursively merges and removes glyph components in font $i$ , recording a font-independent recipe.

(b) Reapplying the recipe to font $j$ produces the same underlying construction in another style.

(c) Skeleton extraction yields a conditioning sketch from $j$ , which is paired with the target glyph from $i$ .

Fonts are a natural starting point for data augmentation: they are available in a large variety of styles, and more importantly, their SVG native representation enables truly geometric augmentations compared to raster form.

However, using real font glyphs directly presents two limitations. First, available fonts cover a relatively narrow set of languages and therefore a limited vocabulary of structures, which may hinder generalization to unseen scripts and, even more, to out-of-domain forms such as symbols or pictograms.

Second, the geometry of a glyph is itself tied to the style of its source font, so the conditioning structure may carry unwanted stylistic cues.

To address both issues, we introduce : a data-generation procedure that expands the range of training geometries while reducing their dependence on font style.

To increase structural diversity, GEE takes advantage of the native SVG parameterization of fonts and constructs novel geometric forms by applying random sequences of geometric edits.

We refer to each such sequence as a .

A recipe may, for example, repeatedly remove or merge SVG parts, producing coherent but unfamiliar structures (Fig. (a)).

Recipes also allow the GEE to address the second problem. A recipe applied to one font can be re-applied to matching letters from another font, producing paired data with but (Fig. (b)).

During UGL training, we form mixed pairs by taking the conditioning sketch from one font and the target from another font to which the same recipe was applied (Fig. (c)).

The sketch and target therefore remain aligned in structure while differing in style, encouraging UGL to learn the supplied geometry independently of its stylistic realization.GEEgeometric recipe

We next describe the editing primitives that drive the geometry enrichment process, first motivating their design and then outlining each one (full details in Appendix ).

C

Structural editing primitives.

A glyph’s structure is determined by how its strokes relate: which strokes meet and where they branch or terminate. Smooth transformations such as warping, shearing, or scaling can change a glyph’s appearance, but they do not create new structural relations between its strokes. To generate genuinely new structures, we therefore need operations that modify these relations. We propose two elementary edits: component removal and merging. This builds on a broader principle: deleting and recombining existing parts can generate meaningful structural variation , and related cut-based augmentations have been shown to improve recognition performance . Repeating these edits produces novel structural relations beyond those found in existing alphabets.[]

11

[, ]

6

30

To make both edits transferable across fonts, we edit the glyph’s structure rather than its contour, which is more sensitive to stylistic variation. We therefore represent each glyph as a graph, with strokes as edges and intersections and endpoints as nodes. A recipe is then expressed as a sequence of graph edits, with component removal and merging each applied one to three times. The edit type and its structural parameters are sampled when the recipe is created, specifying which component to remove or where components should connect. Because the edits are defined structurally, the same recipe can be replayed across fonts to produce the same underlying structure in multiple styles. Structural correspondence across styles is further explained in Appendix .

C

Graph extraction.

We represent each glyph as a graph that captures its dominant stroke structure (Fig. ). Starting from the glyph (a), we compute its medial axis together with the local inscribed-disk radius, which provides an estimate of stroke thickness (b). We prune short branches caused by serifs and other stylistic details, leaving the main stroke structure (c). Pixel chains are then collapsed into edges, with junctions and stroke endpoints represented as nod es (d). Finally, we classify each edge by its structural role: an edge between two junctions is a , while an edge from a junction to an endpoint is a (e).

3.2

Component removal.

Fig.  illustrates the process. Our strategy is to perform the edit in the medial-axis representation and then reconstruct the glyph back in the SVG domain. Outline points unrelated to the removed component are preserved exactly. Only the region surrounding the cut is reconstructed, where additional processing is needed to obtain a clean, style-consistent boundary. Using the graph extracted in the previous step, we locate the component to remove from its structure, which lets us find the same component across styles (a). As seen in Fig. (b), simply removing the red branch can leave bulges where it connects to the remaining blue branches. We therefore trim these regions and reconnect the remaining blue branches. We then separate the pixels belonging to the removed region from those that should remain (c). This produces a pixel removal mask, which we convert to a smooth vector representation (d).Additional reconstruction steps are described in the appendix. The final removal result is shown in (e).

6

6

Merging.

Fig.  illustrates the process. We begin with two glyphs from the same style: a (a) and a (b), and aim to combine them into a single coherent glyph. As in component removal, we perform the edit in the medial-axis representation and reconstruct the result in the SVG domain. Using the graphs extracted in the previous step, we identify where the guest should connect to the host based on their structural attributes. The process starts by randomly generating a candidate merging recipe, combining a set of simple augmentations, such as mirroring, rotation, and scaling, with a pair of connection points selected from the guest and host graphs, shown as red points in (c,d). To assess the result produced by the recipe, we apply the augmentations and connect the glyphs at the selected points. We approve only recipes that produce a clean, coherent shape (e). A merging recipe is retained only if it succeeds across a minimum number of styles. Additional implementation details are provided in the appendix. The final merging result is shown in (f).

Geometry reinforcement.

The few style examples also share a limited family of geometries, so the

Style LoRA may still tie the learned style to those geometries despite

UGL’s structural guidance. To preserve open-form transfer, we mix geometry-enriched

sketch-glyph pairs into its training batches, shown by the connection from

3.4

After training, we apply UGL and the selected Style LoRA jointly to the base diffusion model to map structural sketches to styled outputs (Fig. ).

To control geometry adherence and style strength separately, we adopt dual classifier-free guidance following InstructPix2Pix .

During training, the structural sketch, the style caption, or both are dropped to their null conditions, so a single network learns all four conditioning combinations.

During sampling, we combine three forward passes using two CFG coefficients to obtain separate geometry and style guidance strengths, balancing adherence to the input sketch geometry vs. the target style.

Appendix  provides the guidance formulation and implementation details.

4.1

The training data for the universal geometry LoRA (UGL) is produced by the geometry enrichment engine (GEE) from $80$ base glyphs (Latin letters, Latin Extended letters, and digits) shared across $16$ fonts. Applying $6{,}000$ random recipes yields $42{,}705$ sketch–glyph pairs, on which UGL is trained once (Appendix ). Each style is represented by a small exemplar set with manually drawn structural sketches. We hold out six examples per style for evaluation and train the Style LoRA on the remainder, yielding roughly 20–70 sketch–exemplar pairs per style. During Style LoRA training, $10\%$ of each batch is replayed from the UGL training pairs using their original style-free captions, helping preserve the learned geometry prior while adapting to style. For evaluation, we use a benchmark of $50$ curated sketches per style category (fonts and pictograms). To analyze how well our method and the baselines generalize, the sketches span the in-, near-, and out-of-domain tiers defined above. We evaluate across twelve styles, and for each style all methods receive the same sketches and style references.

What is instead needed is a training distribution with fewer geometric correlations, preventing the model from capturing a specific shape identity.

This is solved by our second technical contribution (GEE Sec. ).

The GEE’s immense augmentation strategy forces the geometry model to rely on the supplied structure rather than recognizing a known geometry.

With this enriched corpus, completing our full method, the out-of-domain score rises to $0.94$ ( in Table ), with a geometry factor of $0.97$ and style within 3% of the ceiling, and the characteristic substitutions largely disappear.

5

We introduced Open-Form Geometric Style Transfer, where a geometric style

learned from one family of shapes is applied to structures well beyond that

family. We showed that learning geometric style requires separating how a shape

is realized from the particular geometry on which that style is observed.

However, . To transfer a

geometric language to unseen forms, the geometry component must itself be

universal.disentanglement is necessary but not sufficient

These findings suggest an asymmetric view of geometry and style. Geometry

should be learned broadly, across a large and diverse space of structures, and

can be learned once as a reusable capability. Style, in contrast, can be learned

from a much narrower collection of examples and specialized independently.

Our Universal Geometry LoRA and Style LoRA instantiate this separation, while

GEE provides the geometric diversity needed to make the former universal.

As with many fine-tuned generative models, some challenges remain. Complex

structures can expose a tradeoff between geometric and stylistic fidelity, while

strong or recurring stylistic elements can occasionally interfere with the target

structure or become overemphasized. Improving this separation, particularly for

increasingly complex geometries and styles, is an interesting direction for

future work.

We believe this principle may extend beyond geometric style transfer, enabling

learned visual languages to be applied outside the domains in which they were

observed.

Appendix A

Sec.  compares against font-generation models and general-purpose image generators. Here we include additional comparisons with three recent methods that are particularly relevant to our setting. B-LoRA  and ZipLoRA , like ours, use low-rank adapters to separate what is depicted from how it is rendered, while Abstraction in Style (AiS)  explicitly models structural abstraction as part of stylization. Fig.  shows the B-LoRA and ZipLoRA results next to ours for the same sketch and style; AiS is discussed separately below.

4

[]

10

24
