19

13

B-LoRA.

B-LoRA leverages LoRA to implicitly separate the style and content of a single image by jointly learning the LoRA weights of two specific SDXL blocks, which can then be used as independent components. We use the official implementation and settings, which we verified by reproducing the authors’ published example. The content adapter is trained on the structural sketch and the style adapter on six training examples of the style, matching the other reference-based baselines. As Fig.  (left) shows, the style block carries only the palette and texture of the style: the geometric style is lost, and the structure of the sketch is replaced by hallucinated, unrelated content, because a thin line drawing provides little reconstruction signal.

13

ZipLoRA.

ZipLoRA merges independently trained style and subject LoRAs by learning per-column merger coefficients that minimize their interference. As no official implementation exists, we implement it on our own backbone, which isolates the merging strategy: the content adapter is our UGL and the style adapter is a Style LoRA trained the UGL, as in the ablation (Sec. ). Both adapters are frozen and only the coefficients are optimized, with the paper’s hyperparameters. With all coefficients at one, the two adapters are simply added, which is exactly the configuration of our ablation study; sampling uses its sketches, prompts, seeds and guidance. The learned coefficients scale down both adapters, averaging for the UGL and for the Style LoRA across the three styles. As Fig.  (right) shows, the result follows the sketch, but the conflict between structure and style remains, only in a milder form: style-specific details such as the pictogram tile and the wedge-shaped terminals of the display font are weakened. Training the Style LoRA with the UGL active, as we do, avoids the conflict altogether.withoutNon-hierarchical

12

Non-hierarchical $0.39$ - $0.48$ $0.24$ - $0.52$

13

AiS is designed specifically for styles in which abstraction extends beyond color and texture to geometric and structural deformation. AiS explicitly separates structural abstraction from visual stylization in two stages: it first transforms the target into an intermediate that reflects the structural tendencies of the reference style, and then renders this proxy into the final stylized output. Both stages are learned from a small set of visual exemplars through its Visual Analogy Transfer framework. This makes AiS particularly relevant to our setting, as it is one of the few recent methods that explicitly treats structural reinterpretation as part of style transfer.Abstraction in Style (AiS).abstraction proxy

: Figure 14Comparison with AiS. For each framed sketch, the result of AiS  (top) and ours (bottom), for two pictogram styles and a sculptural style.[]

19

Fig.  compares AiS with our method on three styles: two pictogram sets and a sculptural style. We train AiS on the same style references and use the structural sketch as the abstraction target. AiS captures the visual appearance of each style, but on the pictogram styles its outputs do not reliably follow the sketch: across the scripts, strokes are rearranged, omitted, or fused, while the runner pose is only loosely preserved. On the sculptural style, whose exemplars are themselves single continuous strokes, AiS follows the sketch more closely, though it renders every glyph as one uniform tube. This reflects AiS’s design: its abstraction proxy follows structural tendencies learned from the references rather than the geometry of a specific target. Our method follows each sketch closely while preserving the same style traits, including the tile deformation and stroke bands of the orange set.

14

Appendix B

Our generator is conditioned on two inputs: a sketch image $c_{I}$ of the target

geometry and a text caption $c_{T}$ that carries the style token. Conventional text-conditioned classifier-free guidance (CFG)

has a single scale: it amplifies the caption, while the sketch enters both

branches as an ordinary, unamplified condition, so the strength of the

geometric conditioning cannot be controlled. We therefore adopt the

compositional guidance of InstructPix2Pix , which

separates the two conditions into terms with independent scales.[]

16

[]

3

Null conditions.

CFG requires the network to model the unconditional branches, so during

training each sample is assigned to one of the four conditioning branches

listed in Table : most samples keep both conditions,

one in five drops the style caption, and a small share drops the sketch or

both. The image null $\varnothing_{I}$ is the complete absence of reference

tokens, i.e. the model’s native text-to-image mode, rather than a blank or

noise image, and the text null $\varnothing_{T}$ is the empty prompt.

2

: Table 2Conditioning branches during training and their sampling frequencies.

Guidance.

Let $v_{\theta}(z_{t},c_{I},c_{T})$ denote the predicted velocity at noise level $t$ .

Each sampling step evaluates the unconditional, geometry-conditioned, and

fully conditioned branches of Table  (the style-only

branch is not used at sampling) and combines them as

2

$\displaystyle\tilde{v}_{\theta}(z_{t},c_{I},c_{T})\;=$ $\displaystyle v_{\theta}(z_{t},\varnothing_{I},\varnothing_{T})$ (1) $\displaystyle+s_{I}\big[v_{\theta}(z_{t},c_{I},\varnothing_{T})-v_{\theta}(z_{t},\varnothing_{I},\varnothing_{T})\big]$ $\displaystyle+s_{T}\big[v_{\theta}(z_{t},c_{I},c_{T})-v_{\theta}(z_{t},c_{I},\varnothing_{T})\big].$

The first bracket moves the prediction toward the sketch and is scaled by the

geometry scale $s_{I}$ ; the second adds the contribution of the style token on

top of the sketch and is scaled by the style scale $s_{T}$ . With $s_{I}=s_{T}$ , the two brackets merge into one and the rule becomes

single-scale CFG on the joint condition $(c_{I},c_{T})$ . Values of $s_{I}$ above

$1$ amplify the geometric conditioning independently of the style scale. In practice we use $s_{I}\in[4,6]$ and $s_{T}\in[2,3]$

(Sec. ).

4

: Figure 15The effect of the two guidance scales of Eq. ; $s_{T}$ grows left to right, $s_{I}$ top to bottom. The framed cell is our default operating point. The structural sketch and three reference examples of the style are shown below the grid.

1

Reading the two levers.

Fig.  jointly sweeps the two guidance scales for a

held-out sketch of a “3”.

The grid makes the roles of the two guidance signals and their characteristic

failure modes clear.

15

With no sketch guidance ( $s_{I}=0$ , top row), the sketch is effectively ignored: increasing $s_{T}$ strengthens the style but does not recover the geometry of a “3”. At $s_{I}=1$ , a coherent letterform emerges, but with incorrect geometry, and strong style guidance can further distort its shape.

At the other extreme, strong sketch guidance ( $s_{I}=8$ , bottom row) reliably preserves the geometry but weakens the appearance signal. Increasing $s_{T}$ restores the red tubular style, though gradients and translucency remain muted. The intermediate regime ( $s_{I}=6$ , third row) provides the best balance, recovering the correct “3” while preserving the inflated volume and warm gradient of the exemplars. We therefore choose our operating point in this regime.

Appendix C

This appendix details the construction of the geometry-enriched training corpus

used to train UGL (Sec. ).

3.2

Generating unfamiliar geometries.

We begin with $80$ base glyphs (Latin letters, Latin Extended letters, and digits) shared across $16$ fonts and treat them

as raw geometric material. We expand this initial vocabulary using two simple

structural operations: , which removes a structural

part of a glyph, and , which combines components from two glyphs.

The operations are applied iteratively, allowing newly generated shapes to

participate in subsequent operations. As illustrated in Fig.  of Sec. , the

resulting forms quickly depart from recognizable characters, producing a much

broader distribution of coherent but unfamiliar geometries.component removalmerging

4

3.2

We represent each sequence of structural operations as a . Importantly, a recipe is defined independently of a particular font

and can therefore be applied to corresponding glyphs across multiple fonts.

This produces related geometric constructions realized in different styles.

Beyond increasing geometric diversity, this correspondence is what allows us to

separate the structural information conveyed by a sketch from the style of its

target realization.geometric

recipe

A GEE recipe is a sequence of component-removal and merging operations, with both operations applied one to three times. The output of one step is the input of the next.

Both operations share a first step, graph extraction, described next.

Graph extraction.

Editing a glyph’s outline directly is fragile, since a removal or a join depends on local contour details that differ from style to style. Both operators therefore act on the glyph’s underlying stroke structure, which we extract as a graph; Fig.  of Sec.  illustrates the steps. Starting from the glyph (a), we compute its medial axis transform, which gives the centerline of every stroke together with the radius of the maximal inscribed disk at each point, a local estimate of stroke thickness (b). Treating the axis pixels as a graph, we prune the short branches caused by serifs and other stylistic contour details, retaining the dominant stroke structure (c). Chains of pixels between meeting points are then collapsed into single edges, junctions become nodes and stroke ends become tips (d). Finally, each edge is classified (e). An edge between two junctions is a , and an edge from a junction to a tip is a . Because these roles do not depend on the exact contour of a style, an operation on these graphs can be replayed across styles.

5

3.2

barleg

Structural correspondence.

A recipe names the component it edits, but only within the style on which it was defined. To apply the same edit consistently across styles, we must identify the corresponding component in each style. We represent the selected component using a compact descriptor consisting of its type (bar or leg), the orientation of the chord connecting its endpoints, its midpoint normalized by the glyph’s bounding box, and its arc length relative to glyph size. For each other style, we compare this descriptor with all removable components of the same type and select the component with the smallest weighted distance, provided that the distance is below a matching tolerance. If no component falls below this tolerance, the recipe is not applied to that style. A recipe is retained only if at least a minimum number of styles remain (we configured as 6).

Component removal.

Fig.  of Sec.  illustrates the process step by step. Given the extracted graph, we aim to remove exactly one structural component, such as a leg or bar, while keeping the rest of the outline unchanged and reconstructing the cut in the font’s own terminal style (a). The component to be removed is described by its structural attributes in the graph. In each style, we use these attributes to identify the corresponding component, so that the same component is removed consistently across styles. Removing only the skeleton associated with the component’s edge is not sufficient, since part of its medial axis may also belong to the junction. To avoid leaving an artificial bulge, we remove medial-axis points near the junction within a radius slightly smaller than its inscribed-disk radius (b). This creates a small gap, which we reconnect with a straight stroke that smoothly bridges the surviving branches. We remove pixels belonging to the deleted limb while preserving those shared with surviving strokes. We then fill small junction concavities using the convex hull of the surviving strokes (c). The removal is defined as a pixel mask, but the output must be vectorized. We therefore trace the removal region into a smooth contour and subtract it from the original glyph outline (d). Geometry outside the edited region is preserved exactly. The newly exposed cut boundary has no counterpart in the original glyph. To reconstruct it in a style-consistent way, we search other glyphs from the same font for a matching outline segment, after normalizing for position, scale, and rotation. We then fit this donor segment to the exposed boundary and insert it into the cut region. The result is a glyph with one structural component removed while preserving the original outline wherever possible (e).

6

3.2

Merging.

Fig.  of Sec.  illustrates the process. The connection between the two glyphs is described through structural attributes of their graphs. These attributes identify where the guest should attach to the host and allow the corresponding connection to be found across styles. We begin with two glyphs from the same style: a $g_{a}$ (a) and a $g_{b}$ (b). Our goal is to attach the guest to the host so that they form a single coherent glyph. The merge has two stages. First, we augment the pair,

7

3.2

guesthost

$\hat{g}_{a}=\mathrm{augment}(g_{a}),\quad\hat{g}_{b}=\mathrm{augment}(g_{b}),$

to generate multiple candidate configurations. The host may be mirrored, while the guest may be also rotated and scaled. These choices are randomly sampled when the recipe is created. In Fig. (c), for example, the host is unchanged while the guest is mirrored and rotated by $270^{\circ}$ . We then merge the augmented pair,

7

$\mathrm{merge}(\hat{g}_{a},\hat{g}_{b}).$

On the guest, the connection is anchored at a stroke end facing the host, marked by the red dot in Fig. (c). On the host, we select the stroke end facing the guest; if none exists, we use the nearest skeleton point (Fig. (d)). The guest is then translated so that the two connection points align. We keep only merges that form a coherent single shape, with a localized overlap at the junction and no narrow gaps or small enclosed holes, as shown in Fig. (e). A merge recipe is retained only if it succeeds across a minimum number of styles, ensuring that the structural relation transfers consistently. Small fragments extending beyond the seam are removed to produce the final glyph, as shown in Fig. (f).

7

7

7

7

Style-suppressed structural sketches.

For each generated glyph, we extract a structural sketch from its medial axis.

A raw medial axis, however, can retain local characteristics of the font from

which it was extracted, allowing the conditioning sketch to inadvertently

reveal style. We therefore simplify the extracted structure by pruning small

branches associated with local stylistic details and approximating the

remaining structure with a limited set of Bézier curves. During training, we

additionally apply random modifications to these curves. Together, these

operations preserve the dominant structure while making residual stylistic

cues unreliable.

We now describe the style-suppressing operations in more detail.

We first remove branches that are more likely to arise from outline decoration than from genuine stroke structure. Pruning is defined relative to the local stroke width rather than by an absolute length threshold. In an initial pass, branches shorter than $0.4$ stroke widths are removed. This suppresses small decorative spurs without systematically eliminating genuinely short structural components. Serifs require separate treatment. At a serif terminal, the medial axis often splits into two short branches on opposite sides of the stroke. Removing either branch independently would shorten the stroke rather than remove only its decoration. We distinguish such serif pairs from genuine bifurcations using the line segment joining the two branch tips. If this segment lies entirely inside the glyph, the branches are treated as the two prongs of a serif. If it exits the glyph, as between the upper arms of a , the branches are treated as genuine structure and retained. A detected serif pair is replaced by a single branch between the two prongs, preserving the full stroke extent while discarding the terminal shape. In our fonts, serif branches span at most approximately one stroke width, whereas genuine structural limbs typically span two to five stroke widths. We therefore merge a pair only when both branches are shorter than $1.5$ stroke widths. A final pruning pass removes branches shorter than $0.9$ stroke widths, except where such a branch independently captures a substantial part of the glyph structure.Pruning.Y

We next approximate the pruned medial axis with a limited number of cubic Bézier curves. This sparse representation acts as an explicit information bottleneck rather than merely a compact encoding. A limited number of smooth curves can preserve the coarse glyph geometry, including stroke paths, curvature, and connectivity, while lacking the capacity to reproduce fine stylistic irregularities inherited from the original outline. Curve fitting is performed adaptively. The axis is initially represented by a single cubic Bézier curve and is subdivided at the point of maximum fitting error only when needed. Capacity is therefore allocated preferentially to regions that require additional geometric detail. Across our data, a glyph is represented by approximately ten curves on average and by at most 12. If this capacity is exceeded, the least significant cues are discarded as intended. The subdivision tolerance is expressed relative to stroke thickness. Because the medial axis is defined by its distance to the glyph boundary, constraining the fitting error in this way keeps the approximation geometrically consistent with the glyph interior. The resulting representation is deliberately lossy while remaining faithful to the underlying stroke geometry.Representational bottleneck.

Although pruning and curve compression remove much of the stylistic information, they cannot guarantee complete invariance. A sufficiently expressive model may still exploit residual correlations between the conditioning sketch and the target style. We therefore introduce two training-time mechanisms in UGL to make such residual information unreliable.

During training, each conditioning stroke is randomly perturbed while the corresponding target glyph remains unchanged. The model therefore does not observe a single exact skeleton as the unique conditioning representation of a target. Large-scale structure is preserved, while small local details become unreliable as predictive features. The curve representation allows us to perturb strokes structurally rather than at the pixel level. We deform the interior of each curve while keeping its endpoints fixed, preserving junctions and overall connectivity. Perturbation magnitude is scaled by curve length and correlated along the stroke, causing the stroke to bend smoothly as a whole rather than introducing high-frequency local noise. Each interior control point is displaced by a Gaussian whose standard deviation is a fraction of the curve’s chord length, capped at twice that deviation so that a curve cannot fold back on itself. We resample this fraction uniformly for every sample at every epoch, from $[0.10,0.20]$ when training UGL and from $[0.03,0.08]$ when training a Style LoRA (Table ), so the model sees a range of sketch precision rather than one fixed noise level.Perturbation during training.

3

Cross-style pairing.

To further prevent the sketch from serving as a style condition, we exploit

the cross-font correspondence provided by the geometric recipes. Rather than

always pairing a target glyph with its own extracted sketch, we can condition

it on a sketch extracted from another font generated by the same recipe.

Although their precise medial axes may differ, the sketch and target share the

same underlying construction while belonging to different styles. This

cross-style pairing discourages UGL from using the conditioning sketch to infer

the target style.

Together, geometry enrichment, style suppression, and cross-style pairing

produce a broad training distribution in which structural sketches primarily

communicate geometry rather than shape identity or style. Training UGL on this

corpus encourages it to follow the supplied structure, providing the universal

geometry prior required for open-form transfer.

Appendix D

Both adapters are LoRA modules  on the attention projections of the FLUX.2-klein-base-4B transformer  ( $80$ linear layers); the backbone, the VAE and the Qwen3 text encoder stay frozen, the text encoder in 8-bit. UGL uses rank $192$ with $\alpha=192$ ; every Style LoRA uses rank $32$ with $\alpha=32$ and is trained with UGL attached as a frozen adapter, never merged. Both stages use AdamW-8bit (learning rate $10^{-4}$ , constant after a linear warm-up, $\beta=(0.9,0.999)$ , weight decay $0.01$ , $\epsilon=10^{-6}$ ), an EMA of the adapter weights with decay $0.99$ , gradient checkpointing, and a flow-matching objective at $256\times 256$ for both the target and the sketch condition. Adapter weights are stored in fp16. Table  lists the per-stage settings.[]

17

[]

2

3

: Table 3Training settings of the two stages.

Appendix E

: Figure 16Sculptural and decorative styles on pose and glyph sketches. Each row is one structural sketch (left): four pose sketches (top) and five glyph sketches (bottom); each column is one style, shown by three reference examples at the top.

: Figure 17Additional results. Each row shows three examples of a style (left) and our results for unseen structural sketches, each shown above its result. The rows cover font and pictogram styles.

: Figure 18Additional sculptural results. Two sculptural styles applied to unseen sketches. Each result is shown under its structural sketch.

Appendix F

We employ a VLM-as-a-Judge evaluation framework to assess generated results in the open-set regimes, where no unique paired ground truth exists: for a target structure outside the style’s own shape family there is no single correct rendering to compare against, so paired metrics such as LPIPS and SSIM are undefined. The judge is asked instead whether the requested is depicted and whether it is realized in the demonstrated .structuregeometric design language

Each judged candidate is presented as a single composite image with labeled panels: a top row of $K=6$ style references, and a bottom row holding the target structural sketch and the candidate. References are drawn only from the style’s training rows, so the judge never sees the ground-truth target of the case it is grading. All panels are rendered at $256\times 256$ on a common canvas, and nothing in the image or the prompt identifies the method that produced the candidate.

We score each candidate rather than in pairs. This has two consequences we rely on: the resulting scalar does not depend on which baselines happen to be included in the comparison, and there is no left–right position bias to mitigate. To remove the remaining ordering effect, the six style references are shuffled per case with a fixed per-case permutation. The judge is instructed to return a single JSON object conforming to a strict response schema, which prevents the answer from drifting into prose and bounds the output length.absolutely

The response to the example query illustrates the two axes being scored independently. Geometry is

$4$ rather than $5$ because the judge locates two nameable departures from the

sketch before scoring it: the rider is given the head the sketch leaves

implicit, and the bicycle frame is redrawn cleaner than the tangle of strokes

it was traced from. Style is $4$ because the candidate carries the references’

badge, weight and figure convention onto a sport none of them shows, while

stopping short of being mistaken for one of them. Both flags are false: the

candidate reproduces no shown reference, and it is not the sketch passed

through unstyled.

F.1

We use the same judge configuration for the entire evaluation: all reported numbers come from gemini-3.1-pro-preview with a structured response schema and medium media resolution. Each candidate is judged in a single pass.

Scores are aggregated hierarchically, matching the rest of our protocol: samples within a case, cases within a style, then styles weighted equally.

Appendix G

G.1

We complement the VLM-as-a-Judge evaluation with a human preference study. Unlike the judge, which scores each candidate , the study is : participants see two results for the same input and indicate which one is better. Relative judgments are easier for non-expert participants to make consistently than absolute ratings, and they directly answer the question of interest, namely whether our results are preferred over those of each baseline.absolutelypairwise

Each question is presented as a single composite image with labeled panels: a top row with the style references and the structural sketch, and a bottom row with two results, A and B. One result is ours and the other is produced by a baseline, both generated for the same style and the same sketch. All panels, including the two results, are rendered at the same size on a common canvas, so that the native output resolution of a method is not revealed, and nothing in the image or the text identifies the method behind a result.

The study contains $12$ questions: three for each of the four baselines (MX-Font, FontDiffuser, Gemini, and GPT-Image), each on a different style, covering black-and-white fonts, decorative fonts, and pictogram styles. The sketches span held-out glyphs, non-Latin glyphs, human poses, and symbols. For each question, participants answer three multiple-choice items, on style, structure, and overall preference, each with the options , , and .Result AResult BAbout the same

To control for ordering and position effects, we prepare four editions of the questionnaire. Each edition shuffles the order of the questions, never placing the same baseline in two consecutive questions, and randomizes which side shows our result. Within every edition our result appears as A in exactly half of the questions, and the side assignment is mirrored between editions, so that any preference for a side cancels out. Participants reach the study through a single link that assigns them to one of the editions at random. Responses are anonymous, and each participant answers one edition.

The example illustrates why the two axes are asked separately. Both results depict a recognizable treble clef, so the structure item mainly asks whether the particular structure of the sketch is preserved, such as its proportions, the spiral around the stem, and the hooked tail. The style item asks something different: whether the result carries the distinctive traits of the references, such as the rounded, asymmetric blue tile, the bold white strokes with rounded ends, and the thin parallel lines that accompany the figures, rather than merely sharing their colors.

Before the first question, participants are shown one worked example in the same layout, with the intended answers marked and a one-line explanation of each. Its two results are not method outputs: one is a letter of a reference font and the other is the same letter in a plain serif font, so the intended answers are unambiguous and do not bias participants toward any method.

G.2

For each baseline and each of the three items, we report the percentage of votes that prefer our result, prefer the baseline’s result, or rate the two as about the same, pooled over participants, editions, and the three questions of that baseline. Significance is assessed with a two-sided exact binomial test against $50\%$ on the decisive votes, i.e., after discarding answers. In total, 32 participants completed the study.About the same

要点：

Abstract

A geometric style learned from one family of shapes is typically applied to

new shapes from the same family. We consider a more challenging setting:

learning the geometric design language of a stylized Latin alphabet and

applying it to new forms, from Greek glyphs to entirely different structures

such as human poses. We introduce Open-Form Geometric Style Transfer,

where the forms to which a learned geometric style can be applied are not

restricted to the shape family in which that style was observed.

This setting is deceptively challenging: the difficulty is not merely learning

a style, but learning the style without learning the shape family in which it

was observed. We represent target forms by structural sketches and disentangle

structural adherence from style realization using a Geometry LoRA and a

style-specific LoRA. Critically, open-form transfer requires the Geometry LoRA

to be universal. To achieve this, we devise a geometry-enrichment

strategy that constructs a large and purposefully diverse collection of

synthetic structural sketches spanning a broad range of unfamiliar geometries.

Our experiments and ablations demonstrate the importance of both

disentanglement and this universal geometry prior, enabling geometric styles

learned from glyphs, pictograms, and other shape families to be transferred to

substantially different, unseen forms.

Style transfer is a long-standing and intriguing problem in visual computing:

given examples that contain both content and style, the goal is to capture the

essence of the style, separate it from the particular content on which it is

observed, and apply it to new content. The separation of style from content has

been studied for decades , and has more

recently become central to neural style transfer and generative

modeling .

In this work, we focus on , where style governs how an

underlying structure is geometrically realized. A canonical example is a font:

different glyphs have different structures, yet their geometric realizations

Existing approaches typically learn and apply such styles within a shared domain: a style observed on letters is transferred to other letters, and a style observed on human figures is applied to other human figures.

We remove this restriction and consider transferring a geometric style to an .

As illustrated in Figure , a style learned from a

Latin alphabet may be applied to Greek glyphs, or more radically, to human

poses; conversely, a geometric style learned from pictograms may be applied to

glyphs. We call this new setting ,

where the forms to which a learned geometric style can be applied are not

restricted to the shape family in which that style was observed. We focus on

forms whose underlying structure can be represented by a sparse structural

sketch, which serves as the geometry to be styled.[, , ]

The open-form setting, illustrated in Figure , is deceptively challenging.

The difficulty is not simply learning a style, but .

Existing font-generation methods can transfer styles to unseen

glyphs , and some explicitly

separate character content from style. However, their structural component is

A straightforward LoRA trained on a limited styled shape family learns an entangled

4.2

Our approach addresses this entanglement by separating .

A Geometry LoRA is responsible for faithfully following the target structural sketch serving as a geometric-adherence prior, while a Style LoRA learns how that geometry should be realized in the desired style.

Accordingly, the Geometry LoRA must be : generalize across the vast universe of styles, responding to structure rather than shape identity or residual stylistic cues.

Acquiring such a universal geometry prior is itself non-trivial: a corpus of ordinary glyphs provides a limited and familiar geometry vocabulary, allowing the model to recognize known shapes rather than truly follow the input structure.

We therefore introduce a geometry-enrichment strategy (GEE Sec. ) that systematically leverages SVG font data to construct a large collection of unfamiliar synthetic geometries, untangled from their source style.

This strategy proves vital for successfully learning a universal geometry LoRA.structural adherence from style realizationuniversal

Our contributions are threefold:

•

We introduce , where a geometric style learned from one shape domain is applied to universally arbitrary forms.Open-Form Geometric Stylization

•

We show that open-form stylization requires separating structural adherence from style realization.

•

Finally, we introduce a geometry-enrichment strategy for constructing the broad and diverse structural training distribution needed to acquire this universal prior.

We evaluate these ideas through controlled ablations and increasingly challenging transfers, from held-out glyphs and cross-alphabet transfer to unrelated forms such as human poses, demonstrating that a geometric style can be extended well beyond the family of shapes on which it was observed.

Our work builds on three lines of research: the separation of style and

content, font and glyph style transfer, and structurally conditioned

generation. Below we review each line, clarify how our notion of

style relates to them, and how they relate to our approach.geometric

2.1

Our work is closely connected to the seminal work of Tenenbaum and

Freeman  on separating style and content.

Using bilinear models, they showed that a common style can be inferred from

multiple observations and applied to new content. Particularly relevant to

our setting is their treatment of fonts, where style is shared across

different letters and can be used to synthesize previously unseen characters.

This provides an early and elegant formulation of style as a factor that can

be learned across a family of shapes and separated from their individual

geometry. Our work builds on this perspective, but considers an open-form

setting in which the new content need not belong to the same family: a

geometric style learned from one alphabet may be applied to another alphabet,

or even to a different class of structures such as human poses.[]

25

More broadly, style transfer has a long history in computer vision and

graphics, with much of the literature focusing on style as visual appearance.

Early example-based methods  synthesized and transferred texture by sampling local neighborhoods or patches

from example images.

later introduced neural style transfer, demonstrating that content and artistic style can be represented separately within a deep network and recombined to render new content in the appearance of a reference image. Recent diffusion-based methods

such as StyleAligned , B-LoRA ,

InstantStyle , and ZipLoRA

substantially extend the quality and flexibility of reference-based style

transfer. Across these works, style is predominantly expressed through visual

appearance, including texture, color, material, brushwork, and shading.[, ]

Our notion of is different. Here, style determines how

an underlying structure is geometrically realized: how curves are formed,

junctions are connected, strokes vary in thickness, gaps are introduced, and

structural elements terminate or interact. Such a style is naturally revealed

by a of related shapes rather than by a single reference image.

Glyphs provide a particularly clean instance of this setting: individual

characters differ in structure, while together they reveal a consistent

geometric design language. Related notions of transferring geometric style

across shapes were also explored in early work by .

More recently, geometric stylization has also been explored for 3D shapes  .geometric styleset[]

2.2

Modern font-generation methods provide the closest setting to our work, as

they explicitly transfer a common style across glyphs with different

structures. FontDiffuser  formulates one-shot

diffusion-based font generation, using multi-scale content aggregation to

preserve character structure and contrastive learning to capture style. It

generalizes to unseen characters and also demonstrates cross-lingual

generation. MX-Font  addresses few-shot font generation using multiple

localized experts that disentangle content and style while capturing different local style characteristics.

It also demonstrates cross-lingual generalization to unseen writing systems.

VecFusion  approaches font generation in the

vector domain, explicitly modeling glyph topology, paths, and Bézier control

points, and supports applications including glyph completion and few-shot

style transfer. Skeleton-Guided Diffusion  is particularly

related to our structural representation, using character skeletons to guide

diffusion and preserve structure during font generation. StrokeStyles  decomposes font glyphs into

meaningful stroke structures and uses this representation for consistent

geometric stylization across characters.[]

FLUX-Font  is particularly close to our work architecturally.

It adapts a pre-trained diffusion transformer using separate LoRA

modules  for glyph content and style, explicitly separating

the two factors rather than learning them through a single adapter. Our method

shares this general motivation, but separates structural adherence from style

realization hierarchically: a universal Geometry LoRA is first trained to

follow arbitrary structural sketches, and each Style LoRA is subsequently

learned with this geometry prior active and fixed.[]

Despite their differences, these methods share an important restriction:

their structural representations and learned priors are designed for the

glyph domain. Their goal is to generalize from observed characters to other

characters, possibly across writing systems, but the target remains a glyph.

Open-form transfer removes this restriction. The target structural sketch may

describe a character, a pictogram, a human pose, or another unrelated form.

Consequently, separating content from style within the font domain is not

sufficient; the geometry-following component must itself generalize beyond

the shape family in which the style was observed.

Spatially conditioned diffusion models provide a complementary line of related

work. ControlNet  and

T2I-Adapter  condition pre-trained text-to-image models

on spatial signals such as edges, depth, segmentation, poses, and sketches,

Our problem, however, is not spatial conditioning alone. The structural sketch

specifies a form whose geometric realization must change according to a style

learned from a separate set of examples. The challenge is therefore to preserve

the target structure while preventing the learned style from carrying with it

the shape distribution on which that style was observed. We use structural

conditioning as a means toward this goal, learning a universal geometry prior

that remains fixed while different geometric styles are acquired. At inference,

we treat structure and style as independent conditions and adopt the

dual-conditioning guidance of InstructPix2Pix , allowing

their strengths to be controlled separately.[]

3.1

The purpose of UGL is to fine-tune a text-to-image diffusion model to follow open-form geometries (i.e. sketches).

Starting from a pre-trained text-to-image diffusion transformer (DiT), we fit LoRA parameters on the DiT’s weights using sketch-glyph data pairs constructed by GEE.

The rich, diverse synthetic data produced by the GEE allows us to select a high LoRA rank without overfitting, giving the UGL significant learning capacity.

After this one-time training, we freeze UGL and share it across all Style LoRAs, providing a common geometry prior beyond each style’s specific training examples.

: Figure 4GEE overview.

(a) Geometry generation recursively merges and removes glyph components in font $i$ , recording a font-independent recipe.

(b) Reapplying the recipe to font $j$ produces the same underlying construction in another style.

(c) Skeleton extraction yields a conditioning sketch from $j$ , which is paired with the target glyph from $i$ .

Fonts are a natural starting point for data augmentation: they are available in a large variety of styles, and more importantly, their SVG native representation enables truly geometric augmentations compared to raster form.

However, using real font glyphs directly presents two limitations. First, available fonts cover a relatively narrow set of languages and therefore a limited vocabulary of structures, which may hinder generalization to unseen scripts and, even more, to out-of-domain forms such as symbols or pictograms.

Second, the geometry of a glyph is itself tied to the style of its source font, so the conditioning structure may carry unwanted stylistic cues.

To address both issues, we introduce : a data-generation procedure that expands the range of training geometries while reducing their dependence on font style.

To increase structural diversity, GEE takes advantage of the native SVG parameterization of fonts and constructs novel geometric forms by applying random sequences of geometric edits.

We refer to each such sequence as a .

A recipe may, for example, repeatedly remove or merge SVG parts, producing coherent but unfamiliar structures (Fig. (a)).

Recipes also allow the GEE to address the second problem. A recipe applied to one font can be re-applied to matching letters from another font, producing paired data with but (Fig. (b)).

During UGL training, we form mixed pairs by taking the conditioning sketch from one font and the target from another font to which the same recipe was applied (Fig. (c)).

The sketch and target therefore remain aligned in structure while differing in style, encouraging UGL to learn the supplied geometry independently of its stylistic realization.GEEgeometric recipe

We next describe the editing primitives that drive the geometry enrichment process, first motivating their design and then outlining each one (full details in Appendix ).

C

Structural editing primitives.

A glyph’s structure is determined by how its strokes relate: which strokes meet and where they branch or terminate. Smooth transformations such as warping, shearing, or scaling can change a glyph’s appearance, but they do not create new structural relations between its strokes. To generate genuinely new structures, we therefore need operations that modify these relations. We propose two elementary edits: component removal and merging. This builds on a broader principle: deleting and recombining existing parts can generate meaningful structural variation , and related cut-based augmentations have been shown to improve recognition performance . Repeating these edits produces novel structural relations beyond those found in existing alphabets.[]

11

[, ]

6

30

To make both edits transferable across fonts, we edit the glyph’s structure rather than its contour, which is more sensitive to stylistic variation. We therefore represent each glyph as a graph, with strokes as edges and intersections and endpoints as nodes. A recipe is then expressed as a sequence of graph edits, with component removal and merging each applied one to three times. The edit type and its structural parameters are sampled when the recipe is created, specifying which component to remove or where components should connect. Because the edits are defined structurally, the same recipe can be replayed across fonts to produce the same underlying structure in multiple styles. Structural correspondence across styles is further explained in Appendix .

C

Graph extraction.

We represent each glyph as a graph that captures its dominant stroke structure (Fig. ). Starting from the glyph (a), we compute its medial axis together with the local inscribed-disk radius, which provides an estimate of stroke thickness (b). We prune short branches caused by serifs and other stylistic details, leaving the main stroke structure (c). Pixel chains are then collapsed into edges, with junctions and stroke endpoints represented as nod es (d). Finally, we classify each edge by its structural role: an edge between two junctions is a , while an edge from a junction to an endpoint is a (e).

3.2

Component removal.

Fig.  illustrates the process. Our strategy is to perform the edit in the medial-axis representation and then reconstruct the glyph back in the SVG domain. Outline points unrelated to the removed component are preserved exactly. Only the region surrounding the cut is reconstructed, where additional processing is needed to obtain a clean, style-consistent boundary. Using the graph extracted in the previous step, we locate the component to remove from its structure, which lets us find the same component across styles (a). As seen in Fig. (b), simply removing the red branch can leave bulges where it connects to the remaining blue branches. We therefore trim these regions and reconnect the remaining blue branches. We then separate the pixels belonging to the removed region from those that should remain (c). This produces a pixel removal mask, which we convert to a smooth vector representation (d).Additional reconstruction steps are described in the appendix. The final removal result is shown in (e).

6

Merging.

Fig.  illustrates the process. We begin with two glyphs from the same style: a (a) and a (b), and aim to combine them into a single coherent glyph. As in component removal, we perform the edit in the medial-axis representation and reconstruct the result in the SVG domain. Using the graphs extracted in the previous step, we identify where the guest should connect to the host based on their structural attributes. The process starts by randomly generating a candidate merging recipe, combining a set of simple augmentations, such as mirroring, rotation, and scaling, with a pair of connection points selected from the guest and host graphs, shown as red points in (c,d). To assess the result produced by the recipe, we apply the augmentations and connect the glyphs at the selected points. We approve only recipes that produce a clean, coherent shape (e). A merging recipe is retained only if it succeeds across a minimum number of styles. Additional implementation details are provided in the appendix. The final merging result is shown in (f).

Geometry reinforcement.

The few style examples also share a limited family of geometries, so the

Style LoRA may still tie the learned style to those geometries despite

UGL’s structural guidance. To preserve open-form transfer, we mix geometry-enriched

sketch-glyph pairs into its training batches, shown by the connection from

GEE to Style LoRA training in Fig. . These pairs expose the

model to geometries outside the target style’s examples throughout adaptation,

reinforcing its ability to follow new structures while learning the style.

3.4

After training, we apply UGL and the selected Style LoRA jointly to the base diffusion model to map structural sketches to styled outputs (Fig. ).

To control geometry adherence and style strength separately, we adopt dual classifier-free guidance following InstructPix2Pix .

During training, the structural sketch, the style caption, or both are dropped to their null conditions, so a single network learns all four conditioning combinations.

During sampling, we combine three forward passes using two CFG coefficients to obtain separate geometry and style guidance strengths, balancing adherence to the input sketch geometry vs. the target style.

Appendix  provides the guidance formulation and implementation details.

4.1

The training data for the universal geometry LoRA (UGL) is produced by the geometry enrichment engine (GEE) from $80$ base glyphs (Latin letters, Latin Extended letters, and digits) shared across $16$ fonts. Applying $6{,}000$ random recipes yields $42{,}705$ sketch–glyph pairs, on which UGL is trained once (Appendix ). Each style is represented by a small exemplar set with manually drawn structural sketches. We hold out six examples per style for evaluation and train the Style LoRA on the remainder, yielding roughly 20–70 sketch–exemplar pairs per style. During Style LoRA training, $10\%$ of each batch is replayed from the UGL training pairs using their original style-free captions, helping preserve the learned geometry prior while adapting to style. For evaluation, we use a benchmark of $50$ curated sketches per style category (fonts and pictograms). To analyze how well our method and the baselines generalize, the sketches span the in-, near-, and out-of-domain tiers defined above. We evaluate across twelve styles, and for each style all methods receive the same sketches and style references.

We tailored our main technical contributions, the universal geometry LoRA (UGL) and the geometry enrichment engine (GEE), to open-form generalization and the challenges of fine-tuning large models.

In this section, we demonstrate the necessity of both components; later in Table  we also present a quantitative evaluation that supports each claim.

While this formulation preserves both the target geometry and the learned style on held-out examples from the , it does not generalize to structures. Instead, the model takes a shortcut by producing results resembling the closest training example, best seen in the bottom rows of Fig.  (), where the model outputs styled examples similar to English alphabet letters rather than the desired geometry.

A natural hypothesis for this phenomenon is that each geometry is observed only through a single realization in the target style, providing too little variation to disentangle the geometry and style.

An intuitive solution is to train a geometry adapter on ordinary glyphs drawn from a broad corpus of fonts, using the same training settings as UGL but without employing GEE, and then train the same Style LoRAs on top of it.

Unfortunately, the failure persisted, now in an even more revealing form.

The UGL is even more biased towards common geometries from the train set, e.g. alphabet letters, as again seen in the bottom row of the section of Fig .

What is instead needed is a training distribution with fewer geometric correlations, preventing the model from capturing a specific shape identity.

This is solved by our second technical contribution (GEE Sec. ).

The GEE’s immense augmentation strategy forces the geometry model to rely on the supplied structure rather than recognizing a known geometry.

With this enriched corpus, completing our full method, the out-of-domain score rises to $0.94$ ( in Table ), with a geometry factor of $0.97$ and style within 3% of the ceiling, and the characteristic substitutions largely disappear.

5

We introduced Open-Form Geometric Style Transfer, where a geometric style

learned from one family of shapes is applied to structures well beyond that

family. We showed that learning geometric style requires separating how a shape

is realized from the particular geometry on which that style is observed.

However, . To transfer a

geometric language to unseen forms, the geometry component must itself be

universal.disentanglement is necessary but not sufficient

These findings suggest an asymmetric view of geometry and style. Geometry

should be learned broadly, across a large and diverse space of structures, and

can be learned once as a reusable capability. Style, in contrast, can be learned

from a much narrower collection of examples and specialized independently.

Our Universal Geometry LoRA and Style LoRA instantiate this separation, while

GEE provides the geometric diversity needed to make the former universal.

As with many fine-tuned generative models, some challenges remain. Complex

structures can expose a tradeoff between geometric and stylistic fidelity, while

strong or recurring stylistic elements can occasionally interfere with the target

structure or become overemphasized. Improving this separation, particularly for

increasingly complex geometries and styles, is an interesting direction for

future work.

We believe this principle may extend beyond geometric style transfer, enabling

learned visual languages to be applied outside the domains in which they were

observed.

B-LoRA.

B-LoRA leverages LoRA to implicitly separate the style and content of a single image by jointly learning the LoRA weights of two specific SDXL blocks, which can then be used as independent components. We use the official implementation and settings, which we verified by reproducing the authors’ published example. The content adapter is trained on the structural sketch and the style adapter on six training examples of the style, matching the other reference-based baselines. As Fig.  (left) shows, the style block carries only the palette and texture of the style: the geometric style is lost, and the structure of the sketch is replaced by hallucinated, unrelated content, because a thin line drawing provides little reconstruction signal.

13

ZipLoRA.

ZipLoRA merges independently trained style and subject LoRAs by learning per-column merger coefficients that minimize their interference. As no official implementation exists, we implement it on our own backbone, which isolates the merging strategy: the content adapter is our UGL and the style adapter is a Style LoRA trained the UGL, as in the ablation (Sec. ). Both adapters are frozen and only the coefficients are optimized, with the paper’s hyperparameters. With all coefficients at one, the two adapters are simply added, which is exactly the configuration of our ablation study; sampling uses its sketches, prompts, seeds and guidance. The learned coefficients scale down both adapters, averaging for the UGL and for the Style LoRA across the three styles. As Fig.  (right) shows, the result follows the sketch, but the conflict between structure and style remains, only in a milder form: style-specific details such as the pictogram tile and the wedge-shaped terminals of the display font are weakened. Training the Style LoRA with the UGL active, as we do, avoids the conflict altogether.withoutNon-hierarchical

AiS is designed specifically for styles in which abstraction extends beyond color and texture to geometric and structural deformation. AiS explicitly separates structural abstraction from visual stylization in two stages: it first transforms the target into an intermediate that reflects the structural tendencies of the reference style, and then renders this proxy into the final stylized output. Both stages are learned from a small set of visual exemplars through its Visual Analogy Transfer framework. This makes AiS particularly relevant to our setting, as it is one of the few recent methods that explicitly treats structural reinterpretation as part of style transfer.Abstraction in Style (AiS).abstraction proxy

3.2

Generating unfamiliar geometries.

We begin with $80$ base glyphs (Latin letters, Latin Extended letters, and digits) shared across $16$ fonts and treat them

as raw geometric material. We expand this initial vocabulary using two simple

structural operations: , which removes a structural

part of a glyph, and , which combines components from two glyphs.

The operations are applied iteratively, allowing newly generated shapes to

participate in subsequent operations. As illustrated in Fig.  of Sec. , the

resulting forms quickly depart from recognizable characters, producing a much

broader distribution of coherent but unfamiliar geometries.component removalmerging

3.2

We represent each sequence of structural operations as a . Importantly, a recipe is defined independently of a particular font

and can therefore be applied to corresponding glyphs across multiple fonts.

This produces related geometric constructions realized in different styles.

Beyond increasing geometric diversity, this correspondence is what allows us to

separate the structural information conveyed by a sketch from the style of its

target realization.geometric

recipe

A GEE recipe is a sequence of component-removal and merging operations, with both operations applied one to three times. The output of one step is the input of the next.

Both operations share a first step, graph extraction, described next.

Graph extraction.

Editing a glyph’s outline directly is fragile, since a removal or a join depends on local contour details that differ from style to style. Both operators therefore act on the glyph’s underlying stroke structure, which we extract as a graph; Fig.  of Sec.  illustrates the steps. Starting from the glyph (a), we compute its medial axis transform, which gives the centerline of every stroke together with the radius of the maximal inscribed disk at each point, a local estimate of stroke thickness (b). Treating the axis pixels as a graph, we prune the short branches caused by serifs and other stylistic contour details, retaining the dominant stroke structure (c). Chains of pixels between meeting points are then collapsed into single edges, junctions become nodes and stroke ends become tips (d). Finally, each edge is classified (e). An edge between two junctions is a , and an edge from a junction to a tip is a . Because these roles do not depend on the exact contour of a style, an operation on these graphs can be replayed across styles.

5

3.2

barleg

Structural correspondence.

A recipe names the component it edits, but only within the style on which it was defined. To apply the same edit consistently across styles, we must identify the corresponding component in each style. We represent the selected component using a compact descriptor consisting of its type (bar or leg), the orientation of the chord connecting its endpoints, its midpoint normalized by the glyph’s bounding box, and its arc length relative to glyph size. For each other style, we compare this descriptor with all removable components of the same type and select the component with the smallest weighted distance, provided that the distance is below a matching tolerance. If no component falls below this tolerance, the recipe is not applied to that style. A recipe is retained only if at least a minimum number of styles remain (we configured as 6).

Component removal.

Fig.  of Sec.  illustrates the process step by step. Given the extracted graph, we aim to remove exactly one structural component, such as a leg or bar, while keeping the rest of the outline unchanged and reconstructing the cut in the font’s own terminal style (a). The component to be removed is described by its structural attributes in the graph. In each style, we use these attributes to identify the corresponding component, so that the same component is removed consistently across styles. Removing only the skeleton associated with the component’s edge is not sufficient, since part of its medial axis may also belong to the junction. To avoid leaving an artificial bulge, we remove medial-axis points near the junction within a radius slightly smaller than its inscribed-disk radius (b). This creates a small gap, which we reconnect with a straight stroke that smoothly bridges the surviving branches. We remove pixels belonging to the deleted limb while preserving those shared with surviving strokes. We then fill small junction concavities using the convex hull of the surviving strokes (c). The removal is defined as a pixel mask, but the output must be vectorized. We therefore trace the removal region into a smooth contour and subtract it from the original glyph outline (d). Geometry outside the edited region is preserved exactly. The newly exposed cut boundary has no counterpart in the original glyph. To reconstruct it in a style-consistent way, we search other glyphs from the same font for a matching outline segment, after normalizing for position, scale, and rotation. We then fit this donor segment to the exposed boundary and insert it into the cut region. The result is a glyph with one structural component removed while preserving the original outline wherever possible (e).

6

Merging.

Fig.  of Sec.  illustrates the process. The connection between the two glyphs is described through structural attributes of their graphs. These attributes identify where the guest should attach to the host and allow the corresponding connection to be found across styles. We begin with two glyphs from the same style: a $g_{a}$ (a) and a $g_{b}$ (b). Our goal is to attach the guest to the host so that they form a single coherent glyph. The merge has two stages. First, we augment the pair,

In Fig. (c), for example, the host is unchanged while the guest is mirrored and rotated by $270^{\circ}$ . We then merge the augmented pair,

Style-suppressed structural sketches.

For each generated glyph, we extract a structural sketch from its medial axis.

A raw medial axis, however, can retain local characteristics of the font from

which it was extracted, allowing the conditioning sketch to inadvertently

reveal style. We therefore simplify the extracted structure by pruning small

branches associated with local stylistic details and approximating the

remaining structure with a limited set of Bézier curves. During training, we

additionally apply random modifications to these curves. Together, these

operations preserve the dominant structure while making residual stylistic

cues unreliable.

We now describe the style-suppressing operations in more detail.

We first remove branches that are more likely to arise from outline decoration than from genuine stroke structure. Pruning is defined relative to the local stroke width rather than by an absolute length threshold. In an initial pass, branches shorter than $0.4$ stroke widths are removed. This suppresses small decorative spurs without systematically eliminating genuinely short structural components. Serifs require separate treatment. At a serif terminal, the medial axis often splits into two short branches on opposite sides of the stroke. Removing either branch independently would shorten the stroke rather than remove only its decoration. We distinguish such serif pairs from genuine bifurcations using the line segment joining the two branch tips. If this segment lies entirely inside the glyph, the branches are treated as the two prongs of a serif. If it exits the glyph, as between the upper arms of a , the branches are treated as genuine structure and retained. A detected serif pair is replaced by a single branch between the two prongs, preserving the full stroke extent while discarding the terminal shape. In our fonts, serif branches span at most approximately one stroke width, whereas genuine structural limbs typically span two to five stroke widths. We therefore merge a pair only when both branches are shorter than $1.5$ stroke widths. A final pruning pass removes branches shorter than $0.9$ stroke widths, except where such a branch independently captures a substantial part of the glyph structure.Pruning.Y

We next approximate the pruned medial axis with a limited number of cubic Bézier curves. This sparse representation acts as an explicit information bottleneck rather than merely a compact encoding. A limited number of smooth curves can preserve the coarse glyph geometry, including stroke paths, curvature, and connectivity, while lacking the capacity to reproduce fine stylistic irregularities inherited from the original outline. Curve fitting is performed adaptively. The axis is initially represented by a single cubic Bézier curve and is subdivided at the point of maximum fitting error only when needed. Capacity is therefore allocated preferentially to regions that require additional geometric detail. Across our data, a glyph is represented by approximately ten curves on average and by at most 12. If this capacity is exceeded, the least significant cues are discarded as intended. The subdivision tolerance is expressed relative to stroke thickness. Because the medial axis is defined by its distance to the glyph boundary, constraining the fitting error in this way keeps the approximation geometrically consistent with the glyph interior. The resulting representation is deliberately lossy while remaining faithful to the underlying stroke geometry.Representational bottleneck.

Although pruning and curve compression remove much of the stylistic information, they cannot guarantee complete invariance. A sufficiently expressive model may still exploit residual correlations between the conditioning sketch and the target style. We therefore introduce two training-time mechanisms in UGL to make such residual information unreliable.

During training, each conditioning stroke is randomly perturbed while the corresponding target glyph remains unchanged. The model therefore does not observe a single exact skeleton as the unique conditioning representation of a target. Large-scale structure is preserved, while small local details become unreliable as predictive features. The curve representation allows us to perturb strokes structurally rather than at the pixel level. We deform the interior of each curve while keeping its endpoints fixed, preserving junctions and overall connectivity. Perturbation magnitude is scaled by curve length and correlated along the stroke, causing the stroke to bend smoothly as a whole rather than introducing high-frequency local noise. Each interior control point is displaced by a Gaussian whose standard deviation is a fraction of the curve’s chord length, capped at twice that deviation so that a curve cannot fold back on itself. We resample this fraction uniformly for every sample at every epoch, from $[0.10,0.20]$ when training UGL and from $[0.03,0.08]$ when training a Style LoRA (Table ), so the model sees a range of sketch precision rather than one fixed noise level.Perturbation during training.

3

Cross-style pairing.

To further prevent the sketch from serving as a style condition, we exploit

the cross-font correspondence provided by the geometric recipes. Rather than

always pairing a target glyph with its own extracted sketch, we can condition

it on a sketch extracted from another font generated by the same recipe.

Although their precise medial axes may differ, the sketch and target share the

same underlying construction while belonging to different styles. This

cross-style pairing discourages UGL from using the conditioning sketch to infer

the target style.

Together, geometry enrichment, style suppression, and cross-style pairing

produce a broad training distribution in which structural sketches primarily

communicate geometry rather than shape identity or style. Training UGL on this

corpus encourages it to follow the supplied structure, providing the universal

geometry prior required for open-form transfer.

Appendix D

Both adapters are LoRA modules  on the attention projections of the FLUX.2-klein-base-4B transformer  ( $80$ linear layers); the backbone, the VAE and the Qwen3 text encoder stay frozen, the text encoder in 8-bit. UGL uses rank $192$ with $\alpha=192$ ; every Style LoRA uses rank $32$ with $\alpha=32$ and is trained with UGL attached as a frozen adapter, never merged. Both stages use AdamW-8bit (learning rate $10^{-4}$ , constant after a linear warm-up, $\beta=(0.9,0.999)$ , weight decay $0.01$ , $\epsilon=10^{-6}$ ), an EMA of the adapter weights with decay $0.99$ , gradient checkpointing, and a flow-matching objective at $256\times 256$ for both the target and the sketch condition. Adapter weights are stored in fp16. Table  lists the per-stage settings.[]

Appendix F

We employ a VLM-as-a-Judge evaluation framework to assess generated results in the open-set regimes, where no unique paired ground truth exists: for a target structure outside the style’s own shape family there is no single correct rendering to compare against, so paired metrics such as LPIPS and SSIM are undefined. The judge is asked instead whether the requested is depicted and whether it is realized in the demonstrated .structuregeometric design language

Each judged candidate is presented as a single composite image with labeled panels: a top row of $K=6$ style references, and a bottom row holding the target structural sketch and the candidate. References are drawn only from the style’s training rows, so the judge never sees the ground-truth target of the case it is grading. All panels are rendered at $256\times 256$ on a common canvas, and nothing in the image or the prompt identifies the method that produced the candidate.

We score each candidate rather than in pairs. This has two consequences we rely on: the resulting scalar does not depend on which baselines happen to be included in the comparison, and there is no left–right position bias to mitigate. To remove the remaining ordering effect, the six style references are shuffled per case with a fixed per-case permutation. The judge is instructed to return a single JSON object conforming to a strict response schema, which prevents the answer from drifting into prose and bounds the output length.absolutely

The response to the example query illustrates the two axes being scored independently. Geometry is

$4$ rather than $5$ because the judge locates two nameable departures from the

sketch before scoring it: the rider is given the head the sketch leaves

implicit, and the bicycle frame is redrawn cleaner than the tangle of strokes

it was traced from. Style is $4$ because the candidate carries the references’

badge, weight and figure convention onto a sport none of them shows, while

stopping short of being mistaken for one of them. Both flags are false: the

candidate reproduces no shown reference, and it is not the sketch passed

through unstyled.

F.1

We use the same judge configuration for the entire evaluation: all reported numbers come from gemini-3.1-pro-preview with a structured response schema and medium media resolution. Each candidate is judged in a single pass.

Scores are aggregated hierarchically, matching the rest of our protocol: samples within a case, cases within a style, then styles weighted equally.

Appendix G

G.1

We complement the VLM-as-a-Judge evaluation with a human preference study. Unlike the judge, which scores each candidate , the study is : participants see two results for the same input and indicate which one is better. Relative judgments are easier for non-expert participants to make consistently than absolute ratings, and they directly answer the question of interest, namely whether our results are preferred over those of each baseline.absolutelypairwise

Each question is presented as a single composite image with labeled panels: a top row with the style references and the structural sketch, and a bottom row with two results, A and B. One result is ours and the other is produced by a baseline, both generated for the same style and the same sketch. All panels, including the two results, are rendered at the same size on a common canvas, so that the native output resolution of a method is not revealed, and nothing in the image or the text identifies the method behind a result.

The study contains $12$ questions: three for each of the four baselines (MX-Font, FontDiffuser, Gemini, and GPT-Image), each on a different style, covering black-and-white fonts, decorative fonts, and pictogram styles. The sketches span held-out glyphs, non-Latin glyphs, human poses, and symbols. For each question, participants answer three multiple-choice items, on style, structure, and overall preference, each with the options , , and .Result AResult BAbout the same

To control for ordering and position effects, we prepare four editions of the questionnaire. Each edition shuffles the order of the questions, never placing the same baseline in two consecutive questions, and randomizes which side shows our result. Within every edition our result appears as A in exactly half of the questions, and the side assignment is mirrored between editions, so that any preference for a side cancels out. Participants reach the study through a single link that assigns them to one of the editions at random. Responses are anonymous, and each participant answers one edition.

The example illustrates why the two axes are asked separately. Both results depict a recognizable treble clef, so the structure item mainly asks whether the particular structure of the sketch is preserved, such as its proportions, the spiral around the stem, and the hooked tail. The style item asks something different: whether the result carries the distinctive traits of the references, such as the rounded, asymmetric blue tile, the bold white strokes with rounded ends, and the thin parallel lines that accompany the figures, rather than merely sharing their colors.

Before the first question, participants are shown one worked example in the same layout, with the intended answers marked and a one-line explanation of each. Its two results are not method outputs: one is a letter of a reference font and the other is the same letter in a plain serif font, so the intended answers are unambiguous and do not bias participants toward any method.

G.2

For each baseline and each of the three items, we report the percentage of votes that prefer our result, prefer the baseline’s result, or rate the two as about the same, pooled over participants, editions, and the three questions of that baseline. Significance is assessed with a two-sided exact binomial test against $50\%$ on the decisive votes, i.e., after discarding answers. In total, 32 participants completed the study.About the same
